name: Fobia - St. Dinfna Hotel
detailed_description: Treze Trilhas is home to the St. Dinfna Hotel, a decadent site that is the subject of numerous rumors including mysterious disappearances and paranormal activity. Hoping to break the story, amateur journalist Roberto Leite Lopes travels to Santa Catarina following a tip from his friend Stephanie. His investigative skills will be needed not only to uncover the truth but to survive when reality is turned upside down with his discovery of a camera that reveals different timelines, a fanatical cult, human experiments, and apparitions roaming the halls. Solve puzzles and scavenge for anything to stop their hunt as the past, present and future collide. • Explore a Grand Hotel – The Unreal Engine brings terrifyingly realistic visuals to this first-person horror experience. • Survive the Horrors – Scavenge for supplies while you run, hide, or fight the monsters that stalk the corridors. • Unravel the Mystery – Worlds collide in a twisting narrative full of puzzles and conspiracies. • Look to the past and the future – Interact with different timelines using an enigmatic camera that connects parallel realities to uncover the many secrets hidden in the walls of the hotel. _childDocuments_.review: Really standout game that on the surface looks similar to Resident Evil 7/8, but feels more like Silent Hill or even From Software's Echo Night series with its focus on slower, methodical exploration. As you play through it, the game gets progressively larger and really rewards the player for remembering all of the areas they couldn't access before whenever they get a new key item. It isn't particularly scary compared to other horror games and the bosses (and shooting mechanics in general) feel sort of unnecessary, but Fobia's atmosphere is so great that it doesn't really matter. Well worth your time if you like atmospheric and slower-paced games.

_childDocuments_.review: Fobia - St. Dinfna Hotel is a survival horror game with an emphasis on puzzle-solving elements. It tells the story of Roberto, a journalist trapped in an evolving hellscape of the St. Dinfna Hotel. While it suffers from fighting recurring enemy types, it is still one of the better indie horror games I’ve played lately. Fans of the genre will find something to enjoy in this delightful, gruesome adventure. Roberto Leite Lopes is an aspiring journalist hoping to catch a big story to publish. Through a contact named Stephanie, he learns about the strange disappearances and unusual hauntings surrounding a local hotel called St. Dinfna in the state of Santa Catarina, Brazil. He travels there to uncover the bizarre phenomenon, but when he arrives, he loses communication with his friend as if she vanished herself. He is about to leave until a ghostly apparition of a gas mask girl manifest before him, causing him to black out. Suddenly, the hotel morphs into a grotesque version of itself, housing dangerous creatures, and a monster carrying a red lantern stalking the blood-covered hallways. Divided into 8 chapters, the story shifts between the present and the past, with our time spent mostly in the modern days with Roberto, but on occasion, we adopt the role of Christopher, the founder of the hotel. I love the attention to detail in both periods and how they’re bridged together, with the past filling in the blanks that players may have needed an elaboration on when roaming around in the present. The pacing is also well done, keeping enough mystery in each segment, but still divulging enough for players to digest. It’s a complete story too, and although I think the two endings are too black and white, it is enough to answer most of my questions.  Enemy encounters are slow-paced and deliberate, reminding me of older Resident Evil titles. You’ll have access to weapons like the pistol, but later on, you can acquire a sawed-off shotgun, a machine gun, and a revolver. Whatever weapon you choose, when you aim, hold still for a second, and the reticle will focus, making a critical hit more possible, especially if you shoot at the weak spot. I don’t find the combat difficult at all, and since you are constantly fighting the same tiresome monster every single time, no strategy is needed. I find the lack of variation in the common enemies rather disappointing. However, the bosses require some planning because they have their tricks, have larger health pools, and provide a slight challenge. They use the environment to their advantage, like the horrid spider that burrows into fleshy holes dispersed around the walls, trying to sneak from behind and spit acid at you. Using curatives like bandages can increase your chances of survival, but applying them completely stops Roberto in his tracks, leaving him wide open. It's frustrating, and I’ve died a few times just trying to heal myself.   Half of your time is consumed with deciphering a variety of puzzles that bars your way, and their level of difficulty can range from easy to “what do you want from me?” It can be as straightforward as a combination lock written on the wall in front of you, or an object that matches the 7th-floor puzzle. Naturally, having common sense and satisfactory observational skills will tremendously help with your endeavors, but if you’re a clueless oaf like me, the trial and error method can be a viable approach. Fortunately, the more head-scratching ones are secondary objectives, but the developers have sequestered some lore bits in them, which can be a satisfying reward for lore hunters like me.One of my favorite addition is the camera because its lenses can reveal the olden days, opening up sections that are normally inaccessible in the present, spot clues for nearby puzzles, and even detect items not seen with the naked eye. A handprint and a sudden “glitch in the matrix” are your typical visual cues whenever it is active around an area. This provides a unique way to explore, such as revealing bolted doorways behind bricked walls, and if you have the bolt cutter, you can reap the rewards for your efforts. Besieged with dread, you slowly trudge across blood-ladened corridors, and the ominous drumming of heavy stomps clashes in your eardrums. You hear a thunderous roar, and a bipedal creature equipped with an overgrown mangled claw and a flashlight customized with a crimson light adorned on his hip blocks your path. At this moment, you have to run since nothing can touch him, but out of curiosity, you linger, and he kills you. This is exactly what happened to me when I met the “Red Lantern,” a patrolling monster who sporadically appears out of nowhere. He doesn’t overstay his welcome, and I find him an effective way of introducing stalker enemies to the player since he is not a persistent presence until the very end. He supplements the atmosphere by being there when you least expect him rather than becoming a continual hindrance. You are still able to look around with little interruption, take in the deafening silence, and allow the environment to do most of the intimidation. Primarily taking place indoors, the layout of St. Dinfna is always evolving as each section of the hotel becomes available, exposing the ghastly transformation the building went through over the years. When delving into different timelines, the vivid colors of the present contrast with the drab, muted hues of the past. Cutscenes can be awkward to watch due to stiff, robotic animations of enemies and NPCs alike, but I don’t mind it considering the general experience isn’t ruined by them. In terms of glitches, I fell through the world once and was able to “leave” the hotel, running towards the moonlight without a care in the world. Other than that, I hardly had any performance issues at high settings, and the frame rate remained at a stable 60 with or without DLSS. The graphical options are considerable and can be changed between DX11 and DX12 with ray tracing.With 15 hours on my belt and most secrets and puzzles unearthed, even when it’s done, there are notes to read, audio logs to listen to, and Easter eggs to dig out, on NG+. I remember playing the early demo last Halloween with a friend on Discord. We were mulling over how to solve the puzzles, getting startled by the atmosphere, and generally loving the long preview for Fobia. Playing the full version is undoubtedly worth the wait, and I look forward to whatever new project the developers might have in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: Don't feel like reading the whole thing? Down at the bottom is the conclusion and score given to the game! :)Fobia is a game criticized for the wrong reasons, such as its textures, backtracking, and enemies. A classic survival-horror experience is rare, so I appreciate a game that brings back the genre's roots while adding its formula to the mix: the different dimensions with the camera. It's not an actual horror game due to a lack of jumpscares and fear elements, and it doesn't shine as a survival due to the combat being so rare. That being said, Fobia has a good quality put into its presentation. I don't mean the textures; I am referring to the environments and attractive locations the hotel offers guests. From infested halfways to elaborate secret areas, the hotel has more going on than one might think.The best aspect of Fobia, along with the presentation, is the combat; it's slow but tactical in its approach as enemies while lacking variety, do feature a familiar topic: keeping as much ammo as possible. Monsters have a specific weak point that can take them down in one shot if you can hit it, that is, and that challenge of trying to aim for one to three shots rather than eight adds tension to the gameplay. The abominations roaming the areas are terrifying in aspect and can appear when less expected, creating a sense of being watched as you transverse locations.One of the biggest complaints is the backtracking, but rather than thinking of the hotel as a level; it is far better to think of it as a giant labyrinth. Attractive designs take the spotlight so each floor can strike its memory in the player's head. It will be necessary to memorize the complex as you move around and solve the puzzles. The camera changes the hotel's layout completely, revealing hidden halls, ammunition, and secrets hidden at first glance. In that aspect, it is a satisfying and gratifying experience to explore every mystery and riddle in the hotel.The game's strong point is the presentation, as I stated before. Fobia is a game that doesn't pack many scares but features heavy doses of tension. It adds that eery feeling that there is something grotesque around the corner waiting to eat you, and for the most part, it strikes right when mixing that concept with the bosses. The foes are not too complex, but their simplicity allows their appearance to shine, and the scenarios in which boss fights are situated reinforce that.An example could be the piano monster; it gives an atmosphere of the unknown mixed with tragedy as it prepares to devour you. The stage appeals to the setting, and multiple ways exist to engage in the battle. From taking refuge on the lower floor to moving to the center, where the piano is located, for a better view of the creature, that fight illustrates Fobia's strengths in art direction.Visually the game could be a lot better when it comes to textures. It helps the title back from unleashing the environments to their utmost potential and leaves a sour aftertaste when seeing surfaces looking horrible. If Fobia stood to sacrifice the complexity of bosses and combat for a more straightforward approach, focusing more on making the visuals match the art styles would have been a better choice rather than balancing everything out.Most enemies look original and terrifying, but the main one chasing you through the hotel looks like a copy of a Tyrant from Resident Evil. It's weird to see Fobia undermine itself so much; for all of its originality and classic experience, it keeps bringing down its best elements as much as it empowers them. Fixing the visuals and changing the pursuit enemy model would have done much for the game.Regarding the sound, Fobia does a solid. It could be more impressive, but it gets the job done, as weapons firing have enough power to feel right but lacks the expected impact. The voice acting does good, but the dialogue and cliches play down the delivery of certain lines.Regarding replayability, the game has an achievement expecting you to beat it three times so that the completionist might be in for a rocky ride. It is not a game that deserves a second run, but it is well-deserving of a first one. A playthrough will last 9 to 14 hours, depending on how fast you resolve the puzzles in the hotel.Performances-wise, the horrible textures are at least a blessing to the FPS, as the game can run at max graphics without issue. I used the max preset in graphics and was getting 105 FPS on average. My specs are RTX 2060, 36 GB of ram, Intel Core i7-11700K - Core i7 11th Gen Rocket Lake 8-Core 3.6 GHz LGA 1200.When it comes to crashes and issues, the majority of the game was clean and perfect. The only problem comes with the piano boss fight, as I would get stuck without being able to move or couldn't change weapons anymore for unknown reasons. Luckily the issues are not too frequent, but there is a 50-50 of getting some problem during that encounter.Fobia is a fantastic game that revitalizes the genre of survival-horror games; it features some flaws, but the experience itself is excellent and something that must be played. The ambiance and exploration of the title are incredibly well done and a note for developers to notice on how to decorate their horror titles appropriately. If you like survival-horror games, I recommend you try Fobia, and if you fancy classics, it is a must-buy.8/10  GREATIf you enjoy and find the review helpful, please follow my curator StarsDeck!

_childDocuments_.review: After finishing FOBIA St. Dinfna Hotel, I had one repeating thought in my head: A puzzle is always clever if you’re the one who made it.And it’s true. If you created the puzzle and know the solution to that puzzle, it’s always going to be clever....to you. But to anyone else, that puzzle could be an obtuse, impossible, ridiculous nightmare.This is what about 75% of FOBIA was for me. Not a horror romp. Not a fun, monster-shooting time. Just a head-scratching, obtuse...experience. And yes, I‘m still recommending the game even though it was a slog of repeated puzzle-induced frustration for me. I liked the story and the characters. Technically it ran well. The limited voice acting is acceptable. And the UE4 graphics are nice and spooky. (There are gamma issues throughout, but they are manageable. And there's no real in-game map which is irritating at first, but eventually it's a non-issue.) When there was shooting, I thought the guns (pistol, shotgun, machine gun, and magnum) and aiming worked fairly well and created a good deal of tension. There really are only two varieties of enemies, but I’m okay with that as long as they are horror-game-weird, and these foes were suitably monster-y. The various texts in the game were well written. FOBIA is the first game made by a dozen or so Brazilian dudes. When I take all that into account, yeah, I say thumbs up.But take this scenario: On one floor in one room of a multi-level building, there are a series of filing cabinets. The room looks like an office and also contains a desk and some chairs. And let’s say this room with the filing cabinets is on floor number 3 of his multi-level building. Just everyday filing cabinets of different sizes with a differing number of drawers placed up against a wall. Always on the hunt for resources in the game, you can open and close all the drawers to see what’s inside—in this case, no bullets or health pickups, but just a few notes that you can read. Eh.Then 30 minutes later, on a completely different floor—let’s say three floors up on level 6—there’s one of many, many paintings hanging on the wall. You’ve already walked past dozens of them in the game. Nothing out of the ordinary here. But also, you are equipped with a special camera that, if you peer through it using night vision, you can see your environment from a different perspective. Sometimes the night vision lens may show a hole in the wall you can walk through....or whatever. And let’s say, with no prompt at all, you decide to look through your camera at this one of a dozen different paintings hanging throughout the place. And when you do that, this single painting changes into a series of simple lines of different lengths, some of them broken, some of them not.Well, it must mean something, right? But what? “Oh well, I guess I’ll figure it out later,” you say to yourself. But you never figure it out later.Only by reading a very thorough walkthrough on Neoseeker did I discover that this image of different-sized broken and unbroken lines is actually an indication for you to travel back down three floors, in an area you ran through 30 minutes ago,  and open specific drawers of those filing cabinets so they perfectly match the lines in the night vision painting to reveal....whatever. I don’t even remember what the reward was because all I actually remember is thinking: Seriously? No one would ever be able to connect any of this unless that player is spending 50 hours turning over every single stone in the game. No one.This is just one example of what FOBIA ultimately is. It is a lengthy (and I mean lengthy) series of obtuse, impossible, disconnected puzzles (like 50+ of them throughout the entire game) with little rhyme or reason. As soon as you might figure out one, there’s another one a few steps away. Think of the silly key-collecting puzzles in the various Resident Evil games. Only here, it's all on steroids.I’m sure the guys at Pulsatrix were very pleased with themselves that they had created these very clever puzzles. But I come back to my first statement: These puzzles are clever only because they already knew the solutions. For the average player looking for a good, horror-time, this does not make good gameplay.And these obtuse puzzles—which often have the player traveling from floor to floor to collect the various pieces or to connect various elements—naturally come with another problem. This is (mostly) a single-location-based game (hence the title St. Dinfna Hotel). Like one reviewer here on Steam rightly noted: The real name of this game should be “Backtracking: The Game.” Couldn’t say it better myself. You go from floor 1 to floor 4, back to floor 2, then up to floor 8, then back down to 1....and on and on. And throughout most of the game, the hotel has been devastated by some science-fiction-y phenomena (I’m cool with that), but this makes your traversal indirect. You can fix (and then ride) an elevator to some floors. But then you are required to exit, walk through collapsed floors, then backtrack through a hidden night vision area, and then through a few rooms (you get the picture), just to get to your destination. You traverse these twisting paths relentlessly—like for hours—back and forth as the hotel slowly (and I mean slowly) reveals itself, room by room and floor by floor. I twisted my way around this hotel so much, in the end I felt like a damn pretzel. During this endless back and forth, you are sometimes attacked by kooky monsters, which helps to break the monotony. (And like I said, the shooting and guns work fine for a game of this caliber.) But unfortunately most of the time there are no foes, and you are walking these figure-eights to wherever just to collect puzzle piece number 3 of 8 parts. I did fall asleep once during my play through (in the middle of the afternoon) running through the same areas endlessly. Not a rousing endorsement for a “horror” game.But I also wonder that maybe this game is just not for me. I see a horror game on Steam that seems competently made, and I immediately buy it. I love my horror games (as long as they aren’t asset-flips pasted together by 12-year-olds). And Pulsatrix is definitely going for a Resident Evil vibe here, as many Steam reviewers note. The story has evil science guys doing evil science things way underground where they think no one can see them. Above ground everything seems hunky dory, but then there are terrible consequences for their actions. And you show up right before the crap hits the fan. Cliché? Sure. But it’s all good for me. The problem though is that this is not a Resident Evil game. It looks like one on the surface, and it smells like one when you watch the trailers. But when playing RE, I could actually figure out most of the rudimentary puzzles in short order. Sure, some of the puzzles may have stalled me for a few minutes in RE, but not for long. Then, I was back into the action. But here? Not even close. Each time I stared at an obtuse, disconnected puzzle for 20 minutes trying to figure it out (over and over and over), I actually forgot I was playing a horror game at all. RE doesn’t make that mistake. But maybe that’s because FOBIA is simply a different kind of game and one that doesn’t jibe with my sensibilities overall.Just be forewarned before buying or playing. If FOBIA gives you the RE feels, you may want to adjust your expectations....and also bookmark the Neoseeker walkthrough so you can figure out most of the “clever” puzzles here....

_childDocuments_.review: I'd describe this as a very pleasant (for a horror fan, at least!) cross between Resident Evil 7 and Outlast. Only with a bit less action than both, and perhaps a slightly greater emphasis on exploration and puzzle-solving. Sound good? Sure did to me!Of course, it is still a video game, and not an especially logical or impressively written one at that. Take the first scene after the prologue: I check into a hotel, get a bit of the cold shoulder from the robotic receptionist when I say I'm a journalist...and immediately proceed to run around in front of him like a three-year-old who's on a play date! I perish to think what the poor fellow thought of me after that. Probably deserved everything that was coming to me thereafter, in all honesty...But let's get down to the more essential stuff, shall we? (We all know by now that asking "logic" from a horror game is like asking good behaviour from a rabid pup!) The atmosphere and environments are excellent, the puzzles never terribly obscure, and the (infrequent) combat sufficiently satisfying (though you really do have to watch that supply of ammo and healing like a hawk)! There's also a very nifty camera mechanic through which you can see an alternate view of the area you're in, in that wonderful shade of green that the likes of Outlast (and movies like REC) have trained us to be instantly unnerved by. A camera that sometimes shifts the very nature of time and space so we can access areas we couldn't before...yes, it's yet another one of those "constantly altering architecture" horror games that some of you get irked by; me, I love 'em, so no complaints here!About the most notable complaint I  make is the lack of a map you can bring up at whim...though there are intermittent floor plans spread throughout the hotel - only showing the floor you're currently on, of course - that resemble maps from the first Silent Hill, scribbled notations and all...so I won't grumble  loudly about "references" like that! There's also a few bits where the (manual) save points are less than generous in their frequency, but...well, let's try and pretend that's a positive thing, 'cause it sure as heck ramps up the tension for a wee while!On the whole, this is a surprisingly well-accomplished game for the fledgling endeavour of a newbie developer. With a little luck, Pulsatrix Studios will be a name we'll be on the constant lookout for in years to come...Verdict: 8.5/10 (alright, so a couple of the boss fights are a bit on the mediocre side, but it's a pretty impressive achievement nonetheless)!(PS If you enjoyed this review, feel free to check out my two Curator pages: Cheers!)

_childDocuments_.review: So it's really not a bad game at all, but for me it's more of an escape room style game with elements of horror, rather than your typical survival horror... The game never really scared me or made me feel on edge, in fact the scariest thing was the poor lighting optimisation. To be honest, the game doesn't run great. It's not a particularly demanding game but it still feels poorly optimised and combat doesn't feel satisfying at all. The puzzles were fun though and I did really like the overall vibe of the game so still worth a play through.PS - I don't get all of the reviews comparing this to RE7. RE7 is a brilliant game, and in addition to it probably being the most  adrenaline inducing RE game ever, it plays great and has really satisfying graphics/combat/pretty much everything. This game genuinely isn't bad, but it doesn't stack up to that.

_childDocuments_.review: I won't write much at the beginning, I'll list the pros and cons and then write more in the conclusion.A fun game to kill time (you can easily finish it in 10h). Not much horror here ( sadly 0 survival horror elements). The game has potential which has not been fully realised. The beginning of the game is very polished in many aspects, but with the flow of time and the next places on the map, it becomes obvious that there was a lack of ideas and motivation. Many missed moments to make the game more scary. Many untold stories and events. The game is not bad, but it could use a few improvements. But still better than RE3:RE :)

_childDocuments_.review: - Can't disable stupid effects.It's insane to have things that can't be disabled, specially when these are known to cause headaches and sickness to some players (Blur, Bloom, DoF). Beyond these, the horrible Chromatic aberration and Lens flare that always suck to deal with. Grain is alright, since it gives the game some of it's atmosphere. Still, all these should be optional (I used a guide to disable them by editing engine files). - Not consistent nor logical.Some items (Keys, etc) disappear automatically upon usage, others stay in your inventory and you must destroy them yourself. Other items, even if you don't need them after one usage (Cassette tapes, a specific coin, etc), you can't delete them.It wouldn't be much of an issue if space wasn't so insanely valuable in this game, with so many different items... - Too many, too obscure.At any given time you might be tracking 7 or more different codes and clues that you must run around between unsolved puzzles, trying to punch them in to unlock something, anything. Not only that, some items are so obscurely hidden, you MUST use a guide or have the memory of an elephant to remember one thing you might have noticed 6 hours ago. Many clues and items don't indicate where you will need them, nor when. There's items you collect that you'll use 8 hours later in the game, all while having an extremely limited inventory. Truly horrible experience. - Even with upgrades, RNG fest.Are you an excellent aimer? Well screw you, RNG dictates you'll never hit dead center, miss all critical hits and spend far too much ammo on one enemy. Thing is so bad, the game even has a "Give free ammo when needed" option... Why should one EVER be punished by RNG is beyond me, why a dev realizes on playtesting that players were running out of ammo and STILL DOESN'T DISABLE STUPID RNG IS UNFATHOMABLE! - Gripping, until you realize it's just a bait.During the whole game I was thinking this was a deep, well thought out, brilliant story that would reveal itself beautifully at it's end. I was sorely disappointed and left the game utterly confused, as did another  that watched a Fobia story explained video on youtube (For reference, at the time of writing, the game has 760 reviews...) 6/10 3/10I followed a guide, as it was clear from the start that the puzzles and items were too many, too nonsensical and too scattered to make this game an enjoyable experience otherwise. I got around inventory issues due to the guide (And it was still a struggle at times). I disabled the stupid video effects by editing the engine. I had a decent time with the game, but it's not supposed to be so hard to enjoy a game.It's a fairly well produced game, but it's flaws taint it severely. I'd only recommend to die hard puzzle and escape room fans. Any fans of horror, survival, shooters, quick-time events or quality lore games, look elsewhere.

_childDocuments_.review: You are Roberto Lopes, and you are a journalist investigating- ugh, who the heck knows anymore... Anyhoo, your source invites you to stay at the St. Dinfna hotel because that’s the goldmine for scoops, but then things take a turn for the weird as reality bends before your very peepers~ In true journalistic fashion, it is up to you to chip away at the big picture that is the unfathomable causes behind the disappearances of many an individual. A story that seemingly takes after a collection of classics, the most profound being Resident Evil’s mad genius and God complex. But it also has  infatuation of an artefact possessing unspeakable power, tearing the fabric of reality, and then a little bit of  and  for good measure. It’s one merry survival horror party in the lobby, but just like a hotel with several competing thematic décor, it doesn’t have a grasp of what it desires to be… The end result is a convoluted plot that comes off as a prequel, sequel and yet still the first entry to a non-existent series. The manner in which it chooses to tell its tale through “secondary puzzles” hints at the lore as mere afterthought, despite being interesting. As for the pacing, it tries to be action-packed but lags much too frequently, giving scraps of cryptic messages in the hopes of dangling you. Lastly, I found the default Portuguese littered everywhere to be realistic, as it’s set in Brazil, but presented an additional language barrier…Fobia has a broad, even mainstream appeal to horror fans in that it’s suited for those who fancy living on the edge comparable to ; backtracking, gunning down abominations, inventory management and all. But also those who wouldn’t mind untangling a few knots in their brains. It captures the best of both worlds, and while we’re on that- so does the special camera, which allows you to discern and interact between differing planes of reality to gather clues, scrounge for resources or hide from enemies.Your first playthrough should clock in at about 10 hours, but if you ever decide to extend your stay vis-à-vis turning the premises upside down to find mementos or solve the infamous puzzles, the length could be double that. And with new game+, it’d be triple that in a heartbeat but I don’t see any reason to as I already 100% the secondary puzzles! Even though the rudimentary shooting can get stale, alternating from having to point the camera can be hassling and it perhaps could use a firm disclaimer of sorts to warn players of the puzzle-heavy temperament, however I believe there are pleasant times to be had~1. You are safe in the 2. Playtime determines ranking.The sights and locations presented to you are like a bartender asking whether they can top off your glass, meanwhile you are already intoxicated as hell. From an untainted grandeur, the best five-star hospitality that present-day St. Dinfna can offer you, to a sundered warzone iteration and even to a warm moist  nest writhing uncontrollably. But they go beyond the eponymous structure, arriving at a cabin of similar and stately progression situated in an idyllic village of a distant memory swallowed by vast woodlands and percolating dimness.Then it travels deeply to… well, why not let your imagination fill in the blanks!? You would think that I’d bring up the matter of the repeating and restricted monster designs to be an issue, but no, not right now anyway. The sole complaint I would raise is the blatant disregard of appropriate brightness adjustments, namely the forest and mine areas where there are no light sources on hand.If the visuals of St. Dinfna were an all-you-can-eat buffet, then together with the sound design, they’d make up impeccable room service! The concierge is a bit of a miser with the music, reserving them only for key moments like boss fights or when you’re stalked by “Nay-mesis” for instance, but I respect that. What you’ll wind up hearing most of the time are snarls, squelches, reverberation from your shots and of course the Moonlight Sonata-sounding save theme emanated from the pendulum clocks. The latter serving a dual purpose of stirring tranquility and guiding you to safety. Two things I would comment on are; one, there’s not much musical range by way of expressiveness, closely attached to piano instrumentals. And two, the audio getting subdued while you have the camera pointed is troubling yet it stifles the oppressive mood~  As much as I enjoyed the voiceovers, no amount of good acting can deliver salvation to the inane script or characters whose counterparts from the classics mentioned earlier fared much better. Emily, with her brief appearances, commands a brooding presence but is essentially a watered down cross of Alma and Alessa, only without the sympathy pains worth in backstory.Stephanie is Zoe from RE7, down to her "knows too much but won’t say zip" operator role. And as for Roberto, he’s just a guy offering commentary and throwing an expletive from time to time, just so things don’t get too quiet! The hotel had more personality than any of the people~For like the first quarter of Fobia, you are persistently besieged by the unknown. Whether it’s a shrewdly-positioned item made to give the impression of jumping out at you when you suddenly switch to the camera. Or your mind races to produce the worst-case scenario whenever the screen flickers, kind of like the hotel itself is seizing… But then things soon become devoid of surprise up until the end, and you can see what’s coming from a few floors ahead. The same Mr.X-like encounters, being forced to go the long way around that gives “backtrack” a bad name and of course, the few tired creatures who, like you, dread every waking second when you approach them. Why else would they return to hibernation when you are not looking? I can’t believe I’m even spouting this, but this is probably the only game in history where I’d use the phrase “where are the jumpscares”!? There weren’t any particularly shudder-worthy moments, and for a survival horror title, that spells doomsday~x Audio gets muted in one of the labs for no reason.x Entire sequences repeat, along with enemy placements. Experiencing them for the first time!x Reloading saves sometimes despawn and other times respawn enemies…x Enemies bound to specific areas walk into surfaces and get stuck chasing you.x Modular key pieces visible one at a time.~ Unfriendly puzzle interactions; outlines as to which parts you are moving are so faint. ~ There’s a “C” shortcut for camera, but you have to equip it in 1 of 4 equipment slot anyway.~ Maps should be jotted down in the notebook as well!~ Notebook should have a bookmark feature. Instead of having to flip through each page with every game reload.Not as the rave reviews advertise it to be. Bland characterization & unimaginative plot without payoff. Still, it has that AAA factor in terms of treatment & presence. They’re what made it sell~

_childDocuments_.review: This game had so much potential. The story feels like it was just on the edge of starting something special, the gunplay was decent, the detail is clearly thought out usually in the enviroment.Then everything falls apart.The same two enemies will be there from start to end. Either the basic enemy which is very easy to deal with even though hitting their weak spot is a coin flip. The other known as the "spider?" A pain. Unless you know where they are they will hurt you. And it will be a long, drawn out animation once they do.Long and drawn out. That is the game.In total I beat it in about 8-9 hours. Most of it was running in circles. While backtracking in survival horror is a staple this game makes it feel like a chore. It cuts off some shortcuts which added an hour to my playtime just going back and forth for the side stuff that was staggeringly unsatisfying. For the main missions it LOVES to make you wander through mazes and more. It was brutally clear that it was set up to slow you down since the areas are actually small.The story? It loves to create these little threads that kinda connect, but it leaves a ton more questions than answers. And not in a fun, mysterious way. In a "why was that even a thing?" kinda way. It felt like elements were put in to explain the bosses and monsters, but it all felt hollow.This game does not respect your time at all, so it deserves no respect. Do not buy it.EDIT!:Took a breath, now its time for "how to fix it!"-Locked shortcuts: Let the game be short. I could tell when gates were left locked and certain things disabled to draw out playtime. Let people unlock gates, restore shortcuts, and other little features. If they are not being forced to go through the same hall ten times staring at a locked gate each time it will allow them to pause and look. Plus, unlocking shortcuts is SUPER satisfying in survival horror games.-Add small variants to enemies. Even if its just cosmetic. A little shirt that you can recognize from a note can really help the atmosphere and reduce "oh. its this thing again. Lets go through the steps once more...." -The camera was great. However it at times was reduced to "you have to have it out to get by a blockade." Turning it into a time wasting key. Do not do this. This was a great feature of your game. Embrace it.-Let people be more scared of your bosses. You barely built up most of them. Let us get glimpses, bits of lore, characterise them more.-Your lore needs to be tied together more. You have lots of VERY good elements that feel like they are there in service of the "survival horror" aspect rather than the characters and setting. -Be careful "drowning" the player with detail. Puzzle elements and small enemies were super hidden by the enviroment. While it does encourage exploration be sure to give the player breathing room for the eyes.-Some of the cutscenes at the end need trimming. One part with a ton of red and swirling truly hurt my eyes. Another at the very end kept on and on giving hints at interesting things for only a super small part. The rest was pretty much nothing but waiting for the end trying not to get motion sick.-Be more careful with the "easter eggs." A few were funny, but some were so blatant it didn't just ruin the immersion, it was an ejector seat out of the setting. -

_childDocuments_.review: This game is good, it looks good, has a good atmosphere, mechanics and is spooky.However, its major downfall, in my opinion, is obtaining items. How do I mean that? Well...The game barely navigates you, and I can't even name how many ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ times I was stuck, because I didn't know what to do or where to go. Sometimes you have to literally run around the whole hotel just to find a room you went through a decade ago, in which there's an essential item that you couldn't access until you had the right tool for it.MY SUGGESTION: Don't make the same mistake as me and write down somewhere every time you see a puzzle, a lock or anything you aren't capable of solving/accessing at that moment. There might come a time when you'll forget about it and tear your hair off because you'll struggle on how to progress.It also has A LOT of unnecessary things. Like finding a combination for a safe, just to find a key inside, for a lock that's in that very room, even the same place. Or having the code for a lock literally right next to it. These are some examples that aren't complicated to describe, but trust me there are way more of them.There are a lot of puzzles that aren't really difficult. If you see a lock with a combination, you have a 90% chance of finding it either in the documents or in that room or room complex (usually using the camera). And I don't really care if they are creative, or intelligent, or whatever. If I would want a puzzle-horror game, I would reach for something else. The puzzles are just a cool thing to experience and not to make the game too dry.I'm here for the spooks. I got them. Thus, I'm satisfied. The story is kind of everything and anything. I won't talk about every single detail to not make this section a whole paragraph.It is well-placed, but still chaotic. It can be really difficult to keep up sometimes with all this time travel, documents, lore and characters that are important for the story, but you get to know them for about 10 minutes in total and at the end you are just holding your head and telling yourself wtf was this.It's good in my opinion, just plain. Like it could be better just by adding some explanations and expanding it a little bit so everything that happens there is actually interesting and keeps you wanting to know more about it. Unfortunately it doesn't always tell you, or you have to be really observant, reading documents, finding some secrets and stuff to know at least something about the different things that happen/happened.Even though I had a rough time playing this game, I enjoyed it most of the time. It's pretty polished and well made game.PS:I give you a 100 bonus points for that USB stick animation.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR It's basically an indie Resident Evil, it was obviously havely inspired by RE series as it uses the same formula, and has some direct references to RE as well.The game starts off strong (for an indie title), but quickly becomes very tedious. First of all, it has only two regular enemy types and three bosses (which are horribly designed, sorry for the pun). And both of those enemy types are more annoying than scary or hard to deal with. Talking about scary or survival, the game kinda fails with that: there are plenty of resources, and cutscenes or enemy fights are not frightening at all. Also, no jumpscare, but that's more like a good thing.Then, Fobia has some ungodly amount of backtracking. Even though it takes less than ten hours to beat the game, I felt like half of that time was running back to the places you already visited just to use some newly found item to progress (and new enemies usually spawn). And if you want to solve all optional puzzles and find all collectibles, you'll have to backtrack even more!Even despite these flows, I was going to recommend the game before I finished the first part, which is actually the hotel as the game title says. But then you travel to another location which has even more backtracking, subpar visual and level design, yet offers nothing new compared to the hotel – just more of the same enemies and a frustrating (not because it's hard, but because it's really boring) final boss fight. So unless you are a die hard Resident Evil fan and want more of the same, I recommend you pass on this one.P.S. But if you are interested, it's part of Humble Choice In February 2023.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is objectively good and if you're starving for a survival horror game I can see the appeal. Wouldn't advise against getting it if it goes on sale, for sure. But I can't recommend it because I hated it. Here's why:- Bad/vague puzzles, often hinging on easy to miss clues. An example being the intuitive puzzle where you have to open cabinets in a certain order, with the clue being that you have to use your camera while looking at a painting.- Awful save system. I've never understood why horror games do this, as it merely adds to the frustration rather than to the fear. It isn't a desirable result that people become "afraid" of having to redo massive parts of the game over and over. I know that the inability to save frequently is intentional design, but I think it was a poor one. - Completely overstays its welcome. I have no idea why this game is so overly long, but the game drags on for hours longer than it needs to. Being too long isn't really that bad of a flaw though, all things considered.- Incredibly bad pacing. Obviously the MC has to move similar to how a 70 year old man with Rheumatoid Arthritis would, since the map is so small. But man does this game just never pick up. - Laughably bad "scares". Cheap jump scares without setting up any atmosphere. Many games try to scare the player with dudes walking behind a corner in sight of the player while deliberately ignoring the player (they know you're there) before disappearing, and I can't think of a time where it has succeeded. - Hard to see enemies that jump out at you with no way to avoid them (bugs)- Those gym-bro Zombie things get a speed boost for some reason (seriously why?)- MC is unintentionally hilarious. Absolutely way too calm about the situation he's in, and seems to only be slightly annoyed at best (mostly taking it out on poor Stephanie). If he gets afraid, the fear lasts for one scene and he never really questions anything beyond "WTF was that". Nothing wrong with having a silent or fearless MC, but Roberto just seems more like he's getting bad service in an actual hotel rather than being in St. Scary's Helltell California or wherever. It's very comical.If you can look past these issues, you'll have fun with the game. The game is by no means bad and is very high production quality. It's one of the best indie survival horror games you can get on Steam, and it does right by the genre. I simply didn't like it, and have good reasons why it didn't click for me is all. Other people may not be so bothered by some of this, and may even have a different perspective than me. I'm in the minority here.

_childDocuments_.review: This game needs way more recognition. It's a beautifully crafted survival horror , more focused on exploration and that makes the player actually analize the environment, making it REALLY engaging. It has Resident Evil 7/8 as a core inspiration but still manages to have a personality and take the great things from various games such as Fear or Silent Hill to some extent.Puzzles are nice, fun and satisfying. Same goes for the atmosphere and graphics, they are actually really good. The plot is interasting and the voice-acting (the english one at least) is cheesy enough to add layers to the overall experience. There isn't a great variety in enemies and they tend to be pretty dumb, but it's fine for what it is. The only big problem is the backtracking: the game lasts way more than it needs to be and it's pretty tedious to traverse the map, expecially when a lot of ways are stuck or become unaccessible. A shoutout to the developers: for being their first game, this is a marvel. If you are reading this, you have a new fan guys. You did great, thank you for developing this game, you have a great potential and i can't wait to see your future work.

_childDocuments_.review: Classic RE fan? Play thisClassic SH fan? Play this (although, not quite as lonely or nightmarish)Classic Survival Horror fan? Play this+ Solid Survival Horror mechanics, all in first person, from start to finish+ Guns and ammo and littered secrets to discover the Story and Lore+ A stronger focus on certain puzzles (vs fighting enemies), while not mandatory, are more difficult, and give more understanding to the overall plot+ The visuals are pretty good. Not great, but they are good. And they run great+ The Camera mechanic is outstanding. I love it The Flash Drive animation+ A decent length, at about 10-12 hours. Don't mind my 18 hours. I was thoroughly trying to solve every last puzzle+ Collectibles for post game if you're into that+ For the animations that they worked hard on, they are fantastic. Little things like opening doors, to the gun animations, reloading, taking out your weapons from the holster, and so. They look great.+/- Story is meh. It has a great foundation, but some of the voice acting (for English) really hurts it.+/- While I did not play this game in Portuguese (speaking), there is an option for that, and it appears to be the native. It might be better to play on that, as the English cast is hit and miss.- Our main character's voice actor needs some work on his acting. Our Side Characters and Antagonists overall did a great job though. I am more understanding since this isn't a AAA game, despite how well they pulled this bad boy off to feel semi-close to one (even lip syncing), but if you can get a few really good or close to good voice actors, I feel you should be able to nail the Protagonist. Whoops.- One single puzzle towards the endgame is so cryptic because it requires a mechanic that you've been able to use all along, but never use it once until this final puzzle. I won't spoil what it is, but it kind of annoys me. I feel it would've been better to use it just ONCE in some other part of the game, and only once. - Some missing sound effectsI loved it. _childDocuments_.review: This game is a very obvious love letter to the original Resident Evil trilogy. The puzzles feel like RE, the layout feels like RE, and there's even a Mr X equivalent to chase you around every now and then. Not only that, the story structure feels like it used the first RE as a foundation, with the bulk of your time exploring the mysterious hotel (mansion), only to eventually uncover some big secrets in the final act underground.In many ways, this love letter does its source material justice. The puzzles are genuinely interesting, and in some cases quite challenging! The way the hotel gradually opens up as you explore is very satisfying! The voice acting is terrible, but in the best possible way! But this game is missing something that, for me, spoils the whole experience: A map. Imagine exploring the Spencer Mansion in RE1 without any sort of map to guide your way. Sure, it would be POSSIBLE, but it would be much more difficult in a very not-fun way. While playing, I often found myself stuck — Not because of a difficult puzzle or challenging enemy, but because I missed an important item in a dead end on the other side of the building, and I had no idea what it was I was meant to be looking for. And in the few cases I KNEW what I was looking for, it was a tedious and frustrating mess just trying to find my way through the maze of rooms and elevators trying to find my way back there.I want to love this game so much more than I do. And I really do feel like the simple addition of an RE-style map would instantly make this game a staple of the genre. But without it, I just cannot recommend it to others.

_childDocuments_.review: Fobia has some good horror mechanics with tricky puzzles. Nothing special about this title and achievement hunting for this game was extremely tedious. Personally I would say skip this game as it is not a challenging game, more of another tedious indie.-Sound: Pretty good overall. Adds tension to the game very well. Most of the sounds are environmental, some sound queues help with enemies nearby.-Graphics: Basic and several FPS drops meaning lacking optimisation. It looks alright but not great. I guess it looks good for an indie.-Horror: Jump scares here and there. Weak weapons at the start can make you panic. I was more terrified of getting damaged while getting an achievement than the actually game itself. Most of the game you can freely run around with no repercussions. This cuts the horror and plays against what the game is trying to achieve.-Gameplay: Basically a glorified "going to point A to point B then back to A" type of game. Backtracking and getting items to continue is an exhausting venture and gets tedious very quickly. The shooting in the game is a nice addition that can add to the intensity and dread. If this game was a dial, it stays at a 5 or 6 and never goes above that. Boss fights are a joke and enemies are quite easy to dodge or kill. Spiders are the most annoying to deal with in my opinion. Inventory is limited, even with upgrades. Inventory boxes and save points are quite abundant so inventory management should not be a problem and you can constantly save. Puzzles are alright and mostly easy as the game literally puts the hints on the walls in front of the puzzle. Not very difficult but can get super frustrating when you miss a piece of paper with the answer.-Story: Basically makes not a dime of sense. It was intriguing at first but once you start to learn the key features of the story, it starts sounding like a failed horror movie. It is not written well and it tries to be smart. Character actions have no logic behind them.-Voice acting: I loathed the journalists voice acting. Everything thing else was fine.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game, but came across several janky/buggy interactions. I think there is a great framework for a game here, but it is held back by how frustrating some of the gameplay elements feel.Movement/Camera control feel like a chore, swapping between inventory items such as your camera/weapons is an incredibly lengthy animation that really starts to drag after the first couple of times. Accidentally swapping to the camera was a pain as you had to go in and out of it to continue moving at a very slow pace throughout the game. Additionally, occasionally throughout the game, you get kind of blurred vision for a few seconds that unless I'm missing something, doesn't actually effect the gameplay, just forces you to stop moving, until you can see again.Fighting enemies is a bit confusing as there is very little feedback about whether or not you're causing damage/progressing through a fight. On the first floor boss, after unloading a lot of bullets in to it, I figured maybe it was immune to damage and perhaps it was a "puzzle fight" where I needed to find a way out, to later be told that you just have to shoot it a bunch more as a giant bullet sponge, some kind of feedback/UI system could really help here.The story is solid and I think has a lot of promise, I honestly couldn't bring myself to finish it as I found the gameplay too frustrating, but I want to give credit where it's due. There are also plenty of intuitive puzzles that feel good to solve and you can feel the intentions and care of the developer(s). I hope that maybe there are some quality of life patches in the future and I would consider revisiting this game.This next one is not a complaint so much as feedback, but I took a week off between playing and couldn't remember anything about what needed to happen next as the objective is shared as a single line. You can't go back and replay previous conversations (in this case, the one from the phone on the first floor) and so I felt my only option was to look up a walkthrough to figure out where to go next.

_childDocuments_.review: It's good! Considering the size of the team and that it is a Brazilian game, this game is an extraordinary achievement.Great atmosphere, puzzles, graphics and animations, story is kinda all over the place and hard to piece, but it is not bad. Audio is also great and the double reality mechanics are always nice!The only real criticism that I have is a very weak combat component, premade death animations, no physics, no gore, no damage, no flavour at all. Bossfights are also pretty annoying due to the bullet sponges, but are so easy that they don't really bother much.Overall, good game, if you are a fan of the genre it is easy to recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: If there was a “survival horror” (and I used quotes, as the term itself should be used very loosely here…) I would pick as a textbook example, a case-study on how NOT to design one in the first place, then it would - by all intents and purposes - be  (FSD). Please go  for all my screenshots of the game, if you want to check some out and see how dated it looks, both in 1440p and 1080p!One fateful day, investigative journalist… uh… Bob (sorry, he’s so unremarkable I forgot his name) decides to undertake an investigation about the mysterious events surrounding an obscure cult residing in the Spanish (?) city of Treze Trilhas, such as murders, kidnappings, occult happenings, and all the fun things usually associated with a bunch of fanatics. He decides to stay in the totally-not-cursed hotel of St. Dinfna, that soon becomes an actual hellscape he has to find a way out from. FSD is clearly set before the current days, something clear by the absence of smartphones, old-style decor (or maybe Spanish countryside is just like that, I’ll ask Leon Kennedy) and so forth. The general ambience is dimly-lit and desaturated, with color palettes that tend to the faded-out side of things, fitting for a worn-out hotel in the middle of nowhere even without all the cursed monsters and gore pumping out of every conceivable crack - which will indeed be the case. The main problem is how inconsistent the quality of models, textures, effects and well, pretty much every eye-candy actually are. A few elements are of noteworthy quality, but most textures seem low-res and blurred out even on the highest settings, while distortion effects can’t be disabled for the most part, adding insult to injury. Most locales you’ll traverse, save for rare sequences, will feel static and devoid of life - but not in a good way. The storyline follows Bob’s exploits through the hotel, but never succeeds at being interesting, as it utilizes overused horror and mystery tropes that feel like already-seen from the get-go, and never really hook the player. Despite an interesting dual-timeline concept, which will put you in the shoes of another character besides Bob, this highlight alone can’t salvage a story that is, otherwise, composed of jumpscares that aren’t scary, chase sequences that aren’t tense, and ‘mysterious’ happenings that don’t feel mysterious at all; it doesn’t take a 300 IQ genius to understand what happened not before long.The hotel will be where most of the game will be set in, exceptions made for the alternate timeline phases which will take place elsewhere. It articulates on ten large floors, most of which are unserviceable due to the damage caused by the cursed crap pouring from everywhere, and on top of that, boasting a security system made of code-locked doors, combination gates and so forth that would make Fort Knox green with envy. It’s clear this enormous amount of nonsensical security measures was put in place for gameplay reasons, as the story gives feeble motives as to why a hotel would need them, nevermind make sense or not arouse suspicion. You’ll need to find keycards, codes, old-fashioned metal keys and more esoteric means to traverse your way.Given how complex and “broken” the layout is, the absence of a map (other than the low-res, barely-comprehensible wall-map found on some floors…) makes orienteering a depressing chore because most locales look nearly the same, and have no ‘landmarks’ (exceptions apply) for the player to reference. Good luck in remembering all the safes, doors and so on you can or must backtrack to hours later for upgrades, extra resources or whatever else. There are a lot of secrets, most of which will only be revealed by using your camera, which for whatever reason is also an inter-dimensional tool that allows you to switch between alternate realities, to overcome obstacles and see secret writings. It’s incredibly fun and satisfying (cough…) to comb every millimeter of every floor in the search of minuscule codes, or hints, to open an optional safe that will give you three bullets and a dirty piece of gauze as a reward. Ugh!The combat, be it against normal enemies (totaling at a grand three types!) or bosses is always the same thing: shoot them until they’re dead. It’s the most basic form of first-person shooting, with a forced virtual crosshair having a set random spread for each weapon, which becomes tighter if you aim for a few seconds. Enemies, some at least, seem to have weak-spots like pulsating, glowing hearts, but it’s unclear if hitting them actually does more damage or not, since there’s no visual or physical feedback of “critical hits”. All enemies behave in the same way: they stumble or rarely rush at you in a basic way - bosses are depressing, braindead hunks of meat that may have a trick more up their sleeve, but nothing you can’t solve by just strafing, backpedaling and keeping the bullets going. The ammo economy is for the most part generous and almost all enemies can be easily avoided anyway… Why even shoot them since they drop nothing?Puzzles will have Bob backtrack ad-nauseam for half the hotel in the search of endless amounts of keys, knobs, devices, codes and whatever else will be needed to unlock the next door. Normally this would be standard in a survival horror, but the amount, frequency and repetition FSD spams these puzzles / fetch tasks at, is unbearable. It becomes so tedious and repetitive, that puzzle-solving and item-fetching will occupy most of your time, with everything else be it combat, lore or survival aspects like item management, being only a vague shadow in a corner, trembling at the big, bad ‘puzzle monster’ ravaging the other poor gameplay elements.These enigmas will often entail deducting a combination, a code or a logical sequence to input. In some cases, you will need some additional pieces of machinery or specialized equipment before being able to solve an enigma - as to where to locate these items, it’s anyone’s guess. The problem here is that important containers that hold key items look like normal pieces of furniture half of the time, without any hint that they are important whatsoever. Dearest developers, did you ever think about why say,  most -good- Survival Horrors place key items in adorned chests, or memorable / easy-to-recognize locations? Yeah that's right, to avoid players going around like an absolute muppet combing every box, locker, drawer and so on for hours.You’ll be able to find glowing dodecahedrons scattered around, usually out of the main way. You can use these anomalous spawns worthy of STALKER to upgrade your weapons with intangible, barely-perceptible improvements that aren’t worth the absolute pain of finding these things around the hotel. Enemies and bosses are so dumb and predictable that you don't need them anyway. Something more worth looking for are inventory expansions, sometimes found in safes, but most of the time just scattered around and suffering from the same issues as puzzle pieces: they just seem like part of the decor, and in many cases I found them by sheer luck. As customary, saving is only allowed at fixed places that you’ll struggle to remember the location of, and excess items can be discarded (destroyed) or put in the stash, shared between all boxes.

_childDocuments_.review: I was a little worried I wasn't going to like this one since I saw people complaining about the difficult puzzles, but I ended up really enjoying it and honestly think it's one of the best horror games that came out this year so far. Fobia is definitely more of a slow burner and requires some patience but if you can get into it it's very rewarding. Exploring the hotel and no spoilers other areas is really fun and immersive, the sound design is really solid. The visuals are nice and the game run flawless, menus and inventory are all polished enough and work well. Some downs sides would be the gunplay/combat is kinda meh, it's really stiff feels jank ect. Story wise it's rough especially the ending, it leaves alot to be desired, and yes I read every note and paid close attention and still didn't grasp everything, might be that some things are lost in translation. There is also a TON of backtracking which imo goes with the territory, but it didnt bother me personally but might be a turn off for others. And yes there is an insane amount of puzzles even a bunch of secret/optional ones, but they mostly fun and could be solves even by me. The price wasn't what I was expecting but it's actually pretty long especially for a horror game and has quite a bit of content and the quality is higher than expected, imo it's worth it I had a good time with this. Highly recommend to horror/puzzle fans and look forward to the devs next project. 8.4/10
_childDocuments_.name: Fobia - St. Dinfna Hotel

_childDocuments_.review: Worth more than the $30 I paid for it. My only irritation are the 'spider' thingies that jump one after the other...kind of gets annoying when you have no recovery or iframes. But other than that, solid gameplay with well thought out puzzles.I think a map as an item that I can access anytime would be more preferable (if I missed it, please let me know) - though I do like the idea of not have a map in a 'real' situation like this and using the hotel maps by the elevators that are marked up instead, I unfortunately tend to forget things and my in-game sense of direction is abysmal.P.S. - Loving all the references/easter eggs!

_childDocuments_.review: It was an enjoyable experience. The atmosphere is great as it definitely put me on edge when exploring the hotel. The gunplay is similar to Resident Evil 7. Actually the entire game is looks to be inspired by RE7 except way more puzzles. WARNING! If you don't like puzzles then I don't think you'll like this game. A lot of them just give you upgrade points and ammo or another piece to another puzzle. This also means there is a lot of backtracking and being lost since they don't progress the story in any way. In my opinion, like half aren't really hard just needs some thinking but the ones for hidden achievements are tricky. It is clear that the devs put a lot of time making these puzzles, and I like them, but they probably added a bit too much since it makes it seem like the player might get a key item from it but doesn't which leads the player lost especially since some of them you can't solve till late into the game. The enemies are scary looking but aren't a threat after an hour after you encounter them. The designs are cool but they really aren't threatening. As long as you keep your distance they are never a problem except for the spiders as they are kinda sneaky. It would have been nice to see more enemy variety or just give the regular monster more attacks.Game is easy so anybody can jump in but be prepared to work your brain for those puzzles. I don't know remember seeing  a hard mode tho so I played on normal.  7.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: I really, REALLY wanted to like this game. But the controls are just so.....bad.God help you if you try it with a controller. The stick dead zone is so large you can't precisely aim at anything in this game and it's not exactly generous with ammo. I'm fairly good at survival horror games and came into what I guess you would consider the first "boss fight" with a decent amount. Used every last bullet and shell on it, it didn't die, and I was essentially softlocked. I suppose this is why they added an "ammo assistance" mode under accessibility for bosses but I didn't expect it to be a requirement to progress. If every enemy is going to be a damage sponge, you gotta give us more than 1-2 bullets per pickup. This isn't tense so much as it is artificial difficulty.It's a cool concept and a solid effort, but unfortunately it falls pretty short in execution. I hope the devs put out more like this though, and maybe polish the next one up a bit more.

_childDocuments_.review: Decent.Reminiscent of Resident Evil, naturally, and some aspects of FEAR.Could do with more monster variation/aggression/ambushing.Little heavy on the horror/jumps from the onset, fall-off of any attempts later on.While kind of the point the story was going for, could do with a 'true' ending or something to work toward - lacks a certain satisfaction to all your efforts.Can spend a lot of time searching for anything you've forgotten the location of. Can understand not wanting a highlighted map telling the players 'here are the puzzles you've missed', but need some balance of not spending hours searching for Stephanie's Safe (it's in the library, not a bedroom). I do not know how I missed some notes after how long I spent double and triple checking locations by accident.Inherent to any game with a 'special vision' mode, a lot of time gets spent rechecking areas, again. The game does have markers where you should need the camera, but cannot confirm if it covers all of them.Appreciate that there are some puzzles, or at least safes/keypads that require a bit more exploration or attention to notes that give small advantages like another shortcut or more ammunition/information/upgrades.The memory room is an interesting touch. Though a note on the writing, it does make the whole hotel feel like there were -only- those people in the entire hotel.Had some fun though, thank you.

_childDocuments_.review: Best parts of the game are the visuals and ambience, It has similar mechanics and style as RE7 but I won't be calling it a clone as it is really not. It is a game of its own that plays well within its limits. Compared to many horror indie games, It doesn't come off as try hard with cheap jumpscares & lame twists.  There are subtle details that when you notice it, it delivers either a cold chill or even a smile due to how clever it is applied. The visuals of the surroundings are what I like the most, beautiful and perfect for screenshots or file photos & it gives off some RE1 vibes where even an empty room creeps you out. I didn't expect the game to be more longer than it  actually is and I'm not complaining, I like it. The camera mechanic is interesting too, similar to the REC movie where you get to open up and see surroundings/paths that can't be seen by the normal eye and contributes to the creepy atmosphere but it also make the game quite frustrating which I would point out in a bit on the negative part. The storyline isn't special but as I've said, the game isn't trying to be tryhard so all the other aspects of the game meld with each other well and the result is a decent horror indie game.The only negative thing I can point out is how the game show very little or no indication to when and where to go especially in a game where it incorporates a camera mechanic that can make the map twice as big because not only new paths will be available while using the camera but also the surroundings that may contain key items. So if you have no idea where to go next then you may have to use the camera in its built in night vision mode all over the place finding the next key item and after all that you still have to consider more time for tedious backtracking to figure out what to do with the found item because there is a lot of puzzles throughout the game. The game difficulty is not easy either, ammo and consumables are very crucial yet manageable but if you add up "having no sense of direction" that is where it gets annoying. Checking a guide for hints on direction every now and then would be recommended instead of trying to figure out things on your own, it wouldn't be enough to spoil the experience since it outweighs getting stuck.All in all I would rate Fobia- St. Dinfa Hotel a decent

_childDocuments_.review: The game offers an interesting experience. Let’s start with the positives:--The presentation is really good. The ambiance and the way the hotel connects each floor are well thought out. Despite needing to backtrack a lot, I found myself enjoying the time spent solving puzzles and exploring. The game looks fantastic and the atmosphere is well set.Now, the negatives:--The monsters and horror elements felt a bit dull. The boss fights, in particular, were disappointing.--The gunplay is functional but feels somewhat random. Many gunshots felt awkward, and it was hard to tell if I was doing good or bad damage.--The story also suffers from poor pacing.--Additionally, many items and puzzle artifacts are easy to miss. I often found myself revisiting areas multiple times, struggling to find what I had overlooked.Despite these issues, this isn’t a bad game. I completed it, and had a great time. It's an incredible production, and I can’t believe it was made by only eight people. They are definitely doing something outstanding here. You can tell they love horror survival puzzle games.
_childDocuments_.name: Fobia - St. Dinfna Hotel

_childDocuments_.review: In my opinion definitely not a survival horror, let alone a horror game. I'd sooner call it a (at times) creepy walking simulator with very simple combat and heavy emphasis on exploration and (especially) puzzle solving. The only time I actually was frightened was when I backed up into a sliding door towards the end of the game and it loudly beeped and slid open.Only real gripe I would have is how backtrack-heavy it is, especially as throughout the game old paths became blocked/inaccessible and you have to find a longer detour to get back to the same place you checked 10 times to find a small flash drive due to a lack of a map system.I still recommend giving it a shot as it combines a lot of interesting ideas and the game definitely isn't a bad one. It has a modern RE-like inventory, passable to sub-par VO, interesting setting, and decent story. Feels like it puttered out towards the end or maybe I'm just dumb and lost track of where the story was going.
_childDocuments_.name: Fobia - St. Dinfna Hotel

_childDocuments_.review: I really want to like this game, but in the end, I just can't recommend it. Fobia is going for a Resident Evil 7 style of gameplay with puzzles, combat and so on. The game looks and sounds great, but that's the main positives if you ask me. Puzzles can be fun, but a lot of them are annoying and it can be confusing where to go or what to do next. This is coming from someone who loves old school Resident Evil, like the first game, and puzzle games in general by the way. Combat is super boring and slow too, and the animations for taking out guns are very slow. You also only have one enemy type thoughout the entire game: humanoid zombie thing. That's it. Well, there are a few bugs as well, but I wouldn't count that. The story is also a bit of a mess, and super slow-paced. It all makes sense in the end, but it does drag on quite a bit. If you NEED a survival horror fix, then I suggest getting it during a sale. Other than that, I find if too annoying and slow to be worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: I've put about 4 hours into this at the time I am writing and I can safely say that this game is well worth the price of admission but it has a few problems that I'll outline using a Pro/Con systemPROS:1. Gunplay, while not the most polished is pretty solid but lacks impact but other than that its good2. The game oozes atmosphere and feels tense walking through the hotel, this is accompanied by creaking floorboards and doors and a creeping soundtrack that feels like it doesn't overstay its welcome.3. The puzzles are great and give a great sense of satisfaction from solving them.4. The voice acting while not amazing isn't the worst I've heard, while this isn't really a pro I can't say it's a con either as it's somewhat hit or miss.5. The game very clearly takes a lot of its influence from Resident evil especially the recent titles of 7 and village but I was surprised to see some elements of Silent Hill with there being a corrupted version of the world and also some of Fatal frame with using a camera to view said other world for exploration, puzzle-solving and also to find useful things such as ammo and healing items.6. I also like the upgrade system for your weapons, you find these little cubes that give you a certain amount of upgrade points for your weapons that get more expensive as you buy them, things like faster reload times, more damage and accuracy, you get these side puzzles that aren't necessary to complete the game (these puzzles also offer you other items) and also by exploring and observing your surrounding's.CONS:1. There is this mechanic for scaring the player that at first was somewhat never wracking but over time just got annoying, as you can see in the cover art above a small girl wearing a gas mask is in the game, she's not really a threat but some in-game note explains that when she's around all light flickers including natural light, this happens to you sometimes and it starts to get old quick especially when it happens near enemies and this really is annoying as it happens frequently and all I do is just stand there with my thumb up my ass until it passes.2. The flashlight is in my inventory, this is a small nitpick on my part but it annoys me that something that should just be for me to see in dark areas takes up a spot when in similar games it does not.3. No map to look at makes backtracking frustrating which is something you have to deal with a lot, there is a map in all the halls of the hotel but I wasn't sure if they were being updated or not but even if it was I shouldn't have to go out into a hallway to look at a map to see where I need to go next.4. While I am only 4 hours in the enemy variety is a little sparse but this could change as I have only played about 4 hours of the game so far with that said slight SPOILER ahead for the enemies. I have fought small spiders that don't look like spiders, some men with mouths that go all the way down to their neck with hearts in their throat that you shoot as a weak spot, a large version of the spiders that is a boss fight and a Mr.X style creature that shows up only on certain story beats and also can easily body block you in certain hallways as they are quite small, this happened when he first showed up and I took a lot more damage than I should have and I spent a lot of ammo stunning him 3 times before I managed to get around him which didn't feel fair. 5. This game is not a native English game as the studio that made it is located in Brazil so there are some slight translation issues but this was surprisingly not as common as one might expect but I'm including this as cons as this made one puzzle a little confusing for me and hopefully won't happen again and will probably get patched sometime soon and so far only happened once.With all that said and done the Pros of this game vastly out-way the cons and the game is a solid 7/10 so far. If any of the issues that I had got better or worse by the time I finish, I intend to update this review.
_childDocuments_.name: Fobia - St. Dinfna Hotel

_childDocuments_.review: It's alright - I didn't *dislike* the game, but I'm not sure it was worth what I paid for it. Pretty decent graphically and the ingame camera's function was pretty neat. Puzzles were not super complicated and obscure which was nice. But the negatives.. clunky movement - the run/walk is clunky, the camera movement and head bob are a bit over the top. Inventory management is often painful (do you like playing inventory tetris? I don't). The save system can be a little frustrating; you need to remember to save often at the clocks. Probably the biggest crime for me was the slow pace and lack of action. Yes, you can collect weapons and there are some monsters that you can kill but you're seldom in any *actual* danger and I found myself worrying more about my ammo than my health when it came to boss fights. If you want a game where you are constantly tense and at risk of imminent death this is not the one; there are horror elements but this is imo a pretty relaxed game in general.
