_childDocuments_.review: So I got this as part of a Humble Bundle. It's a little pricey in my opinion, but $20 isn't bad for what it is. With the other options out there, I thought it might have been $15.The graphics are pretty good and things are usually easy to distinguish. As others have noted, a way to switch between two equip sets would have been nice, but once you get used to the game the inventory management really doesn't feel that bad. It's mostly the first playthrough that it feels a bit much. That said, the game reminded me quite a bit of Circle of the Moon, one of my personal favorite Castlevania games so maybe I'm just used to opening up my inventory to switch minor things around.I will say that once you get into the artifacts and how they affect your weapon swing speed, it honestly kind of hurts the game. Some weapons show up too late to be particularly useful and even "fast" weapons can feel pretty sluggish, so knowing your character's attack speed is pretty important. It makes some weapons kind of superfluous though. And that's kind of what makes the inventory more bearable after you have more experience with the game too: some weapons will just feel better or be able to do better things.Due to the dev's focus on survival, there are no quick refill points. You either have to spend an artifact slot or weapon slot or eat a consumable. The inventory sorts by newest by default, but it can also be sorted by name, so knowing that is also very helpful towards good inventory management once you understand what items cure or nullify certain effects.Enemies can be run past or cheesed in various ways (water has several cheesy things you can do to enemies inside while mitigating the effect on  your character through consumables or artifacts). They either drop consumables or pittances of gold, so don't worry about fighting every enemy. Bosses are where the combat really comes into play in figuring out patterns, openings, vulnerabilities, and even environmental hazards that you can take advantage of. Most of the bosses have two major phases: a player-sized form and a big form that has its own phases. If you know what you're doing late-game, the bosses with defined phases are pretty easy to cheese, which is kind of good if you want to attempt the Hardcore difficulty.Overall, it's good and can be beaten in a few hours. Once the game is beaten, you unlock a Castlevania-like boss mode and two modes that focus on spellslinging or crits that really remind me of COTM's extra modes. It's a nice little bonus that changes the way you play without making tons of changes. The major weapons and artifacts with effects that don't make sense for the mode (such as attack speed buffs in Witch Mode) get new effects thematically appropriate to the mode (like a casting speed buff instead) and become either active or passive artifacts instead of normal equips. I'm not kidding about a few hours per playthrough either. I've beaten it four times so far on different modes with only assassin and hardcore left.So it has balancing issues with its weapons and spells (there are a few absolutely amazing options and a lot of eeehhhh.... ones by comparison). I really wish the default attack speed was faster and didn't stop your forward momentum dead in the air. I also really wish there was some sort of more plentiful healing available that wasn't consumable or equipment based since that partially exacerbates the balance issues. The story isn't going to blow anyone away and it's a little ecchi at times with character designs. The music is balanced pretty low and is fairly lowkey "ambient sense of dread" for most of the game though there are a few nice tracks. That said, finding the little tricks to recover health or make certain rooms easier when attempting to collect most of the stuff is still fun. Finding the best boss strategies to balance out your damage and survivability was quite fun, like little puzzles, and environmental effects add a bit more depth that I appreciate. The extra modes add a bit more replayability to the experience as well. It is a little hard to recommend for $20 with its flaws and quirks, but it's a solid game built around map exploration and equipment combos.

_childDocuments_.review: Cute little metroidvania. The pixel art is quite good. Movement and controls feels intuitive and smooth. The overall sound design is well done. The combat is punishing at first but later on you can gather more equipment and magic that helps a lot. _childDocuments_.review: A fun little Metroidvania with only a handful of very minor stumbling blocks.As the biggest pro, the spire artwork and animation is consistently amazing. Light sources reflect dynamically on the characters which gives the scenes an incredible feeling of depth. Attack animations have a good amount of heft to them, though slower two-handed animations look a bit floaty instead of giving a feeling of 'gravity' to the swing arc. For enemies, all attacks are well telegraphed and simple to read.Combat has an odd mix of slightly floaty weapons with punishingly strict committal, though enemies are forced just as much to watch their attack whiff as you jab them in the back with a dagger, which makes the combat 'fair' for both parties, at least as long as you manage to keep it to a 1v1. Fighting multiple enemies at once is more often than not suicidal and sometimes you best choice is to run away or leave and reenter the room, resetting all still living enemies while dead ones remain temporarily disposed of (moving through enough rooms will revive all enemies in passed rooms). Weapons can feel somewhat floaty because one-handed and two-handed weapons are swung in an arc, but that arc has a steady speed throughout the entire animation, which can make especially slow attack swings feel very weak and weightless. Since being able to modify the swing speed through equipment is an option, I'm not sure if there is an elegant solution to that however.I think the biggest roadblock a lot of people will face getting used to combat isn't its grounded attacks, but the fact that attacking mid-jump will completely void all horizontal momentum, meaning that if you attack while jumping forward you will just drop straight down instead. This paired with how the game likes to place ranged enemies across precarious jumps makes platforming a lot more dangerous than one would expect from a very platforming-focused metroidvania.The typical solution to that of course represent magic and the disposable single-use wands that litter the environment. Magic is tied to MP which does not naturally regenerate, meaning you have to rely on consumables to refresh your MP or use equipment with provides you with some level of MP recovery. Wands are a reasonably abundant resource, but they are still limited in use, so they're best reserved for situations where melee would be too dangerous to commit to or open a handful of doors that require magic to activate their respective levers.For the minor stumbling blocks I brought up in the beginning, while combat is pretty fun once you get the hang of it, the game has somewhat of an over-reliance on status effects and DoTs. Pretty much any attack won't just deal flat damage, but also give you increasingly long stacks of bleed, burn or poison, freeze you in place, invert your controls, and so forth. On Veteran difficulty these can also stack repeatedly on additional hits, frequently providing you with DoT effects that exceed even your maximum possible HP. Most ofthese effects can be countered and even temporarily negated with consumables, but in the heat of combat it can feel rather frustrating to have defeated a a single enemy but losing several items just to counter the DoT and replenish the health you've lost just as the result of burning.Traps and trickery are our best allies in this game, learning which enemies are too dangerous to take head-on and how to bypass and/or defeat them without even allowing them to fight back are typically your best choices.

_childDocuments_.review: The story is kinda crap and if you were to really classify it as Metroidvania (which I don't think you should) it lacks pretty much any ability progression (meaning the only thing stopping your path are doors and enemies), but aside from it - this game is pretty great. _childDocuments_.review: 8/10 This game is pretty good. (9/10 for me personally)The Story - itself is what i would say is the 'DMC3 effect' where in that it's entertaining as hell but has some surprising depth to it (and some dark messed up implications) that at some points gave me the feels.Gameplay - will be quite difficult for new players as it was for me but once you narrow down the mechanics it feels really good with all the weapons, ranged weapons and magic at your disposal. The variety of builds you can conjure up is astounding. Not to mention the amazing enemy variety that the game presents that will keep things not only entertaining but challenging as well. Likewise, the bosses really test your skills (and knowledge of mechanics as well).Visuals - are gorgeous and aesthetically pleasing.Loses points - due to the certain items being a bit too strong in that magic builds in the (very) late game are a bit too strong (for me personally). Inventory item swapping and usage (which you'll be doing a lot) can be streamlined further to lessen the monotony of it a bit. Finally, there should've been a new game plus for the veteran difficulty which in my opinion could've added late game enemies to the earlier stages whilst keeping your inventory so you can use all that OP stuff as well as your skill throughout a new replay. Maybe throw in even harder new enemies because why not?Conclusion,Instead of wasting money on some in-game micro-transaction, buy other games and experience something new. Lost Ruins is one of those experiences, simple and entertaining with surprising depth to it. Has its flaws yes, but it is an overall satisfying product in the end.

_childDocuments_.review: A really charming game with beautiful, breezy pixel art, lush animation and lighting effects, endearing characters and character portraits, and an enjoyable, fairly mellow soundtrack. The storyline is straightforward and accessible, the finale is satisfying, and overall the game just feels very complete. I really loved the tremendous variety of melee and ranged weaponry, spells, and equipment with powerful and distinct perks - there's a lot more potential for buildcrafting here than you might expect in a typical 2D metroidvania.Combat can be a bit janky; each speed category of melee/spell attack feels a few shades slower than it should, enemy stagger thresholds are a bit inconsistent, etc. Difficulty and damage scaling occasionally feel off - some negative status effects last way longer than feels necessary and are particularly punishing.But these are minor annoyances, and ultimately I found they only encouraged me to dig into the game's diverse toolkit for creative solutions to trouble spots. Enemies who spam shields can be overcome with heavy weapons that ignore blocking; flying enemies who are impossible to target can be brought down with auto-strike spells like Chain Lightning; monsters with low stagger points can be crippled with Orb abilities, etc. etc. The game throws a lot at you, but always equips you with the tools to handle it. I found myself constantly switching up my loadout throughout the game's reasonable ~7 hour runtime. It was a great feeling that made for a varied gameplay loop, and I really credit Altari Games for engineering that.Lost Ruins might not satisfy people looking for a more hardcore experience or snappier combat, but I really enjoyed my time with the game, and definitely recommend it to anyone looking for a quick metroidvania with some gentler anime aesthetics.

_childDocuments_.review: I guess you can say the game have an Isekai story, but sadly it is so simplistic and it have an OBVIOUS AS ♥♥♥♥ villain that you won't bother with the details. Well, to be fair it has a plot twist that could have been interesting…but let be honest, we are here for the action and the cute girls. So it is metroidvania with a classic save system! Normal to God save! YES! I like those so much! No ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ autosaves and collecting your exp again trying to not die again. The start feels a little hard at first, but believe me when I say this: you will end up changing different play styles to suit your needs non-stop because it is so much fun! My earlier build was using a fast axe and a shield which with each block I healed myself, then I switched to magical swords and healing spells with armor/weapons filling my mana pool over and over again,oh and a demon bear doll that when it gets hit I get mana back. Getting back on track, another thing I liked a lot was the nice art of the characters when you had a chance to talk to them. I have big praise for some specific monster girls. My favorite from all of them is Jun. Ironically her reveal was also the biggest plot twist as well. A big negative I had (aside from the forgettable story) was the map. It is detailed enough to show you where you are going, painfully bland when you want to reach specific items. Also you can fail a mission if you are not careful, a very important one. If you are a metroidvania fan who also wants an extra challenge managing your loot and gear, and cute anime girls, "Lost Ruins" is the perfect choice.8/10

The game has a much slower pace to it which threw me off after playing much faster metroidvanias such as cave story, iconoclasts, and the ori games. - The story is predictable but has a lot of cute, charming character moments. - The sprite based art is excellent and the 2d portraits are cute. - If you are coming off of Momodora or Minoria and want more of that, then this is for you!

_childDocuments_.review: It's... fine. The art's nice, it sounds fine, the quests are completely forgettable, and it's insanely easy to be juggled from full health and have to redo a ton of rooms. _childDocuments_.name: Lost Ruins

_childDocuments_.review: Fun little metroidvania! Recommended for fans of the genre who want something with some bite, or for those who like cute anime girls.Takes a little bit to get the hang of the rhythm of combat, but once you do it's pretty smooth and not too terribly difficult, while still having some challenge. Has a good focus on resource management that a lot of metroidvanias lack. There's a ton of build variety, it's very fun to play around with different gameplay styles and it's fairly easy to swap between them at will. The pacing of the game does lack at times though - the ability to swap equipment in the middle of combat is both a good and bad thing. It provides lots of flexibility, but also slows things down as there's no reason NOT to constantly swap equipment in the middle of combat as the situation changes, which really slows the otherwise fast-paced combat down. If you don't like fiddling through menus, I'd maybe give this one a pass.
_childDocuments_.name: Lost Ruins

_childDocuments_.review: This review is a direct reply to all the negative reviews saying that the combat is clunky.First: I am a total metroidvania noob. I just found interest in the genre a few days ago and this is the first game I am playing. I'm not experienced and also not a die-hard fan who plays every title that comes out.From those reviews, I get the impression that the authors went into the game expecting a hack'n'slay action game. And that is why they were disappointed. "Lost Ruins" is not about rapidly hitting your buttons and slashing though enemies.There ARE enemies that are easiest to defeat if you rush in and hit them before they know what is happening. More often than not though, you need to know what you are doing. Think of it as a beat'em'up, as if you were playing "Guilty Gear". If you mess up, the enemy can often get you in a stunlock and kill you no matter how many HP you had, especially if you face several enemies at once. At the very least, you will lose a lot of HP. If you know how you have to approach an enemy, chances are you can down him without losing any HP at all.Such was the case with the first boss, which frustrated me massively. It didn't help that I was playing the demo and that you couldn't skip cutscenes there (you can in the proper game). Once I found out how to kill the minions and then the boss, I am confident I can do so without getting hit at all. It's not even about hit zones or immunities, it's just movement and attack patterns.The game doesn't want to give you endless action. It's about ressource management and tactical combat movements. The gratification does not come from going in with guns blazing and slaying foe after foe, but from executing just the right movements in just the right timing. That's not to say the game has no speedrun potential, in the contrary. I'm sure you can rush through it if you perfectly memorized each enemy's patterns.Now the game HAS its downsides. Consumables, especially ranged attacks, are semi-finite. You get money and the occasional item from drops and opponents respawn, but mana does not regenerate (HP can, to an extent) and potions are really expensive. This makes me not use anything at all except for boss fights. There are also no quick-use slots for consumables so you have to enter the menu each time, and with a lot of very situational consumables you often don't end up using them even when it would be beneficial. Which is not a real problem if you can stand retrying a room over and over and are not playing hardcore mode or speedrunning.The characters are interesting and quirky and there is a slightly clichéd but entertaining story unfolding. I'm 3 hours in (2 more hours in the demo) and just facing the second boss, and I still like what I am seeing.
_childDocuments_.name: Lost Ruins

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed this game.  The art is absurdly good, and I found the gameplay enjoyable.  I do still have my gripes with this game though.  The story is bare bones and predictable, so if you're interested in amazing story and lore in games, you should look pretty much anywhere else.  The combat is interesting, in the fact that I have zero idea how 3/4 of it works.  I mostly just used melee weapons, however there are bows, a magic system, and items you can throw around to try and give yourself some advantage.  I can't really advocate for anything but melee combat, as I didn't use anything else, but from what I've seen, it's all well made.  I strayed from the others though, as the game kinda forces you into melee early on, and it's hard to break out of that when it works well.  The game is very short.  It only took me a couple hours to beat it the first time, but it has some replay-ability in a separate game mode and multiple challenge modes.  Overall, I'd give the game a 7/10, although maybe wait for it to be on sale since it's so short.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is outstanding, it does a great job of implementing what makes metroidvania great and then putting a unique spin on it all. All of it was fun, and I ended up feeling that me expectations were exceeded. If this was all the game had, it'd be worth the cost. _childDocuments_.review: Pretty good at what it's trying to do, but definitely not for everyone.The game sets itself apart from most platformers with a veneer of player hostility in most of its design elements--weapons attack slowly, many weapons are single use, your dodge roll is clumsy, enemies deal brutal damage with quick attacks, HP and MP aren't refilled for free anywhere, etc.However, it's kind of a smokescreen. Healing items are showered on you as you go, the AI is braindead, and many of the items are gamebreaking (including items that grant infinite free healing/MP refills, negate all traps/bad terrain, and infinite use ranged weapons).Fortunately, none of that stops it from FEELING like you're triumphing over stacked odds and an unfair game. It's just hostile enough to feel good finding and using the stuff that's broken. You will have to proceed slowly and use your brain, but it's not actually that difficult except a few spots.Other stuff: Visuals are quite good with great monster design and great animations. Enemy design+variety is pretty good. Boss design is hit-or-miss. Despite looking like a metroidvania basically none of the stuff you gain are used for exploration or movement.
_childDocuments_.name: Lost Ruins

_childDocuments_.review: Really good artwork, pretty good music. Storyline feels half baked, but not too bad. The combat has a bit of a learning curve, since it's timing system is something not seen in a lot of games. And the boss patterns could be a bit more interesting.As others have mentioned, magic is totally broken. End of story. As soon as you get good mana regen, you're set. As soon as you get HP regen, you're set. Runes are broken, especially when you get the rune stone. The puzzles were honestly the absolute worst part of the entire game. They were stupidly easy, and really ony served as a annoyance. There was one good one though, where you had to . That got me for a while, and it was actually a bit satisfying. But it was so unlike the others.
_childDocuments_.name: Lost Ruins

_childDocuments_.review: A metroidvania that feels like it was made by a small team which has some truly awful combat.  You can equip one special item and two weapons, but early enemies are either slow and plodding or have ranged attacks that they let off in quick succession.  Many fights were 'hold shield to block projectile, move up, block projectile, move up, block projectile, strike, wait, block projectile, wait, block projectile, strike...'Arial combat causes you to stop moving and drop as you swing.  You can equip a special item to slightly help, but this is in place of better options like a damage booster.  Other items are misleading, such as a 'slingshot' not being a weapon but instead an item that improves the damage of a limited number of consumable thrown grenades.  Magic is already powerful and if you have MP you can waste difficult enemies. The thing that made me end up refunding the game so early on is the save system.  You can save at a small number of computer stations and you automatically save when you encounter a statue.  But you can't autosave at the same statue until you've saved at another one.  This feels like an attempt to make a slower, more deliberate form of gameplay but it feels overly restrictive along with the other issues.  It seems average at best and even watching a few videos showing where the story will go did not make me want to continue.  The cadence of combat just isn't worth the frustration to me, but I'm dead certain that it will 'click' for the right people and be an enjoyable (but too short) experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Lost Ruins

_childDocuments_.review: Fairly simple action game that's somewhat on the short side but is bursting with charm. Visuals are top-notch. I especially like the giant monster girl boss art. Gameplay is pretty fun. The story however is predictable and nothing special, but there are giant monster girl bosses. More games should have giant monster girl bosses.Combat is quite good for how simple it is. Equip weapons and/or spells and press button to use. For the most part (boss mode has some special attacks when jumping) no fancy combos, special attacks when crouching, jumping or dodging, just swing your weapon or cast your spell. There's a fair variety in weapon and spell types with different attack speeds, reach, damage and status effects which when combined with the accessory system that allows you to further affect those offensive as well as your defensive capabilities leaves a plethora of approaches all perfectly viable. Experimenting with different builds throughout the game was pretty fun. Enemy design is done well and encourages that experimentation with various builds; you can't always just run up to all the enemies the same way, attack and back off, a somewhat common fault of more simple action games. The downside to the equipment variety combined with amount of different consumables is that you'll find yourself in the menu longer than you'd like to be. This hassle is somewhat offset by the ability to favorite items bringing them to the top of your list, but still can be an annoyance.

If you want a challenge then you may want to selct a harder difficulty to begin with, although I haven't tried it yet myself.The first couple of encounters will feel a little tough, until you get the hang of the timing and such. The first boss is probably the hardest, after that things get progressively easier due to the sheer amount of weapons options you collect.My main criticism would be that the final boss is a bit dissapointing, The game is about 8 hours long on the default difficulty, if you take your time, but I'd still say it was well worth it. _childDocuments_.review: This was a short and sweet but very entertaining game for me!  It is most easily compared to as being a Souls-like side scroller, where fighting even the simplest enemy takes a bit of thinking and patience, and save points are preset bonfires that reset the entire area of all spawns.You are given free roam very early on, to explore and find enemies in any order you see fit with almost no hand holding whatsoever.  It is a small content filled world with a lot to discover and a lot of interesting little sidequests to complete.  And the way you can build your fighting style can vary quite a bit.  You could go for quick attacking weapons with bleeds, slower hard hitting weapons, or numerous spellcasting builds to get through the game in any way you see fit.  Some things are a bit awkward, such as momentum loss when attacking midair, but they are all just the rules of the world you abide by to get through.  The writing and humour is charming, and the story itself is simple but fun to experience.Would recommend this game.  It has lots of replayability as well, with different challenge modes unlocking by completing the first run of the game, as well as multiple endings depending on how you do things.If anyone's interested in my blind run through, here is a let's play I recorded! :)

_childDocuments_.review: It's not the longest game and is kind of predictable in some things story wise, but it's a solid metroidvania (sort of); I finished it in 6 hours doing 100% of the map and the secret ending (at least I think it was secret?, again, I saw it coming) and honestly, the game is not hard as long as you don't attempt to brute force your way ahead. _childDocuments_.review: Lost Ruins is a fun game that doesn't overstay it's welcome.  As far as Metroidvanias go, it's not overly complex, which is something I appreciate.  Playing on "recommended" difficulty, I never had much of a problem progressing, but that's not to say it isn't easy to die, especially if you aren't careful or appropriately prepared.  Most encounters, including boss fights, can be made significantly less difficult by having the right combination of spells and equipment, so the game becomes less about overcoming difficulty and more about puzzling out the correct strategy.  Other things worth mentioning are the fact that check points and save spots are numerous and forgiving, minimizing the frustration of dying.  Also, the game is rather generous about marking stuff like treasures, NPC locations, and quest items on your map, and the fast travel system makes backtracking to find stuff you missed pretty painless.  There also seems to be quite a bit of replay value with the extra modes that are unlocked after finishing the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Lost Ruins

_childDocuments_.review: Lost Ruins is a metroidvania that tries to offer combat that rewards throughtful use of tactics and cunning rather than quick reflexes, and though i think it fails in that regard i still think it's an enjoyable game.Simply put, there are too many OP pieces of equipment for the combat to ever significantly challenge the player. The only challenge comes from analyzing a situation and equipping whatever pieces of equipment deals with it. Player creativity is rarely required, mostly exploiting game mechanics. However, since death comes very easily, it still feels good to overcome the obsctacles Lost Ruins presents you with, even though it is usually in spite of its design rather than in tandem with it.Knowing this, what does the game get right ? simply put, it feels good to play; movement hits a good balance between weighty and responsive and weapons are varied enough to justify switching loadouts often. It's also pleasant to the eyes and ears, with a fitting if forgettable soundtrack and wonderful pixel art. Finally, the story is surprisingly enjoyable: it is self aware and jokey in tone, but the finale adds an unexpected layer of emotion that sends it off nicely.If you're interested in a metroidvania with slow, almost puzzle like combat, give REDO! a try. I think it succeeds in that regard much better than this game. Otherwise, Lost Ruins is a perfectly fine way to spend 7 hours exploring a good looking world and interacting with a flawed but interesting combat system. Some of the game modes you unlock after beating it are also very cool and let you get more bang for your buck.

_childDocuments_.name: Lost Ruins

_childDocuments_.review: Obviously the game is very beautiful, great visuals/lighting, music and sound, lovely art style and characters with some meme dialog. That much you know. I'm waiting warmly for the anime~Has a cute story, with a twist that only comes by completing a specific quest. Story is a balance of being interesting enough without slowing down the gameplay too much, all the dialog scenes are skippable and they're not too long. Some metroidvanias suffer from too much forced story sequence slow-down of the gameplay but that's not a problem here thankfully. So you can easily just pick up and play the game for an hour without being bogged in some forced cut scenes that you've already seen 30 times or having to spam past pages of dialog and tutorials, this makes the game very replayable for me. This is so rare in modern games, probably as an attempt to pad out the playtime. With Lost Ruins there's a world and characters that are there if you want it, but its short and sweet, direct and to the point and also skippable. This alone is a huge plus for me.There's three endings and five modes, all of which are fun and unique. This is good because be aware that each playthrough is not very long. In 25 hours I have completely 100% the game, I plan to replay it more even though I've seen all the content.Gameplay is excellent each enemy has certain weaknesses and status effects they can inflict, the gameplay loop is almost Pokemon-like, at each screen you pause to consume some items and equip some loadout that is suitable for the specific weakness / strength of the enemies on that screen. Finding the optimal config for each screen makes it, in a way, more of a puzzle game than an action game. One flaw is that after some time it can get tiring to be constantly swapping equipment back and forth. You can mark favorite equipment that will stay at the top of your list, but it'd be nice to be able to save equipment configurations and then swap between them. Half of my playtime is spent in the menu manually swapping between 3-4 equipment setups. Also the sorting seems to keep resetting for me, I can never get the menu to stay in alphabetic sort mode for long.The game makes a solid attempt to balance all the playstyles that it offers, you can max bleed damage or dagger criticals or slow two-handers etc, some loadouts are strictly superior to others though. The game is also simply not that difficult so once you get a good feel for the controls you can choose your favorite build and beeline through the entire game with it if you want to, it will just be less optimal than switching equipment for each screen / area.There are many status effects and environmental reactivity, a lot of the fun of the game is discovering all of these. You can beat enemies in many creative ways if you want to.Both your character and the enemies are bulky and slow so this is more of a souls-like feel as opposed to other metroidvanias where you zip around the screen double-jumping with tight controls. You can easily die simply because you swung too early or you rolled one pixel too short or you misjudged distance and didn't land within your weapon's reach before you swing. It's not a flaw just be aware that's the type of game this is.In the normal mode magic is powerful and scarce for the first half of the map because your MP is so limited, in the second half of the map this flips and you suddenly have infinite MP. Because the map is not that long, the power creep feels wild, you very quickly go from helpless scared schoolgirl to an enemy-shredding god. Initially most healing items are heal over time, which is great, then you quickly get many instant-heal items. The game would be much challenging if instant restore items were more rare or didn't exist at all. There are also items that heal you over time when you're under some status effect, this makes for some cool combos but kinda makes the game too easy because you can exploit this. There are other items that heal you whenever you deal some type of damage to enemies, it'd be better if the game forced you to rely on those more or exclusively, meaning that you have to take a risk to restore your health, which is a little more engaging. It's weird that the game has this cool "you have to deal damage to heal" mechanic built-in but then invalidates it by giving you so many other easier options to restore health.I would love to see a sequel with a larger map and more challenging enemies / screens. The biggest "flaw" if there is any, is that there's simply so many cool weapons / spells / abilities / etc that don't truly get a chance to shine because there's just not enough truly challenging encounters. The health of enemies is pretty low, so there's no bosses that last more than 2-3 cycles and most enemies explode with one or two shots. This game would be a perfect candidate for some kinda lunatic mode DLC. Double the amount of enemies, double their health and make enemies a bit more mobile, and this would be a radically different game with way more opportunity to milk the different mechanics.As it is though the game is still a joy to play, absolutely worth the money, to me this is an almost perfect metroidvania. It feels like playing through an episode of an anime. Also what happened to poor Jun-chan ;_;

_childDocuments_.review: This game should be blasted for being basically a waifu-vania with how plentiful the amount of suggestive monster girls are the selling point of this game. Surprisingly though, game is about as hard as Momodora while still being forgiving as metroidvanias go, in a sense that with the right item combination in the right situation any level can become almost a cake-walk.And that's where I'm impressed by how well utilized are many of the equipments and weaponries you find throughout the game. Besides notable exceptions, many items in this game feel like they're perfectly made for their right purpose and for the right area, which makes the extremely limited equipment that you can use at once the more strategic  to utilize since there are many items that would make for outright broken hero thanks to clever damage stacking.The only main issue I have with this game, as common to any game I have with consumables is that if you're being too careful with the resource management you just end up getting through the game just fine without seeing much of other possible weapon strats, simply because they become less lucrative when, for the most part, melee can solve almost any combat scenario just as fine, and later on it even becomes possible to not run out of mana so that spamming magic from afar is totally an option as well.Not that I think the game's difficulty is any too easy per say, but rather that I'd wish there were more difficulties like witch mode or other creative ways to be able to experience the rest of the varieties in combat the game has to offer.All in all, game has an acquired taste in style that might put some people off due to excessive anime looks, but I'd still recommend this as not only a good metroidvania, but a metroidvania that actually felt different for a change.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is good. Have heard several people describe this as a Metroidvania - and while I can see where they're coming from, because it superficially LOOKS a lot like one, there really isn't this sort of "gain ability and backtrack a lot thing". Sure you can do that, but there's no required backtracking, though some enemies are easier to kill and some obstacles easier to bypass with later abilities.There's an elemental system with limited environmental effects (freezing/electrifying water, setting goo on fire, that sort of thing - but also things like "you recover HP when you set yourself on fire", "electrified water doesn't hurt you"). This can be quite fun to play around with as you discover ways to abuse this to your advantage.This is also generally how boss fights play out. While there's still the whole thing of learning patterns and what not, and technically you *could* beat all bosses just like that, the most effective way to deal with enemies is finding what combination of equipment and consumables works best, disable your opponents strengths and target their weaknesses. Again, to me that was very fun, but people used to some other games might be disappointed that fights are more about picking the best tools for the job than they are about super skillful moment to moment gameplay. Basically, the enemies are cheating bastards but you can throw everything they do right back at them.The game has a decent length for what it is, it took me about 15 hours to reach the true ending, and there are some challenge modes that unlock afterwards.If there is one somewhat disappointing aspect it would the plot - or rather, the lack thereof. The character designs are all pretty neat, but the characters themselves are all pretty one-note, and there's not really that much going on other than a bit of banter and then tearing each others throats out. Some of the characters have some more background or quirky character details, but it never amounts to a whole lot even if there's individually nothing wrong with it per se.Overall a pretty solid game, definitely worth the price of admission.

_childDocuments_.review: This game sits in a rather interesting cross roads of genres. In basic concept and overarching gameplay loop, it's a Metroidvania. You explore a series of rooms making up an interconnected world, defeat bosses and gain upgrades or adjustments to your kit along the way.That's about as far as the comparison goes however.The moment to moment gameplay is not like any other Metroidvania, it's combat and attacks are slow and seemingly clunky. The fastest attacks still leave you standing still for a good while, and while you have a dodge roll it's start up and recovery times mean it's not good for much beyond dodging an attack and disengaging, you'll almost always get hit if you attack to counter after rolling. The game is rather difficult initially as a result, though I did play on the Veteran difficulty for my first play through.However, this kind of gameplay is intentional, and the game is for the most part built around it. It's much less focused on the action of the gameplay, rather it rewards care in exploring the world and taking to careful preparation. The game lacks real upgrades to it, bosses drop stat upgrades or equipment slots rather than new abilities, and throughout the game you'll be collecting an entire variety of spells, weapons and accessories that can drastically modify your loadout and how you can approach situations. Early on the slow nature of combat made me gravitate towards the fastest weapon I could find, but soon I found that using a large heavy weapon was much more successful thanks to the range it gave me and the ability to control the fight by making enemies have to close the distance with me instead, and often times I could kill enemies in one or two hits. The game wants you to be slow and careful, and use the right tool for the job, and you'll be much more successful adjusting what your kit is depending on what you're fighting.The game does have a bit of a difficulty issue around this though. Being very stingy with money and offering no free heals, the early game is arguably the hardest part of the game as you lack the tools needed to properly strategize and play around the situations in front of you. The first boss was certainly the hardest for me, even with equipment that let me move quickly or heal in her arena, it'd certainly have been even worse if I hadn't explored before approaching her. However by the mid game, with the proper use of consumables and equip loads I was able to start killing bosses in only a handful of hits, with the final boss needing less than ten hits if you set yourself up to deal large amounts of damage. As well, magic started out as a valuable and scarce resource in the early game that slowly became my main method of clearing out mobs once I'd gained items to let me passive regenerate mana in the late game. While being able to fight only with spells was cool, magic is also incredibly strong and much of the game's moment to moment difficulty was diminished. On one hand I was rewarded for gathering and using all the tools I could, but I given the ability to simply roll over any non boss enemy purely with spells. Also, dev if you read these, please add some kind of loadout system, often times I had to menu through a cluttered inventory as I wanted to get the achievements for collecting items and it became rather annoying to swap everything out even with a favorite's system. As well, the ability to resave at checkpoint statues instead of having to leave to activate a different one is a much needed QoL change.Over all, I'd recommend the game. It's not a hack and slash, and shouldn't be approached that way. The art style obviously has a bit of a lewd anime girl trend in a similar vein to Shantae, but I wouldn't say it detracts from the game much and the overall aesthetic and featured art is quite good. There's not much to write home about on the story, it's alright with a decent twist at the end and some of the characters can be amusing or quirky.
_childDocuments_.name: Lost Ruins

_childDocuments_.review: A fun little game that can be cleared in a day or less. The combat feels nice and continuing is not too hard, but checkpoints don't restore health which means continuing is painful sometimes. One criticism I will level at the game is that if you want the best ending you have to actively refrain from opening chests that grant some very useful equipment, which means spending the majority of the game underpowered. While this is an appropriate level of challenge for the "golden ending", it takes the form of a side quest with no indication that this side quest is crucial to attaining said golden ending. Worse is that the reward is very mediocre gameplay-wise by the time you get it, so people who don't look up guides/don't care about the story will feel disappointed by this. Combat balancing is rather...iffy. As mentioned earlier, if you follow the side quest then you'll probably spend the majority of the game running away from enemies as there are no experience, gold can't get you good equipment (which is where most of the gameplay benefits come from). On the other hand, if you ignore said quest and open every chest you find, you will soon discover some very broken combo like infinite mana regen which makes most bosses a cakewalk. This can be achieved before fighting the third story boss. But if you're into min-maxing strats then this is an obvious buy.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this on a whim while it was on sale. Normally I would play a game like this once and put it down, instead the first time I played I kept going until I beat it on recommended difficulty. The game is hard but it doesn't feel unfair or cheesy like Dark Souls (personal opinion - sue me). I then went on to beat the extra modes and Hardcore (Deathless) difficulty over the next few days.The primary source of fun I found, while partly in difficulty and mastery, was in figuring out different build combinations from all the different items and weapons in the game. _childDocuments_.review: Sometimes developers come up with concoctions for game ideas that sound fantastic on paper, but when thrown into the pot, mixed up and served create something... interesting. Lost Ruins is a game with elements of difficulty similar to what a player would expect from Dark Souls, with tight controls that work flawlessly and of course the spice of beautifully done pixel artwork and animation. Lost Ruins’ goal is mostly to present a difficult metroidvania style game, with an emphasis on combat, which the game is wildly successful at doing. The player is present many ways to dispatch their enemies from a good variety of melee weapons to throwable items and magic. Of course that's not all as you also have a variety of items that can alter the game mechanics such as giving you health back with attacks or allowing you briefly float. These types of items can vastly change your approach to combat.There is more here than running and gunning or just slashing away like a madman until things die. The player will have to actually really take care with their approach because this game is relentless. Don’t come into the ruins expecting to not die, because you most certainly will.Not only are the enemies and combat very thought out, but the level design had some consideration that shows. Some encounters with your foes almost are like puzzles with multiple solutions. At times there can be the very simple solution, but others not so much due to very creatively placed dangerous traps. Within the labyrinth in Lost Ruins you will find traps and hurdles in many forms. Obviously there are enemies, but we are talking about something very different. Elements such as poison toxins and oil on the ground that can slow you down, but even more alarming, oil can catch fire, burning you.  Also, even getting wet from water has its effects that the player must consider. These elements can be used to your advantage, so be vigilant in using your head as well as your sword.As far as story goes in Lost Ruins, there is a dash of it here, but nothing more than most would expect from a metroidvania title. More-so than not, the story-line is just there as an excuse to move you from point A to point B. Story is there, but don’t come in looking for some classic RPG depth as this is not that style of game.Although I have to admit, this type of game is not for everyone, there is a part of me that thinks there is something here that creates a nice blend that anyone could enjoy. Some players may find a little more struggle than others, but it isn’t so difficult that it’d be hopeless  for an average player to succeed. Lost Ruins is a fantastic game that not only presents a very well done gaming experience, but also comes at a very affordable price-point. If you are a player who wants the best bang for your buck, then you have just come across a stick of dynamite. Lost Ruins is a must buy in my opinion and from a development team we definitely want to keep in the development world.

_childDocuments_.review: Fun and brief. Worth picking up on sale, for sure. I finished my first playthrough on hard mode after just a handful of hours, no guides or breaks needed.Enemies are varied, but extraordinarily simple. Most have exactly one unique attack; a handful of larger minions have two; bosses have, by and large, three per phase. Their art is well-styled and cohesive. All enemies have tells and consistent AI. The bosses are all young women that embody various fetishes, like slime girls, succubi, and a few other less-decent ones, but only the art plays off of that; the limited conversations and lore are completely nonsexual (with the exception of one comedic quest giver who exists to reference erotica from The Elder Scrolls).It controls like a classic post-SotN Castlevania game, with a few exceptions. The most notable is that swinging a weapon cancels all sideways momentum and controls. Startup and end lag is significant on most weapons, and you'll have to learn how to approach and disengage from each enemy individually. Back dashes are replaced with a Souls-like dodge with very forgiving i-frames and infinite uses.While I've heard complaints about the combat feeling slow or unwieldy, I enjoyed it. Some enemies or bosses are fast enough to swing twice before the slowest weapons can swing once, but they're rare. (Plus, slow weapons are going to be the least flexible -- why should you be able to tackle every threat that exists using only a greatsword?)While this game is tagged as a Metroidvania, you don't collect new movement options, there are no secretly-breakable walls, and the game is entirely linear with no necessary backtracking. Attack options (weapons and spells) are collected or bought throughout the game, including in one-screen optional areas that are barely hidden. Puzzles are simple and small.The developers also describe the game as "survival", but I disagree. Free, unlimited, unconditional regeneration is available before the first boss (for a toggleable penalty to max HP that you can switch off once you're healed), there's a checkpoint every third or fourth screen, and unless you choose the permadeath difficulty, you can simply treat the consumables as you always do: as things to be hoarded and unused.Lastly, I very much like the flexibility offered by the environment. Acid on the ground will poison you, but if you light it on fire, it will burn anything that touches it until it's exhausted. Casting ice spells in water will indefinitely chill it to damaging levels for both you and foes. Certain surfaces and regions are "sticky" and slow you down. It's all intuitive, and it's neither over- nor under-used.Overall, heartily recommended. It's a cute fusion of gameplay elements that doesn't overstay its welcome.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game after refunding another game for around $20, and decided I'd play this as a meme to stream to my friends. Then I kept playing it. Then I beat the game, then I started a new game, then another one. Needless to say, this game is really good, addictive certainly, with a gameplay loop that really gripped me.Lost Ruins is a classic dungeon crawl. The controls are clunky, which perfect encapsulates the idea of being a stupid high school girl swinging a zweihander around. However, the clunky controls are likely the biggest hurdle, and in my opinion they warp what seems like an action game into a strategic one. There are many weapons to choose from, all of which halt your momentum when you use them, forcing you to take it slow. If slow isn't your style, this probably isn't the game for you. You can also lobotimize yourself and make the game a cakewalk by using spells and exploiting weaknesses; there's nothing quite like fighting the first boss, getting annihilated, taking a step back and thinking about the nature of the boss and the arena, and then cheesing the boss to death by abusing the hell out of elemental combinations. This is replicated for most bosses, and even sitatuations, you don't have to bash your skull in and just "get gud", there's different strategies to try, and I managed to make the game a cakewalk before the halfway mark just by minmaxing my stats to godhood. Truly euphoric.The artstyle... look, let's not beat around the bush. It's anime, monster girls, and the like. I can't even pretend to do the "horny" joke, because I'm not a huge fan of the genre, but I will admit the farther along I got, the more tolerable, and even enjoyable the artwork became. This is a discussion on the artwork, as in still frames, if we're talking about pixel work, dear lord it's amazing. The Japanese anime thing might not be a selling point for some, but it's undeniable that if it could be done justice, they have gone above and beyond. You can tell that Altari Games really care about the game they made here.So, after having no lifed the game and nearly completed all modes, I can say this game is pretty dang good. I do have some minor gripes with it; for example, I was looking forward to the idea of unlockable characters after the game, and while I did get that, it wasn't really the length I was hoping. Again, what you get it well worth it, I just wish after playing all the modes there was more here, a compliment if anything, and a testament to my enjoyment of the game. Also the story is... not great. It's serviceable, but don't get this game if you want a branching story. The game seems to do best when it does the story of: "small snippets of messages left behind, you fill in the blanks" kind of story telling, the main story itself is nothing to write home about.Finally, this isn't a particularly long game. Once you figure out what works, the game is going to start breezing, or at least it did for me. Still, with the alternate game types you'll get around 10 hours or so, and even still something you could always boot back up to mindlessly play in the background once you've mastered it. Great game, would recommend, Witch mode is busted.

_childDocuments_.review: Nice game. If you played Momodora/Minoria and enjoyed these games, you will probably like Lost Ruins. The items play a major role on the gameplay, consumable or equipment. Controls are really responsive too.The game isn't as oppressive as it seems. _childDocuments_.review: This game is a triumph. The animation is gorgeous, evocative of an extremely well made doujin game but without the jank. There's just world's of choice for how you tackle the combat and puzzles, daggers, swords, magic, status effects, item combos that stack together for enhanced effectiveness, this is a game that begs you to try and explore all it has to offer you. The combat is tough, not unfair, but learning enemy patterns and your own range and speed is crucial to success. The game itself isn't terribly long, my first playthrough with tons of deaths and playing around with items came out to about 6 hours. But the end isn't the end, especially on your first playthrough. There are alternative modes, you can play as some of the bosses in a side campaign, and the variety of items and weapons invite trying multiple play styles.I came into this game blind, and at first the combat felt very slow and deliberate, but it doesn't have to stay that way. Before the first boss you've got access items which will increase your attack speed, weapons with various speeds, spells, one use combat items that pack a punch, and a variety of ways to tackle the problems the game puts in front of you. You get very few upgrades, basically those only come in the form of the artifacts you get from bosses and sidequests. In a normal mode game the max health appears to be 35, and you start the game with 20. Most of the growth in the game comes from your own abilities and experience with the mechanics. If that sounds particularly punishing, don't worry, there's an accessibility mode that eases the difficulty while still offering some challenge. In accessibility mode you're granted a relic at the start which heals 1 HP every few seconds, reduces enemy health and damage by 25%, gives you an extra item slot (VERY USEFUL), recovers your HP/MP at save points, and prevents bleed, fire, and poison damage from stacking. It's a big help!If I have one criticism of the game, I don't always love its sense of humor. The art seems very geared towards the male gaze, lots of big jiggling breasts, some of the artifacts are women's underwear, and for some reason the little hidden areas you'll find that add photos to the gallery all feature toilets. It wasn't enough to detract from my enjoyment of the game, but your experience may differ.For me, this game's an absolute 10/10, and I hope you love it too!
