_childDocuments_.review: It's mid and inoffensive, honestly that's what I expected, but it is not worth $30. It should be $20 at most, but I dunno, it's just not that great nor terribly ♥♥♥♥.There's things I like, the backgrounds representing Volcadera Bluff are actually very nice and pleasant, sells the coastal town vibe very well. I did like a lot of the music, maybe it's just my all over the place taste in music, but I enjoyed it. And the D&D inspired sections have some of the best art direction in the game IMO.The voice acting is good, I didn't really have issues with anyone's performances, I dunno what else to say about that.Now for the spicy takes I think a lot of people that enjoyed the game will tune out I'm sure.There's much better story based games out there with good LGBT representation, if you're looking for it, that are far cheaper like, Night in the Woods, VA-11 Hall-A and maybe more I am forgetting I dunno.And if that's not why you're here and you want a more tightly written story that probably involves these characters or a similar setting, as generic as it sounds and I can hear some people groan and start typing a massive ♥♥♥♥♥ fit about it, play Snoot Game or the original option without the anit-fangame baggage, the I Wani Hug That Gator demo, here on Steam, by the same devs as Snoot Game. Honestly, the story starts off fine and then just kinda speeds up fast by the third act, like the devs desperately want get this over with, despite that, it feels way longer than it actually is with a lot of the tolkien #Relatable dialogue that so many writers nowadays feel the need to just, drop in here and there. Like the devs really didn't want to go on for to long either because they didn't have any confidence they could do a longer more tightly paced story or they were afraid whatever audience they were going for wouldn't have the attention span for it.I also got a problem with the choices or sometimes lack there of, they literally blatantly tell you to your face multiple times in the game with choices going static and graying out "No, no, no, you can only choose this choice and only this choice because ♥♥♥♥ player freedom". Like, if I want to be a complete edgy ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ let me be one, it honestly comes off as smug and pretentious on the developer's part, like they're saying they know better than the player, at least TellTale and even David Cage games let you be a huge dickwad and not care.The rhythm game sections are...just boring. You can literally miss one or two notes and still get a 90% score or higher, its literally just for show. I get it, this is more about the story and such, but so is Night in the Woods, a similar story based game that I can tell influenced this game a bit here and there, except the rhythm game sections in that are an actual challenge and have a proper score system based on how well you do and you don't even need to do well to progress. My point being the challenge should be there for people that want it, I mean hell, they already got accessibility options, just make the mini game as it is now the one of those on by default and let people turn it off for a challenge, can even make achievements for it.The animation, hoo boy, it's kind of a mixed mess. The puppet rigs for the characters freak out often just spazzing for like a second really took out of the story the few times it happened. The lip syncing is, certainly not great, but not horrible either. Honestly despite the start of this paragraph, the animation is fine, it got the job done and from what I hear is leagues better thant whatever the ♥♥♥♥ was going on in the demos and especially the 2020 PS5 Showcase trailer, but I kinda expected less jank from 3 years of work.I overall don't think this game is awful nor do I think it's amazing like I'm sure Twitter addicts are all saying, it's just mid and not that memorable in sea of games just like it and to me that's a far worse fate than being so ♥♥♥♥ it's funny or just plain bad. Still I feel somewhat grateful for it birthing Snoot Game, even it was initially for spiteful means, that game did touch a lot of people emotionally, I know it did for me and it certainly helped advertise this game better than whatever KO-OP was doing for advertising. Truthfully, whatever KO-OP does next I have hope it's better and goes well for them, I can see beyond all the BS and see it's a team that really wants to make great art and I appreciate that, but man this just ain't it.

_childDocuments_.review: First, let's get to what the game does best first. The music, it is phenomenal. In fact, I was disappointed by the amount of times that I actually got to do the song writing and rhythm sections. You get to play about five songs throughout the story and each of them are down right amazing an fun to do. There were so many times when the story got choppy and I wished that I could just have Fang sit down and practice her music instead, but it unfortunately never really went that way.The animation was all around very good as well, there were some hiccups that I saw in the cut scenes, such as Fang having an extra thumb in one of the talks with Naser. But despite the small flaws you can nitpick out, you can really tell there was some love put into this game. Which is why it disheartens me so to write this next part of my review.The story. The main, integral part of this game, felt all over the place and confusing. At the start of the game, you are told that the scene you see is 8 months after the start of the real story. But then it feels so contradicted by the fact that scenes jump from one to the other, with no real sense of timing or pace. During my play-through I really tried to befriend and compromise with each character as best as I could, and yet, there were moments that felt random and disjointed. Some characters would be upset with my actions for no apparent reason, and it felt like scenes were cut from the final game that were necessary to tell the tale in it's entirety. I truly feel this game could have been so much better if the story line was just the slightest bit more sensical.Despite all this, I really did enjoy the game. It was a pleasant story that told the tale of a group of great friends, supporting each other through the toughest of times. And with this, a meteor is coming soon, and we're all going to die. So I'll say to everyone, Goodbye Volcano High.

_childDocuments_.review: Three years in development. Millions grifted from the Canadian government. Multiple delays and the head writer being fired in a huge scandal. The main price of the game being hidden until release date. It is difficult to see how Goodbye Volcano High came into existence, but even more baffling to see how the development team pushed out this deeply flawed, unfun, poorly written title. It is perhaps one of the worst examples of queer fiction in all of media: it should serve as the gold standard on how NOT to create a game, manage a community or run a company.GVH has one of the most troubled development histories of an indie game…ever. The main writer, Kate Gray, wrote an article which she had underage lewd drawings of Harry Potter character Hermoine Granger in it…she did not explain or apologize this until a YEAR after the article was published. Fired from the game, Ko-op had to completely rewrite the story and characters. Why did this require a rewrite? Leave that to your imagination dear reader…the differences were never detailed. Some of her influence still seems to be present though: the game opens with teenagers drinking alcohol (4.0% ABV beer!) on a beach. Other games usually get a Mature rating for this: does GVH get around ESRB ratings because the teenagers are dinosaurs?The development team also went into an immature tailspin when a knockoff game, using the characters likeness, was made in less than a year and featured more story and gameplay. They banned people from entering their Discord and tried to drop a meteor on anyone discussing that fangame. Why? It only amplified people being aware of that game and the awful contents in it. But hey: at least the game is trying to be edgy by having the dinosaurs swear! …which usually gets a game a Mature rating by the ESRB. Did Ko-op lobby the Canadian government to get an exception for this?Visual novels like Validate (Struggling Singles in Your Area Volume 1…we will never see the other volumes due to Dani working on Black Panther and abandoning her game) use the Unity engine to make putting their games on consoles easier. Unfortunately this is one of the worst engines for visual novels: it creates uneven pacing issues, audio glitches/bugs, and prevents players from going back to decisions or skipping dialogue they’ve already seen. This is truly baffling in a story game that wants to give players the illusion of choice…but kneecaps any effort to do so. You want to romance a different dinosaur? Play the game over again. You only have one save file, so make it count…or erase all progress and start a new one. If you decide to pause during the “good” music scenes or button prompts? You cannot click any of the menu buttons or go back to the main menu. You’ll need to wait until the musical number is done before being allowed to close this $30 game…was this used to pad out the length to avoid refunds?Audio: the game’s main menu has no sound or music. At all. Just a completely silent menu with some buttons. This might be OK for a mobile game, but a well financed, Playstation showcased game that took millions to create? Unbelievable as underage talking dinosaurs drinking beer. When performing a song, your input doesn’t matter. At all. You can fail every single note, the main character will still play the same song and sing the same way. Failure isn’t a thing in GVH: the VIBES just seem to be more important than player feedback. If you decide to click when a character is talking? The dialogue cuts out completely and you are treated with watching that character silently mouth the words. Again, this is an issue with Unity and a dev team who didn’t know how to program a game. Want to select your song lyrics? Watch the main character stand there, mouth closed, as that part of the song is sung. When you click the “Done” button, the main character will sing their own version of the song. Your choices or ability to pull of a lyrical miracle do not matter.The developers boast that there’s accessibility options, but there are no descriptions for some of them. What does “Disable resistant choices” mean? No clue: it is not explained, just toggle it on or off. That will be $30 please!It’s extremely heartbreaking to see such a promising title come out as an abysmal failure. If you want good queer games and media: there is an ocean of good titles for you to explore. If you want another Life is Strange: there are better games out there. If you want a good, queer, teen romance game: Butterfly Soup is free. The fact that this is $30 is a travesty: hopefully this is ‘Goodbye Careers’ for the Ko-Op dev team.

_childDocuments_.review: I definitely wanted to give this game the benefit of the doubt. This game always kind of lingered at the back of my mind since it was revealed at the Future of Gaming reveal for the PS5 just from how bizarre it seemed. And then I learned a year later that a group of users on a Bosnian sausage forum made a parody of GVH called Snoot Game, and I absolutely fell in love with the game (it's art style, it's story, it's character, and the messages about empathy encouraged me to better myself) and so because of that, I was somewhat interested in checking out Goodbye Volcano High.However... I was kind of disappointed. I didn't think it was offensively bad as some people tried to say before release but at the risk of sounding like a zoomer, it's very... mid. While the issues in the demo where fixed, there were still a lot that were still there. The sound mixing for dialogue was pretty bad the majority of the time (or dialogue would unnaturally pop in). There was still a lot of bugs with the game (graphical, sound, technical wise, etc) Like for example Borderless Windowed mode will still treat the game as if it was full screen. And I just felt the story and characters fell flat in certain areas. Like for examples none of the characters felt particularly compelling (except for Reed and Trish), Fang felt pretty self-centered, only really caring about their own goals until the very end of the story for being selfish (and even then everyone gives up their final moments for their dream, which makes that growth kind of pointless). And for a story about the apocalypse and the extinction of the dinosaurs, it seems pretty mellow and boring until they shove all conflict in right after the battle of the bands to remind the player of what's happening making it feel rushed. (and don't get me started on the ending).Another issue I had was with the world-building and passage of time. For the former, the world feels very isolated since you aren't really given a clear idea of what the world in GVH is like (or even Caldera Bay), all you know is that there's Caldera Bay (with nothing elaborated on the city, it's history, or different regions), and the other mentioned areas like the vacation Fang's parents are going to feel more like it's trying to be nothing more than a reference than an actual way of expanding the world. As for the passage of time, it's very unclear how much time passes in between the events of the game since it takes place over the course of 8 months (but it feels more like 8 days), between those 8 months society still feels relatively sane for their imminent demise, and not to mention that Fang's parents are going on a 8 month vacation for some reason. The only time it feels like time has passed is after Fang and Trish's argument at Lava Java where you see the school trashed the next day, but even then it's so unclear how many days or months have passed.And the lack of replayability options such as Episode select, or maybe even the ability to fast forward or rewind  makes playing through the game again an absolute slog, especially if this is supposed to be a game where your choices impact the story and characters, that's another issue I had.However, I will give credit where credit is due and saying I thought the soundtrack was pretty good, a lot of the songs were beautiful and well made. The art was also pretty good for the most part, more specifically the background art, some of the character art was hit and miss (some were good, some were bad, and others were meh). And same with the voice acting, I thought Ozioma Akagha, Allegra Clark, and Mark Whitten as Trish, Naomi, and Reed respectively did an incredible job. One scene that stood out in particular was nearing the end of the later two L&L sessions where Reed narrates the dire state of the game's world, and you can see how much of his despair from the imminent apocalypse is carrying over when you hear his voice start to break and become more grim. The rhythm game was a cool part too, although I feel like it was far too easy.Overall, I tried to have an open mind for Goodbye Volcano High due to how much I loved Snoot Game, but I feel a bit let down. However, there were some good qualities of GVH to that I do like.My Score:5/10Pros:ArtMusicVoice Acting (for the most part)Cons:StoryWritingTechnical BugsLack of character growthUnsatisfying conclusion.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this one, but unfortunately this isn't quite for me. One hundred props to you if you liked it, and I can totally see how other people can like it, but it didn't resonate with me at all. A short personal review with some spoilers.-----First of all, I can see that this is a highly competent project, built with pretty solid tech, good art-style and legitimately great music. Don't get me wrong, these folks are experienced gamedevs (coming from gamedev myself), looking closer at their servers and talking with them solidified it even more. However, I can't help but dislike the overall narrative of the game, something that is the most important aspect of a game like this, and I feel this is what tanks it for me...The concept itself is rather interesting, about making amends and realizing your dreams with friends and close ones when apocalypse is nigh on you. But... I can't resonate with these people, you know? Maybe because I was a soggy, depressed turd in my schoolyears, but I really don't like most of these characters. The writing and character dialogues are very irritating and off-putting most of the time and, for lots of times, it's a painfully slow mess (looking at you, LnL). The game never builds enough interesting drama to keep you on your toes (it's a bit more noticeable closer at the end, but not much) and you can spot twists and general plot directions from miles away. It's... boring, you know? And even if you want to just vibe around with characters, I could never force myself to, due to issues mentioned previously. At least for me, keep that in mind.One thing that I don't really get entirely from the marketing... you marketed it initially (shortly after announcements) as a "totally gay story", IIRC. But there's, well... Barely anything about it. There is LGBTQ+ representation, sure, but they are barely explored, it's simply there for representation. And don't get me wrong, that's perfectly fine! I feel this was done elegantly (for the most part) and if you're happy with it then go for it, but this is definitely not a "totally gay story", it doesn't play too much narrative importance to be considered that (even if you decide to date Naomi, but is that necessarily "gay" if Fang is non-binary?). Either way, Fang being non-binary does not play much in the course of the game, maybe besides the moment at the end where Fang's parents are genuinely happy and are proud of them, which was a good moment after the game layd out that there was some friction between them.I can totally see how this would be a pretty good game for a lot of people, but personally for me? I didn't like it enough because of the slow and boring writing. The rest of it is most generally gorgeous and a bliss to my ears.Good luck to your next projects.-----Now onto something that is unrelated to the game and the review itself, but which is pretty dear to me and to the community.All of this is coming from someone who enjoyed Snoot Game quite a bit. You know what I didn't really like about the developments of both of these? That Snoot Game, as a game, came out of incredible passion and love for your project and your characters, and you banned any and all discussions about it, accusing it of harassment of the studio. I get it, 4channers aren't usually the best of the people, far from it, but if you were to only play it for a mere second, you would've understood that you can't get any more respectable and loving than Snoot Game, which actually tackles and explores very serious issues, has great messages about compassion and has a substantially more compelling narrative. And what did you do? You claimed it as a "harassment project", which feels very disingenuous. I guess that's also why you never let me in the discord server for more than half a year for merely mentioning the name, despite being nothing but supportive to you and your work.Dumb haters harrased you, not the creators and certainly not the game. But I guess your producers or community managers, if not most of you, couldn't see past it, and that saddens me immensely. I didn't like such a behavior coming from you of all people, where one of the most important messages in your game is about acceptance, of any and all kinds.This rant is not weighing on my overall decision on Goodbye Volcano High as a game.Once more, thank you and good luck on your next projects. I truly wish the best to you.

_childDocuments_.review: If a 10 kilometer asteroid was going to hit the earth in a few months, how would you change the way you lived your life?That’s the question Goodbye Volcano High explores. The game follows Fang, a senior in high school who is also the lead singer in a rock band. Their goal? To make it big at the local Battle of the Bands and then go touring with their bandmates after graduation.As their luck would have it, however, scientists soon spot a huge asteroid hurtling towards the earth, and there's a good chance of an impact. Predictably, this causes biggest global existential crisis in prehistory. Could life end on Pangea as they know it?This game performed very well on the Steam Deck OLED -- it seemed to run at 90FPS with no hitches, though I did limit it to 60 FPS for 5-hour battery life.Unfortunately, the game had some noticeable bugs throughout. Some of these were minor, but others were more of a nuisance. Here's a list of the ones I noticed, from most severe to least severe:- Some settings were lost every time I restarted the game. For example, I needed to turn colored character names on every time I started the game or it would reset to "off".- Twice, the game stopped detecting button presses on both my PC and steam deck. Restarting the game fixed it for me- Some dialog was auto-skipped without a button press after a word or so which made me reload my save so I could listen to it- Every so often, a character's lips wouldn't move when they were talking- The background glitched out every so oftenGoodbye Volcano High is a great game. It explores many difficult topics -- from trying to become a rockstar while everything is falling apart to growing up LGBTQ+. It also examines diverse character's psychological states during times of crisis. The characters are well written and develop uniquely throughout the game. I found the story to be poignant, thought-provoking, and even triumphant at times.The blend of visual novel and rhythm game added a lot and made the story more impactful. Not to mention the top-tier music that I'll continue to listen to.My chief complaint about this game is that I want *more* of it. The game is rather bite-sized with a 7-hour runtime, but I can't help feeling like it should have been at least 10. There were story beats which felt underdeveloped and could have (*should have*) been explored more thoroughly. The lack of a chapter select, unique save files, and replayable rhythm game sections with customizable difficulty also seem like glaring omissions for a game of this price and caliber.Overall, I recommend this game!**3.6/5: Very Good**

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT: just finished the game, it's very good. I'm going to have to do some replays because like... I gotta see everything this game has to offer!I love this game so far. Love the characters so much, the voice acting does a great job of bringing them to life! The graphics are pretty, beautifully drawn backgrounds, I just... love the vibe of it all. I don't know about anyone else but for me, this game brought back a lot of memories about my own high school experiences. I had two friend groups, the friends who are like the friends Fang has in the game and the friends who were raised on a diet of South Park and Halo.I wish I would have just completely ditched the second friend group and hang out with the friends I had that were weird, fun and supportive. But I didn't because it was a different time, being not-straight meant a lot of possibly bad things... being made fun of/beaten up more at school, parents might disown you, among worse things. If I were to have just been myself back then, I feel like I could have had friends like Fang.In the game, there's not the bigot, South Park/Family Guy quoting "friend" that's "jokes" around with you about how all the stuff you like is gay/stupid such as Pokemon and Final Fantasy. But that makes it better imo. I like this group of friends because they feel genuine with each other. The writing does a good job of capturing this.Anyway, the gameplay is the usual point and click VN stuff. There's rhythm game sections which I suck at. But there's an option to make the timing on those games easier which is great. They do some cool stuff with the UI where you can tell some choices are *really* important because you need to hold both shift buttons while selecting it. There's choices that are a bit wobbly or sometimes the box they're in is wobbly or shiny (what that means, not sure yet exactly), sometimes they change if you wait to long or "test press" the options to see whether the choice has some huge weight to it. I feel like the choices you're given do a great job expressing the kind of character you play as. You're Fang. They're an awkward teenager, it's their senior year of high school. They want their band to take off, they want to live a life as a musician with their friends. But everyone is kind struggling with the typical things that come with the last year of high school. Then, of course, there's the meteor coming. The last time a giant rock about the hit the planet had this much plot weight to it was Final Fantasy 7 on the ps1!I'm stopping here because I'll keep going on about the characters otherwise... so, sure, your mileage may vary but just after a few hours of playing, this game has something special going on. I'd recommend it someone who's interested in a cozy VN with some high stakes or anyone who's a furry (or both).

_childDocuments_.review: In short, it's fine. The story is all right, the music and art are great, and the mechanics are good. But, and this is incredibly unfortunate, there were so many points throughout the experience that took me out of it that I can't recommend the game in its current state.I can't critique it from a narrative standpoint because I'm not good at it, but it felt okay overall. There weren't any parts I was particularly annoyed about or disliked, and there were multiple personally touching moments.One of the big positives I saw in it was the discussion of LGBTQ+ issues, specifically how families of those identifying as such deal with it. Most games I've seen in this genre(?) don't tackle these topics, and it's a shame.The only massive issue I had with the whole story was all the choices. They don't feel like they make any profound impact; the overall plot still goes over beats that feel contradicting to your actions. Even though we're only directing someone's actions, I felt significantly more out of control than other games with player choices that impact the story. At points, I felt like what was presented didn't have to be interactive.The dialogue selections work great, especially with the way different options occasionally have extra thematic highlighting or require additional confirmation. The band performance mechanic was executed fantastically! It feels far less demanding than in , while still offering enough of a challenge that I had to focus during these sections.Other game UI elements worked alright, despite some minor gripes with the navigation in the pause menu. The only feature I still don't fully understand is the Affinity graph, which doesn't appear to update after choices are made and honestly feels like it has a mind of its own.The music was amazing, plain and simple! I expected it to be outstanding, and it definitely delivered, even going above and beyond, in my opinion. Several songs stood out enough to where I'll very likely give them another listen outside of the game.The sound could use some work. The VAs did a great job, and the audio levels were good, too, but the mixing between dialogue and game audio was very distracting. Practically every other sentence, the conversation would get cut off near the end, and every loading screen or scene transition was accompanied by a click as the audio inevitably got interrupted by something else in the game. This issue even happened to the music a few times, which was unfortunate.Unfortunately, the artwork took me out of the experience the most. Don't get me wrong, it's well-drawn, the character designs look great, and the backgrounds work fantastically. But there were so many technical issues with displaying this artwork that I couldn't stay engrossed. There were the small things like backgrounds loading in slower than the characters, resulting in a very perceivable flicker, or characters having small seams of oddly-colored pixels around areas of their face that animated in a scene (eyes, mouth, etc.). But there were also serious errors, like a scene with the characters facing the wrong way (which I still don't understand how that would be possible with 2D sprites) or getting cut off at the bottom, revealing the backgrounds. The most egregious issue was the many scenes featuring multiple characters where characters who weren't animated for speech stood completely motionless like cardboard cutouts. Even something as simple as them blinking or slightly swaying in place would have been a perfectly good solution. The strange thing is that the sprites were animated this way during the  L&L segments.I had an okay time. There were parts of the story that touched me and those that I felt too disconnected from; I bopped to pretty much every track, and I loved the design of the environment, characters, and overall setting. But, the technical and story impact issues impacted my enjoyment and immersion enough to where I can't really recommend this game, at least not at this price.Hopefully, some of the problems will be patched out in the future. But for now, I would only pick this game up if it's 50 or more % off.

_childDocuments_.review: Disclaimer: I work on the Vidya Gaem Awards, whose voting source is 4chan, and awarded "Goodbye Volcano High" the Most Pretentious Game award for 2023. I also have limited connections to Cavemanon: they made Snoot Game, and submitted a trailer for I Wani Hug That Gator to our 2021 show.The staff of Cavemanon do not work on our show, and none of the Vidya Gaem Awards staff work on their projects either. This review below is my own personal opinion on Goodbye Volcano High, and is not the opinion of anyone else.___Goodbye Volcano High tackles love, identity, and the emotional turmoil of adolescence through a looming specter of doom. The protagonist Fang and her best friends, who make up the band Worm Drama (Trish/Reed), serve as the backing track throughout the story.Unlike the past winner of "Most Pretentious" (We Are OFK), Goodbye Volcano High earns its visual novel tag. While its rhythm games are similarly inconsequential to OFK, the rare opportunities to customize and the emotive dialogue choices lend a relatively greater autonomy for the player to express themselves.The game fleshes out its world and characters through a variety of techniques, such as unvoiced comics in the pause menu, snapshot memories, and Dungeons and Dragons sessions. You get a feel for all the characters and what they're about. Their personalities, their passions, and their social proximity to Fang.However, because Fang's moral support system is demonstrably rock solid, not much can go wrong. You can completely flunk all performances and no one will act much differently than if you aced them. However, it's not absolute apathy - although GVH ultimately ends one way, your playthrough experience will differ based on your dialog options, and obviously some paths are more fulfilling than others.The game throws in a clever nod to Cavemanon with the Swamp Babies band—a thinly veiled metaphor for Snoot Game. Each 'Swamp Baby' is color-coded to serve as a masculine-presenting punk-rock rival to Reed, Trish, and Fang. After all, LJ "found them" first, and they're "good, but not like 'good' good". The whole thing is cheeky as hell, but just as  Snoot Game's devs showed up for the release of the game and gave it the respect of a full run.For the purposes of contextualizing GVH's win for the Most Pretentious Indie award, I played through Goodbye Volcano High first, and then followed it up by playing Snoot Game. It was the most fun I had in years. While Snoot Game wouldn't have possible without Goodbye Volcano High existing, the fanwork clearly served as its own inspiration. It buoyed interest in the original, and set a high bar for KO-OP to match. Still, I feel a certain degree of sadness for the team that, in the pursuit of "taking the high road", waged a multi-faceted war on the parody and lost up to 60% of its audience as a result. Getting banned for sharing, honestly, that Snoot Game was how I found Goodbye Volcano High only serves to remind me that KO-OP views with contempt people who enjoy the "forbidden fruit", and furthers a cycle of victimization and resentment for the other side.Turn the other cheek, and play the game anyways.I hope my $30 serves as encouragement for the creation of future works that are impactful and inspiring, without the unnecessary drama that plagued this one.

_childDocuments_.review: I'ma keep it a buck, ts is not good. I'll admit, I got this game after playing Snoot Game + IWHTG and being a part of that general community, but this game actually went BELOW my already low expectations. I have many gripes with the game, and I'll go over a few of them. Dialogue selections where they force you to pick a certain option...what the ♥♥♥♥ is the point? I understand the concept or what they were going for,  but it makes my choices feel useless (which they are anyways because the game has one ending no matter what you do) and they should've just done that stuff in a cutscene. And if I wanna pick a rude dialogue option, I should be able to? This is supposed to be a choose your own story thing, yet you can't actually affect anything other than how close you get with certain people. Speaking of those people, THEY'RE UNBEARABLE! These characters just feel like they were made to fill out the most generic, quirky, LGBTQIA+ archetypes. The only characters that felt like ACTUAL people in this were Reed, Rosa, and Fang themself, and some of them have really questionable moments. For example, Fang willingly talking to some random number claiming to be their fan AND meeting them after their show??? Trish BORDERS on feeling like a real person sometimes, which is nice since she has quite a bit of dialogue, but point is the characters could've been better. I do want to stop and give credit where it's due, because this game legit has amazing music. Songs are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ killer, 100%. Great work there, along with the actual rythm sections of gameplay. However, the music does not save this game from it's most horrid flaws, and what was easily some of my least favorite parts: L&L. Apart from the last L&L with Reed's really depressing ending, all the other sections were just padding to the game. It was actually agony to play through, and it felt so slow. Also, locking achievements behind Nat 20's and Nat 1's? Really? Considering you can't do pack to specific sections of the game, you'd have to replay the whole game to get back to those parts and THEN reset if you don't get the rolls. Actually outlandish. The final problem I'll talk about is character designs. For the most part, they're actually pretty good, but just some certain nitpicks I have. Why tf does Stella (love her despite her being one of those quirky archetype characters tbh) not wear shoes? It just feels really random. Naser's weird cheeto puff fingers, but more importantly his messed up wing?? From what I've seen and heard, the game gives no explanation for his wing being that way. I'd say birth defect, but it's also covered in scars? The game has an achievement for getting all the Naser content, but they never explain that. I was avoiding directly comparing this game to Snoot Game, but Snoot Game actually has a reason as to why Naser's wing is like that and it's actually important to his relationship with Fang. It feels like GVH missed the chance to do something similar here, but in a different kind of way. And with Naser's wing being like that, it sort of ties into my earlier point of them seemingly having a checklist of quirks and archetypes of characters they needed to have, and Naser filled out the role of being disabled. Anyway's, this game has great music and a decent rythm section, but overall I just can't recommend it, especially with a $30 price tag.

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr: A game with some positives but has noticeable issues that take away from the overall experience.  I prefer its free parody called "Snoot Game."I want to like this game. But given the price and the issues I noticed I just don't think I can recommend it. It does have a unique artstyle that is quite interesting (not a furry, I promise). The voice acting is decent. And it's got some fun quirks to it like a certain character's obsession with a velvet worm. Never thought I'd see that fascinating creature represented in a game!However, I found myself looking for missing features present in other visual novel type games. And the pacing is like a roller coaster; starting out slow, fast, then slow near the end. Also, I didn't feel like my choices mattered that much besides maybe one moment near the end. Most of the fun I had from playing was really from seeing how GVH compared with Snoot Game. I found myself missing Anon and his adventures living in a wacky dino world. Or great side characters like Moe! How can this game not have Moe?? At least Trish isn't a monster in this game.But anyways, yeah. I give this game a 5.5/10. It's an interesting concept and I'm glad it exists as a concept, but I think could've been better. The best thing I can say about this game is that it introduced me to Snoot Game. Give it a shot. It's free!

_childDocuments_.review: Remember the golden era of high school movies and TV shows? These were more than just shows; they were a defining part of growing up. But what made them truly special was their use of music as a narrative tool, capturing the essence of teenage life like nothing else. Goodbye Volcano High, a unique blend of visual novel, rhythm game, and interactive animated movie, takes this magical high school vibe and weaves it into a coming-of-age story that's impossible to experience in any other medium.High school memories are often tied to sensory cues - the scent of a particular cologne or the way the sunlight hits your street in the evening. But more than anything, it's the music. A catchy riff, a vocal hook, a melody - these are the soundtracks to our youth. Goodbye Volcano High harnesses this unspoken connection between music and teenhood. It immerses you in a world filled with exquisitely catchy power-pop, crafting a compelling tale that combines the ordinary struggles of dinosaur teens with an impending and inescapable catastrophe.The story revolves around Fang, a student at Volcano High, who's about to embark on their senior year. Fang's summer has been far from ordinary, filled with personal challenges and self-discovery. They've also been working on music for their band, Worm Drama, dreaming of a tour after graduation. However, life has different plans for Fang. Their bandmates have different aspirations, and Fang's path to becoming a musician is fraught with obstacles. These personal struggles are compounded by a looming disaster, echoing the unfortunate fate of the dinosaurs.Gameplay in Goodbye Volcano High involves dialogue-based choices that lead to various narrative paths and rhythm game sections that truly come alive with a controller. Fang's return to school requires them to rebuild relationships with their friends, including a mysterious admirer who communicates anonymously via text messages.The game's true triumph lies in its simplicity. Goodbye Volcano High offers an intimate glimpse into the lives of its characters, moving beyond one-dimensional teen stereotypes. It beautifully captures the essence of high school, showcasing the dynamics between different personalities without relying on overused cliches. The conflicts in the story feel genuine and personal, steering clear of the typical dramatic plot points.The music in Goodbye Volcano High is not just a background element; it's an integral part of the experience. Fang's journey as a songwriter is intertwined with their struggle to navigate the challenges of their senior year. The songs are masterfully composed, and tracks like "12 o'clock" and "Pretty Heroes" resonate deeply, evoking raw emotions and creating a truly memorable gaming experience.Goodbye Volcano High reminds us of the unyielding spirit of youth, the determination to live life on our terms, and the pursuit of our dreams in the face of adversity. It breaks free from the conventions of high school narratives, offering a genuine and heartfelt exploration of teenage life.In conclusion, Goodbye Volcano High is not just a game; it's an emotional journey through the complexities of teenhood, accompanied by an unforgettable soundtrack. It allows us to relive the high school experience without the burden of adult perspectives, making it a truly remarkable and touching gaming experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Goodbye Volcano High has been an up and down battle for me to regain my sanity because the visuals and personalities of each and every character do not always work well together, while also boasting the ability to make a choice in dialogue that will affect the story, but in reality forces you to choose something "nice" rather than "mean" because you have no choice.I'd want to mention that I am not a person who is drawn to drama or social media; I have no dislike or over-affection for most things; instead, I am impartial and honest in my opinions. I really don't care about the Snoot Game or the I Wani to Hug That Gator drama, because you know why? I would never have altered my review about this game or returned to it if it hadn't been for the tremendous impact those two games had on my life, particularly the so-called 4chan hate game, which many claim to be anti-LGBTQ+. When Snoot Games' main character initially appears, he acts like that, but man, you wouldn't believe what the game has to offer. The information that people spread like wildfire through social media is simply awful and better off ignored for your own viewing eyes. While each game was controversial in various scenarios, they were all amazing in their own unique way. You will spend the most of your time staring at characters from various angles as they speak and tell the story, primarily from the side facing view, which just does not function well. It's good if you stare at them straight on! However, any pterodactyl displayed, or anyone with a avian snoot, the proportions and aspect ratio they are attempting to achieve do not resemble 2D or 3D. It's just awkward, if you understand what I mean by looking at most of the previews or my video review which does have spoilers. I had more fun with the L&L sessions for a variety of reasons. First and foremost, Reed and whoever did the writing for that portion of the game were fantastic, with excellent use of voice acting and immersive story telling, as well as an art approach that focused on one character at a time rather than many at once, making everyone appear good and fleshed-out. The story is dull, with no feeling of structure or true agency, and while I liked a few characters, particularly the stoner girl she unfortunately is just some back up character with no reason to be voice acted or animated, it's as if the game feels very unfinished because of their writing issues they had when the lead writer quit I hated almost everyone in the core group of friends, particularly because I couldn't interact with them outside of the primary protagonist Fang, who acts self-centred and only caring about her self until the later portions of the game.If you are like me, you will originally hate this game at first because it didn't feel complete and was overly chaotic. Trust me, you are not alone because it is simply just that. Voices do not match lip sync, frames overlay on top of one another, making transitions feel clumsy, and many other issues arise as you continue to rise and fall with your attention to the game as a whole. Why did I alter my review from negative to positive? It's simply due to Snoot game. Sounds surprising, but as I already indicated, many people are mistaken; without this game, those (2) games would not have been born from the parody and genuine story, and therefore I would not have come here to rate it positive it for being created. It was simply "ok."

_childDocuments_.review: Goodbye Volcano High is a gameIn fact it's a pretty ok game. I have had my eye on it for a minute, and I went in with rock bottom expectations, and it surprised me by being actually competently written, with characters who have basic emotions and motivations. A rarity in visual novels from what I've seen.My problems with the game stem from it's content. It is about 5 and a half, 6 hours to slam through the whole game and in that time you will see everything the game has to offer, all the content. You will maybe miss 2 cutscenes if you're going out of your way to be a ♥♥♥♥ to the other characters. Even within those 6 hours too you'll start to see the rough edges of the game.Character models snapping hard between animations, lips not even remotely synched to the speak, whole bridge sections between chapters going entirely unvoiced, subtitles not lining up wit voice lines, the whole shebang. I was genuinely shocked considering this game had multiple delays, and had studio backing from Sony, how barebones it feels.even a lot of the story elements feel lacking. There's also little screen time for any of the side cast. Anyone who isn't vital to the story are seen in 1 frame pngs, a single time. And characters who are secondary to the story barely get any screen time at all. Including the main character's love interest, who comes across as something of a creep at first.This review has been fairly negative but I want to stress I did like the game. If it seems like the kind of game you would play from the marketing, you will prolly enjoy this game. I just wouldn't recommend it at this price point, it has barely anything going on aside from the music which is genuinely good, and the presence of voice acting, at all.

_childDocuments_.review: I wish Steam had a 1-10 scale for rating, because if it did I'd give it a 5/10It's not bad, it's clearly well made and it has very pretty visuals. But a lot of the voice acting is a little stilted and some of the dialogue options don't give you as many options as you'd hope (by literally showing you the option, but then blocking you from using it).Some story moments we genuinely very good. But most of the game feels a bit aimless in what it wants to do. The meteor flip flops between having too much importance or no importance at all, the game is technically divided into episodes but you don't have an episode selection option, nor multiple save files (Which I believe was a BIG mistep with the type of game it is.Also not being able to fail the musical sections does make it feel like they're just filler (despite being fun, were more fun when I thought you had to flick to hit the notes, rather than just point to them, but a hard mode or a free mode for the songs would actually be a fun extra).By far the worst part of this game is the DnD knock off they play in universe called L&L. It horrible that it literally interrupts two big story moments in the story to meander into some generic fantasy universe that couldn't be any less interesting. And while it tries to make a metaphor for the story in the game, it really just feels like an excuse to not have to animate any characters, or record more voice acting. The LnL sections drag the pacing to a complete halt, and takes you away from the actual character moments which, again, in two cases, get INTERRUPTED by it. You could remove these scenes from the game and end up with 95% the same experience but maybe and hour and a half less play time, if any part of the game feels like filler, it's this. The short runtime of about 5-6 hours is actually not that bad, every episode has quite a bit of original animation interspersed among the reused default animations (which are good, for what they are). I believe actually separating these sections into clear episodes, would also greatly help in pacing the game better, I ended up playing it all in one go because I didn't know where an episode ended and where another one started. In truth, the short runtime might be a blessing in disguise.If you don't like the trailers, you won't like the game, that's just the simple truth, it's not a game made for everyone, and some of the characters *cough* sage *cough* can be a little too annoying if you have a limit for overly enthusiastic characters.Music is good! Better than I expected! But different from what the game would make you believe their band plays from the song titles. You have songs called "Puke factory" and "Rabies babies" which end up being very soft pop rock tunes, and not the type of energetic trash rock you'd expect from them.Again, just wish your performance in the rhythm sections actually meant anything and affected the story. (although I have only done one playthrough, I'll play it again and fail everything to see if it makes a difference).If it weren't for the LnL sections, I could maybe shakily recommend it to people with a 6.5 rating, but those sections are genuinely so awful I can't get past the mediocre 5/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Goodbye Volcano High is a charming game that follows a group of teenagers in their (quite literally) final year of high school. At its most basic level, it's a game that's about young adult relationships and the resilience of youth in the face of adversity and great inevitable change. A lot of the game deals with feelings of existentialism and the futility of life, ideas that often fill the minds of teens. Goodbye Volcano High encompasses those times when life was more free- when everything had more colour and before society taught us to value material and goals over people.If you aren't comfortable with LGBTQ+ people and the community as a whole, you might not like the main cast. Just about everyone is LGBTQ+ in some way. I, personally, think that's awesome. However, seeing as how the gaming community tends to feel anything remotely out of the norm of hetero-norm, I can definitely see it upsetting some people.The soundtrack is amazing and worth a listen even if you don't want to play the game. The devs really nailed it with the music. I was excited throughout the entire game to get to the next singing part. However, I feel like the rhythm part of the game kind of betrayed itself. I'll admit that I'm not a huge fan of rhythm games (I'm terrible at them) but I felt pushed to play it anyways. Hyperfocusing on the rhythm minigame kind of takes away from the imagery and song. I found myself having to relisten to the song I literally just performed to appreciate the lyrics, since I was too heavily focused on the minigame. Especially at the last performance of the game, I really wanted to appreciate the visuals as well but the focus on the minigame took me away from that.The story is a real tear jerker but is bitter-sweet. It's kind of doomed from the start if you understand the game's premise. It may leave you feeling unfulfilled since we are conditioned to expect good endings, but I think that's the beauty of it. In a lot of European cinema, good endings aren't always a given. I think in American cinema especially, any time we don't get a good ending a lot of people write it off as unfulfilling and anticlimactic. But I think Goodbye Volcano High handled its ending exceptionally well. A part of the game that kind of dragged was the L&L scenes for me, personally. I didn't feel like they added a lot to the story but they definitely reminded me of when I allowed myself to geek our in highschool. Those scenes were very wholesome parts of the game, if nothing more.I think the price is a bit steep for a visual novel, even though it is really pretty. No matter what way you slice it, 5-6 hours of gameplay is hard to justify a 30$ price tag. The game was excellent, but the price is a bit too steep. Overall, I would give the game a 4/5. If the price was lower, I think this visual novel would have been a complete masterpiece. A bit of the pacing could have been adjusted a bit to make the game a bit smoother but overall, it was a simply wonderful experience. I don't regret paying full price for it, but I do think they devs could have settled on a bit less.

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game. It has an extremely relatable story, wonderful music, amusing and dramatic characters, and on top of this, a cinematic-like experience. Plus, the interface is not properly optimized for PC and frustrates a bit.Overall, I am extremely pleased with the game and would highly recommend it to anyone who enjoys cinematic story-driven games with little gameplay. It's a very relaxing and emotional experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Someone told me to give this game a fair shake before I call it trash, so here is my fair shake after 7 hours.GAMEPLAY-Player Agency	The game plays like a VN, but the choices barely mean anything aside from additional content that adds nothing to the one single ending. There are many times when options presented get grayed out, despite the game saying at the start	"Your choices matter". Especially since there is only one ending, do these choices really matter at all? I get that may be part of the story, but I'll save that for the story topic. The rhythm game sections have this illusion of feeling necessary until you realize you can just put the controller down and just watch as the game hands you a victory. Really? No fail condition? And the affinity system didn't provide much insight into the characters.-Control Feel	The controls felt pretty standard. Menu navigation was swift, which I liked. And the selection of options did feel a little engaging when some requires additional button prompts to select. Then the rhythm game prompts did feel pretty nice in how it was meant to play. The prompts seemed pretty synced up to the music. But that's where my praise ends. -Misc others [GUI, Menu, settings, game tools, save files, etc.]	For a VN that promotes its "choices matter" warning, there is a lack of save states to go back to and see alternative options. You messed up? Gotta play from the beginning. Hell, you skipped dialogue and wanna see what was said before? Sucks to be you, there's no history to look back on. I saw in the settings an option to slow down timed prompts, which felt unnecessary since those prompts (especially in rhythm games) achieve little to affect the entire game. Also the most entertaining thing I have experience was crashing the game.ARTS-Visual	It was fine for the most part. Though a couple things that bugged me was how stiff some animations looked, and how lacking the lip-sync was. I mean I get it, can't exactly depict anthro dinos talking in a realistic way if said talking isn't realistic at all. But the talking animations were choppy. And also I noticed some mouth details like little "horns" on the lips(?) would disappear when a character was talking for when the mouths opened. Which disappointed me. I don't remember a whole lot from the scenery, since there was a lot of indoor scenes regardless. Some character designs I didn't like, but didn't hate. I felt nothing about it. Other times... you don't wanna see Fang when they're front facing. lol-Auditory	The music (when present) was actually fairly good. I think that was the main focus on this game here. The tracks were emotional and engaging, and the only things I truly remember from the game. That counts as a positive and a negative point. Some of the voices sounded pretty bored, or like they were half-acting when reading from a script. Other voices sounded like they had to do the direction themselves as a result of lacking voice direction. I am not saying all the VAs or even some of the VAs in the game were terrible at their job. That fault lies with the voice direction, which I assume was pretty lax. Sometimes I wish there was more music in scenes. There were quite a few scenes of silence in a game with music as one of its focuses.STORY	Meh. I mean I get it, teenagers are dramatic dudes. But when drama happens, it felt like it just comes from nowhere, no build up. No signs of it. Specifically the whole "battle of the bands" took place and Trish just let out shouts, I didn't feel anything about it. I had thought that maybe it was because I didn't focus affinity for Trish. I thought "oh ♥♥♥♥ consequences for my actions?" Nope. That drama happens regardless if you pay attention to Trish or not. Then there was that whole campfire scene that also felt pretty unrealistic. Out of nowhere, only for shock value. Again, I know. "Teenagers". Besides those two, there wasn't a whole lot even happening. Fang spent most of their time standing in a room and talking to their friends. A lot of scenes were just standing around talking. When the story ended, I felt nothing. Absolutely nothing. Also the "L&L" segments in the game? Lame. I know why it was in, so that the friend group had a better mindset tackling the meteor coming for them. L&L seemed like a waste of time to pad out time, and to put characters in a situation where their actions have "consequences" but for some reason you can't do that in the actual game.-Characters	I felt nothing for the characters. Fang, nothing. Didn't really get attached to them or their passion as I saw only victory and not struggle. Not saying all characters need to struggle to be good, but Fang lacked something to make me really feel like they're a real character. I got annoyed at Trish talking non-stop about worm ♥♥♥♥. Reed went from being cool to being a ♥♥♥♥ with how he just kept reminding people "ay yo we're gonna ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ die" at nearly every meet up. Naomi, Sage, Stella, and Rosa were incredibly forgettable. Those characters just didn't move me at all. Their actions felt shallow, and their drama was resolved as quickly as it came up.-Setting	Volcano High, Caldera, a garage, the beach, and other places. It felt a little... empty to be honest. Aside from the Battle of the Bands venue, these locations really felt like you could swap them out for one another and the scenes wouldn't change much. Because they weren't involved with the plot enough. They were just places to put characters in so they're not talking in a blank void, where they might as well be talking anyway.-Conflicts/Events	Oh no the meteor is going to kill us all. Oh no the band. Not the band.	Nothing might as well be my word of the day because ♥♥♥♥ man, I didn't CARE. Mentioned before, the drama at the place I already forgot the name of and the beach lacked any build up. They also lacked consequences, because oh suddenly after Fang and Trish fought, it didn't matter because they still all attended Reed's Lame Ass DND Sesh. Oh also, before Reed's LADS, he pretty much said "no dnd cuz meteor" then he did do dnd, and for some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ reason he felt the need to go all "okay now here's a depiction of a meteor shower and it's all hellfire and rain and" Reed shut the ♥♥♥♥ up stop doomposting. To sum it up, the conflicts were either frustrating (in a bad way), meaningless, or just absurd.PRICE WORTH-"Dollar per hour" measure (Typically "1$ ≤ 1hr gameplay" to 'justify' the cost)	One regular playthrough took me 7.6 hours. I spent 30 dollars on this game to find out I only beat it in a 1/4 of that number in hours. The dollar per hour thing may not be everyone's focus in a review, but it is mine. And I say this game is terrible for its asking price. In my personal experience, I've tried to get ample playtime from games I spent money out of. Bought the most expensive Like a Dragon Infinite Wealth thing, got more than 100 hours on a save file. Bought Ace Attorney, got more than the price number. And well, bought I Wani Hug That Gator... you can figure what I got.-Production Value	KO_OP had 1.2 million dollars from the Canadian government, generous amount of time through development hell, support from fans that didn't like 4chan's anti-fan game, some rewrites IIRC. And what did I get?Disappointment.My score is a 3/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Goodbye Volcano High is... god.  what to even say to sum up Goodbye Volcano High.This is a game about dealing with the end.  It's a coming of age story set when there's no age to come to.  Everyone is dinosaurs and other prehistoric reptiles, because this is set just before the K-T impact, 65 million years ago.  An asteroid is approaching, and over the course of this visual novel, the people of this world slowly come to realize that they're ultimately doomed, and have to make the best of what time they have left.What do you do when the world is coming apart around you, when long-held plans are shattered and broken because you know, you don't just suspect but you KNOW, that you and everyone you know and love will be dead and gone within the year?  This is a game about missed chances, about regret, about grief.  About coming to terms with mortality, and doing the best you can with what limited time you have left, to find yourself, to do what you've always wanted at long last, and to be kind to the people around you, lest you drive them away without the time to repair what was broken.Also it has genuinely one of the most clever and enjoyable rhythm game mechanics I've seen?  Seriously, KO-OP, spin this out into its own full game, I love them so much.  There's plenty of room to build this out into something complex and skill-intensive and I love it.

_childDocuments_.review: I was given this game as a gift, with the express purpose of playing it to laugh at it. From the word go, it's incredibly clear that this is one of those games that's clearly not for me. I'm not a furry, I'm not a member of the LGBT, I'm not into this lo-fi emotional rock music, I'm not into all the interpersonal high school girl drama. Most of my friends don't fit this category either. I think most of us expected the worse, given the reputation of this game's rocky development, and it's shadow being cast by a parody game that beat them to release. That's all I really knew going in.What I was met with was a fine story with characters that the creators truly cared deeply for. The tiny minute intricacies that only someone deep within their own writer sauce would care about. They're not all details I particularly care about, but they help these characters feel grounded within their paleontological world. A major section of this game is the group playing a DnD game, and it really captures the feel of playing the game while encapsulating it with the themes of the Goodbye Volcano High as a whole. It's where I liked the game the most, and wished the game was just this. It was charming. I could sit here and go into detail about the sometimes rough transitions of these animated scenes switching on the fly, the mouth flaps going out of sync, the memes that'll surely date the game in a few years, the climax of the plot feeling rather forced with my playthrough, motivations not quite lining up with all the possible choices they've laid out, etc. But doing so would be pointless. For what it is, Goodbye Volcano High is a game not for me, but I could see this impacting someone who relates to these characters much more. I can't necessarily recommend it, but I can't, and I refuse, to hate the passion put into this game. Someone cared, even if I didn't.

_childDocuments_.review: There's definitely worse cinematic CYOA narrative adventures out there, but Goodbye Volcano High is rough in every area where it counts, and in a lot of areas where making fun of it is just petty. Like, the audio production. The actual voice acting is great, but EQ is a mess across the board; Reed's mic is way too hot. And many games use low-res models to save on performance when characters are far from the camera, but GVH has the worst implementation of this I have ever seen. How does a 2D version of a Telltale game have LOD problems?But big picture, the pacing is unbearable, the overall concept is cool but takes far too long to get to the point, the teen drama is at once uninteresting yet frustrating and unbelievable, and it all just feels a bit half-baked. The game is meant to take place over about nine months, but time progression is inconsistent and left me feeling like the CYOA aspect was broken with how many scenes were repeated, or referenced at the "wrong" times. While Fang had great potential to be an interesting and relatable character, the moments where this is true are fleeting and incongruous. Seeing them grapple with following their dreams at the end of the world is occasionally touching, but seeing them drag their friends down with them, with no input from the player, is maddening. Seeing them deal with clothing dysphoria or coming out to their parents is stark and hits right in the gut, but it doesn't feel as honest when their talking voice is rough and always changing, while their singing voice is crystal clear and perfectly controlled, and it's just a bummer this theme feels a bit surface level, because by the end, I just kind of hated Fang.I suppose that sums up my feelings. Volcano High ticks a lot of my boxes on paper; it's queer, it's music-based, it has a distinct look, the CYOA stuff is winding and byzantine, it's sorrowful and morose as it touches on contemporary issues. But on all these fronts, it feels amateur, and not in an endearing way. It's easy to point at the botched, contentious production and blame all the technical idiosyncrasies and general glitchiness on that, but the story and storytelling being as bland and flat as they are points to a bigger direction problem. Even at six hours, it feels flabby and bloated.

_childDocuments_.review: mixed opinions.  When I originally played this game, while my opinion on it wasn't exactly shining, I thought it was an altogether well-done experience, albeit one with some noteworthy kinks. However, after replaying it several more times in order to get 100% achievements over the course of the following month or so, and then giving myself much more time to mull over it some more, its narrative issues  started to pop out to me.  While the characters are enjoyable, with them especially lifted up by their good vocal performances and believable writing for them, and there's just enough meat on the game's bones to feasibly say that it's a complete experience, the narrative as a whole is incredibly disjointed. There were multiple points throughout the game where I felt like I was suddenly dropped into a completely different version of the story: character relationships felt different out of the blue (Fang and Rosa have an arguably contrived one-sided rivalry that only rears its head when the game wants to drive the point home that there's a rift between Fang and Trish, and they're otherwise friendly with each other by midway through Episode 4; and in Episode 7 everyone meets up at a hangout spot that has a nickname despite it never being seen before, and with newcomer Naser being pals with the rest of the friend group despite being otherwise isolated from them before Episode 6); the timeline and pacing was all over the place (the entirety of Episode 3 is structured like it takes place only shortly after Episode 2, when in actuality there's a multi-month timeskip between them); and events and scenes that you would think would get more development, either for being hallmarks of teenage dramas or because of their relevancy to the game's plot, just get kind of glossed over inexplicably (everything to do with Fang's parents despite them being the main source of external pressure against Fang's ambitions (and personal identity), and all the montage moments in the final performance bit in Episode 8 that feel like fun slice-of-life scenes that had gotten binned in varying stages of development). It feels like there were three or four drafts that were chopped up and then stitched together into the game that I ended up playing. It's not an absolute mess despite this, and the flow of events is at least reasonable enough on the surface (barring a couple of bits, chief among these being how it drives the wedge between Fang and Trish after Battle of the Bands, in which the core drama of said wedge is ostensibly hashed out in the episode before, which was then immediately forgotten afterwards for the sake of the scene), but the game does have its fill of headscratchers all the same.  Really, the game sits in this ugly middle ground where it's simultaneously too long to be a concise, focused story,  too short to really dig in and explore its cast and get you immersed in them. However, making the game any shorter would make its $30 price a very big ask, while any longer was evidently not feasible from a production standpoint. For its part, the game feels like it wants to be longer and explore its characters and their shared history, but never ends up doing so outside of a choice few moments scattered throughout the game, and instead is forced to work them into the plot that it's trying to tell wherever it can. As a result of this, Fang, Naomi, and Trish are the only characters that get substantial development throughout the game, largely because they're the most relevant to main plot by being the main character, the , and the deuteragonist/primary source of conflict with Fang respectively. Everyone else (in descending order of plot relevance and thus content: Reed, Naser, Rosa, Sage, and finally Stella) is sidelined to varying degrees. You get nuggets and pieces of their personal lives, and semblances of character arcs, but never anything that feels complete or especially satisfying with them.  The apparent compromise for this was the  sections, which tries to be an alternate way of exploring (a majority of) the characters and their personalities through the lens of an in-universe  campaign versus more expensive and expansive scenes, which even comes with a fun downer ending that ties in nicely with the game's angsty tones during the final third of the game. For the most part, though, the writing during them was so dry that it ended up feeling like an uninteresting sideshow that long overstays its welcome, especially when you consider the fact that it takes up at least  of the game's six hour runtime across three sessions. Ironically, these scenes did such a good job selling the point that it was just a dumb tabletop game among the characters that I was constantly going "can we just get back to the not vapid stuff?" while I was mashing through dialogue on all of my repeated playthroughs -- and got close to doing so on the first as well. There's a couple chuckles to be found in them, to be fair, but for the most part they feel like poor substitutes for the character moments I really wanted and the game has in too scant quantities.  I've glossed over the fact that there's extensive branching dialogue which lets you shape Fang's behavior, and an entire system measuring Fang's sense of closeness to other characters, referred to as "affinity". However, all of the game's reactions to these choices are almost entirely clustered in the first half of the game, and after Episode Five, dialogue options become both scant and generally insignificant. Even during that first half where they're a more significant factor, these branching choices mostly exist to  character relationships, and how you choose to interpret Fang (e.g. you can have Fang be significantly more hostile to Rosa and Naser, and you can have Fang be in much heavier denial of Trish wanting to distance herself from the band), rather than  them, per se, and otherwise they simply change who you get affinity points with. Speaking of affinity, only two major moments (one with Trish in Episode Eight, and one with Naomi in Episode Five) are unlocked by getting enough affinity. Otherwise, it's only used for unlocking a portion of in-game "photo" collectibles; six "flashbacks", short comic book-esque sequences that give a bit more backstory for characters; and on some occasions to check for access to optional "wedge" one-on-one scenes, of which each character gets one throughout the game (barring Trish as mentioned earlier, who gets two; Naomi's second, however, is woven into the pre-show scene that it takes place in). The dialogue choices in this game are best treated as offering variety on replays so you're not having to hear the exact same dialogue all the time (though, if you're going for achievement completion, you generally have to pick the same choices each time to build affinity), rather than as a way to meaningfully alter the flow and events of the story. For all intents and purposes, barring a couple of alternating scene choices, this game's story is entirely linear.

_childDocuments_.review: I REALLY want to like this game, and I would love to recommend it, however there are a few too many issues I experienced in its current state that just won't get it over the line for me.There are very few opportunities to truly influence the outcome of events to come, and the interactivity is quite sparse. As a visual novel, I understand that a lot of the plot will progress through its storytelling, but there were scenes where minutes of dialogue passed without the opportunity to participate in the game. Once I realised I could skip dialogue, I found myself clicking away to get through a mundane conversation. It's slow; really slow. And yet, the story seemed disjointed and rushed at the same time. There was no indication of time passing, yet it spanned eight months. It was a jarring experience.The most engaging sequences were the songs, though they were far and few between. And the actual mechanics for the rhythm aspects were odd. I played with keyboard and mouse and it was impossible to keep up with the different keys required to perfect the songs. Visually it was confusing and all over the place, and the pressing of buttons don't actually sync in time with the beat. It was frustrating more than anything.The story arc itself was an intriguing one, however the ending was anticlimactic and felt as though the devs couldn't decide how to wrap it up, and so left it as is. And the fact there is no option to replay chapters or music segments is a crime in this day and age.The visuals were gorgeous, and the theme of the narrative was so gripping. Though flawed, if the devs address the rhythm and replayability issues, then I would recommend grabbing this when it's on a steep sale. Until then, as much as it pains me to say, I'd de-wishlist this and say Goodbye to Volcano High.

_childDocuments_.review: Best story in a video game ever. Best of the genre.Goodbye Volcano High is a cinematic story game I have been eagerly waiting to release for nearly a year. Having now played the game through beginning to end twice, the wait was worth it.The memorable soundtrack and music mini-games help to keep the story tight. Fang's main passions in life are their musical career and their friends, and sometimes they have to decide. I immediately connected with Fang and empathised with their struggles.The game takes about 6.5 hours to complete, but has definite replay value. There is new content to be discovered on the second, and even the third play, if you make different choices along the way.Goodbye Volcano High is a fantastic game. There have been, and there will continue to be, comparisons drawn between this game and Night in the Woods. In a world of mediocre furry-themed visual novels, Goodbye Volcano High has unseated NITW as the finest ever made. It's earned a permanent place in my heart.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wani to like this but their are some big problems that set this back in my head. There are parts that really make this a hesitant buy with your money or other choices. If you wani a quick review, Its a Honeymoon game. The Story has certain moments where they do a great job at showing good moments, and some will stick with you. Reed speeches and the Finale are two i really liked. The problem becomes the moment you reminisce on the how and the why, It starts to fall apart at least for me.Lets at least start with The good which is easy.+ Music is really great. Reunion really is a great song and if anything listen to that song and the others that i wani others to listen to.+ Fang is an interesting character that I liked the plight of. If nothing else this movie at least tries.The parts that were not bad but once you notice, its hard to really not notice it. * The big one is the amount of time that past in this movie. Certain events happen months after the previous, and no real way of knowing how long. This makes certain events really weird to think about like the DND sessions, and where certain people are at.* I Cant tell if the Meteor is an allegory for growing up or if its a real thing. I Wani see more from this Studio in the future and their next projects. Keep up the work and cant wait to see what you guys make next. Pick it up on Sale otherwise this was what I saw in this Movie.

It variates on background characters (if you see them or not), but overall, it's the only story and nothing will be changed in second and more playthrough. It's just my opinion, but I believe games like this should have at least two endings.Gameplay (7 out of 10)Mostly, i's like an anime. You just watch the story, occasionally pick answers in some scenes. These answers only affects how close you be to background characters and if you will see their story. Also, there's rhythm game segments during songs. Gameplay is not comlex, more like Visual Novels, but it still require your attention. If this game would've been longer than 8 hours, I would've give it 5 points, but game is short enough for not getting tired of such gameplay and actually allow you to relax during it. But, still, not much action and involvement of a player. Not best, but good enough.Music (10 out of 10)Music is always about taste and being subjective, but for me it was straight into heart! I loved it! It's calm, vocals are calming, instrumental goes through soul and give you so much vibe! All the people who were responsible for songand music part outdone themselves. I bow to each one of them, it was beyond perfect.Sound design (7 out of 10)The most conflicting part of the game for me. Voice actors did the bomb, Their voices made this game awesome. But sound designers kinda messed up in some places. Like, a lot. Always there's either cut of beggining of the sentence or it's ending, you literally hear how it was cut off. Also sound effect on voices, when someone was, for example, speaking on mic - background noise from the microphone is simply cut off. And it ruines the atmosphere. It's sad, especially, when vocie actors did great.Visual (8 out of 10)Another subjective thing, like every form of art. For me it was good. It's simple, eyes not tire from looking through it. Through every story I noticed only one fail - in club episode with blackout, when Fang played solo on acoustic guitar, in final frames they stay with electro guitar instead of acoustic =) Overall, good job, I won't scream like this is a masterpiece, but it's a job well done.To sum it up, even if I point out some cons, music won this game for me. I recommend to play this game to everyone, just because of music. Just try to read through story and admire art, it may catch your eyes more than mine. KO_OP studios, you did great, I definetely gonna look for your other projects. Good job, guys.
