_childDocuments_.review: Goodbye Volcano High has been in the spotlight for a while, hyped up as an emotional, narrative-driven game with a unique art style. But it doesn’t live up to the hype at all. Let’s give credit where it’s due: the soundtrack is genuinely great. Every song feels carefully crafted to match the emotional beats of the story and the moments where you participate in musical minigames are some of the most enjoyable parts of the entire experience. Choosing how the songs are performed adds a nice layer of connection to the characters’ emotions and it’s honestly the one thing that kept me playing through the game. The music does a lot of heavy lifting in trying to sell the game’s emotional tone; especially in the final moments. If there’s anything that Goodbye Volcano High gets right, it’s the music. But let’s be honest, this isn’t enough to carry an entire game.The concept of the story is strong on paper. A group of high school friends, in the shadow of an impending world-ending event, grappling with their dreams, relationships, and a looming sense of finality. It’s the kind of setup that should have given the game room to explore big themes like life, death, and finding meaning when time is running out. But instead of focusing on these stakes, the story gets bogged down in petty interpersonal drama that feels completely disconnected from the bigger picture. The festival, which seemed like it would be the core event, is sidelined in favour of characters arguing about trivial things.There’s a scene where characters are discussing their regrets about not spending enough time with family and friends yet they’re the same ones who willingly joined the band in the first place. It just doesn’t make sense. The narrative lacks any real direction or depth and by the time the asteroid is mentioned again in the last hour, it feels like a cheap way to force drama.One of the most frustrating aspects of Goodbye Volcano High is how it constantly teases the idea that your choices matter—but they don’t. The game goes out of its way to limit your options, often giving you nothing more than half-hearted dialogue choices that don’t feel like they actually affect the story. Even worse, sometimes the game blocks off choices entirely because it wants to reflect the character’s emotional state. In theory, this could add a layer of realism, forcing you to confront the characters’ struggles, but in practice it’s just frustrating.There’s one scene where I was ready to pursue a relationship with a character, but the game only gave me two weak options: turn away or say I wasn’t ready. It’s moments like these that make the game feel more restrictive than engaging. The developers clearly wanted to create emotional tension, but instead, it ends up making you feel like a spectator in a story you’re supposed to be directing. If you're going to promise meaningful choices, deliver them.Speaking of romance, it’s barely there. The game teases at relationships but never actually lets you develop them into something meaningful. The characters themselves are flat and forgettable. None of them are interesting, and their interactions feel forced. Trish is supposed to be the quirky best friend, but their chemistry feels fake. It’s not that romance can’t be subtle or understated, but here, it’s just undercooked. The game introduces these romantic possibilities, but then never does the work to make them feel meaningful. As a result, when these relationships are supposed to matter, they don’t resonate.What’s most disappointing about Goodbye Volcano High is that it wastes a genuinely interesting premise. The looming threat of an asteroid should have added tension, urgency, and depth to the characters’ actions. Instead, the game spends far too much time on side plots and character interactions that feel trivial. The characters have long, meandering conversations that add little to the story and by the time the threat of the asteroid returns, it’s too late to care.This pacing issue is what really sinks the narrative. For the first four hours, almost nothing happens. You get bogged down in scenes that feel like filler, with characters talking about things that don’t matter in the grand scheme of things. The game wastes so much time on irrelevant drama that when it finally starts addressing the impending end of the world, it’s rushed and lacks any emotional weight. It’s like the game suddenly remembers it’s supposed to be about something more significant, but by then, it’s too little, too late.For a game that’s so centred around music, you’d expect the rhythm game segments to be top-notch. Unfortunately, they’re not. The rhythm sections are basic, overly simplistic and a joke. You don’t even need to pay attention to win. You can just mash buttons and it’ll still count as a success. The background visuals during these sections are often distracting, pulling your focus away from the actual gameplay. It's clear the rhythm segments were meant to be a highlight of the experience, but they end up feeling like a throwaway mechanic.The ending of Goodbye Volcano High is probably the most disappointing part of the entire experience. After all the buildup, it turns out none of your choices mattered. The game has a single ending and it doesn’t even try to hide it. The characters spend the last 30 minutes of the game panicking about the asteroid and then… nothing. The asteroid presumably hits and the game ends. No resolution, no payoff for the relationships you tried to build and no acknowledgment of the choices you made along the way. It’s like the game throws its hands up and says, “Well, that’s it!” For a game that constantly reminds you that your choices matter, it’s a slap in the face to find out that they don’t. It makes the whole experience feel like a waste of time.In the end, Goodbye Volcano High is a game with great soundtracks, but not much else. It’s frustrating, disjointed and ultimately unfulfilling. The music is the only part of the game that’s worth any praise, but even that can’t save the weak story, flat characters and lacklustre gameplay. If you’re looking for a deep, emotional narrative with meaningful choices, this isn’t it. Go listen to the soundtracks, but don’t waste your time playing the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent visual novel game. Characters are all unique, memorable, and distinct. Narrative is fantastic and the pacing/audio/voiceovers are all home-runs. Best part of this game for me was how well nuanced its handling of an enby protagonist and queer identities in general were. Game's worth it at full price hands down, mostly because games like this tend to be expensive to produce due to quality voice actors.This game does have some hiccups, like occasional glitches of progressing dialogue and such, but it rarely took away from the overall experience. It's also not super replayable, but I knew that going in and don't tend to see VNs as super replayable anyway, so I didn't mind. Overall while there are some minor problems, it's very rare to see genuinely good queer representation that isn't queerbaiting or painting queer people as villains. I enjoyed this a lot, and I think if you meet this game halfway, you will too.

_childDocuments_.review: There are few things in life as difficult as accepting that your best and closest friends are now on a different path in life than you are, especially when you're young and they've always been there by your side.  Decisions no longer feel as simple or as clear as they once did... even finding common ground starts to become a challenge as you wonder how these people, once so connected to you, are no longer in sync with your dreams and desires.  Goodbye Volcano High is a glimpse at that struggle, told through a the lens of an aspiring musician and their drive to become more than a high school kid playing guitar.  Their band mates, however, have other ideas for their own lives ahead of them.  The character you play, Fang, hasn't fully accepted the reality around them, as a typical teenager would do, and struggles with their best friend becoming preoccupied with her own future.  All the signs are there, but they still want their dream to come true in spite of the shifting dynamics.  On top of that there is also the existential dread about the end of the world on the horizon, a nod to current day teenagers facing global catastrophe that cannot be avoided.  The cast of the game is very colorful and diverse, populated with realistic feeling queer characters.  As a trans person, it was nice to feel seen while not feeling pandered to.  Conversations between Fang and the other trans characters felt like ones I've had with my own friends about these struggles, especially ones about overcoming family dynamics and parents thinking this is all just a temporary change until you grow out of it...My only real complaint is that I wish we had more time to talk and interact with everyone, or that everyone's story could be explored in a single playthrough rather than having to go through a series of "Groundhog Day"-like plays repeating the same few days over and over; I've found that this lessens the charm of the game on each successive pass as you try to see everyone's additional content.  There also isn't much of a game, more a series of low-impact decisions that don't affect the main plot, but only change what scenes you get to see play out.  Even the music mini rhythm game is overly simple and doesn't give very good feedback to how well you're doing... and it doesn't actually affect the game even when you fail.  So, this won't be everyone's cup of tea, but if you would like to watch an 8-episode TV show with cute anthro dinosaurs in a high school drama, pick it up on a sale.  Get the soundtrack, too, as that was the best part of the whole game.

The DnD campaign adds absolutely nothing to the games story, and is just straight up filler, and as someone that was intrigued by the plot and was curious about how it would end, having this huge side tangent was not enjoyable for me. I also did experience a few audio cuts throughout the game, but that was the only bug I experienced. I enjoyed the story and I thought the ending was pretty. Its a game finish that left me thinking about it for a few days after, and while those aren't for everyone, I really enjoyed it. I thought the characters were memorable, and its very slice of life, so once again something that is not made for everyone. I had very similar feelings about Night In The Woods, so if that is a game you enjoy then you will have a good time with Goodbye Volcano High. Just... Skip the DND session... unless you are huge into DnD (or LnL as they call it, ha) then I feel there is no benifit to that side story.This is like the Serial Experiments Lain of gaming. You might hate it, you might love it, theirs a good chance you will have no idea what is going on, but it will leave you thinking about it for weeks to come.

_childDocuments_.review: What would you do if the world was ending? That’s the main conceit behind Goodbye Volcano High(GVH), also set at the end of high school. That transitionary period means a lot is about to change and the familiarly trodden ground is about to be uprooted, it’s how the characters deal with all of this that makes this such a compelling story.Growing up is a big part of GVH, especially the part where the world starts to feel real, our group of friends is still together but there are tensions as they have different interests in what they want to do with their lives and worry about what that will mean for their friendships. While the main character Fang, isn’t able to see this at first it’s obvious and just waiting for the realization to sink in, that moment is tense. As Fang seeks a life in music with their bandmates Reed and Trish it’s clear they don’t share that enthusiasm. Trish is more into bugs and entomology while Reed is less sure but his love of L&L (GVHs version of D&D) sets him on a path of creative writing or game design. Not having the same interests as lifelong friends can suck and how to navigate that is an important reflection of your friendship, one that GVH deals with exceptionally well.There’s already a sense of finality to the end of high school, an almost unfathomable break from the normal routine of your whole life until that point, and it certainly doesn’t help that the world is also ending, this raises the stakes but it still feels very grounded in reality with regards to high school. Fang has recently come out as non-binary, and while their friends are very accepting of this it’s more difficult for their parents especially their mom who keeps referring to them incorrectly. It’s not clear if this is out of malice or simple difficulty accepting the change but it speaks on the experience that some people might have with their parents.I’ve talked a lot about story and characters, they are the most important and focused part of the game but it is a bit more than a visual novel. While there are many visual novel elements such as dialogue choices the game also features a few rhythm sections to go with Fangs’ music playing, None of these are particularly hard and there isn’t a fail state so much or even a score(aside from a few achievements related to playing well) they do make a good break from the more laid back and text-heavy story. Some of the controls for it are a bit finicky and in the background of the songs is a slide show of moments that are happening to the characters that was hard to watch while focusing on the rhythm game.As previously mentioned the game features a D&D-like game that you get to play a few times, this involves choices about where to go and what to do, what attacks to make, and who to assist or attack with, much of it is controlled by a dice roll as well which allows for some extremely light RPG combat elements through again this is mostly for the story and not a fully realized concept, these sections did a great job at bringing the friend group closer together though and were quite memorable. A further expanded or even fully realized game in this style would work well.Most characters are well-realized with their personalities and intricacies they don’t always agree with what you doing or disagree, it’s more complicated than that, unfortunately, some of the more secondary characters don’t get similar treatment which makes them a bit lacking, the the main 4 or so are very well done. The story as a result of being heavily character isn’t as important, it’s about the characters and their interactions and lives, there’s always that sense of dread in the background for what’s coming, and as the game goes on this builds and builds into some pretty heavy moments that play out in a way that makes sense, maybe I would react similarly while not a perfect depiction of high school it’s quite well done and the writing is the strong point.The end of the world may seem distant but it's something that is at least somewhat on the minds of younger generations today as they look at the increasingly dire problem of anthropogenic climate change. While GVH isn't about climate change and climate change in general won't be such a specific single apocalyptic event; the sense of doom and helplessness is the same and represented well here with competing viewpoints on it. Some characters take a more nihilistic approach, others work to get as much done as possible before it's too late, some hope it'll work out in the end and keep going on like nothing happening. That last one doesn't work so well with the climate change metaphor but each perspective is an important one.It would be difficult to perfect an ending to something as big as the end of the world and here is the same, there’s no perfect solution to it, not everything is solved or figured out but by the end, you’ve kind of just accepted it and focused on what’s important to you, simply put they made the most of what they had and while it might not be the most satisfying outcome it works for them.

_childDocuments_.review: Goodbye Volcano High explores its various themes--friendship, love, ambition, uncertainty, and many, many more!--in a way that deeply touched my heart. The characters are messy and imperfect, and after taking Fang through several interactions with their family and friends, you start to feel connected to all of the characters even when conversations are tough, and you find yourself rooting for them despite their mistakes and flaws.The art, animations, voice acting, and audio in general are absolutely incredible; you can feel the love that went into making this game, and it really brings so much life to the characters and the world. The rhythm gameplay is hard, but he game doesn't appear to punish you for being less-than-perfect, and I liked that since it allowed me to focus more on the story.If you're looking for a game that will allow you to experience Every Emotion associated with being a high school student who also happens to be facing the end of the world: you've found it.

_childDocuments_.review: Goodbye Volcano High is a narrative-driven game set in the final year of high school for Fang, a non-binary dinosaur dealing with the challenges of adolescence and an impending apocalypse. Developed by KO_OP, it combines coming-of-age storytelling with rhythm gameplay, making for a unique and heartfelt experience.Story & Characters:The story is central to Goodbye Volcano High. You play as Fang, who navigates the ups and downs of teenage life, including relationships, self-discovery, and the pursuit of dreams—all set against the background of an impending asteroid strike. The narrative is full of emotional beats that resonate, especially for anyone who has experienced the bittersweet nature of high school graduation and stepping into the unknown. The game does a great job of making characters feel authentic and relatable, each with distinct personalities that add depth to the story.Art & Music:The visual style is vibrant and expressive, with a cartoon-like design that suits its dinosaur cast and high school setting. Characters are animated with strong attention to detail, which enhances the emotional scenes. The soundtrack is another standout, blending indie and rock vibes that suit the rebellious spirit of Fang’s band and add an extra layer of immersion, particularly during rhythm game segments.Gameplay:Goodbye Volcano High is mostly a narrative experience, but it mixes in rhythm gameplay where players perform music. The rhythm sections are engaging, though they may feel simple compared to rhythm-focused games. There are also dialogue choices that allow players to shape Fang’s relationships and narrative direction, making each playthrough potentially different. However, the choices are generally minor and don’t drastically change the story’s main outcomes, which might be a downside for those expecting more narrative branching.Themes & Emotional Impact:The game doesn’t shy away from deep themes, including identity, friendship, family expectations, and the uncertainty of the future. The impending apocalypse metaphorically represents the end of adolescence and the inevitable change it brings, adding weight to each character’s decisions. For many players, these themes may resonate on a personal level, making the story impactful and, at times, genuinely touching.Pros:	•	Strong, relatable story with emotional depth	•	Beautiful, expressive art and soundtrack	•	Well-developed characters with diverse identitiesCons:	•	Limited replayability due to less impactful choices	•	Rhythm gameplay may feel too simplistic for some players	•	Pacing can be slow if you’re more interested in gameplay than storyVerdict:Goodbye Volcano High is a heartfelt journey that’s more of an interactive story than a traditional game. It’s perfect for players who value narrative depth, emotional storytelling, and character-driven experiences. While it may not satisfy players looking for complex gameplay or impactful choices, it excels as a narrative game that deals with the bittersweetness of growing up and letting go.

_childDocuments_.review: Goodbye Volcano High has an interesting premise: what if the dinosaur apocalypse but in a modern world like ours? I think the game needed an extra episode or two to make me care more, even though *most of the characters are decent. Sage and Stella in particular felt barely like characters. It's a shame since all of the main cast is voice acted and the voice actors do an excellent job.Overall this should be a $20 in my mind, it doesn't quite get to Night in the Woods' level but the premise was good enough for me to give it one go around.

_childDocuments_.review: While I don't share a lot in common with the main character, Fang, I really enjoyed my time with them and their crew of colorful dinosaur friends. For those who don't know, the story follows a group of anthropomorphic dinosaurs during their senior year in high school when they find out a giant meteor is coming toward Earth, and there is a very real possibility that the planet will die right as their adult lives are getting started. The soundtrack is lovely and beautifully performed and the game has some pretty rad rhythm game mechanics that I haven't seen before. All of the characters were appealing and the premise behind the story made for some very poignant moments. It's one of only a few games that really got to me emotionally by the end (in a good way), as the looming potential end of the world frames the story in a very compelling way.  Plus, even though there is only one ending, you can choose how you interact with every main character, and it affects some aspects of the story in a lot of ways. You can tell quite a lot of love went into this project, and I recommend giving it your time.

_childDocuments_.review: It's really amazing to see indie developers come together to make a project as large and as quality as Goodbye Volcano High.This game caught my eye due to its unique art style and gameplay elements that you can see in the previews. But what really sold me is the story and music. After reading the game description and hearing the music in the previews I definitely had to experience it.The actual player experience is weird to explain though.The game both looks and controls really nice, with the exception that a controller is recommended. But there are also some inconsistencies with the overall player experience.Sometimes the game audio will cut itself short or omit certain dialogue or cinematic sections entirely. During my one playthrough of seven hours though this did not prevent me from experiencing any important dialogue or scenes, just something to keep in mind if you plan on buying the game.The actual game itself is incredible.Everything from the animation to music composition and story writing was all done expertly.The animation and art style is quite unique, to me anyway. With the use of 2D images plus shading and perspective to really make environments and characters stand out from other games.Music is obviously subjective but I couldn't name a single track that I didn't enjoy in my playthrough. Not every track is the same or even have the same vibe for that matter. They're all composed specifically to convey a certain "feel in the moment".The story writing was also excellent, with each character being uniquely dynamic and relatable to the player. Almost every scene is equally necessary to the story and equally unique from the others, with the exception of band practice and L&L. I kinda wish there were a more in depth conclusion to the story, but that's subjective.Band practice is probably the most fun and enjoyable element in this game, with its unique but not complicated controls it's perfect at creating an immersive and enjoyable experience.As scores go, I'd give Volcano High a 9/10 (10/10 without the audio cutting issue if that ever gets fixed) and I definitely recommend anyone who's into story rich indie games with unique gameplay elements to pick it up and try it out!

_childDocuments_.review: This was an emotional experience from start to finish, and I teared up multiple times over the course of my playthrough. I love visual novels, and I love rhythm games, and this game was so creative with its design of each aspect. Using dialogue choice boxes to represent the character's emotional state, jumbling around during an emotional moment or false options fizzing out to show hesitation. Furthermore, you go into each song blind; there are short snippets where you get to workshop the lyrics, which really gives you the feeling that this is *your* song, but when you actually get to play it out, it's so much more in every way. And since each song is only visited once, it really feels like a once-in-a-lifetime, don't-mess-this-up experience. I was honestly blown away by the beautiful music. There were moments where I fumbled the notes because I was distracted trying to watch the visuals, but once I allowed myself to just let go and lose myself in the music, it became a lot easier for me. A lot of rhythm games have gameplay that's fun to play but not to watch, and that isn't the case with this game. This game has something for both the player and the audience.The story flows so well. It all plays out like a very long movie. I feel like the best experience is playing it in one sitting, or as close to one sitting as you can.

_childDocuments_.review: So steam is Unfortunately very binary  in its review system and if I had the choice I’d leave a more “Meh” rating on this, so don’t treat this review as an absolute condemnation from me.Goodbye volcano high is a pretty interesting concept, teenagers having to deal with the fact the world might end in a few months, it’s kinda hooking at the start, I quite like the art personally..it’s not Disney or anything but it’s got that sort of Cartoon Network vibe and I kinda like it., lotsa bright colours for the various dinosaursSpeaking of said dinosaurs So the astroid takes backstage for most of the story as Fang and her friends gear up for their first major concert which in typical fashion goes off without a hitch, after that point it becomes obvious the astroid is hooking to hit.Absolutely zero hell breaks loose, people will get desperate in these circumstances and yet the entire population of this world seems to be of the most emotionally calm or dead people around, the only time did I see fang actually cry is when they realised they won’t ever see their mom and dad in person again.Speaking of which these teenage dinosaurs reallt don’t act like teenagers but more how mellenial collage students think teenagers act, infinately progressive and sentimental always talking about their feelings and always figuring things out in the end.There was little To no teenage drama here as the group either panned to another scene or delt with the issue with wisened adult levels of maturity, when I was fang’s age I could barely use a dishwasher nevermind understand these complex emotions.and needs kf everybody at such a vital time.There are large portions of this game’s story occupied by Reed’s DND session which is fun for maybe a section but the amount of time this game uses just for that kinda signals to me that the devs didn’t really know what to do with their own  story The ending is VERY lacklustre if not beautiful and while it was pretty to see everybody get together it was the only time in the game where I could genhinely beleive the emotion going on. There was a very big lack of good chronology here though becauee the entire scene suggested the meteor was coming right now? But then apparently in 48 hours?The ending itself is sorta ambiguous, the screen just fades halfway through the ending song, so we’re not even sure if the meteor hits or not, I don’t know if it’s sequel bait or just bad writing.I won’t say it’s terrible but I will say if you coming in expecting teen drama and end of thee world drama you’ll be dissapointed, so it’s a downvote from me

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very special game: meaningful and poetic, funny and tragic, colourful, realistic - and the voice acting and music are just the icing on the cake. It's instantly one of my all-time favourite games, and I was so attached to the characters and story that I dove right back in for a second playthrough, maybe to experiment with some different choices.I took my time, and with a few save reloads when I hit the occasional crash on Steam Deck (see below), and a few re-runs of certain songs I wanted to nail better with the rhythm action gameplay (not because of any sort of score, but just because I was so into the roleplay), I completed it in about 10 hours, which was a perfect length for me. But I think there's more to see on later runs too, with different choices changing the journey.I know I'll be revisiting this year on year like some of my other all-time favourite games, whose run-times are just right to slip back into like a favourite TV show under a warm blanket (198X and Sayonara Wild Hearts have been similar titles for me in recent years; and perhaps not so coincidentally, also feature a similar musical, shoegazing tone)."What’s a worm drama?" Play it and find out!--Some details, though I will try and avoid spoilers (you can tell I'm really into a game when I write waaaay too much in a Steam review):The presentation is sublime - this is less like playing a visual novel (even though it is, mechanically), and more like watching an animated movie. Gone are the conventional VN static/animated portraits that slide in, replaced with a cinematic or TV presentation of characters moving naturally about scenes (though I think with subtle, clever reuse of animations, so it feels like every scene is bespokly animated). The pastel, tropical backdrops, and frequent pans from the huge sky are gorgeous to behold; it really makes you want to step into the screen, like it's a beautiful painting.I suppose the story is fairly linear, but I don't think that's a bad thing. I've not played many visual novels, but I believe they usually let you freely explore their (high school) setting; whereas here, except for very occasionally, you're taken from one scene to the next by the narrative. But this does create good pacing, and less (perhaps RPG-style?) aimless wandering. And unlike most visual novels there are frequent dialogue choices, which let you customise the journey and feel engaged (there's some imaginative presentation of dialogue choices and their mechanics too, which feels very fresh). From a single run I can already see various aspects of the story that could be customised based on my choices, so I'm eager to do another run. There are also fun mini-games (aside from the rhythm action), and even some of the more conventional visual novel dialogues at times, which nicely vary the narrative delivery - as do the rhythm action sections themselves obviously.I struggled a little with the rhythm action (and routinely got confused about what to do when the L and R prompts appeared - it means pull the sticks down, not pull the L and R triggers), but you can't really derail the songs or even the music too much, so you don't spoil the experience for yourself. But there is nice reactivity too, like in one of the first songs where I'm demoing it to the rest of the band: Fang seemed to stop halfway through when I made a few too many mistakes, and said "Well obviously I'm messing it up..." which was a nice touch. And I love how you can customise the lyrics to the songs too, pulling you into some creative compositional roleplay, perhaps a bit like Stray Gods does (and it's a nice feeling when lyrics you've customised in band practice, then get performed at an actual show!). When I did mess up a song, especially at key moments for the band, I found myself wanting to do better, just because I was so into the roleplay, and didn't want them to fail; so I'd reload the save and go again.The game works really hard to put you into the POV of Fang and the band, and at one point, without spoilering anything, this really came to an apex for me at one of their shows. I really felt that I was experiencing this pivotal career moment with them. And I had one of the sweetest and most realistic romantic engagements I think I may have ever had in a game - I genuinely felt like I had a secret admirer, and all the excitement and uncertainty that goes along with that.I mostly played on Steam Deck, docked to my TV, for a relaxing sofa experience, and the game looks amazing on a big screen. I did hit a few crashes, which I think were probably Deck-specific; with a quick save-reload (the game autosaves at every scene break) I was back into it though. I emailed the devs my bug reports at the email address I found on the Steam forums, and they replied soon after saying they'd logged them in the system, so they may very well be fixed now. But it was small fry compared to the highs of the rest of the game. (Though I still prefer games with an in-game bug reporter, to make it easier to report any issues.)The characters and writing are extremely fun and engaging (with a subtle sprinkle of famous dinosaur references from popular culture, which will make you smile if you spot them). Importantly there's a lot of attention paid to the small, specific details of people and their relationships. As with all good stories, it's the characters that will stay in your memory. I definitely recommend reading the Eurogamer review too, which really shows how strong the writing is - not least in how it captures a sincere and authentic teenage voice. I'm in my forties, and sometimes I feel modern dialogue (not just in games) can be too busy and fast-talking, mistaking quantity for quality (though fast-talking is fine if it's also witty and deliberate); at first I was a little put off by the frequent modern slang and busyness of the dialogue (and arguably that's fine - I'm not really the intended audience). But if that's something you think might put you off too, then I'd say give the game a few scenes; before long I think you'll find that the sincere character writing will have you onside and invested for the long haul. The game also does a lot with silence: dialogue is sometimes sparse, with long pauses, or just no dialogue at all, relying instead on actions and atmosphere, so you really get to soak up the contemplative mood. I think it's sophisticated, even literary, in its execution.This game had me hooked with its tragic concept and title right from its unveiling in 2019, combining the extinction of the dinosaurs with leaving-high-school sadness and coming-of-age drama. It's an incredible setup for a story, and I think the game completely nails it.I think the game is also a blueprint for how to live well during the end times, should we ever need it. Would the world really descend into a frenzied, selfish panic, Mad Max-style? Or would people come together and be kind? The game very much leans into the latter, and I think it might be right.

_childDocuments_.review: 10/10Goodbye Volcano High is an absolute triumph in the world of narrative-driven video games. From the very first moments, it captivates with its stunning visual style, seamlessly blending hand-drawn animation with a vibrant color palette that brings its prehistoric world of humanoid dinosaurs to life. The art is not only visually appealing but also expertly complements the themes of youth, change, and self-discovery that the game explores.At its core, Goodbye Volcano High is a deeply emotional coming-of-age story that focuses on the relationships and struggles of its main characters as they navigate the complexities of life, love, and loss. The dialogue is sharp and heartfelt, with characters that feel relatable and real, despite their reptilian appearance. The writing does a beautiful job of capturing the angst and excitement of adolescence, while also providing moments of lightheartedness and humor that give the game a balanced tone.One of the standout features of the game is its choice-driven narrative, where every decision feels meaningful, and the consequences are felt in profound ways. The game allows players to shape the story through their choices, giving a sense of agency while also reflecting the uncertainties that come with growing up. The relationships between characters evolve in such a natural way, making the bonds and tensions feel authentic.The soundtrack is another highlight—an eclectic mix of indie and alternative music that perfectly complements the emotional beats of the story. Each track feels like it was carefully selected to enhance the mood, whether it’s a moment of joy or a more somber, reflective scene. Would love to have a vinyl.Overall, Goodbye Volcano High is a game that leaves a lasting impression. It’s a beautiful blend of heartfelt storytelling, compelling characters, and stunning artistry. Whether you're a fan of narrative-driven games or simply enjoy stories about youth and self-discovery, this one is absolutely worth experiencing. It’s a truly unique gem that resonates on a personal level and lingers long after the credits roll.
_childDocuments_.name: Goodbye Volcano High

_childDocuments_.review: I'll get it out of the way, comparing this with Snoot Game feels meaningless.  That's coming from someone that loves both.  They both do very different things, go for very different feelings, and it's a genuine shame that people will write off one or the other because they're both worth experiencing.Now, Goodbye, Volcano High is less like a normal VN and more like a small interactive movie.  Scenes will play out pretty directly with a bit of variance for choices.  This is more of a Walking Dead style of variance, the very concept of the game is upfront with where it will end and there's no surprise Deus ex Machina that saves everyone because you went down the Trish route instead of the Naomi route or something similar.  If you're looking for that you'll obviously be upset, but if you want this kind of experience it's fantastically done.The characters are all teenagers, all on the cusp of experiencing life outside of school and figuring themselves out.  You'll want to punch almost all of them for how frustrating they can be, but that feels in line for what stage of their lives they're in.  It's only made more stark because of the looming threat of death hanging over their heads.  Despite that...  it feels extremely honest.  Messy relationships, bullheaded mistakes, grand gestures to fix things that are hard to follow up on in smaller moments.In the end it's a story about living in the face of certain death.  Whether the threat is nuclear warfare of our parents' generation, climate disaster of ours, or a meteor that will wipe out all life in this game, we have what little life we have.  Making the most of it, celebrating it, fighting for who you want to be, and experiencing it with ones you love.  Whether it comes in days or decades it's something we each have to reckon with, and while GVH isn't always perfect with its tone it DOES capture that feeling powerfully in its closing chapters.Give it a shot.  This is well worth your time if you're craving something bittersweet and lovely.  The soundtrack is beautiful, the art's often gorgeous, and in the end the experience lingers after the credits roll.  Give Fang and their friends' game a shot.

_childDocuments_.review: Alright, so where to begin? I first found out about this game shortly after it was announced back in 2019? 2020? I will not lie, it was from a meme on ifunny that was a screenshot from 4chan. I forget the details but it was more or less 4chan being 4chan and ripping GVH a new one 10 fold(Yall know how they are). After that I forgot GVH and didn't follow the development process of this game at all with the occasional bits and pieces flowing in from ifunny. Thats when I saw another meme from (guess what?) ifunny and it was a trailer for a "Parody" game called 'Snoot game' Then about 9 or 10 months ago (from the writing of this review) when I got to my duty station in the dead of winter (AK) I was convinced by a dude to give it a try. Snoot game is free so I wasn't at a loss for buying it, so I figured "why the hell not?" I played Snoot game and beat it all 4 endings of it. At one point I was so balls deep in Snoot game that I was apart of it discord and ♥♥♥♥. While I was in the community I saw alot of people saying they wernt going to give GVH a chance since (just from the trailers that were released at the time for GVH) Snoot game and Caveanon blew GVH out of the water.Me personally didn't agree with that stance, so I was fighting for GVH in the Snoot game community for atleast the better part of 9 months. With varying levels of success mind you, I stuck true to my preachings and bought GVH when i saw it came out and as you can see sunk a good day into it. This is where im going to get political fair ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ warning!So one of the main draws to Snoot game was that 4Chan is notorious for being politically right winged to the point of being extreme, and KO_OP is politically left. Look im not picking sides on which is better right now, I just want to have fun and enjoy the story when I play games. I THOROUGHLY enjoyed the take and approach that Snoot game took and the same for GVH. I might not agree with every stance that KO_OP has taken in their game BUT I feel like they focused on some hot topics just enough to where it wasn't shoving it in you face or so far in the background that its irreverent. Lets get into the Audio aspects of both games. So GVH has a rhythm based mini games that are there, I wont say they are good or bad because im extremely biased on that part (mostly because I have no rhythm and I sucked at them) but i did have fun playing them i feel like it kinda took me out of the songs but that a skill issue not a developer issue. Snoot game has no well mini games at all and it just a visual novel so if you want to start keeping score thats 1 or GVH I guess. When is comes to the songs ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ i was blown away by the music and vocals of GVH applauds Lachlan Watson ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ she can sing. Snoot games OST is good and well choreographed but in my opinion just dosent have the same impact as GVHs OST. Dont get me wrong 'Amberlight Brilliance' still gives me the feels and ♥♥♥♥ but Amberlight Brilliance is a punch to the face while any song from GVH is fully loaded freight train to the head. (GHV 2 SG 0)The humor. GVH is tagged with the "Dark Humor" tag I would like to disagree with that one I acknowledge that humor is subjective, but from memory I think there was one maybe 2 or 3 jokes that I would consider "dark humor" Now for Snoot games humor... every joke that games has is dark humor and I love it especially ending 1 and 2 they will be a gut punch. (GVH 2 SG 1)Im not really sure how to put this part into words but for me atleast, GVH made you feel more for the universe that they were building with KO_OPs narrative while Caveanon made you feel more for the characters and not for the universe as a whole. (so a point to each GVH 3 SG 2)The choices While GVH has more choices when it comes to creative liberty like choosing your own song lyrics which in of itself I have to congratulate KO_OP, because just changing 1 line in 1 song means the development team has to make a whole new version of the same song which must have been a nightmare for all of the options. Snoot games choices boils down to "do you want to be a ♥♥♥♥/adult or not" so i have to give this one to GVH (GVH 4 SG 2)Animations GVH no contest OK not going to lie this ♥♥♥♥ has gone on for far too long now. While Snoot game has garnered interest in GVH (for better or worse) one couldn't have survived without the other whether KO_OP wants to admit it or not. TLDRSnoot game is good game if you like being edgy that has a good love story and decent soundtrack. 7.5/10Goodbye Volcano High is a amazing game with a amazing soundtrack and good story if you want to be mainstream. 9/10My personal opinion? PLAY BOTH!!! They are both good for their own reasons.

_childDocuments_.review: Finished the VN now. Twice actually The second time I tried to go an "evil"/bad route by being mean to everyone hoping for different dialogue options, but the novel was more linear, not having many branches. But once again, those decisions are basically for achievement purposes only, as either the game doesn't allow you to be bad (sometimes dialogue options that pop up at first will be grayed out (looking at the piano naming scene)) or just roll with it. Anyway, I did enjoy the story and the art (especially in the pen&paper rounds) and this is what a Visual Novel is about, isn't it? Also, really cool soundtrack.Overall, I'll give it a 7/10

_childDocuments_.review: I´ve seen the game in the PS5 reveal back in 2020 and was pretty interested in it. Im not a sucker for visual novels - usually - , but this game had some "aura" about it. Anyway, three years after waiting, it released today and I was pumped to play it, after all, this seemed pretty well animated for an indie game.If you are looking for a quick answer, I´d say its worth a shot. Im only at the beginning, but it seems promising. Good music, good voice acting, good visuals. The topic of the game is not for everyone, so if you don´t like LGBTQ and all these topics, you might wanna look elsewhere. Its definetly a "unique" game, let´s leave it at that.HOWEVER, there are a few issues:1. the Menu - it looks like someone made it up in an hour. No music, no scenery or anything, no nothing. For a visual novel, it is very underwhelming.2. the Scenes - there´s a lot of problems with lip syncing and just frames jumping to the next one. it all seems like it lacks polish - its gotten better when compared to the demo, but still not good. 3. lack of saves - you can´t save and reload any scene you like - thats a must in a novel, especially when it comes to decisions that are very important - WHY can´t i save when I want and reload the saves? Thats like the basics of a good visual novelAnd the last problem, though that might just be a "me"-thing is the fact that you can´t look around freely in the scenes- thats something most visual novels allow to do - it just rushes you to choose and doesn´t give you the freedom to enjoy the scenery, considering it´s really well drawn.As I haven´t completed the game yet, I will not be rating the story just yet. I would personally say that the game is good so far, but it just feels like a pre-production build. If the problems are fixed, I´d say its a good visua novel, right now, only if you don´t mind the problems and the high price. It´s definetly more expensive then most visual novels, gotta decide yourself what its worth to you.In its current state, I give it a 7/10. It´s good, but not great. I expected a bit better, but it could be much worse.Also, I would like to point out the ridicilous behaviour of the developers towards fans of the "Snoot Game", a game which, despite it being shorter and having less content, does not suffer from all of the problems mentioned above and, simply because it chooses a different story not as "LGBTQ"-friendly, the developers at KO-OP seem to prohibit any talking about it, PLUS it´s impossible to get into the discord, way to strict. _childDocuments_.review: High school can be a rough time.  Some can do school well and guide the foggy waters of the educational system, but for others it's a hard road with bumps along the way that test who you are and what you think you are.  This is a statement and understanding that developer KO_OP has learned good and well with their newest title.It’s been a rough few years of development for the team.  Facing a full narrative reworking after having to hire a brand new writing team, undergoing the challenges of navigating the COVID-19 pandemic, and swallowing their pride and avoiding crunch with delays of almost 2 years, the road to bring Goodbye Volcano High has been dreadful: not to mention the unacceptable but ultimately unavoidable internet outrage involving games with LGBTQIA+ characters at the helm.  So after all this, we finally were able to witness Fang and company navigate their last year of high school with one small caveat: the threat of worldly annihilation via meteor..erm, asteroid.  Sorry, we all get that mixed up.Goodbye Volcano High is a branching path but overall kinetic visual novel involving senior student and non-binary lead singer/guitarist for Worm Drama, Fang.  Fang has been prepping for this year’s Battle of the Bands with bandmates and best friends Trish and Reed, as well as dealing with the expectations of career-pathing and life-choices expected of people who just got allowed into Rated-R movies.  Volcano High’s 8 episodes tell the journey of Senior Year, the reaction to breaking news involving the asteroid, to Fang making amends to end their year, and potentially their life, on the right note.The main benefactor of positives will start with the first chord you hear.  The soundtrack shines brightly with artists Dabu & Brigitte Nagger composing an EP’s worth of indie rock tracks that beautifully encapsulate the fleeting emotions of their lead singer and the sentimental values of their personal life and band life held on by a single thread.  While the gameplay for the score are simple rhythmic pieces to let the audience engage with timed guitar plucks and snare drum hits within the song, the music carries so well and is by and far the standout portion of Volcano High.  The art direction shines just as brightly, boasting a piquant pastel palette with starry night skies, beautifully spacious and inviting outdoor backdrops, and colorful imaginative characters.  Each character is brimming with emotion and individuality and the game as a whole is such a treat to gaze upon.Volcano High’s voice acting and script really phone in the “high school cringe” aspect and I mean this in the most positive way I can.  The multiple layers of anxiety, apprehensiveness, and pseudo-confidence cover the characters like a winter blanket and exude the snarky and snappy nature their emotions would be handled during the most tumultuous points of their lives.  Feelings will be hurt, kindled, and reconciled as fast as they are put into place, but who didn’t have emotional breakdowns with friends every once in a while, especially in predicaments such as Fang’s?The audio direction of this script and audio miscues though brings the volume down a few notches.  Lines feel as if they were recorded in bunches and cut for each sentence to let the game space out and ingest each line accordingly, which is no big deal.  The problem with this is when lines get post-editing done to them, like adding echo from a microphone or any after-effect on the audio, there are prominent and noticeable cuts where the audio stops to let the game require a button press to continue.  It’s super jarring hearing this and makes these scenes feel rushed and disjointed knowing a simple extra half-second of audio to fade out the extra pieces would’ve made these moments sound much better.  I also ran into a few instances where the Autoplay feature would misfire at random causing a full line to be skipped immediately or would cut off voice lines prematurely.  Since there is no Log feature to access previous lines that I could find, you lose what was said during these moments.The animation felt uneven at times as well.  The musical scores boast buttery smooth animation to really heighten these impactful moments where Fang’s heart and soul are pouring into every nook and cranny of each scene.  But the in-between moments of day-to-day routines feel disjointed and mislaid.  Animations for walking scenes feel Flash-era in how clunky and stiff the animations are presented.  Mouth movements don’t have enough frames to cover the lines being said.  Scenes have a tendency to “pop” in place where character positions don’t connect with the end of one line and the beginning of the next one.  And most cutscenes suffer from a lack of In-Betweening which make characters look disjointed in their movements.And, look.  I understand going through a full narrative rework is bound to cause issues especially when under the time constraints that video game development provides, but some issues are too much to ignore.  The amount of L&L (Legends & Lore, GVH’s version of Dungeons & Dragons) sessions in the game feels like artificial inflation of the game’s playtime.  While there are some beneficial moments for the group play sessions, these take up nearly a third of the game which could have been used to hash out other scenes and plot points or provide more world building within Volcano High.  This move, combined with the omission of most voice lines outside of the DM of the game, makes a rushed game feel even more rushed and nets more negatives to its inclusion than positives.Another is a scene about halfway through the game: within the day-to-day sections of going through school, Fang is texted by a secret admirer from an unknown number.  I loved these scenes as it really nailed the grounded feeling of pouring emotions within the anonymity of a text conversation.  The feeling of unequivocal mutual intimacy, being able to rationalize the confidence of a confession without removing the mask of uncertainty is done so well here, and were many of the highlights of my playthrough.But the scenes are pieced together with the intention of figuring out who the secret admirer is, and the fun is playing the whodunit up until the moment the two meet.  But for reasons angrily unknown, they up and .  I tried to mock it up as a potential bait-and-switch to get me later in the game, but they proved my theory wrong and flat out confirmed their own killing of their suspense not 30 minutes after the suspected cutscene.  It felt disloyal to the building of tension it slowly seeped in and left a horrid taste in my mouth when the truth was revealed, instead of whatever emotion they were hoping for.And it’s pieces like the above that really showed how in dire straits Goodbye Volcano High was.  The uphill battle KO_OP had to push through after numerous delays left the game in a scrambled state.  This kills me because as a fan of this game, there’s so many things I adore about Goodbye Volcano High: the characters, the music, and the instilled love of their creation is shown in so many ways that I feel visual novel fans should absolutely play this game.  But as a reviewer I cannot look over the distinct lack of polish in several aspects and the despondent writing direction with its own plot setups and finishes.  Goodbye Volcano High, under less tumultuous circumstances, had the makings to create a genre-defining experience that would carry the narrative weight to captivate audiences much past its expectations; but this title, much like some of its main characters, just needed more time to show who they really are and what they can really be.

_childDocuments_.review: As a snootbro, I went into this with high hopes but low expectations. In all I would say the experience was decently good. Nothing groundbreaking, but the game is definitely far from horrendous. Here are a few of the things I feel the game did quite well at:-Firstly is the Art, say what you will about some of the story or dialogue, but the art itself was extremely enjoyable. The backgrounds were always super solid to downright beautiful, and for the most part the character art was also very good. Although there were definitely a few minor issues (limbs or clothing looking a bit off), but the large majority was just fine. I particularly enjoyed all the little extra shots shown during some of the musical bits that show off individual little moments or energy, definitely helped add what depth they could to the characters that otherwise had a tendency to feel a bit disconnected and random (especially with the complete lack of transitions or time gauging. The game is supposed to take place over 8 months, but there is practically 0 way of knowing roughly where you are on the timeline.)-Much like the Art, the music itself was incredibly enjoyable, and you can definitely tell they did not skimp on the budget for the performances. Audio was clean, clear, and very well done, and for a visual novel it is certainly much more than necessary. Major kudos to the vocalists, and Dabu for the instrumental and mixing.-Lastly, the Minigames. Though I feel some people definitely will disagree, I personally found the minigames to be at the least decently enjoyable. The musical aspect was not overly challenging, but not so much that it could be done mindlessly. As far as the L&L stuff, I found it pretty entertaining (for the most part, chill stoner reed > d&d nerd reed). I enjoyed the branching paths those sections offered, and the art was very interesting during these moments as well.Overall the game definitely has some weaker points (like the character and time stuff mentioned earlier as well as some internal issues during the dev cycle), but aside from that, on it's own and completely separate from snootgame, it's a solid release. Worth $30? I wouldn't say so seeing as it's only around 5-7 hours depending how fast you go, probably about 10 for 100% completion with all routes. If the game is on sale however, or if you were a huge fan of the Anthro Dino Pangaea setting in a VN style, it is definitely worth checking out at the least. Hell, try the game for the 2 hours steam lets you and refund if you dislike it, but it deserves a try. I do have to say though, the writing definitely could have been a bit better, it wasn't absolutely atrocious, but it just felt very detached at times. The flow was not that great either as I mentioned before. I also wish that Final rating: 6/10. Strong Art, Music, and Minigames. Weak story and flow, with writing that felt like it was ripped straight from tumblr. Honestly this rating is definitely being a bit generous, but that's what I'm settling on.

_childDocuments_.review: I like this game. I like this game a lot, in fact.When I first heard about Goodbye Volcano High, the discussions I had about the game were surrounded by a mix of skepticism and curiosity, and I'm extremely glad I let curiosity win.Throughout the whole game, I experienced a touching story about the transition from adolescence to adulthood, represented with an amazing variety of things that made the game not only feel alive but full of soul.Right off the bat, I have to mention the visuals. Things such as the backgrounds are so detailed and simply wonderful to look at, and the game makes sure to switch between camera shots constantly. This, along with the character designs and clever use of 3D, makes for interesting interactions and storytelling. Regretably, there are things like the lip syncing and some scenes, namely the ones that show characters from afar, that do lack some of the detail the rest have. The devs have improved upon some of these scenes since the last demo, but there are still some of them, and they do contrast with the rest of the game.The sound design is good, and the music is great. The game makes excellent use of sound cues and feedback that makes the game feel more immersive, even more so if the player chooses to use a controller thanks to the haptic feedback. There are some lines that cut off either too late or too early and are fixable, while others sadly have some recording errors. These are all rare mistakes, but they do exist. The music, on the other hand, is what really not only sells the game for me but also inspired me to end up writing this review. Dabu, Brigitte, Lachlan, and Co. have done an almost excellent job at expressing the themes of this game through music; the soundtrack is pleasing to hear and to play. I think this is why me and so many other people find the music minigames to be our favorite parts of the game; they look, sound, and feel good to play.While it is subjective, I quite enjoyed most of the writing. We have to keep in mind that this is a game about teenage dinosaurs, after all. I personally did enjoy many of the interactions the characters had with each other and the world around them; they were surprisingly endearing and quite nostalgic. When it comes to things like how characters react to things like the "main antagonist" of the game, so to speak, and alternative routes or paths, I understand that some players may not like the linear nature of the game, and that's understandable. I personally enjoyed the direction the developers chose to go. If you can look past this, you will find that the message that the game is trying to express is actually admirable. Interactions with characters like Trish and Naomi are what stood out the most for me.To wrap it up, despite initial skepticism and differing opinions, Goodbye Volcano High shines with its captivating visuals, touching narrative, and immersive sound design. Give it a genuine chance, and maybe you will agree with this review.

_childDocuments_.review: To sum it up, Goodbye Volcano High is a short coming-of-age story. It doesn't get too deep in the weeds it creates around its premise of the literal end of the world, or to any of the drama it creates, but it has fun characters and great art and music. I would not praise it as much as the obvious comparisons like Night In The Woods or Snootgame, but what's there is still decent, and I would rate it highly, if only given the rocky development history it's had.The story is lacking and there are some confounding design decisions, which sucks, given it's a visual novel.Having played the demos released what feels like half a year ago now, I can say confidently they've fixed most if not all of the bugs I experienced there. I didn't notice any significant hitches in performance, any major game-breaking bugs, any crashes, or really anything else that soured the experience. The game also works fine on keyboard and mouse. The worst I saw program-wise were minor visual oddities and audio hitches that seemed more on the part of the choreography team than the programmers.There is a little bit of jank to the game, some things don't sound quite right, or cut off too soon- some animations are choppy, some scenes have strange framing, and so on. Most people would not notice or care, but it is a little off-putting sometimes. It's not bad enough to be jarring, but for how long this game has been in development, it's definitely rough around the edges. The developers went through a total story rewrite at some point in the game's history, due to their lead writer being canned for some fanfiction they wrote years and years ago, and the length of the story (and to an extent, its content) seems to reflect that. There's a certain "catching up" feeling to everything. There was love put into the game, absolutely, but it feels panicked at times. Some things are just Good Enough, not quite as perfect as they probably could be. Some things make sense at a glance, but when you think about them, really, really don't.The art and music are without a doubt the best part of the game, though I don't know what else it would have to stand on, being a visual novel. There are some oddities, though having a fair bit of art experience myself (7 years of drawing and painting as a hobby, now), I can say they were probably unavoidable. Front-facing snouts are always going to look strange on humanoids, that's just how it is. They did the best they could with the style they chose. The style clearly is where the love is, and it's wonderful visually and aurally.The rhythm game sections are nice, though it feels a little weird to play. The main arrow keys (joystick) input is done on , not on press or release. It goes against everything anyone will ever learn from any other rhythm game and any conclusion anyone would intuitively come to. if you're supposed to jam out to the music, you intuitively press and release the key or joystick, which results in missed inputs because it only allows input before the button has been released, so you have to be constantly rushing or EXACTLY RIGHT, and it feels off. It just doesn't make any sense. The other parts work fine, though, WASD (ABXY) popups and the Q/E (shoulder buttons) arrow things are forgiving enough to be accessible but have extra indicators for precision and seem to be timed properly.The little details like the extra photos, the flashbacks, the little social media tab, etc, are all really charming and cool as well. Not sure if they left in a placeholder asset or something, but one of the social media posts you can see in the auditorium is verbatim just a discord screenshot. The media tab is probably the funniest thing about the game. It adds flavor.******As for the story, it's okay. For the generation who was still in high school in 2020-2023, I think this would really hit home with them. A lot of the topics covered are really pertinent to highschoolers who lived through Covid, but only some of them seem applicable to a more general audience. The game covers themes of friendship / relationships, love, life goals, aspirations, and it feels like it wants to say something about having empathy and understanding what other people want despite your own desires, or how to compromise or something, though I'll get into why that doesn't quite work out a little further down.It feels a little bit... Padded, maybe? The first 2 chapters of the game felt like there was a lot of time where not much was happening.  of the game feels like not much happens. Not much drama, not much intrigue. Just life happening and going on for people who are in a school and have a few friends around. What drama there is, aside from the obvious meteor thing that hangs over everything like a giant cloud of dripping pitch, feels forced. Most conflict is caused by what seems like intentional bad faith rather than misunderstandings or lack of information or however arguments in real life usually start. One character will say something inflammatory or slightly angrily and then another character, rather than trying to assume the other is just sad or angry about something general (they are usually friends or have been friends for a long time), will take it personally and start a half-hearted, mostly mean-spirited argument.This happens on multiple occasions, and it feels fabricated. Like the argument itself was manufactured specifically for the purpose of creating drama in a story, rather than anything anyone cares about in . This does not feel or flow very good, it just makes me groan at how bad everyone seems to be at listening. Fang is especially guilty of being mean like this with little or no instigator, which feels awful, seeing as I am the one making decisions for them. I Have shouted out loud, "why are you making it worse?" It's just so obvious that these things did not need to be said. There could be a lesson about understanding others, like I mentioned before, but in the situations provided, the answer seems closer to "people will get over it eventually." The characters never seem to learn to just shut the hell up or think before they speak. Naomi, Trish, Fang, Reed; all of them end up saying something inflammatory that absolutely did not need to be said, or could have just been phrased better. And everyone else somehow manages to take it completely the wrong way, seemingly on purpose, exacerbating the problem for literally no reason. This would be less of a problem if the characters' reactions to others was less immediately aggressive, or if they actually learned to The ending is very wish-fulfillment-y, which feels like it takes away from the impact of the story. We never see what happens with the whole meteor thing, only that people panic and get freaked out. There is something to be said about the whole meteor thing being blown out of proportion or how modern news media exists to spread bad news and create worry because it creates panic and divides people, but I don't think that was even a sparkle in the devs' eyes when they included the 3 or 4 scenes that have a TV playing, or the social media tab on the pause menu. It seems more like an afterthought.Kinda like the whole non-binary thing, too? That was pushed big in the marketing, and that was something a lot of people brought up when this game was mentioned (on top of being the crux of snoot), but it was barely  in this game, and never brought up again. I get the feeling this was done in a similar vein to the whole LGBT thing with Fang x Naomi and Reed x his boyfriend, where it's just supposed to be a normal thing, which is an agreeable way to handle it, but with today's society, and what was advertised, I think it leaves something to be desired. It ends up as just a label that allows discriminators to discriminate.

_childDocuments_.review: I was introduced to this 'universe' by a friend with Wani hug that gator, not a game I thought I'd be a fan of but I absolutely loved it, eventually went on to try Snoot game myself and it was the same, a fantastic experience and story with wonderful characters.After hearing about Goodbye Volcano High I decided to jump into the game that I suppose 'started' it all (sort of), I'd heard plenty of negative things about GVH, I am aware that there was some sort of beef/conflict with the creators of the previous mentioned games and the makers of this one but I wont dive into that, end of the day just enjoy what you like and have fun.With that in mind I jumped into this with fairly low expectations and was rather surprisedDespite having a non-unique story, regular characters and its general quality and finish... this has been 1 of my favourite games this year. People will often compare this to the games mentioned above and I feel that while understandable given Snoot shares the same roster of characters (at least in terms of appearance), the games in question couldn't be further apart.The story was enjoyable but without doubt the highlight has to be the soundtrack which is phenomenal. The game is lacking some quality of life features such as a multiple saves, chapter selection and a better gallery for viewing specific scenes (all features that the 'fan' games incorporate). The game suffered with development hell and it shows, there are plenty of occasions where the quality dips and rises such as character animation where 1 character seems more animated and well done than others in a scene as well as the general story pace feeling a bit rushed at times.The game is also relatively short and while I doubt its an intended affect I found it sort of does help in a way to relate to the feeling of the characters and the lack of time to do and see certain things due to ongoing events, the feeling of things moving too fast and to wanting more time to experience and see things before the end.I wouldn't advise getting this game at full price due to the points I made above but I do feel it offers an enjoyable experience to those willing to try it but I would emphasise to not compare this to the fan games and go in with a clear mind.In a nutshell this is a experience that despite the opinions and drama I'd heard surrounding it, I am very glad I jumped into and enjoyed, I only wish there was more to it to enjoy.

_childDocuments_.review: Genuinely the first game to have ever blown me away enough to warrant writing a review for it, this game was the single most immersive visual novel I've ever played and my only gripes with it is that it doesn't have an extras screen to be able to replay scenes or songs, as well as there being some weird issues with pausing and voiced dialogue being cut off unnaturally sometimes (which is really brought out when a character is speaking into a microphone for some reason).The base gameplay of this game being a visual novel is enhanced in so many ways, as even though there's a max of only three choices (at most points), the dialogue boxes can sometimes fizzle out or are presented in a way that represents a specific emotion. In any situation, the choices could be moving around or have an electrifying or maybe soft-and-bubbly border that would perfectly encapsulate how, if I were in said situation, would have my own thoughts be moving around in my head. And then, past the regular dialogue-choosing gameplay, the rhythm game incorporated into the story is also one of the most fun rhythm games I have ever played, and I only wish that there were more songs to play with its mechanics.Past the base gameplay, the story is phenomenal and is what earned this game the top spot of the list of my favorite games of all time, if you're queer or you like music or you're neurodivergent or you don't really feel like you know what you're doing with your life, and ESPECIALLY if you're all four of those and more do NOT play this game you will be sobbing for a good half hour at least after it ends and you may possibly have your life be changed forevermore (speaking from personal experience). All in all, 19/10. It can't be 20 unfortunately because of the fact that I will never ever get to experience playing this game for the first time again, SO worth it!

_childDocuments_.review: Goodbye Volcano High is a game that wears its heart on its sleeve. If you saw the announcement during the Playstation showcase many years ago, it lives up to the potential there and more so.Goodbye Volcano High is a different form of visual novel. Rather than strictly text based, it is more akin to School Days where it takes the form of watching a cartoon where you would at times be given a chance to choose dialogue / thoughts / vibes for the protagonist Fang. Throughout the chapters of the game there is also a challenging and well done with gorgeous music. If you're not into the whole purely animation style game, you can turn it into a more traditional visual novel with making it click to progress through the text at all times rather than a few intentional points. There are collectables in the form of photos for a Yearbook, achievements, and a relationship system that revolves around the people that are in Fang's 'orbit' and how close they are to them.Goodbye Volcano High isn't an adventure game. You won't take control of Fang during their final school year, walk around the school or engage in much point and click gameplay. There are a couple of portions where things slow down and you do get a chance to get Fang's thoughts on various other dinos. It also isn't a harem style dating sim.The game is gorgeous. Playing on my set up the animation was smooth without any noticeable latency in the rhythm game. Character designs stand out apart from each other, and the profusion of colours really makes any crowd scene pop and not look monotonous. The original music blew me away, and I wish there was a music video mode to just watch what played during the rhythm game scenes and listen to the lyrics as opposed to trying to pass the songs. If there was a game I'd want to just sit down and watch, this would definitely be one of them.It does have support for mouse and keyboard as well as controller, but I can't speak for how well they are as I stuck with controller, which definitely works well with the rhythm game portions. Other than that, the controls that you have to use are clearly telegraphed at any time.I'm sure mileage will vary in regards to this point. So, out of the bag, its a story about a group of queer dinosaur friends. There aren't many other characters that appear beyond the core eight that are in Fang's orbit (and you can see who is in their orbit and their relative closeness to Fang through the pause menu). So beyond the core 8, the others are little more than a couple of supporting characters and aptly named 'randos' (of which there is one who I wish she played a larger role!)Each of the character feels human (I know, dinos being people too!) While you might look at them at a glance and think that they're stereotypes, taking the time to get to know them and there is a sense of the depths to who they are that can make them universally relatable. A couple of them in particularly were painfully resonant for me personally.Being a queer group of friends there is the peril that they would fall into the stereotype of 'everything is shiny and perfect', but it avoids it with a vengeance. They're flawed, and its up to the player whether how they want to act or react in regards to it, whether to push away or try to pull back together. Fang themselves isn't flawless, and at points comes across as the single most flawed of the primary cast.But they've got the chance to develop and grow on their journey together, one final high school year before the end of everything.For the core, I'd say that the replayability i tied to the achievements which will take 2 - 3 playthroughs to obtain. Theres only the one save file, hence the mandatory 2 at least. After that? Maybe after some time has passed, and if you enjoy the stories and characters enough that you want to go through them again.I could keep this review going, glowing along like Fang with all the things I liked and loved about their story, and that even at the moments they made me cringe, wince or cry, it was all worth it. Its a game that I could definitely recommend to lovers of animation, coming of ages stories, anthro dinos, queer stories, and the end of the world. Or various combinations of those.If you'd be hesitant because of who the cast are, please give them a try. They may seem like standard tropes at first, but they do have depth, and while they do talk about their identities both because its safe to do so with who they are, it feels like natural moments and conversations.I wish I hadn't sat on grabbing this so long, since I'd been genuinely interested from the trailer, and been a part of the community, but I did start playing a day before its one year anniversary. And it is all worth the journey. So if the trailers or my review have made you even a bit curious, I definitely recommend checking it out.

_childDocuments_.review: Edit: this discussion has some valid points that you should read beforehand: Writing this review after my first playthrough, and it certainly won’t be my last. I still have some achievements to claim as my own.It took me three of the song minigames to realize that you need to drag the analog sticks down instead of pressing them. It might be helpful to have the instructions viewable again after the initial introduction, somewhere other than just the game’s wiki.That minigame could easily be its own full-title rhythm game. I enjoyed it a lot—it requires intense focus and serious thumb coordination to hit all the notes. The way you embedded it into the cute story about our prehistoric ancestors was spot on. My only complaint is that there were too few of those minigames. There were a few song-writing scenes that could have been perfect opportunities to play through them again.Aside from that, the music is beautiful and gave me goosebumps. I was even forced into a relationship—can’t complain!I got 6 hours of entertainment from my first playthrough alone and will probably spend more time farming to 100% the game. At just under 20€ on sale, it’s definitely worth it in my experience. If you enjoy short story-driven games, a touch of rhythm gameplay, and are open (you don't have to be pro, but not being anti helps a lot because you will be confronted with it the whole time) to LGBTQ+ and furries—or in this case, scalies—take your shot.
