_childDocuments_.review: Recently, it’s become standard fare for Devolver to publish somewhat odd yet interesting games from up-and-coming studios. After Carrion, Loop Hero, and Inscryption (to name but a few), Cult of the Lamb is the latest game to follow this particular trend.The story of the game starts as four mysterious entities called Bishops order the death of the last sacrificial lamb. With all of them dead, the Bishops believe, no one will be able to perform the ritual and summon back the fifth, imprisoned, entity, The One Who Waits.However, The One Who Waits decides to resurrect the lamb and task it with rebuilding his cult so that one day he may return and take his place as the supreme deity.Mechanically, the game is a mix of a settlement sim and a roguelite. Controlling the lamb, you’ll build your cult’s compound and take care of your followers’ physical and spiritual needs. You’ll also perform crusades into the realms of rival Bishops, exploring maps, killing enemies, and collecting resources.I first heard of this game during the last Steam demo fest, when my GF downloaded and tried out the demo. After watching her play for a while, I was especially impressed with the audio and visual design of the game.The game world is designed to look like a children’s storybook, with cute and colorful characters and vibrant and detailed backgrounds. The soundtrack is superb (the track that plays in your cult compound is a real earworm) and works really well to immerse you in the experience.Thematically, combining this type of design with the macabre and occasionally disturbing storytelling creates a nice contrast. I also found that the fact the characters are so cute creates more of a connection with them. This is especially true when your followers turn old and start shuffling around with a cane wearing a perpetual smile.Cult of the Lamb tries to do a lot with a little, both in terms of themes and storytelling, as well as gameplay and mechanics. Unfortunately, none of these aspects seem fully thought out and developed.From a storytelling perspective, the game touches on themes of dead or dying gods, sacrifice, and the abuse that lies at the core of every cult. However, none of these are explored in any depth.The fact that the creators also include things like polygamy, cannibalism, body horror, and many others, suggests that they thought that the mere inclusion of content like this would be enough to shock people. After all, this is a game about building and running a cult of an eldritch god. But in a world where games like The Binding of Isaac, Sanitarium, or re:Kinder exist, this seems a little tame and insincere. Of course, I might be completely off the mark here, and the creators just wanted to make a cutesy, but violent game, but then why use the cult angle?Running the cult compound in this game usually means constant hand-holding. Your job is to boost your followers’ faith by holding sermons, keeping them fed, and keeping the compound clean and tidy. In return, your followers generate devotion, which you use to upgrade the lamb’s powers and unlock new buildings you can build.This requires a lot of busy work on your part since very few of the tasks mentioned above can be automated in any significant way. Let’s take food production as an example.One of the very first things you can unlock is building farmable plots. Each one requires you to plant a seed, water the plant, and harvest it when it grows fully. You can then take the produce you harvested and use it to cook food for your followers.If you want to automate this process, you can unlock and build a farm. Assigning a follower to the farm makes them plant and water the nearby plots. But you still need to harvest the produce. Much later in the game, you can unlock an upgraded version of the farm, where a follower can now harvest the plants on their own, but you still need to pick up the produce and cook the food yourself.Every other aspect of life at the compound follows the same formula. The latrines need cleaning out, the resources and devotion need to be claimed, dead followers need to be buried, and it seems you are the only one who can do it. I understand that this is probably there so you’d have to come back to the compound during the late game, but it turns players off investing in more complex buildings if they only provide a minimal benefit. It begs the question of what’s preventing you from speedrunning the game with a basic compound, 20 sleeping bags, and your followers doing their business on the ground.The fighting is also fairly basic: you can swing your weapon, lob a special attack, and roll out of the way. Each crusade randomly generates a new map and you can choose which path you take by going from node to node. There are enough different types of nodes to keep things interesting (eg. fight maps, resource nodes, special encounters), but after a while, things can get a little predictable.Tarot cards are an interesting addition. Collecting them gives the lamb passive abilities (like extra HP or poisonous weapons), but they can only be found on fighting nodes. This presents the players with a choice of weighing the potential benefits of a full deck of cards vs the risk of fighting more enemies in order to collect them.On occasion, the combat RNG can feel slightly unfair, especially when fighting enemies that can spawn more units. This can quickly turn into a fight against a horde where it’s difficult to even see where your character is.It’s always kind of disappointing running into a game like this. There are so many elements that, with just a little more polish, could have brought Cult of the Lamb from pretty good to great. Still, the game offers a very enjoyable experience wrapped in one of the prettiest packages I’ve seen in a while. A combination of roguelite hack-and-slash and settlement sim where you run a cult and kill gods. Beautiful design, compelling atmosphere, enjoyable gameplay. Feels slightly exploitative, gameplay and story not deep enough.

_childDocuments_.review: Cult of the Lamb is a casual game with little depth, which appears to be its intent. This does not make it a bad game, but rather, a good one for its audience.If you've ever found yourself interested in the Roguelike genre but unable to dedicate time or mental energy to popular staples, Cult of the Lamb is great. The same is true for colony simulators. It touches on the very basics of each genre in a way where you can safely play with them as a casual player, which is a great thing, as both genres are typically rather intensive.The game is not very deep. You learn how it works and that's it. The things that change in the mechanics don't actually change them much, making it very easy to cruise. As a game intended for casual play, this makes perfect sense. At the same time, there is space to make your own challenges and create your own difficulty. You simply have to make that choice yourself.That's not to say it'll be as fun for non-casuals. Optomizing is easy, combat rather dull due to the roguelike elements not really mattering and runs needing to be short to account for the colony management, and as many elements can't be changed to make things harder or more interesting as those that can. (Many being staples, such as locking yourself into a specific weapon, not upgrading your skills, etc.)All in all, it's not a great game, but it is a good one. It's made for a specific audience and caters to that audience well, but it lacks pull for those outside of it. If you're looking for a casual experience, Cult of the Lamb is a great choice. As a lover of roguelikes and colony sims myself, it's actually refreshing to have something to play even when I can't give it my all.

_childDocuments_.review: This is what happens when arts people try to make a game, and don't listen to technical people on how to balance it properly.Nothing is balanced properly. There's no concept of risk/reward.I kept waiting for the game to start making sense, but it never does.The game was too easy, even on Hard difficulty, until almost 20 hours in. The weapon you get at the start of a run makes ALL the difference between whether that run is going to be easy or hard. If it's hard, it's hard in an incredibly tedious way-- not in a challenging way. The faster weapons are objectively better, and if you don't get a fast weapon at the start (sword or dagger), then it's best that you cut the run and start another.The rewards you find along the way are 95% useless cosmetic junk. The other rewards are followers, which are effectively interchangeable faceless commodities, or Tarot cards, which have so little influence on your runs that they are pointless.If you've played Binding of Isaac, especially the last expansions for Rebirth, then you know what it's like to 'unlock rewards' which just add useless items to the item pool, and are therefore actually handicaps for you as well as making the game a lot more boring.This game does that too, with ALL non-cosmetic unlocks being either 'make all weapons marginally stronger' or 'more curses added' or 'more weapons added' or 'more Tarot cards added'.Curses are just a secondary weapon, and they are all useless by the way.The thing is, there's no synergy between curses or weapons or Tarot cards. When you unlock things, you're just letting the random dice roll have more available outcomes. There's no player agency, no decision-making, it's just boring.I encountered one rare room where I was offered a reward if I didn't take damage for 3 rooms. I did that, and the reward was a worthless 'large gift' which I could give to a follower for a small increase in loyalty. These gifts are so time-consuming and pointless to give out, that even if I have infinitely many of them, I won't use them because the process of giving out gifts is extremely tedious.Also, I can use the 'confession booth' once a day to have more effect every day than a large gift!The followers you get are indistinguishable; nothing about their behaviour changes with increasing loyalty level, except some numbers go up faster. You'd think the high-loyalty ones would be the last to dissent, but no, the game appears to pick a dissenter randomly.Followers don't remember the jobs you set them. So you need to keep telling followers to do the same job, especially farming.The game gives you so many shops to buy things, but they are all either Tarot cards which have nearly no influence on your game and you have no control over anyway, or cosmetic junk.At 20 hours in, I was wondering how the game expected me to get all this gold to buy anything from these shops. I never bought a single thing because I couldn't afford it.Turns out that even if you have tax-collecting followers, and send 3 follower out on missionaries to collect gold at all times, these things don't give you any appreciable amount of gold. Turns out the only REAL way to earn gold in this game is to perform a ritual which collects gold. Sucks if you didn't pick that ritual as a permanent binary unlock choice, by the way.That's one example of how the game is grossly unbalanced-- it introduces several mechanisms to get gold, but none of them matter except one.But everything in this game is like that. It makes you feel like you're playing the game wrong, but actually the game is so poorly balanced that it's surprising they were even willing to release it in this state.Also, regarding the game's aesthetic: from the moment I started it up, I found it too visually complex to be comfortable with. I thought maybe some younger players would be okay with that though. But I think my initial feeling was right-- the artists got carried away. The game wastes a ton of screen real estate, showing huge amounts of space on the edges of combat rooms. I had assumed that the game would introduce enemies that shoot at you from off the edge of the room, like a bullet hell. But nope, they just wasted that screen real estate for no reason.The final straw for me was when I was doing a run, and I collected a whole ton of resources I was glad to have. Actually, just bones for rituals, and an 'eye of the witness' to give to some guy. The other resources don't mean anything at this point, anyway. I brainwashed my followers because the game more-or-less arbitrarily took away all of their faith due to random events I have no control over, and I headed into combat to replenish my bones so I could perform rituals to restore their faith when I got back.I went into a "?" room, and the "?" room took away all my resources that I collected in that entire run. All of it. For no reason. I had no control over this. It even took away the 'eye of the witness' which appeared to be a one-time thing per run.That was when I had enough. The creators of this game don't know how to make a game. They should have stuck to an interactive art project or something.

_childDocuments_.review: Cult of the Lamb is a delightful twist on the cult genre, where managing an adorable cult becomes simultaneously funny and challenging. Picture this: fluffy cult leaders, sacrificial rituals with cute sheep, and an unholy dose of chaos. The game taps into the unexpected joy of herding sheep, turning it into a strategic, yet amusing experience. Forget traditional world domination – here, it's all about embracing your inner shepherd and navigating the whimsical world of fluffy followers. Cult of the Lamb takes the cult game concept to a whole new level, proving that the key to a successful cult is, unsurprisingly, a flock of fuzzy companions. It's a quirky, humorous journey where you might find yourself chanting "Baa-men" instead of the usual "Amen." So, if you've ever wondered what it's like to lead a cult with a woolly twist, this game is your ticket to an entertaining, sheep-filled adventure.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wish I had a "this is fine, BUT" option, because that's where I'm at.I pre-ordered this with the DLC completely going in with no expectations or awareness of the hype; my spouse just told me that I'd enjoy the game. And I did get a lot of enjoyment out of it! But I also ran into disappointment and frustration around every corner and felt vastly underwhelmed at times. I'll try to break it down (be mindful that some gameplay spoilers are ahead):Like everyone else has said: aesthetically, it's a great artistic endeavor. The character designs are original and fun and the environmental concepts are downright unsettling despite the cutesy art style. However, a lot of detail is lost in that it all blurs together. Maps are monochromatic with slightly variant shades that provide no real contrast. Enemies (with maybe one exception per layer) match the map palette and blend seamlessly into the tall grass (which makes the already obnoxious combat even moreso). With the game's fast pace, it's hard to really take in and appreciate all the talent and labor. Not to mention that if you have any significant degree of visual impairment, good luck trying to hack and slash your way into hitting, uh, something?--CotL did a great job adding in many necessary accessibility features that sadly lack in many AAA titles, and I'm totally grateful, but I and several other friends were severely nerfed by not having a colorblind mode.Speaking of nerf: the curve between easy and medium mode is ridiculous. Easy may as well be renamed "story mode," as that more accurately represents what it is, while medium requires significantly more skill and familiarity with roguelites to make substantial progress. There's no in-between "normal" mode that helps newbies transition to more challenging gameplay nor an entry level for players who enjoy a balance between casual and stimulating. And as for the combat itself, your success has less to do with your skill in rougelites as it does with how lucky you are with your pull of tarot cards, cache of spirit hearts and curse and weapon levels and buffs. Randomly generated weapons aren't foreign to roguelites, but the lack of meaningful growth in combat reflects the lack of meaningful advancement in the simulation portion of the game.I love choices matter games, and I love Animal Crossing: Pocket Camp, so I thought that the compound progression system and follower recruitment system would be a real treat for me. For a good portion of the game, it was! Sure, you spend most of your early game cleaning up your followers' ♥♥♥♥ (and sometimes feeding it to them--which gets old real fast), but you could see the fruits of your labors and reap the rewards through building mills and mines and through planting crops. The concept of unlocking functional upgrades and cosmetic assets through the devotion system is honestly quite enjoyable, and many of the rewards really do feel worth the effort. But by 15 hours in, provided you have a substantial number of followers and tabernacles/gravestones, you can acquire virtually every upgrade the game has to offer. There's no real planning or strategy you have to put into your tree. You're not going to miss out on anything in this playthrough that you'd have to go back for in a future replay.And all of your progress feels for naught when you unlock doctrines and acquire rituals. You may never need to touch your crops or send your followers out on missions for meat if you spam the fasting ritual (after you pick up the "half the cooldown time" perk in the devotion tree, of course) or pick up the cannibalism doctrine. You may never need to rebuild another mill or mine again when you come back with campaigns with more grass than what you could ever use in spamming decor to farm loyalty. You will never want for coin when you can extort your followers individually at no loss of loyalty or demand a large tithe during a ritual at a small loyalty debuff (which you can more than make up for by spamming other rituals or by locking in your loyalty with another ritual unlockable via a sidequest). In short: your choices don't matter. Your cult will be successful regardless of how you choose to play. The consequences that are built in (faith dissenters, loyalty hits and item hits from martyrdom) make such a small impact that can easily be overcompensated.The gameplay identity itself is... all over the place. There are several minigames that are not particularly fun or rewarding that don't contribute to the main story--knucklebones definitely isn't what gwent is to The Witcher. Your progress in the dungeon crawler portion only amounts to cosmetic upgrades for your compound. The dungeon crawler is the strongest portion of the game with randomly generated maps that don't feel stale and a compelling narrative told through npcs you encounter by chance depending on the path you take to the boss arena. Each of these components feel totally separated from each other, as if they were their own individual games and not part of a unified world.I won't go terribly deep into the issues with the game bugs themselves as, quite frankly, the developers' patch updates really spell it all. The game is a hydra: for every bug that's allegedly fixed (e.g., the infamous arena soft lock that still persists after the patch that addressed it), more bugs crawl out of the woodwork. I'm currently sitting just shy of 20 hours (at least 5 of which is me retracing my steps after being repeatedly softlocked), and I'm not planning on touching the game again until I'm sure that my game won't be totally bricked. I don't want to lose my progress because, frankly, I have no interest in rebuilding my compound.The majority of what made the game fun for me was streaming, and from what I can tell, Devolver really went hard on ingratiating this game to streamers from the get-go (largely to promote the hype through influencer-granted early access) all the way to the point where the devs made an ambitious Twitch extension to allow direct follower participation. However, the extension has been about as touch-and-go as the game itself. Every other day the help/hinder functions are turned on and off (and when they are on, they don't seem to work), the follower creation raffle (when it does recognize a winner) is occasionally softlocked to where the streamer has to close and re-open the raffle screen. Without the consistent and fully-featured extension, that engagement is just not there, and frankly the streaming experience is just not nearly as fun.I genuinely want to finish the game and to have an honest final opinion once I've seen the whole plot come together, but in its current state and having exhausted the entirety of the compound progression (the only reason I'm behind in story progression is because I've given up on combat so many times out of pure frustration from being softlocked in the boss arena), my motivation to keep playing is just not there. I don't have any buyer's remorse, and I don't feel like it was a waste, but I do feel that maybe I should have held off on purchasing the game.EDIT: to the people who really think they're doing something by giving me clown awards, thanks for the free steam points!!

_childDocuments_.review: Elder gods decide to sacrifice you. They make a sacrificial lamb of you. Ironically, you are literally a lamb. But not the one who resigned themselves to their fate. Luck in the form of the enemy of elders gods saved you from a tragic final. Now you are alive, dangerous, and ready to take revenge. The only thing is to get strong enough to challenge the enemies. To do that, you need followers who give you what you seek. With the help of a supernatural patron, you will run your cult and kill elders gods.It`s how your Cult of Lamb will be started (or not "Cult of Lamb"—it's yours; you can give it whatever name you like). And it`s up to you how your cult will finish. The adventure of the little cultist lamb has started.The game provides us with two main mechanics. First is the cult builder sim. You manage your village, look after followers, build buildings, hold ceremonies, etc. Second is rouge-like dungeon rides called “Crusade”. You collect resources, get new followers, and, of course, defeat bosses. Also, there are mini-games and some interesting mechanics which make the game process deeper. All of these things combine ideally you don`t have a chance to be bored (maybe a bit with a village). Tired of building a village - move to crusade, tired of dungeons - your followers are awaiting. Switching mechanics imperceptibly moves you to the game final, providing a lot of joy. What else provides joy is the game style. I`m sure Cult of Lamb developers hardly see this review, however, I need to say that the character design and visuals are terrific. Your designers are rocks. Characters look not only cute but also scary. Which is not so easy to achieve, obviously.Cult of Lamb is practically devoid of cons. Someone might say modest duration is the main minus of the game. But developers works on that and the latest update provides us with additional quests after beating the last boss. So I would say the major con is not addictive base-building mechanics. Yes, it`s good to get rest from the crusade by building a village but it might be much more interesting if we have some reasons to improve the cult, except to be stronger on crusades. Or to build a more posh-looking village.However if you are fan of unusual settings, not trivial ideas and rouge-lite games choosing Cult of Lamb would be great idea!  Be sure to try

_childDocuments_.review: Cult of the Good Game DesignCotL is two games in one the likes of which many have been made before but all to often these titles are shovel ware rogue lites that all feel the same. This game really tries to innovate the genres whilst master crafting the experience to feel immersive and ultimately fun.The game consists of base building and the binding of issac style dungeon crawler and both feed off each other. Both games feel really fun with beautiful top tier artwork and snappy animations whilst you craft your experince throughout. The cult theme really works here and is a pillar of much of the games great humour. Maybe this theme isnt normie friendly enough for the masses I'm not sure but arent we all sick of dnd fantasy themes or done to death simplistic sci fi rogue lites I for one am and CotL is super refreshing by contrast. Given the games clear replayability factor and the price I think this is a no brainer in terms of recommending and buying at full price and I would not be surprised if this game makes it into the top 10 games of the year at very least for art direction which for me is a 10. Overall there are moments in this game to which the medium of video games is truly emboldened in its ultimate form. The graphics the music the feel of combat all sing in unison triggering the buzz only video games can give you when all your senses are being stimulated. I have had no bugs up to now and tbh this game feels alot like something you would see made in Nintendos gold era it has that level of a quality feel to it but with a darker tone which I love alot. Like drdisrespect says its a snooze fest out there in the gaming world so love it or hate I recommend giving cult of the lamb a shot its at the very least trying to stand out from all the terrible games being shoved out right now.

_childDocuments_.review: I've beaten this game and I am now on the road to 100%.This game is unlike anything I have ever played and I mean that in a good way. There has never been a game as endearing as this one. It has all the charm of games like Animal Crossing and LittleBigPlanet but with the dark and moody atmosphere and feel of Binding of Isaac. The gameplay is far from that however, while still not straying too far from its influences. You will crawl dungeons in a room by room fashion, a-la Binding of Isaac, however you don't lose everything when you die, nor are you forced right back in. This is because a lot of the things you will be gathering on your dungeoneering (crusades) is materials to level and build in your cult "base". The majority of this game focuses on growing and expanding your cult, getting them to be more loyal to you and then sacrificing them (is one of the options) to grow even stronger. There is multiple choices for everything in this game and it's such a unique experience I will wholeheartedly give this game a 10/10, once a few bugs are patched that is!tl;drThis game is cozy, it's heartwarming, its sadistic, its intense, it's rewarding, its FUN. My game of the year 2022, buy it if you like rogue-lites and base building.Stay away if you're scared of demonic imagery, otherwise, rock-on!EDIT: I forgot to say in the original post, THE MUSIC IS INCREDIBLE

_childDocuments_.review: Some of what I say may seem negative, but in practise, I had a lot of fun with this game and it didn't overstay its welcome (though if it dragged a little longer it might have).For the super positives, this game is visually stunning and the soundtrack is excellent. Not much to say on this.For the regular positives, I enjoyed the simplified dungeon crawler gameplay (slightly less than I thought I would) as well as the simplified colony sim (slightly more than I thought I would).The main issue, which you probably know if you've read any other reviews, is this game is a bit shallow. There's not much variety to the gameplay - this shows especially in the doctrines, which at first glance seem like they'd shake up the formula a lot, but I found myself using only one of two rituals throughout my entire playtime and the modifiers had little effect. It seems vast at first but by the end you use like half of what the game offers you because you have no reason to use the rest.The action sections were fairly easy, even on Hard (though the final boss took me a while), though still enjoyable cause they required decent focus.The cult sections were actually super relaxing, despite not having that much variety. This is in no small part helped by the aesthetics mentioned earlier, but generally it's fun to just get resources and manage your group.The empty 'Roadmap' icon implies there will be big content updates, which I think this game sorely needs and I'll probably revisit it if/when they come out. I 100%ed this game, and it didn't take me much longer than just beating it normally, since I naturally got most of the collectables and could sweep the rest up quite quickly.Also it's worth mentioning that this game was very buggy on launch, though they fixed pretty much all the major ones very quickly. I have encountered a couple graphical glitches, one minor error that was a bit annoying and I got softlocked once (but I could easily get back to the same point so it was fine). If you're buying it now, you will probably have a decently smooth experience.I feel incredibly mixed about this game, but looking back on it, I had fun throughout despite my issues - it was only that I had quite high expectations going in.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a great concept with more content than most indie games. This isn't trying to be a retro game (and I get the homage to Binding of Isaac, Saturday Morning Cartoons, Animal Crossing, etc.) so hopefully, if there's a sequel, it will have more 2.5D graphics and elaborate character animations. I have to mention that the combat doesn't really do it for me. But, thankfully, that's only about a third of the game. There's so much to do an explore, and you'll be so distracted running your cult, you'll barely notice the simplistic hack and slash mechanics of your rogue-lite runs.  I also want to say that the game's engine stability is strangely all over the place. My Steam Deck crashed 5 times in my 30 hours...but that could be a Steam OS issue maybe?Anyway, play this game. It's great.

_childDocuments_.review: No where near finished on this game and i can already see myself coming back to it for a replay. _childDocuments_.review: I think a lot in this game is done right.Mixing management with an Isaac-like Roguelike Combat Formula works quite well.Its a good contrast. Despite a lot of peoples opinion that the management aspect is tedious, I find it quite simple and relaxing. Combat wise the game lacks some level of depth tho. Most of the cards are just clutter and some things are just not worth upgrading at all. While the types of melee weapons play a little bit differently, all feel very similar in a way, because they basically just differ in their attack speed. They have different move sets, but when you try to avoid getting hit, its more like hit and run for every type of weapon and it doesnt really matter which one you get. Secondary Upgrades like Poison, Vampiric, Necrotic attacks doesnt really add up in a way that it alters the gameplay greatly. Art wise the game is gorgeous but it has some problems with "design follows function". The point of view in the game with a very small character makes the game hard to play on small screens like the Steam Deck. While the art design in combination with the diagonal point of view is very nice to look at, it would most certainly play better in a more traditional point of view. Getting hit by stuff you just didnt see properly happens a lot of time.8/10

_childDocuments_.review: The game itself is good and enjoyable, I recommend you to play it.BUT!At the end of the day it's a patchwork of other different, more successful games. It takes a bit of everything and clumps it together in a way that somehow works but, if you played said games, feels like something you've already played... but without the depth that you've already seen in such games.Cult of the Lamb has Hades' combat, Isaac's rooms system, Animal crossing's base management and art, Stardew Valley's fishing and so on. You can clearly feel that you're not playing an original formula and that's where you start losing interest: copying other games' successful formulas it's not a sin, but if you're not trying to improve those in a substantial way you'll end up with an "averagely good" patchwork game that doesn't really shine. If you've played none of such other games, Cult of the Lamb may be a great gaming experience. If you are a seasoned player you can still enjoy it but you will definitely notice the unoriginality of it through the patchwork, which will prevent the feeling of having played a memorable experience.

_childDocuments_.review: So I recommended, but see this as a mixed recommendation. not because this game is bad, it's good, but if you're going in expecting a full blown roguelite like I did, you're gonna be disappointed.The gameplay loop revolves between managing your cult (making sure you cultists are fine, building infrastructures until they become as self sufficient as possible) and going into crusades (the actual roguelite part of the game) with randomized dungeons and such.The first part is where the game shines. The animations are cute and funny, ressources management and scales are great, it's honestly huge fun and very satisfying to see your cult grow.However, I feel like combat and dungeon crawling are where the game is weaker and more flawed. Basically, it's one of those "wtf hit me" kind of game. I put most of the blame on the graphics that, albeit very cute and pretty, tend to make hitboxes very hard to read. Sometimes you're like "how did I hit/not hit?" or "how did I get/not get hit by that", though I also think runs lack variety. Add a couple of annoying, unintuitive enemy design and "button-mashable" bosses, and you're in for an explosive cocktail of "eh, could be better."When I say unintuitive enemy designs, which is by far the biggest flaws, it consists both in the difficult to read hitboxes, but also in enemies that will be way too hard to avoid (because if you dodge ahead of the attack, they're gonna instantly reposition and hit you anyway)One enemy straight up "breaks the rules" of the game by having deflectable arrows that you're supposed to deflect back to him. It is, to my knowledge, the only enemy of the game with that mechanic, and the overall mess of combat and animations will make you think that you managed to damage it by chance more than anything else. Note that this enemy can absolutely ruin your run if you didn't get its mechanic (which, as I said, is very very oblivious).Anyway, very fun and cute game, with great town building gameplay. But if you're looking for intense roguelite combat, I'd recommend going for Hades or something.

_childDocuments_.review: Cult of the Lamb is a cute base building game with rogue-like elements which involve growing your cult, building a little commune for your cult and also going into the lairs of evil demonic-like entities so that your god can be the last one standing.The games art direction is phenomenal, I've always been a fan of games which handle what could be quite serious topics, especially in real life, but with a cute charm to it. Of course you're still going around indoctrinating people, stealing their money, sacrificing them etc but its all very light-hearted. The roguelike elements come from you going into the woods and going room to room defeating enemies with a plethora or weapons and spells but they start off weak. However as your cult grows stronger you can invest you inspirations and fellowship into different tech/skill trees to make you a lot stronger.You unlock more buildings, decorations and mechanics as the game progresses. You can even name every little woodland creature that joins your cult so its a great game for putting your friends into; a feature I'd have in all games if it would let me.Overall Cult of the Lamb is a great game, there's honestly not much to dislike except that maybe the food system is a little hard to fully get to grips with and doesn't reflect properly. A few bugs here and there but they can be solved with a restart. The game isn't difficult but its still rewarding, I'd recommend this to anyone. 8/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Cult of the Lamb is a combination management sim and roguelite, which sounds like an odd combination, but works fairly well. You play as a lamb, recruited by an imprisoned god to overthrow a cadre of false gods and restore the imprisoned god to their rightful place. The lamb must build and manage a cult of followers, establishing tenets of faith and collecting their devotion, while using the resources gained on crusades to feed and build the cult. The game is, once again, a combination roguelite and management sim, with the roguelite elements providing the resources used to build and improve the colony.  The roguelite elements follow the traditional beats of providing several weapons options, varying those weapons options between runs, and allowing upgrades and swaps throughout the run. Each run lasts ten to fifteen minutes, with progressively more difficult enemies as the player progresses, and different items that can be acquired along the way.These items are then used for thee colony management side of the game. Here, the player feeds and cares for their followers, building different buildings that allow for resource harvesting, and generally maintains the colony. The player can also choose what the cult actually believes in, ranging from being free-ranging hippies to merciless cannibals who sacrifice their elderly and feast on their flesh. It’s a bit difficult to decide how I feel about the combination of elements of the game because I am, once again, playing on a touchpad, and there is no roguelite in existence that is optimised for touchpad. By linking resource harvesting to the roguelite elements, more management-minded players have no choice but to plow into fights they will almost certainly lose. In my playthrough, I got to a frustrating point where, no matter how I tried, I could not progress through the combat, and therefore, couldn’t progress my colony any further either. While the roguelite crusades make absolute sense from a narrative perspective, they can get frustrating, especially with a difficulty that seems to scale up just a bit faster than I do. Upon seeing certain weapons spawn at start (I’m looking at you, giant axe), I knew the entire dungeon run would be a wash. My dislike of Cult of the Lamb’s dungeons isn’t solely a result of my own lack of skills. There is a shallowness to these dungeons that is the natural consequence of the player having to split their time and energy between two radically different genres. As the player moves through the dungeons, time continues to pass outside, and with it, the actions and needs of the cult continue. The dungeon runs must necessarily be brief to give the player time to complete them and still hurry back to manage their cult. This means that Cult of the Lamb never gets the chance to be a true roguelite, but remains an odd malformed dungeon crawler, more reliant on being quick on the controls than on the careful planning and building that characterises many other roguelites. I am generally bad at roguelites, yes, but I am uniquely bad at Cult of the Lamb because it doesn’t provide me the opportunity to make a build that makes the game work for me. It provides a shallow hack-and-slash as one of its fundamental progression mechanics, leading to slogging gameplay. The dungeon elements can be fun, but they require a skill I don’t have, and a patience for hack-and-slash that I will never possess. The flipside of this mixed-genre gameplay is the colony management elements. Much like with the roguelite elements, the colony management elements recognise that they are sharing space with the roguelite elements, and as such, are less developed than they might have been otherwise. While there is space to customise and build a cult following a specific vision, that space is limited. The colony will always face the same situations with the same choices, creating no real incentive to do anything but the ideal play. This becomes coupled with the more tedious elements of colony management. While the cult members can be assigned to tasks, many tasks have to be unlocked over time and with the resources gathered through the dungeon crawl. Tasks like cleaning and watering crops are, at least initially, the sole purview of the player character. When coupled with the mechanics to raise followers’ loyalty, the gameplay loop becomes a cycle of talking to people, cleaning up messes, and solving every problem ad infinitum. I spent my time managing the colony thinking about the automation I could build if I had the resources from the dungeons. I spent my time in the dungeon thinking about the time I wasn’t spending managing and leveling up the colony. Rather than one element creating a break in the routine of the other, each distracts from the other, and makes of it a lesser experience. The final nail in Cult of the Lamb’s coffin for me, though, is its humour and how its art style embodies that humour. Cult of the Lamb has a very specific style that I think of as Oatmeal-esque. It’s a style that accentuates over-the-top cartoon violence and gore, fixates on poop as one of its core sources of humour, and draws its characters as hyper-cartoonish versions of themselves. It’s a juvenile style of humour that lacks the self-awareness of something like Crush Your Enemies, instead expecting its audience to agree with the humour at face value, and laugh because of the references to the thing both the creator and the audience find funny. This is entirely subjective, but I hate this style of humour, and I hate this style of art. While its sense of humour may appeal to some members of its audience, I was thoroughly put-off by Cult of the Lamb’s poop jokes and art style. There are some games where the various components of the game are compelling enough for me to overlook a difference in artistic taste. With Cult of the Lamb, when both game major elements are already a bit of a chore, the humour just cements the sense that the game has nothing it can offer me. Cult of the Lamb is not a bad game. As much as I have torn into what I see as elements that are lacking, the reality is that I have also sunk a dozen hours into it in the hope that it would become something more than it was. I wanted the colony management elements to work. I wanted the dungeon crawler to be fun. I kept coming back to it in the hopes that the game I wanted this to be would appear. It never did, and I am disappointed by that. Instead, I’m left with a game that combines the most shallow elements of its gameplay with an off-putting art style and sense of humour. It has the potential to be interesting and more than what it is, but flubs it, instead becoming a tedious slog of poop jokes and monotonous chores.

_childDocuments_.review: This is an adorable little fusion of Animal Crossing and the Binding of Isaac and it somehow managed to merge two entirely different worlds almost seamlessly to create an incredibly addictive gameThe story is interesting, the music is killer, the visuals are the perfect blend of dark and adorable. The core gameplay loop revolves around you running roguelike dungeon crawls to progress the story, gather resources and cult members, etc, and going back to your main hub where you manage your cult and tend to the needs of your base and your cultists. Both aspects of gameplay are enjoyable and if the game becomes too difficult for you in the dungeon crawl, you can simply spend some time growing your cult to snowball the other part of the game into a cake walk. If you like games like binding of isaac or animal crossing, you'll feel right at home with this one.If I had any complains about the game, it would be that there is a certain limit to how self-sufficient your cult can be which means there will always be a somewhat tedious level of micromanaging to make sure your cult is happy, and that, though you can continue playing after you beat the story, there isn't much to do past find any unlocks you missed before. I beat the game in about 10 hours? and that was taking my time. And yet, despite my complaints, I keep finding myself coming back to the game, creating more cute little cultists for my cult, and testing myself to see how far I can get along the dungeon runs again.This game is an absolutely must-play for me and I highly reccomend it.

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely love this game! The art design is very charming and it has some great looking characters. The story is fairly interesting, but I wish we learned a bit more about the Lamb's past and the world as a whole. The combat leveling system is fun and can allow you to make some customization. The combat does leave something to be desired, but all around is decent and fun with a lot of variety.  I LOVE the soundtrack. It creates a fantastic atmosphere for the game and makes it really enjoyable. The cult management is good, but I'm used to dealing with more environmental pressures like you encounter in Don't Starve and Oxygen Not Included, so by comparison this game feels rather simple and lacking in depth. This game would be great for folks less experienced with platformers or point and click games (or even games in general). Playing on the easiest mode is very forgiving and even playing on the hardest mode really isn't too bad if you don't mind spending more time doing combat. Unlike a lot of games that come out, this one doesn't fall victim to being too hard, thus causing folks to stop their play-through. Overall, great game! What's really annoying is that your town continues to develop in the background, so that many of your followers at the beginning will keep getting hungry, angry, or sick from you just going for a simple normal dungeon run to get ressources you need for them. There should be a shop to trade ressources and there's just nothing to do with all of your money and ressources after you get past some point in the game.Also, I think the release definitely could have used some more time for polishing: Apart from several bugs which could still be considered teething troubles, the game just seems very poorly optimised and made me suffer from some very extreme lags during some activities like cooking in my town and even in dungeons while things were being built in my town despite using a very stable PC setup.I am afraid I must say I'm mostly disappointed that this game may have come out a tad too early. _childDocuments_.review: How can I not recommend this cute but demonic mini soulslike & roguelike game?The premise is simple, it doesn't need to be best writing of 2022 award kinda level. You will start a cute little cult with animal followers that you gotta level up, keep sheltered but also...EXPLOIT! The game gives you much freedom about all of the above, depending on everyone's choices. And I loved that aspect because it offers many ways to do this goal as well as maybe hinder with your later gameplay because of these choices or by forgetting to do sermons or rituals to keep the folks as loyal as possible.The combat is simplistic yet satisfying. I like to combine my dodge roll with tarot cards that damage them or shoots projectiles. The cards even if random, offer a variety of playstyles along with the weapons you receive at beginning of each run. The game's not insanely difficult but I think on its highest might be challenging but I didn't try much.Overall, I enjoyed all my 20 hours of gameplay even if most of the time has been spent around the cult, not on combat, but I loved both the aspects and how well they tie together.

_childDocuments_.review: If you’ve made it to the review section, you already know you want your own cult of adorable animals worshipping you. So let's cut to the chase.This game sits somewhere between roguelike and roguelite. You’ve got permadeath, permanent upgrades outside of battles, and a self-generating, dungeon-like world. But outside of that, you’re also running a base-building sim with some exploration and character-building mixed in. Progress in both your cult and your dungeon runs is equally important, and the balance between the two feels just right.Design-wise, it’s a charmingly cute take on a demonic setting. You’ll work hard to grow and sustain your cult—because the bigger the cult, the more that can worship you! Feed your ego!If you're a seasoned roguelite/roguelike player, you might find it on the easier side. For beginners, though, it could be a bit challenging.Definitely check this one out and make those peasants bow before you! :3

_childDocuments_.review: B++/A Tier game. This game can be good and rise up to A++ If it fixes some of its main problems which I'll mention soon but overall If you do like games similar to Stardew Valley and Core Keeper so on its the game for you. Anyways lets talk about the problems it has first one being the game crashing issues this would be ok and all If the auto-save saved after doing one activity such as finishing a crusade,finishing a building so on but it doesn't which does allow save scumming which is a must need but damn losing hours of progress because you didn't manually save or did an activity that activates auto-save is rather painful. Secondly the rng can be rather painful for anything that has a rng system. And lastly you can make some bad irreversible choices If you're just starting mainly being choosing bad docturines (I recommend looking up  to avoid this issue) and perma killing a quest needed follower/a follower with a quest item (This can also be avoided via looking up  guides)Tips: If you are finding the quick-time events rather annoying go to the accessibility settings ingame and make them automatic,If you're struggling getting some gold bars try to get some gold pooping cultists as fertilizing crops with them gives you ton of gold bars,Gaunlets are overall the worst weapon you can get unless If its the "godly" version or you're playing with a controller,There are ways to reload/attack cancel via dodging to increase your rpm,Daggers heavy attack can do insane damage If you attack from the left/right side of a boss,If you buy the "Good Die Young" docturine restart your save because its the worst docturine out of the bad ones,The best way to get bones is from missionarys,If your game is stuterring do a manual save or stay still because the game will most likely crash,If you unlock every building blueprint before the final boss is killed any devotion is turned into coins which can make you rich real quick but know that npc Midas will steal most of it during your crusades so this is a great time to turn all that cash into gold bars for further use,Exploding corpses card removes any bone gain from dead enemies so If you're grinding bones from crusades don't pick it up and last of all outfits/costumes are a great way to keep faith levels up during crusades.

_childDocuments_.review: Allow me to regard you, wholly. 25 hours of casual gameplay allowed me to 100% Cult of the Lamb.If you enjoy the idea of a town builder lite with a sprinkling of godgame elements and sim elements, which is then mixed with Binding of Isaac lite then this game will be for you. The components mix quite well so that the two core styles of gameplay feed off each other. Building and expanding your cult will give you more strength, better equipment and abilities to go into the randomly generated dungeons. On the flipside, going on dungeon runs will give you materials, shop items and praise from your followers to take back to your cult. Minigames and side quests are there to break up the core gameplay and allow you to unlock bonus gear and cosmetics. Combat is simple but feels tights and responsive, hitting enemies has satisfying feedback and doesn't feel weak in any way, shape or form. The overall aesthetic is probably the standout part of this game. The cutesy art style doesn't dilute the fact the story, and events within the story, get dark as ♥♥♥♥. Sacrifice, betrayal for profit and satanic worship galore. This game is dark and unapologetic about the fact. If you're looking for replayability, this CotL won't really give you it. The dungeons are randomised but the gear, weapons and spells on offer don't really offer the levels of replayability that a full blown dungeon crawler/roguelite(like) will give you. This is more of a campaign and less of a 'jump in and do a run or two, like your BoI or your Slay the Spires. The game has an evident start and an evident end. TLDR; Cute but very dark game with two strong, core, gameplay elements with a clear and fun story which offers some dungeon crawling and roguelite elements to keep you going until the end and doesn't outstay its welcome. Replayability not there, but a single playthrough is worth your time and money. 8/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Cult of the Lamb can be described best as a half Rougelite half managment sim that in my opinion combines really well into each other. The two gameplay styles really blend well into each other. The rougelite elements remind of Hades, you get a random weapon and a random projectile each dungeon run with different attributes and each room will have a random benefit and each run ends with a boss fight that typically grants you a new follower. Combat is pretty simplistic but otherwise enjoyable. The cult and base building element reminds of Animal Crossing, feed your villagers, treat their needs, gain faith points and become stronger through them in the dungeons. Building your own religion in your own image is mighty fun too in my experience. The synergy boils down really well. Game also has a lot of nice and fun side content minigames to partake in. Game can clock you about 9-15 hours depending on how much you focus on the base building aspect as you raise your total follower count. Easily one of the best games to come out this year. A pretty good buy for its price too.

_childDocuments_.review: After 100%ing, I'd say it's worth buying on sale, and maybe after a few more rounds of bug fixes/content updates.10/10 for style and charm, but by midgame it starts to feel like a super high quality mobile game. As far as being a roguelike and basebuilding game, it feels more like a basebuilding game with occasional roguelike dungeon when the base can finally be left alone for 5 minutes. 90% of the time is triaging the base. It's decently fun to do, but it's a lot of balancing different timers and meters and pressing A on different things, hence reminding me of a mobile game.The roguelike element kinda isn't. Most roguelikes are set up some kind of build, then go until you die or win. There aren't builds in this game other than small modifiers, and the weapons/spells you get are randomly selected at the start. You might find a replacement later, you might not, so you just have to go in hoping you don't get 1 of the 2 useless weapons and hopefully a good spell. I'm not particularly good at these games and I never died once, so no idea what even happens. The combat is simple enough that it probably was designed with smartphones in mind. Despite all that, it's short enough to not feel tedious at any point. The visuals and character interactions were fun. Building the base and setting it up for success was an interesting balance. Doing cult rituals was very fun.

_childDocuments_.review: Aside from the bugs which can be fixed and hopefully will be fixed I gotta say the game is rather shallow.First the three big positives: Art Style, Music, Theme & Presentation, those are incredible and put together so well that I gladly spend 23€ for the game.The gameplay itself feels like they've half heartedly glued together Hades (The Dungeon Crawling Part) with Oxygen Not Included and Don't Starve Together (The Village System / Cult System).First of all the Major Problems for me with the Dungeon Crawling.- The Dungeon Crawling Upgrade / Tarot Cards are just useless out of 36 cards there are only 3 useful ones which will help you in the run itself.What's the point of adding cards like "Enemies drop Fish", "Harvest more resources" (in the dungeon)? Feels like those effects should be something unlockable through something in the cult system and not upgrades in the dungeon itself.They only dilute the pool of the 3 cards that are useful for a dungeon run.While other cards are even counterproductive, the bomb Tarot card made me go paranoid since I didn't know if the bomb was my bomb or a bomb of an enemy, the faster movement speed made it harder for me to position myself in a game about positioning.At 10 hours in I've just stopped picking up any cards.- The Combat is boring and to easy.You run in hit the enemy once run out, repeat until the enemy is dead.I just started using the golden fleece which gives you more damage for each enemy killed until you get hit, to fasten the combat up.To talk about the easy part (very small spoiler about endboss mechanics) I gonne use the last boss as an example: it's partly a bullethell boss, so dodge bullets get in hit get out.Except there are barley any bullets to dodge, it feels like they had more bullets since the arena is quite big to manuvere but removed 300% of those bullets at some point in development, it's as if they've tried to develop the difficulty for small children.The Village Part / Cult Part:-The building part is that there is barley a building part there is maybe 5 total buildings you build and then upgrade through them to level x while some of the levels are literally just filler and don't add any value to it.Like as an example there are sleeping bags > tents > houses, the upgrade from bags to tents is that tents don't crash as often as bags. That's it nothing more, there is no real value to upgrade to tents. - Running the cult itself is also very bland & very micromanaging there are two things you have to watch out,  followers believe and their hunger.For the believe you just do a sermone each day and a ritual every few days. For the hunger you just cook every few days.So a daily day in the cult is sermone > bless your members > collect devotion > either cook or do a ritual > go into the dungeon repeat from step 1.That's all there is sadly, I expected a lil bit more.Weirdly enough I managed to get all the upgrades there are in the game by hour 9 so the other 10 hours I just dungeon crawled and did the quests.In other words 10 out of 19 hours I barley engaged with the cult mechanic at most feeding my followers and doing a ritual like once every 3-5 days. I'll defininitley return to the game once the endgame has been added hopefully they add more systems to the Cult System and actually engaging bosses with those updates but at the current time I would only say buy the game when its on a deep sale for like 5-10€.

_childDocuments_.review: Cult of the Lamb is a game where it was like the love child of Don't Starve, Binding of Isaac, and Hollow Knight. The art style, the soundtrack, and the building/material mechanics are very similar to don't starve, with some hollow knight inspiration in there as well; While the combat and the randomization of rooms, curses, and weapons is that of Isaac.Now in regards to its story, its simple. You're a Lamb, you run a cult for THE ONE WHO WAITS, and you kill the current "gods" or bishops, of the land. I won't go into more detail, but know that it is kind of a short story if you blast through the game all at once (which is why you should pace yourself for a bit). My favorite in regards to story, is the side characters. Some give advice, info regarding plot, or their own stories and struggles in the current game. They're unique, and I do love the little chitter noises they all make. That all to say, the story is enjoyable :).If you're into rogue-likes, settlement management/character management, and LOVE to hyperfocus on this kind of loop-able gameplay, you'll definitely love this.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm really torn on this game, I was looking forward to since it was first previewed, I loved the art style, tone, and general vibe of the game, And all of that is still here.My main issue with the game is it took me around 12.5 hours to beat, which isn't a issue in it's own right, But around 8 hours into the game, I effectively reached "Full build" as far as my in game character would go (Meaning i couldn't upgrade my rougelite side with weapons and abilities any further)which makes the cult side of things effectively have no link to the rougelite side of things, while also letting me breeze through the rest of the story i had left with the best weapons in the game, When at full build there's also a fair bit less incentive to actually push your cult as well, As the only real way that matters is in the form of converting your followers to demons to assist you in dungeons.It really is a shame though, Because the base building side of this game was fantastic.. It's primarly what i focused on before, and even after reaching full build (Partially why i got it so fast i imagine) It's great seeing the cute little animations of your followers working, and seeing them slowly get more and more levels to them is a huge appeal to the game, It's just a shame this aspect, and the rougelite seperate so fast.Overall though the game is still a good one, It's just a very short game, with bad pacing contained within. I'd probably still recommend this game on a sale, And a lot of my issues could potentially be fixed with future updates, Don't let me stop you if you think you're fine with paying full price for a 12-15 hour game, but ideally wait for a sale, or a major content update.

_childDocuments_.review: Insanely fun dungeon crawling roguelike with a mix of hack-n-slash to bullet hell, and the mix of slower-paced play with organizing and tending to your cult while also decorating your base to make resources, do passive resources, fish, play some board games, and also to prepare sermons and doctrines to make the cult of what you like with different benefits. t's both addicting, a nice mix of two features that work together while helping ensure a balance if one part gets a bit much than the other to swap to, and its style is overall cute and appealing without trying to be too edgy with itself, given the subject matter of cults. All of it being a really great package of a game!Some of the complaints I do have are the controls being somewhat iffy. It's most noticeable when on keybouse/mouse, since both mouse and keyboard can also aim where you attack, so sometimes you'll accidentally attack backwards from the enemy as you try to move the opposite direction to aim your dodge roll towards. The other one is the game having a bit of limited content; the content in the game is decently plentiful, but afterwards you might run to a spot where you're beefed out a lot, especially with the game being somewhat short. It isn't too bad of a deal when you're playing the game at a somewhat slower pace, as you'll be put in a steady grind to getting everything unless you're gonna be speedrunning really hard to completing it so quickly. Otherwise, problems that are there, aren't too bad problems, though playing on keyboard and mouse can somewhat affect controls a bit.To top it all off, the best feature:Press the B key or press the right thumbstick >:)

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game, but unfortunately for me, it falls short in a couple of areas.The general idea of the game is that it's a roguelite and a management game rolled up into one, which is a very cool idea. While you are off in the dungeon, your villagers are eating, pooping, getting sick, worshipping, etc. When you get back from the dungeon, you can unlock new skills and also you can go off and do other things like fishing (same as Stardew Valley), play card games (pretty cool idea), and do quests for people if they show up.However, I found that the game feels weighted towards the beginning. By the time I was finishing the second dungeon (of 4), I had already unlocked all of the skills in one area of the game. There wasn't anymore gameplay to be had in getting relic pieces. So I was maxed out on skills in that sense. The only other stuff to purchase (using other currency), was new buildings, new decorations, and cosmetics for followers (new skins). And at about 16 hours of gameplay, I've beaten all the bosses and there really isn't much left to do other than rerun the same 4 dungeons.HOWEVER, THE MOST EGREGIOUS THING, was that as a mix of management/roguelite, it doesn't mesh well. Whenever you complete a run of a dungeon (about 5 "floors"), you can choose to do a new run or to go back to your cult. As someone who likes roguelite games, of course I want to keep running floors so I can get super OP. That's where the fun is! But, you can't. Why? Because your cult back at home is now starving, losing faith in you, pooping everywhere, and getting sick because you aren't there to baby them. I think I did 2 runs of a dungeon because I was feeling cool and then went back and everyone was dying. Even with blessings, you can fix a couple things to not decrease for a couple days, but in the end, you'll always have to stop your dungeon run to go back to your children and baby them.I might recommend this on sale or if there's a better "endless run" option but right now, I'd pay maybe $10 for it instead of $25.

_childDocuments_.review: I recently got 100% in this game, as of the Sins of Flesh update. There are a few bugs and my game would freeze at times. Sometimes I'd be soft-locked in a mini boss room. Once I died on a crusade and I was supposed to be able to sacrifice one of my followers to revive, but none of them showed up. I was soft-locked in Narinder's realm and my crusade progress was lost. I understand that the new update only came out recently, so bugs are to be expected, so I didn't mind anything too much. I do recommend this game, though. Even after completing the game fully I still have the desire to play it. As this was my first save, I tried being very nice to my followers. Next save, I think I'll sacrifice followers and murder dissenters more often. The game doesn't take too long to complete, either. I have a bit over 100 hours on this game, though it'll probably take others less time, since I wasn't speedrunning the game or anything. The music and sound effects add to the atmosphere and I love the cute and creepy art style. I highly recommend it! ^^

_childDocuments_.review: Cult of the Lamb (COTL) delivers a specific experience that I personally have wanted out of a game ever since I stopped playing Fallout 4 for mental health reasons (would spend more time fixing it then playing it.)COTL is one of the few games that lets the player create and manage a settlement/town/city/cult as a  not as a camera. I thoroughly enjoy this, as I prefer to feel immersed as a character in a game world, as compared to seeing the world through a flying and no-clipping camera. To be able to not only walk around the cult I built, but to also interact with its followers in more ways then just greeting them or telling them to work like other games, feels really good.Sure this isn't exclusive to COTL but I've recently found it frustrating that nearly every mainstream or popular sandbox never has a real STORY or characters. Don't get me wrong developing a sandbox AND writing interesting characters and story is asking a lot from a developer, its just really nice to see a game do that. Sozo and Plimbo my beloved. (♥♥♥♥ Dr. S.).I love the art style and theme of the game. Simple.I really hope the developers see this. I would love to see this game get modding support, if not then I hope if they make a sequel, they consider that.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a mix of rogue-lite and colony management, and it's not good in either of them.There are no meaningful upgrades or changes in your run. You see the same rooms, same enemies and same weapons over and over again.You never try to build synergistic load-out. you are given a load-out and simply you have to play with it.On the management side, there is a lot of manual work. You have to individually go to the followers and do the same repetitive actions over and over again. There's nothing interesting or challenging about the colony management aside from gathering enough food for the people to not starve.To summarize, this game is simply a washed-out base-building game with a sprinkle of rogue-lite.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly as a  (or roguelite, whatever you wanna call it) this game doesn't hold a candle to most games in the genre. Combat can be pretty clunky, and some enemies blend into the background of the arena. To top it off, some obstacles are not active as soon as the room loads (specifically the fire ball things) and I have been hit by them unduly as a result, since if you're on the move it's hard to notice the spawners by themselves. Additionally, sometimes enemy spawns are quite frankly ridiculous when compared to the room they're in. Overall the roguelike sections of the game are not fun for me at all, and maybe that's to taste, but when half of the game is built on these expeditions I wish there was a bit more QoL. Although I guess if you don't play this genre a lot this issues wouldn't be as obvious.The other half of the game is very fun and all the mechanics work together great, complimented by the games art direction and music, but I don't want to have to do horrible dungeon crawls just to experience it. Cult of the Lamb is really a management sim with a roguelike tacked onto it.Tl;Dr: came for the cult management, left because of roguelikeOnly really playing anymore to get 100%.

_childDocuments_.review: I originally played the demo during the Steam Fest they had for new upcoming small team games. I went through all of the games offered and then found Cult of the Lamb. Since I played the demo, I was extremely excited to try the game out.After beating the game and spending time with everything, I think I can safely make a review. The game as a whole is really addicting and fun. You will be able to beat the entire game within 20 hours of playing maybe more if you spend a lot of time building stuff for your camp.The weapons in the game are good enough to get the job done. There is some personal preference for them. Some are better for aggressive play and the others are better for passive, slow play. It really just depends on your play style. The paths themselves are pretty straightforward. You enter rooms progressing through and killing enemies. You face a few mini bosses and then move onto the main boss for that area. Each main boss has its set of unique powers and attack patterns. Once you can figure them out, it's pretty easy.You can basically max out your cult extremely quickly. If you spend all of your time at the cult, you can easily get all upgrades in under 10 hours of play. That is one of my negatives about the game. It felt like you unlock everything way too quickly. Far before the final boss, you already have everything unlocked.  The game (as it stands, first couple weeks of release) has its fair share of essentially game breaking bugs. I have been soft locked in rooms several times. I also had an invisible enemy spawn in and was essentially unkillable. Make sure you buy the Omnipresent upgrade early on as that will help with any soft locks. I have also glitched through the wall of the main worship hall and was able to walk through the void and come back. That's my second negative (this will change with the updates given). The game is replayable. You can create multiple saves. However, your saves wont be as unique when it comes to your cult itself. You can basically only go two different pathways with doctrines, once you do the opposite of what you originally did, there isn't much else you can change. The only replayable aspect is the different difficulties. But, if you end up mastering the attack patterns, this will become a breeze.Overall, I love the game. I spent over 20 hours playing from release day until now (and counting). I can excuse all of the bugs because it is to be expected. The developers have said they will update the game down the road as well. There have been updates released these past couple days. I personally think the game is worth buying. I also hope they add more to increase its replayability, because right now it needs more.

_childDocuments_.review: Alas, despite its phenomenal presentation, Cult of the Lamb is too shallow to garner an honest recommendation from me, and, forced to a hard Yes or No, I find myself leaning negative here.This game knocks it out of the park when it comes to the superficial - it's visually distinct and full of very crunchy and punchy effects.  The combination of combat-roguelike and colony sim is intriguing, and the game is absolutely effective at ... much like any cult worth its salt strives to be.Would that the similarities had ended there, but, also like a cult, a hollow existence awaits those who delve deeper into the game.  Every system introduced into this game, though many appear interesting at first, turns out to be disappointingly shallow.  The upgrades to buildings/tech offer little variety and are underwhelming in terms of any actual feeling of .  The combat upgrades are even less inspiring; you get new weapon types (insofar as just adding Poison or Crit to existing ones is ), you get new spells (which I found unsatisfying to use), and there's little else worth mentioning.  These are arranged into a truly meager tree, with little apparent reason for its hierarchy and no sense of customization, since you must take nearly every option from one tier before advancing to the next.  Doctrines and Rituals are probably the most interesting systems, but these too lack depth, and don't feel very balanced or tuned for good pacing.It feels strange to say about a game that, outwardly, seems so polished, but Cult of the Lamb felt almost .  It's not that you can see any gaping holes at a glance, and it's not that anything is evidently ... Rather, what's not done here is the expansion, evolution, and finishing touches that allow good ideas to mature and coalesce into great games.   It's as though there were a few solid brainstorming sessions, and the resulting high-level ideas were developed, arranged to look as enticing as possible, and released.  With such excellent alternatives in the roguelike genre, it's hard not to feel that this approach is in some way a deliberate cash-grab rather than a true attempt to make a game the best it can be.The shortcomings are not immediately apparent, and there are procedural obstacles (tiered trees and mandatory repeats of the same combat area) which do little other than extend playtime, so many who might've gone for a quick refund will remain enticed just long enough to make that impossible.  I wouldn't refund it myself, as I did have some genuine fun here, but the more I think about this game, the more a thumbs-down feels like a correct response.

_childDocuments_.review: Cult of the Lamb: A Unique and Captivating Game with Innovative GameplayCult of the Lamb, developed by Massive Monster, is a unique and captivating game that offers an innovative gameplay experience like no other. With its charming art style, engaging mechanics, and intriguing story, Cult of the Lamb has quickly become a standout title in the gaming world.One of the highlights of Cult of the Lamb is its refreshing gameplay mechanics. As players take on the role of a lamb-turned-cult leader, they must manage and expand their cult, recruit followers, and perform rituals to grow their influence. The blend of strategic decision-making, resource management, and exploration creates a compelling gameplay loop that keeps players engaged and invested in the outcome of their cult.The art style of Cult of the Lamb is also a standout feature. The game's hand-drawn visuals are charming, whimsical, and full of character. The unique aesthetic creates a visually captivating world that is both inviting and intriguing, drawing players into its mysterious and darkly comedic story.Furthermore, Cult of the Lamb boasts a captivating story that keeps players engaged throughout their journey. The game's narrative is filled with twists, turns, and unexpected events that add depth and intrigue to the gameplay. Players will find themselves emotionally invested in the outcome of their cult and the fate of its members, creating a sense of attachment and investment in the story.The game's innovative gameplay, charming art style, and captivating story make Cult of the Lamb a standout title that is well worth playing. It offers a fresh and unique experience that pushes the boundaries of traditional gaming genres and delivers an engaging and memorable gameplay experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Good art style and idea hamstrung by tedium. I found this to be very frustrating experience. Things that should be unlocked early game seem not exist. I was around 75% through and still haven't unlocked the ability for my followers to harvest food??? Many of the cult-management pieces early game are very frustrating as you haven't unlocked the mechanics to solve the problems that the game presents you with. I wanted to set up and automate the camp management pieces, but there was so much manual tedium involved in camp maintenance, it turned it into a chore. Additionally, your camp suffers every time you die, so it almost incentivizes you to not fight difficult bosses. I wanted to keep going on runs to try my luck against the bosses, but every time I did, I would have to spend days building my camp back up. Food creation was bad and I was almost never able to cook food that didn't make my followers sick, again, things that should be unlocked very early game and automated, became a manual process. Overall, it's a pretty fun game that I wish I could actually play instead of babysit.

_childDocuments_.review: An endearing mix of rogue-lite and town building that doesn't overstay its welcome. At a glance, someone could look at the charming presentation and confuse the game's adorable denizens with defectors of Animal Crossing, not realizing the true darkness that lies underneath the cuteness. As the name implies, Cult of the lamb is a cult simulator through and through, complete with  animal sacrifices and questionable leadership and its game-play loop of dungeon runs and cult management is diabolically efficient.The game is rather short though when compared to other rogue games, with its main story line lasting for approximately 30 hours. Not a bad thing if you're struggling to squeeze gaming sessions into your schedule but it may leave the aficionados of the genre wanting for a little more.All in all a great addition to the genre with few strings attached, so what are you waiting for? Join the Cult.
