_childDocuments_.review: I've finished all of the current content, so I think I'm in a good position to critique the game as it is currently. Overall, this game is a real gem. I'm a fan of Lovecraftian-styled games along with rogues and sidescrollers, so this game is perfect for me. The character movement and combat starts out sluggish, but once you unlock some more dashes the pace becomes faster. The developers have already addressed this in an update today that bumped up the character movement, among other improvements. However it's still a game that favors defense, and the bullet-sponge nature of the enemies is my biggest criticism. At times it can borderline on ridiculous. Also, the second level of Act 1 feels way too long, and in my opinion, doesn't earn its length.The sounds and aesthetics are perfect for capturing the eldritch. Here's a quick example from a recent playthrough: I descend into an expansive cavern and hear a roar from somewhere in the darkness. Soon a leviathan looking monster is hurling itself toward me with crab-like claws crashing down from fifty feet above. I try to back up when a troop of smaller creatures spill out from the ceiling behind me. As a pyromancer, I throw up a wall of flames to hold off the big guy as I dash behind the little guys spewing out of the ceiling and torch them just as the giant monster is crashing down upon me and already drenching me in poison.It's moments like the above that make the slower moments worth the slog, and I think a Lovecraftian world is better explored in a cautious, almost timid manner to what may await in the shadows beyond. As expected of an EA game, some balancing work needs tweaking. Certain classes like the pyromancer seems superior to others like the geomancer and some weapons are almost useless. But perhaps I just haven't played around with optimizations well enough. The runs are divided into independent acts and it takes me about two hours to get through Act 1, though I tend to explorer every nook and cranny of the levels. Act 2 is only partially done and is about half as long as Act 1 so far. According to the roadmap, three acts are planned.Anyway, this review is longer than I intended, but I felt it necessary to support a small team that's willing to take risks in creating something so original. Small criticisms aside, this a fantastic game that I'm really happy to have discovered.
_childDocuments_.name: Source of Madness

_childDocuments_.review: features a 2D action platformer with some roguelite features; however, the content available so far likely is not enough to drive enough variability so run to run actually feels very similar in level design. The enemies are multi-tentacled eldritch masses of flesh and there is some randomization of what spawns as well. Of course there are differences run to run in terms of character traits and also abilities from the equipment, so there is decent replay value. But the price seems a bit much for what is available as the game only has a couple of bosses among the somewhat random large and small seething piles of monster flesh while running through several different biomes (currently in sequential order). Artistically this game is quite nice and is what drew me in at first. Of serious consideration though, the controls feel rather janky at times, and I have on more than one occasion been stuck in the environment and not been able to get out due to moving floor/environments. The game itself feels slow in all aspects of movement, combat, and it's just difficult to see a lot of times when the enemies will lash out at you, especially when you are being swarmed. Thus to counter balance this, I do find it necessary to hit and run but that makes the slow-appearing game move along even slower. Finding cheese going from run to run while maximizing damage output while also keeping yourself safe seems to be the biggest priority, and as such, runs tend to get bogged down with unnecessary movements.The game for me at first was a rather artistic and visually pleasing adventure with notable slowness in gameplay. Later on I was ignoring what I didn't have to pay attention to and blasting through enemies a lot faster, after getting accustomed to the game itself. Still, with runs of an hour or so for the currently available content, I cannot imagine the length of a run should the full game be completed with all of the sections that seem to be planned. I am estimating by what I see wandering around the "hub" area before the run starts.I am having fun with this game and I will look forward to seeing it in its completed form, though it would not be unrealistic to wait and see how it turns out before you decide to dive in yourself. 1. The maps are sizeable but as far as I know, there's nothing in terms of a mini-map overlay that you can toggle. Maybe it's there and I just didn't know how to get to it, but when I was doing my due diligence and exploring some areas that had a lot of vertical layers and not just horizontal left-right orientation, I would often wish to be able to see some kind of a map to give me some reference points about where I was or where was the shop I had come across, etc.2. The lengths of the runs seem a bit long, and almost burdensome at times. The game just has a slowness factor that is difficult to ignore. I cannot exactly see myself having the time to sit through whole runs without being able to save when the game is complete. They would be too long and I am sure other things would get in the way and I would need to quit and lose a bunch of progress.3. I can see from the game updates that there are plenty attempts to fix the monster attacking patterns and making them not so deadly. I think some of these changes were probably necessary. Nevertheless, it is still at times difficult to visualize their attacks especially within those challenge rooms where several monsters are around you simultaneously. It is difficult to get away and also difficult to see how they are dropping their attack cues.4. There are only two merchants that I have run across and they always show up together. It would be nice to have some more merchants with more varied items available down the line. I suppose this actually goes for all of the items/drops. More variety would be great.5. There was an auto-attack with aiming the right stick that was removed from a previous update. While most might prefer to not have this, I think I would find it a better experience. Perhaps turning this into a toggle option and allowing the players to decide would be great.6. The different spells/magic attacks are pretty fun in their differences, but there are really not very many weapons, tools, or modifiers available. More visual designs and more types of items available would be nice.7. Definitely need to fix some of the areas where it is easy to actually get stuck in the environment, making it difficult for the player to move. This adds nothing to the gameplay other than frustration at the most inopportune moments. (Specifically I got stuck in Forest of Lies, where there are mobile/wavy floors that could create just the right pocket to fit me and for the floor to engulf me, with the floors unresponsive to attacking and jumping just bonking my head instead.)There are definitely areas that the controls could be improved. Smoothness of actions would be priority for me. I suppose part of it is the limitations of the engine physics, but there are so many times when the jump/double jump feels like it should get you where you want to go, but you end up just short, etc. I only moved around and tried out the controls on KB+M, and that felt fine. I played primarily using a controller, which worked well. However, working well does not yield the same satisfying feeling that I usually look for when playing a 2D platforming style game using the controller.The artwork is rather visually appealing, with a consistent dark and eerie mood/background while the monsters are pretty interesting to look at. The different spells have varying appearances and look pretty cool as well. So many times the artwork in this game made me think "creepy" and I think that's the intended effect.The music sets the mood reasonably well, though it isn't too exciting. Some of the sound effects are a bit overused and can get jarring on the ears after a while.If you are looking for eldritch style horror in a highly artistic 2D platformer, you have found a really nice game choice here. Just keep in mind, that death and repeat cycle keeps happening and this game is rather slow-paced. As for people looking to play a 2D action platformer with significant roguelite elements and only wanting buttery-smooth gameplay, this is not it. All of the janky movements and physics make for some additional frustrations at times.I do think the game is priced a bit high for its current version of Early Access. Not to mention it has the same number in baseline pricing in both USD and Euro. When I am thinking $17 is high for the content right now, and seeing that it's that many Euro, I would not be surprised if most people wait for a heavy sale before even diving in. It's unclear how much the price will go up by in the finished product either. is pretty fun but could also use some additional work. It's completely reasonable to wait before heading into this game, though doing so now could mean that you help to shape the final version the game in some manner. Recommended with caution for current version of Early Access.Thank you for reading.Review written October 17, 2021.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a weird one for sure. There's a great ambiance throughout. The monsters are weird and freaky and scary. There's a large variety of effects and items you can combine to build your mage every run.I get why people would complain about the controls, since they're different, but I wouldn't call them "bad". They're responsive, they do what you expect them to, and you can definitely get to control your mage with finesse once you get the hang of it.It's definitely not perfect though. There are a lot of balance issues in my opinion. The game feels like it's missing some items (why is there a hat for every element except 2?). Some of the spell-rings feel really bad to use in comparison to others. The classes are a bit weird (some of them really don't do much), and you can't fully choose which class you get at the beginning of a run. Some of the effects don't scale at all, like Poison and Burn. For example, Burn deals 3 damage a few times to enemies (per burning body part). It deals the same 3 damage when you start the run and enemies have 200 health, as when bosses have 20'000 health at the end of the game, becoming completely irrelevant. Similarly, the "blood" spells heal you for 1 hp when you land a hit. You start the game at 100 hp, so those spells are great, but towards the end, you can easily have 400+ hp, where they just don't really do anything.Overall it's a fun game, but I'd rate it something around 7/10. It could easily become a 8 or 9 to me with just a few balance changes though.
_childDocuments_.name: Source of Madness

_childDocuments_.review: Good, not great. It's a rogue-lite, procedurally generated game without much variation. I think some monsters and bosses are random, but a lot aren't. Also a lot of levels variation isn't really relevant, its just variation without much actual effect. Compare with Sundered that makes the bite sized chunks interesting to traverse versus this. It doesn't help that by default your movement speed is on the slow side.I love the style of the game (Gustave Doré-esque) and the combat is fine pretty good even if the dash gets a bit sticky sometimes. Generally you'll fall into a decent build pretty quick especially once you learn what everything does. I went with arcane damage and cooldown, using King's Rings and Arcane Bursts almost exclusively from start to finish.It's too long per run, with levels like the caverns being tedious to explore. You'll have seen pretty well every variation after a few runs. The tower of knowledge is ridiculously large, just to explore for NPCs who say the same thing every time even after you complete the 3 Acts of the game.From there it's a rogue-lite, meaning you gradually get stronger. The issue for me is the left upgrade tree makes more items drop and opens up more classes. This just dilutes the pool of weapons and classes I want. You can set their drop rates to low but it still adds more that I don't want compared to what I want.Now that I've beaten the game I just need some more boss blood and to be poisoned a bunch of times before I've 100% it. Except for killing 10,000 monsters which is an obnoxious amount.Pro-tip: In the forest there are red rings that sometimes spawn which continually teleport in monsters. With precision weapons (like King's Rings) you can farm at a rate of 30 per minute or so. At the very least get a bunch of money from them before killing the ring.Main criticisms:Story is severely lacking despite being able to draw upon the whole Lovecraft Mythos. See Hades and Rogue Legacy 2 for effective rogue-lite storytelling.Physics engine. Pardon me but I wasn't finished with those monsters that shot into the sky, and I'm sure they weren't done with me.Level length: too long, too winding in many areas. Also no maps. The more linear levels are generally about the right length.Item and monsters sometimes spawn in solid rocks. Not often but enough to be noticeable and fixable.The randomness adds little, if anything, to the game. It rarely makes encounters interesting. Again, see Hades or ScourgeBringer for meaningful randomness of encounters.
_childDocuments_.name: Source of Madness

_childDocuments_.review: At this point in early access I cannot recommend this game, as it is in a half-baked state that is not very enjoyable.  That said, the game has a lot of potential so maybe check back later when its more fully fleshed out.  The graphics and atmosphere of the game are a unique-feeling and gorgeous take on Lovecraftian cosmic horror.  The monsters are truly monstrous, moving in unpredictable and horrifying ways.  This is a positive for atmosphere but potentially a negative for gameplay because unlike other great games in the genre, the player cannot memorize the attack patterns of the monsters and react accordingly.  This creates a frantic gameplay experience, which might be good or bad depending on your concept of fun.But by far the most major issue is the progression system.  The skill tree is full of meaningless upgrades that do little to improve a player's power curve and actually in many cases hinder it, for example by unlocking unlabeled friendly fire weapons that some players won't even want to use.  Buyer beware.  The devs themselves have stated that the only upgrades that matter are dash and potion uses, so the other 50 or so upgrades are nothing but fluff.  The skill tree is not nearly juicy enough to create a rewarding feeling of progress or an interesting diversification of playstyle.The weapons the player has access to are not balanced with each other and there are clearly superior options, meaning most of the time you will be playing with weapons that are ineffective and unfortunately there is no progression system in the skill tree to upgrade any of their base effects.  You can spend a lot of time playing this game and your 100th run will be just as much a roll of the dice as your very first run, unfortunately.  Due to these balance issues, many of the weapons just feel bad or ineffectual to play with. With the randomized nature of which weapons you are assigned at the start of a run, this means that the majority of your playtime will be wasted on dud runs unless you manually end the run over and over and over until the game gives you better starting weapons (which, if a player has to do this to enjoy your game, you're probably doing something wrong).  These make-or-break RNG aspects coupled with the already slow-pace of combat makes it feel the game is just disrespecting my time.Your weapon upgrades during a run will most often come from the shop periodically encountered.  It's inventory is completely RNG based and many times will have nothing useful to offer you, making this another painful RNG point of failure for a run because without proper upgrades, the player cannot continue.Many of the unlockable weapons contain friendly fire elements which do not mesh well with the inherently frantic nature of the combat, as there is often little planning or muscle memory involved in how the player fights and responds to the actions of the monsters.  As such, these weapons will be passed up by many players and simply not used.  Unfortunately they are also not labelled as friendly fire in the purchase tree so the player will likely spend hard earned resources unlocking weapons they may not even want to use.  Buyer beware, and so goes with this game.If you want to play out the fantasy of becoming a cosmic horror badass, this game in its current state falls far short.  Which is a shame, as it has the potential to satisfy a large audience if there are some simple mathematical balance changes implemented to make the game feel better from the start and feel better over time.  Right now its not worth a player's time.If the skill tree is fleshed out better with permanent stat upgrades and features that improve the base stats and/or  abilities of the various weapons, reduce or eliminate friendly fire, or give the player some degree of control over their starting weapons or the shop inventories it will go a long ways towards alleviating  the many, many RNG feel-bads this game currently offers.  More fun, less RNG feel-bads, I say.
_childDocuments_.name: Source of Madness

_childDocuments_.review: I think a lot of the negative reviews are being a bit too picky. Carry Castle is a one-man development studio, and they're trying to do something pretty cool. I think we should be generally supportive of such efforts.The AI generated beings in Source of Madness are quite possibly the closest we've gotten to the unintelligible madness at the core of lovecraftian cosmic horror. AI is particularly suited to this, since it is, well unintelligible, having no actual connection to logic. I wouldn't accept AI being involved in any other game, but strangely, it works here. It's a bag of jank, to be sure, but it's fun and intriguing. The crazy things still manage to pop out at you with one, none, or 1,000 legs. It works.
_childDocuments_.name: Source of Madness

_childDocuments_.review: Nice art and style.  Problem is that the controls are too floaty.  Combat is awfully slow, and constists of running backwards and shooting at the enemies and then dashing through them forward.  Spells don't feel different enough.  Takes forever to kill things.  I like my combat to have nice rythm to it, that's just not here. The slow pace of combat causes runs to take a lot longer.  Hence I'm less likely want to play the game from Steam or jump right back into another new run after dying.

_childDocuments_.review: caught my attention right away just from browsing through its , as its twisted,  themes looked enthralling enough, making me want to give it a go. While I am not a rogue-lite enthusiast per se, I adore playing them from time to time; thus, this seemed like a perfect opportunity to satisfy my thirst for such a subgenre.The start was promising, and I thoroughly enjoyed the initial two or three hours. Moreover, the visual presentation of the opening locations hooked me; galavanting through the pompous yet dilapidated temple of your fellow acolytes felt strangely engrossing, whereas hopping near a lake that seemed to be hiding its horrors underneath the calm surface was a bit haunting. These parts work well, managing to create an eerie, captivating atmosphere. However, it does not last long, as the latter areas are lacklustre: a bland, uninteresting combination of generic environments like deep caves or dark forests. Additionally, the audio is underwhelming, presenting a barely noticeable soundtrack and repetitive sound effects that are rather irritating to your lovely ears after a while.Nevertheless, these audiovisual shortcomings are just a minor issue compared to the half-baked mess that this title is as a whole. Sure, it has an intriguing premise and ideas that perhaps sound good on paper, but its implementation is horrendous at best, and a bunch of balance inconsistencies and glitches do not make it better. Due to that, its simplistic and repetitive gameplay loop – where your one and only goal is to get to the end of the level, fighting with tons of monsters in the process – becomes rather frustrating to experience. tries to turn this mundane approach into an exciting one by focusing on magically-oriented combat and randomised algorithms that influence every bit of the game, whether it is the design of environments, items dropped from foes or chests, as well as enemies’ appearance and abilities.Thus, instead of wielding ordinary swords, spears or bows, you have rings and supportive items at your disposal that grant you spells, such as unleashing a volley of arcane shots, stunning lighting, poisonous clouds and much more. Yet, these abilities are highly unbalanced, making me feel like I am either obliterating everything in my way or just merely scratching my foes—as if there was no middle ground. Additionally, most boss fights are easier to deal with when you have the right tools. Then, neither of that is enjoyable since you rely on randomised loot than your skill.Like, running around with powerful homing missiles and explosives that obliterate everything in your way is not joyful, and neither are playthroughs that “blessed” you with poisonous clouds or firey effects that take too long to kill anything. Both are tiresome in their own way, especially when you get stuck with the said items because the found loot is worse, and even vendors do not have anything to offer. Consequently, I found myself dying unnecessarily a few times due to this system until the game decided to provide me with an overpowered spell against which enemies could not do anything. At times I died due to unreliable dashing, as sometimes it makes you stuck to an opponent or limb you previously dash through without problems, taking those crucial health points from you.Monsters’ appearance and abilities are problematic, as well, because they purely rely on the said randomised algorithm, which chooses what and how many limbs and types of attacks will they possess. Sure, their looks are unique, fulfilling the goal of presenting them as weird abominations, but that is about it. Most of the encounters feel the same, as foes will just crawl toward you, trying to hit you with a tentacle, occasionally casting spells, as well; it does not matter whether they are big or small, fast or slow—they all behave like that. As if that was not enough, their physics tends to glitch out, pushing them dozen of meters above you or even getting stuck in walls and ceilings, which especially happened with larger minibosses.The said bugs happened more often in the second and third acts, which seemed less polished compared to the first one, turning it into a half-broken experience. By the time I reached the final part, I was exhausted. There was not a single aspect that I would enjoy. My only hope was that the randomised loot would make me suffer less. Yet, the third act somehow managed to top this atrocious mess, as it forces you to go through almost a whole first act yet again; what a marvellous design decision to slightly boost the playtime.Since you might die often – it is a rogue-lite, after all – you have a chance to buy some permanent upgrades at the start of each run. These can boost the amount of found currency, increasing the chance of dropping rarer items or improving your health flasks. However, the prices are way too high, and even after finishing the game, I still had more than half the upgrades to unlock. Not that it matters much, as most of them were rather useless; I would even dare to say that some handicap the player. For example, the unlockable character classes felt worse, constantly having subpar stats and rings than the starting one. Sure, I could decide not to use them, but they filled one or two of the three starting slots.Well, that is all. It is a shame, for sure, as the premise of a mage fighting with  monsters sounds amazing to me; however, the implementation of strong randomised elements ruins the whole game completely, making it a tiresome mess that I sadly cannot recommend. Just avoid it.

_childDocuments_.review: My girlfriend asked me a question, Do I think this game is actually fun? It stunned me for a second because I realized then I did not.But I do find it extremely interesting.Currently beat Act 2 moving onto Act 3 Interest is waning though-------Spoilers ahead-------Below are Cons that I hope are improved/added in a DLC or sequel. As I think this is the start of something absolutely spectacular. This game achieves something in the first hour or 2 of gameplay that I think isn't really ever been achieved before in a game. (I'll talk about that at the end for a bit)-------This game struggles with repetition, After the very first zone the enemy "variety" (procedural) doesn't matter.The only thing that has a chance of killing you after that point is probably the actual bosses and not the mini bosses. I found the minibosses easier than most enemy encounters.Bringing me to my first 2 points of the game that need improvement- Minibosses are a chance to showcase the point of targeting certain parts of an enemy during a long engagement and instead you are just fighting a ball of arms and legs, it makes the targeting aspect honestly pointless which could drive the combat to be really exciting- Enemies need a way to be define-ably different the only enemy i ever noticed that was different was the flying thing that shots vertical beams pointing down on Planet of Yith and some elemental enemies but those did nothing. Because this has led me to honestly be bored for most of the time i've played doing the same strategy clearing each zone pretty fast with a huge abundance of money and blood, because enemies don't throw any curve balls forcing me to learn the AI machine learning doesn't seem to have an impact.Which leads to my next point- AI Machine Learning from a player perspective seems to have zero impact. I'm assuming when you say this it's just a mix of AI animation and AI machine learning to adapt with the AI animations to make it work to some degree but not actually learn how to overcome the player. Would be cool if there was a hive mind aspect to the game that increased the difficulty in certain areas of the AI based on the players actions from using certain strategies over and over but I assume this is probably an incredibly hard thing to do.Moving on to 3 other points- By far the best thing in this game is the Art and Atmosphere. So it really sucks when there is a curse called "Colorblind" that muddies the Art so you can't enjoy it for a 2hr run through Act 2 :upside down smiley: I beat Act 2 on my first and only run and the only thing was spoiled by the Curse "Colorblind" I love the concepts of the curses, not saying remove them, but maybe not add one that is permanent and spoiling one of the best aspects of your game during hour long runs.- Curses: I wish... Curses were more prevalent. I've only been cursed twice, and with the same one "Colorblind" from the guy that heals you in exchange for a curse and he gave me the same one both times. This is fine not a big deal. But in the E thing that that has a random chance of getting a positive or negative I've never got a curse. To my knowledge these are the only 2 things that come to mind to get a Curse, I imagine some of them are pretty fun and cool but I probably won't experience this even though I keep taking the risk over and over, it's just too rare. So maybe add a way to cure Curses and add in a couple other random encounters that offer curses but you also get a free item or something. Or some demon that wants to consume a Curse that you have. To enforce suffering with a Curse through a run in the hope of running into that to get a huge boon. Things like that could be really interesting.- Atmosphere & Story/Lore: I'll just say it straight up this probably has been my biggest disappointment, I thought completing Act 1 and 2 would impact the hub world but it seems to have done nothing. This is one of the most underutilized things in every game, People write it off as non-important but I think it's little work for huge pay off for drawing people in. It's cool talking to random people and then getting a weird image, but these images are just silly at this point to me and have zero meaning or impact in the world. I'm not getting enough lore thrown at me. I beat 2 whole acts and got a few lines of dialogue that connect the acts, is the games story really 3 Acts of less than 50 lines? I'm hoping something unlocks or happens to the game after the 3 acts since there are weird gates in the Hub that look like they could do something but don't as of now.Last point- Sound/Audio: It's strange to me that some of the best sounds and music are in the hub world which currently has very little impact to the game from what I've seen so far. Like going down the elevator the music starts playing is really strange but this is the only time you hear this. Some of the monster sounds are great but again it's pretty rare or maybe it's hard to pick it out with all the explosions and body explosion sounds going off--------Ok time to talk about some positives.This game with the enemies and the weird artstyle really does unsettle you at the start kinda unheard of before honestly. With weird Art filters/distortions and shaders that are really cool. I think this is the first game that was "lovecraftian" and actually hitting notes of what I expected in my head besides just adding mentions of Cthulhu and adding a tentacle monster like other games do that claim to be that. (I understand theres other types of Lovecraftian besides Cosmic Horror but a lot of others that go down the cosmic horror fail imo, except Bloodborne)The enemies put together procedurally and them just figuring out what they can do is really cool, it really does throw out undescribable monsters at you which is the first I've seen this well executed on in media.-----------Final Thoughts:This game could be much better.But I hope/believe there will be a sequel that builds off of this and learns from this one. I think there is a lot here that is worth seeing and playing and do recommend this game and think it's worth supporting.

_childDocuments_.review: Early impressions review: The game has potential, but so far feels strange and lacking.The combat indeed is brutal and unforgiving, but it also doesn't feel satisfying and generally is floaty and confusing instead. It's hard to tell if you're hitting an enemy or if an enemy is hitting you, and it's even hard to distinguish between enemies that are alive or corpses that are being flung towards you because of physics. Ranged moves generally don't feel very different from one another, as far as I can tell, and the lack of variety makes it not very fun unlike other roguelites that tend to distinguish between different weapon types.Because of all of the above, I don't find the combat or exploration that fun. _childDocuments_.review: is a rogue-lite Metroidvania that features procedural generation of environments and monsters, guaranteeing fresh scenery and uniquely nightmarish monsters on every Run, and offering infinite replayability with its diverse array of skills and items to suit various play styles.Monsters are masses of procedurally generated combinations of torsos and limbs, relying on neural network AI to automatically animate them, resulting in enemies being unable to move naturally, so they simply throw themselves like ragdolls at the player. You take damage when any of the designated "danger points"- which are points on the body such as tentacles, spikes, appendages or projectiles- come into physical contact with you.Because of this mechanic, the game becomes a matter of both skill and luck in avoiding the ragdolling enemies flailing about and tossing themselves at you. Combat strategy becomes all about moving backward while shooting forward. Indicators of when you are taking damage or when the enemy is doing damage to you can sometime be unclear or unreliable.Enemy appendages can be individually destroyed to get rid of their attacking parts. When killed, enemies explode into clumps of body parts that clutter the screen, blending into, while at the same time layered atop of, the environment, obscuring your vision of item drops and important environmental objects.Players earn Blood (red orbs) when killing normal monsters, and Evenstar (blue orbs) when killing rare special monsters. You require from hundreds to thousands of these red orbs and tens of these blue orbs to unlock each node at the skill tree found at home base. These allow you to have access to new item drops, starting specialist classes and passives that increase your resource gain (such as extra Gold and Blood).The player almost always has to adopt a run-and-gun approach when fighting enemies because of how readily and quickly the enemies propel themselves at the player. Enemies do massive damage if they touch you, so players should keep their distance.While players can unlock a flask and increase its charges from the skill tree, these flasks have a limited number of charges and can only be replenished at transition areas which take a long time to reach.There is a Diablo-style inventory and stats screen, where you can collect and equip rings (which function as the two main weapons), crystals (as two sub-weapons), a Hood, and three accessories which provide passive buffs such as increase in HP, Cooldown reduction, Movement speed and more.On Runs, you can encounter shops to trade equipment with the money you earn from that Run. However, because this is a rogue-lite, everything you've acquired on a Run is completely erased when you die, except for Blood and Evenstar. These resources provide the only form of persistent progression across Runs through unlocking nodes.The aesthetics and visual style of the environments, monsters and also the music are all excellently done. Controls are responsive and convenient, and animations and movements are very fluid and smooth.I highly recommend this game for players who enjoy a fun challenge and appreciate the dark fantasy theme.

_childDocuments_.review: Let me start by saying that this game's art is an ode to H.P Lovecraft's work. Through the choice made by the art-director, the visuals beautifully capture the uncanny, unsettling & unnerving aspect of the 'elder ones' and the eldritch terraforming of our environment that comes with them. Whilst I commend what they have done with the presentation, the gameplay in my opinion is paying the price for all this eldritch artwork. I have some major quibbles with this aspect of the game. However. before that let me tell you what pulls me to the game.Being a souls-borne fan, the game's theme, presentation and narration style didn't take too long to captivate me. With its machine learning and procedural system, it just nails the Lovecraftian weirdness. The game takes a grip on your senses as soon as you step out from the small tiny room you start at. The world, the NPCs, the dialogues, the eldritch library we get to explore in the beginning all captures the strangeness of this world and sets the mood of the game perfectly. The navigation feels a bit awkward but you get used to it and also it sort of adds into the whole uncanny visual treat of this game. The sound design of enemies and overall atmosphere is something that will take you back into the pages of The Dunwich Horror. With all this said, let me get into why I still am not recommending the game.I will try and be gentle, it's still in EARLY ACCESS, so having played about 90 minutes of game, I couldn't continue though I wanted to - whilst the unknown pulled me into the game more, I was constantly fighting the game due to how (in my opinion) the art direction got in the way of the gameplay. Keeping the subjectivity of 'art' in mind, let's get into it.The background environment, combat & enemies:Skipping the introduction part, I am going to jump ahead into combat and enemies.As soon as you step out of the eldritch library, you are presented with these grotesque deformed unknown beings that look like they came out of Lovecraft's pages. As per the dev's, the movement of these beings are procedural generation and through AI machine learning - which is great in terms of the look and feel, it adds to the weirdness, however it's so hard to understand how they are attacking us. It was so hard to read and telegraph their moments for us to time the dodge. When I started playing I was timing my dodge but as enemy waves increased I was button mashing and scrambling as I wasn't able to understand which enemy is causing my health bar depletion and the combat can get brutal pretty quick. Another issue that popped up here due to the art designs taking precedence over gameplay was the depth perceptions. This was one of the most annoying aspects, the background environment art and the enemy art merge during action. It's so hard to understand what's a tree truck and what's an enemy because they have similar ragdoll-like movement and they look alike. One of my good runs came to an end as I was attacking an inanimate object that was swaying like an enemy while the real enemies were swarming me, I got thrown and tossed around into areas I am sure I can stand on, my health bar started depleting and I was frantically trying to figure out what's causing it - parsing details during combat is such a mental gymnastic. Enemies do have a 'red' slashing graphic, personally for me that's hardly enough to make split second decisions during combat. Some areas where the colour has very less contrast for us to make sense of what's going on.So, the environment tends to have hazardous areas/regions like most platformers do and again the issue comes in where you do not understand if the particular stretch of land will end up damaging you due to the graphic choices made by the devs. It does have a different colour palette to indicate the dangers, but then I entered a portal to find colours that are similar to the  hazardous areas.Also strangely enough. while tinkering with the settings, on display I changed the graphic to lowest and that actually slightly improved the look - I could read the environment a bit more.Menu and its art choice:This aspect of it is subjective. For me, in Source of Madness the gorgeous artwork is truly getting into the way of gameplay and this is an extension of my gripes mentioned above. It's not a good user-friendly design. Especially when your art & iconography choices are accompanied with a lot of flourishes, noisy details and a general lack of separation of contrast. The character ability trees are alright, not much to talk about, however the inventory is just too detailed to a point where it's simply a cluster noise. Everything has this grain on it as if someone took art and ran a sharpness filter on it. The icons are super hard to parse while you are in the heat of the game. This also affects the UI's on the bottom left that shows your health bar, abilities and their cool down timer.  They are all so hard to read at a quick glance. Conclusion:The brutality of this game isn't because enemies are too hard or because it's an unfair design, it comes down to the fact you have no idea what's going on on the screen during combat.So it comes down to one main aspect - what makes this game so attractive to gamers like me, who love this theme also makes this game hard to recommend or even play.There is an amazing game here, Thunderful Publishing has created something very special, but until they tweak the overall gameplay experience that's getting overwhelmed by it's visuals I am going to keep away. However, I will be keeping a watch on the game as I am still extremely interested in trying it again in the future, like I said above the theme and the overall presentation is just bizarrely creative.TLDR: Awesome game & theme that captures Lovecraftian eldritch horror, but it's gameplay is held back by its art-design that gets in the way constantly, making it hard to parse what's going on during combat and environment, accompanied by a really overwhelmingly noisy UI design.

But slowly, steadily, I witnessed despicable landscapes of torment and cyklopean towers wirthling like maggots surrounded by living mountains, eating the horizon.The sun, black as the darkest ink, shining it's unlight over us as we stride towards a goal that is as ill-omened as the maelstrom of chaos. _childDocuments_.review: I've put a few hours into this game. Enough to know that I've no interest in continuing with it. The art style is appealing in the strange grim Lovecraftian horror sort of way that I love. Unfortunately, that's where my interest ended. Source of Madness feels to me like a mishmash of ideas drawn from other places without understanding what made the key components it's borrowing successful. Side-scrolling gameplay, a world heavily inspired by Dark Souls, Diablo-style loot drops and equipment builds, and some roguelike mechanics. It's an interesting experiment, but I just don't think it works very well. I'm also not inspired by the AI-generated content. The enemies are strange looking but mostly nonsensical jumbles of bodies and limbs and they don't seem to exhibit any sort of compelling behaviours or encourage any particular strategy. If, like me, you were drawn to the idea of a side-scroller that feels a little like Dark Souls: my recommendation would be leave this one on the shelf. The are better options out there.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR : Fun sidecrolling roguelite with floppy monsters, fun builds that dont need hours to invent and the best kind of cheese there is, and is relativly easyThe thing that is notable about this game is the artstyle made with AI, which works very well with the procedural generation of the levels. But the most unique thing is the monsters and physic interactions of them, objects, and player. They are floppy, get stuck often, and are made from parts, which some are just solid flesh, some do movement and some damage, melee or ranged. Due to physic simulation, this game is unigue compared to Dead cells or other roguelites or likes : Cheese. Its possible everywhere, and its fun and basicly intended : You can stand on enemies, deal big damage with some rings that do AOA or penetrate, jump over walls, snipe them from places that they cant reach and other stuff. Also, there are some funny builds that are possible, and they can become broken to god run level, even if you just take random cool looking stuff(My favorite being a ring that drops bombs that explode after a while, dealing BIG damage, and friendly fire, and are affected by gravity. Take two of them and anything that allows for faster cooldowns => god run potential and self damage if you forget to dodge the 16 bombs that you planted as charged attack.) Game has also great replayablity, you wont have every upgrade (and item that can be broken) unlocked once you beat it, and can serve as a more chill roguelike after raging on other games (wink wink, Dead Cells)
_childDocuments_.name: Source of Madness

_childDocuments_.review: The game ironically suffers from its very concept of things which exist beyond human comprehension. The visual style is immediately striking, but it quickly becomes obvious that in terms of video games, it is a mistake. The game doesn't actually feel like a game most of the time, just a visual mess of random garbage that does not contrast nearly enough with the environment or the plethora of particle effects which litter the screen. This is a serious problem in a rogue-like game with an emphasis on dodging attacks which you will never really be able to see coming, even with the visual indicators which blend in with all of the other nonsense. This visual style extends to the inventory UI, which is embarrassingly bad. At the risk of being really rude, it is genuinely confusing how they messed it up this bad. Everything about the UI is just absolutely unacceptable. It is borderline if not literally unplayable in its current state and I don't think it's going to be fixed considering it's the entire gimmick...
_childDocuments_.name: Source of Madness

_childDocuments_.review: Ok.I will say that the concept is neat and the artstyle itself is pretty dope. If this was a different kinda game where precision isn't such a factor, I'd be all over this just for that alone. But, man, I don't think this works. Even ignoring the cluttered gameplay, where you can't tell what's going on and what's hitting you and where it's coming from, the UI itself, which i'm assuming you will be spending a lot of your time starring at later on, is such an eye-killer. Keep the stylized borders but fade out the grid or something in the damn inventory, dear god.Anyway. The game itself is pretty much what's it advertised to be, so I can't fault it for that. I think it can really use some more player-friendly additional design choices though. For me, all it did was make me wanna go back to Noita lol

_childDocuments_.review: Okay so this game is slop. The games description states that it is "set in a twisted Lovecraftian inspired world powered by procedural generation and AI machine learning." Now the reason this is a terrible description is that it fails to even describe just how much of this game truly is AI. I came in assuming that maybe it was just the levels that were AI generated, which, fair enough, its not a new concept but maybe they did something cool with it. What i don't like to see is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ LAZY ideas. Not only are the levels themselves AI generated, but the enemies are as well, and so are the cut scenes. What this means is basically, the enemies are totally random, cool concept BUT instead of being cool, it fundamentally breaks the game at some points, enemies will just be completely unable to attack you and will basically be useless because the AI has NO concept of structure to make the enemies actually work. Another thing, the AI levels, heres the real kicker, I have seen GREAT randomized level layout type games, it is a thing and it can be cool. But this is NOT. you have about what seems to be 5 levels, and what the AI does is splice them around to make variations that are just these Frankenstein monsters of levels that have no cohesion or any kind of sensibilities. And of course, the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ LAZY uninspired AI cut scenes. I try to give ever game a fair shake, And i made it 12 mins into this game before i was subject to one of the most awful looking cut scenes i have ever seen. Now why was it bad? Not because the art was that terrible, no it was because of how LAZY it was. It was just a panning shot of some building, not sound, it was probably like 7 seconds in total, but it looked AWFUL because of the AI generated style which made it look like a building made of spaghetti and just ruined the whole vibe, it could have taken them just a single commission from a talented artist to make stills for this cut scene it wasn't even a complicated shot, yet these lazy fools decided to just AI slop it. That alone made me shut the game down and immediately ask for a refund. DO NOT support this game, This is one of the laziest things I've ever seen in a game. Support real artists and screw these losers for putting a blemish on what can be considered art.

_childDocuments_.review: While this game can be addictively fun as you go the course, there are balancing issues that make this game more of an annoyance than something that's actually fun to play.  I will admit, I really do enjoy this game's play loop. It's something that will keep you pushing further and further as you go along. That is, until you are met with elemental status effects.  I'm not one to complain about those type of issues because usually other games have a way of mitigating the effects, or even to avoid them all out.  So far, I have not found  that to be the case in this game. The elemental effects can happen just by jumping over an enemy and barely touch the top of them. When you've got multiple enemies on the screen who are poisonous, they'll continue to nik at your health until you're left with minimal health to continue going forward.  The size of these monsters and it's RNG generally cause more frustration than actual intuitive means to get through. Once you're hit with the elemental statuses you will see what I mean.
_childDocuments_.name: Source of Madness

_childDocuments_.review: Normally, I would complain of games being too mundane, too safe and riskless. As a product of art, a soulless game defeats its own purpose. Source of Madness has the opposite problem - it's too alien, too esoteric.There's a game here, it's a roguelike as any other - but the graphic style, the heavy use of filters, the incomprehensible masses of enemies that float haphazardly in your direction meshing with the strangely flat blackground give this game the feeling that you are stuck in some kind of fever dream, a realm that you aren't meant to understand entirely and just yet the components of sense are there, scattered all over the place for you to get the feeling that it's not the world lacking in coherence, it's you that can't piece it together. Personally speaking, I don't enjoy the floaty combat, the messy fights that consist in spamming spells and watching healthbars go down, or the senseless flailing of limbs that makes discerning what is supposed to be movement and what is an attack skill that you should avoid an impossibility.If that sounds interesting to you, by all means, give this game a try.
_childDocuments_.name: Source of Madness

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly at first its fun. But then it very quickly gets very tiresome to play. The way it controls reminds me of QWOP. Which isn't a compliment. dealing with enemies as they fling themselves at you haphazardly as random parts of them seem to shoot or swipe at you fits the name of the game. The source of madness dealing with enemies gets so nauseating it sucks the fun out of the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Source of Madness

_childDocuments_.review: I am no soulslike/metroidvania/roguelike officionado. This game is sort of like if Noita was written by HP lovecraft and someone on the team was perversely obsessed with procedural generation. I love it. You do casting, not melee, and your spells are things you spam, with low cooldown. You avoid being killed by monsters by hiding in their hundreds of armpits, looking for when the telegraph that that armpit will start emitting poison gas. I wish the time taken to restart a game was lower because I die every 5 minutes.
_childDocuments_.name: Source of Madness

_childDocuments_.review: Incredible game, very innovative with the usage of neural network ai. Enemies you face are something you have not seen before so it is hard to describe. They have very weird shapes (thanks to procedural generation) but their attacks are indicated with certain visual indicators so fighting them does not feel unfair. It takes a few mins to get used to the game's art style but after that it grows on you. Movement is so smooth. Environments are so cool. Controls are also great  on both controller and keyboard-mouse. Basically a hidden gem so yeah don't sleep on this one
_childDocuments_.name: Source of Madness

_childDocuments_.review: Sloppy, disappointing, and almost beautiful. I was so delighted to see this game on steam. A roguelike with a Diablo 2 style item system, inspired by eldritch horror? everything seems to coalesce to something truly wonderful, but the game falls short on every margin. the AI art looks awful, the enemies come off as pure nonsense (I get that it's "incomprehensible", but I can comprehend it, it's a ball of trash with eyes), the maps aren't well designed, it's just a slog to play. I think if there was a real, devoted effort to replace all the generative elements, remove the dinky AI cutscenes of buildings with scary swirls, and have several dedicated enemy types with defined physiology, the game could be genuinely very fun to play. But none of that is here. Save your money, DO NOT BUY THIS.
_childDocuments_.name: Source of Madness

_childDocuments_.review: Firstly, I love the art style - like a sinister Terry Gilliam gone mad(er). The look, sound and atmosphere are fantastic; otherworldly and Lovecraftian. The overall aesthetic is awesome.The AI assisted aspect works perfectly for this subject matter - so much of the background and creatures look like I can kind of identify it, but can't quite focus on it, so it adds to the feeling of being surrounded by otherworldly madness extremely well.Gameplay is really good to! I'm very much enjoying the battles and killing the monsters is very satisfying. Difficulty balance is pretty good also, keeping a decent challenge to the progression.Some UI functionality could do with a bit of polish, but it doesn't interfere with the game.I would really like to be able to save a game mid-run tho, and not have to restart if I have to leave. A run can take more time than I often have available to complete.Overall a great game - really hits the spot!

_childDocuments_.review: Initial impressions: Delivers everything it promises. It will become more refined later I'm sure, but what's here is wonderful. It's like Noita meets barotrauma.Criticisms: -low variety of spells and spell behaviors / currently early access -Only the specialist class pyromancer is unlockable at present-Physics being wonky / in the bad waysBiggest Praises: -Atmosphere / Aesthetic-World building / Lore-Monster design / creepiness and behavior-Physics being wonky / in the good waysI recommend getting this because what exists is fun and clearly a great running start towards what could become an amazing game. Help the developer finish this and polish it into the gem it clearly is already shaping up to be.*********************************UPDATE***********************************July 2023:The game is still reccommended on sale, for the atmosphere, concept, and for the potential fun that can be had. But to be perfectly honest, it never really got much more advanced after the release. More content got added, but the effects and spells never really got the true polish they deserved. The FX isn't bad and there are many good ideas going on, it just never went from 75% to 100%. It's a decent 75% though.That's what I give this game. a 75% as good as it should be rating. If there was a neutral option, I would make this review neutral, but I don't think it's bad enough to not recommend. It's still very unique and interesting and has tons of cool moments, but the sluggish bogged down combat and for the most part unsatisfying spell effects/feel/sound synchronization make what could be a transcendent eerie experience into a nightmare where you're running in jello at times. Bosses pin you against the wall and your dash doesn't always help (especially with Krampus).

_childDocuments_.review: Recommending this game almost entirely from an artistic standpoint, and for trying something really unique with its art direction. The gameplay itself is ok, and for a roguelite the progression is a little slow. Certain upgrades are massive (healing flask, getting refills per biome) but other than that it feels like there's essentially no meta progression. Combat is basically "backpedal while holding your trigger buttons" for the most part, but it's done well enough. The randomly generated monsters are a cool gimmick, but more often than not it turns in to "idk what's going on so I'm just going to hope it dies", which unfortunately applies to the bosses as well.Overall, worth it on a sale if you're a sucker for Lovecraftian weirdness. The game is noteworthy for that on its own, and there's a really solid foundation of gameplay / progression present. With some time and patches, this could be a really great game. For now, it's firmly settled in the "good" category.
_childDocuments_.name: Source of Madness

_childDocuments_.review: MASTERPIECE. This game is  a gem and a total blast to play. Source of Madness will be a big deal when it exits early access. The game is just graphically beautiful, and captures the mood it is going for, so so so so flawlessly. In another review, a reviewer wrote if "Noita and CARRION had a baby", these are the exact thoughts I had while playing this game, and it captures these two games perfectly. The magic and abilities that you pick up, and the long flowing robe of the main character is very reminiscent of Noita. And just like in Noita, the main character is tasked with entering dungeons and areas with foul, hungry,  monstrosities that are usually reminiscent of CARRION. These monsters and  disgusting creatures that lurk in the area's that you'll be exploring, are all generated by an A.I (and the locations are also generated by an A.I.) . CARRION and Noita were very physics heavy games, and the true is also said with Source of Madness. These games rely heavily on they're fun physics engines If you're a fan of either of those games,  do yourself a favor and put this in your checkout cart. This game is shockingly good and captures Lovecraftian horror perfectly.The combat is awesome. You start with and can only have equipped two rings, and you collect more. These rings give you different spells. These are arcane spells, pyro spells, lightning, and others. They have heavy spells and light spells. This game has a lot of cool physics, and the heavy spells can cause your character to launch back when he fires it, which is a cool effect.. And along with the rings, you also collect two other gem sockets and  other attachments that also give you other abilities and stat increases, for example it may summon two arcane like crystals that follow you around and shoot at enemies. And the monsters are created by an AI within the game, and the monsters look pretty weird and cool. A lot of them have tentacles like the monster from CARRION, that you can blast limb from limb. it's rad as ♥♥♥♥.All the environments have been extremely different from each other. There is a lot of variety. This game is really good. BUT PLEASE ADD WAY MORE RINGS AND SPELLS. THIS GAME HAS A LACK OF SPELLS. Potential customers, please be aware that there are a decent amount of spells for an early access game. But the game definitely could use a lot more, like Noita. I love this game and it is my favorite new game that is out, I think it's a game that is hard not to love. I already have over 18 hours played, as of writing this review. If you love Carrion and Noita, you'll feel right at home here.
_childDocuments_.name: Source of Madness

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not very far into this game but I'd already recommend it. On the surface, Source of Madness is a lovecraftian Dead Cells clone, which by itself is already good enough for me. Yet, for whatever reason, it feels like more. Perhaps its the art style, the funky monster physics, the particle effects, or the underlying intrigue of an esoteric setting, but this is a roguelite that I actually want to finish.
_childDocuments_.name: Source of Madness

_childDocuments_.review: If you want a fair, nightmarishly moody side-scrolling action roguelite with substantial persistent progression, equipment and abilities of consequence, Source Of Madness is your title. Great to play a sorceror, with many sub-classes unlockable, and also great to play a game that is fun, challenging, yet not brutally difficult - intensity is here, but not to the extent that you can't actually take a few milliseconds to think. Physics feature prominently. Save points occur in between every major section. Definitely hooked. Worthy!P.S.: Plays great with keyboard & mouse.
_childDocuments_.name: Source of Madness

_childDocuments_.review: I expected this game to feature horrid enemy design, (horrid in a good way) very high combat difficulty and quick do or die moment instead I got the exact opposite experience. The enemy design is terrible, I understand that there's only so much you can do with AI machine learning but good god. When I think of lovecraftian I think of giant all consuming entities where even attempting to whitness the most common of entities is a dead wish so I expected quick hard hitting enemies but they are closer to a loose collection of tentacles hopelessly failing to comprehend the purpose of a door rather than a world ending threat.Most of the enemies you'll face will just aimlessly flop towards you while you keep backing up until they get stuck on the terrain at which point you just start trimming their bodyparts like it's a particularly overgrown hedge. They are also excessively bullet spongey with most fights taking up to a minute which would fit the aesthetic if that minute wasn't spent tossing fireballs at the old tentacle hedge.The attacks also feel way too hard hitting, this may sound like a weird complaint considering my issues with the enemies but they really just feel way too powerfull. Like the before mentioned fireball shoots massive balls of exploding fire that deals AOE damage, it pushes you back when you use it and it can be charged to the point where it's closer to a carpetbombing with enough knockback to literally send you flying; frankly you feel like a god chipping away at lovecraft branded bullet sponges.If there's anything I can recommend this game on it's most likely the art style as it is a very interesting style but then there's also the issues with the ambience. To keep a creepy atmosphere a lot of the background noises are whispers and groans something that is rather effective for the first 30 minutes at which point you notice that some guy with a soar throat keeps telling you to look behind you every thirty seconds at which point the novelty becomes more of a slight annoyance which really brings home the main issue of the game.The vast majority of obstacles that you face are presented as overwhelming and incomprehensible threats but play more like minor inconveniences with the tentacle slider set to max, at one point I even got a curse which caused random hostile tentacles to spawn on top of me every minute or so which usually ended up in my favor anyway as it often just caused me to rocket up in the air while the tentacle was attempting the comprehend the concept of aiming. In my first run I managed to get to the third biome at which point I died not to an enemy but to a black hole that I spawned myself and got myself trapped inside of because my dash got stuck on a platform. Considering how the game presents itself and how it actually plays clashes so heavily with with each other I almost feel entitled to compensation for severe tonal whiplash.My critiscism is very harsh but I would be lying if I said there wasn't some insane talent behind this game, The combat is impressively varied and unique, the visual design of the enemies are top notch and the one time I had an enemy that actually physically funtioned I was genuinely tense as it dashed around the area smashing into walls as it kept gaining on me but the moments where it all comes together are way too rare for this game to work.
_childDocuments_.name: Source of Madness

_childDocuments_.review: *** Several edits made after the newest patch and more time i invested into the game ***To be honest, i just bought this game because i was immediately attracted by the unique art.And i must say that the Source of Madness is a very unique experience.The art is just great. The game is dark and dreamy, just as the H. P. Lovecrafts world and books are.Sounds and music are pretty good as well, as the overall flow of the Lovecraftian inspired world.The combat is as unique as the world design, but not only in a good way - and i think it needs some improvements to be more enjoyable, especially for the new players.I understand that the slower combat is here for purpose, and i really like the movement and animations, with good old double jump and dash moves.The combat itself is more about gaining advantage from your and enemy positions, using dashes to gain distance, and just like in DS series - don't be greedy. You have to have enough patience if you don't wana die fast.On gamepad, you can move by left analog, while changing the spell direction with right analog (for some spells it's 360°, while some are only left 2 right) - this way, you can cast the spells in opposite direction you're running.You can even cast 2 spells at one time, which is very effective considering you want to do max DPS.Dash can provide a nice additional damage, some spells gives your dash a special effect, like fire bomb - with nice burn DoT, but it can damage yourself as well, so you have to use it wisely :)Sometime it's hard to dash or avoid attacks, because of the confusing enemy movement, especially when you encounter multiple enemies at once.Some enemies tends to blend with the environment, so you will find yourself confused in some cases, wondering if that thing in front of you is an enemy, part of environment, eventually a piece of another enemy you killed.I have met enemies who went up to the highest roof or tower and it was really hard to kill them just because of it.Sometime, you will have to put yourself at a disadvantage just because the enemy is stucked somewhere where you can't hit it.The game is hard. I found myself a little bit confused by overall combat flow and speed when i started. The learning curve is kind of high, but after few tries, my runs became much better, and not just because of the permanent upgrades i unlocked.In the Source of Madness, you don't create your character and level it up. Instead of it, it comes with more unique "roguelite" system, when you have to choose a new Acolyte when you'll die, loosing all your items and gold, but you can keep all upgrades related to "skill trees" and you can keep your "souls", which makes unlocking of new classes and skills easier.Permanent skill upgrades let you increase the ammount of healing flasks, ammount of dashes you can perform and lower it's cooldown, unlock new classes, starting items etc.Every time you start the game, you have to start with new acolyte (one of the general unlocks let you choose from 3 different acolytes, with different stats and start items). At the beginning, I found myself restarting the game often, just to "roll" the Acolyte with life drain/leech skill, which makes the HP management much easier. Now i'm rather using more DPS skills.Speaking of HP management - the options to replenish your HP are very limited at the beginning. You have to unlock the healing flask through the skill tree, and the first unlock only gives you half a bottle. This, combined with sort of high damage enemies can do, kinda increases the diffiCulty - especially during your first tries. Good thing is, that HP (even healing flasks) replenish when you enter new zone (not the hidden / bonus areas) or boss area.You can use the gold you collected to buy new equipment in shops (located in "combat zones"), which is really helpful, but just as gold, your items dissapear when you'll die.Despite some current cons, i can only recommend this game, just for the unique experience it is. I think that it will be only better, as the new content looks promising, but i hope that the combat will get some improvements as well :)
_childDocuments_.name: Source of Madness

_childDocuments_.review: Note: I received this game for free from the Intel sweepstakes giveaway promotion.This game is really cool.  It has a dark Lovecraftian theme, with amazing procgen monsters, in a changing world, and a lot of replayability.  I love the art style.  The music is pretty good.  I found the gameplay a bit clunky but once you get the hang of it, most of the flaws become trivial.Art/graphics/theme: If you enjoy Lovecraft/Cthulhu themed games, you'll enjoy this game.  The art is top notch and the way the game sets the tone of the 'non-euclidean geometry' in certain parts of the game is amazing.Monsters: This game has these amazing procgen monsters.  They have body parts that each have a function (ie. legs to make the monster walk; tentacles to attack with; etc) and the body parts can be destroyed if they take enough damage.  I would recommend playing the game just to experience how they implemented the enemies - it is truly unique.Gameplay: The biggest issue at the moment is the balance.  There are a ton of different items to customize your build with but I found only a few that were useful.  I hope the devs look at reworking and balancing the ways items are used.The game has a progression system between "runs", but for the most part it is used to unlock new items/classes.  A few perks give more survibability (ie. a life potion).  This means the only way to gain stats/power/surviveability is via the items found in the world.  Because of the balancing issue of items, this limits the creativity of some builds since you will likely be using certain items only.  The lack of vertical power progression makes the game a lot more challenging, which may affect peoples ability to progress.  Further, unlocking new items dilutes the "item pool", making it harder to obtain desirable items (the devs said they are considering ways to address this).It took me about 12-16 hours to complete the game.  Probably about 20-24 hours to unlock everything.Other: I hope the devs add steam workshop support.  There is so much potential by allowing players to tweak/modify elements of this game (especially the monsters/body parts).The devs are active on the steam forums and regularly respond to questions/feedback.  It is really refreshing to see the way they interact with the community.  I provided some feedback in beta and saw it added to the game for release.Score: 60.5 out of 69

_childDocuments_.review: Source of Madness is a side-scrolling roguelike set in the Lovecraftian inspired world of Loam Land, with wonderfully aesthetic visuals and interestingly designed creatures.Gameplay with the exploration and combat is extremely fun to explore and conduct as you encounter the various dark and gritty areas and fight all the unique and strange Lovecraftian inspired creatures. As you go from area to area, you earn powers and tools as you gain equippable weapons and clothing and earning power ups to become stronger. The world is powered by procedural generation and AI machine learning, which keeps the game entertaining as playing the game is a bit different each time. The combat itself is while not bad, is mostly okay. Occasionally I got stuck in between the enemies when there were too many of them but did manage to get out eventually. For the most part it was enjoyable to play.The visuals are the main highlight of the game with the dark tone and appealing aesthetics consisting of several biomes and plenty of nightmarish looking creatures. The background and environment are both very well detailed and the all the characters from the foes to the shopkeepers are all designed very interestingly with the Lovecraftian look. The use of colours is well done with the darker colour palette. The music and sound effects are another nice touch with some action and eerie music and sound in the background and coming from the monsters. The sound effects from your attacks and abilities are also satisfying to listen to as they hit the enemies.Controls are fine to play with on keyboard and mouse as it isn’t too complex to play, though it is controller supported and was my preferred way to play. It is mainly just the movements and various keys for combat and spells, but it was more satisfying to perform them using a controller as you move around enemies and fight them. Price is around the norm for indie games, though seems like it will be increased later when it leaves early access. Currently, I’d say it is worth the current price and worth checking out for the engrossing visuals. Am looking forward to seeing what comes out of the game from its early access phase as it develops further. Overall, it is a compelling action roguelike with very interesting visuals of the Lovecraftian theme. At times it can be a bit wishy washy but all in all was a fun time. It should improve throughout early access, making it a more worthwhile time.

_childDocuments_.review: This game kind of mixes my feelings. It has decent builds variety, interesting overall concept, creative art style and some neat ideas in it's combat system such as dismembering enemies, counterattacks, riding large enemies' back. But... The problems arise at the start of second act. This act has larger amounts of complex enemies with dangerous abilities, narrow corridors, poison and freezing traps everywere, and all of this just mixes up together. Your mobility is already limited by narrow guts-like location, and now everything is trying to slow you down, freeze you, entangle you, you constantly get stuck in something or get flung in the air and your entire screen ia covered in moving mass of eyes and tentacles, which constantly swings it's claws and casts something. It feels slow and tedious; it's not hard, just extremely unfun, and you can't just run past all of these, because path is blocked by obstacles and monsters move faster than you. Also, I had a need sometimes to change equipment mid-fight, and inventory at this point started feeling very clunky, because I can change equipment while inventory UI is still in opening animation, but I can't close it until it finishes this animation. This led to a couple of shameful death, when monsters damaged me in inventory opening animation. I think, clear understanding what is happening and responsive controls must be at first point in the roguelike. Next thing is Krampus, second boss of the second act... This guy enrages me. You can't beat him with clever moves because of freezing and small arena with spikes. This boss is kind of damage rush, and you must kill him before he chip damages you enough or freeze and one-shot you. After all, I recommend the game, but with one caveat: keep in mind that at one point you may to grind your way through the game, which is not a very pleasant experience. Also geomancer sucks

_childDocuments_.review: This game perfectly shows how important Art Direction is, and how "AI-Generation" should not be a genre on its own. Not only does the look and feel of the game suffer immensely from the lack of clarity, which leads to unclear objectives or spacial orientation, the enemy design makes fighting and exploring not an exciting endeavor but more of a slog. The idea of linking attacks to magical rings so you can mix and match different attacks for different encounters, and the 'skill-tree' based design of unlocking new attacks is fun though. However this alone does not justify the lack of vision that clearly shows itself in the level design. I would compare my first play session as trying to finish a maze, with one entrance, one exit, and now path deviations. With no tactical challenge in defeating enemies and no clear path in the levels, I could just hold left and attack and get pretty far into the level. If you are interested in AI generated game design, I would suggest just playing around with Dalle2 or Midjourney yourself, and trying to generate a lore-heavy story for the artwork using Chat-GPT. That would be more fun than this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Wow the critics who rated this game so poorly have no idea what the point of this game is suppose to be.It’s a souls rogue like game. You grind through levels, slowly power up throughout. While also having a “home base” for a lack of a better word where you put talent points in skill trees. It’s similar to Hades in some elements as well, but your hand is not held. You have to figure things out and experiment just like Soul style games.The art is fantastic, the combat is good, despite some blandness, and despite what critics say it’s been exciting finding builds that work well. The story is very mysterious and the occult theme feels great. There’s a few issues. The lack of imaginative spell customization. You use rings as a source of your spells. It would have been great if they let you upgrade the rings you had so you don’t have to wait for a drop of the same ring but more powerful for the build you created, or at least make the rings you’re looking for more accessible. The UI is a little tiring to look at, as there is little color contrast. So cool down timers are hard to see. That being said, if you head to the discord, the creators are active and take in feed back well, and have a desire to continually improve the game based on feedback. Would absolutely recommend this game to anyone who likes soulborne type games, who feel like the genre is a little over saturated atm and need something refreshing.

_childDocuments_.review: REALLY glad I decided to pick this game! Something about Lovecraftian-based games that always offer something extra special, and this is no exception! It's quickly become my current fave to play. Though I often steer away from 'souls-like' games, something about the game-play here does not discourage me from dying over and over...as it never seems  fact, you kind of see it coming once it happens, so no frustrating, rage-quit kind of deaths really. Plus, there are some benefits to dying, as you can transfer the monies earned from each run to buy upgrades, or do so over time, that make it worthwhile. There is a varied feel to each play-through which is unique enough to feel fresh, the battles are challenging, yet not unfair, and several comments here from players who find themselves frustrated by backgrounds which seem to confuse them, visually, from foregrounds is something I personally find appealing...even quite sublime, IMHO.  To me, Source of Madness is fun, fair, gorgeous to look at, and I have bought in to it all. Plus, updates I have seen since I have had the game seem to address many if not most of the feedback in the comments sections and/or reviews, so the complaints from gamers have been addressed and taken seriously, while this game is in early access, so they follow gamer issues to heart, in deeds as well as words, which is nice to see. The Developers do make rather clear that they intend to take players' issues seriously, and it seems they mean to in earnest, something always cool to see actually happen...lol. And no...I do not know them or write this Review for their behalf...I simply find this game to my liking, to my surprise and delight. I took a chance getting this game, while not normally my 'cup of tea', and thus far it's paid off handsomely, and I am having a blast playing it, and feeling smarter for taking a risk in getting Source of Madness. I even included it among my Nominations during the Thanksgiving Sale Event here on Steam...giving it my choice of 'Outstanding Visual Style' Award for 2021! Source of Madness plays, at least for me, like a gift that keeps on giving, with an EA game with Updates showing they listen to their players, and good variation in-game to prevent feeling a 'same-old' kind of sense, while already knowing the further you get, the more varied things become. Well done!! :)
