_childDocuments_.review: Even though I know exactly what I should expect from Zeboyd's games (I've played all of them), I'm still surprised by how consistently they manage to pull off turn-based jrpg combat that doesn't bore you to death. Fast-paced fights, every encounter is high-stakes, various party compositions and loadouts.It had enough potential for the full duration of the game and in a way even left me craving for more. I played on highest difficulty and I think it was perfect, so I recommend it to pretty much anyone who's up for a bit of a challenge. The story... I've no idea what was happening there, but it sure was fun. It definitely lives up to its title.
_childDocuments_.name: This Way Madness Lies

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game and I wish it was longer. The characters are great and I felt like I only got a proper handle on the battle system in the last quarter of the game. But I'll definitely be playing it again at some point (hopefully in NG+, which has been mooted but at the time of writing isn't in the PC version).As it is, it's a snappy JRPG with visual novel interludes. It's absolutely linear - the only choices you have are cosmetic ones in the visual novel sections, and your party is preset until you gain the final member towards the end - at which point you can switch any of the girls aside from leader Imogen. There are no towns, shops etc. - the only downtime aside from the visual novel bits is a brief section in between each act where you can chat to your teammates and change your setup.You'll probably get more out of the magical-girls-meets-Shakespeare setup if you know Shakespeare's oeuvre, but it's not necessary. The narrative is extremely slight - nothing about the gameworld is explained, you just go along with it. But the girls themselves are the stars of the show - breezily-written, distinct, and just generally nice in a way that feels rarer than it should.The battle system will be familiar to anyone who's played Cosmic Star Heroine (and I imagine the other Zeboyd games, but I haven't played them yet). It's a mix of traditional battling with heavy emphasis on buffs and debuffs, along with resource management (in terms of within individual battles - your health and items regenerate after every one). What I like most about it is how all your actions are connected to each other - you probably won't get very far randomly attacking and using skills. It's really satisfying to set up a plan and then see a screen of enemies defeated in one shot.My main complaints are linked to the battles, though. It's odd that in a game where buffs / debuffs are so important, a lot of the information is hidden. You can't see at a glance if your party members are poisoned, stunned, powered up and so on. And while there are no random battles, the enemies in the field are all represented by the same purple ghoul-type figures, and you only find out exactly who you're up against once you're in the battle. A lot of the enemies have opposing elemental strengths / weaknesses which can make this a bit frustrating, but there are abilities that get around it.But overall, I'm really glad I've played this and I'm a little sad it's over. Recommended to anyone who likes JRPGs with likeable characters and clever battle systems, and doesn't mind a lack of exploration. Oh, and the music and art are also fantastic - please don't skip the transformation sequences!
_childDocuments_.name: This Way Madness Lies

_childDocuments_.review: A fun, charming RPG that respects your time. I love the creativity of taking Shakespeare's work and combining it with magical girls in a turn-based RPG. I comfortably finished this in just over eight hours and had a lot of fun doing so. The cast is immediately likable, the combat has a good amount of depth despite the shorter runtime, and the writing is enjoyable throughout.
_childDocuments_.name: This Way Madness Lies

_childDocuments_.review: Do you like the idea of a JRPG but hate the execution? That being multi-hour long tutorials, insufferable padding and absolutely horrendous pacing and filler? Get this game. Cut all that crap out and you're left with a really fun yet still deep combat system with a good progression system and challenging gameplay. From the creators of Cthulhu Saves The World comes another real banger from Zeboyd.Combat is pretty fun in that you have your typical turn-based battles with leveling up and character progression but the fun Unite, Recharge, Rows, and Hyper systems add some depth to make the game interesting/The Soundtrack and Sound Design are great and totally weren't what I was expecting. Every piece of music is really good in this game and there's a lot of variety to it.The dialogue and writing are entertaining, the dialogue feels believable and some of it got a chuckle out of me, pretty good considering I can't feel anything anymore. Aesthetic execution is not my cup of tea, it's definitely American art trying to do Sailor Moon with its own direction and it's fine, it's a good effort. The sprites look amazing and most of the game looks great. Just not into some of the character portraits and a few other nitpicks here and there.Everything is solid here and for 10 bucks it's hard to really complain. There's nothing convoluted, frustrating, or oversimplified about this game. Everything is paced well and extremely fun.Thanks for reading, if you want more recommendations, I have a curator page here:
_childDocuments_.name: This Way Madness Lies

_childDocuments_.review: Ah Zeboyd, never change. Whenever I start a new Zeboyd game, a warm comfy feeling washes over me. When you know what you like and you like what you know, sometimes you just want more of the same and Zeboyd game really rides that line between familiar yet different enough to be fresh. I think they really nailed it here. It is a tight, brisk moving game that doesn’t waste your time.A few things I really like:•	They throw you into a mission without any backstory. You play as a team of thespian highschoolers who can transform into magical girls and portal into Shakespeare book universes to help fight off monster and corruption that shouldn’t exist. Why or how do they have these powers? How do they know which worlds need saving? Don’t know and the pacing is brisk enough where I honestly didn't care. •	The humor is pure Zeboyd. Similar to their Cthulhu and Penny Arcade games. A handful of laugh out loud moments for sure and I enjoy how the game gets increasingly zany as the story progresses.•	Combat is fast paced yet engaging. Battles last just long enough for strategy to be a necessity but not long enough to drag. Obviously, this will vary based on difficulty setting but I found moderate to be perfect for what I am looking for.•	Great soundtrack! Strongly considering picking up the ost which is reasonably priced.•	Easy 100% completion. Thanks, Zeboyd!Some meh things:•	The magical girl transformation is a mixed bag. On one hand I really like it because it highlights the differences in the girls. Each girl has their own music and slight differences in stance and headpiece and you can get a good sense of who they are without the need for dialogue.o	On the other hand. It kind of drags and isn’t worth playing every time in my opinion. You can skip it, but you kind of feel like a dirtbag (Thanks Zeboyd!)One last thing which may be controversial, but I found it refreshing that none of the girls were lesbians. I know that’s all the rage now a days, but it is just nice to see a bunch of girls hanging out, putting on plays, and just enjoying each other’s company without the need for some kind of romance. It’s more of a meta thing and not necessarily good or bad, but I felt it worth mentioning. Zeboyd if you are reading this, sincerely thank you. I’ve been enjoying your games for about a decade now. You manage to create a style of game that you cannot find anywhere else. I look forward to checking out your next project!
_childDocuments_.name: This Way Madness Lies

_childDocuments_.review: This Way Madness Lies is a mixed bag. The concept is great: magical girls who are in a theater troupe/class by day, magical girls by night? Well, maybe? It's not very well spelled out, which is my biggest problem with the game: the narrative is extremely half-baked and only moderately fleshed out.TWML kind of takes the 'toss the player into the deep end' approach to storytelling. You never really get an introduction to any of the cast, you just tag along on their wacky adventures and figure out as you go. How did they become magical girls? How did they meet? What kind of school do they go to? There's all these questions and more that the story doesn't really bother answering. The narrative occurs in sporadic 'chapters' that just toss the player randomly between events in the story without any real time to let them breathe or get to know the girls.This could work if the narrative maybe offered flashbacks or more character-specific moments to flesh them out, but it doesn't provide any. The characters are fun, bear in mind, and have some fun dialogue, but without much backstory or history on them, they sadly boil down to little more than tropes with slightly more personality than average.That's really my main(only) gripe with the game, but beyond the narrative issues, the combat is a blast. All the girls have wildly unique combat functionality, so the possibilities of party customization are through the roof. I personally used the MC(Imogen, a mix of support and strong attacks), Rosalind(wears glasses, has AOE elementals), Viola(heavy physicals), and Beatrice(status effect queen), but just about any party formation will work. It also takes a lot of the irritation out of RPGs with how battles are on the map, and all the party heal after every battle. The developers are born-and-bred RPG veterans, so I'm sure they know how to keep the genre fresh, and it shows. Each character has both traits and abilities, so even if you decide to use the same party I did, they could wind up being completely different than my setup. (Another small nitpick: you can't pick who you want to use until near the very end of the game, but that's fair to an extent, since it forces the player to see what each of the girls has to offer.)It's also a very breezy, largely simple game. The combat is fun, rarely gets old, and it has some fun dungeon varieties. I just wish that with a rich pool of stories to pull from with both the magical girl genre and Shakespeare as influence, the writing better lived up to the premise, especially with more fleshing out of the cast and interactions between the party.Also, there is a neat feature to """translate""" the Shakespearean dialogue into "Zeboyd text", which really just boils down to making the dialogue silly and sadly not as clever as it thinks it is, so I always preferred using the original text.
_childDocuments_.name: This Way Madness Lies

_childDocuments_.review: This is not a terrible game by any stretch, but I didn't find myself enjoying it. My main issue is that, for a game about Drama students, the writing was disappointing. They're also magical girls, so I was expecting a mashup of tones, and the Old English translator was fun! But pretty soon I found myself clicking through the story and not really connecting to any of the characters. If that doesn't sound like something that would bother you, then this is a turn-based RPG with its own take on abilities you might enjoy playing with. I had fun finding character and move combinations, switching it up once or twice every area to try new approaches. That said, by the last area or two, as the battles got longer and no less frequent, things started to drag for me. Maybe if I had levelled more and learned new things to try out, or found ways to speed through battles faster, it would have been a smoother ending.
_childDocuments_.name: This Way Madness Lies

_childDocuments_.review: And with this game done I have now officially played and completed every  game.This was a pleasant weekends diversion and I feel it's a great choice for a relaxing weekend RPG that respects your time, (Code speak for short and sweet, rather than long and grindy.)Minor critiques would include that the training wheels that allow the player to choose his party freely come off a bit too late for my personal taste, I understand that showcasing a character or two for the first few chapters to teach the player their mechanics and synergy with the others, but forcing character parties for most of the game works against full enjoyment. If there were a few more chapters to enjoy and play with varying character setups would have alleviated this feeling as well, but then of course the game would be a bit longer, which in  (humble?) opinion would have been fine as the game could have gone on a few chapters more before the final curtain call and  for it!Ultimately I'd rate this highly if you enjoyed the style of games Zeboyd is known for.
_childDocuments_.name: This Way Madness Lies

_childDocuments_.review: Cute little game.  As I expected going in from my experience with the developer, the combat is REALLY good, at least on hard mode.  And the writing is extremely clever and funny.  The "translation" of the Shakespearean English lines into modern English is hilarious, and the game is the right length to realize its premise without feeling like the story is getting repetitive.Took me about 13 hours on the hardest difficulty.  Supposedly the average play time is about 7-8 hours, which I guess is apparently being measured on some other difficulty setting.Saw another review where someone was complaining about the combat being boring, but they were clearly on an easier difficulty.  I thought hard mode was calibrated almost perfectly, which is to say that I died about 50 times but I always knew what I did wrong.  Every skill and trait felt useful, and the characters felt balanced and unique, and the forced party shifts kept the battles feeling fresh.It's an extremely linear game, but it's not trying to be anything else, and the linear path it leads you down is a well-crafted experience.

_childDocuments_.review: I love all of Zeboyd games work and this is no exception. It's a quick, funny little JRPG with some nice little mechanic innovations (Stats and traits are tied together, letting you customize your team a LOT, especially along with all of the different options for abilities and how traits change them) my only complaint is the game is so short you don't get to try out as much as you'd like at the higher levels... but it's got enough little fluff choice branches in there to add some replayability.Also, AMAZING soundtrack

_childDocuments_.review: A wonderful mash-up of Shakespeare, magical girls, and JRPG. I played the game on Challenging and the difficulty curve was enjoyable (matched to my party's abilities throughout). The story is split between Shakespeare inspired nightmares and High School Drama life. We follow a group of Shakespeare nerds while they attempt to put on creative renditions of Shakespeare plays and also fight nightmare demon creatures as magical girls. It's breezy and does a good job of providing enough story to make the dungeon segments compelling while not getting in the way of the dungeoning. The only negative is that near the end the amount of menuing required to level-up/equip characters slows down the pacing, but never fatally. Recommended!

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely fantastic!"This Way Madness Lies" does not waste your time and delivers a great experience in less than 10 hours. The story is full of laughs and the gameplay works really well.Unlike other RPGs, each battle is self-contained. Any items you use, abilities, and hp are fully restored at the end of each combat. So instead of lots of combats that slowly wear down your resources, you have fewer combats, but each one is a more intense. It's a different way of looking at RPG combat and lends itself well to a shorter experience.The story is lighthearted and enjoyable. I was constantly laughing at what the characters said or a monster description. I recommend this game.And don't skip the transformation sequences.
_childDocuments_.name: This Way Madness Lies

_childDocuments_.review: Interesting concept, poor game design. The TLDR of it is that it's mostly kinetic novel story combined with a frustrating combat system. Overall this game feels like a gimmick selling itself on the Magical Girls x Shakespeare concept and not by actually being a fun game to play.Starting with the combat, because that's the most interactive part of the game, it's JRPG-style but it comes off as different just for the sake of being different and fails to be good. First of all if you want to see enemy HP and weaknesses, you have to choose an attack that targets only one enemy and move the selection amongst them. Then you cancel and choose what you REALLY want to do. If your attack-one is spent (disabled) then you can't even see any enemy stats and plan appropriately. Why make it so cumbersome to see enemy HP and weaknesses? Secondly a lot of the abilities lack good descriptions so i don't even use some of them because i don't know what they actually do. And then the most obvious annoyance is that you are forced to waste turns by resting to make your abilities available again since they get disabled after using them. But don't worry, it has the same old problems most JRPG games have in that you keep fighting the same enemies over and over in a single stage to grind up character levels and you end up relying on the same attack patterns anyway. The few bright spots are that there are no individual character levels, leveling up is handled as an entire group. It doesn't matter who's in your party or if someone got KO'd. You can also change the difficulty at any time but that's like taking the entree out of a meal.Speaking of the party, you can only take 4 at a time but you have no idea what you'll be facing so you can't plan who to take. But guess what, that doesn't even matter because when you begin a combat stage the party you get is scripted and it ignores your picks anyway. So why even let me choose?As for the story, i'm 4 hours in which i guess should be near the halfway point but it's still superficial. By now there should have been a captivating plot point to bring depth to the story but there's no feeling of a need to save the world or anything like that. It feels episodic in the sense that the girls are just going about normally until an evil power shows up. If there is something big at play that's behind all the encounters, it's taking too long to get there.Unlike the usual JRPG's, there's no free roam outside of the combat areas so there's no story exploration or NPC's to talk to. Outside of combat it's just like a kinetic novel. All you're doing is pushing a button to advance the text with the rare chance to answer a question. This wouldn't be so bad if there were at least nice high-res visuals to go with the story but there aren't any. If you're like me, you're just skipping through the text and accidentally answering any prompt that does come up. The problem is that there's still no buildup in the story so i'm not interested in what they're talking about. Thankfully the Shakespearean dialogs aren't very prevalent because they feel cringey.I've played a lot of games based on the older style of JRPG like this one is and this is just trying to be different but isn't doing anything better. It still feels like a grind to play with a lot of irrelevant dialog to skip through. The aspects it does differently are just frustrating. This concept would have been better served as a visual novel.
_childDocuments_.name: This Way Madness Lies

_childDocuments_.review: A Magical Girl game in the style of a JRPG.  If you've ever played a Zeboyd game before like Cthulhu Saves the World this game has the same humor with retro game references and pop culture jokes.  Mixed in with Sailor Moon and Shakespeare and you have This Way Madness Lies.This game has the most polished RPG combat that Zeboyd has ever made.  The battles are so enjoyable I went out of my way to fight everything I could.The story is held up by the characters.  The girls all have interesting personalities and their banter is on point but never feels like a Marvel movie.The game is quite short, but priced accordingly.  I think it's well worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: This Way Madness Lies

_childDocuments_.review: Zeboyd generally makes good games and this one immediately grabbed me.Rather than their traditional 8-bit look and sound, this one leaps forward, still maintaining the general feel but adding a lot more depth in terms of animation and especially through voiced attacks and music. Booting it up and immediately being greeted with electric guitar and a three minute opening song, only to find moments later that all of the music holds that same standard, was a welcome surprise that I haven't seen in even most modern style games.The gameplay systems are simple, so far it feels like the normal enemies are more of a time waste than a challenge since you start with full resources each battle, but even the boss fights felt good and required some strategy to stay standing. I'm also looking forward to playing with the customizable Traits and Abilities, which allow you really shift how each character is used.The game throws you right into the story and makes it very clear exactly what you should expect. It immediately embraces the zaniness of the setting, with your first mission being to save Romeo from a man-eating plant. It frequently breaks the fourth wall. It subverts expectations. Most importantly, it is genuinely, laugh out loud funny at times.I've only played through the first area so far and will post an updated review once I've gotten further. So far, highly recommend this one if your'e a fan of JRPGs.
_childDocuments_.name: This Way Madness Lies

_childDocuments_.review: This Way Madness Lies is about a group of drama students who enter worlds of Shakespeare, which have been corrupted, to cleanse them (more or less). The girls are sweet and entertaining; nothing inappropriate or "offensive" here. The game is some good quick fun, though I confess I know very little about Shakespeare and had to look up all the answers to the occasional questions they ask. The game took about 6 hours to complete on easy; it's probably longer if you play on a harder difficulty. Overall it is a well-made game. My only "complaint" is that I want to keep playing. :p There are a couple things that you get to select, which likely lead to different cut scenes, but for the most part a second play through would likely be much like the first.
_childDocuments_.name: This Way Madness Lies

_childDocuments_.review: This Way Madness Lies is a quick and breezy RPG designed to be finished in a weekend. It really reminds me of B tier Super Nintendo RPGs, something in the vein of Paladin’s Quest or Secret of the Stars.The setup is a group of high school girls travel to Shakespearean inspired worlds and make their way through a RPG dungeon to liberate it from some big bad. Interwoven between the dungeons are brief visual novel style sequences to add story bits and humor.Up until the end, each chapter forces you to play with mostly different characters, each of which has unique battle abilities. You can also equip traits on each party member to add stat boosts or passive abilities, which helps to add a little bit of depth to the party customization.The music is great and I really liked the visuals as well. There are neat transformation sequences at the beginning of each dungeon that drive home the magical girl aesthetic.I clocked around 7.5 hours and that length felt about right for the depth of the game. I think if it were longer I’d be looking to get more out of either the story or the gameplay, but for a RPG designed to be finished quickly it’s well tuned.Just play on one of the harder difficulty settings to get the most fun out of it.
_childDocuments_.name: This Way Madness Lies

_childDocuments_.review: It's cute, it's funny, and it's fun! This Way Madness Lies delivers gameplay in bite-sized segments. You'll do a dungeon, then see short scenes with character interaction or plot development, then dungeon, etc. The game presents you with choices that vary which scenes you see and how those scenes play out. The combat system isn't groundbreaking, but it does enough to keep turn-based RPG gameplay interesting. Each character has a slate of abilities to choose from, and in battle these can change significantly if a character is powered up or not. For instance, one character's single targets become AOEs, one's AOEs become higher damage single-targets, skills change elements, healing changes to damaging enemies, etc.In short, it's great & you definitely won't feel like the game is wasting your time or padding unnecessarily. Also, the soundtrack is full of bangers.

_childDocuments_.review: Fun game, worth the price if you enjoy the genre imo. The battle system keep getting more streamlined and overall better from game to game.You'll have for about 7 hours of gameplay in normal mode.Recommended, and hoping it gets enough sales for a sequel!

_childDocuments_.review: Big disappointmentI suppose it was too much to ask that the game would treat magical girls and shakespeare plays as something serious. But the references to shakespeare are just shoehorned that just spouts it as references like a smartass rather as anything meaningufl, and the magical girls seem to just be an excuse to have girls doing jrpg combat and not something that's actually inspired by magical girls and have some sense.The bad part is that the game begins in the middle of a dungeon and assumes you understand all the characters, understand the plot and understand what's going on. At first I though this was just the typical case of the introduction of a game being an event that happens later in the story and that once it was over the first act would properly start and I would get an intro of who are the characters, why are they magical girls and why are they entering shakespeare worlds. I was baffled that didn't happen and that the game was going to continue in such an inorganic manner. I can't be invested if you just throw me in and won't give me a reason to care. I can't care about the magical girls because the game doesn't care to tell me where they come from and what are they doing. I can't care about the shakespearean fantasy elements because the game didn't care to not treat shakespeare just like a joke. I can't care about the characters because the game doesn't care to tell me who they are. I can't care about the plot because the game doesn't care to tell me whats going on and just prefers to make shokingly bad jokes and memes mocking shakespeareI wanted to like the game, but I'm disappointed

_childDocuments_.review: Absolute insanity! One of the most bonkers RPGs I've ever played, and likely counting all RPGs I ever will play.I don't know if the menu is as polished as it should be, but this game offers *A LOT* of fun for the money! My only complaint is that it's so very short, but at the very least it doesn't overstay its welcome. Not too short, not too long, not so insane it loses its charm.This is not going to be a profound experience, just a lot of hearty laughs from start to finish.

_childDocuments_.review: Although this is not an RPG Maker game (see Bollehopp's comment regarding my original assertion that it is), it certainly   like one, both from how it plays and from its OK artwork. To give it a unique sales proposition, a very Japanese-style treatment of a fantasy Shakespeare theme was bolted on. I expected all of this when buying this game (and in fact thought it was an RPG Maker game with bought assets); it's consistent with an enjoyable experience, and I am not too picky.Unfortunately, this is not an enjoyable experience but a lazy job. If I had bought this game directly on Steam, I would have it refunded. Clearly the game also gets a lot of things right, and I will give it a chance and maybe update this review later. But you can likely find everything you need to know among the positive reviews.There is absolutely no volume control. This is a problem because the game plays rock music at maximum volume. It is therefore impossible to listen to something else on the same computer while playing this game.The control scheme is displayed in the Options dialog, but it cannot be changed at all.Since nobody else has reported this, this may be specific to my setup. (Running the game on Ubuntu Linux.) However, I still hold it against the developer because this is the first time ever I have had this problem, so the developer probably did something non-standard that causes this. (Another Linux user commented below that they do not have this problem.)The issue is that there is no way to leave the Options dialog or the Save dialog other than by using Steam or the operating system to shut down the game. According to the Options dialog, the Escape key should do the job as usual, but at least for me it doesn't. I have never had this problem in other games (especially not in RPG Maker games, so this supports the claim it's not one; maybe it would be better if it was), and in gameplay mode the Escape key does work: it opens an exit confirmation dialog.Whoever wrote the "Olde English" texts clearly had no idea what they were doing. The English of Shakespeare's time is called Early Modern English. Old English (also known as Anglo-Saxon) is a far earlier stage of the language and much closer to Old German than it is to Modern English or even to Shakespeare's English. Does the following example of Old English sound even remotely like Shakespeare? "Fæder ure, ðu ðe eart on heofenum, ..." This is the beginning of the Lord's Prayer, which in Shakespeare's time went like this: "Our father which art in heauen, ...".Unfortunately, the developer wasn't content with copying random Shakespeare quotations into the game, sometimes in a way that makes no sense. They also tried to write in Shakespeare's English, while clearly having no idea whatsoever of Early Modern English grammar.For example, Early Modern English for "Help me!" is definitely not "Helpest thou me!", but is simply "Help me!". Although you  use "Help thou me!" if you want to make it sound more antiquated."I beseech thee, brave women, ..." is ungrammatical because in a sentence addressing more than one person (in this case four women), you can of course not use the singular pronoun thou/thee to refer to them. Even if Juliet had addressed only one of the heroes, the singular would still have been questionable in context because the situation asked for the polite form of address which in Modern English is the only one: "you", or its alternate form "ye". So the developer should have used "I beseech you, brave women, ..." or, to make it sound more antiquated, "I beseech ye, brave women...".Given the developer's linguistic incompetence, it is no wonder that the "auto-translations" into "New English" are no such thing. They are alternative text versions that often are not translations of the "Olde English" sentences at all, and tend to make more sense.All of this may be a non-issue for most native speakers of non-Indo-European languages and even for native English speakers with a relatively poor education (such as seems to be standard in the US, for example). But for someone with a good grounding in a European language that makes the same grammatical differentiations that Early Middle English does (and Modern English has lost), it is too painfully obvious to be ignored easily. This certainly applies to native German speakers such as myself.After a short monologue by "Shakespeare", we find ourselves controlling a group of four female protagonists. The only thing we learn about them are their names, their stats, and that they are members of the "Stratford-Upon-Avon High Drama Society". For some reason, the group stands in front of a portal, and the only thing we can do is enter the portal. The rudimentary context given on the Store Page is significantly more than is present in the game, and is all we get.

_childDocuments_.review: At its core, it's a game that rewards constant tinkering with character builds, party compositions, and strategy. _childDocuments_.review: I am not a big fan of Sailor Moon/Magic Girl-esque anime or material, nor Shakespear in general, and yet, I have found myself pleasantly enjoying the game, its humour, and its vibes with a smile on my face.Each girl has her own character without being overbearing on the screen or the script, the game doesn't overstay its welcome, and the mechanics are, actually, simple yet very engaging! Each character has its own VERY unique set of abilities (No single skill is shared between them), and Unite skills bring another layer to the game where you are rewarded for playing defensively or sticking it out, plus giving another venue against bosses or if you feel outmatched.The trait system (Where each character has 3 passives, and you mix and match them as you level up and gain more) was an interesting replacement for the gearing, and I REALLY liked how I could customize my favourite character to my own liking.Really nice! If you are remotely into Turn Based Combat in a Final Fantasy/Golden Sun kind of style, this is a banger. Worth every penny, and just a no-brainer to buy on any kind of discount. Just go for it! You won't regret it.11 Hours was enough to beat it on Challenging (Second to worst difficulty), and I never felt outright overpowered, died only few times, and easily won with a little change in my approach.

_childDocuments_.review: The magical girl aesthetic and Shakespeare aren't usually my thing, but This Way Madness Lies was charming enough to hold my attention throughout the 14-ish hours it lasted me. The way this game handles the unite mechanic is pretty interesting. They start at a 'level 1' of sorts and become stronger the more turns pass before actually using them, with a cap of level 10. It was a neat idea that sometimes had me wondering 'oooh should I use my unite now because I need it in the moment, or should I save it for when it's stronger?'. It's worth noting that going hyper will boost unite levels by 2, but iirc they still abide by the level 10 cap. Going hyper on turn 9 would not give a lv 11 unite for example.Another neat layer of decision making is in the traits that the girls unlock as they level up. There were a few traits that came with very good stat boosts but I didn't find their main effects to be particularly useful, while others were the opposite, having very useful effects but with smaller stat boosts. Even after beating the game, I'm still not sure if it's optimal to just prioritise the stats, but it was fun to experiment as the game went on. One of my favourite traits was the one that gives you the Unstoppable buff immediately. It was a nice safety net. On the topic of buffs, one of the problems I had with Cosmic Star Heroine unfortunately persists in This Way Madness Lies. I still couldn't find an indicator on the battle UI pointing out how long buffs last, so I would sometimes forget that someone even had the Inspire buff active for example. I hope Zeboyd Games considers adding some sort of buff indicator to their future games, for the sake of convenience. A more minor complaint with the gameplay is that I wish the game would let me experiment more with the party members. You're forced to use specific teams in each Act and you're only given the option to swap freely starting with... Act 9 I think? And there's 12 Acts in total. Given the game's short runtime, I would have liked more freedom sooner. I wanted to use Rosalind more in particular. I liked Rosalind because she has a lot of type coverage! Instead, we're forced to use Miranda for a lot of the game, and her starting attack move is very RNG-dependent! It's funny to gamble sometimes, but she doesn't unlock a consistent attack option for a while iirc. As for the story and characters, don't go into this game expecting a deep narrative or thought-provoking character writing. Even with the game's short runtime and fast-paced plot, I feel there was a bit of room to flesh out the characters that the writers didn't quite take advantage of. Still, a lot of the lines had me chuckling. At one point, Imogen wonders why this game doesn't have a Run Away command and I'm like 'I don't know, Zeboyd, you tell me!'. At another point, Imogen finds Miranda slacking off on her assignment and instead playing... Cosmic Star Heroine... Very clever, Zeboyd.Great game overall! It's got funny writing, an engaging gameplay loop and from my experience the higher difficulties can put in quite a bit of work! I'm very pleased with what Zeboyd produced here.

_childDocuments_.review: The game has a ton of good going for it. I've seen other reviews compare it favorably to other games from the same developer, but this is my first title of theirs, so I can't really make those comparisons. If you've played the Sailor Moon RPG for the Super Nintendo through its fan translation and enjoyed it, this game feels very similar, but has a much, much better script and more balanced combat.  The short synopsis of the plot is magical girls meet Shakespeare without forcing you to really have to know much about either to enjoy the game.  The characters are memorable and distinct from each other in combat, the Shakespearean "translations" are silly and fun, and the ability, item, and even "magical girl title" system all put a fun spin on what can sometimes be a drab, standard turn-based JRPG experience in other games.I just wish it stuck a little bit closer to some of the norms of the genre. This game has that combination of "you can't run from combat," and also "you can stealth around enemy encounters (but there's no stealth gameplay)", and also "there's no soft reset," and also "your grind is kinda not rewarded." At "normal" difficulty, the bosses are relatively easy to beat at what feels like a minimum level. At higher difficulties, your only rewards seem to be pride and a longer grind for the extra numbers.Additionally, after introducing you to an ENTIRE TEAM of fantastic magical girls, one of whom is an AOE expert, the game takes all of them away and pigeonholes you entire specific party setups. You'll end up fighting big groups of enemies where you're lucky to get an elemental advantage, have no AOE, are lucky to have a rez ability, and the rez ability requires two separate characters to be upright because it's a rare, once-per-fight Unite ability. The end result is what, to me, feels like some arbitrarily long grind fights with no reward, fought by party members the game chooses for me despite teasing the ability to pick my own team. This isn't the first non-AAA RPG I've played that does this. Clearly it's a gameplay loop that other people like. And aside from that, I love love LOVE everything about this game! The soundtrack is fantastic, the game looks like a Super Nintendo RPG which is exactly how I like my RPGs to look, and when the game finally lets me pick my party at the end of the game, I'm having a blast blowin' everything up with the characters I want to use. It even uses a "party XP" system so everyone levels together! No level gap! Seriously, the game hits every single note for a game I look for as a speedrun, and I want to make it the next game I speedrun. I really, really do.But I'm a cranky old man when it comes to my games sometimes, and back in my day I had a run button and soft resets so I could pick and choose when I wanted to fight knucklehead enemy peons. As it stands, it feels like if I get caught in a "normal" enemy encounter, the best thing to do is hit Alt-F4 and try again.  The combat mechanics are unique and fun, but not so unique and fun to warrant grinding when I don't need the EXP.  I definitely recommend this game to lots of other people, even if it wasn't entirely my cup of tea from start to finish.

_childDocuments_.review: this is a relatively good tb rpgit can be a little slow at first before you've unlocked anything, but there's a good selection of abilities and mechanics that prevent it from ever falling into that annoying 'mash a' purgatory a lot of games fall into.it also has a bunch of options to customise how you fight as well, so you will generally always feel like you're winning because of your own choices rather than because you're following a strict template.this is 90% of what I want to see in this kind of game, so I'm largely happy with it at a mechanical levelthis game is kind of shy of being great though, it suffers from a few larger structural issues that prevent it from being as much fun as it should be.the main issue is that the overall narrative flow isn't goodnot so much in that it's story telling is bad but more in that it's pacing is not greatput simply there's not enough down time; you're just not given much of anything to do outside of fighting enemies, you get a few cutscenes between dungeons, but they're all very short and aren't enough to stop you from feeling like you're being shunted from one dungeon to anotherwhich is an issue as the dungeon design itself is kind of the other big problem here.the dungeon design is best described as being pretty but confusing; the pixel art is all very good but the amount of asset reuse makes it very hard to hold bearings in my head between battles, they're also kind of abstract in that ff XIII way where they explain so little about the world, that I am often left feeling existentially confused about where I am or what I'm doing in a way that leaves me feeling very disconnected from the setting.I suppose you could say that it is trying to emulate a stage with that kind of abstractness, but alas, I don't think it works particularly well.these problems were tiring enough that I had to take multiple breaks over the 14 or so hours I played this, but they didn't stop me from appreciating my time here overall

It doesn't sound like much but even normal fights can be ruthless if you're not planning things properly. I did play on the hardest difficulty though. The soundtrack is truly impressive. There is some singing with some of them. Usually I'm not into that but it's done well here. The story is not really deep or even trying to be serious. The dialogue is entertaining and I enjoyed how the characters interact with each other. There are some minor flaws with the game. They're not game breaking but they would have made the experience better.  I would have liked having the % of attacks/ailments mentioned during fights. You get that kind of info when you go to the party menu outside of fights, but it would help with planning during fights. Also there needs to be a better way to check character buffs and unite moves. _childDocuments_.review: Faithful to the playwright’s comedic sensibility yet open to the potentials of the gaming, THIS WAY MADNESS LIES transcends both stage and strategy. Zeboyd Digital Entertainment's sublime take on the Bard’s immortal tragedies breathes new life into the oft-told tales by adding magical teenagers. From the tragedy of young lovers whose affair threatens to inflame the tensions between their feuding families in Renaissance Verona, to combatting the titular Tempest from The Tempest, this is a sensory banquet thanks to the delicate score and the exquisite pixel art. THIS WAY MADNESS LIES is Shakespeare at its most deeply felt and passionately alive.

_childDocuments_.review: It's charming and doesn't overstay it's welcome.  If you've played a Zeboyd game, you know what you're in for. If you've got $10 to spare and don't need those to have a good time, This Way Madness Lies has all the dimension-hopping, Cthulu-containing, Magical Girl adventure you can Shake a Spear at.

From this menu players can navigate to the credits, which show  that the music was composed by Joshua Queen, while the vocalist is Sarah Queen. _childDocuments_.review: (full review with screenshots here:  )This Way Madness Lies is the latest game from Zeboyd, developers of very silly RPGs like Cthulhu Saves Christmas. Difficult as it is to top that for silliness, I think they've managed to do it with a game that is basically the result of cramming Sailor Moon, Shakespeare, and yet more Cthulhu into a particle collider. It easily could've been too dumb to be coherent, but it's self-aware enough to tell a good story despite the complete absurdity of everything that happens. And it does it all in as little as five hours, which is remarkable. Gameplay will be immediately familiar to anyone who has played any of Zeboyd's previous games. You wander around mazelike dungeons with overworld enemy groups (as seen in Chrono Trigger) and alternate between finding treasure chests and fighting those enemies. Abilities can be used freely since there's no SP, but most require you to rest a turn before they recharge. I'm sure this makes for a very interesting system on higher difficulties when combined with all the different active and passive skills you can equip, but it fell into a loop of using the same abilities in every battle on easy. I'd have appreciated a way to speed up or skip combat since it wasn't what I was playing for in the first place, but thankfully combat sections are brief enough that it never became too grating. When you're not fighting or exploring dungeons, you're in overworld sections that consist of dialogue and a few choices. I don't think any of those choices impact the overall story, but they can definitely change what kind of silly thing happens in future cutscenes. The writing is consistently funny and although the story is hardly the next great gaming narrative, it's easily good enough to keep you playing. I enjoyed the character interactions and got quite a few laughs out of the classroom sections in particular. This Way Madness Lies is without a doubt my favorite of Zeboyd's games so far. It's exactly as long as it needs to be, has one of the year's best soundtracks, and is on-point with its comedy. A somewhat repetitive battle system holds it back from being the perfect budget RPG, but that's really the only thing I can criticize about it. I'd consider it a must-play if the concept sounds at all interesting to you.
_childDocuments_.name: This Way Madness Lies

_childDocuments_.review: Zeboyd delivers another hit. A delightful combination of magical girls and Shakespearean plays sounds strange but they delivered a wonderful tale with plenty of fun characters. I'm already hoping for a sequel.Blind, but well earned, praise out of the way.. if you've played Cosmic Star Heroine or Cthulhu Saves Christmas, you can expect some familiar gameplay elements. Every battle allows for you to go all out, as upon victory everyone is fully healed. This makes battles more fun since you don't have to worry about inventory management or item conservation. Grinding is also optional as there are  random battles; a fixed number of enemies patrol dungeons and once they're gone you're free to move on. If you wish to get even stronger, battles can be initiated at any time from the game's status screen.Another familiar mechanic is the characters gaining a plethora of skills which can be mixed and matched to your liking in the ability menu; up to 7 spells or attacks, plus your rest & recharge defensive move. When you battle, everyone's abilities can be used once (with a couple exceptions) but resting will recharge them all. Items can also be set from the menu and are available one time per battle, but always refresh afterwards.Unlike previous outings, however, where you could obtain weapons & armour for the party members, the girls of Stratford-Upon-Avon High School gain a series of special traits as you level up. You can equip three at a time and they range from increased elemental damage to starting the battle in hyper mode. What they  do is increasingly raise your stats. Starting traits do not have many stats, but ones learned at level 40, for instance, will have significantly higher bonus HP and attack power.There are more girls than there are available party slots, but the game swaps them around per the story chapters so you get a chance to experience them all. As an added bonus, they all maintain the same level as EXP goes towards the team as a whole. Nobody gets left behind!If I do have one complaint, it's that there are not enough opportunities to see the girls in their day-to-day lives. The focus is squarely on the plot, which is important, but I'd have liked a couple sidequests or to maybe explore the town or the school. Not a deal breaker, though. I still highly recommend this game as the writing is excellent.

_childDocuments_.review: A delightful romp. I'm not really into the magical girl aspects, but I was sold on the Shakespeare side of things. It's a fun, straightforward game with vibes of Persona, looks of Shining Force, and the silliness you can expect from a Zeboyd Games game. Some of the descriptions of the monsters had me cracking up.They really cut away from a lot of the extraneous fluff a ton of JRPGs, and game companies, are guilty of stuffing into games. I appreciate that respect for the player's time. Also, the different difficulty levels seemed fair to me. I played through on Challenging and thought it was fair.There were some minor hiccups here and there (walking through a pillar or two due to collision not being set), but nothing game-breaking. If you enjoyed this and haven't played some of their other works, I highly recommend Cosmic Star Heroine.

_childDocuments_.review: Another very solid piece of work from Zeboyd, if you liked their previous post-Xbox arcade games, you'll likely enjoy this one as well.  This is a shorter game than Cthulhu Saves the World or Cosmic Star Heroine; clocking in an 6-8 hours for a first playthrough.Zeboyd games have always had a flimsy 4th wall, but this one goes far beyond any of their previous offerings.  You the player are an active participant in the story, which makes things quite fun.  The story blends Shakespeare, magical girl anime, and high school relationship building together with a large dose of humor.The map graphics are a bit plain, but still very servicable and very varied between the different dungeons.  The menu, character art, and battle sprites are extremely well done.  The battle sprites and character art in particular show a lot of character.  Sound and music are top notch, sound has always been good for Zeboyd games, but this title really shows a huge improvement.  The soundtrack is wonderful and I strongly recommend it when/if it becomes available for purchase.Combat wise, it's fairly similar in design to how Cosmic Star Heroine and Cthulhu Saves Christmas operates.  Each character can equip up to 7 skills, most of these exhaust after one use; then there is one defend which reduces damage for a turn and recharges your exhausted skills.  There are no chaos skills like in CSC, so you have full party build control.  Imogen is forced in your party at all times.  In most of the game, you'll have a forced party, which will be different between dungeons.  This makes you alter your strategies for each dungeon, but it can make some dungeons rough when you have little to no AoE damage, especially on higher difficulties.  Late in the game, you will get the ability to select which three party members to bring along out of the full compliment of characters; so you can create a specific party build with complementary skills.Like with previous CSH/CSC titles, there are also items, which are 1/combat skills any character can use; unite skills that get stronger as the battle goes on; and the Hype (Hyper in previous games) system where every few turns a character's skills get stronger.  Different in this game is that equipment is gone.  Here, you get traits which unlock as you gain levels.  These traits (aside from the first one Magical) give you passive bonuses or modifications to skills and a set of stat boosts.  Each character can equip 3 traits which helps customize that character's role in the party.  This feels a lot like a collectible card game, and reminds me a bit of creating hero builds in the original Guild Wars.  Synergy between skills on a single character and synergy with other party members is quite important to making combat easier.I ran the game on the "normal" difficulty (second choice), and it was pretty solid.  I could easily die if I didn't pay attention or used my party synergies and skills inappropriately.  The last boss got a bit tricky as well.  Like with all of Zeboyd's other games, foes get stronger as the fight goes on to discourage turtling strats, so you will need to play fairly aggressively.  Luckily like CSH and CSC, you are at full power for each fight so there is no risk in going all out each fight.The final aspect is that between missions, you have interactive scenes with your fellow characters.  There are only a few places during these scenes where you have to choose between options on what to do.  This is unlike CSC's wide array of choices.  Note that there is some combat that can happen during these scenes, you'll have a fixed party for these for the most part.Criticisms are fairly minor overall.  I feel that full party customization is unlocked a bit too late.  Loot in this is a bit more boring than in previous games, it's mostly similar items (which are still good as they can fill in gaps in your party's skill set) and backpacks that allow you to carry  more items.  Leveling is more important, as the replacement for equipment, your traits are almost only unlocked by leveling up.  Map design is good but doesn't feel as creative as some of CSH's dungeons; and the graphics of the maps are a bit more plain when compared to the excellent battle, sprite, scene, and UI art.Overall I feel it's a great game and one of Zeboyd's best entries to date.  Almost anyone who likes 2D turn based jRPG's, especially those with the theatre or magical girl themes, will enjoy this one.  The short nature of it is a nice change of pace from the long epics that many jRPG's are; and the more humorous and whimsical nature of the game is a nice departure from the grim nature of many other jRPG's.  Those with familiarity with Shakespeare's plays will probably get a kick out of the silliness, obvious and less obvious references, and the humorous "translations" that are available whenever any early Modern English is displayed.

_childDocuments_.review: This is everything a short RPG should be. It has a joyfully broad and deep skill system that it throws you right into and constantly adds interesting, meaningful abilities to right up to the end. On Challenging mode (the second-highest difficulty out of four settings, which you can switch between any time), there were virtually no trivial enemy encounters the entire game. Because the system doesn't include stock-able items and refreshes everything after each battle, the game expects you to make full use of your party's plentiful abilities with each encounter. This is a major part of why the regular battles are more fun than many RPGs' boss battles. The combat is exhilerating and immensely satisfying, even by Zeboyd Games's exceptional track record.At first glance, the game appears very trimmed down compared to what's typical in an RPG, but make no mistake: the battle and skill progression systems are as deep, rewarding, and fun as any 50-hour RPG's. The game is short, but there is more fun to be had per minute (and more laughs to be had per minute in the script) than any other RPG I've played. Don't think of it as being trimmed down or shortened: it is in fact highly concentrated. If you're looking for a sprawling, epic, emotional story played out over real-world weeks, this isn't that, but I highly recommend changing your expectations and giving this a shot anyway. If you ARE looking for a deep game that you actually have time to finish and makes you laugh a lot, this is exactly what you want. Although the ending is more abrupt than would be ideal, it will still put a smile on your face.I haven't even touched on the premise yet, which is singular and delightful. If you enjoyed studying Shakespeare in school even a little and have at least heard of Sailor Moon, you will have a blast. And if you love either or both of those, this game was made specifically for you. The "modern translations" of the Shakespeare and Shakespeare-esque dialogue, which you can press right to see on each applicable line, manage to be genuinely semantically helpful, illuminating on the subtext of the plays, and side-splittingly funny all at once.tl;dr: 10-ish hours of tremendous, satisfying, fun JRPG combat and laughs galore. It doesn't have everything you would expect from a JRPG, but what it does have, it has in spades, and this MORE than carries the whole experience. Must-play.EDIT: I had included a bug FYI here, but they just patched it!
_childDocuments_.name: This Way Madness Lies

_childDocuments_.review: I have thoroughly enjoyed every game by this studio, and this is no exception. The combat isn't quite as polished as Cosmic Star Heroine (their previous game), and it's way more linear. The story is a lot more light-hearted though, and it's definitely funnier as a result. The entire premise is just hilarious, and it's an absolute blast to go through the story. The sound track is just one amazing song after another, which definitely helps.Personally I prefer the more serious tone and deep combat system of CSH, but I still had a great time with this. If you've played any of their games before you pretty much know what you're in for. If you haven't, and you have even a passing interest in JRPGs, buy this game, play it, and then buy every other game they've made and play those too! Their games are seriously the best indie JRPGs out there.

name: Fashion Police Squad
detailed_description: Calling all officers! I've got a Fashion Crime in Progress and I'm mobilizing all Fashion Police Squad members. Grab your Belt of Justice and your Tailormade Sewing Machine, we've got some Fashion Justice to dispense! Fashion Police Squad is a humorous Retro FPS where you fight against fashion crime using attire enhancing weaponry. Clean the streets of socks in sandals as Sergeant Des, and experience a single-player story full of fabulous characters, dazzling encounters, and fierce runway shows! Pit yourself against all kinds of Fashion Crimes, from saggy pants to neon brights Utilize a specialized weapons arsenal, including weaponized Sock Gnomes Jump, climb and swing your way around Trendopolis to uncover its secrets Fight against the biggest, baddest bosses in the fashion industry Solve the mystery of the resurgence of Fashion Crime and take out the villains at the top Each fashion crime has a fashion solution, and you'll need to choose between your weapons carefully to fix each fashion faux pas! Each enemy needs something, be it a splash of color or all the seams taken in, so you'll need to switch to and use the right weapons for the right situations! Picking the wrong weapon will do nothing to your enemies, so time to choose wisely!

_childDocuments_.review: It's more than a boomer shooter. There's an interesting twist: you need to always use the correct weapon against a given type of enemy, otherwise it doesn't do a thing. You can't fix a bad fitting dress with a paint gun. It ups the difficulty quite a bit, but trust me - they made it work.Obviously the concept is ridiculous, and the game embraces that fact. When "fixing" an enemy instead of hearing a death scream, you hear the announcer say how amazing the refashioned person looks: SEXY! DEBONAIR! DAYUM! FIERCE! And of course you get to see their new self standing there, thankful and much happier. It doesn't get in the way of fighting, as the "reformed" criminals are almost invisible when there's still danger around.This light tone lends itself well to humour and classic memes. And by classic, I do mean classic. Since it's a boomer shooter, it contains some "boomer memes" (this is a misnomer, but let's just roll with it). Make no mistake: whoever made this is well-versed in the language of the early internet and uses that knowledge to make ridiculous mishmashes which, when combined with creative and fun game design, create some incredibly memorable and fun moments.I need to stress this here: normally I  memes and pop culture references in games, they just yank me out of whatever immersion I had. But here they not only work, they get away with insane levels of meme saturation. It's just that kind of a game.It also breaks some conventions of the shooter genre, but it does it with gusto. Your weapons (except the ultimate one) have unlimited ammo, and only one of them requires reloading. Your melee attack isn't so melee, it actually has quite a bit of range, and it's main utility is stunning. Exploding barrels contain glitter, so they hurt your enemies, but heal you. And there is no sprinting, instead there's... making the floor slippery.Okay, this part actually sucks. In order to move fast, you must use a specific weapon to spray water on the floor, and then "slide" on it. It doesn't really work so well; what makes things worse is that there are some platforming/parkour sections which require you to use this. I fell so many times because I just couldn't get the feel for it. Luckily, the most annoying of those sections is an optional challenge, so at least there's that.Oh, and some people are complaining about the belt swinging. I don't know, I found it cool. Maybe they made it easier? I think it works just fine. You don't have to use it all that much, anyway.Finally, something that I really liked is that even though the game's protagonist is a male fashionista, it doesn't contain  direct LGBT references. I don't mean it in a homophobic way, though - quite the opposite. I think it's ridiculous that we associate good fashion sense in men with being gay. This kind of mindset hurts all men - straight and otherwise. If I want to slay some puss while wearing high heels and a red overcoat, let me. Okay?I think the game's great. It's pretty, it's fun, it's got good humour, and there's some really good music, too. I've played most of the game on Hard difficulty ("You reap what you sew") and I had to lower it towards the end because the fights got a little too tough. Enjoy!
_childDocuments_.name: Fashion Police Squad

_childDocuments_.review: Well, this one was surely a breath of fresh air in this stream of "boomer shooters"! No blood, gore and guts here, it's all glam, fashion, style and silly light hearted references packed in a neat set of varied missions and accompanied by an amazing OST worth the price on its own if you are a fan of SEGA-style music with a funky approach, in fact, if you like that sort of piano/grand jazz/keyboard synth ultra melodic songs that glue to your mind, this is for you. Indeed, sound design is just as prominent as the visuals here.Anyway, quick mechanics rundown: your character is extremely agile and fast, there is no dash but there is a melee weapon used to hop and climb to greater distances. You get a small set of weapons (including one that let's you jump further ahead and move even faster) and they are arranged in a system where each one needs to be used on different enemy types to stunlock them or deal damage, that is until you get the equivalent of the BFG (which the devs kindly provide infinite ammo for if you clear the game). Each weapon fits a certain purpose and they will not be effective against certain enemy types. This is telegraphed both via audio and visual cues so you are quickly told you need to switch weapons.Now, things get extremely chaotic and challenging once you face enemy waves with enemy combinations that require you to move around and switch like a madman until you fashionize all those terrible criminals. Each time you eliminate a target an Unreal Tournament/Devil May Cry 5 style loud voice will scream phrases and that already elevates the game above others. It just oozing style and I loved it so much more for it. It's a good way to accompany the combat! Again, it may not be the wailing of demons and electric guitars and an angry armored dude but it sure is a learning experience on fashion words in English, heh. At the end of each mission you are evaluated by the amount of secrets, swag (basically, armor items) and enemies arrested for that sweet-yet-OCD 100% completion goal. These tallies are done incredibly well in a silly fashion parade style, with bosses getting their own special screens.The story is kind of a spoof full of references (not gonna spoil) and certainly not quintessential to the experience although I would certainly love if the next game contains even more voiced dialogue (only the intro is voiced, the rest is what I can only describe as Banjo Kazooie noises), although the delivery and writing could make or break it. Having all enemies voiced is also great as the quotes they spew are just as ridiculous as expected, chockfull of memes that keep the arenas engaging.While for many it may not reach the heights of some of the new torch bearers of this new old school era like DUSK or Ultrakill, the style is extremely well done, entertaining and packed with enough humor to get a special highlight. My only gripe was that a few of the encounters are confined into extremely small arenas for the amount of enemies you face and that gives you little room for maneuvers and there were a few performance hiccups using the melee belt, other than that the game ran smoothly on my PC.I really hope the devs are working on a sequel that refines elements and ups the ante or just brings us more joy and fun to cut it up a bit with all the disembowelments and violence. Sometimes we just need a break from that with some colours and laughter. Props to the devs, hats off and suit up!It's not a terribly long game so even aiming for the 100% should be doable. Very recommended and if on sale, even more recommended but also get it with the OST! It comes with FLACs which is always a huge plus!

_childDocuments_.review: This game is what it appears to be - a catwalk of stylish ideas rekindling an old flame with a plethora of fresh twists. It's almost unbecoming how long it took me to connect. I wasn't feeling it until a multitude of mechanics finally clicked together. It's a slow starter, but I think the devs acted wisely by introducing them gradually instead of making a mess. After a couple of hours, I could see the full picture and caught myself deeply engaged with the systems in place. Now, let's dispense some judgement on this proudly judgemental game.The story takes place in Trendopolis, a leading city in fashion, dizzying heights, and breakneck chases. Gazing at the vibrant vistas from the rooftops, I felt like I was visiting a town from Transport Tycoon. The striking colour palette is seeping juice and the pixel art is meticulous, emanating craftsmanship. On top of that, the game periodically delivers cool gags, brilliantly spoofing bigwigs like MGS, Wolfenstein, CoD, even old-fashioned racing games. And not by making some feeble references but through well-made playable sketches that fit into the world aesthetically and don't overstay their welcome.Aside from aesthetics, FPS emphasizes its story and characters. The protagonist, Sergeant Des, is trusting and confident, he even gets a clever little character arc at the end. His fashion sense resembles that of M. Bison. Cosplay is all the rage, I suppose. His partner officer Haley is featured prominently by partaking in most conversations. She plays a role of a level-headed and strict archetype, talking sense into Des, yet she doesn't come off as condescending when doing so, being a loyal and respectful companion. Soon, Deep Coat enters the picture, bringing with him a voguish mystery that unfolds throughout the playthrough, culminating in many hilarious payoffs.Looking holistically, the story is gratuitous nonsense played for a joke. The game is aware of the fact, treating its characters and twists with sass, paying more attention to its clothing puns all three-and-a-half fashionistas may fully appreciate. I can't help but respect this tailored approach! If anything, this commitment to the thematic throughline is impressive. Only a niche audience could make the most of it by recognising all the nuances, yet the game was made to be enjoyed by everyone. I did, and I'm a notorious fashion criminal. Despite the inherently divisive subject matter, FPS never gives off any elitist vibes. It's too nonchalant and cheerful for such antiquated notions.The beginning levels are flat, lacking in branching or environmental interactivity. I also wasn't happy with unlimited ammo, because it made me almost indifferent to secrets, which, despite being inventively tucked away, don't contain interesting items to find, only your old health and swag (armour)! Vital stuff, just unexciting. But I forgot all about it when the game began to open up. Its map design always stays straightforward, however, soon I gave in to the sheer charm of its crazy ride through the beauty of surreal absurdity. I adore the abstract set pieces like that Transport Tycoon city, a subway with inventive platforming fights, bathhouses with labyrinthian wardrobe hells, and a colossal cruise boat boasting vent tunnels coated in gold.Every environment is thought-out, full of imaginative challenges that wouldn't fit anywhere else. Fun acrobatic elements with good air control as well as many hazards get introduced later in the game. They range from traditional explosive barrels to trampolines and poles to swing from by using the Belt of Justice as a grappling hook. Thus, platforming in search for scissors to cut ribbons Des "can't possibly get past", your analogue of cards and keys, never feels like a chore. Finally, someone tackled that ancient trope in a manner most fabulous! In the same manner, the game makes sure to entertain you between battles while doing its best to diversify gameplay scenarios.With those getting more exciting the more stunts like jumping from one side of the metro station to the other over electrified rails you get to perform. Not to mention several intense challenge missions and these wonderful spoofs of classic franchises presented in hands-on, interactive ways. Take the gnome-shooting sniper segments with "unfit" and "hair" bullet types. Although I sucked so hard I kinda hated those, I must admit they're solid. But I loved the other ones a lot, be that a lightning-fast vehicle turret segment or VR speedrunning parkour levels. None of them felt superfluous, enriching an already saturated game even further.It's a non-violent game, by the way. Des doesn't kill, he fashionizes his grateful victims. You still shoot people though! Spilling no blood or gore, but the paint clouds, resounding thuds, and impactful feedback compensate for it. Refashioned enemies keep standing and it would've been a problem if they didn't become elegantly transparent during fights. And some fights they are! Local boss battles, for one, are some of the most complex engagements I've ever seen in a shooter! This is where the game's playful nature goes truly wild, letting its mechanics shine, and the best gags get introduced. Normal brawls don't lag far behind. FPS is one of these classic Doom-like shooters that, while having dedicated arenas that lock you in, constantly drips intermediary side gigs that can be just as layered as the main attractions.Each encounter forces you to correctly assess your ever-changing predicaments and rapidly swap guns according to your targets' overlapping weaknesses. It's a quaint take on rock, paper, scissors. But these tools aren't glamorous enough. Instead, get your hands on an assortment of thematically coherent guns that put commitment to the themes on display. Use the Belt of Justice as a stunning melee option, a paint shotgun to brighten up the day, a sewing machine gun shooting buttons and grenades, and sock gnomes for special occasions. A water cannon deals with loud and oversized garments and can be also used to spray soapy water on the floor in front of you to run faster and jump further. Finally, the Ultimate Fashionizer shooting vacuum-packed wardrobe rockets crowns this humble but effective collection. To boot, every weapon gets a cool secondary fire.By refashioning people, you fill the Fab Meter to slap some fashion sense into them with your Fab Slap Glove. Basically, it allows you to skip an odd fight in style. But it won't always be that easy, you'll have to learn your enemy. The criminals represent a range of tacky stereotypes, possessing unmistakable shapes and easily distinguishable sound cues. From suitcase-tossing office drones and jumping Karens with pepper sprays to nefarious scooter bastards or beach dads in speedos, and every one of them demands special treatment. To underline how complex it gets, the beach dad first demands the use of sock gnomes to get rid of the armour, then a grenade to blast off the speedos, and a quick button-up to finish him off, all in this exact order. Here's how a myriad of little quirks come together to form a hardcore and highly entertaining combat system. Des is quick on his feet and slick, being able to lash his way out of trouble in most circumstances. I had to use everything in my arsenal, jump, swing around to survive, and did it make me feel good! This game carries a bright spark inside, giving it a special kind of cheerful energy strong enough to light up your mood and make your worst day a little bit better. Mopeful Games, thank you sweethearts for being as you are! Be that your first and last creation or one of many, know that you did a swell job, you magnificent hype beasts. Your game slapped my frumpy cheeks happy.My curator

_childDocuments_.review: I feel like I have to make this review just for people who might have similar expectations to me. This is definitely not a bad game, but I feel in various ways it's a letdown for me. I don't do reviews too often overall but these problems definitely added up in the later levels of the game. I'll just do a pro and con list because it's pretty simple. Pros:Great visuals and localesFun humourA set of mechanics that initially work wellSecond boss has a lot of cool segments if a bit tediously longCons:Mechanics become overwrought and tediousVisibility on screen of enemies is a genuine problem when too much is going onA later enemy absolutely tanked performanceVarious minor bugsPlatforming segments become jank and unpredictableSniper sections, which I feel are rarely enjoyable but are certainly out of place hereI wish the devs well, I think this is a creative game. But to anyone buying this expecting a more typical retro shooter experience, this is really not that game.
