_childDocuments_.review: I wish I could give Death Come True a thumb up, but unfortunately this interactive movie that barely qualifies as a game has been a disappointment. Read the summary at the end if you want a tl;dr.Let me explain. First of all the gameplay element is very light. Every scene in Death Come True (DCT) is acted out by real people in live action. The game is closer to a visual novel but in film form, than say interactive adventure games from Supermassive or Quantic Dreams like The Quarry and Heavy Rain where you can fully control the characters’ movements and is able to interact with multiple objects within a scene to trigger branching paths. However, what makes good visual novels a game is that choices are consequential and branching story paths and scenarios are distinctly different and have substantial length. This is not the case for DCT where one can finish under two hours, and it is more linear than it first appears to the player. The general gameplay flow goes you view one scene, at the end of it you make a choice among two or more actions (except the first scene serving as a tutorial where there’s only one choice). Where DCT falls short is that there is only one story scenario, you either pick the action that advances the story or pick from the rest of the actions which immediately results in a very brief dead end scene or an invalid choice where the protagonist goes “that’s wrong, pick from the other options”. Granted some of these dead ends can be rather humorous, but they are not enough to make up for the illusion of choice.Okay, so how does DCT fare as a film? In my opinion, a B movie. The story and premise is uninspired and the central ideas have been explored many times over past decades in much greater depth and sophistication. Those ideas were used quite shallowly in this game and without spoiling too much, I’d say this is a murder mystery crossing the Matrix minus the action, with gaming tropes like reloading a death, like in Re:zero. There are flashes of the quirkiness and ingenious absurdity from director Kazutaka Kodaka who created the Dangaronpa series, but the script is mostly mediocre and forgettable. The dialogue can be quite corny at times, like when you watch a live action adaption of an anime. Sometimes real people saying anime stuff just don’t work. Video quality is not very good either, the game being ~5gb and 1.5-2 hours long means you can expect Youtube 1080p quality with visual artifacts. Visual effects, music and sound, and the acting are not bad but nothing to write home about, aka mid. I feel like most of the budget went into hiring the actors, many of whom while not A listers are likely familiar faces to people who watch many Japanese films, TV shows and anime, like Chiaki Kuriyama from Battle Royale and Kill Bill, or Yuki Kaji who is primarily a voice actor with roles like Eren from Attack on Titan.In summary, what I liked:+ Recognisable cast.+ Ability to fast forward and rewind right from the start. Important because you can only have 1 save and you can’t do chapter select until you have 100% the game, meaning if you want to redo an early choice you have to start over.+ Extra footage, behind the scenes, blooper reel, like you would find on a movie DVD. Some of them are funnier and more interesting than the main story LOLWhat I didn’t like:- Lack of gameplay and meaningful choices.- Mediocre story and writing.- Short length.I bought it heavily discounted during a sale, and even then I find it debatable if it was worth my money.My score: 4.0/10

_childDocuments_.review: Since I got all the achievements for this game I'll try to leave a complete review.  I loved the female detective, I thought she was a great character and I wanted her to prevail, so I played this over and over to get all the scenes.  The gameplay mechanics were perfect for an FMV game.  It wasn't complex and didn't get in the way of the story.  As you played, you unlocked behind-the-scenes footage.  So once you finish the game, it's like having a movie on Blu-Ray with a bunch of extras that you can skim through to enjoy the experience more.  Very rewarding.  The good ending was very satisfying and it ends like a good Japanese movie.  Made me want to see more!Something I really liked about this game is that you often have to fail and end the game to move forward.  You can't play a 'perfect' game.  Dying is a part of it.  A lot of FMV games, when you die, you think you failed and you just have to try again, and not die, and that can get tedious.  When you realize that dying in this game means you're progressing, you don't mind playing again and again.  There are just a handful of characters, and they all have great twists and turns to their story. This is one FMV game where, like a good movie, I'll be revisiting this every so often.  When I played it though, I was compelled to play it nonstop because it was so enthralling.  I think you'll like this a lot if you enjoy this genre!

_childDocuments_.review: Something about the "You wake up in a room" genre has always fascinated me. Perhaps it's how there's an instinctive need to find out what's happening that motivates you and the character to work in unison to learn out the truth. And coming from the creator of Danganronpa, this game has quite the pedigree in that genre. Sadly, that's most of the game's appeal. It's a rather small story all things considered, clocking in at about 2-3 hours of play and there's not much happening. No grand reveals about the world the game takes place in, no big conspiracy and only a few meaningful choices to make. On my first playthrough, the game felt much bigger than it really was because I was somehow avoiding all the random ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ deaths. And that's a shame because the random ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ deaths are great, and the game knows it because finding all the deaths is the way you earn achievements and bonus extras.But on the other hand, in this genre I would normally expect the random ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ deaths to be part of the interlocking mystery and they just aren't in this game; they are just completely random and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. More than one of the characters in the cover art only show up in one scene to kill you in what is basically a complete coincidence (to the extent of creating a plot hole once you know the big secret), almost like the story is trying to punish you for not following the aggressively linear story. But hey, it's the creator of Danganronpa, aggressively linear stories seem to be their thing.Definitely a recommend: The mystery is fairly interesting and the characters are fun to engage with for a while, but it's not a game changer and you'll probably never come back to it once you've beaten it.

_childDocuments_.review: I would say this is more like a Novel moreso than some of the other FMV games out there. It's a very interesting story with twists and turns and lots of epic Shots (Great lighting and Photography/Directing) as well as clues that keep you guessing about things. _childDocuments_.name: Death Come True

_childDocuments_.review: The Steam page lies a bit by saying it's the "first interactive film of its genra", because it really much is a simple FMV game.The gameplay is pretty simple : watch a video telling you what happens, make a choice, see the consequences. Sometimes your choice will lead you to your death. Sometimes it will further the plot. Sometimes, it will do both. Even though the gameplay is very simple, I really like the fact that the death routes are not synonymous with bad choices.The game does not tell you this, but you can bring the menu out by left clicking during a cinematic. There, you can rewind, pause, or skip forward the video.Each time you discover a new way to die, you will earn a "Death Medal" symbolizing the death. It's like an achievement menu. Earning Death Medals gives you access to extra videos.You have two main endings. If you play your cards right, you can see every scene and earn every Death Medal in two playthroughs. It takes about 2 hours to reach one of the two endings, and 4 hours 100% the game if you skip the scenes you already saw, not counting the extra videos unlocked by the Death Medals. Yeah, this game is really short.This game is an FMV, so talking about difficulty is a bit weird since you are bound to finish this type of games as long as you don't re-do the same mistakes. Even by this standard, this is a very easy FMV. I dodged like half of the bad ends simply because I have enough brain capacity to remember what worked or did not work a few minutes earlier. There are only two times when you have a time limit to make a choice, and they give you plenty of time to make up your mind. There are no real puzzles, and the few moments when you have to investigate, the game will tell you when your choice is wrong and ask you to choose something else.As I said earlier, the game is really short, and it shows in the story. The mystery around the main character's amnesia and presence in the hotel is solved pretty quickly, especially if you "play it right". You pretty much understand most of the truth after 1 hour, and the next hour is spent solving the main problem of the game and discovering the last missing pieces.I would have loved to see more of some characters. Maybe, this way, the game would be longer. You can see 7 characters on the game's poster (if you count the monster in the foreground), but only 4 of them have a real importance to the plot. The others are pretty much cameos. Getting to learn more about the 3 others would have been nice.Still, the story is the true strength of this game. Even though the story points are a bit "classic", the game uses a combination of those classic tropes and presents them to the player in a well written and articulated manner. Sometimes, you don't need to have something never seen before to write a good story. You just need to know how to write in an interesting way.The worldbuilding is alright. Nothing grandiose, but tight enough to be coherent and to not destroy your suspension of disbelief.Finally, your choices, good or bad, have an influence on the story. Well, not that your choices matter in the classic sense of the term : in the end, you are railroaded into a single course of actions, and the story doesn't change wildly depending on your choices. No, what I mean is that this game is a bit... meta. The story does take into account the fact that you can make "bad" choices. You'll understand once you play it.I can't tell you much more about the story, because it is such a short experience that you can easily spoil it. You'll have to believe in my words when I say I liked it ;)Another point where this game is pretty good. They really outdid themselves on this, if I compare this game to other FMV games I played before. Each character is really recognizable with nice costumes and "character design" ; they all have little something that makes me think about manga/anime characters. On some characters (especially Nene), you can see the influence of Danganronpa, the author's previous work. The SFX are nice. Contrarily to other FMVs where they have a nice interface and that's it, SFXs were used in the videos as well to enhance the visuals and accentuate the "abnormal" aspect of the situation and are pretty clean.There are also some really nice, pretty cinematic shot compositions. Instead of just filming someone talking in front of the camera, like some FMVs do, they took some filming techniques from movies and applied them. If you ignore the occasional choices you have to make, you really feel like you are watching a movie.Also, this game has one of my favorites Game Over screens.You can feel that this game is experimental. It's really short, the gameplay is barebones, and it uses classic tropes in its story. It's nothing grandiose, and it does not try to be more than it is. Still, it does what it does pretty well. I especially liked how the story was told to the player and the visuals.Because of its short nature and its quality, playing this game feels like playing a very polished proof of concept. It was a nice experience, I had fun, but I found that it ended too soon. If the studio makes another FMV game, I would love to check it out - juste make it a bit longer ;)If you want a nice story, are looking for something easy to play and/or are searching an interesting 2-hours movie, I think you will like this game.And the ending song is a banger \m/

_childDocuments_.review: The gameplay is just like any choose-your-own-adventure book, with the wrong decisions leading to imminent death. However each death awards you with collectible death medals which in turn unlocks behind-the-scenes videos. As for story, the beginning 30 minutes are really good at keeping your excited and tense. If anything the endings are the really enjoyable part of the game. Death Come True's real weakness is it's inflexibility to develop the story beyond the "correct" path. Many times I felt the story was going to make a twist but instead I was murdered in less than a minute. It's a real same since it leaves it's interesting side characters to appear for less than two minutes.[v]Verdict[/v]If you decided $16 is worth it to support a rookie game company by all means. _childDocuments_.review: Very short game.  Looks like it has lots of choices and branching story points, but at least 90% of the choices are meaningless and lead to the same path, near identical alternate results, or just plain out not letting you choose the choice and make you reselect the single right choice.  The game is definitely a linear story with the only true branch being the final choice at the end of the game.  Also the title screen shot is a lie.  Theres only 3 characters in this story.  The others appear for all of 30 seconds and are gone and done with, totally irrelevant.That said, I recommend this game/movie.  This would be horrible rip-off as a full priced Danganronpa / Zero Escape -esque dark mystery game, but for $15, its quite good for what it is.  I enjoyed the story and mood of the game.  It just felt like a concept demo and too short to be something awesome.
_childDocuments_.name: Death Come True

_childDocuments_.review: I would say that price-wise it is quite worthwhile. It is indeed more a little bit longer than a movie-length experience but not really as long as a full-fledged game. Nonetheless, It was very interesting to see the history and mystery unfold. Sadly due to the limited time and resources, and additional routes, I guess it could not get more complex than it was, but still was enjoyable. I think the format does work and would be quite interesting to see in a multi-part series where the history and mystery can unfold in more complex ways. The acting had a little bit of issues here and there, but I only had more issues with one scene in particular, the others were worthwhile.  Sadly if there was one I totally missed any Danganronpa easter eggs. Would love to hear an official "pupupupu" somewhere hinting at something that we know it is not the case. Even if it was only for the hype and a nod to the fanbase.

_childDocuments_.review: It's very good! I found the plot to be somewhat unexpected. If you're a big fan of Kodaka's work this is definitely a must buy for you. The game (movie?) isn't really on your face at all times with the lore since you have to piece things together yourself, so even if you find some parts confusing, everything will eventually be explained. Also, the protagonist reminds me a lot of Junpei from ZE999, so there's that. Love that guy.

_childDocuments_.review: The idea of the game/movie is good. The option to choose what is going to happen is very interesting, as you can get yourself to think about what you would really do in a similar situation. But what the game promises is an interactive movie. Instead, it gives the watcher more like an interactive episode. I was already expecting a short thing but did not know it would be this short. You can spend more time playing again, going through all deaths, and watching the Deathtube, but the first-time game experience is too short. Even though the game has basically 6 characters, it just focused on 2-3. Maybe it could have presented more of the others story during the game, which could have made it longer and more enjoyable.Overall it is a nice game, but for the playtime, it should be much cheaper. I would give it a 5/10.Playstyle: 9/10Story: 7/10Playtime: 3/10Price: 4/10

_childDocuments_.review:
A new wave interactive movie game where your actions, and the ending of the story, are determined by your choices.

A completely new science fiction mystery, in full-length live-action movie format, from genius creator of the "Danganronpa" series, Kazutaka Kodaka.

Player controls are simple and straightforward: just swipe to look around and tap to make a selection. Even if you are a beginner, you can enjoy the game as if you were watching a movie.

The protagonist acts as you make choices in each scene, moving the story forward.
What ending awaits you after you've made your choices?

name: Cassette Beasts
detailed_description: Check out another turn-based title About the Game Adventure. Battle. Transform. Collect awesome monsters to use during turn-based battles in this open-world RPG. Combine any two monster forms using Cassette Beasts’ Fusion System to create unique and powerful new ones! Welcome to New Wirral , a remote island inhabited by strange creatures you’ve only dreamed of, nightmares you hopefully haven’t, and a cast of brave folks who use cassette tapes to transform for battle. To find a way home you’ll need to explore every inch of the island, and record monsters to your trusty cassette tapes to gain their abilities! Transform into monsters...using retro cassette tapes?! Faced with the constant threat of monster attacks, the residents of Harbourtown, New Wirral choose to fight fire with fire. Record a monster to tape, then play it back to take on its form for battle! Fuse monster forms! Getting close to your companion has benefits–while transformed you can combine your strengths to gain the upper hand in battle! Any two monster forms can be fused to produce unique, fully-animated new fusion forms. Explore a rich open world Certain monster abilities can be used in human form. You’ll need these to help you get around, solve puzzles, and locate dungeons. Glide, fly, swim, climb, dash, or turn magnetic! Take on the Gauntlet – a never-ending battle mode where you’ll face fearsome enemies for precious material and glory! Travel alongside a diverse cast of human companions Never fight alone! Form bonds, spend time together, and help your selected partner complete personal goals to become a better team. The strength of your relationship determines how well you’re able to fuse! Master a deep battle system Take advantage of elemental chemistry to apply extra buffs or debuffs alongside your attack, or even alter your opponent’s elemental type! Play with Friends Team up with a friend in local multiplayer to explore, transform, and fight together! Party up with Online Multiplayer to trade monster tapes, challenge your friends to 1v1 battles, and team up to take on powerful Rogue Fusion beasts for great rewards!

_childDocuments_.review: This is my first Steam review, but this game is so great that it compelled me to share my thoughts. I went into this game expecting a cute, if rather generic, monster battling game. What I found was an unbelievably thoughtful and wonderfully crafted experience that is a steal at $20. It improves upon Pokemon in nearly every way, and I hope someone at GameFreak takes notice. Here's a list of the things I love about this game, as a lifelong monster catcher.1. The moves. Most monsters have around 8 move slots, which can be filled with attacks, status moves, or passive abilities. You can freely remove and add these moves (called "stickers") on each monster and easily transfer them between monsters. You can stack attacks and passives to build really interesting beasts. For instance, you can use 7 "Random Starter" passive stickers with one really strong attack sticker. At the beginning of battle you will have 7 chances to trigger the strong attack right at the beginning of battle (and can trigger it up to 7 times).2. The AP system. There are no useless moves in this game, and none become "outclassed" as you progress in the game. You will never see a Pokemon packing "Tackle" in a competitive environment, but every move in Cassette Beasts retains value. The stronger the move, the more "AP" it costs (which regenerates at a rate of 2 AP/turn). Using "Tackle" (here called "Smack" if melee and "Spit" if ranged) costs 0 AP, so you can save it for a stronger move next turn.3. The Bootleg system. As an avid shiny hunter, this is my favorite feature in the game. When you find a bootleg monster (1/1000 chance for normal encounters), the monster will not only have a different color palette, but a different type (which determines the color palette). These off-type bootlegs learn different moves than usual (and they are often rare moves with extra characteristics, like a chance to hit the whole team). You can hunt for your favorite monster in your favorite type. Wait until you see how cool Glitter-type monsters look!4. The Alchemy system. In this game, type matchups don't give damage multipliers. Instead, types react in a way that makes sense, and has effects that would naturally result from the interaction. For instance, using Fire against Plastic melts it and releases fumes, turning the Plastic type into a poison type. Hitting a Glass-type with a Metal attack shatters the glass, spreading glass shards across the battlefield that damage melee attackers. This system is so fun, and using these reactions in smart ways makes you feel like a boss.5. The new wave-inspired original soundtrack is wonderful and has some unbelievably catchy vocal tracks. I think "Face Down" will be stuck in my head for a long time.If you like monster battling/training games, you've got to grab this game. And if you're reading this, Bytten Studio, please consider expanding this world in the future!

_childDocuments_.review: Cassette Beasts: it's high time we dispel the notion that it's merely a Pokémon clone. Developed by Bytten Studio, this game offers a fresh and exhilarating take on the monster taming genre that stands tall on its own merits. Here, we'll dive into what makes Cassette Beasts so unique and why it's a complete masterpiece.A Unique Twist on Monster Taming:At first glance, some may draw parallels between Cassette Beasts and the Pokémon franchise. After all, both involve capturing and battling creatures, but Cassette Beasts distinguishes itself with its innovative "cassette" mechanic. Unlike Pokémon, where you simply capture creatures, in Cassette Beasts, you capture abilities and splice them together to create your own unique monster hybrids. This adds a layer of strategy and creativity that sets it apart from the traditional monster taming formula.A Riveting and Fast-Paced Story:One of Cassette Beasts' most outstanding features is its gripping storyline. From the moment you step into this pixel-art world, you'll find yourself engrossed in a narrative that unfolds at a breakneck pace. The plot is full of unexpected twists, complex characters, and thought-provoking themes that keep you invested from start to finish. It's not just about capturing monsters; it's about uncovering the mysteries of the world and your character's place in it.Challenge for the Experienced Gamer:Cassette Beasts doesn't hold your hand. It offers a refreshing challenge for those seeking a more demanding gaming experience. Battles are strategic and require careful planning. The variety of cassette combinations and the dynamic AI make each encounter a thrilling puzzle to solve. It's a game that rewards skill and strategy, keeping even seasoned gamers on their toes.Visually Stunning Graphics:The game's pixel-art style is a work of art in itself. The attention to detail in every environment, creature design, and character is astounding. Cassette Beasts manages to evoke a sense of nostalgia while still pushing the boundaries of what pixel art can achieve. It's a visual treat that enhances the overall immersion in the game.A Masterpiece in the Monster Taming Genre:In summary, Cassette Beasts is nothing short of a masterpiece in the monster taming genre. It successfully distances itself from the Pokémon comparisons with its innovative mechanics, and it offers a captivating story, challenging gameplay, and stunning visuals that set a new standard for the genre.While Pokémon may have laid the foundation for monster taming games, Cassette Beasts takes bold steps in its own direction. Bytten Studio's creation deserves recognition for its dedication to delivering an unforgettable gaming experience that stands tall on its own. Cassette Beasts is more than a clone; it's a genre-defining title that has undoubtedly earned its place among gaming greats.10/10

_childDocuments_.review: Cassette Beasts to me is the perfect Pokemon game, but it feels unfair to call it that since the game ends up sharing so little with Pokemon by the end besides the loose idea of "catching monsters" to use later.  Be warned if you are looking for more Pokemon exactly as you know it this game will not be for you, but if you want to try something wholly new with the genre give Cassette Beasts a try!If you just are looking for a random opinion I highly recommend this game without caveat, but if you want a break down of how this game differs from Pokemon games I will be spoiling most of the games mechanics while trying not to touch any story or specific secret spoilers.  This game has a lot in it, but it is good at giving you the information concisely when it is relevant (it doesn't all seem this overwhelming in game).  I am sure I will be forgetting to mention some mechanics here, but these are what I found to be most relevant to playing the game.If you are curious how the game differs from Pokemon it has a lot of the fat stripped from it replacing it with wholly new mechanics and ideas.  Gone are the random differences in individual mons (for the most part).  No more IVs, EVs, Natures, or Abilities. Any mon you catch will start the same as any other of the same species.  Similarly levels of individual mons are removed for the most part.  In its place is a mechanic of "stars" (basically levels), where each star grants a new move and at 5 stars the mon can evolve if possible.  Stats are only changed on evolution rather than on star gain so there will never be a need to grind up newly caught mons to try to match the rest of your team.  The leveling up system is not gone entirely though, instead being tied to the player instead, so a sense of progression and the ability to over level still exists.  If you want though you can change the way that other npcs level scales to the player in settings.  That might be one of the greatest strengths of the game, an absolutely fantastic UI with so many quality of life features.The game is choked full of great QOL of features:  you can see what abilities do while you use them, status changes and types are visible on the mon itself during combat, a very helpful tutorial message (can be turned off) pops up the 1st time a new effect happens, the type matchup chart can be pulled up in combat, healing items are replenishable for cheap but capped on how much you can hold, fast travel is unlocked from the start and has a hotkey, dialog animation and move speed are quick, the location of interesting events are marked on your map when an npc mentions them, moves can be removed and added on the fly (even switched between mons that can learn them).  There are so many impressive QOL that it is hard to remember them all.  I know I will struggle to go back to other games that lack them.The game isn't just refined Pokemon, it has new takes on some of the tropes of the genre.  The game has unique types, with some familiar ones from other monster training games.   The big change to typing though is the interactions.  There are no super effective/not effective moves, instead all interactions with types are more complicated then that, often giving a debuff/buff on interaction or rarely even changing the type entirely.  For instance a fire move on a plastic mon turns the plastic type to poison type. Another fire move on the now poison type will set it on fire giving it a damage over time effect for 3 turns.  The type changing element of the game is a core mechanic, every mon has a unique sprite for every other type it could be.  Shinys in this game are instead one of these type changed mons, equipped with unique movepool as well as a different type from what is normally found.  The way moves are learned is also a big departure.  All moves can be removed from any mon and added to any other mon that is compatible.  There are also passive moves which function in the way abilities do in Pokemon.  If you miss grinding out catching Pokemon for better stats the closest equivalent for that here is a chance for moves to have extra (generally not very significant, or a restriction on using to its fullest) effects on them.  Any time you gain a new move you have a chance to have an added effect on it, with shinys having a boosted chance.  Finally another departure is that the game focuses exclusively on double battles, as well as fusing together of two mons to create a temporary stronger mon.There will of course be a lot of comparisons to Pokemon, but the game stands on its own in many ways as well.  The game's focus is on traversing an open world while gaining abilities to solve puzzles and unlock more of the world.  There are many boss battles, separate from trainer battles, quests, and environmental puzzles throughout the world.  There is no universal currency, instead the game has a theme of recycling and raw materials are used in place of a currency.  Items are only obtainable with the relevant material and more of it can be found through breaking down similar items, battling monsters, finding chests, or completing quests.  Perhaps the last big selling point is the "romance system".  As the game focuses exclusively around double battles you will spend the game with one of several partners growing closer with them as the game progresses.Ultimately this game won't be for everyone.  I personally love the mon designs and art direction, but I know for some people the differences between this and Pokemon's style will be an instant deal breaker.  Additionally you aren't really catching mons, but rather transforming into them.  In practice this changes very little but I know weirds out some people. The game focuses more on story than the original Pokemon did which will be a mixed bag for some people.  To me this is a game that takes the mechanics of Pokemon, refines it to perfection, and then creates a world out of it that the creators seemed to have truly put a lot of love into.  Despite all of my comparisons to Pokemon I think this is a game that stands on its own apart from it, and if anything is helped by comparing the two.  I would highly recommend giving this a try if you have ever hoped Game Freak would try new things or even if you just like the style and tone of the game.  It is a perfect Steam Deck game and should be coming to Switch in late may if you would prefer to play this handheld.

_childDocuments_.review: Cassette Beasts is an interesting take on the mon genre (monre) that passes more often than it fails when it comes to presenting a cohesive experience.Major disclaimer: this game might resemble a popular mon game series. This game, while borrowing elements of that series, is absolutely NOT like that game in the least. You will be mercilessly obliterated in your battles if you think it is. Prepare for shenanigans. We're entering romhacklike territory.Pros:- Colorful monster designs are inspired and not at all derivative or overly generic (glances at temtem). You can definitely make out each monster's visual influences even when they're smushed together with other monsters, or evolved ("remixed").- The sticker system presents an enormous amount of mix and match potential for almost any pick you go with. You might find yourself favoring other picks over your starter as more choices are made available to you.- No monster breeding means that you can just obtain one tape of any given monster and not have to endlessly fish for optimal stats or moves. (glances at temtem again)- You still have a reason to acquire more monster recordings because you can use extras for materials or fishing for more stickers. If you like collecting things, there's no shortage of hoarding here.- Gameplay is quite challenging. You will find yourself often on the back foot because new faces and gameplay elements can turn a situation on its head very quickly. On the other hand, you might just find a way past the problem just as quickly as things spiral out of control. Sometimes the problems are the solutions?...- Music, as a core theme of the game, is the game's strongest element and continues to impress at every turn, as long as you're into the aesthetic it is presenting.- The only thing that gates you off from advancing is the main story and unlocking new modes of overworld movement. Everything else is your choice as you see fit, no matter how reckless this is.Cons:- The visual aesthetic is somewhat muddled, even given the context of the multiversal trash pile that the game world is set in. This makes it sometimes difficult for the theme of "80's/90's americana I guess???" to get across through these limitations.- The game somewhat suffers from romhack mechanical overload, which misses the point of the most popular mon's pick up and play style. (Of course, since this is a common problem to have, you mostly have yourself to blame if you go searching for somebody else's take on the monre.) This is somewhat alleviated by the fact that the game does take the time to explain new mechanics to you when they happen, but oftentimes you'll get bogged down in multiple pratfalls when some elemental matchups cause numerous status effects to pile up in a chain reaction that can feel somewhat discouraging when you get penalized two or three times by different things that happen from one mistake. Of course, it is somewhat evenhanded in that some mistakes can actually result in benefits for you, but all of this is happening by accident and makes the experience vary greatly between players for no other reason than luck of the draw from your previous choices. This can make counterplay and mitigation difficult to perform on the fly.- Having so many choices can easily lead to choice paralysis. This is even more of a problem if your monster has multiple evolution paths, and then on top of that we find out that stickers have rare variants that are better and have additional effects. Thankfully, given how flexible the game makes everything, if a choice doesn't work out, you're not super committed to it forever, or even in five minutes of resourceful thinking.- Materials are somewhat of a chore to farm early on until you get your footing, since most fights are never as simple as you think they would be, and there's no settings option to skip attack animations.- If you eat ♥♥♥♥ because you picked a fight a bit too big for your britches, you will lose a significant (to a new player) amount of resources, and then the game salts the wound by autosaving afterwards. It will also give you some healing items to help you, but if you went into a fight that killed you so fast you couldn't use them (action economy is extremely tight in most battles), it's somewhat unintentionally insulting, and you can't even hold them if you were already holding the maximum amount of healing items when you were wrecked. Although you can't lose anything that isn't replaceable, this can be extremely punishing to newer players who just wanted to see if they can beat a new challenge that they can only sort of guess how strong it is because enemy sprites are all roughly the same size in the overworld. Losses should have been scaled more towards relative player levels rather than a set percentage for the entire playthrough if the players are encouraged to take risks in a very off the rails experience, as there are no backsies if you fall down a hole filled with angry monsters or catch the attention of anybody dangerous.- Battles are somewhat skewed in favor of your opponent (romhack syndrome part two), because the assumption is that you know what you're doing, except you don't if you're going in blind. Yes, breaking them over your knee is easy once you do know what you're doing. May the fates help you if you don't though.- All of the above elements leads many players to have to consult the wiki in fear of putting their foot in a beartrap, which seems somewhat counter to the game's presentation of a wilderness where freedom is king. This is definitely not the kind of thing you can pick up casually, which leads me back to my original major point; most mon games seem to favor mechanical complexity over being easy to pick up, and it's weird that players and developers think that mainstream mons are overly simplistic and that being easy is a negative thing.That being said, I can still recommend this game because they actually make this sort of design work for what they're shooting for, instead of being somewhat aimless like many romhacks. The design is tight enough that it can work with what its given, and that effort has largely paid off. The main thing you should be asking is if this kind of thing is your wheelhouse. Thankfully there's a demo for that.

_childDocuments_.review: On one hand, this is really good. The art is great, fusion is a perfect mechanic, I love the music, I love the writing, and it outperforms Pokémon all the time (I say this as someone with a lifelong obsession with Pokémon). Hence so many stars.On the other... it has problems. Mostly quality of life problems that should have been solved during user testing. And they're not that big a deal if you're playing the game once, only a few will come up, especially if you don't do the postgame. But if you love the game, and really want to engage properly, and get 100% achievements, they discourage that which is sad. It honestly feels like the game is fighting you sometimes... 1. Menuing: No easy way to see which types of beast learn which stickers. When adding stickers to tapes, your position in the list of stickers is randomized after clicking, which is disorienting and makes rescoping your beasts really tedious and difficult. Also, sorting only applies at the time of sorting. So if you sort alphabetically, and then get another sticker, that will be put at the bottom of the list instead of alphabetically, unless you click sort again /every time you unequip a sticker/. This is a huge problem because you always want to be rescoping your beasts and this means you're scrolling for so long to do this basic aspect of gameplay! It discourages builds and making cool beasts which is really sad. 2. Saving: If you reset to use a ritual candle, a priceless item you would be a fool not to savescum (see currency balance and cruel and unusual achievements section below), they make you wait 4 real world minutes before anything spawns again. This is vindictive, especially when considering the achievements list. Once you've bought a game, you should be able to "cheat" if you want. You paid for it.3. Currency balance: Fused material is immensely scarce and valuable, to a mean and stingy extent. For example, you only get 75 fused material for 100%ing EVERY CASETTE BEAST TYPE IN THE GAME. That's 1.5 ritual candles, for doing something many could consider definitively "completing" the game. After spending 0 fused material for the entire game (which involved never upgrading my character) I had 100 after completing the main game. So, 2 candles. And after that they dry up. For doing long "raid boss" equivalents you get... 1. So that's how you farm it. 1 by 1. Meanwhile all other currencies like wood accumulate in massive quantities you couldn't spend even if you tried, with no way to convert them to the only useful currency. To make this even worse, the same currency you need for these candles (which are obligatory to 100%) is the one used to upgrade your character. So if you want to 100% achievements, something only possible with several candles, you can't upgrade your character once or you're wasting resources that will literally take hours to grind to get back.4. Physics: Physics in this game is nasty. You get caught on corners, the obligatory platforming segments (especially the one with Alice) are very frustrating, where endlessly respawning enemies keep knocking you off platforms... doesn't help that stamina is lower than I would like, even in the postgame. Honestly, this is probably Godot's fault, but it goes to show that the engine has limitations. Also, your partner who follows you everywhere haws a hitbox, so you keep bashing into them and they keep knocking cubes off buttons which is very frustrating. 5. Text speed: Text speed is slow, and there are strange pauses in loading text when characters are talking (within the same text box onscreen) that make it unclear when the text is going to end. I couldn't press to skip, because I kept accidentally pressing through dialogue options because the load speeds were so irregular and sometimes characters would say short things. I would like text speed options. Again, a minor complaint, but it would be nice...6. Cruel and unusual achievements: See section 2 and 3 for why these are cruel and unusual, but honestly what a nasty grinding postgame to get 100%. Literally hours of grinding to get 1 of the item that gives you a chance, and if you use it, what do you get? Possibly not the thing you need, unless you save scum. But the game tries to thwart that at any turn. I can't imagine authentically getting an astral traffikrab (hyperspecific achievement) without savescumming, but even with that the game is fighting you and giving you "time out" wait periods between resets like you are a misbehaving child.tl;dr: good game, but some fixable flaws make it frustrating at times, and the nastiest endgame grind I've ever encountered

_childDocuments_.review: This game surprised the heck out of me with the demo (now unavailable) so much so that it's an easy day 1 purchase for me, and I played it straight to finish, which I rarely do now with games as an adult, maybe playing it on the Steam Deck helps hah.The combat is turn-based and is interesting, you mostly have a partner with you and you can change the type of beasts that both characters could become leading to a dynamic mix-and-match strategies. Each cassette that holds the beast forms have a set of stickers, those are the aggressive, passive and support moves that the character could use and each stickers have their own rarity with additional effects on them, leading to the possibility of creating some very interesting (even borderline unfair for the enemies) strategies. Main feature of this game is the fusion mechanic which combines both beasts that your character and your partner currently equipped into 1 mixed beast, combining both their stickers move pool and stats. Love every time this happens as the current soundtrack switches to vocal version and it just fills me with that feeling of "LETS GOOOOOO".Enemies of various types like beasts, bosses and other characters can be very challenging and requires you to switch and try other strategies, especially the bosses and some character fights when they also fused with their partners. The bosses are some of the most unique designed characters I've seen especially when you first see them in your fight.This the only game where I feel like I want to go out and record the bootlegs version of the beasts, they're like shinies in Pokemon but with a different type than their original version with a look that matches that new type, this leads to creating more interesting combat strategies and there are mechanics that makes the bootleg hunting/grinding easier.There are end-game contents and even new game+ contents and gives you the ability to turn on some challenges like a cassette is permanently destroyed if it gets defeated and randomizing all of the beast locations.All and all I completely love this game and I highly recommend people to at least give it a try.

_childDocuments_.review: Probably the best overall Monster Tamer game and by far one of the most (if not the most) original one.The island you end up on is very intriguing and fun to explore. _childDocuments_.review: There is absolutely some initial clunk, but this game takes wild and unexpected swings for something that could've just stuck the formula and been a perfectly normal pokemonlike.There's Shin Megami Tensei and Digimon DNA mixed in. There's a working physics engine. There's a vocal version of seemingly every song in the soundtrack. There's surprisingly deep lore. You can fuse every gad dang pokemon into every other gad dang pokemon. I don't... I don't actually know why they did that. That's a monumental amount of design work for a payoff that the average player is barely conscious of. And the whole game is like that.Cassette Beasts is casual and cozy. It's got heaps of sidequests, Legend Of Zelda style puzzles, and mons to catch. Character customization is weirdly deep, and you can peel moves off of mons and put them on other compatible mons, and this includes passives and specials. The move list is also bonkers wide, and a *lot* of them aren't just +damage +type stuff. Every tenth move I see is metagame defining in its potential. Not to mention type interactions aren't just plus damage. There's an unhinged number of them, all with highly specific effects, and STAB bonuses don't seem to be much of a thing, so you can aim for really wide coverage with your movepools.Or you can leave move slots open, because some moves scale their effects based on the number of open slots.It's good.Now, on the downside, the game does start a little slow. Before you've gotten a few mons and acclimated to the way combat works and gotten some traversal abilities, map exploration feels clunky. This improves, but you have to be willing to get over the initial hump. Also, the game's cozy tone is not always... completely cozy. There is *stuff* going on in the metaplot that is extremely compelling, but less nice than you'd expect from the genre.Ultimately, I'd say Cassette Beasts feels like a weird DS monster catcher rpg that never quite took off, but developed a strong cult following ten years after launch. If you like specifically that type of game, you're going to have a *phenomenal* time here. If you're just looking for a pokemonlike, this is still a good one, but be prepared to spend the first few hours getting acclimated.Edit: Rolled credits. Holy crap this was made by like three people, publisher and voice cast excluded. Also Yuri Lownethal is a voice in this? What a weird gem of a game. Definitely a bit neither-fish-nor-fowl with its pokemon color palette and SMT tone, but it takes some wild swings and hits more than it misses. Strong recommend if you like monster catchers and you're looking for something cozy.

_childDocuments_.review: I really love this game. Its one of the best monster catching pokemon-esque games that doesn't image itself as a direct pokemon clone. What I love most about the game are the quality of life features. When you make a game using gameplay already set in stone, like turn based rpg elements, you don't want to keep the terrible qualities that come with them that other indie devs don't seem to understand.For example, cassette beasts allows;-your entire party to gain exp (even when they're knocked out)-levels are based on your player character's, so all your monsters share the same level.-you can't one shot this game's version of shinies-you can adjust difficulty and level scaling to let grinding or main gameplay to be less annoying-your moves are able to be swapped in and out to other monstersThe only problems I have with the game is mostly to the menus. Giving multiple level up items to your characters or monsters takes too long when you can only give them one at a time. Or how there isn't a system or menu to know what moves each monsters are allowed to have instead of relying on hope. The story also had problems that is prevalent in other trapped in new world need to return home, but I won't spoil the obvious. The notice board grind to complete 100 quests was also mind numbing on the way to 100% the game, but overall Cassette Beasts was the most fun I had 100%ing a monster catching game like this. Overall 9/10 for a clean experience. Fountess gang rise up.

_childDocuments_.review: This playtime is not a joke. Neither is this review.I work two jobs and don't always have time during the week for a lot of video gaming, so I tend to pick up one or two "main" things at a time to slowly chew through. I recently picked up the excellent Tears of The Kingdom and have been loving it, when this little indie monster tamer popped up on my radar, and after a couple recommendations I decided to try it out a little bit.I now have well over 100 hours within the two weeks I've owned this game, to the point where I still haven't beaten Tears  I don't mean to imply that one game is better than the other... rather that this game scratches a  of specific itches for me personally, and it will only continue to get better as it receives both free and paid updates from an attentive and caring dev team.tl;dr - Game's good, highly recommend. Probably a Top 10 of all time for me personally.Feel free to scroll past, or keep reading for some more in-depth thoughts.I feel like this is probably the most important thing to mention: Cassette Beasts is NOT a clone of a certain multimedia monster catching franchise, nor is it even trying to be. This is something that personally bugs me about a lot of other monster tamers on the market (such as Temtem) - they have unique spins on game mechanics, or changes to certain systems, but at the end of the day it feels like they  want to be Pikachu,  they wanna be Pikachu  but they never will be. Somewhat open map with settlements and routes in-between, elemental weaknesses and resistances, a professor-like mentor figure who hands you one of several elemental animals... you know the routine, right?Cassette Beasts, on the other hand, immediately says loud and proud that it is very much so its own  that it has its own unique colorful identity. The player transforms directly into the monster forms; monsters themselves are never "captured" or "tamed", but rather a copy of their abilities is recorded onto a cassette tape. The type system is much more interesting than "effectiveness means big damage"; using an effective type will instead apply unique debuffs to an opponent, such as inflicting damage over time or reducing their attack stats. Boss fights range from silly and whimsical, to (at times) mildly disturbing, and the game isn't afraid to touch on more serious themes in-between lighthearted jabs. Mild spoilers for some character arcs:  The monster designs themselves are also fairly varied, with intimidating beasts and unusual cryptids populating the world of New Wirrel right next to Christmas elves and crabs with traffic cones for shells.Despite all the appeal of New Wirrel, I'd easily say half of why I adore Cassette Beasts so much is because it's really  approachable. Not that great at devising attack sets for your monsters? Having trouble with a specific boss? Open the Options menu at any time, even while a save is loaded, and tone down the AI difficulty or the overall level scaling. If the game starts to feel too easy, you can also greatly increase these settings to your liking. Are all the interactions between types too much to keep track of? There's an in-game type chart accessible even during combat, conveniently tucked inside of your Items, and most elemental moves will show preview icons to remind you of any possible reactions. Accidentally defeat a rare monster that spawned in a specific area? That species will begin to randomly spawn across the overworld after you first battle it, regardless of whether you recorded it or not. Late-game even introduces an item that makes it much easier to obtain "bootleg" monsters, which are variants that have a different type than normal (and a different coloration to match).If that weren't somehow enough, you can also unlock "custom modes" after reaching the credits once (or inputting a command code on the title menu), enabling things like randomized encounters, changing the types of every monster in the game, setting a specific RNG seed for speedruns, or a mode where defeated monsters are permanently removed from your collection. Factor in the upcoming addition of online multiplayer, and you have a game that both has plenty of replay value, and one where you can spend dozens of hours within a single save file.Oh yeah, the PC version also supports a good variety of user-made mods, with more being developed over time thanks to the increasingly comprehensive official wiki. That's right, the  wiki has modding advice, as well as details on every monster and ability in the game - most details filled in by the developers themselves. It's honestly incredible to see so much support for Cassette Beasts, both with the devs interacting with the community and with the players contributing and giving back to everyone else.... Okay, so nothing can actually be  Don't get me wrong, these are fairly minor gripes, and I still believe Cassette Beasts is easily the best monster-tamer I've played in the last decade, but I still feel I should go over them in the spirit of full honesty and transparency.The main issue I have is with the relationship system. I honestly really like the concept on paper; after meeting a partner character, they assign you a personal quest tying directly into their own storyline, and completing said quest will unlock the ability to build bond levels with them. Simply defeating enemies and completing sidequests will strengthen your bond over time, and once you get to the fifth bond level, you can enter a relationship or choose to remain as just friends. The problem I have is that  that cannot be reverted in any way, as of this review's writing. Wanted to date Kayleigh, but didn't click the romantic option during the  bond event? Sucks to suck, you are now PERMANENTLY friend-zoned! What's even  is that if you pick the romantic option, you are  locked into committing to that relationship, and can totally sweet-talk a different partner until you eventually romance  instead! With how easy it is to retry boss battles, encounter "unique" species repeatedly, or even hunt for the rare bootleg variants of monsters, I'm honestly baffled at how easy it is to completely lock yourself out of romancing a partner character. "Oh, but romance is optional," you might cry out... except it's actually not if you care about 100% completion, because there's an achievement  to forming an intimate bond. The only other "major" gripe I have is kind of a huge spoiler? It's mostly feedback for the dev team, so come back once you've played a good majority of the main game. Also I kind of hit the maximum review length typing this all up, so I'll append it as a post below. Don't say I didn't warn you if you decide to look!Aside from those two complaints though, I honestly and wholeheartedly believe Cassette Beasts is a fantastic adventure,  for the modest asking price of $20. I've already bought at least four other copies for friends, not even sure they'll totally enjoy it, just because I had that much fun - and am continuing to have a grand time. Especially looking forward to the upcoming DLC!

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those magical games that appear once in a long while. I found it by chance and tried the demo, and on the very first few minutes I was already very interested on it. And then I learned a bit more about the setting, and then the first vocal track dropped.... And I fell in love with the game immediately. And the more I play the game, and unlock new stuff to do, it gets better and better.I won't spoil anything of the story, nor the setting. All I can say is that it has such a great mood to it, and some unexpected contrasts at some points!Gameplay-wise, it's not just a Pokémon-like game. It has a lot of unique twists to the formula, and also has some cool mechanics probably inspired by other games as well. Like Persona's Social Links, essentially you can get closer to your NPC partners and know them better as time goes, also making your Fusion stronger.This game does so many things great that a lot of monster collecting games should do as well. The difficulty is very customizable. And I'm not saying like the usual "make the game nuzlock mode". I mean you can actually make the AI more challenging, which I love it.No random encounters by walking in grass a few steps. You can actually see the monsters in the world. This should be a staple in every monster collecting game, in my opinion.tl;dr, This is one of the best monster collecting RPGs I've ever played, even with my little play time it's easy to tell that. Fantastic soundtrack; great mechanics; not just another Pokémon-like; very cool story and setting that keeps me interested of learning more, side-quests, an interesting open world that doesn't feel like it's constantly railroading you, and many more.I highly recommend it!

A lot of NPCs reference things in a twisted or real way, it's always fun to hear what your next opponent will say.The gameplay is challenging, but not grindy. You have a lot of freedom with where you can or want to go.Last but not least, the soundtrack is exceptional and well placed.

_childDocuments_.review: Only a handful of hours into the game, and I can clearly see why it's ***very*** highly rated! The gameplay is pokemon-esque, with cassette tapes instead of pokeballs, but has some very clever changes to the standard recipe that most pokemon inspired games follow. Instead of commanding your beasts, you transform into them, leaving you with a human health pool that can be reduced if your beast form breaks. Enemies who also have Beasts follow this same rule, so this introduces new strategies into the game. There is also the fusion mechanic, which lets you fuse the 2 Beasts you manage mid-battle to help deal with some significantly more difficult enemies. Variable difficulty sliders in the menu means you can change how easy or hard the game is, so you can get just the story, or really amp up the challenge.The game runs very smooth, although some small quirks of the physics engine can cause interactable objects like crates to go flying. The world is filled with many puzzles to get to various areas, or to access loot chests, and some of them do require character powers to access. On the plus side, unlike Pokemon Scarlet/Violet, you just need to capture certain types of beasts which are in the wild, and these (as far as I've seen) aren't restricted based on story progression.As far as world ambience, the music and art are phenomenal! I bought the base game initially, but am buying the deluxe edition bundle to get the extras just cause it genuinely is worth it!

_childDocuments_.review: Legitimately one of the best monster collecting games I've ever played, and I've been playing since OG Pokemon Red/Blue, played all the Dragon Quest Monsters games, played the best of the Monster Rancher's Series, and several others. This game has beautiful art, phenomenal music, an interesting story that isn't too directed at any age group or another. The typings in this game are done in a way that feels incredibly interesting to use not just "oh man I take more damage from that type" or the opposite. The fusion system is an incredibly interesting way to brute force your way through some fights you might normally have trouble with. The game has built in difficulty settings that make it much harder if that's what you're interested in but at a certain point if you're one of those players you can absolutely just turn the cheese on and become a god. (8 random starters and Headshot or Last Rites will end a fight before you even start a turn.) But that's not easy to achieve until mid game and then I mean if you're the one that gets rid of your own fun in the game that's kind of on you.My *biggest* gripe with this game if it can even be called this is that there are some absolutely phenomenal characters in this game that aren't available as companions and it makes me so sad. I would *love* to see some of the captains, or Sunny as available companions but sadly their roles are very limited right now.This game could drop a DLC at the same price as the base game and not only would I buy it but I'd feel like it was a better investment than buying the DLC for pokemon at the end of the year. I really really love this game. Thank you Tom and Jay, and your team. While everyone's attention is on Tears of the Kingdom you guys got game of the year in my books. _childDocuments_.review: Review in short:"Cassette Beasts has a better story, theme, world building, level design, soundtrack and ideas than any Pokémon game in the last decade. An extremely solid game that goes beyond being just a 'Pokémon-like'."Info on how I played:* Played on PC* Played in single playerPro:+ Amazing OSTs+ Simple but effective character creator, with everything (also name and pronouns) that can be changed any time during the game+ Optional Quest Log+ Special types interactions+ Visible enemies on the world; no random encounters+ Original beasts' designs and names+ Difficulty settings+ All cassettes in the team gain exp+ Original mechanics (capturing beasts, world movement skills, fusions, ...)+ Good level design with shortcuts; well done open world with Metroidvania mechanics+ Interesting world building+ Good characters+ Post-game content+ Huge replayability thanks to special New Game options+ Unbelieavably huge amount of unique beasts sprites for fusions; each pair of beasts has one for a total of more than 16kCons:- Cannot remap joypad's controls- Captured bests go automatically to the "box" and cannot be added directly to the party- Cannot add pointers or markers to the map- Cannot skip or speed up animations, making battles against many enemies incredibly long- Completing the bestiary requires heavy RNG-based mechanics and some unclear ones- Bad handle of sorting/filtering of moves- Bad handle of re-ording beasts between the party and the "box"Miscellaneous:* Pokémon-like, but more JRPG* Cassettes' level is tied to evolving; in battle, it is the character's level that matters* The game is not all "happy and colorful", but has some relatively creepy parts and designs. It's NOT a horror game, mind you, but it's not a kids game either.* Strongly altered status-based combat system* [Minor spoiler] In order to finish the game, the player is required to solve a riddle which is "unique" to each game.

_childDocuments_.review: I have tried SO HARD to love alternative monster training games to Pokemon. Temtem, coromon, various other indie titles...They honestly felt like soulless copies. I couldn't enjoy any of them, and found myself crawling back to Gamefreak and their latest buggy mess of a game for that fading flicker of brilliance that was left.That all changes today. Casette Beasts is an absolute labor of love. Every inch of the game is dripping with care, polish, charm, and adventure. It feels like a mix between classic Pokemon Emerald with all of its secrets and remote locations, the openness and traversal of Scarlett and Violet without the bugs and graphical glitches (you can challenge the archangels and ranger captains in any order you so please, and enter dangerous areas from the start of the game), and the best parts of the storytelling in Black/White/2. It's a more mature story that maintains much of its light-hearted charm, and even carries around Stardew Valley-like relationships that actually reward you with better effectiveness in battle.I am in love. The story has drawn me in and kept me hooked from the very beginning, and the island is full of secrets and puzzles to keep you entertained as you travel around. You can even sequence break in a few areas, and the level design encourages it.My favorite feature (spoiler) The combat mechanics are also truly unique. Instead of the standard rock/paper/scissors of effectiveness/weakness, each type has certain status conditions it can receive when hit by another type. Astral types, the psychics of the game, get the Beserk condition when hit by metal or poison types. This restricts them to using only attacking moves. Fire types lose attack power when hit by water or air types, ice types melt into water types, metal types can retain poison that they are hit with and dish it back as contact damage. It's absolutely amazing.If you love Pokemon, GET THIS GAME. Even if you haven't enjoyed any other indie monster battlers. THIS is the one with all of the love and soul that Pokemon used to have, and then some. I will be buying every title that this team releases in this series. If we get sequels and followups, they have already secured me as a customer. It is THAT good.

The beasts are interesting and some have hidden ways to "evolve" or remaster as Cassette Beasts calls it. Overall this is an 8/10, but it scratched an itch for a Pokemon-like game that wasn't a direct copy. If this got a sequel I'd buy it instantly.

_childDocuments_.review: I initially purchased on switch, but this game has not only been my favorite game of 2023, but one of my top 3 games of all time. It's like a monster taming game but instead of taming monsters you transform into them with a cassette player!This game really just wants the player to have fun. Fully customizable AI and scaling (even customizable mid-playthrough!), with perma-death and randomizer options after beating the game once, and the main puzzle of the game differs each time you make a new game. This and the other options allow for a unique experience even on your 2nd, 3rd, or 20th playthrough! So, even if I uh completely accidentally solved the main puzzle so early on that I was completely confused as to what happened and why (as I couldn't even do anything with solving it until later) it actually took me a while to solve on my second playthrough due to it being completely different!There is a local co-op feature, but I haven't gotten to use it yet so I can't really comment on it. However, there is an online multplayer and PvP update being heavily worked on and planning to release early this year, so there's that to look forward to! As far as characters in the game, there are several characters and you can improve your relationship/bond with them. There are some cutscenes and light romantic events that can happen if you select the right options when you are close enough to a character, but they are entirely optional so if light romantic elements don't interest you, you can just avoid them. It has a phenomenal soundtrack, fun and unique designs, complete customization, many huge Quality of Life features, (stickers are SO NICE and have INSANE competitive potential(for those who've played Pokemon, think of one-time-use tms but then you can take the move back off the creature and get the tm back to put on another one, or just take off a move that was part of its learnset and make it a tm)), and many unique and fun features! I mean, the typing system itself is actually really fun! They made a freaking typing system FUN. I didn't even know that was a thing I could enjoy so much until this!!!I will absolutely be trying to get all the steam achievements, and while the Bestiary is able to be completed, I probably won't truly complete it as the  do have their own section. On top of that, it keeps track of all the  so uh yeah good luck if you truly want to 100% this game!So yeah, that's my semi-spoiler free review for this phenomenal game. I would pay $60 for this game if it was priced that high- I cannot recommend it enough for those who want a monster taming game suited for an older audience!

_childDocuments_.review: If you are bored of pokemon and want something new, but still familiar, this is your game.Though that's how it's easiest to describe, I feel Cassette Beasts is something special, something of it's own.The game is definitely more mature and doesn't handhold as much as most monster collector games I've played did, and the freedom it gives, while overwhelming at first, is one of the best things about the game in my opinion.The artstyle is charming and the both the character and monster designs are nice, and have some real gems.The game's story is nothing to write home about(though the setting itself is quite refreshing) but it's nice, interesting enough and made colorful by the characters themselves.The music is one of the best I've had the pleasure of hearing in a while, and hasn't gotten boring at all so far.Gameplay-wise, the battling is solid(if a bit RNG dependant sometimes, which can be annoying), and the sticker system is just amazing and gives so much freedom in costumizing your builds and team. _childDocuments_.review: Cassette Beasts is an absolute gem of a game, seamlessly blending nostalgic charm with innovative gameplay mechanics to deliver an unforgettable experience. From the moment you boot up the game, you're greeted with a vibrant world teeming with personality and possibilities.One of the standout features of Cassette Beasts is its unique cassette mechanic, which allows players to transform ordinary objects into powerful creatures. This mechanic not only adds an exciting element of discovery and experimentation but also serves as a clever homage to the beloved cassette culture of the past. Whether you're turning a humble toaster into a fire-breathing dragon or transforming a cassette tape into a lightning-fast cheetah, the possibilities are endless and endlessly entertaining.Cassette Beasts is more than just its inventive gameplay mechanics. It's a beautifully crafted world filled with memorable characters, breathtaking landscapes, and secrets waiting to be uncovered. The art style is a delightful mix of retro pixel art and modern flair, evoking a sense of nostalgia while still feeling fresh and contemporary.The game's narrative is equally captivating, weaving together elements of mystery, adventure, and humor in a way that keeps you hooked from start to finish. Whether you're unraveling the secrets of the island or forming bonds with your quirky companions, every moment feels meaningful and rewarding.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm just gonna come right out of the gate and say these 4 words about the game:  Quality of Life ImprovementsMovement is so wonky.  Jumping and gliding and dashing all do not feel very smooth.  There are many times I get frustrated because I can't quite make the jump or move fast enough.  You can only change your party while resting.  They don't really tell you this until you remove a party member from your party in the middle of nowhere and then you're left with a huge gaping hole in your roster because of this.  Why can't I just switch out between battles?  There are places you can quick travel to but in some of those places, you have to go a few screens to get out of the train station and then off to wherever you wish to go in the over world.  Why isn't this more consistent so that I can plan my travels more accordingly?  Some puzzles are just wayyyyy too obscure for anyone to get.  For instance, in the thirstalot chamber, I unlocked all of the puzzles and got a key.  Only for there to be one last puzzle to stand in my way.   I know that this might sound silly but I thought all of the puzzles were solved for the main line once I grabbed the key and opened up what I needed to.   NO!  There's one last puzzle and the only clue is far off in another room with a depiction of the same puzzle you had to do earlier!  No point in grinding levels as the whole world levels up as you level.  This is understandable as this is basically an open world map.  However, it's slightly annoying when at one point you were one-shotting the trash mobs and now you have to 2 hit them because you and your allies have leveled up.  I'd rather they just stay the hell away from me if I'm 30+ levels above it.  Or at least just stay put.  This game suffers from the "same party syndrome".  Why should I switch out my party members when clearly leveling them all up together and creating beautiful synergies with them is the way to go!?  I basically got my 10 poke...I mean cassettes that I will switch in and out depending on which secondary I take with me and that's it.  Speaking of builds, there are some digi...err cassettes types that are clearly better than the rest.  Lightening types are hands down the best, and if they are weak against lightening.. ouch time.  There are some unique strategies that can play out... HOWEVER...  trash mobs are normally 1 or 2 shotted making you very ill prepared to fight boss battles.  Get ready to have your cassettes consistently knocked out as those boss battles are ALWAYS difficult, these fights will take huge chunks of health off of your guys rendering many predefined plans laid to waste.   Forget about healing skills as rewinds and roll backs are the way to go.  As previously mentioned, the trash fights are a joke but the boss fights are so difficult that casting one heal will actually set you back too far.   Better to just use rewinds and heal all the way up when low.  Lots of times the quests will put a plot down on the map of where to go.  That's great, until you get there and you are still scratching your head thinking: WTF?  Once again, there are times which go unexplained on what needs to be done.  For instance, go check out a metal lady.  Are they talking about the robot that needs a coin??? Ah yes..... they were.   There's a whole separate quest/rumor for the coin so it's a bit confusing.  Now you may say to me: Hey VG - you gave this game a thumbs up but all I see are big time complaints.  Well...Yes, but it's because underneath all of these QoL issues, there's actually a pretty good in depth game here.  Sure things could be smoother and things could be more readily accessible but there's a lot of fun to be had here.  Try messing up your party synergy to put in this new cassette and see how much fun you'll get from trying to make it work.  Getting lost on the overworld map is good fun as there are a lot of puzzles to figure out.  Even moving objects around and jumping on them trying to get to new places is eye opening.   TLDR:  More quality of life fixes are needed but a diamond in the rough.
