_childDocuments_.review: Cassette Beasts is fantastic. Go get it for that reason alone, no matter what console, Steam, Switch, otherwise.The game looks like if Pokemon Diamond and Pearl refined its style, soundtrack is fantastic. Gameplay invites you break it in so many different ways, by giving you massive variety in Uncommon/Rare stickers (attacks). Maybe you got a 30% chance of Confusion in a 0 cost attack, and you build in to spamming that. Or you opt to commit to turtle strats, by combining Leeching and regen effects, and spamming walls until you can one shot anything that's in front of you. Combine Ghost and Gambit statues, and become a powerhouse that can't be hit with damage. Drawback? There's no drawback if you're counting in Dog Years. And that's not counting your freedom to adjust your own stats once you've collected half of the Captain Stamps. Go for it, 200% Melee Power with only 50% Ranged Power, 75% for each Defence. Bootlegs are also interesting. Different colour, but also different type, and movepool. Go ahead, collect 14 variants of every single monster. Go and collect and fuse in combat every possible combination of over 16 thousand possibilities. If you want to be a collector, you've got room to collect here. Oh, and Custom Games are a thing! There's enough possible random elements that you can do randomized runs too. You could randomize the typing and movepools, the main quest location, even what partner starts with what beast. Complete with timer, if you wanted to race and master the game. Oh, and you can also scale the AI up so that even random encounters could have the logical AI that human encounters would have. If you want to have a harder experience, and prove yourself, you can do so. This game was made with love. This isn't just a bi-yearly edition of Pokemon, with corners cut. And on the sliding scale of Pokemon to Digimon, I'd probably put it closer to Digimon anyways. Especially with context wrong Archangels and transforming in to the beasts yourselves.
_childDocuments_.name: Cassette Beasts

_childDocuments_.review: After completing Cassette Beasts entirely, I have to say this has been one of the most refreshing and entertaining sorts of monster-catching game I’ve ever played, as the charm, aesthetics and music all work together perfectly to create something that goes far beyond the gameplay itself in terms of the meaning and messages that are conveyed in the game. While I won’t go into too much detail to avoid giving spoilers to anyone that hasn’t played it through to completion, I will at the very least say that the gameplay, story, soundtrack and deeper meaning behind the game and the events that unfold within it are likely to keep me coming back for more playthroughs. The gameplay itself very much is reminiscent of franchises like Pokémon, of which I am a long-time fan, so the combat felt familiar enough for me to easily grasp the combat system, but still felt complex in its own right and different enough that it was fun to learn how to make the most of my adventure throughout its world, with plenty of new mechanics that can help to make each and every beast in the game unique and worth learning about and experimenting with. The combat felt incredibly engaging on a regular basis and really demanded my attention to make the most of every fight, and the way that enemies scale in power to make them a challenge to handle even in later parts of the game really helped to keep my attention focused on getting as much done in the world as possible and making the most of every single monster that I could get my hands on. The story takes a simple trope of waking up in an unfamiliar world and makes it feel fresh and colorful in the wide cast of characters that you come across over the course of a journey, and I can’t say that I was ever disinterested in the adventure, both in term of NPCs and those that are playable in the course of the game. Everyone feels like they’ve got personality and just enough background to make them all stand out distinctly, and they all mesh together well to create a gaggle of characters you feel invested in learning more about and how they have come to find themselves working for the betterment of all around them in the world the game takes place in. You honestly will grow to feel attached to them all as the game progress, and that attachment to them, whether it be heroes of villains, helps to make the game stand out from others where the characters in a game might only relevant for short periods of time here and there.The soundtrack of the game if perhaps one of the most standout features and something I highly recommend also investing in if you’re looking for something totally original that goes far beyond the sort of music you might otherwise expect from a game like this. The music is just as colorful and vibrant as the world the game takes place in and really helps to keep you engaged mentally as you make your way through your journey, with tracks that help to set the tone wherever you might be in the game. The fact that vocals can even come with the music is highly impressive and is something I normally would expect to only see in a high-budget video game production, so the extra effort that was taken with the soundtrack there is more than appreciated. Lastly, I just want to briefly mention that the game is much more than just a game in its existence, as it offers fresh perspectives into the way that our world interfaces with the world the game takes place in and fiction as a whole, and I was not expecting for it to really hit me as hard as it did. Not only are there emotional moments that really serve to tug at the heart stings in how you can relate to the characters, but what they represent in this world and what meaning can be gleamed from the events that unfold in it proved to be profound to me, and highly enlightening in regards to how the dreams and thoughts of people everywhere can create things greater than our expectations might otherwise ever imagine. There’s so much more I could say, but at the very least, the game is one that will leave you thinking about its events long after playing it, in ways too numerous for me to truly mention. As a whole, I can’t recommend this game enough and honestly found it to be a thrill ride with plenty of secrets and messages within it that everyone should give a try for the sake of experiencing it and the amazing adventure it presents for all those that choose to delve into it.

_childDocuments_.review: Decided to get this on a whim, as I've recently been hooked on Pokemon nuzlocke runs, but didn't know much about it. So far, I'm very impressed. It's obviously in the same genre as Pokemon, but every single variation and new mechanic I've seen is absolutely brilliant. I love that type-effectiveness adds unique effects, like debuffs and type changes, instead of doubling or halving damage. It's cool that you have to build up power to use your strongest moves, so it's harder to just brainlessly sweep enemy teams. The trainer dynamic, where you merge with monsters and you yourself take damage if they're defeated, is really interesting, and gives you another option when fighting opposing trainers. The first boss fight I've run into is well designed and forces me to think about and change up my team line-up.Stickers are also really interesting as a way to assign abilities, where you can freely shuffle moves between beasts, without having to faff around with move deleters and relearners. Adding Diablo-style affixes to moves is also something I never expected. The dynamic soundtrack is fantastic. I was really surprised to have song lyrics kick in during intense moments, and it works so well. I'm also glad to see another creature collector go in the direction of avoidable wild beasts which you can see, instead of random encounters, which feel increasingly outdated as a mechanic.The only thing I struggle with a little is the overworld aesthetic, which isn't really for me. The physics in the world feel out-of-place and a little janky, especially when your AI partner starts to bump into things. I was also slightly put off when the first monster was crab under a traffic cone, but I warmed to the style of the beasts quite quickly. I'd say I couldn't remember the last time I was so pleasantly surprised by a game, but I've bought Helldivers 2, Palworld and Dave the Diver this year. It's been a great couple of years for video games, hasn't it? Hopefully the 'AAA' industry will learn some lessons.

_childDocuments_.review: Cassette beasts is a game that's flawed, unique, and also really ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ hard to write about.Let's get this out of the way first- yes, I recommend cassette beasts, and yes I like it a lot, but it comes with an asterisk. Oh, and yes, it's also pokemon but actually good. This game sets out to do a lot of things, but it sometimes misses the mark, and on at least one occasion, misses it pretty hard. This review is going to be rather harsh on the game, but it comes from a place of genuine love for the game. Some of these points, especially quite a few of the negative ones are just weird little nitpicks that bother me quite a lot for reason, so be warned. Cassette beasts gets to sit along side games like CONTROL as games won't play again, not because I don't like them, but because they had a big impact on me and I want those memories to remain untainted.And so, without further adieu, let's actually talk about the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ game.The Pros.- The music. THE ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ MUSIC. This game's soundtrack is great. If I had to, I'd place in in A tier. A little higher than DMC5 but lower than Laika Aged Through Blood or Alan Wake (which are high A to S tier imo). Some of the instrumentals are pretty forgettable, but the ones with vocals are excellent and a majority of the instrumentals are, bare minimum, good (or great at best). I listen to the ost on a semi regular basis, and considering how that was one of the game's selling points, at least for me, it knocks it out of the park. - Elemental interactions in this game are good. Instead of having Pokemon's system of "Oh this pokemon is middle aged type and takes x2 damage from midlife crisis type attack", they actually put ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ EFFORT INTO IT. Take notes, Nintendo. Instead of a binary damage multiplier or whatever, type advantaged advantaged attacks can buff, debuff, or even change the type of the target or attacker. Fire type attacks might cause metal type creatures to melt, but could also cause healing mist if used on a water type. There are tons of factors to consider, and these kinds of interactions can easily trip up even prepared parties.- The story. It was interesting enough for me to keep playing, and was the driving force behind playing the game. The climax was satisying and well written and I really enjoyed it. There are some really cool ideas , but unfortunately, not all the ideas and writing sticks the landing, as I'll go into detail later. Regardless, the story is good, and the writing is leagues better than what you'd see in any other game in the creature collector genre.- The Cassettes. I just really liked it. It's cool and unique, and even if it's mechanically the same thing, I still like it a lot.- The Character portraits. They're good. I really like the art style for them.Eh- The game was easy, aside from a couple spikes in difficulty. It's not a huge deal. I'd glad I don't have to spend too much time with the combat system, but I think it's something to note.- The graphical style is pretty standard as well, nothing special. The pixel art didn't really stand out as anything interesting, but not every game has to be Rain World or Hyper Light Drifter. The art was charming, but there's still room for improvement. - The movement. This goes without saying for top down rpgs, but the movement was eh, even in a 2.5d space (which I liked the inclusion of). There are movement abilities you get, but aside from the dash and wings, none of them felt decent, and of the dash and wings, only the wings truly felt good. But you only really use the dash and wings, so it's not a huge deal. The movement isn't bad, it's just okay and I thought I'd mention it here.Cons- The big portion of the review where I dump my issues with the otherwise good writing goes here. I didn't like the characters in Cassette beasts, well not all of them at least. To be fair, while I did get everybody but viola to max relasionship level and saw their special cutscenes, I didn't romance any characters. I liked Kayleigh, though felix was fine, and was either neutral or disliked most of the other companions. It's a baldur's gate situation where they added too many and as such, some ended up half baked. I think it would have been better if they just had 2 or three (plus barkley, because yes) and focused on giving more time for them to develop and expand upon the characters.  The game has tonal issues. Dealing with both a serious and light hearted tone can be hard, and while skilled, the writers didn't pull it off. Sometimes it felt like they were trying to keep the light hearted tone for the sake of being a "pokemon like", and as such doesn't quite fufill being "Pokemon for adults". It's certainly a mature game, and there's some super cool stuff, both light hearted and not, but the light heartedness feels a bit forced. I don't think the game should have been serious all the time, but I wish they'd actually dive into the darker or more serious and grounded aspects of the world and characters that were mentioned  and just brushed over. It is a testament to the writing, however, that I really do want to know more about this stuff though.- The illusion of choice. This is a minor one but the game often offers 2 or more choices for dialogue and they're both the exact ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ same thing but worded slightly differently. It just feels a little condescending. Offer us choice or don't. Just don't pretend you're doing so.- The combat was pretty eh. Not much to say here, it's the boring standard affair. Things do become interesting once type advantaged attacks are thrown into the mix though.- Fusions look ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ugly. It's not a real gripe but i thought it would be funny to put it here.- This is less of a con and more of a missed opportunity. A lot of the designs for monsters are solid, but forgettable. I wish they did something unique and go with some more music (or any design that fits with the cassettes) inspired designs. It felt like they went with what was familiar rather and sticking with the general theme. As a result, the cassettes kinda felt like a nice bonus rather than being at the forefront as the title implies.Anyway, thanks for reading. I live in your walls. BYYYYEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEE

_childDocuments_.review: + Loads of monsters to discover and they're generally very well designed and fun with interesting themes+ Evolutions hit the sweet spot of keeping in line with a monster's theme but being different enough to distinguish it i.e. it's not just a bigger buffer version of the previous one+ Some monsters have multiple evolution paths which is interesting+ Monsters have excellent sprites and animations and the battle backdrops are really nice+ Game mechanics are really tight and leave lots of room for experimentation, especially with every battle being a 2 vs 2+ Loads of flexibility in what moves each monster can have as you can switch abilities (Stickers) around freely (providing the monster can learn the ability)+ A lot, if not all, of the monsters feel viable in combat+ The difficulty is fairly well balanced - it isn't a complete cakewalk and there are some challenging fights+ Minimal grind - you have your own character level that influences how strong all of your transformations are, and monsters have their own 1-5 star rating that you can level up and influences how strong they are - it cuts down on level grinding massively and in turn makes monsters viable a lot more quickly rather than having to grind up their levels a lot+ Type effectiveness results in buffs and debuffs as opposed to massive "I win" damage, you can still be at an advantage / disadvantage but it doesn't mean you're completely guaranteed to win / doomed - additionally, whenever you select to use a move, you get a pop-up that tells you the buffs and/or debuffs you're about to apply which is really handy+ You can fuse 2 monsters together and every single combo has its own sprite (not all are created equal but its impressive it works across all monsters)+ You have the freedom to tackle quests and the map largely in whatever order you want+ There's decent endgame material to progress if you want more to do after beating the main story+ Music is nice and fitting with the game/ The story is decent but the characters and writing are just okay and not super memorable- Sometimes there are minor performance issues when there really shouldn't be considering it's a 2.5D game- When you swap out partners, they keep the monster cassette that they had on them, sometimes making it frustrating to switch around to get it back- Not made with any kind of competitive play in mindMy first game ever was Pokémon Yellow so it's hard not to compare it to Pokémon, especially considering how big and well-established that franchise is. I haven't been tempted to a monster-collecting-and-battling game until now because I didn't think anything else really looked that good or had much of its own identity beyond "PST hey wanna play a Pokémon knock-off on PC?"Cassette Beasts definitely has its own identity and has plenty of innovation to stand out on its own - it has excellent mechanics and memorable monsters that made it a blast to play. If you have any kind of Pokémon itch this will definitely scratch it, but it's also just a great game even without the comparison. Hope to see more of it in the future!

_childDocuments_.review: TL:DR. This is probably one of the best "Pokéclones" out there, but it still doesn't really escape feeling like a Pokéclone. If you're really hankering for something in that peripheral line, by all means get this, this is one of the best ones. If you want something that truly feels more unique, get Siralim or Monster Sanctuary. And if you want a Pokémon game but you can fuse them, you should try infinite fusion before you shell out the bucks for this. This is another game trying to be "Pokémon but better". Like a lot of those games, it starts in Pokémon's shadow and tries to take steps away to escape. Unlike most, to a degree it does... but unfortunately, it escapes from Pokémon's shadow into the shadow of what I can only describe as painfully generic indie tropes, something that feels like it should be an oxymoron.Here's the retro pixel-style graphics with oh-so-scary eldritch abominations being represented by art shifts. Here's the main cast of people somewhere between 15 and 30 with no identifiable traits in any direction. Here's the world of people from dozens of different times and cultures, by which they mean "Stranger Things aesthetic, modern tumblr sensibilities and a few jokes about historical events that didn't happen". And I can't be the only one that immediately figured out the "ooh beeeg tweeest" pretty much the moment that the game tried to play coy about who the strongest warrior fused with.This game is also a victim of timing, which I feel sorry for, because it was at least a little bit smarter than most games of the sort. Unlike a fair few indie and indie-adjacent mon games, it understood not to try and rush itself out to capitalise on the scorned fans from Sword and Shield or Scarlet and Violet, because those sorts of scorned fans do not a healthy game ecosystem make. Unfortunately, right as it's coming out, so does Pokemon Infinite Fusion take the spotlight, a game which much more directly answers the fantasy that Cassette beasts wanted to use as it's niche, and doesn't hold back on letting players indulge in it by using it's unofficial status to let players toss in their own ideas and fan-references, and by letting players do it early and often. Cassette beasts' own fusion system, meanwhile, is algorithmically generated, and if you're like me and like to explore other characters and test all of them first, rather than diving deep with your starter character and doing all their content at once, then the game can feel very stingy with it during your first few hours. (Fusion runs on Steven Universe rules, with the exact same implications - specifically I believe you need to hit Bond Level 1 to unlock it with a given character, which means you actually need to quest with the character and can't just get it by adventuring with them). Even when it's not, it doesn't feel like something you get to really play with as much as you kind of need to to make it a tentpole of your game. So what's meant to be this fairly pricey indie game's core feature is completely overshadowed by a free fangame of the thing it's trying to distance itself from. The starters are... merely okay. There's nothing strictly wrong with either one individually, it's just that they feel like they have a hefty amount of thematic overlap (to the point that the question of which starter you want being framed as "spooky" vs. "sweet" felt kinda ridiculous). Monsters overall are pretty good, having a notably more civilised theme of being largely associated with human jobs or tech than most rosters. A shame that the potential of that is largely wasted, as you don't catch monsters, you just copy their forms, and it does change how you perceive them. You're not collecting a team, you're collecting a closet.Catching has been frustrating. You tether on to a monster at the start of the turn, skip that character's turn then anything that happens to that monster or to you over the course of the turn affects the likelihood of success. This means that it feels just... bad a lot of the time, as you watch your HP and your chance of recording it plummet because i guess the monster or monsters both decided to make the catch harder. A classic case of making something worse from the baseline to try and make it more unique, as well as not understanding that sometimes showing the exact number is a bad thing.Another thing that the game tries to distinguish itself with, but instead makes the game feel less interesting, is something I can only think of as monster symmetry. When you start doing things like the bootleg system which means every monster can be any type, and have so many moves that just inherit types from the monster, they just lose identity. And if I have one more game that thinks "monotyped Pokéballs and nothing else" is a great idea for their specialty Pokéballs I will feed them an entire cactus.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who grew up with Generation IV Pokémon, I've always been looking for a game that recaptures the same excitement I've had when I was small - a new creature around every corner, another new sight here and there, and call me strange, but I quite liked the story of those games as well. Sadly, I was quite late to the party, so I never got to share my findings or opinions with my friends.Enter Cassette Beasts, a game that drips with that exact same aesthetic, is a very recent release (as of this review), and is unfettered by the whims of a larger franchise or publisher. While its creature catalogue is rather modest compared to its bigger sibling, with 120 creatures to write home about, the primary Fusion mechanic, in which two creatures combine in battle, bumps that up to a whopping 14400 combinations of them - and with Cassette's unique spin on rare creatures, Bootleg Tapes that have nonstandard typing for a species with different move pools, you'll almost certainly have a unique experience when you play.The gameplay is fairly conventional, though it also puts a new spin on the classic type chart formula with unique interactions: Using a Fire-type attack on a Plastic-type monster (yes, PLASTIC) causes it to burn and release toxic fumes, which temporarily changes its type to Poison. Using a Metal-type attack on an Ice-type monster smashes it, resulting in severe penalties to the victim's defense. Using Lightning on an Air-type? Makes it Conductive, inflicting damage to it whenever ANY combatant uses another Lightning-type attack, regardless of source and target. Its base in chemical reactions means that despite looking intimidating, it's fairly intuitive.If I have one complaint about the typing system, it feels like Glass type is an unloved "middle child", with very little, if no interactions with other types.The music in the game is phenomenal, with the game heavily utilizing modern music genres for its music - many cutscenes have variations on existing tracks in them, for instance.Special mention goes to all SIX of the combat themes, which have dynamic layering for vocals that kick in when a Fusion occurs in the battle, to prevent them from getting stale. Might just be me, but I've had some of those tracks stuck in my head for ages now.A complaint I have about the sound design, if a very minor one, is the footstep sounds can be a little grating, but they could be far worse. The game also tries to be a little overly generous with its usage of directional audio, which can be jarring in certain cutscenes.Story- and art style-wise, this game is nothing like its competitor, and instead leans more into its more distant cousins of Persona and Shin Megami Tensei, heavily exploring its own setting of New Wirral and how it works (or doesn't) via its characters. Building relationships and completing the partner characters' questlines is encouraged as this allows and strengthens Fusion with these characters (romantic relationships are available, but provide NO additional gameplay benefit), and also paints a larger picture. The game feels quite nonlinear - you're tasked with locating 8 beings known as Archangels to find a gateway, and completely separately from that you may also prove yourself by defeating the 12 Ranger Captains stationed around the island, but the order you do either of these things in is entirely up to the player, with a rumor system directing any lost players towards potential goals.Without spoiling too much, suffice it to say that this game's indie status gives it free reign that its larger sibling would never have, discussing and handling unique themes and doing its own things with its setting and story. Archangel encounters in particular feel quite interesting and unique, with their battle gimmicks chosen very carefully - same for the Ranger Captains. Every single story battle gave me some sort of Eureka moment, which I've found very delightful.On the other hand, I'm a little sad to see some questlines in the game conclude so early or abruptly (How Does It Feel comes to mind), and once story dialogue is exhausted, camping with your favorite character has a very small and limited pool of options, which can be somewhat of a dampener in the extensive postgame.The UI is very sleek and modern-designed; navigating menus is not the fastest with a lack of shortcut buttons, but most of the time things are not buried too deep in the menus. This can actually work to the game's detriment on occasion; putting a tape in storage has no confirmation prompt, and pulling them out is only possible at campsites in the world, which can be a minor inconvenience. As of an update that released a little while ago, the Sticker section of the inventory, which stores all attacks and moves which are freely exchangeable between creatures, now has filter options, sorting, and a "mass delete" button, on top of being paginated and having a search bar! This makes finding moves much faster. Additionally, when editing one of your creatures, Stickers that it can equip are bumped to the top of the list temporarily, to save time.The battle UI is quick, concise, and to the point; battles flow rather briskly, with few pauses or breaks except to explain new status effects (and even that can be disabled or limited in the settings).Ultimately, it's largely polished, but a few patches wouldn't be unwelcome either - this is absolutely a gem of a game in my humble opinion, and with some extra love and attention this has the potential to become another of 2023's major milestones.My thanks to the team at Bytten Studio for giving me a free RPG with my music album.Oh, right, we're getting Online Multiplayer. I guess that's kind of big.

_childDocuments_.review: The truth of the matter is not every person is a Nintendo fan.  That being the case, those same people, like myself do enjoy a good "catch em all" game when they come around in order to get my Pokemon fix.  Cassette Beast is a really unique take on the familiar genre.  What I enjoy the most is the 80's/90's art style.  The colors are vibrant and a pleasure to look at.  Mechanically, the game is very familiar with what Pokemon fans may have played before.  It's cool that the beast are collected through retro audio tapes as opposed to the "poke-ball" that we are all accustom to.  I also like how when you are attempting to catch your potential beast, you use a "walk-man" in order to get it done.  The game has relationship mechanics and plenty of quirky characters for you to meet and impress.  The quest/sub quest are plentiful and the dungeons within the game are tricky but fun when you figure them out.  I recommend this game to anyone who enjoys Pokemon mechanics with a Stardew Valley feel.  It's a charming game that I hope a lot of people get to experience.

_childDocuments_.review: So I'm not too fond of pokemon-like games, so have my bias up front.This was suggested to me by a friend who was trying to sell me on the "you fuse with your monsters" and more important "you can combine monsters" - since I do enjoy games with high end customization.While graphically the designs and fusions are fantastic, the mechanics behind them seemed relatively lacking in terms of tactical nature.  They're a little less 'fuse' and a little more 'sync' if that makes any sense.So I thought I was missing something so I went to check the discussions.When I found multiple locked threads from an apparently controversial design choice.While I've little issue with such mechanics being included, I can't say the same for noticing one half of the divide all getting locks and bans and the other half all getting a free pass. _childDocuments_.review: I'm 14 hours in now and I'm sad to say that I have to clap back against some of these reviews when it comes to how good the writing. This is a very character focused story. The overall plot is not very important and only vaguely moves you forward. Main takeaway = The more the characters talk, the more I think the writers don't actually know how to write interesting characters. A personality trait and some quirky writing to describe that personality does not make an interesting character.  As a basic litmus test, go back and read how often do MANY characters say, "Anyways...Moving on... In other words... Now then... Alright then..." at the start of a sentence to try and change topics. I counted. The 11'th sentence from the first person you meet starts with 'Anyways.' Again from the same person at sentence 22. This keeps going on near constantly and its excessive use is just 1 example of how young or new writers try to use character dialogue to get the plot moving forward without realizing that it only makes the characters sound like they all have the same voice. This is the type of writing we teach to kids in English or creative writing class just to impart some level of structure and consistency to them, not to have them produce good writing for stories.So the dialogue writing isn't great and the above was just 1 example that stood out to me. What about the characters themselves? Are they good in the sense that they are written well? Do they have compelling motivations, personalities, back stories, or actions? No, kinda, for the most part. I restate, this is a plot-light (so far) character driven game but the characters are not that interesting. Some people put up Merideth when talking about the characters being good and I'm just here thinking, 'that was enough for you?' A couple lines establishing that her personality = moody/prickly and some black eyeliner away from being a stereotypical goth girl depiction, a few brief campfires hinting at a tragic past and some stunted social growth, and a 1line persona 5-esque awakening for her fusion vs the [redacted] with no actual character development, challenge, or change counts as a good character!? The writing is already not great and I don't trust the writing to somehow make the character more interesting later if I even bother putting her back in my party.The guy who's life mission in fighting back the 'vampires' FOR JUSTICE as a warrior was almost interesting until it was revealed just how cringe the 'vampires' were. I could not take him or any of the vampires seriously OR as a joke, because they weren't funny or entertaining either. At least Team Rocket back in the day (idk about the new Pokemon) were interesting and sometimes comedic baddies, even if we didn't take them that seriously either. Thus far their 1 joke is "[mode of governance] = bad" like a satirical newspaper comic that should have only been 2 panels but it was turned into a book. The guy's speech was also uninteresting. I'll see how far I can get without using him. Interestingly enough, I actually did like Kayleigh's (the first person you meet) writing of her character for the most part after having done her first quest. There actually seems like there is some level of nuance in the writing,  with her reflecting over her actions and inactions in the world around her, and her personality is not annoying by default. It's too bad that the actual baddies of her arc are also not interesting. The game does a very poor job of SHOWING why that group is bad; her main baddie gets maybe 10 lines of text total, and we the audience are just supposed to accept that this group that keeps sending people at us like the Axis from Konosuba are causing serious harm to everyone? Enough that Kayleigh is not just embarrased as if she was just part of a weird crowd when she was younger but seemingly sincerely distraught over being associated with them as if she were an ex-mafia member trying to turn over a new leaf? I'm not buying it. People are dying to monsters with some level of regularity in this world, this group was not SHOWN to warrant Kayleigh's angst, despite how surprisingly well written I thought she was thus far in this storyline.All that said, no one is playing Pokemon for the strong character writing, deep interpersonal romance between Brock and Misty, or the political struggles of Team Rocket. I think that's the case for this game too. Thus far in my 14 hrs in, the Exploration, Combat, and Team Planning are fantastic and somewhat reminded me of why I loved playing Yellow and Emerald way back in the day. Difference here is that those games barely had ANY character writing at all. Prof. gives you a pokeball, and away you go. Everyone else pretty much just gave generic npc lines, and the game was better for it. I think the same would be true here. If the game did NOT try to make the reader simpathize or sympathize with shallow personality checkboxes and that the characters just stayed as generic npcs, I think the game would be better off. Good writing can elevate mid or good games to greatness. Bad writing can bring a good game down to mediocrity. No writing will at least keep a good game good. For me at least.I'm almost reminded of the game Unsighted. A kinda good game, but I didn't get even 5 hours in because the writing was so aggressively boring that it took me completely out of the experience. At least this game has some' redemption in it's writing thus far. And the gameplay, again, is REALLY good.It's also a little weird that fusing is being treated as a thinly veiled metaphor for sex. Not the first or last to do it, but its still weird.A top steam review was great: " You turn into monsters like Ben 10 and then DBZ fusion dance with your depressed bisexual millennial friends to fight the witches from Madoka Magica. " Despite 'technically' being a millenial I have a feeling I'm outside this game's target audience. Or maybe I'm just a curmudgeon and people just get easily invested in shallow sob-stories, because ppl also said P5(one of the best modern jrpgs imo) had great writing when it just ranged from passable to horrible over 100+ hours of gametime. I guess a take home lesson is that stories don't need to have complex or even good writing for someone to get invested in its characters. And this game clearly has done that for a lot of people.Last thing, the music in this game actually is pretty good. Some of the tracks were a bop. Too bad I need to mute it most of the time because the main theme that you're going to be hearing all the time is some smooth R&B / Jazz tune and I'm not interested in being told through the lyrics every 1.5 minutes that 'it's ok to be unsure' or imperfect or some other generic life+self affirmation. AS THE OVERWORLD BGM. Wtf are these lyrics? Why did they go with this instead something actually catchy? Why not a chiptune given the game's aesthetic is clearly inspired by the 16+bit era but with some modern graphical improvements?7/10 so far. Great game but the writing drags it down. I'ma keep playing it. I had the same opinion with Octopath 2, only I stopped playing that at 70hrs in and probably won't finish it. I'll probably finish this game though.

_childDocuments_.review: TL:DR: What starts as an innovative and exciting experience unfortunately ends up devolving into a mundane and messy one.I appreciate the innovation when it comes to the platformer and traversal aspects, however the camera angle and movement made several encounters very janky, repetitive, and a chore. As for the battle mechanics - the forms and walls are a welcome addition. While I appreciate the wider variety of types and advantages, this turns into a spreadsheet headache if you care about battling and using that system. If you don't you can get through most of the game just using astral and plastic types. I think it would have been better served to narrow down on the available types and advantages and flesh out those options more to make battles more involved aside from spamming attacks and the occasional buff/debuff. The game also becomes very grindy and repetitive as a whole, fairly quickly. If you're someone like me and care about achievements/completion, you may find yourself dipping into QOL mods or the debug console to help expedite things. The art style was very pleasing - The music was not. It's not that the music itself was bad, it's just like 5 songs and thats it. 2 or 3 are mainly in rotation, with the hub town that you revisit a lot featuring one of them and it just loops, and loops....and...loops. The lyrics, the voice, it all gets really annoying 20 hours in hearing it over and over.

_childDocuments_.review: I really like games with the theme of catching monsters, as I've mentioned in other reviews, since I played a lot of Pokémon at the time (although I won’t lie, I still play it), and I’ve kept that attachment to the genre. That's why this title caught my attention (besides being a fan of Raw Fury!), and I was more than happy to have the opportunity to give it a try. Cassette Beasts is an open-world RPG game and monster “catcher”, which presents itself with a somewhat retro theme, and where we can assimilate the appearance and power of mysterious creatures using a curious music recorder and cassettes. The  will revolve around the mysterious island "New Wirral", a place where we'll be shipwrecked as soon as the game begins, and that hides countless secrets across its lands. we'll take control of our character on a beach, and we'll wander around until we find what seems to be a coastal town. But, before we even set foot in it, a strange creature will get in our way, threatening to end our story abruptly. It will be here that we'll meet one of the various characters of this adventure: Kayleigh, an energetic girl who will come to our rescue, and who will teach us how combat works and gradually explain to us about this place and its inhabitants.New Wirral seems to be a kind of dimension where travelers from different times and worlds have ended up, but who have in common that they don't know how to return to their homes. However, our character will be involved in several events that will lead him to have a clear goal: to find the way back. For this, it will be essential to use the skills that can be used in this island: the power to "record" creatures on cassettes in order to transform into them. With this power at our disposal, a varied repertoire of allies, and a powerful entity that will guide our way, we'll go through this adventure full of fun and neat moments. There is a lot to see, and little that I can tell, as I feel that you should go as blind as possible for greater enjoyment. It was a very entertaining story, and left me extremely satisfied, charming from beginning to end and with an ending but that touched me very much.In terms of , the title is presented as a typical rpg seen from above, in which we can explore the island almost without obstacles. Some places are more accessible than others, requiring specific skills to reach them, such as swimming or destroying rocks in our path. These skills are obtained by recording specific creatures, and I’ll get around to explaining that topic; for now I want to add that if you’re resourceful you can get anywhere!The combat is the classic turn-based style of the genre. We'll have two characters at the same time in battle, and both can switch to any of up to six creatures in the team. In the beginning we'll recruit Kayleigh, but we'll also be able to meet other people who want to join our adventures. In addition, there are several companions (including a dog that uses the cassettes!) and we'll have an affection system to increase our affinity with them. I always like this kind of detail, especially because reaching the maximum friendship can also result in romance; and what can I say, I'm a sucker for those little things. Apart from our companions, there are several other important npc, such as the "rangers", who try to safeguard the peace, and the inhabitants of the town of Harbortown, who will give us missions, provide "rumors" to pursue in the world, or simply sell us objects.Now, let's move on to the creatures. In this universe, the monsters are "recorded" to cassettes using a special music player, allowing us to create copies of them in which we can transform; a creative twist in my opinion, that marks the theme of the game very well. Some of these monsters will give us special abilities for exploration, as I mentioned before, and many of them have evolutions, called "remasters" that can be acquired by leveling up and other objectives, so it never hurts to record the ones we don’t have.Each creature has an innate element, out of the fifteen in the game, with its own strengths and weaknesses. Elemental advantages are somewhat peculiar, since they can create buffs or debuffs on the beasts. For example, wind extinguishes fire and lowers its attack, and water benefits plant by giving it self-regeneration, among *many* other combinations. And speaking of combinations, we'll also have a fusion system, where we'll be able to see up to.... 14400 variants?! Something that will keep completionists busy, no doubt. The fusions maintain the two elements of the units, and are performed between our character and their ally. This mechanic can be used by filling a specific bar to the max, and its effectiveness rises along with the affection with our companions, so get to socializing!I want to add that since we are the ones doing the fighting, changing creatures will not eliminate the buffs or debuffs, which can be both beneficial and negative. There is quite a lot of complexity and depth put into the combat system, especially with the stickers and the order in which we equip them. The stickers are the base, learned, or purchased skills that we can give and take from the monsters at will, allowing us to customize their attacks; in particular, it should be noted that the same skill can come in different rarities and with additional effects, which is awesome. At the same time, there is a wide variety of things to do while exploring, from puzzles and fights against rangers, to resting in bonfires to recover and interact briefly with our companions, for example. It really exceeded my expectations, it's a section that I found very robust and interesting!The  is represented with a very nice pixel style for both sprites and the world itself, although the latter is rendered in a more 3D-ish style and it really fits well with the vibe of the game. The characters in conversation have beautiful digital portraits, and some important enemies have super stylized art styles that give them a special touch. The designs of the monsters are very creative and varied, and although I can't say that I liked them all, I can say that they are very unique, especially with so many fusions. Something I kept to mention in this section is that the "shiny" of this game, called "bootlegs" (hehe), are not only color variants, but they have different elements depending on their color; this opens the possibility of more team compositions without having to change your favorite critters, and I thought it was spectacular.The soundtrack is, as you would expect from a game with such a musical theme, stunning in every aspect. All areas have their own background song, which changes in rhythm depending on the time of day, and there are several different tunes depending on the kind of enemy we are facing, such as bosses, for example. On the latter, I want to highlight that when we use fusion the song on duty acquires vocals, sung by a girl with a sublime voice and that kept me super energized throughout the game. Overall, I found this section to be a beauty, and one of the game's strongest points, to the point that I found myself humming the combat songs throughout the day.In , Cassette Beasts is a captivating game from start to finish, with a story that has comical moments but serious when it counts, and I thoroughly enjoyed it. I really liked the cast of characters, and the stories of each of them! The combat with the various creatures and their abilities is extremely fun, and the amount of secondary content (of which I left a few things for later), opens the way to a good time of entertainment. It’s a charismatic game that shines in practically all its aspects, and although I had some random fps drops, the effort with which it was developed is very noticeable. I recommend it to all fans of the genre looking for a sparkling jewel, or at least try it for the soundtrack!

_childDocuments_.review: Gotta Record'em all!I brought out my old cassette tapes just for this occasion!It’s Pokémon, but cassette.This isn't Pokémon at home, Pokémon is Cassette Beasts at home.One of the best RPGs, it's a mixture of Pokémon Platinum and Persona + Shin Megami with the puzzles of The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past.I don't think there has ever been a game that I have craved more people knowing and talking about more than Cassette Beasts. Honestly, from the moment that I heard the lyrics to Wherever We Are Now, I knew this game was something incredibly special to me. I was kinda scared to actually finish it, so for a while I just stayed away from the ending, not willing to say final goodbyes and watch the credits roll. This game is complex, but the themes of friendship and personal power are very important to me, as naive and pathetically unrealistic and childish as the real world seems to find them, the notion that we can change reality, and that the combined power of multiple people working together is limitless is something that I will never ever let go of.I loved the gameplay, monster designs, fusion gimmick, and of course the soundtrack. The story is also really well done, with very unique and challenging boss battles. The gameplay is engaging and challenging. There is so much to collect and there are so many quests to complete. This is the kind of game that could easily take over someone's life. So I think that makes the ending all the more stronger, telling you to put it down. You didn't turn into a monster and go to another world, and date a redheaded guitarist, but you still had to give up something comforting to get home.I think one of the things that makes Cassette Beasts truly excellent is the way it handles combat. You can't just go in guns-blazing because your stronger moves require more points to spend, meaning you can either use free moves and save up for hard-hitters, or use medium-hitters on every turn. And because HP doesn't recover between fights and your healing items are limited, it makes even the most mundane fights meaningful. The music kicking in vocals when you're fused is mind-blowingly smart. Every song sounds good both with and without vocals, which is hard enough to do. But the lyrics are so perfect for the situations you find yourself in that I can't stop praising Joel Baylis' work. I'm just thankful the OST is finally on Spotify.I think a subtle, but really big reason why I'm enjoying CB more than Pokemon is the way they handled leveling, capturing, and moves. Stickers you can swap + your character leveling up vs the monsters makes it way less grindy and easier to change out your roster. The capturing also is easier since you don't have to worry about the monster "fainting". I really liked those changes as I feel like they took the most annoying aspects out of Pokémon and improved them. I don't feel like I'm stuck with one roster the whole game with CB.Cassette beasts is the first Pokémon clone that doesn’t feel like Pokémon. It is very unique and changes up quite a bit of things. It’s got tons of unique mechanics. It feels like a Pokémon clone that went out of its way to fix a lot of problems that Pokémon had, like much more interesting bosses, a more elaborate status effect system, etc. Does enough different from Pokémon to be distinct and engaging, but it still has a familiar feel for anyone who wants that kind of experience. Great story and companion system. The Archangels are FANTASTIC, such phenomenal designs! And the creatures actually have quite a bit of background as far as their naming and/or design, and the sticker and bootleg systems makes things quite entertaining as far as build diversity.This game will forever hold a special place in my heart. The mechanics are amazing and unique. I love how it made more of a buff and de buff with the type chart… it’s just so different and opens a world of combinations and strategy. The story is really really good… a lot darker and it has a lot of real life stuff but of course it’s presented in a way where it is still cassette beast and not Romeo and Juliet or aliens and angels. The dark atmosphere (they did such an outstanding job with allowing the player to feel certain emotions specially when fighting the arch angels) felt like a dream/nightmare. The monster designs are the best ones hands down… the fusion system is amazing I loved the characters and how cassette beasts make you actually care for them. The world is so vibrant and the night and day cycle is such an amazing touch. Literally everything about the game screams classic.There are minor things it does worse than Pokémon (the storage system is not very efficient and it kills me there isn’t some kind of dex) but overall it’s a really great experience. Honestly, if Pokémon can be riddled with issues and still be popular, then I will happily overlook the couple of issues Cassette Beasts has. It's nearly perfect and that is more than you can say about all the recent Pokémon games. Scratched an itch I didn’t know needed scratching. The game is a great time, felt like I was returning from vacation when I beat the game, however, and now I’m kinda stuck feeling depressed and just wanna go back and never return to the real world, I’d happily spend some time on that island! Damn near cried my way through the entire final boss. The sheer climactic majesty, the positive message about human will, the music, the thematic resolution of the entire game... it was beautiful. I hope they continue with this series!! I can’t wait for the future of this game!10/10

_childDocuments_.review: One of the first series that ever got me into gaming was Pokemon. I mention this here because Cassette Beasts is so inspired by the groundwork Pokemon set up in games that it’s impossible not to mention it at least once in this review. Cassette Beasts rings more similar to early game Pokemon than the recent fare. This is a positive, because newer generation Pokemon has proven disappointing in a number of ways to myself and other fans alike. If you’re looking for a great monster-capturing game with a fantastical story, you’re in the right place.If you’re familiar with the isekai genre, you’ve got a good place to start with the base story in Cassette Beasts. After you make a player character, the protagonist finds themselves within the world of New Wirral. Falling into an alternate universe is strange enough, but things get weirder. There are monsters in New Wirral, and the residents need to protect themselves. To fight back, they use cassette tapes to transfer into the same beasts after them, using various elemental attacks to force their foes to retreat. That’s right, in Cassette Beasts you turn into the monsters.The first companion you’ll meet, Kayleigh, is a bright face that acts as a guiding hand to the way things work. She helps lead the way to the main city, where multiple rumours and paths forward can be found. That’s right, despite all the side quests, main quests, and errands available in the game, your main goal is to get back to your own reality.For the most part, the main story quests are split into three categories: companion quests, archangel quests, and captain quests. These can be tackled in basically any order that you want, though the game does make it decently clear what areas might be too difficult for your current level. Level scaling can also be adjusted in the game’s settings, making things harder or easier depending on what you’d like. My favourite part of the game has to be the Archangels. These fights are great, the “dungeons” and puzzles to get to them are fun, and they act as boss fights within Cassette Beasts. Pursuing them is a requirement to “finish” the game, though there are hours and hours of game play to get there. I’ll admit a close second  are the companion quests. Felix and Kayleigh have the best companion quests of all time, and they both genuinely make me feel warm and fuzzy once I completed them. Don’t sleep on the companions either, you’ll find more throughout the world and by following rumours in Harbourtown. Each companion has their own personality, their own quests, their own Cassette Beast, and their own scenes to unlock by resting at the campfires or cafe. While I typically avoid spoilers in my reviews I’ll say this: you can benefit from keeping companions leveled up, even if they’ll train on their own some without you.Catch as many beasts as you’d like, pursue friendships with all six companions, become a ranger, and enjoy potentially getting back to your own world. Love pixel graphics? Me too. Cassette Beasts has a wealth of pixel sprites for each beast available, with each one varied and easy to tell apart. Even the remasters of certain beast lines change things up enough to be different while also being clearly related. What really astonishes with the graphics are the varying sprites for every single fusion in the game. Each one is a little bit different, and discovering what two beasts look like fused was sincerely part of the fun of gameplay for me. Character sprites are colourful- except when they’re not supposed to be- and most of them are unique. Archangels are incredible to see, and seem to break all graphical rules within the confines of the game, appearing in true unpixelated 3D, 2D, static images, and more. The world is also bright, three-dimensional, and loads of fun to explore. There are multiple regions to traverse, with plenty of unique obstacles and terrain.Yes, you turn into a beast, but each Cassette Beast takes the main player's level and stats and combines it with the stats from each cassette. The cassettes don’t have their own level, every beast you equip will scale to the level that your player is. Stats can be adjusted once players pursue the captain/ranger quest further, allowing players to train at a gym to raise or lower particular stats for their player. There are 14 types of beasts in the game, and every single Cassette Beast is a monotype until fusions get involved.  Certain types impact other types differently, and there’s plenty of moves to also swap yours or an opponent's type in battle. For example: a plastic type beast will turn into a poison type temporarily when hit with a fire type move. The game is chock full of instances like this, which keep combat fun and reactive. The game also hands players a number of ways to interact with the environment and get from place to place. First will be gliding, eventually you’ll be able to swim, and more. This also allows the ability to double-back and grab things missed at first, so you can really round stock up on items and stickers. Moves in this game are dictated by stickers stuck to a beasts cassette, which can be swapped out and learned by compatible beasts. Each move can be used based on the amount of AP (action points) the player gets per turn, though more AP can be generated with certain stickers. AP also builds faster when players fuse with their partners, and this is also the only way to get dual type beasts that have access to both beasts moves. The fusion meter builds naturally in battle, though there are also items that can be used to fill the bar. Certain enemies can also fuse, and rogue fusions can be found throughout the world as well. These monsters are harder challenges to tackle, though there are potentially rarer stickers and even a higher chance for bootleg (or shiny) beasts to be found. Did I mention there’s romance? That’s right, you can romance companions as well, if that’s the sort of thing you enjoy. They’re not exactly deep romances, of course, but they’re there!There’s boundless amounts of passion present in the small team that created Cassette Beasts, and you’d be doing yourself a disservice by not checking it out if turn-based monster-collecting RPG’s are a genre you enjoy. I played this game for many hours back-to-back, and aside from a few issues that are beyond easy to overlook compared to some recent similar releases in the genre, I thoroughly enjoyed my time. This game is great, and one I’ll be recommending to most of my friends.

_childDocuments_.review: The monster catching genre is stuffed to the brim with misses that don't understand what makes the genre great, but Cassette Beasts stands apart by really knowing the genre and playing with the traditional mechanics in interesting ways. This game is completely inundated with clever decisions that make the game sing. Monsters all use your level, not their own? Check. 'Trainer' stats used as the basis for monster stats? Check. Every monster can be any element in the game, with proper color changes? Check, if you're willing to work for it. Interesting type matchups that aren't just damage multiplers? You bet. Traditional indie Cute/Creep Story? Oh yea, it's there. The monsters and their movesets are very interesting. Of their 10 slots, you can stuff moves, passives, and even automation triggers (chance to trigger when you crit, chance to trigger at start of battle, etc). There are even Uncommon and Rare versions of the tapes that add special effects to them, like increased duration or heal after use. Every beast has their own total potential moveset but you can swap them out as much as you want. And any two monsters in the game can fuse together into a new monster, mixing body, head, and limbs/etc and swapping the color pallet, and combining the stats, movesets, types, etc as well.Moveset combinations are exciting. Get the status that turns you into an immortal ghost but kills you when it runs out? Better pair it with the attack that extends your statuses! Have a good on-death effect? Ritual to bring you back after death + Self-Destruct might be what you're looking for. Electric types can often pump themselves up to hit all enemies, good thing their Conductive status also damages everyone with the status every time anyone with the status is struck with electricity. Or maybe you'd rather use that ability to place up strong walls at the beginning of the match for cheap?The exploration factor had a lot of love put into it. There is a lot of content out in the wild and plenty of it you can easily miss, to the general benefit of the game. New traversal methods open up (Metroid Style) that allow you to get to new areas, and shortcuts can often be unlocked after getting to key points. The only 'downside' to this game is that it's a single-player focused experience, with no online battles. This makes sense, though, as competitive viability is a decent sacrifice for a good single player game. Overall, a very enthusiastic 'yes' to everyone as for a team that really understands what makes Monster Tamer games fun.

_childDocuments_.review: "Can you feel it? The lack of wind but abundance of air?"This game is quite honestly my game of the year. It's fun, engaging, non-restrictive (A big thing I'll get into in a moment), and does well in establishing it's own identity in a well saturated genre.It introduces some very interesting Quality of Life changes that Pokemon-likes would really do well to implement. I was worried at first that the catch mechanic was a bit handholdy because technically a beast can't die while you try to catch it. But as the game scales up and the monsters/legendaries get harder to catch, you realize that its not easier than your usual "throw ball and pray" strategy. It's actually much riskier and more challenging as you risk your character (not your beast, your actual player) being 1-shot.So that already put the game at a solid 9/10 for me. But what really pushed it over was the ability to play with whatever combination you want. The way type advantages are done make them easy to either abuse, work into your strategy, or ignore. The concept of STAB seems to be removed in favor of bonuses over other typings. For example, instead of Fire critting Grass for super effective damage, instead it guarantees a burn even on a skill with no innate burn attached.Water "extinguishes" fire, causing a drop in damage, both ranged and melee, etc.Baton Pass players like me will love the setup capabilities of this game, as buffs and debuffs are applied to your character, not your tape. So you can have a tape (The "Pokemon" are called tapes) that, at start of battle immediately does 3 buffs, then on your turn, swap them with your sweeper.You can build almost any tape in any way you want, save for some stickers (the "TMs" are called stickers) that cant go on some tapes, giving you an incredibly vast pool to play with. This game is amazing and I haven't stopped playing it since I picked it up. I wish there was PvP or some form of online so I can see the teams and mons other people have come up with.Solid 10/10 for me

_childDocuments_.review: I'll update this review when I'm done. Very fun so far, lots of exploration and although I tend to get bored with turn based combat the combat felt nice. I have only one issue with this game and that is how it can be a bit confusing of what you're supposed to do to advance. There are puzzles around the map that require specific moves from specific monsters like Pokemon. I understand it's meant to motivate the player to capture more monsters but it can be a bit frustrating staring at puzzles while you can't do anything yet.UPDATE: I would still very much recommend this game, and it is a great pokemon style game. However, annoyances I have in pokemon games are can be found in this game. Waiting a long time for moves to go through as each status effect is applied to each monster individually instead of in one is very much annoying. Some parts of the game definitely feels like its padding for time and although I don't mind games padding for time the gameplay has to be fun. Most of the time these moments feel needlessly dragged out. And oh my God, there is a boss in the game that puts you to sleep constantly and I am still malding from it. Other than these problems I enjoyed the game alot. Unlike pokemon games I felt like I could get around and not get lost easily (probably some bias here with the last pokemon game i played being emerald when i was like 8 and I had no idea where to go). I'm not one to listen to music often but the soundtrack is great. The art direction is fun and creative; and the story although not very deep was interesting and had a lot of themes I resonate with. For 20 dollars it's definitely worth it and I hope the devs keep making games because they know how to make a good one.

_childDocuments_.review: Cassette Beasts is cute. Cassette Beasts is one of those cute RPGs and if that’s what you’re looking for, you probably won’t be disappointed- but I can’t say why the “probably” without spoiling the ending.The concept rests on you as the main character being isekai’d to a new, very small world- but in a subversion of the trope, nearly everyone and everything on this new world has been isekai’d there. And, in typical fashion, your main quest is to leave; but it’s not long before you find out that the rules of physics here don’t quite apply, which is how you wind up monster collecting and transforming using Cassette Beasts.I’m not good at video games, and guaranteed some Pokemaniac would know the optimization of it all better, but for the most part: the designs are fun, the branching paths for remastering (evolution) are easy to find and understand, and most monsters have some level of merit to using in battle, at least for a casual playthrough, so you can really play around with making a team out of designs you like rather than optimization.Speaking of optimization of team and strategy, one of the nice things that this game lets you do if change the AI difficulty and the level scaling right from the get go; I chose to leave them be, as I overall thought they presented a good challenge, but as I said before, I’m not good at video games, so I didn’t want it harder or easier. Still, it sometimes slaps you in the face; I mean the basic plotline at around level 65, and in doing post game, I almost immediately got a new quest, only to be slapped in the face by a level 100 boss. And it wasn’t the only one. (The level scaling is nice in regards to the other mini bosses and bosses you face, though.)Speaking of the monsters and gameplay, finding bootlegs (shinies) is not horrible in this game. Upon its completion I had around two dozen. The chance in a normal encounter is 1/1000, but the post game is far more helpful, giving you an item that makes a bootleg a guaranteed encounter (though what kind specifically is only partially guaranteed; getting exactly what you're looking for takes work in quitting and reopening the game). For a while even this was frustrating, since the item is only one use and it costs 50 of another item to farm, but in the end, not horrible. The fun thing about bootlegs is, unlike shiny pokemon, bootlegs are more than just a special color; they actually change the element of the monster from its typical state for a bit of fun!The battling system is mostly simple, but can get complicated as times; there are so many status conditions (and elemental internations that cause status conditions) that, after 70 hours of gameplay, I still don’t remember them all. But the setup makes it far from impossible to win despite this. One of the largest issues I have is the map; the characters are 2d on a 3d map stylized to look 2d artistically. I enjoy the art the the cheesy 80s/90s getups, but sometimes moving about the maps can be a pain; it’ll turn at sometimes unexpected times and has more than once messed up my direction, and there are places you can get… Stuck isn’t the right word, but not not-stuck. At my 8GB of RAM speed (not high, but you don’t need much to run this game) the map would also load for me if I went from one side to the other, in basically the same longitudinal position, which includes of the middle of the main town and in the middle of a puzzle that requires running back and forth so I got it over, and over, and over, and over again. Now that I don’t need to run in the same places 500 times it’s not so bad, but that part was grating- especially with enemies chasing you into encounters and disrupting you. Let me do the damn puzzle!One thing that befuddles me is that I can be roaming the map at level 105 and lvl 1 enemies are still trying to chase me for a showdown. They do get in the way sometimes. Fast travel is useful, but feels inconsistently placed sometimes.Throughout the game, you’ll get six partners that tag along with you (you can choose who one at a time and swap whenever), and five of those six partners are romanceable (the sixth one is not for a VERY GOOD REASON, but I’ll leave that out of this portion). It’s very much a side item to the game and mostly for the achievement, but all relationships have hearts- which is odd, because hearts are about the overall relationship level, not the romance level. You have the option to begin romancing any of those characters at their respective five-heart cutscenes, and you can have each character romanceable at the same time, but can only be in a solid relationship with one. Fortunately, there’s no damage to friendship if you don’t choose romance options at any time. The conversations are fun, and you get either little snippets or dialogue when you rest. The snippets repeat randomly and are based on your relationship level with someone. Dialogue is unique, only occurs once, is a great way to learn about characters and feel a passage of time in the game, and has new dialogue based on different plot points in the game. Unfortunately in the post game, these eventually wear out, and the post game can be far longer than the main game. It just felt stale after a time.There are 123 achievements and they’re all doable. Most are storyline related and the rest are not difficult. The longest I spent on one that wasn’t story related was 4 hours, and that was just due to awful, awful rng luck (trying to get a Glitter bootleg). 100%ing this game is not bad. A couple of them (catching all monsters and getting them all to five stars) can be cheated a bit with the DLC, since “doing them all” is hardcoded by number, so I got the achievements before I did thanks to the DLC (the DLC is fun by the way, if a bit odd in its initial mechanic, I’d say worth the money).(Warning for ending and postgame spoilers.)My biggest issue with the postgame is that- unless I’m stupid- it’s not really explained where the orb fusions are coming from or what their purpose is. Me being stupid is a distinct possibility, though.And now the ending, the sore spot for many: the second you arrive on New Wirral, your goal is to leave. And that’s what the end of the plotline is: leaving. I, like many others, expected the moment where everyone decides to stay. And then, when that didn’t happen, I waited for the moment after the cutscenes where they somehow found a way back.It doesn’t happen. In the end, your friends say goodbye, if you had a romance it breaks, and you all leave on good terms, never to see one another again. If you play after, in the postgame, you’re teleported to the moment before you make this decision, and can carry on in New Wirral (you can start the post game without doing this anyway, from what I understand). This decisions was controversial, to say the least. I saw people disappointed with it, saying it was against the spirit of the game, and I felt the same- until I realized it was entirely wrong. Sometimes plans change or life throws you obstacles. Sometimes you’ll make unlikely friends that will help you through it. But the plan was always to go back home, to friends and family and loved ones; you either don’t see your New Wirral friends again- and they all want to leave- or you don’t go back to your friends and family. You can’t ask them to stay for you. Not everyone or everything is meant to stay in our lives, but that doesn’t mean we don’t grow because of it, that we aren’t affected by it, or that it’s not worth treasuring.Overall, this game is a solid 8.5/10, it was fun, and I’ll miss it.

_childDocuments_.review: I know it says (As of me writing this) that I haven't played long, but I have been entirely playing on the Xbox because I wanted to see if it was worth the 30 dollars Id be dropping on steam for it, and when I say that this game has blown me out of the water, I mean it. This game has so much story, stemming only from your characters want to leave the island they and everyone else have been trapped upon. But that isn't the only thing going for it. It has so many options for what to do, and when you have to do it, because nothing is locked down by a specific time of day or night. You can fight bosses in whatever order you want to fight them, but be aware, the bosses don't scale in level for you, they are where they are, and I feel like that adds a beautiful extra bite of challenge. The game gives you a need to communicate with the npc around you, as anyone and everyone can give you a quest at any random moment, and that quest will only push you twords the next big thing on your plate. And the heart system is just amazing. I know most people say it isnt the strongest romance bar in game history, and I agree with that, but it is certainly up there in my book. In order to make fusions stronger by more then simple stat adds, you can do things with your main partner in order to raise affection points, which, in turn, not only boosts the power behind your fusions by 5%, but also gets you one step closer to popping the question you wait to ask from the moment you meet that specific partner. It isn't much, but you do get a cute dating scene and throughout the rest of the game you will receive romantic dialogue, which I think is plenty. I dare to say that this feels superior to games like Pokemon in my opinion, and while I cant say I trust it will be possible, I happily await the mention of a cassette beasts 2!

_childDocuments_.review: I believe this is my first time reviewing a Steam game, so here we go. This is easily the best monster collector game I have ever played for several reasons.1. Monster DesignI've played a few monster collector series over the years, and a lot of them seem to fail in what I consider to be one of the most important aspects of this genre - making me want to collect the monsters. Cassette Beasts monster design is amazing, I think easily rivaling Pokemon. Each monster has a unique personality, and when they get remastered (evolve), they aren't just bigger versions of the previous stage.2. Story and LoreI have not yet finished the game, but Cassette Beasts is pretty light on story (aside from character arcs). Your main goals are becoming a ranger, and battling analog horror bosses to find a way home. I can't go into much without spoilers, but the origin of the monsters in Cassette Beasts is really cool idea and works well for the themes of the game.3. CharactersThere are several characters in the game. You always have one person with you at all times. When you rest, there is a chance for a small conversation with that character. I've completed 4 quests so far, all of which have been great. This ties in with the games themes, but there is a focus on art and creativity, as well as people's interaction with media, in the quests. Once you complete a character's quest, you can build a relationship with them by battling with them, which lets you learn more about them. I've liked what I've seen so far, and really related with some of the characters.4. ThemesThis game focuses a lot on the creativity and imagination of humanity. Especially on the idea that once something is created and people believe in it, that thing is essentially real. This theme is reinforced by the characters, the monsters themselves, and the main story. I think it all blends together really well.I love the society in-game as well. The community is money-less, running on a trade-and-barter system which meshes in with materials gained from combat. There is kind of an "enemy team" like Team Rocket in this game - the Landowner's Association. One character's quest is to wipe them out completely. Also, the society seems to be government-less, with the Rangers being a group of community members who do what they can to help everybody out.5. CombatI think combat is more dynamic than Pokemon's. Super-effective moves in Cassette Beasts cause a status effect based on the specific type matchup, it isn't just more damage. This has more consequences than the Pokemon system, and I really felt it when my Astral-type starter got AP Drain from a Plastic-type move.Combat in general is about medium difficulty. You can carry 6 monsters, while enemy teams never seem to have more than 4. Boss battles and Rogue Fusions definitely tip more into the challenging side which I liked. The fusion mechanic is enjoyable and felt required for a couple fights.I expected the Ranger fights to be kind of like Gym Battles in Pokemon, and they sort of were. Instead of just being type-based, there was a gimmick or effect that they focused, which I think is a better way of doing things. I only have 2 fights left, and unfortunately I have felt underwhelmed. They mention at the beginning that you can't just brute force the fights and need to adapt to their strategies. This is just wrong. It is very easy to brute force the fights, so I wish there was more of a challenge there.6. SoundtrackThe soundtrack in all areas and situations in this game rocks. ---TLDR: Monsters have personality, cool lore, fun character stories, great theming, good combat if a bit easy sometimes, and awesome music.9/10
