_childDocuments_.review: This game is pretty hard to review fairly for me so I'll just summarise the things that stood out. TL;DR: I wasn't sure whether to rate it positive or negative as its many upsides are countered by also many downsides, but after all decided it was net positive. It scratches the creature collector itch and has interesting parts. 6/10 tho.Upsides:1. The good ol' rock-paper-scissors type system is innovated in that hitting an enemy with an attack they're weak against on top of dealing increased damage will debuff them or even change their type, while hitting them with one they're strong enough will buff them. For example hitting a plastic type with fire will melt it, changing its type to poison for 3 turns, and then hitting that poison type with fire again will ignite it, inflicting burn DoT for 3 turns. This is also taught well, except I'm still not sure if transforming type interactions count as advantaged and deal more damage or not.2. The overworld movement is fluid with metroidvania-like skills that allow traversing obstacles after catching a specific monster. This is cool.3. Instead of "lucky" or "shiny" monsters this game has "bootlegs", which have have their type changed. This is also cool.4. Attacks are learned via "stickers", which can be taken off one monster cassette and attached to another. Monsters keep unlocking stickers even after reaching max level, and you can buy more stickers in shops. This results in a good build variety.5. There's enough types and interactions to make things interesting.6. They somehow managed to make every two monster fusion I've tried look good or good enough. The game has over a hundred monster species.7. Again, there's a lot of monster species (140 as of version 1.5) and some have interesting branching remasters (evolutions).8. The graphics are nice.9. The soundtrack is good and in some cases even awesome, with some caveats. It uses the trick of playing the instrumental version and seamlessly switching to one with vocals when the situation gets more intense.10. There's a friendship/romance with your NPC partners element, which is cute.11. Defended by the hp bar of your monster is the hp bar of your character, this also applies to enemy trainers. Meaning that if you bring an enemy monster to low HP and then hit it hard enough, you can defeat the enemy character and end the battle even if they have monsters remaining, but en enemy can defeat you in the same fashion.Downsides:1. The type system is unbalanced. This is especially obvious with the Beast type, this game's equivalent of Normal, which has *no defensive nor offensive weaknesses* and one offensive advantage. I'll repeat: there is nothing you can do to counter a strong Beast type. It annoyed me multiple times during my playthrough. They're plain OP, which is sad because they're also the most boring.2. Speaking of my playthrough, I finished the game, maxed out all relationships and captured all monsters except for like 2. I have 20 hours of playtime.3. All monsters are single type to facilitate the Fusion mechanic, which combines the two monsters you're using at the moment.4. Some types are under-utilised. The Glass type has a single monster species which you can encounter once or so without chasing random timed events. The rarest type, Glitter, has no species, it's only available via bootlegs.5. The fusion mechanic is kinda bad. I mean, it takes the double battle format and changes it into "you have this single more powerful monster that can spam a more powerful attack every turn lol". It's as if the game creators looked at what modern P*kemon games are doing with introducing a mediocre mechanic the combat is centered around every generation and removing it in the next one, and thought "that's a great idea, let's also center our combat around a mediocre mechanic that everyone will sure wish gets changed or removed if this ever gets a sequel".6. Bootlegs are an important part of the game's appeal, so it's a shame that they're so rare. Before finishing the game I caught one or two, and I don't think I ended up using it/them. This is especially bad when you consider that this meant I didn't have an opportunity to use a single Glitter type at all, didn't catch one even in post-game. And that some remasters (evolutions) are unique to a given bootleg type, which means that if you wanna fill out your codex or whatever it was called, have fun hunting for a certain type of a certain monster via random wild fusion events that don't specify what you'll even be fighting. (They have a higher chance of bootlegs, but still not very high.) There's one saving grace in the form of a ~post-game item that guarantees the next fusion battle will include a bootleg of a given type *or* species, but it's the most expensive thing in the game (prepare to grind) and requires sacrificing a monster of that type and species. Either type or species is still random. 7. Since movement abilities are unlocked by capturing a given monster, you can easily miss them if you don't capture everything as you go along. The last ability is available via another monster that you encounter once without chasing random timed events which aren't even trackable before ~post-game, that is also extremely hard to capture.8. Capturing monsters exposes one of the characters' main HP bar to attacks. Against stronger, hard to capture monsters this can mean that they'll just kill both of your characters before you get a good enough capture roll, even if you constantly put them to sleep with the other character, if they're even still alive. As this is an exposed character, there is no option to mitigate this with a monster with better defence or advantageous type.9. Branching remasters are only hinted at what triggers them. It's a fun egg hunt, but also means that unless you're looking up every monster on the wiki and spoiling the later forms for yourself, you *will* end up in a situation where you remaster a monster you like and later learn that you got a generic version you can easily encounter in the wild and you missed a cooler form.10. The plot is generic and feels kinda bad.11. The characters except for one are your standard set of forgettable tumblrwave gender/race/orientation/culture combo tokens that manage to be quirky and generic at the same time.12. The soundtrack grew on me over time, but the town theme version with vocals, which you're gonna hear *a lot* since it plays whenever you're inside a town building, ground on my nerves nearly the whole playtime. Like the characters, some soundtrack pieces give off tumblr vibes and not in a good way.13. The hype, vocals-included, versions of battle themes play only when you're fused. I only grew to appreciate the main battle theme in the latter parts of my playthrough when I was fighting a lot of wild fusions and so used fusion more than against normal monsters. Another case of the fusion mechanic harming more than helping.14. The evil organisation you can fight as a sidequest is literally a tumblr zoomer's strawman image of landlords. And I mean literally, that's what they are in-universe. Prepare to cringe.

_childDocuments_.review: A fun game with interesting mechanics, an efficient and enjoyable level up system, and major quality of life features. Game is well-balanced and adding a new beast to your team doesn't mean retraining it all the way up to your current level to match the rest of your teams' levels since it's based on character level and not an individual beast's level.It's everything Pokemon wanted to be before Pokemon turned into a weak, yearly Fifa cash grab, and it's far more worth your time to play. _childDocuments_.review: Despite the juggernaut that is the Pokemon franchise, monster taming/catching games are rather sparse. I think a large reason for this is that these games live and die by their monster designs and it can be a tough thing to nail. Cassette Beasts manages to (mostly) accomplish this while also bringing some welcome additions to the genre.Just like Pokemon, in Cassette Beasts you catch monsters using a specific item (Cassettes in this case) and then transform into them in battle against other monsters / trainers. The vast majority of battles are double battles where each side has 2 (or more) monsters. CB diverges in a handful of ways from Pokemon's formula such as:1. Monsters cannot be defeated while attempting to catch them, but you can damage them and they can damage you.2. Monsters do not have levels, instead the player does and their companions does. Monsters instead are able to rank up to 5 times, earning a move each time, and in many cases being able to remaster (evolve) upon reaching the 5th rank. Ranks do not increase a monster's stats, but remastering does.3. The player and their companions have a health bar separate from their monsters that is exposed when their current monster is defeated, meaning that if enough damage is dealt in a single turn, you could be defeated despite your entire team not being defeated.4. Cassette Beasts version of "shinies" goes beyond a simple palette swap and changes a monster's typing and even moveset.A lot of these changes remove the tedium that would be commonly found in Pokemon titles. There's a smooth level curve that keeps the game challenging but never left me feeling like I needed to grind to overcome fights.The combat system feels overall less complex than Pokemon, and you can build some truly busted monsters that are able to end nearly any battle in a single turn, but by utilizing the multiple difficulty options for the enemy AI, there can be a greater challenge found here.Outside of battling, you traverse the world of New Wirral that gradually opens up as you solve puzzles, progress the story, and acquire player abilities which are essentially this game's version of HMs. These abilities include gliding, a dash that can break boulders/crates, and more. New Wirral isn't the most exciting location in a game, but it is fun to explore and traverse once you've gotten a few abilities under your belt.Graphics are charming and the monster/character designs are memorable and creative. The soundtrack is also very well done which ties in well given the theme of the game. Many tracks have vocals which were great but I did find a bit distracting after some time so the option to disable just the vocals is a welcome addition. I think the story is okay, certainly better than the usual Pokemon story line, but the writing sometimes had a little too much "millennial sappiness" that made my eyes roll. That being said, there are certainly funny moments of dialogue within the game.There is a post game with a handful of repeatable quests that unlock further tidbits of story and rewards as you complete enough of them but I felt the grind to do so wasn't enjoyable so it's unfortunate to see story content locked behind it.Overall, Cassette Beasts is a great monster-catcher that I'd recommended all fans of the genre check out. It scratches that Pokemon itch very well, despite a few shortcomings, and adds enough to keep it from being an outright Pokemon clone. Check it out!

_childDocuments_.review: When I play a game for 20 hours in two days, usually it gets a positive review. So don't be surprised when I give this game an absolutely glowing review while I'm still honeymooning with it. I'll probably write a more in-depth review later that only I will really read, but the main thrust of this is me being baffled that I'm the first one on my whole steam list to have played this. What's wrong with you people? College changed you.I don't usually push out review like this, but this game is 50% off at time of writing and I felt like I was going to try the game and refund it if I bounced off of it. Instead, yesterday was a blur where I did nothing but play this game and occasionally rose to eat and drink.Why should you play cassette beasts?Cassette beasts is like if Digimon loved you back. Somehow basically every gripe I have with other mon-games has been addressed. And that's hard to lead with because Cassette Beasts isn't a subtweet of a game, it's something that clearly takes inspiration and lessons from other mongames and then takes that ball straight to the net. This game was not meant to carve out a niche like Temtem or made to be bitter and edgy while eating nintendo's lunch like Palworld. It stands alone as something unique and special, a lighthouse of a game in between oceans of disappointment.-Simplistic type matchups that lead to the game turning into rock-paper-scissors? Not in Cassette beasts baby, while there are type match-ups they lead to unique and in-depth interactions that tip the battle in your favor but don't guarantee a win. It pays to learn them and they can be part of chipping away at tough fights, but they aren't the major deciding factor for most fights, rather just a little bag of chips that comes with the meal.-Weird leveling system that makes you stick with like 4 mons and leave the rest of them in the dust? Don't worry about it. The game uses a system that makes even the most route-1 pidgey-lookin' mon that you have in your box at least passable in a fight. The evolution system is a bit weird but it's easy to get used to and the way it's set up leads more to having a big book full of mons that you can assemble different parties out of rather than a few staples that you always use. Also because the evolution system doesn't take multiple hour grinds for every mon, I ended up clearing the finish with around 80% of the mons collected. Even if they will be in my pack forever.-Static environments and boxed in quests? Try schmoving around an enormous 3-d world with quests you can tackle in any order you like. The game gives you the ability to bullet-dash very early on and with the physics engine at play you can do really wacky stuff with it. I think I've already sequence-broken a few times on accident based on some level gaps.-Divides its attention better than its contemporaries. Breaks the mold from pokemon more and isn't as hobbled by random jutting MMO aspects. Plus, the artstyle is better. Yes, I am bitter.-Parting from other mongames that leave story swinging in the breeze, Cassette Beasts' video-gamey plot is made very flavorful by the many different fun characters and interesting small twists in its structure, along with one or two legitimate little beats that make the story more than just a glorified gym leader hunt. Plus, the undertale-style shirt-tearing ending, while a little clumsy, did succeed in making a sentimental little bozo like myself get misty-eyed. If I had it my way they'd inject a couple more decibels into the ending because it's such a showstopper.Also, the game has a bunch of really cool other stuff.-Companion characters ahoy! So far I like all of them but one. Meredith you are too much of a drip and I have already pledged my heart and soul to Kaleigh. Even if her name is spelled like that. She's irish, okay? It's fine. This is fine. It's fine.-The way the game uses music and its artstyle are amazing. The first time I played I spent a while just hanging out in the Harbourtown cafe listening to the amazing vocal performances.-Just oodles and oodles of charm. I love that the healing item is a pencil you use to re-spool  your tape, I love the stupid pun names that some of the mons have, I like that you can just camp in an area where you're grinding or hunting for a bootleg (shiny, kinda), I like the fact that the "team rocket"-like in this game is actually just- well it's really good but I won't spoil it here, I like the way the vocals for the soundtrack come in when you fuse- it really feels like they added a bunch of small details that nobody would have even thought to ask for.It adds up to create the same wonder and exploration that I felt when I first played pokemon all those years ago. To paraphrase youtuber and cool-sounding guy Steak Bentley, "Less de-constructive and more re-constructive. Bringing back the magic, but a little more honest, because you're a grown-up now."In leiu of a rating, that's just my pitch for why you should play Cassette Beasts. If you feel let down by any of the larger mongames (pokemon, digimon, etc etc) or even if you love the genre and can feel how tight the constraints can feel on it, then you really owe it to yourself to give Cassette beasts a whirl. It is abundantly clear that stem to stern this game is built with love for its genre and a sincere desire to make a worthy successor to the ailing old throne of Mr. Pikachu himself. Fantastique.Edit: I finished the game, came back to do some more undisclosed edits, and give this game a 9/10. Yeah, hoss, get it in your steam library. Grab a copy for you and that one neice you don't really talk to but could use a fun, mostly wholesome game that takes the bad in the world seriously. Get it burned on a series of 14.35 discs and seal them in your wall so that it will survive the great gloaming. Get it tattooed on your firstborn child's head in a language they don't understand so one day a wise old shaman will caress his finger across the scalp of your now-adult progeny and catch a Springheel. Or just play it, that works too.But, one caveat.If you are my sister, don't buy it. Look I'm not good at christmas gifts okay

_childDocuments_.review: Cassette Beasts feels like a game made by true fans of the genre. Everything about this games is just so well done, if you’re a fan of Pokemon or creature collectors this is an absolute 10 out of 10 experience and a must play. Definitely a top contender of my personal contender for indie GOTY. Unlike the other games in the genre cassette beasts gets going really fast with minimal handholding, just the occasional text bubble of how mechanics and type matchups work as there are some very interesting typings here that shake up the formula. Combat is fast and never feels like a chore of endless grinding. Me and a friend having been playing through it side by side on the hardest difficulty for reference and it’s still not overly challenging for veterans of these games but I always appreciate it when games let you decide your own difficulty or just make the game brutal as I love a solid, rewarding experience. The only thing I wish was that the game made one of its unique mechanics, fusions, a bit more of a requirement on the hardest difficulty. But I’m pulling at strings here as that is nearly a nitpick if I must say one thing, and that never detracts from the experience. Exploration is fun, and fast as the developers implemented a ton of movement mechanics that make exploring the world feel incredibly satisfying. Being a game called Cassette Beats and probably by reading some of the other reviews you’ll come to learn that the soundtrack here is absolutely fantastic. Lots of great tracks at all the right moments make the experience so so much better. The tender vocals of the track that plays while in town really just bring such a sense of belonging and warmth, and if that’s not your cup of tea they give you the option to just play with the instrumental soundtrack. Trainer captains, this games equivalent of gym leaders, bring along more intense tracks with hard hitting guitar riffs that really amplify the moment. It’s all just done so well. Had another friend watching a stream in the discord who began singing the music as he also found it so enjoyable to listen to. If this game pops up on your steam recommendations you would be doing yourself a huge disservice by passing up on it. And I mean that wholeheartedly. I know a game like cassette beasts won’t be what every gamer is necessarily looking for and that’s okay. But for those looking for an absolute indie gem in a sea of games that either waste your time or are just utter hot garbage, this is the exact opposite. A true masterpiece of an experience and the team who worked on this should be regarded incredibly highly. I for one will be patiently awaiting a well deserved sequel and if you take the 30ish hours to get through this I’m sure you will be too. TLDR: Overwhelmingly positive reviews don’t do this same justice, if you even clicked on this title just do yourself the favor and add it to your cart. It’s easily worth so much more than the asking price.

_childDocuments_.review: ++TLDR: This is a fantastic monster taming game with fun exploration, an interesting story, and great combat mechanics.  However, there are areas for improvement with art, odd filler content, and some combat mechanics.+The game is open world, though some of this doesn't open up until you learn certain abilities.  This makes exploration quite interesting throughout the game.  And, by the end of the game, since the abilities that enhance your exploration allow things like double-jumping and gliding, moving around is an enjoyable breeze.+The game introduces mechanics to replace weakness and resistance, which is a breath of fresh air.  Rather, type-advantages cause temporary buffs and debuffs, which, when explained by the in-game tutorials are both hilarious and logical at the same time.+Combat is made more interesting by introducing a point system that allows different moves based on the available points.  Higher hitting attacks cost more points to use, so players need to ramp up and balance their turns instead of spamming heavy hitting attacks every turn.+The game introduces relationship strength to encourage players to pick combat partners and explore their storylines more extensively.  By the end of the game, I had unlocked several interesting combat partners to fight with.  SPOILER: +Puzzles exist in this game and sometimes offer a challenge.  This was greatly missed from games like Pokemon that oddly have removed those in the last several generations.+The story is quite interesting and has multiple, interesting twists.-Combat can be slow because of the points system the game introduces.  This means that some fights against lower level monsters can drag on and cost HPs desired for a boss fight.  By the end of the game, I was largely trying to avoid fights.-Some of the anime art for the characters seemed very amateur.  I would hope that if there's a sequel, more money is put into hiring a better artist that could channel a similar, but more professional vibe for the game.-While exploring, the perspectives sometimes change.  This is interesting when that reveals new, hidden, areas, but often just became frustrating having to change controls or watch the camera shift often just because I'm near the border of an area where the perspective shifts back and forth.-Some of the characters had random interactions to reveal they were gay.  Though, there really was no plot enhancement or story that this added and this never came up for more than 10-15 seconds.  Rather, this seems shoehorned into the game for no apparent reason other than "inclusivity."  I'd rather this be more fleshed-out if it's going to be in the game.  In this case, I just groaned.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a creature-capture RPG with  a great soundtrack, likable characters, and of course, a great lineup of cool monsters.Most characters carry cassette players. Wild monsters you encounter can be 'recorded' to cassettes, and characters physically transform by listening back to the cassettes.Battles are turn-based, and use an energy system for moves. More powerful moves need more energy. You get a little energy each turn.All monsters have a type. Some are elemental, like fire, water, wind, etc. Others are more modern, like plastic, glass, and metal types. Types have advantages over others, but it goes deeper than just "does more damage." When a water attack hits a fire type, it 'extingushes' it, giving the fire type a debuff on its own attack. But if a fire move hits a plant type, it causes a guaranteed burn status that does damage every turn. These are just the absolute basics, there are plenty more type interactions that cause various buffs, debuffs, or status effects.Possibly the most innovative feature of this game is the ability to temporarily fuse any two monsters into a gnarly new beast during battles. You also always have a swappable companion to accompany you on your adventure.I really like this game, and I highly recommend it. It runs great, looks great, and most importantly, it's fun. Also, 20 bucks is a steal for the amount of content you get.

_childDocuments_.review: i first heard of this game by watching alpharad gold play it, thought the artstyle was super appealing and immediately bought it after watching that video, something i have never done before after watching a let's play. being a fan of pokemon my whole life, i was really drawn to this game, moreso than any other monster collectors besides pokemon (and maybe yo-kai watch). i'll list what i think are some really strong parts of the game and some parts i think are a bit weak (while trying to spoil as little as possible). i played this game completely alone so i can't comment on the coop though.stuff i liked+ a lot of focus on human characters. i love the human characters in pokemon so this made me really happy to see.+ music is really good, none of the songs i actively dislike or got bored of. i couldn't find some of my favourites on youtube so i bought the ost just so i could go back to them any time i wanted+ as i said above, the artstyle appeals to me a lot, as well as the monster design. the fact that there are 14k+ animated sprites with just two full time developers is nuts (a vast majority of them do seem to have been procedurally generated but what can you do. it fooled me otherwise a couple times at least)+ the world feels massive, in a good way. in a similar way to how old pokemon games felt massive as a kid. new wirral feels as expansive as i thought unova and sinnoh were as a kid.+ the gameplay took me a bit of getting used to but i still really like it and there's tons of really cool saucy stuff you can pull off. sometimes i'd go into a fight underleveled but with a creative strategy and come out on top and it made me feel really proud for coming up with it, a feeling that i've only gotten from pokemon in the past.+ didn't mess with it too much since i don't like self inserting in rpgs but the character customizer gives like the perfect amount of options such that it doesn't feel too daunting. plus you can change anything at any time. ++++++++++++ the difficulty options are AWESOME. they're kind of tucked away but you should absolutely turn them up. scroll to the gameplay section of the settings tab. didn't feel the need to grind ever on the max setting and every battle was even. there is an order the game lays out certain tasks in, but on the max level scaling settings you can completely ignore it and it's so so so COOL.stuff i didn't really like (might be a bit nitpicky but i do think they're worth airing out)- the overworld puzzles have some janky physics which can be frustrating at times. sometimes i felt like i was supposed to use a moveable object as something to stand on top of but whenever i did the cube would convulse. multiple times during my playthrough movable cubes flipped over or sent me flying, which just became an annoyance whenever it happened. i'm sure these issues could absolutely be fixed in a patch, i hope this part of the review ages poorly.- my game crashed once on an older build, but given the fact that this happened to me only one time and the game has since received new patches, it is likely that they fixed whatever caused me to crash.- i found one of the partner's quests really frustrating, because you're locked out of using a core gameplay mechanic with them until pretty late into the game, especially . it's not the end of the world, it just means that using this specific partner is the hardest to use, so i'd suggest not using  unless it's to work through their quest.+ these issues do not retract from all the positive things to be said about the game, so i really hope this doesn't come across that way.overall for its price i think this game is a steal. every year or so i run into an indie game that knocks my socks off, and this is the most recent one to do so (it's also the first pokemon-like to do so too). i 100% recommend this game to anyone who likes pokemon or just any kind of jrpg. i'm writing this before i play the dlc so i'll write a review for that too when i'm done it. you *can* access the dlc any time after you buy it but i intentionally avoided it so i could just focus this review on the base game. i also tried to avoid being too specific about gameplay and characters and music because i think it's worth experiencing yourself, instead of having some person tell you about it. you can tell this game was made by people who get what makes pokemon work and what makes other jrpgs work, and put their own creative spin on it that also works.

_childDocuments_.review: So when it comes to creature collector games, I’ve only really focused on Pokemon and SMT/Persona. For some reason, I’ve convinced myself that any other creature collector game that aren’t these must be garbage somehow. I’m happy to report that I was completely wrong. This is definitely one of the best games I’ve played this year by far.It’s like Pokemon but you transform into the monster rather than summon it. The difference is that if your monster form goes down, your player character is exposed to attacks. If your character goes down, you’re done, even if you have more monsters in reserve. Another key difference is the fact that you can equip up to 8 or 10 attacks on a monster. That must seem like a lot to Pokemon players, but there are no “abilities”, instead you use those slots to equip passive abilities, thus, giving you greater control over the build of your monster. And yes, you can have multiple passives, unlike Pokemon’s one passive ability per monster. Then there's the battle gimmick, which is fusion. Two of your monsters can become one to unlock a new super attack, and combine move/passives pools into one huge monster with much higher stats. It's fun, and it's impressive what they've done to make all fusions look like the monsters they're fused from. The story is also more mature than your typical Pokemon story. The music is absolutely god-tier. Nothing else to say on this. I wish more games had soundtracks this incredible.Now the negatives, the post game, if you want all achievements, is a terrible horrific grind. You do randomly generated quests in order to get “fusion material” which you need a lot of to get the last achievement (around 450 or so, if I’m not mistaken). I think your most recent Pokemon games handled the post-game content much better. Sword/Shield’s Dynamax Adventures are tons of fun, Legend’s Arceus various post-game side quests, and even Scarlet/Violet’s meager post-game (I haven’t played the DLCs for this one yet…) far outshine the disgusting mindless grind this game has. Which is unfortunate as every other part of Cassette Beasts is better than most Pokemon games, in my opinion.I do hope I get to play a “Cassette Beasts 2” one day. This was far too fantastic to just end like this. There’s DLC to this game, but I haven’t played it. It’s not required for 100% achievement completion, and I heard that the new music in that DLC doesn’t have vocals, which is a huge deal-breaker for me.

_childDocuments_.review: Cool little monster collection game that can probably scratch your itch for a certain monster collecting franchise.The gist of the game is you run around an island, collecting monsters and moves, exploring and battling monsters and bosses. Exploration was engaging but not too rewarding - it's an open level with metroid-like blockers that require new movement tools, and you can find mini-puzzles that unlock chests. Quests have grid markers that point you in the general direction, guiding you through the intended path but are very open-ended.(Worth noting, you can go straight to the final boss but going through the story makes the final fight easier, a-la BOTW. Cool!)As you see more of the island and defeat bosses, the plot unfolds. The setting is interesting and had me engaged at the end, and is a whole lot better than every pokemon story, but it's also a slow burn. Companions are likable, but you don't get too many interactions with them. The overall tone of the game is hopeful, earnest and endearingly cringe, and had a real charm for me, but YMMV.The big draw of the game to me is how different mechanics wise it is to pokemon, and how easy it is to change your builds. Double battle is the default, which I really like. Type advantages provide buffs/debuffs instead of a damage multiplier, and type manipulation is common with moves and Bootlegs (type-specific shiny mon). Your level is independent from your monsters, and moves can be freely added and removed.All of this makes for a great teambuilding and battling experience. I loved making crazy builds that can win battles before it starts, max out AP in a single turn, or abuse type interactions for massive advantages. Unfortunately the early game is a bit of a slow burn, since you don't have access to all the tools and the combat system doesn't really open up. The fusion system is also gimmicky, kind of like the generational gimmicks pokemon has.In my opinion this is a worthwhile purchase at full price if you like monster collection games. This can take up days of your life if you're not careful.As a final note, the only reason I bought it is because someone called it "liberal pokemon". I can, in fact, confirm this game is exactly liberal pokemon.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the greatest take on a non-Pokémon Monster RPG I've ever played and it's not even close. To those who play that series but don't know what to expect from this, it's basically a double-battle focused RPG where you and a partner (who you also control) use monsters to fight wild monsters, other "trainers", and large boss fights.This game nails:-Its characterization and writing, which ranges from sad and relatable to hilarious and uplifting (and it's not afraid to talk about more adult themes)-Its gameplay, where it dips into a vast pool of Passive Equippable moves that you can stack on top of each other to produce tremendous and wild results-Its Type Chart, that blends pure advantages with status conditions and stat boosts to make Typing always feel worth its effort in learning-Its soundtrack, which is LOADED with strong combat music and great emotional gravitas (although the overworld themes are a little bland by comparison, I must admit)-Its world design, which heavily emphasizes PLATFORMING and puzzle solving, but none of it is difficult to learn and by catching new Beasts you get more abilities to traverse where you areSo if any of the above sounds remotely appealing, get this game. GET IT. You will not regret it at all.My only regret is this was gifted to me! I'd have bought it for myself had I had more money at the time... but I'm all in on any future paid DLC, because this game and its studio more than earned every penny they can get.10/10 would fuse again.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the best creature collectors. It's just solid in every category. Good stuff:Type advantage/disadvantage applies a debuff/buff instead of dealing more/less damage. I think this is more interesting than a damage multiplier, but I'm sure someone will have a problem with it. The buffs and debuffs are genuinely good too. You level up your character rather than monsters. This means when you record a new monster, it's already your level and you don't need to train it forever.Bad Stuff:The random chance to record monsters is the most glaring issue. I've spent dozens of tapes trying to record the same rare monster before finally getting it.Recovery items can trivialize combat. Enemies just don't use items, but you can. Debuff removal items can be used without using your turn, which sounds nice but essentially makes you immune to debuffs. Remember the only penalty for type advantage hits are a debuff, so now type advantage doesn't matter to you.Overall, the game does a great job of scratching that creature collector itch and trying new things, a few complaints aside.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a masterpiece. It's not as crunchy as Siralim, but it makes up for it with engaging puzzles, innovative gameplay, and a delightful story. The combat is fun, the difficulty is solid, and bootleg hunting is more addicting (and rewarding) than shiny hunting ever was. I cannot commend the devs enough for doing what Gamefreak and others have failed to do in the past years. The creators of Cassette Beasts put their entire heart and soul into this project, and it shows. Grab this game now, you won't regret it.

_childDocuments_.review: This really is a love letter to monster collection fans. The amount of QoL in Cassette Beasts compared to other games in the genre is frankly embarrassing for other publishers. Visuals: 8/10Sound: 9/10UI: 8/10Gameplay: 9/10Replayability: 10/10Your tapes (monsters) rank up to learn new moves and eventually remaster (evolve) into more powerful tapes. These moves are applied as stickers that you can freely peel and replace onto any compatible tape. There is a unique shiny system in this game known as bootlegs. Any monster can be found as a bootleg of any element. Every monster has effectively 14 different elements that you can find; the color changes to match the element as well. When you factor in fusions (any two tapes can fuse into a unique monster during battle) you end up with a staggering amount of possibilities. Also it’s open world with overworld monster sprites (including bootlegs), abilities, and unlockable fast travel.Do yourself a favor and pick up Cassette Beasts. I’ve played exclusively on Steam Deck and it is a fantastic experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic, fantastic, fantastic game!To compare this to Pokémon is to do Cassette Beasts a disservice. Pokémon feels to me as though it has lost its heart and soul. This game plays not like a Pokémon made for kids or to print money but a game made for all ages, and a game made out of love and passion. I'm so ashamed of myself for sleeping on this for so long. I bought it back when it came out and just never got around to playing it until now. Ironically enough, I kind of put it off a bit thinking it would be “yet another Pokémon clone.”I'll be transparent and say I haven't finished the game, but I'm on track to doing so. It runs well enough on Steam Deck and utilizes the Godot game engine. My playtime has been split between playing on my laptop and playing on my Steam Deck. I leave it set to 50 Hz on Steam Deck, and leave all other battery settings at their default values. Turn off half rate shading if you're using DeckyRecorder. HRS seems to cause some sort of flickering in footage. May cause epileptic episodes if you open footage without realizing you've left HRS on. Steam Deck does get frame drops, and they are noticeable, but due to the nature of the gameplay, they are not game-breaking. I did get some crashes, and I think my issue was limiting the wattage to 13 instead of leaving the limiter off. I have been unable to recreate the crashes after setting wattage back to default. I don’t have an OLED model Steam Deck to compare, but the fans ramp up quite a bit on the old 512 GB LCD model Steam Deck.Cassette Beasts is 100% what I would call a wholesome and cozy game. It's got some creepiness and some cuteness. It’s got a good amount of diversity. It’s got some heartfelt moments, and some good potential for character development. There’s been some really clever moments that made me go “Huh. That’s interesting,” as well. I think I still have quite a bit left to do, and I've been stumped a couple of times. The game could do with some more hints or giving more guidance on what you're supposed to do next at certain points. It just kind of started to slow down at one point, and I ended up wandering around until I stumbled into what I was supposed to do. This actually happened a couple of times during my play sessions.There’s some really good music in certain locations and boss battles of this game as well. I was in a cafe at one point and was suddenly hit with some music that took me aback for a moment. I wasn’t expecting that kind of vibe from this game going into it. As a music lover, I can’t help but love the record-themed stages. The first boss encounter had a really good song, as well. Not quite the kind of music I was expecting from this game, but definitely not disappointing by any stretch. I find the fusion and cassette/recording mechanics to be really interesting. They’re a good twist on the monster collector formula. Type matches and mismatches, abilities, buffs, and debuffs all feel really good to me. They’re fun to play around with, and they make sense in this game’s world. I really like the way the leveling system is implemented as well. I never felt like I was hindered by the beasts I wanted to use. Your beasts level up, evolve, and all that good stuff. However, your player character also levels up. That’s the interesting part. There’s a lot to play around with here, and a lot of interesting twists on the monster collecting genre. It’s really not “just another Pokémon clone.”To just describe it as “Pokémon but better” or something along those lines is to do Cassette Beasts dirty. It’s so much more than that. It’s a love letter to what made those classic Pokémon and Zelda games great. It wears its inspiration on its sleeve, and it does it in the best way possible.Pick this one up. Buy it on sale if you want, but I think it’s worth the full asking price.Edit: I beat the game.  I'm now playing the DLC. Cassette Beasts is definitely worth the asking price. So much so that I've gone back and purchased their previous game, Lenna's Inception, as well.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not really a fan of Pokémon clones (I've only played a few), but this one is great. I haven't got very far but from what I've seen this one is very unique. Lots of interesting designs for the monsters. They remind me of cryptids, some of them actually being based on real folklore (Flatwoods monster, for example). The fusion mechanic is fun, although I don't really use it outside of boss battles. The type matchups are a bit confusing at first but there are a lot of them and they all have unique mechanics. I wasn't a fan of the vocals at first, but once I heard the different tracks a few times I really started to enjoy them.The only real downside I have for Cassette Beasts is I'm not a fan of the 3D overworld mixed with 2D sprites. The camera turning for certain areas and the physics-based puzzles can get annoying at times, but that certainly doesn't hold back the massive amounts of charm this game has.So far this game is fantastic, I can't wait to play more.

_childDocuments_.review: 3.4.24 UPDATE: I would recommend adding the "List of Redeemable Codes (Past and Current)" guide by Sky to your favorites. Here the devs drop limited time codes that get you free bootlegs. When a new code is posted to the guide, you simply go to your mailbox in your room or the Cafe, put in the code and you get a free bootleg instantly and sometimes an additional item. The codes generally last a few weeks before they are deactivated. This is a nice feature because getting bootlegs is definitely a grind. And now you know what the mailbox is for! ORIGINAL REVIEW: I've had a lot of luck when trying out new genres the past couple of years.  Cassette Beasts was no exception.  This game constitutes my first JRPG and first Creature Capture game (nope, I've never played a Pokémon game). I must admit this game has been a ton of fun. The music is quite catchy and the main song is very peaceful. It has an "I ❤️ the 80s" retro theme with its pixelated graphics, limited voice acting and character wardrobe. None of which took away from the gaming experience in 2023. The gameplay is enjoyable with plenty to do on a large map... you can even play with a friend!  Most of the tasks are fairly straight forward, but if you want to 💯 the achievements you will have to grind to find at least one of every bootleg type, obtain a copy of every beast and obtain additional info on every beast (there are a lot of beasts, evolutions and fusions). You can adjust the difficulty to your preferences, but I found the default to be very enjoyable.The price is extraordinarily reasonable. At $19.99 you can feel good picking up this game at full price... on any sort of discount, it's a steal. In fact, the devs could have fairly priced it at $24.99- $29.99, but I do appreciate the lower price point. I haven't said anything about the story or gameplay. Both are interesting and engaging. Most of you are better gamers than I, so suffice it to say,  "you won't have much trouble naturally figuring out some of the less obvious elements as you progress through the game." ... battle strategy, chemistry, how/ where to find bootleg beasts, etc... and for the things that weren't intuitive to me (like how the heck do you beat a ghost!? And where on New Wirrell is that gold coin??), steam guides and youtube videos have been a big help.This one's a 10/10 for me. It's not a perfect game by any means, but the devs have given it a ton of love and it has been a real treat to play. I strongly recommend you give it a try.

_childDocuments_.review: I fell in love with pokemon so long ago, played every game, but slowly became jaded with newer entries. They didn't capture me quite the same- like somehow the "charm" they used to have lessened each time. The stories felt cheaper or more surface-level, new mons more lazily designed. I think for me, part of this was the transition from 2d to 3d. Cassette Beasts wasn't something I expected to love- my first thought was that it was probably another relatively uncreative ripoff with a new gimmick to make it stand out. Boy, was I wrong, and I'm so grateful to the friend who pushed me to try this.I have never written a review before, but I feel compelled to now. I am obsessed with this game. You can really feel the passion the devs have for it! It's innovative, it's original, and man, is it fun. The beasts are WAY more interesting than those in any other monster collecting game I have experienced, and at times, even more than Pokemon itself. The sprites are SO beautifully done and are EXACTLY what I would want out of a modern monster collector- they feel nostalgic but fresh all the same. The environments being 3d while the characters are pixelated/2d did throw me off a lot at first, as did the background music lyrics which were horribly distracting, BUT thankfully the devs added the ability to switch them off in the settings. With time, the mix of 2d/3d didn't really bother me at all, especially given everything else I love about this game. The inclusion of completely new element types (such as plastic, a personal favorite) and their unique interactions with one another made the battle gameplay feel much more energized. Being able to collect rare moves and switch them between beasts is also a huge plus, with different rarities carrying a variety of randomized boons such as +ignores walls or +% chance to activate at the beginning of battle. The "fusion" mechanic is really fun as well, and combines ANY- and I mean ANY of the beasts together in battle for one super-strong beast with its own unique sprite. Shinies, or "bootlegs" as they are called in CB, come with more than just a palette swap. They are more likely to learn rare moves, and can be ANY element- something that can completely switch the way you use it vs. its standard-type counterpart. If you are a shinydex collector, you have the opportunity to find FOURTEEN bootleg versions for every beast, EVEN legendaries! Finding bootlegs can be super addicting, and they spawn at a MUCH higher rate than pokemon- although it isn't so high that they lose their value. You can still go for hours without encountering one.I do wish the characters themselves felt more fleshed out. It would be nice to have character-specific activities (training with Eugene, writing poetry with Viola, drawing with Felix or playing fetch with Barkley, perhaps?) and more character-specific date events. I also think there is opportunity to add additional cast members, even if it's post-game. Frankie and Sunny come immediately to mind. My hope is that these things are expanded upon in the future. And I must say, the future of this game looks bright!Tl;dr- if you are jaded by monster collectors and are on the fence, absolutely go for it. I bet it'll exceed your every expectation like it did mine.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is amazing, if you're a fan of the monster taming genre, it is a must have. This game does a lot to set itself apart and define itself. The music themeing is done amazing, with amazing vocal tracks, music themed items, and even music references in the quest names. It all feels really cohesive. How it changes the typical battle formula is lots of fun, it does more than just being based around partner battles, but the type charts doing complex debuffs and buffs instead of just 2x damage and 0.5x damage is really refreshing. And the fusion mechanic is a gem. When I heard that there were 14,400 fusions done by an algorithm, I was worried some of them would not look great as they were meticulously crafted by hand like the original 120 monsters were. But the fusions look fantastic! And the fact that they are all animated is gob smacking. It makes for a really fun mechanic and shows that my worries were unwarranted. Exploring the world is well done, you unlock these different abilities based off different monsters and they let you interact with the environment in unique ways making for some fun exploration.Amazing battle mechanics, amazing music, amazing graphics, amazing world, what else can I saw, amazing game.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to preface this review by saying that I loved this game. I wouldn't play 90 hours of it and 100% it if I didn't really enjoy my time with this game. That being said, I'm an overly critical person and this game is certainly not perfect. So the good: It's essentially a 2-dev game with custom artwork for all the combinations of all 128   and it's really neat that they put such care into the art. The art itself is also unique and distinct, and the tailored lyrics to the situation your character is in is really interesting to see a game do. The type mixes are confusing, but they're at least scientific, and hey - I liked that it was grounded in more realistic chemical reactions than arguably a lot of creature collector games. Alongside all that, the story itself was engaging and compelling and I haven't enjoyed a creature collector game story in a good ten years. It was mysterious, and kept me wanting to learn more and play further. And it was never easy to guess what would happen. The archangel designs contrasting the game's aesthetic was also a really cool feature, and the bootleg versions of creature types and sticker TMs really gave you a lot of customisation for your teams, along with the fusion. This game was an enjoyable game. But it was also incredibly frustrating, and here's why. I'm gonna be brief: There's a lot of late-game crashes that increase the more you use your sprint/dash. The game cannot load in the world as quickly as you can sprint, and even the "loading in the rest of the world" jarring, out of place loading screens do nothing to help the loading issues. And if the game can't load it in, it either completely stops your character with an invisible wall or hard-crashes your game. The character relationships are ok but ultimately disappointing - The characters are kind of boring, get better as you get to know them but even then, they're pretty mid, and spoilers: but none of the relationships are meaningful nor ultimately matter because you - and the characters themselves - leave it all behind, even with a romantic relationship. Which is weird, because you get the excuse "I can't go there" but then the dog can, so why can't anybody else? Another complaint is that the game  favours Kayleigh, and you lose out on a lot of early game lore, dialogue and flavour-text about your situation and even game mechanics if you ditch Kayleigh and go with Eugene or someone. Which is nuts, because the game is barely voice acted, so it wouldn't have taken them much to adjust early scenes for other companions. So the whole relationship/romance system is there, but ultimately feels hollow. Speaking of hollow, the stickers/TMs and bootlegs somewhat trivialise the gameplay. It ended up being very min-max, with the "strat" being Glitter Kephri with Headshot and Random Starter, or a normal Kephri with "type-change" support that trivialises the types. I enjoyed the fact the game gave you that level of customisation because it gave me the freedom to choose beasts based on aesthetic choices, but kind of killed the incentive of trying out different beasts, because why would I bother when I could just change the sticker? The end grind is also pretty insulting. I finished the main story in 50 hours, and only realised there was "more" after seeing the achievements. The "more" is a handful of quests hidden behind fetch&carry "townboard" quests that have you running across the map (that loads in really slowly!) doing busy work in what is essentially radiant quest padding between levels. I had very much checked out of the experience by the end of the grind, even with the ritual candle "exploit" to speed up the process. It felt like a really lazy way to create extra content when it started really strong with unique quests, especially as this grind was only accessible at the very end. If you'd let me do these missions throughout the entire game? It wouldn't have felt half as terrible. But I found myself struggling to boot up the game for such a grind, which sucked, because it was so strong before that and the cracks started to appear.Anyway. It's not a bad game. It has flaws, but I enjoyed my time with it, and it's definitely worth the price, and an incredible job for a two-person team. I'll keep an eye on their future games for sure, and I don't regret my time with this game - but I'm content to uninstall this and never touch it again.

_childDocuments_.review: With the review scores being the way there are, I am wondering if I ended up with the wrong version of the game. It had so many blatant issues that I am more than a little surprised so few people would mention them here. So, having played through the entirety of it with a friend, I may as well try myself.To at least start off on a positive note, the game does look and sound nice. The artwork and designs, as well as the music in the game, are pretty good. It did give a good first impression, but that is about everything the game really does well. Everything else feels like someone's first attempt at designing gameplay.The combat tries to offer some complexity with various type interactions that cause different buffs, debuffs, and other effects when certain typed attacks are used against others. This sounds neat in theory, but was so irrelevant for the entirety of the game that it may as well not have been there. The observant player quickly notices that a high speed and damage stat are all that really matters, at least early on. It's easy to one shot at least one enemy in a given fight before they get a turn in, far more effectively minimizing damage than any amount of defense or utility ever could.Once you get into the late game and have more stickers at your disposal (The game's version of monster abilities that you can swap between monsters), the game completely falls apart. It is trivial to equip your monsters with combinations of stickers that, in our playthrough, one-shot almost every single fight (Including bosses) before enemies even got a turn in. So the game either breaks the moment you experiment with it, or you restrain yourself and stick to uninteractive loadouts all the way through, there is, unfortunately, no fun way to go about it.Even when you are obliterating your foes, the game is still adamant on playing out every single action in order. Did you proc five random attacks and the single enemy died after the first? The game has to let you know the other four ones all failed, in order. Attacks with type advantage need to inform you what debuffs you put on the enemy even though they are already dead. Multi-hit attacks play out all of their attacks every single time as they whittle away at corpses. There is no way to speed up combat or skip animations.Fusions were a neat idea in theory but became obsolete the moment you get them, not to mention that they effectively delete multiplayer for the duration. Hopefully, your friend doesn't mind sitting out if you ever plan on using them. Either way, they effectively combine the stats of the fused creatures, as well as their ap. In execution, this is pointless because you are also down to one action per round, making anything but spamming high ap attacks a waste of your turn. Even then, the strongest attacks are ones that trigger when creatures are swapped in, meaning you are far better off even damage wise to just never fuse and rely on your passives.The UI in this game is an absolute atrocity. You have 14 different elements attacks can have, and can then roughly categorize abilities into melee attacks, ranged attacks, passives and utility. Guess what options you have to sort them? Alphabetically. That's it. Have fun scrolling through your list of stickers from memory as you flip through a list that can only display ten at a time.Swapping out party members means they have to take the creature equipped to them with them. Had a new party member force your current one back into town during a story quest? Have fun running back and swapping around monsters for a few minutes in order to get back the monsters you were currently planning on using. Someone seems to have understood the general concept of puzzles but didn't actually bother trying with the execution. There are some overworld puzzles that were interesting, requiring you to pay attention to the environment and figure out a solution off of those hints by yourself. Most of the main game puzzles, however, are obvious the moment you look at them, and simply require you to go through the motions for the bland execution, making you wonder why they are even there in the first place.This is exacerbated by the fact almost all chests in this game contain garbage. You get good stickers from shops/leveling up bootlegs (The game's version of shiny monsters) and good materials from overworld rogue fusions, quests, and bosses. As far as I remember, the contents of every single chest in this game have been pointless materials you would also drop from every random encounter ever.The game has made the curious decision of attempting to go for a character relationship driven narrative while also rendering you a silent protagonist. You have occasional response prompts that are usually something along the lines of "Yes" and "Yes but in yellow". No dialogue options in this game matter, except for possibly romance confessions when reaching maximum relationship status with a given character. Naturally, they are head over heels for you after expositing their life story and struggles at you, while you blankly stared back like the soulless automaton that you are. The meta-commentary we haven't paid much attention to, but it is more than a little on the nose with one boss being the incarnation of capitalism, while one of the enemy factions is a group of landlords that are literally just vampires. This was roughly on the same level as the quest to stop an evil cult. You don't really know why they are evil, they aren't actually doing anything in the game that is shown to you, or even mentioned to any significant degree, but it's a cult, what else are they going to be?This game certainly felt like wasted potential. The gameplay didn't really change after five or so hours in, but we wanted to push through to the end to see if combat maybe gets more varied somehow. As far as we could tell, none of the bosses have any mechanics that require you to interact with them, safe for a singular puppeteer that has effigies of your team on his side, requiring you to pay attention to where you place your attacks, lest you suffer recoil. Had the game tried to do more things like this while keeping some semblance of ability balance, perhaps it could have been something.

_childDocuments_.review: (The following review is based on the 1.5.0 version of Cassette Beasts, but not taking DLC into account. These feelings are still accurate as of me writing this review, but praises and criticisms I have exclusively with the DLC are not included here.)I had heard quite a few good things going into Cassette Beasts, and the game's launch trailer really grabbed my attention, but I was not at all prepared for how the game would blow every single one of my expectations out of the water. Cassette Beasts manages to pay homage to its inspirations while crafting its own special experience from that foundation. As a longtime Pokémon fan, I pretty quickly picked up on the gameplay, but was pleasantly surprised at the many individual components that make the game unique. Instead of a MP or PP system, the game uses Action Points that you accrue over the course of a battle that can be spent on moves of varying amounts of power- it's more akin to something like Boost Points in Octopath Traveler. This makes it so that both weak moves and strong moves have their place in battle, which I really like! The game primarily focuses on 2v2 combat, and the synergy you build with the various partner characters you join up with over the course of the story translates very well into the gameplay, especially through the headlining "fusion" mechanic that spices up the combat significantly─ you'll have much greater firepower, but can't take as many actions per turn, which is a fun tradeoff. Moves and passives are contextualized as "stickers" that can be freely attached and detached from monster tapes at will, making experimentation and strategization easily some of the most streamlined I've seen from an RPG. My only minor point of criticism is that by endgame the sticker list is a bit of a pain to sort through to find what you want, but the filter tools make this a little less frustrating at least. As a lover of turn-based combat, I was thoroughly impressed.The characters and story felt very fresh and engaging, especially for an RPG of this subgenre. I'll keep my thoughts here as general as I can to not spoil things. Each of their backstories and personalities added something to the party, and the optional romance mechanic managed to enhance the experience without taking anything away for those who aren't interested (except an achievement unfortunately, but that's not too bad). As a nonbinary person, I felt very at home with the options included for character creation, and seeing LGBTQ+ representation in the game itself was really awesome to see. Everything regarding this feels really natural and well-written, which I love. The Archangels and what they each ultimately represent slowly build an interesting narrative over the course of the game, while each being memorable in their own right, utilizing various art styles that feel foreign to everything else in the game's world. There's a nice balance of lightheartedness and more serious subject matters tackled here, and overall does a good job of keeping a positive outlook throughout without needing to talk down to its players when the going gets rough. The story pacing felt very good, which can be hard to pull off in an open-world experience where things aren't always done in the same order, so I appreciate what the devs and writers were able to accomplish here.The visuals really land in this game in every aspect, from the chibi overworld, to the adorable talk sprites, to the unsettling-yet-badass Archangels, and of course, the fantastic animated monster sprites. To the untrained eye the inspiration is obvious, but it goes a lot further with it than its inspirations by every monster having animations for dealing and taking damage, as well as many of the "asleep" animations being a lot more visually interesting than just having closed eyes. Oh, and reminder that just about all of this applies to the 19,000+ fusions too. Some procedural generation was obviously needed to reach that monolithic number, but amidst the recent controversies around AI art, it's really refreshing to see this pulled off with 100% organically drawn and animated components. Oh, and of course, the monster designs themselves are fantastic. There's a very lovable quirky feel to each one, while having a flavor entirely of their own that you can't easily find elsewhere. The more mature subject matter allows for some really fun names and designs that wouldn't fly in more family-friendly monster-collecting RPGs without losing any of the aforementioned charm at all─ shoutout to Skelevangelist and Miasmodeus, among others.The music is absolutely stellar. The vocals kicking in during battle themes when a fusion happens appeals very heavily to me as an enjoyer of dynamic music in video games. There's some nice motif reusage present, as well as a good amount of lyrics with multiple meanings that were fun to experience. Same Old Story and Arrow of Time will be on my VGM playlist for a long time yet to come.I could go on for ages about all the other things I love about this game, and I'm sure there's some things I'll kick myself for not mentioning here later, but honestly the best thing about Cassette Beasts is the gestalt of the game experience rather than any of its individual aspects. It's not very often I see a game so well-balanced in its strengths, and whether you're a casual Pokémon fan, a monster-collector RPG fanatic, or just want a fun turn-based experience in general, you can't go wrong with Cassette Beasts.

_childDocuments_.review: I've played every Pokemon game, and every creature collection game I can get my hands on. I don't think any of them can top Cassette Beasts, in any way. The gameplay is amazing. Type Advantages in battle aren't just effective/resisted. There's a full chart of Chemical Reactions between types that inflict status effects throughout your battle. The games "Shinies" are called "Bootlegs" and they change creature typing, color palette, and moves they learn as they level up. It's addictive.The story is captivating. Without spoilers, I can just say it's got the capacity to be silly one second, and then have you sitting there in shock and awe over some perspective it's thrown at you. Each of the companion characters has their own quest and storyline, interactions between eachother, and most of them are romanceable.The music is INSANE. It's a solid instrumental track on its own, but the first time I went into the Cafe, which acts as home base, the vocal track had me stop and go "Have I had vocals as a games background music before?" but it gets even more rich and soul-filled. Early in the story you discover that you and your partner character have a special mode you can enter, and when you do, the musical instrumental in whatever battle you're in gains a vocal track. It's a small detail, but it's my favorite part of this game. 11/10

_childDocuments_.review: A phenomenal RPG! If you're looking for a creature collecting game on PC, this is probably one of the best and most refreshing takes on the genre. The combat has so much depth, thanks to a rich assortment of mechanics and an incredible diverse pool of interesting moves. The combat requires a lot more thought than simply selecting the strongest move with a type advantage like you'd typically get in other games, and because of this it can get decently challengin, especially during boss fights. In Cassette Beasts YOU transform into the monster. This means that any buffs & debuffs that get applied to you during combat stick around when you switch forms (upon being defeated or choosing to mid-fight). The combat also runs on a stamina system, where every move requires a different amount of stamina. There are 14 elements in this game, and unlike other games, they don't simply do the whole "X element is super effective/weak against Y element." They've chosen to implement an elemental interaction system. A few examples of this: when an ice-monster gets hit by a fire attack, it turns into a water-type. When a Water attack hits a fire-Monster, it debuffs it's attack stats for 3-turns. When Plastic attacks hit a fire-monster, it increases the monster's evasion.All of these interactions are given an explanation in game when you first encounter them. There is a good logical reason as to why they interact, making them easier to remember and understand. Because the game allows you to attack yourself and teammates, you can actually use this system to buff each other, too! Because you transform into the monsters, you don't have to worry about levelling up newly acquired forms, as it is your character that gains levels. The base stats of the character are combined with the transformation's stats. Though if you keep using a form it will rank up, acquiring stars on the stat screen. Each star gives you a new move, and when you acquire 5 stars you can "remix" the transformation (or in other words, evolve it) into a stronger form with higher stats, more stamina, and more attack slots. Though you can always obtain the remixed form through wild encounters as you progress.What's interesting is that the moves you acquire take shape in the form of stickers, which can then be removed and put into your inventory to be used on another compatible creature form. Basically you are rewarded for using other transformations, even if you don't plan on committing to them, and you can use these stickers to power up newly acquired transformations with fewer moves, or strengthen older transformations. Another neat feature is that many moves change elements to match the transformation, while others have a fixed element. Some stickers are actually passive abilities rather than attacks. If you're lucky, you can obtain stickers that have rarities like "uncommon" attached to them, which grants them passive buffs, like higher crit chances, healing a % of HP when used, etc. All of this is to say that the games combat is insanely well done. That's not even scratching everything else, like the incredible soundtrack, the beautiful pixel graphics, the fun puzzle solving, world traversal, and a solid sense of progression. While I haven't finished the campaign at the time of writing this review, the game's mysterious setting and story have piqued my interest, it seems very promising. This game has an awesome vibe to it that I can't find in any other creature collecting games, and I can't recommend it enough. Cassette Beasts costs under $20.. that's an insanely good deal for a BASE price. Personally bought the collectors edition, as  the devs deserve it, and I really wanted to get the soundtrack with it, as it was the song "Same Old Story" from the trailer that hooked me into following the game initially. Do yourselves a favour and get this game!

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who grew up playing Pokemon, this game is an absolute joy to play. I have a real soft spot for indie games, and this is no exception. The passion for making a great monster catcher game is evident.The battles were challenging at times, especially if I stumbled into an area that easily countered my two main beasts I ran for a while. It pushed me to swap out and try other combinations and led to some really neat combos! The story was cute and I enjoyed playing through it. The main story took around 24 or so hours for me to complete at a leisurely pace. There is also a number of post-game/late-game challenges you can complete that I'm sure will keep me busy for a number of hours more.While I don't think I'll push for 100%, as I don't want to grind that hard for getting a bootleg (like a shiny) of every type, I definitely am going to shoot for a completed bestiary! Also, the move bad joke is one of my favorites and always gives me a chuckle!So, if you want at least 20 hours of enjoyable gameplay, I can honestly recommend picking it up at its current full price as it is worth every penny!

_childDocuments_.review: I was looked forward to this game back when i first saw its trailer- and i had no regrets of it. Is it groundbreaking? No, but it certainly does quite a few different things to set it apart from other creature collecting games. One of the biggest being how type advantages do NOT dish out extra damage, they interact/change things. One example being how fire type attacks against a poison types cause the burn status effect, or hitting a plastic type with a fire type move turns it into a poison type. It forces you to be strategic and plan out how you use the creatures you capture on tape.Oh yeah, you turn into the monsters you capture.Anyways, onto the rest of the review. Otherwise this will get much longer than it should.Story/lore?Good for what it is and certainly had my interest. Leaves me wanting more in a good way. And i'm not afraid to admit i shed a tear toward the end after everything i did. That is all i can really say without spoiling anything.Characters?Different and none annoying- especially the companions you can get/choose from. They reach have a certain leaning toward certain stats, encouraging you to use certain monsters with them, but they do have a certain monster they like and get a 10% stat bonus from using that line. Showing they have a preference based on their character.Gameplay?This is one of those games where over leveling only does so much. It helps, but not as much as having a good build to counter the foe- especially when facing the bosses of the game- all of whom fight in a completely different manner. I will not spoil how they fight, as i found it very tense and satisfying to find out how each battle and plan accordingly. If you do not like overleveling, you can change the difficulty anytime on the settings. because they do scale up based on difficulty settings... Scarlet and Violet- take notes!Soundtrack?Love it. I love the vocal and non vocal versions of them. While i disagree that the vocal versions are somehow distracting, there is an option to turn off the vocals so you only get the music. Up to you.Replayability?After clearing story mode the first time, you unlock a custom mode where you can go full on nuzlocke mode, randomizing the monsters, typing- even the moves they learn. There is also a local coop, but i am not sure how that plays out. But it is there at least.Are there flaws?Some people have complained about crashes and bugs, but the only time anything like that happened to me was when i fell through the map- but that hardly set me back as i was put right where i was before that happened, so no harm done. I personally didn't have any issue with the game otherwise, but that might be the result of me being pretty casual. Some of the achievements do appear a bit... grindy, for the more dedicated sort.Verdict?If you really love creature collecting games in general or even an rpg where you can formulate your own strategy and ways of battling- i give this game a big thumbs up. Certainly feels like it has more love and effort put in than the last few pokemon games as of late- especially on release.
