_childDocuments_.review: I don't often leave reviews (even though I should), but I feel this is one of the times I would be mad at myself for not leaving one. This review is SPOILER FREETL;DRGameplay loop/core mechanics: 9.5/10UI design: 9/10Controls/settings: 7/10Environment design: 9/10Music/sound design: 9/10Creature design: 10/10Partner deisgn: 8/10Character customization: 8/10Final score: 9.5/10Long Version:Gameplay: the gameplay is fun, though I am biased as a big pokemon fan. That said, this isn't just a pokemon clone. It more than feels like its own game in the same genre rather than a re-skinned pokemon game due in part to the evolutions but also the characters you travel with. Objectively I couldn't give it a 10 due to the tedium I know some people will find if they aren't into the completionism like I am (which is also a problem people have with pokemon to be fair), but personally I love it so subjectively I would. The only complaint I personally have with the game is the difficulty scaling. Its open world so if you go too far forward that's on you but some of the special monsters in the base area are unreasonably strong. There were a few times I nearly lost to a special in area 1 but blew a special in area 3 out of the water by comparison even with type advantages and solid strategies. UI design: the various UIs are non-intrusive and generally easy to navigate. You can get to any of the menus from either a shortcut or the default menu button, so one or two inputs. The layouts are for the most part intuitive with the exception of the settings menu which requires you to press the FN button plus the arrow keys to swap pages. The battle interface is easy to read and understand, and turn indicators are more subtle but for the most part effective. The selection menu in battle is very clever but also clearly labeled to avoid any confusion which is nice. There's no flee prompt, and while it would be nice not having one isn't really too big a deal in my personal opinion.Controls/settings: it's a pretty standard control scheme (WASD to move, space to jump, shift to dash), and it can be customized. The only weird choice is the "page up" "page down" option, because I have to hold the FN key in order to use those keys rather than just the arrow keys. And from what I can tell you can't assign the regular arrow keys. The customization is a little confusing as it's the only place that requires you to use the mouse which isn't intuitive when everything else can be done keyboard only. But when you figure it out it's not really a hassle. I can't remember off the top of my head if it has controller support, but if it doesn't that would be the other thing I'd dock points for. Controller support is a big thing for me because it allows people with disabilities to have a better experience with the game.Environment design: in terms of visuals, I really love the aesthetic. It's cute but not overdone. The environment doesn't distract from the characters in it too much, things that are interactive are not made so painfully obvious they distract you but also don't entirely blend in with static environment pieces either, and for the most part the sprites align everywhere they should. The physics can be a little weird but all things considered it's very smooth. The amount of the world that gets loaded doesn't lag anything on my computer and having only 1 loading boarder in the whole overworld makes it far less intrusive which is a big plus in an open world game. The loading screen itself only takes a few seconds at most, so it doesn't really throw off the flow of exploration. The only difficulty I had was one that just comes with the design by default. Navigating a 2D sprite on a 3D plane can make platforming a bit confusing but as you play your understanding of exactly "where" you sit in the world gets better, allowing you to make more precision maneuvers. The map itself is big enough to be initially confusing (in the way that encourages exploration), but small enough to be learned and navigated which is a different kind of rewarding.Music/sound design: It's just good. Plain and simple. The individual themes of each area are unique but all follow a more relaxed overall theme. The choice to include lyrics is apparently a controversial one but I quite enjoy it, and they only appear indoors. It does distract from the reading at first, but after you hear it a few times it fades into the background almost as well as plain instrumental music. Other times the lyrics are a very nice surprise. Voice acting isn't AAA grade which is expected but as far as indie games go its one of the more smooth implementations, and it's quite light-hearted which fits the theme of the game very well. Personally I think the voice acting here feels much more fitting to the game's atmosphere than the more "big industry standard" style of voice acting. The dialog is not fully voiced but the vocal interjections generally do a good job conveying the tone of whatever text is on screen. The battle cries of NPCs are a little funny. I'm not sure if they're randomized or if maybe I just had a bug happen but a character that was very clearly supposed to be a male figure (he was a reference to a real person) made a much higher pitch sound when he saw me.Creature design: in terms of aesthetics I love the creatures. It gives me the same excitement I had when I was a kid playing the pokemon games for the first time. They're full of clever references and cheeky nods to so many different things I had fun trying to guess them all, Each new monster is unique and interesting in its own right, and makes me wonder what it might become, if anything. And the main mechanics give you so many forms to discover, meaning you'll really have to be doing your due diligence if you want to see all of them. And speaking of; mechanics wise, I'm actually quite impressed. This is where it differs from pokemon the most in my opinion. Because of the way the move system works you really can turn just about any of your creatures into a powerhouse who does not stop to ask for directions. They won't be invincible, and no one strategy will work for all occasions, but you can very reliably make a team of just your favorite monsters and you can get to most places and win most fights just fine. They're all versatile and balanced enough to hold their own if you take the time to build them up. Even unevolved forms can bring you pretty far into the main game without needing an absurd amount of knowledge about stats and mechanics.see comments for part 2
_childDocuments_.name: Cassette Beasts

_childDocuments_.review: - Very interesting combat system with unique elemental reactions.- Fusion feels VERY AWESOME to do. Every combination of monsters leads to a unique fusion result. - Exploration with Pokemon HM-styled moves are taken to another level with the abilities being used in creative puzzles. - Very cute mix of 2D and 3D. - Game has a very good feel of atmosphere, whether it be relaxing or spooky.- Simple story line and subplot that feel a bit rushed at time but still do enough to be charming. - Very flexible monster customization system.- Tons of optional and post-game content. - Phenomenal soundtrack. The vocals even kick in when you fuse in battle!- Rewards you for paying attention. Quest markers don't tell you everything and it's a joy trying to figure out the puzzles and riddles on your own.- Boss fights aren't too hard, but have gimmicks to keep them interesting and are very visually intimidating and memorable.I'll be honest as someone going through a rough time i've teared up multiple times at how good this game is. If you enjoy Pokemon, Shin Megami Tensei, Persona or you're looking for an adventure in general, Cassette Beasts should be the next station you make a stop at.

_childDocuments_.review: I cannot recommend this game enough. From the soundtrack and artwork, to its battle system and abilities, this game exceeds a rating of 10/10. I bought this game on a whim after seeing someone play it for a bit and I don't regret it, not at all. This game is an absolute joy to play.First of all: the soundtrack. The game really lives up to its name and theme by having some of the catchiest songs as its soundtrack. I even added them to my playlist and listen to them regularly. I don't think it's possible to play through the game without singing along to a song at least one.I loveeee the art direction in this game as well. Not gonna lie, the art style of the game is what enticed me to get it in the first place. It blends multiple different styles; pixel and 3D in the overworld, Illustrations for the characters in the game, and a unique art style and design for every boss battle, which pushes the unsettling feeling of the encounter even further. I have goosebumps every time I see a new boss. The boss battles really are one of my favourite parts of the game, especially since the best song in the soundtrack plays during said battles. And also, did you know that every fusion in the game, which can happen between any two beasts from a roster of 100+, is unique? That's just crazy. The battle system is super fun as well. Every beast element type interacts differently from one another, not in the way it's usually portrayed (ie: strength vs weakness) and instead focuses on status effects brought upon by those interactions. The movesets of the beasts are highly customizable as well, enabling interesting builds, gimmicky moves, and personalized combat. The levelling system is a unique one. Only the characters level up while beasts gather stars to evolve into more powerful forms, which I find beats the grindiness of most monster-collector games. Although there are a few annoyances in the game (like the physics of some puzzles), I still think that this game is one that can't be missed because there really isn't anything to dislike about it. It's just really fun. Just buy the damn game. You won't regret it
_childDocuments_.name: Cassette Beasts

_childDocuments_.review: Before I go over the game I'd just like to say this: I never played any monster tamer before, pokémon included. This is my first entry into the genre. I do know a few bits and bobs here and there, but I don't have any actual first hand experience of any other monster tamer. Take of that what you will when reading this review.I did not expect Cassette Beasts to be as good as it is; the gameplay is (for the most part) fun, innovative, and easy to understand, it has a great artstyle, and an AMAZING soundtrack. It is overall a VERY good game. If a non-pokémon player like me likes it, I'm sure anyone who DOES play other monster taming games will love Cassette Beasts. Easily an 8/10 for me, my 2nd favourite game of all time (so far).Overall, the gameplay is very good at the start, but after you beat the main game and get to the post-game content (yes, there is post-game content) it starts to lose a bit of it's magic. As for specifics, I'll put them in bullet points here:That's all I'm gonna say; there is still a lot to the game, but I'd rather not spoil too much.The story is pretty fun. Each character/companion has their own quest with their own storylines. The characters themsleves aren't one-note; they feel like real people, and are fun to listen and talk to. The ending is pretty underwhelming, but I suppose it's all about the journey, not the destination. Again, won't spoil too much, but rest assured that it's a good story that might even get a tear or two out from you.It's cute and very pleasant to look at, ranging from the character portraits to the pixel art. The team have done a phenomenal job on these.The beast designs are both unique and random, ranging from a sad water tap to a cat with a flat screen for a head. If you like weird and fun designs, you'll like this game.The soundtrack consists of 80's/90's synths and rock. Some of the tracks even include vocals, which slap REALLY hard and still give me goosebumps everytime I hear them. Think Persona 5; just instead of jazz it's electric guitars and synths. It's really good.The game does have options for same-sex romance, along with the option for your character to have they/them pronouns. I'm indifferent on this, but maybe you might love/hate it. I'm not the one to really judge either way.The community is small but welcoming. The people in the discord server are a great bunch of lads and are really supportive. The developers even also talk often in there. As far I see there is no toxicity at all.That's all I got to say; great game, I highly recommend it if you like fun, innovative gameplay, or even for the artsyle/music alone.

_childDocuments_.review: After a few hours in New Wirral, however, I think Pokémon fans, whether they’re like me and still playing the games or lapsed fans of days long gone, are going to love Cassette Beasts. _childDocuments_.review: Cassette Beasts is a wonderful game that does a great job of capturing the feeling and aesthetic of Gen IV Pokémon, with a battle system that is focused on taking the basic concepts of combat in Pokémon and expanding them in intriguing, unexpected ways. Tied together with a light story that essentially functions as a framework in which the game operates rather than being the driving force, this game is both cozy and challenging, simple and thought-provoking, and a great time from start to finish.It really feels to me like the developers have a great deal of appreciation for what makes Pokémon work so well - one of the things that really annoys me about some romhacks and fangames is the sense that the developers of those always think they can do things a lot better than Game Freak, whereas with Cassette Beasts, it feels like it simply takes inspiration from the basic framework of combat and goes in a fresh, interesting direction. The core of battle is type interactions, which are a lot more varied and diverse than in Pokémon, relying on basic logic for you to ascertain how elements will interact with each other. I was discovering new interactions as late as the final part of the main mission, and I'm still not completely sure I've seen it all.Party management emphasizes experimentation - monsters don't have their own individual levels, instead your player character levels up directly, giving every monster a common base power upon which you can build, and making all of them at least a little bit usable in battle from the moment you acquire them. In place of levels, monsters have a separate leveling system that grants more move slots and default moves every time they level up, though movesets are completely customizable at will via the use of HM-like move stickers that are infinitely reusable. It all just feels very thoughtfully considered, more about creating a satisfying environment for player experimentation than, I don't know, being difficult for difficulty's sake.The story is sparse, and the somewhat non-linear mission system can sometimes leave you feeling a little directionless, but all it takes to get on the right track is to just open the mission list, pick a mission, and start pursuing it. Eventually, you'll narrow the list down to just the core path, and doing the other missions as much as possible first will allow you to properly scale up to match the increasing difficulty of the main mission. The art style is very, very charming, using sprites for characters and 3D models for the environment - very Gen IV Pokémon, as I said before. There's an unsettling aspect to some elements, too, hinting at a darkness at the center of the world you're thrown into, and the variance in art style for the characters related to that core mission is one of my favorite things about the game.This is a game where it feels like every element comes together extremely well, in the service of ensuring the player enjoys every aspect of it as much as possible. It's not perfect - fusion feels like little more than a gimmick, there's an ambiguity to some missions that makes it hard to figure out what exactly to do at the mission marker, you can inadvertently sequence break and get rolled pretty easily even with your partner party member warning you when you're underleveled for an area - but it does a lot of things well, very well, in fact, and it's a game I had a blast with from beginning to end. Worth it at any price.

_childDocuments_.review: Monster-designs are super creative with a lot of variety.World/Dialogue/Story is at least good enough. Didnt blow me away, but wasnt bad either.Music is awesome, especially the different battle themes always pump me up! Inside buildings there is even singing. Which is nice, if i wouldnt have to read A LOT of dialogue at the same time. Its distracting, but strangely fits very well in any other case. If it really annoys you, you can turn vocals off in the options.You can take 1 partner with you, you can take 6 different monster forms with you, each monster has around 8 different attack/skill slots, there are many different elements, buffs, debuffs, attacks, skills and you can temporarily fuse 2 monsters to combine all of those into one powerful monster. There are seemingly endless possibilities to form your own strategies!For example, hitting my wind-monster with a weak fire attack creates a wall that blocks ANY attack 3 times, which can be stacked up to 15 times. _childDocuments_.review: A very enjoyable creature collector with an amazing soundtrack and awesome gameplay elements.I don't think it's a hot take at this point that the more recent Pokemon games have been going downhill... riding on a quadrupedal bike-monster with stiff controls to unlock a gym battle that they'll sweep with one move. This has sent me on a bit of an alternative creature collector quest, and I found Cassette Beasts. Or, more accurately, my friends found it and recommended it to me.Like other creature collectors, you wander around the world catching new creatures and building your team, leveling up and getting stronger as you go along. Unlike Pokemon though, this game does a lot of things to greatly enhance the strategy of play. First, it uses an AP system instead of PP. You gain 2 AP every turn and can store up to 5-10 depending on what creature you have deployed. Moves will use this AP, with stronger moves costing more. This not only prevents you from needing to run back to the healing center after every battle, but it also adds some strategy to the combat; do you use a weaker move now, or save up for a stronger one a turn or two from now? With moves that steal AP or alter the rate at which you gain it, your strategy can change mid-battle too.The way the game handles type matchups is way better too. Certain elemental combinations generate special effects rather than just doing more damage. For example, hitting a fire type with a water attack will "extinguish" them, lowering their attack stats. Hitting an ice type with a fire move will "melt" them, changing them into a water type temporarily. Hitting a water type with an electric move will "conduct" them, causing them to take additional damage whenever any electric type move is used for a few turns. These elemental reactions do a lot to spice up combat strategies, and you may find yourself carrying around some off-type moves just to use for elemental reactions.Speaking of moves, this game manages to one-up Pokemon there too. You can have up to 8 moves equipped depending on the strength of the monster. These moves are called "stickers" and they can be removed and swapped out to compatible monsters any time you're not in combat. There are also uncommon and rare versions of moves that have additional random effects added to them, like 15% extra damage, or a 22% chance to gain a free wall. There are also passive stickers and stickers that trigger automatically at the start of fights, allowing you to customize your monster loadouts beyond which four attacking/setup moves you'll pick.The buff/debuff system is also fairly unique. Attack and defense buffs don't stack in effect and have a limited duration. The duration stacks though, so you can extend the buff longer. If the opposite effect is applied it subtracts some turns from the effect's duration, allowing you to cut down on the amount of time an enemy is buffed, or neutralize your own debuffs faster if you have the right moves.But the leveling is where this game really takes the win. You yourself have a level. The stats of your monsters are determined by your own level (modified by the base stats of the monster form of course), and gaining exp "Stars up" your monster forms, making them learn new moves. Reach 5 stars and the monster can be "remastered" into a stronger form, but base forms are still somewhat viable even into the endgame. It's nice and refreshing to catch something cool and rare and actually be able to use it without grinding for exp for it.And finally, you always have a companion fighting by your side. Most battles will be at least 2v2 (even versus wild monsters), with you and your companion able to support each other with a variety of moves.As for the story, it's pretty neat. There are six companions, and each has a personal quest to complete, but there's also several other questlines you can pursue and of course the main story quest, which involves beating up scary bosses. Most companion quests have one of these bosses at the end, so there's always an incentive to do these sub-quests, though if you really don't want to, you don't technically have to (though you may struggle a bit finding the final boss).Overall it's a really great game and if you're even remotely interested in creature collectors I would absolutely recommend giving this a try.

_childDocuments_.review: This is without exaggeration the perfect monster-catching game. Fantastic art and monster design, an absolutely killer soundtrack, and progression that's insanely open-ended without ever feeling boring or aimless. _childDocuments_.review: Disclaimer: I'm one of the developers of Godot Engine, the game engine used by Cassette Beasts. So I'm naturally rooting for it to be a success that helps outline how versatile Godot is :) Still, I'm playing this on my free time and reviewing it from my perspective of a player fond of indie games.I'm only a few hours into the game so far, but what I've seen really ticks all the boxes for me. Fun and refreshing monster collection gameplay, amazing art direction and OST, and a pretty engaging story. I picked up the game for the first time when it released yesterday and I've had a hard time stopping playing to go to sleep at a reasonable hour ;)I'm eager to see more of the game, and I'll aim to update this review when I do with more in depth insights on what I enjoyed or not. But so far I love everything about it!Oh btw I'm playing on Linux, and it runs great, both on my laptop and on Steam Deck (where I'm going to play it through).---Edit after 20h in-game: Yep, I still love it. It actually gets better after a few hours when you really dive into exploding the overworld, and start recording or "remastering" (evolving) some of your more experienced monsters. You get access to new skills which make the combat a lot more interesting, as well as progressively getting more possibilities to navigate the overworld, unlocking new areas and secrets.I got to find my first 3 bootlegs in the wild, which are slightly more powerful versions of the monsters with a different element, and those quickly found their way to my favorite rooster :)There's overall more content than I first expected, seeing how I haven't beat the game yet. The overworld map didn't feel very big initially when I started exploring it and discovering big chunks in a short time, but it's actually pretty satisfactory.I'm having a lot of fun capturing new monsters, trying to find bootleg versions of them, reading their witty descriptions - Djinn Entonic is my favorite - and experimenting with different play styles.I'm a bit overwhelmed by the sheer number of monsters I now have available, combined with the "stickers" system to assign skills, which makes me feel like I might have to spend a lot of time micro-optimizing the assigned stickers whenever I change the composition of my party. But I mostly play casually and don't bother too much, I'm still powerful enough to go through most areas, and just need to be a bit tactical on big boss encounters.
_childDocuments_.name: Cassette Beasts

_childDocuments_.review: Cannot get over how fun Type Chemistry is! So many interactions and status effects to play around with. Having level be mostly tied to your character instead of the individual monster forms also makes it much easier to experiment with all the moves and monsters you'll stock up over the course of the game. 10/10 only crashed once when I tried to hold all the [overworld movement power] buttons at the same time.
_childDocuments_.name: Cassette Beasts

_childDocuments_.review: If you're looking for a game that's relatively close to Pokemon and Digimon, but also utilizes the 2v2 format? Look no further! Cassette Beasts breathes a lot of new life into the genre! At first I didn't know what to think, but after spending a good chunk of time with the game, I've grown to love it a lot! The references to hit pop culture from the 80s is also phenomenally done! (Spoiler free of course!)One twist the game offers is that instead of catching the beasts you find out in the wild, you transform into them with your cassette player! In a way, it reminds me of a Digivice from Digimon! *insert nostalgia vibes* Funny enough, the game bares more resemblance to Digimon; there are different paths that your beasts can evolve on (some beasts even have 3 remaster options). Monster types even vary a lot, especially when it comes to mixing monster combos for new and strong fusions (a similar aspect for Digimon with DNA Digivolution as well as Pokemon Infinite Fusion, you can utilize both movesets within the newly created beast)!Story wise it all fits nicely in its package; flavorful and memorable characters, twists and turns applied, and subplot tied in with main plot! I have to hand it to Bytten Studios, I don't get attached to a lot of games, and this one really sealed the deal for me on numerous factors! It just hits all the right spots!Ratings:Story: 9/10Nostalgia: 10/10Gameplay: 10/10*insert shameless plug* If you're curious about the gameplay, I happen to have a playlist made for the entire story!Though I will say, if you want to check the game out for yourself, definitely pick it up! I would HIGHLY recommend this game to anyone who enjoys Pokemon and Digimon, as well as other monster catching/taming games! While the game doesn't have multiplayer yet, it will at some point once the Piers of the Unknown free DLC comes out (there's no confirmed date just yet, but hoping this year for the 8 player multiplayer update)

_childDocuments_.review: I'm honestly shocked. I picked this up knowing it was a pokemon-like and knew little else but it captured me from the start. The creature designs have also been incredibly solid so far! The music has been stand out so far and I'm excited for the next chance I get to play. If you like Pokemon, pick this up! Even if you don't like pokemon, if you like turn based RPGs, this may still grab you. It's a great game!

_childDocuments_.review: Edit: 11/21 Nominated Best on Deck. Good luck!Cassette Beasts very quickly shot to the top of my favourites list after just a couple of hours with it. If you're like me and you played Pokemon for years, but didn't enjoy the more recent entries for one reason or another then this game might just fill that void. I find that with a lot of monster collecting RPGs (Nexomon and TemTem, for example) I'm always wondering when my monsters are going to evolve because I'm so used to the conventions laid by Pokèmon. It's a bit grating, finishing a battle, levelling up, and... Nothing. There's no wondering in Cassette Beasts: The system that developer Bytten Studio has in place—a star ranking that raises with each battle until it hits level 5 and then your Beast is ready to evolve—is perfect. I also liked that some monsters had branching forms. Progress feels good and the fact that you can remove and reuse moves at will to build the perfect moveset is brilliant.If any of the following interest you, I would suggest picking it and it's fantastic OST up:*An example of that last one is Rock versus Grass. In Pokèmon, sure, one would do extra damage to the other, but in Cassette Beasts, Grass striking Earth means the Earth type will get seeded, providing your Grass Beast with HP regen. Say whaaaaa? Some of them are just logical: attack a Plastic type with a Fire move and you get a Poison effect as a result. So cool.I could go on about how area progression is unlocked by acquiring new Beast forms to unlock over world abilities and how great the writing is. I could gush about the pixel art style and how wonderful and vibrant the world is. I could tell you all about how this game breathes life back into a tired genre.  Instead, I'll urge you to top off your Steam wallet and get this game. It is definitely a labour of love and well worth the asking price.
_childDocuments_.name: Cassette Beasts

_childDocuments_.review: Casette Beasts takes monster collection games (e.g. Pokemon) to the next level. It's witty, it's fun, it's anti-capitalist, and to top it off it has THE BEST soundtrack. If you love a good 80's/90's retro vibe and love smashing 'mons together to get wacky combos.... do yourself a favor and pick this game up!
_childDocuments_.name: Cassette Beasts

_childDocuments_.review: If you're a fan of indie games that take a genre and make a masterpiece out of it, the I cannot recommend this game highly enough!The style is fun, whimsical and full of character. The music is incredible, the characters are deeply likeable and the monster designs are great. But the mechanics is where this game really shines!Other turn based games focused on creature collection can feel grindy. So this game ties your level to your character (and your companions never seem to drift far behind) so you can switch monsters without worry. This leads to more experimentation, and cleaner gameplay while still giving a sense of progression. The only grind I experienced is the post game, but by that point you're in too deep and its an excuse to stay in the world a little longer.The movement options given based on certain tapes you get don't feel like "Get this to do a specific thing to progress" but rather a constantly used part of your arsenal for traversing the world, tapping into experiences found in metroidvanias.The type matchups feels fresh through usage of effects dependent on the matchup, leading to more creative uses and strategies forming. (Like attacking your own beasts for the buffs, or strategic switching)The fusion mechanic feels great to use, and the addition of adding vocals to the soundtrack makes it feel amazing even when against a level 8 enemy.I feel like I have a whole bunch more to say but who's looking at steam reviews for an essay, so all in all, highly reccommend
_childDocuments_.name: Cassette Beasts

_childDocuments_.review: I like it, my favourite thing about it is how it takes you off guard with the boss fights and how there are complex interactions with different elemental typings and how much room there is for creative strategiesThe environments, the beast desgins and the world and lore are all super cool and I like them a lot too!I started to get very bored of the game by the end though, difficulty being completely gone and just going through the motions. After not playing for a while and returning back to it I found I had no interest in going on playing any more. The characters are cute and endearing but they just don't go deep enough for me to really be invested in the story enough to want to go on eitherMain problem with this game is a problem I have with leveling systems in general. You're doomed to always be overleveled by the end if you do any amount of side quests. I just don't like stat-increasing leveling systems outside of roguelikes because of this.7/10 Nothing really wrong about it, a lot of interesting stuff but goes on too long for it's own good and becomes uninteresting to me
_childDocuments_.name: Cassette Beasts

_childDocuments_.review: Right out the gate I just want to say, this game is great and doing a ton of things right. The genre of creature collecting isn't as flooded as it might feel, it's just one giant Pikachu shaped shadow looming over it. What a game needs to do to be successful despite that shadow, is step out of it and be it's own thing which is exactly what Cassette Beasts is doing. The story has a lot of intrigue, I could go on about how great the music is, or how I love the beast designs and use of pixel art, but what about gameplay?From a much better capture (recording in this game) mechanic, to a very interesting take on beast types, this game has a lot of its own flare going and it's great. Battles play out very differently because of the change in mechanics, and the world is actually open for you to explore with a lot to do. It's a single player focused game, with couch co-op as an option, but no online PVP. It feels like this is very deliberate to allow for a very well put together and focused singleplayer/co-op experience. 4 hours in and there's still so so much more to see and do!There's a demo to try, the demo sold me on it right away so I recommend giving that a go if you're somehow still on the fence. But I will say I highly recommend this one, the devs are great, the game is amazing, almost feels like someone went into my brain and made a game based on exactly what makes it tick. Can't wait to keep going with this one!

_childDocuments_.review: Reviewing this after 100%It's probably my favourite creature collector of all times. Greatest soundstrack to a game I've heard in a long time. It is one of the only ones I've actually wanted to buy (and I'm also listening to it on Spotify, for free, which is saying something). _childDocuments_.review: With 25% of all players having progressed to late stage achievements that take many hours the percentages speak for themselves.I really wish I could write these comments without referring to Pokemon but I just can't. It's a "catch em all" em up and there's just no getting around that fact. What most people will find surprising is that this small (just over 600mb) game by an indie development team is far superior to any of the other games of its genre. It's also pretty amazing in an age where games can be close to 200GB exactly how much can be achieved with vastly lower use of data space. The graphics are typically cutesy made from a combination of pixel, voxel, and cell shading. I'd refer to them as Zelda-esque but there are also areas that can remind you of Mario 3D without the full rotating views. In fact much of the game is centred around working out how to get to certain areas so there is a fair amount of puzzle element to the game. Combat will be instantly familiar to anyone who has played a catch em all before but the range of moves and custom skills on offer here far surpass any others. The music is also very pleasant - not something I usually take a lot of notice of. Add to this a fairly large cast of characters and companions, rpg like questing and multiple quest threads, and you have an absorbing and fun game that is worth every penny of its asking price and some. What a sublimely designed game! 95%This should absolutely be entered in the end of year awards.

_childDocuments_.review: Easily one of the most competent creature collector games on Steam.Pros:-Type advantages are handled in a very refreshing way. "Super effective" attacks debuff opponents rather than just doing more damage, and "resisted" attacks buff opponents instead of just doing less damage.-The action points system adds strategy to movesets and encourages a balance of low and high AP moves.-Party characters are fleshed-out, having development arcs instead of being one-note personalities.-Soundtrack is PHENOMENAL. Town theme is very cozy, while the battle themes get you pumped up. AND THERE ARE VOCAL TRACKS, which is really cool.-The theme of cassettes is maintained very well, potions and revives are tools to rewind cassette tapes, like pencils.-Monsters stats are tied to player level, so it's easy to swap out teammates without worrying about grinding.Cons:- While most of the spriting and animation is good, some are a bit off- Only one attacking animation per monster, whether doing melee or ranged attacks- There is little structure in terms of progression, so it's easy to be a bit overwhelmed with all of the quests that require explorationOverall, this game is an easy 9/10, and I highly recommend it to anyone who wants something that shakes up the classic Pokemon-esque formula.

_childDocuments_.review: Cassette Beasts is an iteration on classic Pokemon that improves on everything that made those games excellent.Combat is more strategic, the catch mechanic has an excellent risk/reward system, mistakes while leveling don't exist, and all the monster designs are fun and inventive.The music is an absolute banger, cover-to-cover. The art and narrative are consistently solid.While family-friendly, the game never condescends to the player.No distasteful cash grabs or perverse monetization. Just good vibes.A modern classic!

_childDocuments_.review: Cassette Beasts is one of the few creature collection games that doesn't just steal from the Pokémon formula. With distinct enough ideas to stand on its own, the game stands at about 20 hours to complete the main story. It includes post-game content too so you can definitely get several hours more out of this.The battle system is unique and encourages more tactical thinking, and with an AP system it doesn't punish the player for using stat-based moves or switching casettes, as doing so can store up AP for more powerful moves. You can also more easily make your favourite beast your main cassette, as the sticker system makes it easy to give them powerful moves.The game runs smoothly even on lower-end devices and I've never encountered any glitches. I absolutely love this game, and the critique is sparse. Here's a few things that could improve the game for the developers, but in its current state I'd still highly recommend it.The amount of different types makes things confusing at times. The game gives you a guide, but it's a hassle to memorise it. Being able to see what moves would be weak / strong against your opponent would go far. The game actually does have this feature but only for major bosses. Bringing this into every fight would be helpful, especially since certain moves actually boost the enemy, so using the wrong ones punishes the player a lot.As well as this, the beasts have symbols to indicate their type instead of words. This becomes a little more inconvenient when the type-tapes you use have words. Putting the symbol on the tapes description too would be very helpful in avoiding confusion.

_childDocuments_.review: At the time of review, I also have 100 hours in the Game Pass version of this game, after which I decided to buy the game on Steam.Cassette Beasts is a creature collecting game which naturally leads to the first question of: How does it compare to a game like Pokemon? In my opinion, Cassette Beasts does its own unique spin on the genre very well, and I'd argue as an avid shiny Pokemon hunter that the bootleg system implemented in this game is superior, which is where I'd really like to take this review as someone who is a big fan of having a huge grind to chip away it, this game really scratches the itch. There are 14 types in Cassette Beasts, and every creature can have a bootleg of any type, so for example a Traffikrab is normally a Plastic type, however you can find a bootleg Ice Traffikrab, or Fire, or Astral, you name it. Each creature has a section of its bestiary entry dedicated to showing which bootlegs you've acquired of the creature. On top of that, creatures can also fuse together with each other, and all 128 creatures can fuse with all 128 creatures (so yes, even itself!) to form over 16,000 possible fusions. Which are also recorded in the Bestiary. So yeah, if, like me, you're a lover of the grind, and a fan of this type of game at all, this game does an amazing job of giving you a lot to do. Of course, if you're not a grinder that isn't to say the game isn't good, it's fantastic regardless, and absolutely worth your time. I just wanted to talk a little bit about the full completionist nature of the game as it may encourage some masochists like myself to pick it up.

_childDocuments_.review: Cassette Beasts had been sitting in my wishlist for a while, mostly out of fear that another upcoming monster taming game would be underwhelming. IMO if a game can put a nice spin on the genre and actually attempt to face the BEHEMOTH that is Pokemon, hats off to them. Giving Cassette Beasts a chance was a great gamble-Story: 7/10The type of open world game that throws multiple objectives on the map and is like "go do all this to complete the game" which isn't my really my cup of tea, but really fun nonetheless-Art: 9/10All the character portrait art and promotional art is phenomenal along with the world and creature design, but the open world sprites felt... off, for lack of a better term. (only when exploring the map, not during battle. Those sprites are nice)  -Monster Design: 7/10   At the time of typing this I haven't completed my Bestiary, but all of the monsters I've encountered have really charming designs. The game kind of loses me at the fusion mechanic though (Granted I know for the sake of game creation they could give every possible fusion it's own hand made sprite, but some of the fusions look a tad goofy)-Soundtrack 1000/10This soundtrack goes HARD! and its only supported by the fact the the music gets more dynamic if you engage with the in-game mechanics. the same mechanic also applies to the mellow town theme. being instrumental as you walk around town, but entering a building ramps up with vocals for an even soother tone-Combat: 9/10Made me think more than in Pokemon. Instead of individual moves having a use amount, you build up spendable points each turn that you can use on said moves. Instead of types just doing more or less damage to each other, they have specific reactions with the games chemistry system, which makes battles less of a mash A simulator. There's also and essence of resource management since you can only hold a limited number of healing items. Now I can't just buy a million revives and beat my opponent via war of attrition-Misc Notes  -The companion are cool and all have pretty compelling stories that are really grounded in the setting. Although some companion quests take you to late game before you can fully utilize them  -The mix of 2D sprites in a 3D environment could be jarring to some people, but I think that's what makes it charming  -OMG the boss designs are so cool and I wish I could ramble about them but its definitely something a new player should go in blind to  -The open world puzzles aren't the most attention grabbing, but they are a nice break from constant questing/leveling/farming and who doesn't like some free goodies

_childDocuments_.review: Cassette Beasts is the best monster-collecting game I've played. Ever.While that may seem like a sweeping statement, it's entirely honest - it hits the perfect blend of story, gameplay and customisation that I look for in a game, while not being particularly expensive or being a hundred hour titan (I had beaten the main story by the thirty hour mark, and that's taking my time to explore!).First, the type system is far more interesting than the classical 'super-effective/not-very-effective' you'll see in many games in this genre. Instead, elements have specific interactions with other ones - hit a Glass monster with a Metal attack, and shards of glass will be scattered across the battlefield, dealing damage to anyone who tries to make a melee attack. Using Fire on an Ice monster will cause the ice to melt, making them change to a Water type - said Water type can then be hit by Ice to freeze them and turn them back into an Ice type, which makes them flinch.The world of Cassette Beasts can only be described as brilliant. New Wirral is an island full of mystery and wonder, with secrets and surprises around each turn. I consistently ran into things that made me momentarily stop in awe or got taken off-guard by a monster doing something completely unexpected that made me decide that I had to record one of those suckers. Your NPC partner will also have things to say as you go to various places and interact with different things, which helps make you feel a lot less lonely in your travels.And yes, 'record'. Not 'catch'. See, you're not actually collecting monsters like this was a Pokemon game - you're using your cassette player to record monsters onto empty tapes, and then playing those tapes to transform into the recorded monster. This is the next part of Cassette Beasts's genius, and it's that you're not just standing to the side and giving orders in fights - you're doing the work, simply taking on the form and powers of your recorded monsters. Combined with how you'll always have a fully-controlled companion with you as you explore and fight, it makes things feel so much more personal than they would otherwise. You're not worried about Kayleigh's monster getting electrocuted, you're worried about Kayleigh herself.This is also a relevant mechanic in combat. Once your monster form runs out of HP, you revert to human until the end of the round when you can pick a new tape. In this time, you still have your own HP - if you're defeated in human form, then you don't get to choose a new tape and that fighter's out of battle completely. This also applies while you're trying to record a monster, since you automatically turn human when using one of your blank tapes and can be have your efforts disrupted by being hit by attacks.I haven't even touched on the plot of the game, but I don't think I will beyond saying that it's a damn good one. Cassette Beasts demands to be experienced firsthand, and I think using a guide or having forewarning worsens the experience. (Of course, there's no shame in breaking one out when trying to complete your Bestiary in the post-game - some of those remaster conditions are really quite obscure.)Oh, and did I mention you can fuse with your partner on the fly and get a unique form based on both of the monsters you're transformed into? Because I have now. There's over sixteen thousand different fusion sprites, and I myself have only seen just over a hundred in forty hours.Play Cassette Beasts. You won't regret it.

_childDocuments_.review: The blend of Persona-style monster-fusion and open, online Monster-catcher/Pokemon style gameplay are novel and enjoyable. Worth a play if you want a cool spin on the Monster-catching/Pokemon formula, but not if you want a really cohesive one.

_childDocuments_.review: Edit: I've completed the story at this point and my stance on this game is largely unchanged. I've touched up my review a bit to elaborate on some things I was too brief on but that's about it. I will say that the final boss is at least decent in the first phase, though the second phase ends up being a glorified cutscene which is pretty disappointing. The ending is also really abrupt, which didn't really bother me but will probably upset anyone who actually likes any of the characters besides Viola (whose character motivation is clear and consistent enough for her behavior at the end to actually make sense) and Barkley (who is a very good boy).----From a raw gameplay standpoint Cassette Beasts is a pretty good game, and if that's all you're after then the current "Overwhelmingly Positive" rating is warranted. It's not perfect - I have issues with some of the UI (too many button presses to perform basic tasks, no confirmation window for irreversible actions like sending party members to storage or fusing) mechanics (unlocking new fast travel points / shortcuts is much more annoying/tedious than it needs to be, Eugene's fusion unlocking at endgame when he's one of the starter characters is baffling design) and balancing (Coaldron is such a mess that it can't use its own level up moves, meanwhile stack 7 Random Starters and a 10AP attack of your choice on a glass cannon and you'll auto-win every fight forever) - but it's overall a refreshing take on the mons genre that's mechanically solid enough that I wanted to keep playing until the end of the story in spite of the rest of this review.The writing however is a  miss. Some other reviews mention woke elements, but honestly they aren't that bad. You have a 3-choice pronoun selection at the start of the game; a bunch of characters with neon hair; and a partner lineup with 1 white (female, Irish) character, 1 ambiguous character with dyed hair, 3 black characters, and a dog; but that's as far as it goes. It's the  that gets me.Several of you have already pressed the jester award button just from reading that much, but if you haven't, please hear me out. There are random philosophers as NPC trainers throughout the world who spout one-liners related to whatever they're most famous for saying, then they lose all relevancy forever because they're just NPC trainers. Most of the partner conversations that weren't utterly forgettable were full of navel-gazing, the main exceptions being Viola (who actively refuses to navel-gaze and is the most based character in the game because of it) and Barkley (who is a dog).The society of New Wirral is pretty clearly trying to portray socialism...or more accurately the quasi-socialist  that so many modern liberals think is cool. If the game's portrayal of "socialism" functioned on more than an aesthetic level, or if it wasn't trying so hard to deliver a message rather than just being a good vibes "all-in-this-together" society, I wouldn't be nearly as scathing as I'm about to be."From each according to his abilities, to each according to his needs" does  mean "you can do what you feel like and if that's sitting at home all day every day nobody will bother you about it" but that's sure how the game treats it. Similarly, in order to seize the means of production  but New Wirral is a disorganized blob of vibes that subsists off of interdimensional detritus and expects a single pumpkin patch to feed everyone. This admittedly works, but only because the pumpkins are video game enemies that respawn faster than you can kill them. New Wirral also straight up  (probably because all the landlords are literally vampires - yes, it really is that unsubtle) and instead relies on barter and favors, which is technically possible in the world as shown, but only because the canonical population is less than 1000 people, everyone who might possibly have less than pure intentions is cartoonishly obvious about it, and the island gets a constant influx of basic resources and refined goods for free so nobody has to bother with things like "infrastructure", "manufacturing facilities", or "supply chains". Even electricity production gets waved away with vague comments about an "energy field"! The only reason this society lasted a full century is authorial fiat, which means the whole thing stops being applicable to the real world and the message is shot in the foot.I think the best summary is that the game has an entire dungeon and boss fight that's all about lecturing the player about the emptiness of consumerism and the need to spend less time and money on hollow things like...video games...when it A) costs $20, which might not sound like much, but the take only needs to be split between 2 people and most games with this heavy an anti-consumerism message are either less than $10 or explicitly give a sizable chunk of profits to charity; and B) will take most players at least 20 hours to beat the main story, while still having a bunch of postgame content + a randomizer mode specifically designed to encourage people to play the game forever. Again, this game has "go outside" as one of its core messages.I hang out with  and they aren't anywhere  as insufferable as this game can be. And their arguments are occasionally somewhat convincing, too.

_childDocuments_.review: It's not that similar to Pocket Monsters™. There were definitely moments at the beginning where I thought, "well that's just [x] from Pokemon," but that went away pretty quickly. The core systems are very different and (for the most part) better. There's a lot of QOL improvements compared to Pokemon, like enemy level scaling, a built-in False Swipe mechanic, and fast travel that's available before the three-quarter mark of the game. I really enjoyed the soundtrack, particularly the battle themes. The visual style is yet another reminder that good 2/2.5D will always be better than mediocre 3D.I did find the dialogue to be pretty bad at some points, such as in the (optional) romance scenes, which were definitely Fire Emblem: Awakening tier (i.e. not good). The main story was just okay, though I guess this is an open world game. The final boss fight was a bit of a headscratcher given how gimmicky (in a good way) the other boss fights were. The post-game is super grindy if you want to get every achievement, as there are only a few non-generic sidequests before you're just doing repetitive fetch and bounty quests for the rest of time.Still, it's a nice game overall. It definitely reminded me of a happier time. A time before responsibilities, work, and Gen 7.

_childDocuments_.review: So many great things to say about this game. The artsyle, music, and monster designs are all so fresh. I don't like to compare games to pokemon but this is exactly what I want out of a pokemon game. It has this great 2D/HD style with lots of nice bright colors that pop. The world is fun to explore and has you unlocking abilities that open up new areas and let you explore the world in different ways.The music is so relaxing and calm when it needs to be and then in the heat of a boss battle, you get this awesome soundtrack that picks up in pace. I love the small snippets of dialogue that some of the characters make during text scenes. It helps to give them a bit more personality hearing what they actually sound like.The monster designs are all so different and quirky with funny combinations that you can fuse together throughout the game. I wish there were even more but the fact that you can fuse any 2 leads to thousands of combos so I understand why there can't be more.This game has a semi-open world that expands as you unlock more traversable abilities. You can do any line of major quests (fight bad guys, progress story, fight the "gym leaders") and there are lots of fun side quests with supporting characters. This is one thing that pokemon scarlet and violet failed at providing as it was "open world" in the sense that you could go anywhere, but it was not scaled properly. With cassette beast, it felt like almost anywhere I went, I could handle myself but there was still a threat if I wandered too far or for too long without healing.I really enjoy the combat system. It's almost always double battles so there are lots of unique strategies and combos to try out. The leveling system in this game is also a favorite of mine. You level your character and a monster simultaneously. The monster provides base stats on top of the character so you can switch to a weaker mosnter to level it and it won't be totaly useless. The moves can be swapped out and stored in a move bank that can then be put on another monster that is compatible. Overall I found it to be a mechanic that was  unique and time saving when I wanted it to be. I'm close to finishing the game. The story has been unique and has a cool cast of characters that make me want to complete all their story lines. The monster designs are great and I love trying out all the different fusion combos. For the price, this game is a great pickup and you won't be disappointed with the amount of content you get out of it. If they were to ever release more content or another game along these lines, I would pick it up in a heartbeat.

_childDocuments_.review: I am gonna be real with you reader, Cassette beasts is an incredible experience, it does with 2 dudes and a modest budget what the most profitable franchise ever made couldn't with a bottomless budget and 160+ devs, it made a world I genuinely love just being in. New Wirral is not some modern 8 hours to travel from one end to the other open world filled with areas that serve zero purpose, every corner of the map every single area has things to do, not an ounce of space is wasted.The gameplay reminds me of Atlus's digital devil saga games crossed with Nintendo's big yellow money farting behemoth Pokemon. The elemental chemistry system feels like a genuine evolution of the old type effectiveness of yore, instead of just rewarding smart move usage with larger damage numbers Cassette beasts decides it's more fun if each type caused unique positive or negative statuses to the attacks recipient, like earth moves crippling electric's ability to hit multiple targets or poison moves being burned up as fuel by fire types causing them to gain increased energy generation. I could gush so much about the intricacies of combat but I think I've said enough.Now the soundtrack, god this soundtrack is perfect it enhances everything to such an absurd degree, the theme of Harbor town turns what would be a cute but not incredible little jrpg town into one of the coziest towns in gaming that I am just happy to be in. The battle themes are no slouch either special mention to "Same old story" and "Your inception" the latter being tied to one of the coolest pieces of fanservice to those who played Bytten studios previous game "Lenna's inception" another great game in it's own right.Look I could keep just gushing forever but please just play this game it deserves so much love, Bytten studio should be so proud of their work here because they've made something truly beautiful here and I look forward to anything they make in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: I initially passed this up as being just another pixel-art Pokémon knockoff, but after seeing a glowing review for it, I decided to give it a shot - and I certainly didn't regret it! Rather than just aping the Big P, it very much provides a fresh take on the Monster-Taming genre, and while it's not without its flaws, the execution is truly excellent. The music is AMAZING, and utilizes dynamic mixing in a way I really wish more games would. Despite the 'kid-friendly' design of the monsters, the story's quite deep and mature, dipping into philosophical and psychological concepts. The characters are well-executed, with your various companions all being fully realized individuals that you find yourself wanting to get to know better, and not just grinding rep with for the sake of boosted abilities or achievements.Now, I DO have to point out a couple of drawbacks, though they don't detract enough to make that thumbs-up waver. Firstly, while the game being moderately challenging isn't a bad thing, the way it often blindsides you in one way or another feels rather unfair. You may sometimes be plunged into harsh boss-fights with no warning, and even fights that ARE thoroughly telegraphed may turn out to revolve around some gimmick or trick that you just don't have an answer to in your current lineup of monsters. In the end-game, the loss of resources you suffer upon death is rather insignificant, but early on it rather stings... and of course, once you ARE in the endgame, it's quite possible for you to create your OWN gimmicky trick-builds, murdering any and all challenge the game has to offer.Second, there's the... ugh... *post-game*. It's a GRIND. Just... a HUGE grind. There's some actual interesting stuff there - extra monsters, extra features, more interesting characters, new types of mini-bosses and so on, but most of it is gated behind a ridiculous grind that just requires you to collect 'Unstable Matter' by either doing hundreds of endless, randomly-generated radial quests, fighting tons and tons of endlessly respawning minibosses, or refighting the main storyline's bosses over and over and over again for hours on end. The later option, for those curious, is the most efficient, once you have the right kind of depraved gimmick-build to effortlessly annihilate them - but it's still a dull, mindless slog.Still, despite those flaws, Cassette Beasts remains a very worthwhile game to play, and a fine example of what monster-taming can be like when you stop trying to just imitate Pokémon -  and if you aren't a completionist obsessed with 100%'ing games, the post-game grind is at least... *manageable*.

_childDocuments_.review: Y'all are inevitably going to compare this to pokemon, and I'm not even gonna pretend that my lifelong love of those games isn't exactly why I bought this. Which is a damned shame, because this game really isn't quite that. I mean, nothing much manages to have the sort of charming monster design and style that pokemon has, but this game feels like its more interested in making a name for itself on other strengths, namely being a really  little JRPG, and I'm not sure how else to describe the vibe of this game, but I absolutely love it.Like, you meet NPC companions, and they all just kinda give off this same, really charming vibe of "We're all in this together" that meshes well with the setting, and just gives the game cozy feels. It captures the  you're looking for in a game trying to capitalize on your nostalgia for older games in its genre without actually trying to  the same as those games in a really masterful way I've never seen before.But it's polished and modern and just  in a way that alone makes it worth recommending. It's got good  and  behind it, despite me coming in skeptical that the cassette thing would be more of a weird retro gimmick from a decade before I was born, but no, it's just , at least from the first few hours I've seen.And the turn-based combat going on has strong pokemon vibes but is clearly trying to make for its own identity- the type chart (which the game hands you as an item early on, and you're free to check in battle, thank god) is mostly built around free status conditions, positive and negative, rather than big damage buffs, and it's a solid take. I'm having fun.Strong recommend on a game I was half expecting to refund when I bought it, tbh. _childDocuments_.review: Loaded with both charm and depth, Cassette Beasts is a snappy, vibrant RPG that knows exactly what it wants to be and executes with style.- Instead of individual monsters leveling up independently, the player characters have levels of their own, which is then applied to every monster form you take. Furthermore, move sets are totally customizable, letting you, for instance, raise a monster with the intent to cannibalize its moves for a monster you like better. Together, these make it incredibly easy and rewarding to experiment, since it takes almost no effort to get a new monster up to speed.- The writing is solid, exactly the kind of lighthearted-but-not-irreverent you might expect from a creature RPG. The jokes land, the characters are likable, the moments meant to hype you up do, and occasionally it pulls out some genuine philosophy. - The open world works surprisingly well for the system; you're heavily encouraged to run around, solve platforming puzzles for secrets, and record every beast in sight to unlock new traversal mechanics. However, you don't run the risk of missing anything, as rumors in town will highlight major objectives on your map, and you're not actually required to hit every major objective in order to reach endgame. Put together, this means that at virtually all times there'll be a new point on the map that you haven't checked out yet- probably several- so there's no risk of getting lost or bogged down.- The music. It's really good. I still have Wherever We Are Now stuck in my head.- The personal quests for each of your partners are great fun, but notably the relationship mechanics for each partner but the first are locked off until you've completed their personal quest- which locks off some important combat abilities. For the early game, it's a little wonky trying out new partners for this reason.- There are only so many overworld sprites, so the game frequently will use a basic beast's sprite for what is actually an encounter with its evolved form. Furthermore, this may be an error on my part, but some monsters don't have overworld sprites, and thus can only appear as add-ons in a fight with a different enemy. This tripped me up for a while when I was hunting for Bestiary completion.That's pretty much the worst I could muster for this game. It's a good game.Ultimately, Cassette Beasts doesn't wear out its welcome- if you're not interested in beating every Ranger Captain or completing the bestiary, you can easily chew through this game in 20 hours of zero fat, just pure fun. There's also a large postgame should you want more, but be warned that aside from some superbosses, it's rather grindy and unimpressive unless you're the type to really enjoy hunting for alt-color variants of monster forms.This is one of the best creature RPGs I've seen in a long, long time, and if you have any interest in the genre, do yourself a favor and give this a try.

_childDocuments_.review: I picked up this game expecting a half decent Pokemon clone. What I got instead was one of the best monster collectors I have ever played. This game may invoke ideas to compare it to Pokemon but make no mistake, this is it's own beast of a game.The elemental system is was of the most fleshed out and well thought out I have ever encountered. Rather than a simple strong or weak, every element uniquely interacts with others to completely alter the tide of battle, like using fire on a plastic type melts the plastic turning it into a poison type, or hitting air with a fire move causing a surging updraft putting up a defensive wall around the air type. This system is fine tune, dense with customization, and just begging you to break it open with a hammer.The monster designs are absolutely endearing with so many that I couldn't help falling in love with. Hell this is the first Monster Collector I've played where I DIDN'T feel compelled to keep my starter because of how many options there were, and I mean that in a good way. Combine that with the unique bootleg system, and this truly is a game just desperately begging for an online battle mode. I can see a meta forming behind the scenes already.The bosses were an absolutely treat, with several of them being permanently stuck in my head. The side quests and partner characters are all deeply interesting with some very relatable and realistic worries. I felt compelled to do everything and meet everyone. I plan to get all the achievements now at this point.The music is the real stand out here though. Every track in this OST is mesmerizing. Lyrics dropping in and out based on the context of the situation, a heavenly voice that draws you in... I found myself unconsciously singing along every time I went to the cafe to manage my team.If I have to give anything negative about the game, it's that as it currently stands I do it a "journey is greater than the destination" type situation as the game itself including the final boss were absolutely fantastic, I did find the main story ending to be less than satisfying, especially given the game does have a romance system in place, but I feel like it didn't really contribute much once I chose my partner. All things that can be rectified with DLC, Updates, or anything else honestly. 9.5 / 10 from me. Recommending it to whoever I can.
_childDocuments_.name: Cassette Beasts

_childDocuments_.review: As much as I adore the monster designs, a good art/sprite team can't save a game from mind-numbingly amateurish writing and tedious "puzzles" that feel like a college student's Unity project. I understand indie dev teams don't have the same resources an AAA studio has, but Cassette Beasts has so much potential and it's painful to be forced to wade through so much drivel before you can get to the genuinely enjoyable parts.While I wouldn't recommend the game for a full $20, if it goes on sale (which I picked it up on) I'd say it's worth it. The combat is pretty alright and can be complex if you want it to be, boss fights are decently fun, and like I said the beasts you collect are pretty great. I just wish they'd either put more time into the overworld + dialogue because atmosphere plays a big role in RPGs, even monster collectors.
_childDocuments_.name: Cassette Beasts

_childDocuments_.review: Having played a few creature collecting games in the past (Including that particularly popular franchise), I was drawn to this game, and then my eyes were opened.It has an extra layer to the type advantages/disadvantages that can make you think more carefully when it comes to your next move which I really enjoyed, it wasn't as simple as "This is better than this, so just does extra damage".The creatures are well designed ranging from cute and cuddly to weird and creepy, and I loved every single one, and the fusion system as well! Such an interesting mechanic that you don't always see. Can't forget the bootlegs either, essentially shinies that make them be any type! Think of all the colours!The story and world is pretty neat as well, with some interesting puzzles that occasionally made me think every now and then.I love the art-style and soundtrack of this game, probably one of my favourite soundtracks from a game for a good while, and fit the situations!(I'm not the best at writing these kinda things but I enjoyed the game so much that I gave it a go, but why are you still reading this? Go get the game already!)
_childDocuments_.name: Cassette Beasts

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who grew up on Monster Raising/Catching games this was a COMPLETE breath of fresh air. I cannot express how good this game is with a TONNE of reasons to pop it open for a few hours. The story is charming, the artwork is lovely and I absolutely love the designs of the creatures- not to mention the spin on the usual monster battling genre of you being the monster.I cannot recommend this game enough and I really hope it gets the attention it deserves.
_childDocuments_.name: Cassette Beasts

_childDocuments_.review: Lovely turn based RPG, where you can collect cassette tapes by beating monsters in combat. By putting a certain cassette in your walkman, you can fight with that particular monsters or even use that monsters skill when fighting with another monster. Every monster has a certain element type like water, fire etc, and for each element type there's another element that results in a buff or debuff when used against it. Picking the right monster when going to combat should be very important because of this, but it really isn't. First of all, you can take only five different cassette tapes with you. Since you don't know what type of monsters you're about to face, you'll always pick the strongest no matter what element they are. Buffs and debuffs can also be applied by using certain attacks, no matter what element the monsters are. This is a bit of a missed opportunity, especially since the battles are 2 vs 2 and could have used more variation. Most of the time, I ended up using the same cassettes in every battle but the boss fights.While the combat is mediocre, everything else in this game is very well designed. The story and characters you encounter are great, there are lots of interesting (side) quests and the overworld is stuffed with secrets and puzzles. Cassette Beasts is not perfect, but definitely worth playing.
_childDocuments_.name: Cassette Beasts

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic evolution of the Pokemon like RPG. The Double Battles really require you to strategize in battles and the tuneable difficulty is a fantastic. The twist on the typical proficiency and mastery of the various types was significantly better than what modern Pokemon games have devolved into and the soundtrack is top notch.
_childDocuments_.name: Cassette Beasts

_childDocuments_.review: 10/10 music 10/10 story 10/10 art 10/10 mechanics. This game did everything right and is easily one of my favorite games of all time and probably the best monster-catching/collector game I have played. Everything about this game is very refreshing and all of the mechanics make it very unique. It takes all of the mechanics already set up in the genre and builds upon them while at the same time also introducing many new unique mechanics such as fusions where you can combine your monsters to create thousands of combinations while still keeping the game very balanced and enjoyable.All of the characters have their own unique personalities and I enjoyed getting to know every single one of them throughout their individual story quests, as you fight along with them, and while taking a break at the rest stops. As you grow your relationships with the characters your fusions when you fight alongside them also strengthen which I found to be a really cool feature. Once you get to know the characters you can also even have relationships with them which while not being super fleshed out still adds some cute dialogue and it makes me feel warm and fuzzy inside :DThis game set up a new IP and world perfectly. The only downside I can think of is that even though it’s a decently long game that took me ~20 hours to beat the main story, I wish there was more. hopefully, there’s some future DLC or second game or something. Anyways 10/10 game, I cannot recommend it enough, if you enjoy monster collecting games, RPGs, or any video games play this, it is very good, and $20 is a steal.
