_childDocuments_.review: This is the writeup for my review, I will add the full video review once it's available.Do you like turn based combat? How about monster collecting? Want a game that works when you install it? Like boom, here’s a full game! Then I have some great news for you!Cassette Beasts brings a refreshing take to the monster-collecting genre. On first glance, one might be forgiven for calling it a Pokemon clone. It does, after all, feature monster collection mechanics and a 2v2 battle system, so why not just play a Pokemon game? Well... Cassette Beasts is, in almost EVERY REGARD, better than Pokemon, while drastically being a different experience. Let’s dig in.Graphically, Cassette Beasts appears very simple at first. It’s a pixel style game, so it probably can’t have that much graphical complexity, right? Well... yes, but also no. The art style in this game looks really good. All of the character portraits are unique, and you can tell most characters apart from each other based on just their sprite. There’s also a shocking amount of customization you can do with your own character, and by changing a few pieces of cosmetics you can go from a big boy with a beard and glasses to a cute girl in a sundress. I still can’t wrap my head around how the artists in this game managed to make the sprites so individualized in what just a few pixels. The monster designs are honestly kind of hit or miss. Some of them are incredibly creative and unique, some are cool takes on existing stereotypes like Yuki-Onna, while others are just weird and off putting. Given the lore of the game, all three descriptions make sense but it’s still hard to get excited about some of these designs, yet others are so cool you just have to have them. With the large varieties of designs, part of the game’s charm is that it has aesthetics to tailor to most personalities. There is also a Fusion mechanic which allows any two monsters to combine into a single monster, but we will get into that IN DETAIL later. The music in this game is also really good and I am reminded of the soundtrack from the show RWBY. If you’re not familiar with RWBY, then it’s all fully instrumental (with a mix of electric guitar, drums, and piano). You get your first real taste when you get to the main hub in the game, Harbourtown. There’s a nice peaceful track playing that kind of gets you relaxed; however, when you walk into a building, the lyrics kick in. Any time you enter the building, the somber lyrical laid back music will send you into a euphoric relaxation, helping you mentally recover before heading back out to explore more of the island. This is a taste that the full game offers. Much like graphics, the music alters drastically when you fuse. Every battle theme in the game has lyrics, butthey only get sung by fusing with your chosen partner, completely changing the atmosphere and intensity of ANY battle, even a mundane encounter with a generic monster on the beach. The game uses the lyrics to reward you for fusing! That music ramps the fight with the game’s many bosses up to 11 and after 2-3 of them and you’ll be belting out the lyrics along with newcomer Shelby Harvey. This girl has some pipes on her, and just thinking about these songs gets me a little emotional. Cassette Beasts seems like her first work and I hope to hear more of her in the future. Similar to Undertale or Persona 5, you will be listening to the soundtrack long after you watch the credits roll.The gameplay of Cassette Beasts is split into two sections, exploration and battling. The exploration is top notch, giving me sweet memories of Monster Sanctuary in that you have to capture certain monsters to gain their abilities for overworld exploration. The first one you get is the ability to glide, which is automatically given as part of the tutorial. As the game progresses, you’ll get the ability to dash through rocks, climb walls, double jump, swim, etc. which slowly opens up more of the map as you progress. There are ways an experimental player can sequence break several parts of the game and are likely intentional, since the game includes speed running options built in. Throughout the game you will find random puzzles that open up to treasures which remind me a lot of Genshin Impact or Breath of the Wild. The treasures can range from materials needed to buy goods in town to common or even rare stickers, this game’s version of moves. Seeing a locked chest will immediately send the player into a frenzy looking for a switch or trick to get it open and get the goods. They usually only take 30 seconds or so to solve, but it’s always a nice mental refresher from battling and exploring, and since the treasure chests are mostly randomized it can lead to an exceptional endorphin hit if you pop one open and see different colored text indicating a rare sticker!The second part of exploration is the questing system. The game checks your level and then the NPCs in town will give you a “Rumor” which will point you to content you have the numbers to deal with. Be it a Vampire hideout, a newly discovered subway tunnel, or the next Captain on your mission to join the Rangers, You’ll always have a quest marker to tell you where to go for your next big throwdown. The quest marker is important due to the large map. While you won’t get lost, it’s very possible to just not know where to go next for some of the less obvious missions. For example, locating the optional partner quests. Every quest you complete also gives substantial monetary and experience rewards, so they are always worth doing.As for the combat, you and your chosen partner participate in 2v2 battles, which can also be 2v1 or even 2v3, and on occasion you can get into a horde battle which pits the two of you against up to 6 enemies. You and your partner can equip any monster cassette tape to turn into, each with its own moveset or, the game calls moves stickers. Stickers can range from elemental attacks, to buffs, shields, debuffs, passives, etc. I could write an entire novel on just this aspect of the game. For example, I had a monster that auto-cast an ability that gave it “Multi-target” which turns any attack into an area of effect attack, and my partner had a monster equipped that had an ability it would auto-cast at the start of battle that would give any monster the ability to land it’s next attack, guaranteed. This allowed me to basically shred any random encounter on turn 1, as I would unleash a low accuracy, powerful single target attack on the entire enemy team. That is just a taste of the many possible combinations that you can use to give yourself an advantage in combat, or outright break the game. And again, that is only scratching the surface. Every single monster can have a “Bootleg” version of itself. Every monster in the game has a base typing, but it can also appear as any other type via bootleg. That means you can get an Astral Traffikrab, or a water type Bulletino. This is already a very cool mechanic, as it also affects stickers, but the more important thing is that it also affects fusions! You do get a random bootleg for free near the start of the game via an NPC, but any time you see that glitchy avatar indicating that a bootleg exists, the excitement is akin to finding a shiny in Pokemon, except it’s better because bootlegs affect gameplay.The game truly shines with the AI Algorithms that the developers added. There are 120 monsters in base Cassette Beasts but ANY TWO MONSTERS IN THE GAME CAN FUSE TOGETHER. During combat, you get a fusion meter with your partner, and once full (by giving or receiving damage) you can fuse into a super powered monster, which combines the moves and stats of both monsters 1 for 1. The game then uses its AI to generate a combined form for the monsters AND a name. This mechanic is the best way to defeat the game’s bosses and many other challenges, and is absolutely paramount to master. Yes, you can fuse any two monsters together, but th

_childDocuments_.review: I wasn't expecting too much out of this game-- most monster catchers aren't anything special to me, and make me feel like I'd rather be playing what they're inspired by. But a halfhearted copycat this is not.Cassette Beasts is very much it's own game, and it is a FANTASTIC experience at that. I've taken the time to fully immerse myself in the game world. Collecting new creatures, trying them out, and seeing who you gel with best is just plain fun. Whether you're like me and plan what guys you wanna use beforehand, or go in completely blind, this game has a little something for everyone.The concept is so unique, and they follow through on the execution. Everything about it oozes charm. The party menu, health and experience bars included, being cassettes is just such a lovely touch. Not to mention, THE MUSIC. Every battle track in the game has two versions, and whenever you use the fusion mechanic that you can build up between fights, the lyrics KICK IN. It makes for an amazingly satisfying experience, especially when no fusion is barred from happening for arbitrary reason. Every monster can fuse with every other monster, making for over 14,000 different possible combinations.All the beasts and the humans who turn into them are rendered in adorable high-quality 2d sprites, against a vibrant and expansive 3d environment. It's not unlike Octopath Traveler in that presentation department. Not to mention, you'll quickly find yourself growing close to the partner characters and their individual quests for something important to them. Meaning, justice, self-expression, memories...and each of them has their own signature monster not found anywhere else in the world. Aside from offering something valuable to a team, be it fast-paced blitzing or valuable supportive tools, you can even romance them if you get close enough...saucy.In short, if you're a fan of monster tamers or not, you should 100% PLAY this game, it's such a joyous and enthralling experience. It makes learning the new type chart it has natural, easy to remember, and intuitive without being intrusive. Recording new monsters for your team is deeper, and far less annoying than the kind of catching you may be accustomed to. In fact, I'd go as far as to say it's FUN in of itself. The bosses are so creative, offer a fair challenge, and feel so good to defeat. The music goes so hard I'm going to purchase the soundtrack, which is something I like, never do for games. Supporting this game is entirely worth it, communities help a game thrive. And this one most certainly deserves it.

_childDocuments_.review: Do you like Pokemon?  Into action, adventure, grinding, and exploration?  Well, if you like any or all of that, plus an extra heap of nice music to go with it, this may be the game for you.+++Pros++++ The overall concept and most of the execution is great+ The game looks decent and the music fits it+ No crashes or bugs encountered so far+ Varied selection of monsters, stickers, and companions to customize your play+ Almost a casual game, but you can get yourself into trouble if you don't pay attention---Cons---- Would like a bit more variety with the music - each monster form has its own unique music since they are "taped"- At the outset the pacing seems a bit slow & grindy, as you have to repeatedly return to a rest spot to heal yourself; you can only carry a limited number of items that heal/repair your monsters/tapes, but not you - the number carried can be upgraded eventually though===Conclusion===While I haven't played any Pokemon games in over 20 years now, I doubt the formula has changed so much that my experience with it would be irrelevant.  This game is cut from a similar cloth, but gives you more freedom to play around with your monsters.Monsters can evolve after awhile, but you also have the ability to customize them via the use of stickers that you apply to the cassette tapes - the higher their level, the more sticker slots they have.  Then, you also have the ability to temporarily fuse you and your companion's equipped monsters into a unique monster - prior to playing, I thought you could permanently fuse two monsters to create a new one that joins your party, but that isn't the case.  Too bad, as I would have loved a breeding/fusion system that allowed for that, but oh well.I wasn't sure what my reaction to this game would be before playing, but I'm pleasantly surprised.  There are a few things I'd like to see done differently, but overall it is quite fun.  Oh, and it plays flawlessly on the Steam Deck, so there's that.

_childDocuments_.review: It plays like a Pokémon game in many regards, the monster designs are great and the fusion mechanic keeps things constantly interesting (although I wish I could fuse more often). The music is neat, although I'm not fond of many of the lyrical additions they added to the song, half the time it feels like I'm playing Life is Strange or something. Because of small things like that, the game feels very "Western", for the lack of a better word. Many mechanics are well fleshed out though, such as traversal, puzzles and general gameplay, including the fact that you can adjust the intellect and difficulty of enemy encounters, which I found very nice. My only gripe so far are the characters. I don't know why people are saying they're engaging, they're about as deep as your average Pokémon rival, and I remember very vividly it had a death scene at one point and instead of being shocked or at least somewhat horrified at a living being just straight up being pulverized in front of them, the "engaging character" simply showed mild annoyance, saying "I told them they'd get killed". It was very out of character, really tone-deaf and just soured the whole experience. Why even have death in your game if you don't know how to write it? I didn't think this was a trope, but the exact same thing happened in the game "Indivisible", which also ruined the experience there.Anyhow, if you ignore that, the game gets a solid 7/10, maybe just short under an 8. It's clearly aimed at a more casual audience but has a lot of features and intricacies that more skilled players will appreciate, unlike most mainline Pokémon games these days.

_childDocuments_.review: Quite possibly one of the best monster-taming RPGs I have ever played. All the monster designs are great, the open world feels expansive and is genuinely fun to traverse, and the game itself is pretty impressive visually. Cassette Beasts also has stellar combat; running off the AP system, every ability a monster has is tied to an AP cost, so stronger moves tend to cost more AP and weaker moves less AP. This creates a very satisfying rhythm in combat, where you have to plan out your AP usage accordingly to utilized your strongest skills. Contributing to the fun of the combat, each monster skill is represented by a sticker, which can be freely removed and reallocated to any other compatible monster. This allows for some very fun build craft, and plenty of broken movesets. The story of the game is nothing crazy, but it's engaging enough to keep you moving. Story really shines, however, with the companions in the game (two in particular). And, of course, the game has a frankly incredible OST.This game feels fresh and fun in a genre that is often more than content to fall into trappings of a particular monster taming RPG series. Cassette Beasts is a truly incredible game. I have fallen for the game, head over heels, and I cannot possibly recommend it enough.

_childDocuments_.review: First impressions after 8 hours are as followsPros:- enemy scaling and AI can be adjusted on the fly (also max difficulty is definitely a challenge)- type matchups are unique instead of multiplying damage, leading to less sweeping even against lower level enemies- the player gains levels instead of monsters, meaning freshly caught monsters can immediately pull their weight- HMs are replaced by moves your character uses in the open world- shinies have different types and aren't just recolors- moves can have additional bonus perks like scaling based on Max HP instead of Melee Attack, bonus Exp gained, chance at higher priority, refunds AP- equip many moves including passives that can trigger at the start of a fight or on other conditionsCons:- open world can be confusing since it isn't linear like Pokemon- open world puzzles are at times finicky since they are based on physics in a game with a fixed top down perspective- minor 'performance' issues, game initially stutters a bitfeel free to ask for info in the comments.

_childDocuments_.review: it's good and i do recommend it, but there's definitely a few problems. first, the good everyone mentions is rly good. the music is shockingly good, the monster designs are great, the characters are a little 1.5 dimensional but are still very enjoyable with overall pleasant art. when the game opens up, the world feels really fun to collect stuff in. the story is alright, it has some very charming subplots and the ending is good, but everything working up to the payoff is pretty shallow. the main problem with the game, for me, was that it is too open ended. i feel like i stumbled upon almost everything i was supposed to do, which i think to some players that's great, but i didn't feel like i discovered anything, i just wondered over to the next open-world-collectible/miniboss. the world is very diorama-esc, which makes it feel very... game-y. again, this likely really appeals to some players, but it made it hard for me to feel emotionally invested in almost anything in the game, and it seems like the game wanted me to be invested. i never felt a narrative arc, no sense of escalation or pressure, just wandering around finding stuff until the game says i found enough stuff to unlock the final last stuff to beat the game. the villain is present here and there but in the most indirect ways, almost every goal of the game is just to gather more resources, do little platforming puzzles (that were fun enough, if a little stale towards the end), or go fight X thing. because it can be done so open ended-ly, they all have to just be kinda hanging out in plain sight, and i started to get serious open-world-game-fatigue.this is not helped by the fact that the game tries to guide you via the level curve of certain areas, but by the midway point you can go most places as it is very open ended, which creates the problem that pokemon gold/silver had: the beginning is strangely hard as it tries to bottleneck you into the areas where you first level up, and then the mid to late game is suddenly incredibly easy once you start to outpace the remaining sections in levels. the post game it gets a little bit harder again, but strategy in the game is WAY more free-from than pokemon, which at first is really fun as you get to handcraft kinda broken strategies by holding onto all moves (stickers) and applying them to the appropriate CBs, with some pretty absurd (and not the best balanced) passives. However, this gets old when you realize the opponents do not have the same access to strategy, or else they too could create CBs that have like a 20% chance to instantly nuke your first starting CBs and maybe even you or your partner. so by the time you get to the end game, you will likely know a few nigh unbeatable strats if your CBs are in a remotely similar level range as your opponent.overall, i'm critiquing the game a lot despite the fact that it is really pleasant to play, just because some of the core design detracts so much from what is good about the game for certain players. it's good to set your expectations accordingly. i honestly still recommend it to pretty much anyone: the music, the visuals, the area design, the side quests, collecting monsters, building your character, all of that stuff is incredibly fun. the game manages to be very funny as well. but if you aren't a huge open world fan, keep that in mind.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're on the fence about getting Cassette Beasts, my advice is to go for it, because I genuinely believe it's the absolute best creature collector game on the market right now. This is something extremely special, the kind of game that you look back on and wish you could experience it for the first time again.With that said, SPOILERS AHEAD!I just got this game like, a week or so ago, and I've played it every day since. I'm pretty confident that I've done about everything there is to do- beat the game, got every achievement, maxed out friendship with every companion, faced postgame bosses, gotten five-stars on all 129 monsters, and yet, I still really want to keep playing. I can already tell Cassette Beasts has serious replay value, not because it has a lot of variation between each playthrough, but because it's just that charming of a game. I would have to seriously reach just to think of a single flaw, there's almost nothing in the game that isn't executed perfectly.I'm struggling to think of which part of the atmosphere to talk about first- the art, or the music, because both of them are just fantastic and really pull everything together.Art: The artstyle of the overworld is totally adorable, and I love it. I don't really know how I could describe it, but something about the comfy and high quality art just makes the world feel very alive. I'm a sucker for pixelart, and I'm an even bigger sucker for those animated sprites that every single one of the creatures has- AND every single one of the fusions. Seriously, I don't even know how that was pulled off, but I'm not complaining. Another detail I really enjoyed is how different the style of every character feels- it really backs the concept of everyone being pulled from different worlds and times and whatnot.Music: I don't think there's a single bad track in the game, and I really appreciate how each one has a version with lyrics. A surprise for sure, but a welcome one- not at all common in creature collectors in my experience, but it just works so, so well. The seamless transition into the lyrical version of the battle themes whenever you use fusion, makes every fusion just feel special. Especially in the Archangel battles- goosebumps! Some of my favorite battle music ever, I was crossing my fingers throughout my entire playthrough that I'd be able to have rematches against those things, so I could experience that backing music again and again.Luckily, the gameplay does match the atmosphere, in that it's also of great quality. Battles are well-paced and fun, featuring a wide variety of moves and creatures to build a team out of. The fact that just about every battle is in a 2v2 format helps a lot, allows you to work with a lot more strategy than you usually could. Each creature has a pretty huge movepool, and the stickers mechanic makes it so that you can get really creative with sets, and switch between them as necessary. There's even stickers for passive effects you can apply to your creatures in battle, which quickly became one of my favorite things.The fusion mechanic is PHENOMENAL. I don't really know what I expected, as I went in blind, but it ended up being one of my favorite parts of the game by a country mile. The fact that you can fuse any of the two creatures, out of a roster of 120+, is still crazy to me even after I've beaten the game. Fifty hours in and I still rub my hands together menacingly every single time I fuse, contemplating which high-AP move I'm going to clobber the opponent with while that vocalist works magic in the background.Also, I haven't tried any of the NG+ options yet (because I am afraid) but they all look extremely fun, and I appreciate having them. Definitely adds on to my plans to go for a second playthrough, not that I really needed any more reasons.Level design is pretty fantastic. Each area is unique and hosts quite a lot of critters, you'll be finding new ones pretty much everywhere you go, each one better looking than the last. The contrast between the areas is noticeable, but nothing feels out of place (especially given the plot and setting). I really enjoyed the mall, in particular, as it was genuinely pretty eerie in a liminal-spacey kind of way. I guess it SORTA helps that there's giant ripped up stuffed animals and ghosts everywhere. Other than that, my favorite spot would have to be the cafe, it's just a really nice environment, comfortable. I dig the friend who sells me healing items for a small handful of garbage scraps, the true MVP of the game.The bosses (the Archangels) are so very cool to me, because I felt exactly what the game was trying to get across with each and every one. A lot of them do, indeed, just feel wrong to look at, just as the characters state- and them all being in different art styles is extremely fun. Alice is probably going to give me nightmares, but oh well, what can ya do?I was only made aware of the existence of bootlegs pretty late in the game, but wow, what an awesome mechanic. It's something rare and special, but also very diverse and practical. The fact that almost any monster can be ANY type makes your options pretty limitless. Bootlegs aren't by any means common, but the odds are fair, and you're not going to be sitting around for days at a time trying to find one. 50 hours in and I've gotten around a dozen bootlegs, most of them in the postgame since that's when the Rogue Fusion battles where they're more common become a lot more frequent and necessary. Not entirely related to bootlegs, but another thing I can't get over is how every monster will swap to a new color palette when they change types- it's going to be REALLY hard to decide what to turn my Glitter Bootleg Carniviper into. How is this game so good? I also encountered that Carniviper with bullet dash, which I think should have killed it... which makes me think the devs made it so that you can't kill bootlegs before the battle starts. If this is the case, thank you so much, I nearly had a heart attack.Last thing about bootlegs, I messed around with candles for like an hour and a half trying to get an Astral Bootleg Traffikrab, only to run into one completely naturally. In other words, I used up all my luck for 2023 on this game.So, bugs. In my full playthrough of the game, I did run into a small handful of very minor ones, but nothing game breaking. I wouldn't at all say that these effected my experience in any negative fashion and none of them are a big deal, but I'd still like to bring them to the attention of the developers. I'll also note that my game did crash twice in my 50 hours of gameplay, but autosaves are really frequent so I literally lost no progress at all. Other than that, the game runs perfectly smooth with zero issues.BUG 1: When fighting a Salamagus, it died after using an attack, but its Roll Again then proceeded to activate after it had already died and left the screen.BUG 2: I have Dual Wield equipped onto my Ripterra, letting it use Smack twice in a row. In one instance, after the first smack, Ripterra died to contact damage, but my player character still went through with the second smack. Might be intentional, might not be, either way not a big deal.BUG 3: A little complex. A fought an Undyin swarm, and the fusion at the end consisted of a normal Undyin and a Beast Bootleg Undyin. The fusion used Ritual or some equivalent of it, and then upon death, the Ritual status was passed to the normal Undyin component. The Beast Bootleg then used Ice Wall, and while the effect was there, the wall itself did not visually appear.Ok, now with that done, I'd like to end off by saying this is one of the best games I've ever played. This is a must play for creature collector fans, there's literally NOTHING else like Cassette Beasts on the market right now. I'm extremely excited for future updates, and that DLC. Thank you for the experience that is Cassette Beasts.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not much one for reviews, and I haven't even finished the game as of doing this review but I feel the need to purely out of the amazing time i've had with this game so far to at the least reccomend this game HIGHLY. The entire world feels crafted to get you highly invested in the people on this island and their every day struggles and as of recent, quite a lot more on the rise and it works. Characters I thought I might get tired of are grew on me and maybe it's just getting older or experiences changing outlooks but I genuinely felt for the people of this island who have been isolated, pulled away from former lives that they can't go back to.The gameplay is everything you'd want in a monster collecting game and genuinely more than I was expecting out of this game to begin with, Typing and move typing is of great importance in this game, even moreso than most. fire moves hitting plastic types turns them into a poison type, fire types hitting metal melts them and that's only about 2 of the numerous reactions to typing that there are, not to mention it being a 2v2 fight for the most part which lends itself to more strategy and one of my favourite things in this game, Fusing. A VERY underutilised feature in these sorts of games, most of which are romhacks or fan made. Also just as a little side bar, the concept of every creature having bootlegs which you can find in any type makes the uniques of these games actually worth something more than a palette swap and for that I commend them and it adds many hours of gameplay if you're a person who loves collecting (which who are we kidding, it's monster collecting we're all on that bus.)The story so far has been good, I can't really divulge on much because a lot of it is just spoilers beyond the first 30 minutes in the game? But it's been enjoyable.Graphics are nice and all the beasties are really well designed, I haven't met one I've not liked yet and if I do then honestly I'd be surprised.It's not much of a super in depth review, but it's something. If you take anything from my random rambling on a review of a monster collecting game it's that this is one of the best of this genre and I HIGHLY recommend it. Don't go in expecting a gamefreak product because that's not what you're gonna get. There's glimpses of inspiration from many different parts of this genre (Digimon in transforming into the beasts, SMT and Persona in relationships, etc.) and to only hope for some complete rehash would be a disservice to the game. Pick this up if you got the 20 dollars to dip into, because it's worth the money.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a stellar monster battler with a wide open map and combat system – the game does not hold your hand in the best way. _childDocuments_.review: Like most 90s kids, I was obsessed with Pokemon. I had Pokemon videogames on N64 and Gameboy. I had Pokemon trading cards. I didn't even understand the concept of other countries existing or having their own cartoons but I watched a ton of the Pokemon anime. The formula of collecting and playing Pokemon was really fun, compelling, and addicting. I've had a Switch for years but none of the new Pokemon games have appealed to me. I haven't played a Pokemon game since X and Omega Ruby on 3DS. And even those didn't hold my interest enough to finish them. But I still think the monster collecting formula is really fun. Cassette Beasts takes the classic formula and introduces some interesting twists. One thing I really like about this game is how types can change mid-battle. For example, if you use a fire attack on a ice-type, it'll turn a water-type. Most of the battles are 2v2, so there's a lot of strategy in choosing to buff/defend your ally or trying to win via bruteforce by having both on the offensive (usually how I play because I'm a dumb caveman). Instead of playing with your Pokeballs to capture monsters, you use cassette tapes to record them.All of the monsters have interesting designs too. Sure, Skelevangelist and Bansheep will never have the name recognition of Pikachu but they look cool. The soundtrack in this game is really catchy too. It especially gets hype when the lyrics kick in during bossfights. Overall, I think this is a really fun RPG. I'm looking forward to the multiplayer update.

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely kind of regret not picking this game up sooner, it's really good. It's familiar enough to scratch the "monster collection RPG" itch but it branches out the mechanics in a very cool way.Pros:+ The battle mechanics feel great and rewarding to work with. I feel like I'm actually making strategies and stuff, versus "switching to a type advantage and clicking the move with the biggest number"+ The writing is also a surprising high point, I've been enjoying the concept and themes while also wanting to learn more about the world+ Boss fights are particularly good at showing off the engine, and highlighting synergies and strategies you can pull off+ Item system, especially for healing, strikes a good balance in terms of enforcing "how much can I explore before I have to go restock"+ Music rulesCons:- Some of the overworld platforming and physics stuff gets a little janky- Open overworld sometimes makes it a little hard to figure out where to go next; NPC rumors point you to quests, but don't give any feel for "what level should I be to go there." It's kind of easy to accidentally get overleveled by wandering around, as a result- It feels disproportionately hard to complete Eugene's quest in particular, compared to the other partner characters- The visuals might be kind of an acquired taste if you don't already have nostalgia for older-Pokemon-style sprite artNone of those critiques are enough to stop this game from being my current ongoing fixation, though.

_childDocuments_.review: Cassette Beasts is such a unique monster tamer experience! The world is filled with numerous adventures, puzzles, beasts, and companions you can romance! Play through storylines at your own pace with whichever companion you want to bring along. This game is perfect for a more casual player like myself who doesn't enjoy punishing death mechanics. You can flee from any battle, even if your flee attempt fails you get the option to leave the battle at the cost of losing a few ressources which can easily be regained.I cannot praise this games variety of storylines and puzzles enough! I am enthralled with the world of New Wirral and my passion for exploration has been renewed with this game.While I usually rely on wikis to help me through difficult quests in games, Cassette Beasts has made me choose to actively avoid seeking out any guides. This game has made me love discovering things on my own, and I'd encourage others to do the same.I love that we, the players, get to choose our companions moves in battle, allowing for more strategy and leaving less up to chance. While recording a beast, it cannot be knocked out, allowing you to try and try again should your recording attempt fail.The type chart is accessible in game at any time, yes even during battle! Unlike a game like pokemon, in which types only effect is a damage increase or decrease, Cassette Beasts type matchups have meaningful effects. If you attack an air type beast with a fire type attack, the air beast will gain a damage absorbing air wall. Attack a metal type beast with a poison attack and it'll be coated, dealing more damage to your own beasts when either party uses a melee move on the coated beast. This makes strategy all the more fun!

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished the game and to say it was worth every penny, would be an understatement. I originally bought it to try and bring the old spark I felt while playing the old Pokemon games, but it was so much more than that.It has a simple, but enjoyable story easy to follow, to the point I didn't read a lot of the dialogue at the start but was still able to quickly grasp the world around me and become immersed.Combat is satisfying with AI who actually pose a challenge especially so far with the post game content, along with the unique typing and how each type can effect each other, stat changes, unique moves that change the fight significantly really allow for some really significant builds.The game allows you to go where you want and unlike another monster catching game that tries to do the same, you really can choose your path, there are places that have much stronger monsters but I never once felt underleveled or overleveled just doing the missions I ran into,  which allowed me to constantly changed my team and enjoy so many different builds.It's really a masterpiece as another reviewer put it, its if Gamefreak still loved to make Pokemon, it's a passion project that really shines through and if you loved Pokemon back when you were younger this is a must have, can't wait to 100% it <3

_childDocuments_.review: Cassette Beasts is an excellent game that made Pokemon look bad by comparison for me. Has a completely different style and vibe with a melancholic, 'comfy' feeling to play. Very enjoyable both if you're looking for a Pokemon alternative or just a solid, fun RPG.-Strong story and setting; surprisingly melancholy tone despite its colorful idea. NPC companions that are all enjoyable to have around (and can be romanced!).-Clever battle system: Type advantage causes unique status effects instead of extra damage, most major bosses using tricky strategies rather than just raw numbers.-Under-the-hood: Leveling is much less annoying than in Pokemon, allowing you to freely switch between team members and experiment without having to grind. Along with that, there is an automatic level scaling system that you can adjust heavily in the settings. You can also adjust AI difficulty, and after beating the game you unlock randomizer and Nuzlocke settings.-Charming monsters: The Mons you can encounter are a lot more 'out-there' than what Pokemon would allow, and are universally unique and enjoyable. Split evolutions abound as well, letting you personalize your team.-Better open world than Scarlet & Violet because it actually scales.-Postgame is a little repetitive, and ropes player into challenges they are probably not prepared for yet-Certain mechanics are gated behind optional quests that may be overly long or obscure to find-Bootlegs, shiny equivalents with unique types, are still obnoxiously rareAll in all, highly recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Cassette Beasts

_childDocuments_.review: Really good and innovative monster catching game. Takes a while to get going but it has unique mechanics, monster design, combat system, and a distinct brand of humor. Really love how you get to pick your evolution path on some of the monsters. I hope to see an expansion or second game with more than 120 beasts eventually.EDIT: I've played way more and am essentially in the endgame/postgame content now. I saw a criticism on Reddit about this game being grindy and repetitive so I figured I'd share my response here as well as it may be a factor to those on the fence: Grindiness applies to endgame/post-story content only, and it's a good thing in my opinion. The main story/campaign is not grindy at all and having stuff to do long term after you finish the main quests like hunting bootlegs (shinies), ranger bounties/quests, getting all of your trainer companions to 5 hearts, and beating harder versions of the captains (gym leaders essentially) changes this game from being an ~16 hour game to 50+ hours. I think it's very good for the player to have reason to pick it back up after they've done the story. A note on bootlegs, this game's version of shinies, they are more exciting as they are a different element from their baseform and have a different moveset and higher chance of getting rarer versions of moves. Moves in this game are called stickers and they're much more modular than other monster catching games as you can peel them off and put them on different monsters that can use the move and there's a rarity system for random bonus effects to each move.This game is also the perfect Steam Deck game, which is the cherry on top for me.

_childDocuments_.review: One of my fav game in years. Pros: - Cute pixel art graphics.- Open world works great. The game can get easy as you become stronger than certain areas, but I did not care: I had creatures to evolve and the fights can be quick enough that It was not a problem. - Exploration is fun. There are secrets to discover and map abilities to unlock. - The story is also interesting and delves into some interesting existentialist questions. - Great variety of creatures to evolve and develop. - Creatures can be modified considerably. Lots of fun combos to try and put together- So many types vs types effects. Looks overwhelming, but I learned them fairly quickly and they add a lot to the fights and strategies- Not too long. I finished the game in 35 hours. I wanted more when I was done, which is rare for me. I usually rush to finish a game in order to start a new one. (There are so many interesting games to play)Cons:- hardcore gamers will find the game too easy.

_childDocuments_.review: I saw a lot of people recommending this game as a Pokémon like. It was enough to sell me on the game, but now that I've played it, I actually take issue with this description. This game is far more than an indie clone, it is inspired by that genre of game but does more to be innovative and unique to the series than any main line Pokémon game has ever tried to do.From charming sprites, great and well implemented dynamic music, interesting monster design, a refreshing take on type matchups, good characterisation and a story that isn't forgettable, this game would be worth the price of a triple A game that a certain, Nintendo Entity might produce and then some. So much so that I actually feel a little guilty for buying it in a sale!Pros:- Refreshing take on combat, Type Advantages and Disadvantages are far more 'strategic'- Great sense of humour interwoven within the world, from funny monster names to the move 'Bad Joke'- Music is well composed, catchy and dynamically adapts to whether there are any fusions up- Sprite Work is well done- Cassette/Retro theme is well executed, and fun to experience. Items and mechanics are appropriately named- Remaster (Evolve) criteria are unique and interesting- Metroidvania style world exploration with abilities allowing you to explore more and moreCons:- Game can't decide what type of achievements it wants to give you, you get 5 achievements in the space of 10 minutes for breathing, and then there's one that will require near enough 100 hours of gameplay- End game options could be a little more diverse to make grinding 5* a little more invigorating- Some movement bugs, one of the stations doesn't like you going right straight after exiting, one of the other stations sometimes won't let you leave it because the loading zone (ironically) doesn't load- Dying feels very punishing, especially as a lot of the captains/archangels won't clue you into their gimmick until you fight them, leading you to be trapped in a very frustrating situation. It never looks good to see 8000 pieces of material disappear.All in all, this game is amazing and I've been absolutely addicted to it since I picked it up, the game oozes love and effort from every orifice, and if you pick this up as an RPG fan, you will not be disappointed.
_childDocuments_.name: Cassette Beasts

_childDocuments_.review: Or, you know, being frustrated to the point of putting the game down. The reason that monster catching games, like Pokemon or Dragon Quest Monsters, work is that there  consistent and well explained rules. Things are balanced around these rules and the player, through either trial and error or type matchup charts, can quickly glean what they need to to succeed consistently.Cassette Beasts, as the developer fully admits, intentionally made these type matchups difficult to understand, which is frustrating. For example, I found a cute lion puffball that I wanted to use, sadly it seemed weak to literally everything. Fire? Yep. Wind? Yep. Poison? Yep. Astral? Sure. Gonorrhea? Probably. It was a liability to even have around.And that sort of unbalanced nature pervades the core of the gameplay. You can create walls, but that requires a) a for you to sacrifice 20% of your health, b) use up your turn's action points, c) use up your only action per turn, and d) make sure your wall type isn't "weak" to anything the opponent has as a single hit from them will destroy your wall. And the wall only lasts for three hits- and there are a lot of moves that hit multiple times (or bosses that one hit walls anyway). At that point, why even have defensive options? Stat boosts are the same way. They take up a turn, require action points, and are generally not worth the damage you would have done if you had just attacked.Just overall, the gameplay is poorly tuned. Sure, your character level informs how powerful the monsters you use are, so  you can use any monster once you catch it-  most base monsters have terrible stat ratios, so end up being worthless to use until remastered. Sure, you can change the moves your monsters know, but a) most are pretty worthless and b) not every monster can use every sticker thereby limiting what you can actually do with it. Sure, you get a partner to help out, but every one of them is basically pigeonholed into using a specific monster.The gameplay is very mediocre. But the art is nice! I do like the art! Is the art worth the price of admission? Not really, because you still have to play the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Cassette Beasts is to Pokèmon what a good cover is to one of your favorite song, intimately familiar while being it’s own jam.The art is stellar, the combat system is deep, and the music is a vibe.Spent two long play sessions making my way through the main story, and have continued to hop in to enjoy both the authored and procedural post-game content. And, with only 120 monsters to catch, I might actually do something I haven’t done in a ‘Mon game since I was a kid, and “catch the all”.There is DEFINITELY a bit of a learning curve about the type matchups, which here take the form of a dizzying number of buffs and debuffs instead of simple “not very effectives” and “super effectives”. Thankfully, the game has great UI around each move, so you can get a rough idea of whether you’re about to hit the enemy hard or shoot yourself in the foot.The “sticker” system is also kind of ridiculous, allowing a level of customization that similar games can’t possibly compete with.High marks all around.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't think I've ever written a Steam review before, but this game is a must buy! I went in out of pure curiosity after seeing a recommendation online - with no idea what to expect - only to find myself completely obsessed.The combat is intuitive and fun, with a level of customisability I haven't seen before. The characters have wonderful designs that you can tell came from a place of passion. All of the game's companions have interesting personalities that are really allowed to develop on account of the abundance of companion-unique dialogue. The story (which I still haven't even finished by the way, I just had to get a recommendation out) is super compelling, subverting your expectations and playing around with some really cool concepts. I found that the difficulty of the puzzles was a tad low (at least so far), but that this didn't detract from the clever ideas and designs put into play; in fact, it felt like the devs struck a kind of perfect balance which always kept you from toiling for ages to find a solution, but still often made you actually think. Adding to this, due to the endless options for battle loadouts, combat difficulties can always be overcome with a little creativity, which is really rewarding. This game felt super friendly to all skill levels/levels of play! I could keep listing pros, but really, I think it's best I hold my tongue and let you craft your own experience with the game. I honestly think the tiny Bytten Studio deserve some serious respect for achieving this with such a small team. I wish you guys the absolute best in any future projects - I'm definitely gonna stick around for them!

_childDocuments_.review: Cassette Beasts starts off executing well on 'quirky, progressive indie game' staples; the sorts of character designs, colour palette, musical style (done particularly well), retro touches, and implied values that suggests are all there. The game definitely wears its heart on its sleeve with respect to those values, with a modernised take on monsters types seeing things like plastic types being converted to poison types by fire attacks, and an enemy group of what are apparently vampires that turn out to be estate agents looking to monetise an otherwise cooperative society. That's a good thing in my opinion, contrary to a couple of the usual troglodytes crying about the game being 'woke' in negative reviews. Better than bland, say-nothing media.It's not all style, though: the game seems to have a really good amount of substance from what I've played so far. The battle system is very solid and comes with all sorts of options. The decision to have type advantages and disadvantages cause various unique effects rather than numerical bonuses is excellent (even if it does mean it's taking me a while to learn them all!), and the action point system combined with highly modifiable, interactive movesets has made even early fights pretty interesting. There are plenty of monsters to collect, and several different types of special fights beyond the usual wild monsters and other collectors, with ranger captains (effectively, gym leaders), rogue fusions (the fusion system doesn't seem that big an aspect of the game for players, but makes for good enemies), and 'archangels' as particularly strong bosses.So far the world is the only thing I've got mixed feelings on. In concept, the setting is pretty cool, but in practice exploring has been somewhat underwhelming. The overworld graphics don't mesh together too well, with pixel-sprite characters, very blocky but technically 3D environments, and jarring examples of fully 3D items like movable rocks in those environments. The rest of the game's art is good - I like the pixel art and animation for the monsters, and I like the drawn character designs, but the overworld isn't very cohesive. It also feels a bit artificial with everything being so rectangular, and while a good amount is packed in and exploration is made dynamic through puzzles and verticality, the actual distances between locations in the overworld is small, making things feel cramped. The process of moving around the world is pretty good (particularly the use of movement abilities obtained by collecting specific monsters), and it's not lacking in things to do, but it could feel so much better if it spread itself a bit wider.Overall I'm having a really good time. I don't know how deep the game goes yet, but I'm enjoying what's there a great deal.PS. A couple of things in the UI could be clearer: showing numerical HP values in battle would help, as would giving numerical values for the way that stat-altering moves work. It's a little difficult to know how much value you are getting out of non-damaging moves because only durations are ever shown explicitly, not magnitudes.

_childDocuments_.review: Cassette Beasts is probably my favorite creature collector game out there. The music is phenomenal in this game, and I listen to the soundtrack often, (please add Arrow of Time and Your Inception to Spotify I'm begging.) Like I would tell you to get this game for the music alone, and the way music is used to enhance scenes, areas, battles, characters is wonderful. I love the design of both characters and creatures. And the fusion mechanic is so incredibly cool and actually useful (unlike another creature collector that attempted it that just padded out battles with bigger health, this game actually brings some strategy to its fusion mechanic.) Not to mention when a fusion takes place, the vocals of their songs kick in?! It really hypes up any battle honestly. The story and world of New Wirral are so interesting with the eldritch lore of archangels and the designs of them being just chef's kiss. I adore the companions (Meredith is best girl) and their side quests too. Stories of people finding love and getting by in a new world, helping each other, as well as the conflicts with other people stranded are so interesting. The game feels very post-apocalyptic (though I'm sure there's a better term to describe it that I can't quite place) and gives it a cool atmosphere with things from different worlds being pulled in and appearing as wreckage (ships, stores, etc.) I won't spoil the ending of the story, and while I think it was very good, I'd love for this game to have a couple more different endings or even variations of the same ending. The endgame is also great with some cool fights (including a boss that has my favorite song in the game tied to them). It can be pretty repetitive, but they mix in some interesting endgame quests here and there among the repetitive bounties. As well as the ritual candle grind for bootleg or "shiny" creatures. I don't think they really take away from the game though, and you can have fun just playing through the story and fights. I'm a completionist so I'll get all the achievements one day, may just take me a while. If you've made it this far into my "review" of Cassette Beasts, thanks for reading! I feel like its more so just me gushing about how much I love this game. I look forward to also playing Lenna's Inception, and since your here I'll talk about just a couple more things. My favorite fight is against Ianthe, it was so difficult and I really had to come up with some ideas to beat that fight (i also went into every fight probably a little underleveled which I think added to the challenge. So I'm not sure how much overleveling takes away from the experience) I also played Piers of the Unknown, which I thought was a very cool little side story. The puzzles are amazing, but outside the final boss I think the other fights in it are a little meh. The creatures it added are so good though especially with the theme of the DLC. Like the creature designers in the whole game just go so hard. I love seeing what fusions of monsters come out to look like to. That's all though folks! Thanks again for listening to my spiel!

_childDocuments_.review: Cassette Beasts dares to ask the question: "What if the Monster Catching genre was good?"- double battles are standard- a mon doesnt need to be isolated to capture it- bosses ACTUALLY USE STRATEGIES AGAINST THE PLAYER- level scaling that you can adjust how you like- pronouns in character customization- storys really good- hint system for finding secrets you may have missed- rewards for capturing and releasing mons- that weird sort of HD Pixel-Voxel Hybrid that some games have to keep the charm of pixels without sacrificing graphics- YOU CAN BE GAY- the type chart isn't "Water does more damage to Fire" they're all ♥♥♥♥ like "Water douses Fire, temporarily lowering Attack stats" or "Fire melts plastic, releasing toxic fumes and temporarily changing them to a Poison type"- "shiny" equivalent have slight mechanical differences- when youre trying to catch a mon you cannot KO it, so no dealing with False Swipe ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥literally better than pokemonedit: lmao hoes mad

_childDocuments_.review: If you don't like the vocals for the songs,  There's multiple settings pages that you can navigate with the Page Down/Up keys.The combat system and the fusion mechanics are definitely great, and make it fairly distinct from a Pokemon-esque creature collector.The way that stats and moves are used for monsters is fantastic. I don't have to worry about monsters having really bad rolls on their stats or trying to do special things in order to get base moves that I want. Simply swapping moves in and out, as well as stats being static per monster & helper make it easier to create a base team that I want to play.In terms of completing the main story, the combat difficulty felt right for me. Even though you can accidentally go into higher level areas before you're ready, it's overall fairly straightforward. The puzzles in the main quest were a bit difficult for me but I quickly found answers on their Discord server.The grind for 100% completion and hyper-optimized movesets does seem long though, if you're interested in doing that.

_childDocuments_.review: I super duper recommend this game! It's so good in fact that I've been itching to do another play through here recently! As a Pokemon fan, it very much scratches that itch of finding and collecting new creatures, but with a lot of unique twists! The story is pretty straight forward but definitely has a number of complexities that were deep enough to tug at my heart strings near the end, especially when it came to the concept of letting go. The overworld navigation is simplistic but definitely gets the job done and I love how, despite the map being rather small, it feels a lot bigger than it really is because there's a new thing around almost every corner!Easily my favorite portion of the game is finding ways to break it by adding certain abilities to your monsters. I'm not sure what the 'meta' is or anything or if the community has found a crazy new tech option but when I played, the crazy combo I went with was to give a monster 1 copy of Headshot, 1 copy of Echolocation or any move that applies Multi-Target, and then as many copies of Random Starter as possible! If you did this with 4 monsters and alternated between them, you could easily melt quite literally any enemy!Beyond the wacky builds you can go with, the bosses were at times very challenging yet never really felt unfair. A handful of the bosses also had art styles that were wildly different from the normal style, creating this really otherworldly artistic feel that popped out spectacularly. Aside from a slightly lackluster start where you're more restricted on what you're able to do, once the game does allow you to start branching out, it's a nonstop roller coaster of fun that I cannot recommend enough!

_childDocuments_.review: I've often thought that the closer any piece of art gets to perfection, the greater my temptation to nit pick the few things I didn't like. That being said, let me spend a boring few paragraphs explaining why Cassette Beasts is not only certain to end up in my top five of 2023 but also extremely likely to be my game of the year.In the ceaseless war between people who think games are about writing and people who think games are for playing, I am very much in the latter category. It is therefore a testament to how well this game is written that the first thing I think to praise is the writing. I adore the characters and the world and didn't skip through a single cutscene or conversation. That is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ unprecedented.The combat feels great, with enough different viable strategies to keep the pokemon nuzlockers (mad people) entertained and an easy mode for people who don't want to grind like a coffee machine on coke.Turning away from mechanics, tho, I love the queer representation. The characters feel like real people from all walks of life with their own goals and personalities. Frankie is adorable, and my only complaint is that she can't be a companion. There are so many things I want to say in praise of the story and writing that I kind of can't because it requires spoilers. Let's just say that my little leftie heart sang when the Team Rocket stand-ins were real-estate agents trying to bring the scourge of capitalism to the land.Okay so where are these nits I picked? Despite what I said about the optional easy mode, I actually still think the game gets a bit grindy. I hit a wall about half-way through where strategy wasn't really helping and enemy levels seemed to be increasing waaay faster than mine. I chose to play through the whole game exclusively with Kayleigh (swoon) and I'm guessing switching out partners frequently would have made the grind even worse. Some later enemies can get a bit damage spongy, especially the rogue fusion bounty quests that are a massive chore to fight.The biggest and grizzliest nit tho is that I realised early on that dialogue choices didn't seem to matter widdly wong. I started keeping a tally of how many times it felt like my choice changed the story.Once.Thing is, I'm not asking for branching narrative. If the devs want to keep control on the story and the protagonist, then I have no issue with removing entirely the illusion of choice. What really gets on my plums is the fantasy of control being cruelly whipped away when I foolishly dreamt my input might matter. It's jarring because the game starts so open ended. Choose pronouns, design an avatar, pick a name, a starter, choose your partner and their monster, but it's so unrepresentative of the rest of the game.The truly baffling part is that they put so much work into designing not just every monster but a unique fusion for every combination of monsters as well as dozens of unique lines said by different companions in different situations. So what, there's only one way to respond to the main villain in the climactic showdown, but there's enough time to write a line that Kayleigh says when I sprint across a narrow bridge telling me to be careful? Sweet yes, but it feels like misplaced effort.Look, none of this is a deal breaker, and the ending is spectacular. It ties up everything nicely and  made me genuinely emotional. This game is so worth your time and I fully expect to replay it.As I said at the start, the closer a game gets to perfection, the more I want to bully it until it gets the rest of the way. That's what you are Cassette Beasts, you're my star pupil and I give you a hard time because I know what you're capable of. Now take this A- and go do something even better.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best games of 2023 by a long, long mile. Combat is interesting and unique, the dialogue is intriguing, the plot is thick, and the world is rich.Strategic planning is a necessary factor in the game, the capture system is mind, the mysteries are fascinating, and above all, the game has incredible graphics and a killer soundtrack.Customisation does lack a little in the clothing department, however, the ability to set your own pronouns, have the ability to wear a head scarf or face mask makes this game a stand-out amongst other monster-catchers.The game is, at no point, overtly difficult, or a cakewalk, and with tweakable difficulties and scaling, this game is incredibly user-friendly to any who wish to hop in and play. With an easy modding system, multiple save slots, and unique creatures, I severely misjudged just how complex and wonderful Cassette Beasts is.An easy 9/10 - my only critique being the somewhat dull Bootleg (this game's version of Shiny) hunting can be, even with late-game items.If you have the money to spend, then definitely consider this your top-most priority.

_childDocuments_.review: I am clearly one of the outliers here, but I cannot recommend this game. I am a huge fan of most creature collectors, from Dragon Quest Monsters to World of Final Fantasy, Digimon, and, of course, Pokemon. This game just seems kind of like a thematic mess to me. First and foremost, picking your starter tape basically explains nothing about it besides "Whats your style," In every creature collection game in existence this is the pinnacle moment of choosing your first partner, in Cassette Beasts in an afterthought. Unfortunately, for what I have played, that's what every character, emotion, or even combat experience feels like, an afterthought.Combat: Slow animations, way to many abilities, having a partner in the first place?Movement: Movement is janky as well, I know it gets better as you get further but its such a turn off to even attempt. Creature designs: One thing creature collector games hammer into you in a digestible way repeatedly is creature types and what beats what. You don't need a novel explaining the mechanics. I have no idea what my first two tapes were until way later on in the battles. I had no idea what things were weak too etc. Secondly the creature designs felt off. Games like Pokemon and Digimon do a really good job of things, starting off small in silhouettes or designs, even matching what spawns to the environment. Cassette Beasts has a giant ass Lunar New Years Lion dog spawn in one of the first areas. It's large and intimidating, doesnt fit the area and also offers no sense of a challenge. Music: Finally the reason people are probably wanting to play this in the first place. Why is it soooooo slow. It's almost like a Minecraft vibe but that doesnt fit here. You are going out on an adventure warding off wild monsters while fighting archangels and you have this really slow lofi music. Going back and having a discussion after fusion and fighting what seems like some higher being with lofi in the background just isnt the vibe. The Hayley Williams-sounding girl lyrical tracks playing while you are listening to characters and reading slowly become grating as well. For a smaller team the game seems like it was an ambitious project, there is strong designs and concept foundations but they just did not land the mark for me. Too much was done without any sense of world cohesion or the way it feels to a player.
_childDocuments_.name: Cassette Beasts

_childDocuments_.review: Cassette Beasts brings back the old nostalgia of monster-catching games, turn-based combat, and pixel graphics. Being an open-world game, there are limitless possibilities on how one may approach and progress through the game. There were a lot more puzzles than I had thought initially after going through the demo version, but these were challenging/engaging in their own way as there are no guides as of writing this review. Overall, really enjoyed my first play through and recommend towards those interested in these types of games!The soundtrack and pixel-graphics are what had drawn me into this game in the first place, it did not disappoint. Appropriate and stellar soundtracks hyped up and really brought out the tension/emotions that Bytten Studio wanted to convey during particular cutscenes. It really did feel like I was on a journey with all the friends that we have made along the way, even if it was not long.
_childDocuments_.name: Cassette Beasts

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic Monster Catcher/Fighter. Really enjoyed the type chart more than in its contemporaries, all battles being Duo battles made for more interesting fights and boss battles, making status moves and team wide moves feel great to happen to have on a monster. The "shiny" system in this game is wonderful and fulfilling to hunt for in both an aesthetic and competitive angle. The story is pretty cute, the post game is plentiful, I really have few bad things to say about the game. It's cute, it's cheap, it's everything the "main" Monster Catcher wishes it was.
_childDocuments_.name: Cassette Beasts

_childDocuments_.review: Great game overall. One thing I really love is how it respects your time and redirects it to personal goals. You can beat the game quickly, or if you're looking for the perfect build it could take very very long. I love how they do the progression system with special abilities (no spoilers). It's a clever system, which feels like the design was from those who were pokemon and digimon fans and put all the quality of life features you'd want to see in the game. Amazing work! _childDocuments_.review: I want to start off this review with a clear statement:I wholeheartedly recommend this game to anyone who has ever played and enjoyed a monster capture game (most likely Pokemon).That being said, I want to focus on negatives first that really grinded my gears (literally) since I didn't see a lot of criticism in other reviews. This focuses mostly on the post game content so minor (mechanic) spoilers there.While the main story was absolutely delightful and meatier than I expected (about 20-25 hours), the post-game content and achievement hunting absolutely dropped the ball for me. I am generally not a completionist but this game gripped me real good which is why I wanted to set out to 100% it. However, completing this game takes an absurd amount of grinding and, most of all, luck. There are missable achievements, you need to get a bootleg version (basically "shinies" of this game) of every typing and there is one specific monster you need one specific bootleg of to get one specific achievement. This is in my opinion a punch to the face for anyone who wants to complete this game, especially on one save file.There is an items you can buy later in the game to mitigate >some< of the rng by using it, then sacrifice  a monster and the next special encounter you trigger has a bootleg of either the species of the monster you sacrified or the typing. However, this items takes 50 of the end-game currency to buy and for each special encounter you beat you get 1. Needless to say, this is an extremely exhausting process that doesn't respect the time of the player. I wish there was some metric that would increase the amount of that currency you get over time, maybe scaling with your player or difficulty level or something.I currently have every achievement not tied to luck and it took me about the same time of post-game grinding as it took me for the main story.Other minor criticisms I have are the lack of a "fast battle" option by either making text and animations faster or have them be skipped entirely. This ties in to my former point of the (end)game being too grindy and time consuming to the point this stuck in my head. Additionally I felt like the game was overall too easy, You didn't really need any strategy most of the time (Disclaimer: I only played on the second highest difficulty, maybe if I had bumped it up there would be some insane difficulty spike).So, this block of negatives and criticism was pretty large. Why do I still recommend the game? Because most of this pertains to the end- and postgame and it only really affects completionists which many people are not. So if you just casually love monster collectors, as stated before, this game is absolutely worth the money. The characters are cute and colorful, the story is pretty good, the soundtrack slaps hard and the monsters are really well designed. The game has a built-in nuzlocke (monsters stay dead when they die) and randomizer feature and even a speedrun timer. Little things like these are absolute delights to me.So yeah, buy the game and enjoy it.

_childDocuments_.review: Completed, 8/10:Pros:-Music is great, and the way they activate or deactivate vocals depending on the situation works very well.-Monsters have interesting designs, and don't feel generic in the way many other Pokemon style games do-Fusion system is very interesting-Monsters tend to (for the most part) be balanced, and even if they're strong in one way, they'll be weak in another-Built in tools for special playthroughs unlocked after your first. (Tapes break permanently, defeat is game over, randomize monsters, types, and moves, and custom seeds.)-Two main stories that you can play through at the same time, that being both the rangers, and the Archangels.-Archangels tend to be actually dangerous, and can defeat your team if you're not careful, even with fusions.-The elemental system involving debuffs rather than straight damage multipliers is quite interesting.-Basically every monster is viable, since you can move the stickers (which are what gives each monster their moves) between tapes anytime you like.Cons:-Mobility system feels very weird, and doesn't tend to work that well. This mostly goes for the rolling ball and electric abilities-There are a few very overpowered strategies that, once discovered, make the combat extremely easy (Glasstain + Gambit + Fusion + Glass Cannon = instant win 99% of the time)-Fusion is made out to be something that's hard to pull off, but once you get a few upgrades, you can pretty much pop it whenever you want without worry of needing it again before you recharge.-Rangers were very underwhelming, and could be defeated without much effort, even without fusion. (Except for the ghost one, that one was just annoying.)-Battle animations can take forever, especially if there's multiple effects being applied to a monster, potentially even multiple times.

_childDocuments_.review: tldr: it's a good game! Cassette Beasts does a great job of adding more complexity to traditional monster tamer turn based rpg stuff without getting overcomplicated. Would recommend!Pros: -Fun monster designs! I'm a zoomer, so I don't really have a soft spot for the 80's vibes they're working with, but I really liked a lot of the monster designs in this game, especially the "hidden" evolutions.-Lots of "secret" monsters/evolutions/etc. I'm not normally a "catch 'em all" girl but I ended up getting 100+/128 monsters by the end of my playthrough, and if the postgame worked a little differently I probably would've put the time in to finish all 128!-Great character designs, decent writing, good music/aesthetics. I really enjoyed all the partners & ranger captains, and the boss designs especially were fun. The music can be a little repetitive (which is just what happens in rpgs like this, imo) but I really enjoyed it, especially because it's unique for a game to have lyrical music like this one.-Excellent battle system allows for a lot of playing around with teams/builds. There's a lot of screwy stuff you can do with passive abilities, type interactions, and the various move pools (especially when you throw the bootleg monsters into the mix). If you're a hardcore optimizer/someone who likes getting competitive in games like this, there's a lot to be done here (especially if you try a permadeath playthrough, I would assume)Cons:-Personally, I struggled to find a good difficulty setting; doing the side content/exploring led to me over-leveling, and I rarely felt challenged even after tweaking the settings up-The open endedness of the game made things feel kind of messy, especially when getting to the postgame. There *is* a substantial amount of content overall though!-Rewards for levelling/finding chests started feeling inconsequential by the mid/endgame-Because the 8 (spoiler) bosses don't really have types, and the ranger captains are a pretty loose theme, i didn't often feel like I had the opportunity to build teams for certain challenges. I would love more stuff like Monster Sanctuary's bosses, where you can really be rewarded for making an optimal lineup for a given boss.Overall I really enjoyed this game, and I appreciate that the devs included surprisingly comprehensive lgbtq options! I'll definitely come back for the DLC (and would def play a sequel someday). <3
