_childDocuments_.review: As a turn based monster-catching RPG,  is yet another take on the Pokemon-like games. However, it does not merely copy Pokemon and provides a fresh perspective with its fusion mechanics, move customization, fun art design, jamming music and zany story. While it has its flaws and a rather weak post-game, it is still a great time and worth playing through at least once for the story and seeing all the monsters. Simply put – it’s a good time.The game opens up with your character (which you can customize name, appearance, gender, etc.) becoming stranded on a new strange land with monsters. The first human you meet teaches you how to defend yourself by using a cassette player to turn yourself into a monster. She also demonstrates how to obtain new forms (i.e. monster catching) via recording said monsters.  The game is very tongue in cheek about how weird this method of obtaining monsters and battling them is and encourages you not to think too much about it.Eventually, as your new friend shows you around town, exploration opens up and you’re free to take on some quests. You can explore the world and try to become a ranger (like a gym leader in pokemon) by defeating other rangers, etc. Eventually the exploration leads to an encounter with a different kind of monster that the characters dub an archangel. These archangels are essentially elite monster boss encounters and stand out from the rest of the monsters. They cannot be recorded and their appearance is cryptic and rather creepy along with some odd dialog. There also seems to be a connection with the archangels and a way to escape the stranded world and so the adventure continues in a search for more archangels. Along the way, you meet yet more friendly trainers in your quest and can complete their character-focused side stories. Upon doing so, they want to share your goal of defeating the archangels and escaping the world as they become your trusted battle companion.Overall, it has a decent enough premise that provides reason to continue battling monsters with a goal to work toward. The characters are all interesting and there is plenty of character-based story telling within the plot as well for players who enjoy that kind of storytelling more than just a general overarching story.I really fell in love with the designs of the monsters and especially the music that played throughout. Harbourtown especially had me humming along as it stirred some nostalgic emotions within me. Sometimes I just sat in town vibing along enjoying the song. Whenever an archangel showed up I really loved anticipating what sort of craziness I was getting myself into next.There are 128 monsters + 1 bonus monster in the base game (excluding the arch angels) and they are all unique designs. As with many monster taming games, there are evolutions and branching paths but also some standalone monsters. In addition to these monsters, you can fuse any two monsters (including two of the same monster) with yet more unique designs and even names. There is a lot to take in!The world itself is cleanly designed with elevation, hidden switches, interactable objects, etc. Typically, I was able to explore the world and distinguish the monsters and interactable objects from the environment. There were some exceptions but the switches or monsters were intentionally camouflaged.My only gripe with the presentation is I did not see a setting to speed up battle animations. They’re enjoyable but get old really fast, needlessly extending the time battles (or even setup time from pre-battle skills).At its core, this is a game about collecting and battling monsters. There is also a stage in between with customizing the monster’s move sets with stickers. Every time a monster levels up (gains a star) it will earn a new sticker that can be equipped. You can also use the world’s currency to purchase more stickers, find them in chests, or even just grab a sticker from another monster (if compatible). It is very fun to plan out and customize a build to make a monster. There are a mix of passive and action abilities including abilities that trigger at the start of battle. Some combinations are extremely broken and will trivialize the game – but it’s fun to come up with solutions prior to then. Even the broken combination is fun to see at first, but I’d recommend not using it until the post-game as it does take the wind out of the sails of fun. As for stats and leveling up – the monsters only get more stickers and sticker slots as they progress down their evolution chain and ranking up. Stat growth and actual levels are only tied to the trainer. This makes it a lot more viable to switch out monsters for variety, although it can be annoying to shift the useful stickers around before you’re swimming in surplus.Battling is enjoyable and can be pretty strategic (outside of the broken sticker combination). I’ve found myself having to mix up strategies and skills rather than using the same build for every encounter. Some trainers or archangels have gimmicks that may make you have to play differently. Such reasons may include status effects or passive skills that hard counter your own, and even type advantage. Like pokemon, there are type advantage/disadvantage but instead of just doing more/less damage, there is always some kind of additional status effect applied. For example, a water type will give a health regen status to their opponent when attacking plant types. Collecting monsters was fun and for the most part not too difficult. No monster is missable, thankfully! However, obtaining the bonus monster is a bit too RNG dependent for my tastes as it essentially requires a very specific bootleg (this game’s version of shiny pokemon) monster. This was around when I started to really have criticism for the game which would only escalate with the post-game.I enjoyed my trek through the story which lasted perhaps around 30 hours. After that was the post-game where the game started to overstay it’s welcome and frustrate me. The additional story content, monsters, and rematches were welcome. But the “100 side quests” achievement is just an insanely needless grind with no respect for the player’s time. There is no reason to force a player to do 100 fetch quests just to see the end of 100% completion.  This number should have been reduced significantly to approximately just 10 and stick to only relevant story content. These quests consist of “kill X amount of monster”. “record X monster and get it to 5 stars”, “fuse these two monsters together”. Etc. It’s mind numbingly dull and I decided to just drop the game at this point and even passing on the DLC. At this point I had enough, sadly.Game runs fine.Operating System: Windows 10Processor (CPU): Intel Core i5-3570K CPU @3.40GHzGraphics Card (GPU): NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1070Memory (RAM) 16 GBWhile the post-game ruined my honeymoon with the game, I do still overall recommend the game. It’s a really nice story and a refreshing take on the monster catching and battling formula. I’d just advise to not bother with 100% completion if you try out the Ranger Sign Board and hate it as much as I did. It doesn’t get any better, in fact it just gets worse. Check out the post-game archangels/monsters/trainers then call it. Overall, despite a weak post-game, the ending itself was fine and it’s a really fun ride through an interesting world. I recommend any monster catching fan to pick this one up, sale or not.

_childDocuments_.review: Cassette Beasts' battle system is wonderfully in-depth, allowing the player to meticulously craft any number of surefire strategies to ensure victory against the numerous adversaries present on New Wirral. To speak of the island itself, exploring it is a satisfying process not unlike a Metroidvania; several of the creatures that the player can "Record" and add to their teams will grant the player new abilities that open up new possibilities for traversal and puzzle-solving. Additionally, these abilities are permanent additions; you'll always be able to use them, regardless of whether or not the creature in question is in your party, or even still in your collection.This game's soundtrack is phenomenal, featuring multiple songs with both vocal and instrumental variations that the game often swaps between dynamically in response to the player's actions. The first vocal theme you hear is practically guaranteed to make you stop playing for a minute or two, just to vibe. Personally speaking, I've wound up with at least three of the game's songs stuck in my head, on loop, and I'm certainly not about to complain.The game's cast of characters is a memorable collection of all-too-relatable personalities, and nowhere else does that fact shine brighter than in the six partner characters that fight alongside you on your journey. Each of them (yes, even the dog) has their own painfully familiar struggles that the player is able to be alongside them for and see them grow past in an extremely cathartic experience. And, for the hopeless romantics (such as myself) out there, yes, you're able to grow closer with your companions through your shared experiences and hardships, and, if you so choose, even romance one of them (aside from the dog, for reasons that should require no explanation), regardless of your selected gender.Unfortunately, this  bring us to...No game is perfect, but there have been games with enough upsides and few and small enough downsides that come close enough to ignore the issues they had. Unfortunately, while Cassette Beasts does have few negative points against it, the ones that are there are too glaring to avoid mentioning.If the player wishes to see all that the game has to offer, and isn't simply rushing towards the credits, they will inevitably have to go off the beaten path and grind to get there. This, unfortunately, holds especially true for witnessing the culmination of the companion characters' story arcs, as their bonds with the player grow as a result of experience points gained from battle (in a system that I can commend for preventing players from simply blitzing through all of the partners' conversations, but this feels like it went too far in the other direction). If you're like me, and want to see the most from all of these characters that you can, you'll be in for a number of extra hours pushing through battles that, after a point, do get repetitive, despite the well-put-together battle system.And then we have the big one,At the end of your journey, you've likely latched onto at least one of the companion characters, or quite possibly grown fond of all of them. Regardless, at the end of it all, you'll eventually shut down the game, and you won't see them again within their original context.  While I do understand what they were going for in writing this ending, it didn't land well for me, and I know full well that I'm not alone. It's this ending that took off at least a full two points from the game's final score, in my book.Regardless, there is always the realm of headcanon, if you find the ending as unsatisfying as I did. Overall, I do still recommend the game, as it's an excellently made experience, and though the negatives of it do hurt, it didn't erase the good times that I had with it.

_childDocuments_.review: I can't do anything but gush about this game. It feels like a mix of Pokemon, Digimon, and Persona with a hint of Undertale/Deltarune. The main antagonist group of the game, the Archangels, have amazing designs and fights. Puppetox cemented my love for the game. It's a great experience that I completely recommend for fans of Pokemon and the genre in general. If you really hate the '80s, appreciating art, and general feel-good stories, this game will probably feel cringe. It's earnest in its hopeful attitude about humanity and the capacity to share experiences with other people.Some of the highlights of the game, imo:- The beast designs are some of my favorite. Lots of creatures mixed with toys, urban objects, folklore, and other figments of human culture. If you hate objectmon, you'll be annoyed by it. But it works so well in the world of Cassette Beasts.- Partners are very likeable and have their own fun character quests. Kayleigh, Meredith and Felix are my favorites.- Engaging type matchup chart. It may be overwhelming at first, but I love it.- The leveling system is restricted to your MC and your partner. Partners will gain some exp when they're idle at the cafe, so level gaps are easy to close (plus items to level partners). Big win for not needing to manage exp gains for a party of 6+. Makes the grind less mind-numbingly grindy.- The moveset of each monster is fully customizable with the sticker system. There's a lot of flexibility thanks to the typeless moves adapting to whatever type your beast is.- Stickers can come in higher rarities that add additional effects -- mostly in the form of +1 Duration, +1 Slot, higher priority/speed, exp bonuses. Sometimes melee/ranged attacks will use a different stat in the damage calculation, making speed/hp/defense builds fun. Tanks can pack some power.- Everything about the bootlegs. Bootlegs are the shinies of this game and become fairly easy to find at end game. You get guaranteed bootlegs from the story and ranger board quests. You can see them on the overworld via different colors and static-glitch effects.- Dynamic difficulty and enemy AI sliders. I played most of it on Recommended, but bumped it up to Hard/Harder when in lower-level areas.- The literal 15,000+ possible fusions still keeps me entertained at over 100 hours of play time.- Mod support -- really helps to slot in global tape storage access and ways to further customize stickers.- The music is fantastic. You can disable song vocals from playing if you're like me and prefer instrumental tracksThe Only Con:- Wonky overworld physics -- boxes are wonky and overly reactive, but there aren't too many puzzles related to moving boxes.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fantastic indie monster-catching RPG with engaging combat and team-building mechanics. In the world of Cassette Beasts, monster are recorded on--you guessed it--magical tapes, which the player character then listens to in order to transform *into* the creature in question. A clever sticker-based ability system allows moves to be freely transferred between compatible creatures, while "chemistry"-based combat keeps things interesting with a bevy of (mostly) intuitive reactions between the various types. Rather than super-effective or weak attacks swinging battles wildly in different directions, combat is a strategic dance of managing status effects:Water extinguishes fire, lowering attack damage, but fire vaporizes water into steam that soothes and heals. Ice yields no reactions when attacking a fire type, but if an ice-type is attacked with fire, it will then melt into a water-type.Astral creatures gain additional action points when struck with any of the four basic elements (air, fire, water, earth) but suffer at the hands of “impure” compounds like plastic (AP drain) and metal (can only use attacks). My favorite is the earth and electric matchup: Earth types can “ground” electric types, reducing the scope and accuracy of their attacks; however, lightning will turn them into glass that still possesses the grounding properties of earth but can be chipped, littering the ground with shards that damage any creature that uses a melee ability, or completely shattered and destroyed by the “resonance” built up by certain metal or air attacks. The fact that combat is predominantly played out in 2-on-2 adds another layer of depth that requires players to delicately balance risk and reward as they choose their NPC companion and leverage those sidekicks' unique monsters and abilities. There's much more to the gameplay than what I've discussed above, but I'm already starting to get a bit long-winded, so I'll wrap up with some of my minor quibbles. The overworld, which the player can navigate using powers "recorded" from certain monsters, run the usual gamut of dashing/climbing/rock-crushing/etc., but the movement can feel clunky, especially when platforming is involved. There's also no way (as of the week after launch) to sort or filter stickers by type--an option that *is* available when browsing your library of monster tapes--making it kind of a slog to transfer moves between creatures after amassing a large collection of stickers. Those are my only complaints as I approach some of the final story bosses--otherwise, I'm enjoying the hell out of Cassette Beasts.

_childDocuments_.review: The premiere creature-collector at the moment, in my opinion. The game does a lot to iterate on the classic pokemon formula in ways that I think other contemporaries like Temtem failed to do. There's a wide variety of creatures that I'm excited to find, collect, and evolve. The world is fairly open and the quests are well placed. Regarding combat, I'm particularly fond of the interesting takes the game has that exemplify that iteration mentioned above. Moves have an action cost rather than "PP" that you accumulate and spend over the course of the battle. You can KO a trainer by overkilling a monster by a particular threshhold. The elemental rock paper scissors doesnt just "make move do more/less damage", but applies status effects, i.e. fire applies burn to poison types, water makes electricity types conductive (allowing single target attacks to hit multiple units). For someone who fell into the camp of "why use status moves over moves that do damage?" In other creature collectors, the game does a very good job of making statuses feel very impactful, and encourages experimentation. Being able to swap moves around freely between units also encourages creating "builds" for each of your monsters, which really appeals to me, personally.

_childDocuments_.review: I am only a couple of hours into the game but it already brings a lot of new stuff to the table.The designs that are not just animal + element, the setting, the story with it's hints of deeply unsetteling elements, the ACTUAL open world(unlike SOME creature collector that promised an open world but didn't really deliver, even though it should, considering it's budget) and a very interesting way it let's elements interact with each other(instead of just 2x or 1/2x the damage, certain elements get certain advantages/disadvantages when hit/hitting specific other ones).The demo had me curious, but the finished product seems to be far greater than what I expected and I am looking forward to seeing all it has to offer.

_childDocuments_.review: I purchased this game the day it released on steam, and I've been so busy playing that I kept putting off writing a review, and now pretty much everyone has already said the things I wanted to say- so instead I'm going to give you some bootleg hunting tips because I've caught well over 50 at this point.As soon as you see any cave, you can go in and out of the entrance of the cave in order to make the spawned tem inside it refresh. This is the fastest way to cycle through encounters. You do not need to fight them in order to see the overworld bootlegs- but if you're hunting something that isn't found in the overworld this method may not work. You may think that the stuff outside the cave will respawn too when you're going in and out, but it will only refresh new encounters if you enter a battle inside the cave- so like the above, if you like something appearing directly outside of a cave I suggest entering one encounter inside the cave and then running to refresh the beasts outside. Anything you can't find in the overworld I suggest going after in the end game with the ritual candles. They'll take a little bit to farm up but it'll still be faster unless you get lucky in a fusion battle, or you just happen upon one during your playthrough.I hope this info helps all the shiny hunters out there! I can't recommend the game more, just go ahead and buy it. It's well worth the price!
_childDocuments_.name: Cassette Beasts

_childDocuments_.review: Cassette Beasts will be the standard I compare all games of either genre to, and I will sing its glory to anyone who will listen. I held off on buying it for a while because I wasn't getting clear answers on questions like "what makes this different from Pokemon"? Reviews were the usual blend of fanboy injokes, story/music description, and nothing actually describing the gameplay, so I'll do my best to explain what you're getting here beyond the obvious. Your lil critters do not have levels,  do. Pokemon pigeonholes you into having one super OP dude carry your team forever or a set squad you never swap out, and everyone else is relegated to soak up exp share. All these cool monsters, worthless because your Charizard is already OP. Not in Cassette Beasts. Since your level is the only one that changes, you can swap in any monster and the appropriate stats will scale.Reading that sounds like some nerd ♥♥♥♥, but consider the ethos of a monster collector; You see a cool monster, you want to collect it, and you should want to try it out. What's the point of collecting hundreds of lil dudes if all they are is a checkbox in a pokedex to say you collected it? Pokemon actively disincentivizes the player from trying different pokemon. Cassette Beasts does the opposite with a combination of quests to use different dudes, how finding new moves works. and the simple joy of seeing a cool thing and wanting to use it. So sure, take that traffic cone right up against a boss, it'll actually contribute.Cassette Beasts has a small roster of 128 (at the time of me playing without DLC) beasts, and each one feels handcrafted with something cool going on about it. You see a cool monster, you actually want to collect it for reasons beyond completionism. There's that joy of discovery; seeing something and thinking "what is THAT? I need it, I need to see what it evolves into". And because level is tied to you, there is never a point you'll need/want to grind for more levels. You'll just see cool dudes you wanna collect and have a grand 'ol time fighting.Never have I felt like I had so much freedom in customizing a team and individual monsters. Each beasts has 8 slots for ~ stickers ~. Stickers can be added/removed at will infinitely, and there are sooooo many! You can even apply the same sticker multiple times (as long as you have multiples of that sticker). Neutral stickers will apply the type of the monster your applying to, so your vanilla attacks will have the type applied and stickers can truly be shared. There are type specific attacks, and there are also passives that greatly affect how you might build a beast. There are the usual slew of buffs and debuffs, but they do not stack to the level Pokemon lets you. +1/-1 only (though it's a dramatic +/-, it's nothing as game ending as a fully set up sweeper).Speaking of buffs, remember how you, the character, are the one leveling up? You're also the one taking all the buffs/debuffs. When you switch/faint, the remaining buffs/debuffs stay. A permanent baton pass. At first that doesn't seem that crazy, but you will see the insane tactical depth such information gives you. Builds will become influenced based on good swapping or devastating one of the opponent's active slots.There is no PP/Mana, you have action points given each turn with maaany ways to manipulate them. No need to fear for ethers or wanting to save your cool moves for important fights, your fun is not limited here. Healing in the overworld is also basically free, so your skill will only be tested on tactical prowess rather than how much time you wasted grinding materials or traveling to towns. Type advantages are also handled way cooler than "this type does 2x/.5x damage to this other type", they have actual tactical effects. Fire on grass applies burn, but on water gives them healing steam. Lightning on water triggers a conductivity damage tick, which will then trigger all beasts with conductivity. Going up against a type disadvantage isn't an auto-loss, but a puzzle to decipher. Whoda thunk boss fights in a pokemon game could be something more than "giant stat stick, but otherwise normal fight"? Cassette Beasts did. They require a change of strategy and dealing with mechanics. Insane that such concepts are novel in a Pokemon game, but that's only because GameFreak hasn't cared about making a game for anything other than milking the franchise in 20 years. No need to innovate when they make millions seeing just how bare the minimum can be. From the gameplay, to being made on Godot (love an open-source ally), and while I have many gripes and things I'd want to see improved, Whether it be just to complete the main story and call it a day (10-20 hours maybe), or complete postgame and achievements (40-50 hours), go full nerd and embrace Pokemon Showdown levels of PvP depth (oh god hours), Cassette Beasts is an easy 10/10 buy even at full price.

_childDocuments_.review: I randomly happened into this game at its release date on the Steam front page and it instantly caught my attention. In just a single play session this already game proved that it's worth the 18 bucks I spent on it.As a monster collector, it's very obvious it takes inspiration from Pokémon, but the connection might as well end there; a simple inspiration. The graphics look stunning, the monster design is awesome, the combat is unique and fun while being simple enough to not get complicated, and the soundtrack is full of bangers.The game is full of the ambition that Pokémon wishes it'd have a fraction of and it shows on everything about it, and I say this without even finishing it yet, mind you. _childDocuments_.review: The biggest problem I have with this game, is that it feels like it is both extremely easy to just out-level content, and somehow paradoxically very difficult to do so at the same time. When you're playing to your monster's strengths, you'll breeze through opponents. If you try to force them to fight opponents with inappropriate moves or type disadvantage, you'll start taking truckloads of damage from enemies ten or twenty levels lower than you. Some of the boss fights are a little frustrating, because they kind of operate inside their own framework. Most lack any creature types and will have resistances to a lot of status effects. However, I felt it was fairly easy to suss out the gimmick on all of them without looking up guides. Some of the fusions are a little lame, but the game will let you squish any two monsters together temporarily during combat, assuming your fusion gauge is full. Typically they perform well enough that you'll overlook the way some of the creatures look like horrible mistakes spawned from a mad scientist's lab.That's it. The story is great. You get to customize your character at the start of the game, and repeatedly at no cost once the story gets rolling. I enjoyed all the monster designs. Capturing monsters starts kind of tough, but gets easier as you go. It definitely helps that you can't KO any monster you're actively trying to capture, and allowing your partner to beat on it actually improves your odds. Moves can be shuffled around from monster to monster fairly easy. There are restrictions, where you typically can't go too "off theme", or attempt to completely eliminate weaknesses from type match-ups. The music for this game is pretty dang good. It has a hand full of different battle themes, and they all are somehow really rad.Oh, every battle is a doubles battle. Some opponents will only have a single monster on the field, but you should expect a mostly 2v2s, even with wild monsters. There are sliders controlling how much enemies scale up with your levels, and how "smart" npcs and wild monsters are supposed to be when picking moves. Those are two separate sliders, actually. If you want everything to scale right up to your level, but kind of just pick moves at random, this game has your back.I have my fingers crossed for some sort of "Cassette Beasts 2" in the future.tl;drGood monster catching/training game. I like the monsters. It's fun. Buy it.

_childDocuments_.review: Cassette Beasts is one of the best creature collection games out there and even exceeds it's "Mon" influence. It's hard to explain what the game does so well but I'll try to summarise it.- All double battles (the best format imo). The fusion mechanic is also neat.- Levelling is based on your level rather than a creature level, meaning there is rarely a need to grind and any new creatures you collect are almost usable as soon as you get them- Lots of settings for scaling a difficulty. You can fine tune the enemy and npc level scaling and also the intelligence of the enemy AI to suit the experience you want.- An actual challenge. The bosses and late game rangers (gym leader equivalent) require actual thought and team planning going into them and all play in a different way. And again if you don't want a challenge (or want more of a challenge) you can adjust the difficulty as you see fit.- Great creature design- Moves are signified as stickers which you can freely put on and removed from creatures. This allows for easy customisation of builds- A decent open world with free exploration. The world is a perfect size of not being too big but also having enough mystery to discover. Whilst there are quest markers you are left to go wherever you please and are usually rewarded with a secret puzzle or area. There is also a slight metroidvania aspect with abilities you unlock as you progress. The rewards for secrets aren't usually that interesting but the joy of finding a secret and solving it is a reward in itself.- MUSIC. One of my favourite game soundtracks of 2023. So fun and I listen to regularly out of game.- Indie game made by 3 people (2 devs 1 for music). All 14000 fusions are hand drawn by mostly one person.My only major complaints are the story being pretty shallow and the platforming/movement around the world is quite often frustrating to control. Otherwise this is one of the best creature collection RPGs you can play out there.

_childDocuments_.review: As of right now, this is my game of the year 2023.Dont look at the game and just think: "oh its another pokemonclone... its so much more...- The new take on the type-mechanic is good, fusions are great, actual interesting bosses.- You get abilitys by recording some monster, they help you traverse the world.- Unlike pokemon, there is also a nice story around all of that, with very likeable characters (there is also romance)...- Also build in nutzlock and randomizer (something still missing in any pokemon game)The visuals are stunning and it also has a killer-sountrack.If any of this and the trailer sparks just a tiny bit of interest in you: then go for it, you will not be disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: A fantastic game.If you're looking for something that is *like* a certain other monster collecting game (that I'll not name), but isn't just more of the same, it's worth checking out. Cassette Beasts has a lot of charm, and has gameplay mechanics that set it above and apart from others in the same category.+ The game has a rather cozy and laid-back atmosphere that I find quite enjoyable.+ Elemental interactions between the different types are much more than a simple 'more damage' vs. 'less damage,' and add depth to the fights. You get a type chart near the beginning that you can refer to whenever. Super helpful.+Moves can be added to and removed from compatible monsters at will, so you can change up your build whenever you want.+Your combat strength is mostly dependent on your character's level, so if you decide to change up your team, it doesn't require tons of grinding to make the new monster(s) combat ready.+Adjustable difficulty, can be made easier or harder than the default. I've played through on the default setting and found a good number of the fights fairly challenging. Higher difficulties adjust things like general opponent intelligence, and make enemies level up with you.+The Captain battles (and some others) use specific combat strategies, rather than necessarily sticking to any specific element. The rematch fights later are tougher, too.+ The game has something called "bootleg" monsters, which are  They're fairly difficult to find early on, but towards the end of the game you get some tools that make it easier. helpful if you're aiming to have a more unique team.+ There's same-screen Co-op. I haven't used it, so I can't speak to how it works, but co-op is almost always a plus in my books.+/- You'll have a partner with you almost all of the time, and almost all of the fights are double fights (at least on the player's side.), which allows for strategies that wouldn't work in the typical 1v1 setup a lot of games have.+/- It's not particularly linear after the tutorial bit, outside of certain movement abilities making parts of the map more accessible.+/- A lot of the game is fairly lighthearted, sometimes silly or cringe. The main story line bosses are a bit out of place, but it's done intentionally. I find these things enjoyable, but can imagine some people won't.+/- At the time of this review, there is no PvP (as far as I know). It's a shame that I can't crush my friends with some OP nonsense build, but I can understand if that's not everybody's thing.- The fast travel system is a bit inconvenient, but becomes less of an issue as you get more movement abilities.

_childDocuments_.review: A solid "-like" that does a lot both aesthetically and mechanically to stand out among the rest. It takes full advantage of the shift to 2v2 battles with lots of little mechanical tweaks, and it's all bundled in a package with fantastic art and music; though the early game can be a bit tedious and the story left something to be desired. Overall, though, it's a good game that got me to dip my toes back into a genre that I normally don't enjoy much anymore, and that's got to mean something. I'll admit, I was on the fence about playing  when my friend gifted me a copy recently. It wasn't due to any fault of the game, it's just that I've found myself enjoying the  style of "creature collector + turn-based JRPG" gameplay less and less as time goes on. Then again, I felt the same way when I tried a similar game called  a few years ago, and I ended up dumping 40 hours into it because the changes it made to this long-established formula made things much more interesting to me. Even though I didn't find myself playing it for quite as long, I can say that  got me to set aside my growing disinterest in the "-like" genre thanks to everything it does to set itself apart.The early game was where I had the most trouble, partly because fast travel can take a couple hours to unlock, and partly because of how the in-game economy works. Buying any healing items and even resting outside of town requires materials found in chests or from winning battles, and these are scarce at first; so I spent an annoying amount of time backtracking into town to replenish until the game got more generous with materials. Once it did, though, things were smooth sailing—mostly. The game was a little buggy when I was out in the overworld, which usually presented itself in the player/object physics misbehaving (e.g. being unable to jump out of the water, barrels flying off-screen/into the ground, etc.). Nothing game-breaking, thankfully, but your mileage may vary.Outside of the main story, you also have some side goals you can pursue: you can try to record all 128 monsters, hunt bootlegs (basically shiny monsters with a different elemental type), pursue partners' side stories to improve your relationships with them, tackle raid bosses that spawn randomly around the map, and solve all manner of environmental puzzles for extra materials/stickers—plus some other stuff you unlock later on that I won't spoil. Basically all of it comes back to battling in the end, though, so players looking to see everything on offer might find themselves doing a  of grinding to get there. Luckily, playing through the main story doesn't actually require much dedicated grinding, if any, but that's assuming you're at least dabbling in this side content and not just doing the bare minimum when playing.Quick side note: you may have seen that this game recently got a multiplayer update, but I wouldn't pick it up with the expectation that it's now a full-fledged co-op game. You can hang out with up to 8 players in the same map, team up in raids, and trade with/battle against one another; but you can't help each other with story quests or fight non-raid battles together, so you're mostly just hanging out in the same world doing your own thing. It can make some completionist goals like farming raid rewards or hunting bootlegs go much quicker, but it would've been nice to have the option to run through the story with the friend that got me my copy in the first place.Finally, it would be a massive disservice if I didn't talk at least a little bit about the game's artistic elements. For one, the visuals are great all around: monster designs are interesting, characters are distinct, the whole map and everyone in it is just pleasant to look at, and the designs of the main antagonists (no spoilers, promise) were really, really cool. The music is, perhaps unsurprisingly given the cassette motifs, a big focus of the experience; and the best way to convey my thoughts on that is by saying that I was ready to buy the soundtrack DLC within my first hour of playtime (which I later did). The writing, on the other hand, is the weakest of the three—far from bad, but underwhelming in comparison. The main story didn't really hook me personally, the partner stories were nice (Kayleigh confirmed best girl, fight me) but didn't get fleshed out as much as I would have liked, and there isn't much going on beyond those two. It gets carried by the art, music, and gameplay, so I didn't mind this too much.You can expect the main story to take maybe 20-25 hours to beat, but you could easily spend twice that long if not more on the game's side content/achievements if you really wanted to, not to mention the DLC and future update content. I didn't try and 100% the game because, again, this isn't really my preferred genre; but the fact that I still saw it through to the end despite that says a lot to me about its quality.
_childDocuments_.name: Cassette Beasts

_childDocuments_.review: Cassette Beasts is FINE. It has many great ideas, and executes them with varying levels of success.The first half of the game is amazing. But by the time you reach the second half, you've basically seen everything there is to see. The content is stretched extremely thin, with some baffling design decisions, and an overall lack of polish. But it innovates so well upon the pokemon formula that it's very hard to not recommend it.I love how the game handles type match-ups. They're so much more intricate. An attack with a type advantage can inflict a very wide variety of debuffs, or change the opponent's type entirely. On the flip side, an ineffective attack can do more harm than good by buffing the enemy. The stickers are also a super compelling mechanic; they provide the majority of interesting build options, a lot of which tie into the type match-ups. Unfortunately, the sticker UI is actively hostile to the player.Exploration feels good once you get used to the movement. Dashing and gliding across the map feels great, and I really like how the map is laid out, but unfortunately, there's hardly anything to actually explore. There are dozens of chests in the game, some of which require you to solve a puzzle. But it's always just a random sticker and some materials. In 40 hours of gameplay, I don't think I ever felt any amount of excitement upon opening a chest, and I've opened basically all of them. And besides the chests, there's kinda just, nothing? As much as I like traversing the map, I have to admit that it's extremely shallow.The monster designs are passable. Most of them are very silly and over the top. They don't really take themselves seriously, but they're not bad by any means. Some of the designs are genuinely really good though. I mean it when I say Zombleat is a better design than anything in the recent pokemon games. The music is pretty good too, but there's just not enough of it. It gets really damn repetitive after some time.Then you've got the writing. Man. It is genuinely impressive how the writing managed to be worse than post gen 5 pokemon. Almost every character is super forgettable, the plot is full of predictable tropes and cliches, and it takes itself WAY too seriously; a complete 180 from the silly monster designs.My worst gripe with the game though, is the UI/UX, and the complete and utter lack of polish. The game loves to waste your time; the animations are inexcusably long with no way to speed them up, and some of the UI is horrid to trudge through. I've also had the combat menu lock up and become unresponsive to mouse inputs way too often for a supposedly finished product.Still, at the end of the day, I find it really hard to not recommend Cassette Beasts, at least for the first half of the game. It has a lot going for it, and the problems are, for the most part, easy enough to put up with. I'm really looking forward to a potential sequel.

_childDocuments_.review: The best Pokemon-like creature collector I've ever played bar none. This game just does so many things so right. It copies Pokemon in the ways you want - cute and varied creatures to collect, and a lighthearted and upbeat tone/setting. But it takes almost every aspect of the now stale Pokemon formula and re-works it in a way that breathes fresh life into it. I'll give you a few examples. In this game you turn into the beasts you capture. They inherit their level from your character. What this means is that instead of capturing a wild beast at X level and now you have to raise it, you catch it and can immediately use it at your character's level. Its moveset won't be fleshed out yet but that's easy to fix. As a result it's really fun to run into new beasts. I found myself capturing and immediately using new beasts all the time. I'm legitimately excited to take the time to catch everything in the bestiary.The type matchup system is significantly more involved and a lot more nuanced. Instead of being super effective and just doing more damage, type matchups confer buffs and debuffs. For example, attacking an earth type as a plant type adds a health leeching effect from you seeding them. Attacking a plastic type as a fire type turns the plastic type into a poison type cause you've just made them start giving off noxious gases. These matchups are pretty intuitive and it brings a totally different way of thinking about them. There are a bunch of new types like the aforementioned plastic, astral, beast, glass, and others. None of them are super compelling on their own but it's fun to have the type chart be that much bigger. The game also deserves props for its art and music. The pixel art is well done and has a really fun mix of kooky and cool. The music is very chill and quite relaxing. I may listen to some of this music offline, which is really saying something. The story and world/setting are a little flat. They're not bad by any means, and when compared to Pokemon they're more than acceptable. But don't get this game expecting a compelling world and story, cause they're not here. My biggest gripe with the game, frankly, is the starter options. You're given two options: a goth cow, and a candy demon. They're both pretty good in terms of their strength/usefulness, but only having two such strongly stylized beasts be your only options as you're first being introduced to the game was a really bad call. I found myself trying both and then being like, "Really? I have to use one of these?" This is a minor gripe though. TLDR - great pokemon-like creature collector with a huge array of innovations and a personality of its own and it's absolutely worth picking up. I'll be raving about this game for a while.

_childDocuments_.review: Wasn't expecting to have so much fun, the game is great, not really balanced but since it's a single or co-op game, that's not much of an issue. lots of content even post-story. _childDocuments_.review: This game is excellent, simply put. The creature catcher genre has seen a boom in entries recently though many fail to be truly unique. Games like Temtem or Coromon often stay to close to the formula set by Pokemon, ultimately feeling like filler fan games.Cassette Beasts is different, retaining the simple collectible charm of the genre while innovating in ways that make it something special. The rock paper scissors format has been reinvented so that various effects manifest depending on the interaction (i.e. fire striking plastic causes it to melt into toxic sludge or wind uprooting plant types, causing a debuff). Learning these matchups is greatly beneficial though you will not be overly punished when you make a bad call, just needing to adapt.A notorious flaw of the genre is grinding (looking at you Temtem) yet Cassette Beasts has sidestepped this issue in a way I've never seen before in this genre. Here, your character and your partners level up while your Beasts match whatever the level of the character using them is. You can be level 56 go back to capture a rare level 12 Beast you missed early on, and imminently use it in the next boss battle as it will now be your level.On top of the innovations they make, the Beast designs are excellent. Cassette Beasts doesn't follow the usual trend of animal + element and instead makes charming and likable monsters that then have an element/type applied to it that matches its design. These solid designs give way to Cassette Beasts amazing rare color monster system, in which a Beast will change its type to match its new coloration, creating a unique creature that you may never encounter again.I haven't even gotten into the npcs, which I'll say little on to not spoil them. All I'll say is that they are wonderful, ranging from classic 80-90s style cartoon goofballs to deeper characters that you feel like you might meet irl.I deeply hope this is not the only entry in this series, for the first time in a long while I feel like a WANT to 100% a game. Cassette Beasts is fantastic and i hope you give it a try.
_childDocuments_.name: Cassette Beasts

_childDocuments_.review: This game blew me away in so many aspects.Mechanically it feels like an evolution on the pokemon formula in every way: - Type interactions are interesting and offer much more depth to the combat than simple +/- damage- The ability to collect and swap moves out on all of your mons lets you customize them in very unique ways- Companions not only add depth to the combat by making you use a team of 2 mons, but also connect the out of combat progression back to the combat in a very clean way- The open world is neatly designed, and exploration provides a very meaningful axis of progress in multiple ways- Shinies can be seen in the open world, and each mon has 13(?!) shiny variants that actually provide gameplay differences- There's a decent amount of post game content, as well as "custom game options" that allow you to create challenge runs on subsequent playthroughsOn top of all of this, the OST is something else entirely. I think the songs themselves are wonderful, but also the audio design and implementation really helps them shine. Each song has an instrumental version and a version with lyrics that seamlessly transition between each other depending on certain conditions. For example: in town, the background track is instrumental when outdoors, and transitions to the lyrical version when you enter a building. It's a little touch that I think adds so much to the character of this game, and it's a great example of how much thought and care went in to the whole package.I could go on but honestly if you have any interest in pokemon style games you owe it to yourself to give this one a shot. It's rare to find a game with so much heart put in to it.
_childDocuments_.name: Cassette Beasts

_childDocuments_.review: Better story than any mainline Pokemon game for less than 20 euros? ✔️Better optimized than any Pokemon game while running on ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Godot? ✔️Able to fight off an horde of zombie Landlords AND Karl Marx? ✔️'nuff said.All jokes aside, this is possibly one of the most uplifting and joyous games I've played - I have immensely enjoyed the story and characters, and its bright and cheerful messages about community and the power of the indomitable human will have truly struck a chord with me. If you enjoy pokemon-style games, I cannot recommend this one enough. Speaking for myself, I don't enjoy this style of gameplay *that* much, I don't care about minmaxing fights, synergies and weaknesses, etc. - yet, I've had plenty of fun playing at my pace and without worrying too much about it, being able to finish the main story in ~17 hours or so, so it gets a strong recommendation even if you don't usually like this style of games.I'm hoping with the success of Cassette Beasts the team will be able to create more, either in the same universe or in different ones, because I think they have tremendous potential!

_childDocuments_.review: Over the past few years, I've had my fair share of brushing off these sorts of creature-collecting games as "Pokemon Clones", but between the current state of the Pokemon series and getting multiple recommendations to get this game, I decided to give it a try and WOW. This game makes Pokemon S/V look like Zip-Lash in comparison! Great battle system that makes me actually have to think about strategy, difficulty is customizable through both Enemy AI and Level Scaling sliders, the artwork and monster design are gorgeous, the order in which you need to do things to progress is pretty free-form, and while not quite as many bangers as S/V's soundtrack (Which, in it's defense, is a high bar to top), there is not one piece of music I have heard in this game so far that I would consider even remotely bad. Absolutely worth the $10 if you're a Pokemon fan still coping with the company's recent incompetence.
_childDocuments_.name: Cassette Beasts

_childDocuments_.review: Now, Monster Taming games are one of my favorite genres of the games, and to see one done so amazingly, is just... well... amazing. if I could I would scream from the top of my lungs in public to tell everyone to play this game.I really love the type chart (chemestry? I think the name is) and how dynamic it is, do I understand it? not really, but I'm getting there, the fact that some attacks can change the target beasts typing is so cool (looking at you glitter type) now I haven't really noticed any issues but that might just be my first reaction hype tainting my views on things but so far everything is just... fun? the monster designs are also really cool, something about the starter options made me look at the screen for 5 minutes before choosing one and any game that does that is a good game in my opinionone of the best things in my personal opinion that this game does is focus on the bonds between the people in constract to normal monster tamers where you befriend the creatures and "human" characters fall to the wayside, as I'm reviewing it I have only unlocked three of the companions and love the campfire interactions so much. it makes me really feel inversed in the characters, and it makes perfect sense as the beasts you tame aren't really real just recordings that you transform into.
_childDocuments_.name: Cassette Beasts

_childDocuments_.review: This is my highlight this year!It's a monster collector like Pokemon, but different enough to feel fresh.There are 14 Types, but unlike in Pokemon there's no super effective/not very effective, instead it's debuff/buffs/type changes. Fire on Ice? It's effective, but turns the Ice monster into a Water Type which extingushes Fire lowering their offenses. Plants on Earth seeds it and puts leech seeds on every attack.But my favourite part got to be the "shinys" in this game, called Bootlegs. Instead of every monster having one different coloured version, it's 14! And that's not all it does, it also changes the Type and the moves it learns. For Example: There's a Fire-type dog but you found a rare yellow one? It's a Lightning-type now and learns Lightning-type moves.The game also looks beautiful and runs smooth. It controls really well and once you get more movements abilities you'll zoom through the map.There are also fusions who look different depending which two monsters you fused together. Oh and there's a built in randomizer.Negatives:- It crashes randomly, luckily it autosaves on every exit and fights and loads fast.- Only 128 monsters. You'll see the same ones a lot, and because there's not a big pool it means you'll get spoiled what your evolution looks like before you get to it quite a few times. The Bootlegs do help here somewhat.- Bad inventory management. You get so many stickers (This games TMs) but no way to sort them by Type or AP cost.- The ending is too bittersweet for me, a 2nd choice would've helped here.Overall probably one of the best games I've played the last 5 years, and I hope we get more monsters through updates and DLCs for years to come.
_childDocuments_.name: Cassette Beasts

_childDocuments_.review: I have fallen completely in love with this game and it's easily the best games I have ever played. don't let my hours fool you... i have spent so much more time in new wirrel through the god tier music. if i added in the music i have been listening from the incredible music producer of the game, which by the way... two man team so even more respect, it would be closer to 300 hours.  the world is absolutely charming and, while you might find exploration slow first, after you find the right beasts to record, you gain so many abilities to make traversal a breeze. you get gliding very early on but the other abilities are tied to random beasts, so it's incentive to keep looking, besides the bootlegs. which, yeah, are shinies but they change your type, give you rarer stickers and visually show up on the overworld.  Secondly the music... with seamless transitions between vocal and non vocal tied to the fusion mechanic in battle, with wherever you are now picking up it's vocals when you enter the cafe, it truly just feels so freaking good to just... sit and listen for what feels like days on end in game, hearing the singer put so much passion into it. and thirdly, the monsters themselves. there's around over 100 different monsters, but don't let that fool you... with the fusion mechanic, there is a grand total of over 16000 fusions, all with unique designs depending on what you fuse together AND the order of them. the two same beasts can become two different ones depending upon which you have and which your partner has. that is absolute dedication right there.I would happily rate this a 15/10. it's setting is easily the absolute most tranquil area... the music draws you in like nothing else and you are free to explore and do whatever story you want and in any order after you finish the starting bit with kayleigh. new wirrel just keeps on delivering. Oh, and you unlock randomizers, which change where which beast is, types, moves... and even offers a nuzlock mode. though those are unlocked after you beat the game. so even after you do it, you can make a new save AND play the same game but with so many different things, like different starters, stickers, bootlegs... try it for yourself.

_childDocuments_.review: So this is a monster collection RPG with a few big twists.  First of all, rather than collecting and training monsters, you're playing as something of a shapeshifter, who can turn into the various beasts on the Isle of New Wirral by recording them in the wild and then listening to those recordings on your portable cassette player!You find yourself in New Wirral after falling through a dimensional portal while sleeping (I spent a good portion of the game running around in my pajamas before I learned how to change clothes, giving the experience a vaguely 'Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy' feel), and are quickly brought to one of its two only active settlements by a young lady named Kayleigh, who is one of the Rangers that have charged themselves with protecting Harbour Town from the dangerous beasts that dwell on the Island.  You quickly learn that the population of Harbour Town, and the rest of New Wirral, is made up of people from alternate versions of Earth, which leads to a lot of entertaining dialogue and some fun cameos from famous historic figures (There seems to be an emphasis on Philosophers and Scientists in particular for these).Kayleigh quickly persuades you to try out for the Rangers yourself, and the early game is largely a matter of you exploring the Island and finding and challenging the various Ranger Captains to prove your worth.  You soon learn of a major and mysterious threat to Harbour Town and its people, but I've gotten too far into spoiler territory as it is.Exploration is handled in a somewhat Zelda style, with certain of the beasts enabling different means of travel once you add them to your repertoire.  This does make some areas gated off initially, but I found a few spots were clever use of powers could get you into higher level areas a bit early, if you were clever and persistant.In the course of your travels you continue to collect recordings and gain new forms, though you can only have five active at a time, and also gain new companions, though only one will travel with you at a time for most of the game.  They all have distinct personalities and stories, and one of them is even a cameo on the part of a well known literary character!  Romance is an option, and the game does not bar you from making any matches you might wish in that regard, with the understandable exception of the dog.Combat is turn based, and offers another twist on the monster collecting formula: Once you have established a friendship with a companion, you can fuse your forms together to make a more powerful, hybrid beast!  This is not something restricted to the player, and battles against hybrid monsters, known as 'Rogue Fusions' and 'Fusion Swarms' are some of the most rewarding in the game!I really enjoyed this.  The plot is reasonably straight forward, but still contains some interesting twists, and the writing and characterization are both super solid, with a lot of fun had with the ideas of so many people being native to alternate realities, and the fact that no one truly understands how the shape changing that is possible in New Wirral actually works.If you enjoy monster collecting games, or if the idea of a Zeldaish game with turn based pokemon like battles sounds appealing, you should give this a try.
_childDocuments_.name: Cassette Beasts

_childDocuments_.review: The first 4 hours of this are great! (the first hour I played in the demo and save transferred over). Unique twist on the monster catching genre which includes fusions and evolution. Includes multiple main quest lines in a limited open world format, including level and AI scaling preferences.The music is fantastic, including some great vocal music performances. The vocals can be turned off in the menu if you prefer. So far, the writing has been a little funny and very charming. You always have a companion character and you can switch between them at will. They have a little generalized voice acting to give you a flavor of their accent/background.The battle system seems deep enough to keep me interested for a few dozen hours. I will update later with a full review, but I wanted to get one in early to show support. There aren't super effective moves per se, but there are type interactions that can create advantages or disadvantages.And last, the animations and visuals seem extremely polished and it seems very well optimized for a less powerful PC.Check the Discord for free event beasts. The current one is "LAUNCHDAY" (enter the code at the mailbox in your room or in the cafe).
_childDocuments_.name: Cassette Beasts

_childDocuments_.review: Well, I have to say, graphics are amazing, OST is amazing, the battle system is very immersive with its type matchups, bootlegs and extra effects added to moves.  The difficulty setting is entirely up to the player (if they know the settings menu) as well. The story overall was great, with interesting bosses that add to the mystery of what is actually going on the main plot that makes you even more curious of what is going on.  The game being an open world setting, has creative puzzles that reward the player that actually feel rewarding, with some requiring abilities that would be acquired later on. Not to mention, the split evolutions that can be acquired can be discovered by the player if they look hard enough, such as one requiring a move that makes all ranged attacks into melee attacks. (although some of these hints are a bit vague at times)Grinding for all of the achievements was definitely worth it, since they are quite easy to accomplish (2 are miss-able however), even those that include the "shinies" of the game can be hunted quite easily with a bit of grinding (unlike pokemon). Completing the Bestiary also gives insight into what the monsters are based of too, which also pulled me in to completing it.Overall? I give it a 10/10. Sure, it has flaws but its something I can leave out since they are not too major. This game should be in a top 10 list for anyone willing to try out a creature collector.
_childDocuments_.name: Cassette Beasts

_childDocuments_.review: Pixel aesthetic, monsters, an actual overarching plot, and cute art. This is the game I never knew I needed. I've fallen in love with the characters and weird little world. There's a sense of nostalgia that lingers throughout the game, but it doesn't interfere with the enjoyment of the game. (I'm just old enough to know what a cassette tape is and have experiences with the wonky little things.)The element system is way more engaging than a simple fire vs water and utilizes things that I honestly wouldn't expect. It keeps me on my toes and a bit more engaged than something like Pokemon for example. The fact that Glitter is an element is just... wonderful.Music is really good.The fusion system is definitely a cool element of the game. Some of the monsters are unspeakably cute (e.g. Macabra x Pombomb) and some got hit with the ugly stick. Either way the fusion system is like a fun addition to help you through a challenging battle.All in all, I adore this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I was very excited to play this game, having seen gameplay and loving the artstyle and designs of the monsters themselves. I love Spitzfyre so much, the design and name are genius lmao Unfortunately, while the combat is a lot of fun, the rest of the game just doesn't feel very fun.I've seen people draw the obvious comparison to Pokémon a lot. I'd say the biggest difference between this game and Pokémon is that the world feels so vibrant in the latter series. Each location has its own atmosphere, the routes are full of features with lots of charm, and the supporting characters are very interesting, and it's a lot of fun supporting them in chasing their motivations.Unfortunately, this game does not succeed in the same areas, at least to me. Apart from the town you start in and a couple other settlements found throughout the world, the game otherwise takes place in very samey, boring areas with no distinct landmarks or features that make one area feel different to another. This made the world very boring to travel through. While you unlock abilities that allow you to move faster and interact with the world further, I don't think they really make the world much more enjoyable to travel through.The quests don't make it particularly exciting to travel through that world either. Using Pokémon as an example again, those games found a way to move you through routes to get to the key towns and cities to progress the narrative and your gym badge progress. It was very easy to know you were where you need to be. This game, however, has you constantly wandering back and forth all the way up and down the map just to receive and complete quests. And it's not that easy to know when you're approaching one of the Captains, this game's equivalent of the gym leaders. "Oh, you didn't talk to that one random NPC in the middle of nowhere? Congratulations, you've missed one of the most important fights in the game!" I just think the game could benefit from being a little *more* linear and guided plot-wise, because I always found myself too bored by the time I got to the locations to actually enjoy what was going on.The characters in the game are also just very boring. I never played far enough through to see anyone but Kayleigh's story tie off, but it was very uninteresting and underwhelming. And the rest of the characters I met during my time playing were all also very boring. Their character designs were AMAZING, I love the designs in this game, but the personalities just didn't follow through and make them interesting to me. The archangel characters were enjoyable to me because of how mysterious and creepy they are, but that's about it.I will say, one thing I absolutely love about this game is the idea of the bootlegs. You can find each monster with every typing, each also giving them a different colour to their base typing. In fact, I just love the way that the cassettes work in this game. "Recording" monsters onto the cassettes and adding "stickers" to give them moves is a really fun idea. Everything is tied back to the musical theme very well!Unfortunately, this leads me to my final big gripe about this game - the music. Don't get me wrong, the music SLAPS, all the songs in this game sound GREAT!! Unfortunately, there are only like 5 songs in this entire game. Hearing the exact same songs everywhere got very old *very* fast and it wasn't long before I found myself playing with the music muted with my Spotify on instead.I'm really really glad other people seem to be absolutely loving this game, with it having an Overwhelmingly Positive rating on Steam. Unfortunately, it just wasn't for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Cassette Beasts

_childDocuments_.review: Cassette Beasts is a nostalgic blend of the 80s and 90s that takes the creature capture base of Pokemon and adds its own twist of flavors. For example, the rock-paper-scissors formula of combat is made more complex with adding special reactions between elements, the leveling system is streamlined by basing creature power on the main character's own level, and evolving your creatures to new more powerful forms can have engaging "choose your own adventure" like moments. These ingredients come together to create gameplay where you never feel like you're wasting time leveling, collecting, and exploring with your beasts through the game's narrative and side quests. Worth a pickup before the multiplayer update.

_childDocuments_.review: Playing it solo and co-op in another save. Pretty good in both cases.Type advantages now come with buffs and debuffs rather than solely a X2 to X4 in output. Some even change type when hit with a "super effective" move:Ground turns to glass when hit by lightning, plastic to poison when lit on fire. There's also shiny variants which change the type of the animal you're catching, so there's 14 shiny variant in their own recolor scheme for all animals. Played solely on steam deck, aside the weird gamepad layout bug (+ when the system falls asleep you cannot reconnect a controller and continue. You are inclined to restart the game) and vibration being bugged i had no other issues while playing. At ~60% brightness i got about 4h of playtime. This is with everything maxed and game profile untouched.Lastly, it's recommend to turn off vocals in OST and to SKIP anything dialog related to companions and their stories. Like you have most likely heard before, it's Pokemon but actually enjoyable, though it seems no one in this "genre" knows how to write a story that isn't incomprehensibly cringe or meant solely for a 6 yearold playerbase. (Counting out SMT because they have yet to port 5 to normal platforms).F.e. Eugene who solely states anime protagonist lines in the most foul and heinous way possible: "I am the Protector of (Loserville) !, Do not worry, i will DEFEND everyone against the EVIL that DOESNT BELONG HERE!" (He's talking about people who look different than him) Making it impossible to 100% all achievements because you are inclined to be friendly to him to get 2/3 achievements. _childDocuments_.review: This game is awesome. Not to bring down the game by comparing it to other things but it's like all of the good openworld improvements of pokemon Scarlet and Violet, the fusion gimmick from the pokemon infinite fusions fangame, and a whole lot of pixel and retro charm.The soundtrack is banger, the sprites are fun, the game has a ton of content, and the companions are cool (except you Eugene).If I had to give some complaints: -I wish there was some sort of speedup for status effects in combat. Hitting multiple enemies and having to watch their defenses increase for 45s is annoying, especially when the attack defeated them anyways.-Also I guess I wish there was at least one more starter cassette beast.-Physics can be really janky sometimes. It can be funny, but also very frustrating.edit: just coming back after finishing most of the post game and doing the final ending. It is amazing. It's consumed a lot of my life in the past week and I'm glad to have done it. A bittersweet end having to leave behind the characters I'd befriended (in more ways than one). _childDocuments_.review: A good game that blends monster-tamer, turn-based battles, and open world into an enchanting and delightful gameplay experience. Though it presents familiar elements from the traditional Pokémon franchise, the refreshing ideas of “humans transforming into monsters”, monster fusion, and sticker customization do make this game stand alone from any other Pokemon-alikes.  – Very decent 20–30 hour length. It is all based on a world where people record monsters onto cassette tapes and play those back with cassette players to transform. With the completely customizable sticker system and huge movepool of each monster, you can apply many creative strategies to your build. Those passive effect stickers, various status effects, and transformation switches bring so much fun and unexpected chaos to the fights.  Personally, I wouldn’t say I like the puzzle element across the map, but still within my acceptable range.  – The pixel art and vibrant colors make the whole world alive, and I do love it. The monster design is a huge plus, creative and distinctive. I was quite fascinated when I first saw the fusion mechanics, and then I realized that YOU CAN FUSE ANY TWO MONSTERS OF THE WHOLE BESTIARY! That’s crazy, as they really sketched over 10,000 combinations! Another standout feature is the groovy retro-futuristic soundtrack that perfectly complements the game’s theme. Some battle music, particularly those with vocals, transient smoothly, making those battles special and immersive. Previously I tried this game from my friend’s library, but for the artbook and soundtrack, I purchased the complete bundle without hesitation XDOverall, delightful, comfy, and unique gameplay with adorable creatures, innovative mechanics, and strategic depth. Highly recommended to anyone who wants to try a monster-taming game.

_childDocuments_.review: Got this game because it was on sale and it seemed kind of like Pokemon. It both is and isn't. It's basically a mix of a platformer and Pokemon, but in a good way. The platforming can be a bit annoying, but there's usually some way to cheese it. There's no exact path to follow, kind of like Scarlet/Violet but with quests and stuff. It's a lot of fun and will definitely suck you in. Maybe the mechanics and the way that it's a bit more challenging make it so, but it's a lot of fun. Also, the music's good and pretty soothing.If you're looking for the cons, there's only a few.The evolutions are so fun that you just wish that there's more because most of the beasts only have one evolution. Also, the [redacted] (the bad guy(s)) is/are a little creepy.The story is pretty decent, although I'm not much to care about it. There is a decent amount of dialogue, which can get a little annoying, but you can usually click through it.If I had to pick one thing that's the most annoying, it's that I can't hide the mouse, which gets annoying after a while.Anyway, I'm posting this because this game is great and if you got $20 to drop, it's worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: Cassette Beasts is a Pokémon game that treats you like an adult, both in its relatively mature themes and its gameplay. It respects your time - dialogue and menus are a breeze to cycle through, you can reference a type chart at any time, and the world map is intimate and easy to navigate with a great fast travel system.This philosophy even carries over to the battle system, which features a replenishing per-battle SP mechanic that eliminates the migraine-inducing "run back to town just so I can use this one move again" loop. Grinding is also practically non-existent as levels are tied much more strongly to your base characters than the titular beasts, putting you in a great spot to take on the final boss as soon as the option is there.Also, refreshingly, the playable characters are all grown adults who you can romance no matter your gender identity, and they all have interesting backstories you can unravel by spending time with them. This is backed by some great, though admittedly sparse, voice acting, a feature The Pokémon Company seems to write off as a mortal sin.I'll admit the creature designs leave quite a bit to be desired, and that's really where Pokémon still reigns supreme. You're probably not going to be drawing any of these beasts in your notebook while you're bored in class or a meeting, but I'd overall describe most of them as "pretty cool."And it's difficult to get completely invested in this world where every inhabitant seems really uncomfortable with the idea of Cassette Beasts existing in the first place; a far cry from the majority of Pokémon's population falling in love with - and often dedicating their entire lives to - a wide cast of cuddly companions.If you're an adult who's felt disenfranchised by Pokémon's inefficient hand holding and laser focus on the younger market, definitely give Cassette Beasts a try. You'll get a short and sweet RPG monster-collecting experience that gives you a firm handshake and buys you a drink. Just don't expect a juggernaut universe that becomes your next personality like its grandfather before it may have done for you back when "2nd recess" was a regular part of the daily itinerary.
_childDocuments_.name: Cassette Beasts

_childDocuments_.review: This is an incredible spin on the monster catching genre that I think really needs to be experienced.While there are a couple things about the game that I've had issues with, such as somewhat clunky menus with regards to switching around party members, I cannot stress enough that the rest of this game is actually close to perfect.The gameplay is satisfying, it's fun to come up with ridiculous strategies and watch them play out live, and I found myself getting giddy even when I lost, because it meant that I'd be able to come up with something stronger and come back twice as greater than they had thought.I adore the characters.  Every single one of them is a joy to adventure with, and the ones I can't take on adventures with me, I so desperately want to. (But that's what workshop mods are for. >:3)The bosses in this game.  Hoooooly crap.  I'm going to restrain myself from talking too much about these because they are genuinely so much better experienced blind, but just know you're in for a treat.  The concept is ridiculously cool to me, and the execution is FLAWLESS, with the caveat of a couple of them being pushovers, but they still come in swinging with incredible designs and just the general rush of being in the fight.The soundtrack is flawless.  There's not even much to say outside of "I HAVE BEEN LISTENING TO THESE SONGS ON LOOP SINCE I STARTED PLAYING THE GAME" and I think that honestly says what it needs to.I have only had this game for around two weeks and it already means the world to me.  I HIGHLY recommend it and would LOVE to see more people get into it.  <3

_childDocuments_.review: This is more akin to a casual strategy game. Due to the nature of the game, rather than over-levelling, you must employ strategy. When you are at an advantage or disadvantage, the game will show you through visual triggers. Changing your forms is necessary for some of the trainer battles; otherwise, it makes no difference if you're level 25 and your opponents are level 5 you can't overpower them. You're going to lose do to them apply an array of different negative effects, at a high amount damage.It does provide a consistent amount of progression, which is nice and the ability to fully craft your beasts. Don't like what their current abilities are? No worries. Rip those stickers off and slap on some stellar ones in their place and customise with super rare and uncommon variants to empower them even further than before. You can find these from the merchants that restock their stores every night/day. So gathering resources from beasts and quests help set you up for more powerful stickers to make the following battles even more trivial. It's enjoyable to theorycraft.Building your relationship with your companion allows you to fuse together, this alone offers so many different types of beasts a new visual appearance. The possibilities are endless. Find a glitter version? That'll also effect it's color. Joy! The game is worth the price and is very cozy. However, it may be a bit too slow for those who want a more fast paced game experience, since you can't really "run" just dash every 3 seconds due to the annoying stamina meter, which makes sense for the gliding, but not for the dashing. It makes traversing new areas take up some unneeded time.
