_childDocuments_.review: Rimworld - Depth + 3D graphics = Stranded Alien DawnIts ok - 6/10 Not as great as I was hoping it would be honestly. Base building is very well designed and incredibly fun. Looks great as well however compared to similar colony sims like this it just doesnt have much depth. It plays exactly like Rimworld in every way, you can tell Rimworld was a huge inspiration for this game.  You can also tell they had to soften the edges for that Teen rating. Unfortunately no effort was made to replace the brutal M rated aspects that made Rimworld so interesting. Combat is exactly like Rimworld however there is no dismemberment and the organ damage has been dumbed down a ton. There is a status panel where you can see what limb or body part is hurt but the effect is almost always the same - a little movement and blood loss until they heal up. It doesnt go beyond that and this panel can almost be ignored completely. Your limbs will never actually be destroyed same as organs, your survivors just take damage until they die. Unfortunately there is also huge lack of variety when it comes to enemies. There is basically just 1 enemy and its waves of bugs that comes in different intervals. Its like they tried to copy Rimworld here too but to get the T rating they cut all human enemies and didnt try to add any variety of their own just left it at waves of bugs who quickly get repetitive and boring super quick.

_childDocuments_.review: Stranded Alien Dawn is a breath of fresh air in a gaming landscape that has felt somewhat stagnant in recent years. For those seeking a fresh and engaging adventure, Stranded Alien Dawn is a standout title that revitalizes the genre with its creativity and polish.

_childDocuments_.review: :Finally, we're at the point, where I can say that  surpassed any other colony survival management simulation game Steam has to offer. With the latest free update (and DLC that comes with it) you finally can build multi-floor complexes. At this point  won't lose to any other game in terms of graphics, features, optimization and moddability. And in some cases, it even surpasses them. Moreover, some existing frameworks (such as detailed body status/information for humans and robots) imply that there are much more things to come.An extremely powerful modding toolkit is supplied along with the game, that allows to modify everything or even implement completely new features. Considering, that most of the logic is handled via LUA scripts, almost every part of the game is open for tinkering.And presence of Denuvo? Frankly, for all the attention, love and care game receives from the developers, the presence of thy Denuvo in thou game can be forgiveth.:I can tell with clear conscience that developer, Haemimont Games, lived up to expectations with release of modding toolkit. There are some bugs and issues to resolve, but main step towards infinite replayability is already done. By the way, all unpacking instructions for Surviving Mars are totally suitable for Stranded: Alien Dawn as well, thanks to both games using very similar engine.:Seems like developers (and publisher) decided to heed the voice of reason and add proper modding tools with Steam Workshop support. _childDocuments_.review: The game is fun. You can easily get 30 hours out of your first play through/scenario. I order it to construct a roof, but it stops halfway and does something else which it deems to be more important.Weapon variety, especially in the early game is somewhat lacklustre. _childDocuments_.review: AKTUALIZACE RECENZE: Hru jsem nakonec rozjel. Musel jsem ale nainstalovat externí program Intel extrem tuning utility a podtaktovat procesor. Další radou co jsem našel na fórech byla deaktivace E-jader, to jsem naštestí už dělat nemusel. Verdikt na hru neměním. Mám i9-13900K takže z mého pohledu relativně nový a výkonný hardware. Musím li tedy používat programy třetích stran, abych hru rozjel, nemohu ji s čistým svědomím doporučit ke koupi.ENG version translated with the help of GoogleREVIEW UPDATE: I finally got the game up and running. But I had to install the external program Intel extrem tuning utility and underclock the processor. Another piece of advice I found on the forums was deactivating E-cores, luckily I didn't have to do that anymore. I do not change the verdict on the game. I have an i9-13900K so from my point of view relatively new and powerful hardware. So if I have to use third-party programs to run the game, I can't in good conscience recommend it for purchase.Původní recenze:Hra samotná je v jádru zábavná, jedna se o jednoduší Rimworld s atraktivnější grafikou. Bohužel asi po odehrání 15h začala hra zamrzat, interval se začal postupně zkracovat na současných cca 10 minut hrací doby před zamrznutím a pádem na plochu. Řešení na fórů nepomáhala (vypnutí autosavu, snížení grafiky). Sledujte zda přijde aktualizace, která toto opraví.  Informace o zamrzání hry jsem našel na fóru už v říjnu minulého roku a problém je zde pořád. Takže občasným informacím od vývojářů, že problém řeší uvěřím až uvidím výsledky, pak i změním hodnocení. Do té doby zvažte nákup, chyba se začala projevovat daleko za hranicí času pro refundaci. Unfortunately, after about 15 hours of play, the game began to freeze, the interval gradually began to shorten to the current approx. 10 minutes of playing time before freezing and crashing to the desktop. Solutions on the forums did not help (disabling autosave, reducing graphics). Watch for an update to fix this. I found information about the game freezing on the forum already in October of last year and the problem is still there. So I will believe the occasional information from the developers that they are solving the problem when I see the results, then I will change the rating. Until then, please consider purchasing, the bug started showing up well past the refund time limit. I really enjoyed the game despite the freeze. Therefore, I do not recommend the game in its current state.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is good. Some more work needs to be done, but it does indeed feel like a 3d Rimworld.As for some gems of other reviews:Denuvo? Contact the developer and let them know why you aren't purchasing it. Or decline the EULA and refund it through Steam. If you explain why, support is generally really good about refunding for DRM that you don't agree with as long as you are under the 2 hour limit."Denuvo has been criticised for high central processing unit (CPU) usage and excessive writing operations on storage components, the latter causing significant life-span reductions for solid-state drive"No. I've played this and other recent Denuvo games on a nearly decade old CPU. Denuvo related processes don't use more than 2% of it. Any modern hardware isn't going to notice it (5800x for example). SSD wear? ((citation needed)). These issues were partially true in the first revision, it has long since been fixed.'The recent change to the EULA that states you do "NOT OWN THE GAME"'You haven't actually "owned the game(s)" since digital distribution became a thing. Read the Steam EULA, if they ban/block your account you lose your entire library. Same goes for XBox, Playstation and Nintendo.TL;DR?1. Stop playing on a potato.2. _childDocuments_.review: This is an exceptionally enjoyable survival base builder, with three unique campaigns (in the base product) (and three unique biomes) that each have their own unique starting conditions and victory conditions, even if the overall gameplay tends to boil down to the same moment to moment activity.  It is generally a relaxing game that has enough challenge to keep one's focus but not so much difficulty that it becomes frustrating.The graphics are serviceable unless you really want to zoom in on characters or the environment, mostly being clear on what you're looking at (some small plants look very similar to one another), and there is a distinct look of all the given materials in the game.The 'give general order but allow autonomy' mostly works, with the characters going about the task that needs to be done, and while there is a system to readjust what priority each of their tasks are, the default system is generally workable if a bit uneven.  Characters might interrupt a task to do something else, like stop transporting an item to have a meal because they're hungry, but then won't resume the task; many items will be left lying around unless task priority is shifted considerably.Characters can be drafted, specifically for combat, but there is little finesse in this area, mainly it's best to gather all your people together and have them well equipped and then send them at a target; characters have to be manually controlled to fall back, most enemies don't have ranged attacks so they merely charge at you and cover is generally only buildable; I've not had a situation where I could get to a ridge that oversaw an area and then rained fire down on enemies who would have to take the long way around.The drafting doesn't allow for precise control of non-combat actions, which is a bit frustrating particularly when you have an item you want a survivor to observe (the means by which you learn about them for resource extraction), but that item might be very far from the base so you want to have them properly equipped and make sure they do THAT task and not try to retreat to base to relax, or sleep, or eat, or whatever.  I suspect this is to prevent the sense that one must micromanage your people for optimal outcomes, but there are fringe cases where it would be nice to have this option.

_childDocuments_.review: I like the idea of it, but there isn't enough control on the characters. As the game progresses, possibly through too many assigned tasks, but it is hard to determine, the characters start doing their own thing. For example, i had an animal attack, which hurt three of the 4 survivors... one went to bed for healing, another one started running more or less in circle, apparently healing himself, but actually eventually died, and another one just went on with her tasks and eventually slept in the snow, instead of coming back to her assigned bed.There is a need for a task manager in the MANAGE menu and a way to view and cancel or re-prioritise given tasks per survivors without changing the tasks priorities all the time.As it stands, it becomes frustrating to not be able to direct the survivors for a function as simple as "go to bed now" despite the fact that they are waiting for treatment... or "go hide in the house", when they are pursued by dangerous animals and don't want to or can't fight.Some features take time to master as well.This said, there are a lot of details in the game as well. For example, in most cases, the actual keyboard and/or mouse action is displayed, which helps a lot.One main function is missing. my survivors are often depressed... i think, after a year, they are more than constipated... no toilet and no plumbing... I would also love that the player be able to choose the number of characters to start with. As soon as i lose one (of 4), i know the game will soon end with way too much work  for the rest, even if the player plays with full 10/10 skills ON.I did get a 5th survivor coming in on day 2 in my last game. That was nice.The game did crash twice, or rather froze, which stopped me from sending any logs.Addendum :After playing many more hours (92+/year 8), i am getting the hang of it. Year 8 now. There are still control issues, but all in all, i enjoy it.New sites are created from "seeds" based on words. I wish the sites could be generated before the game begins, so that one could accept or reject them without needing to restart the crash scene.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is currently in the Humble Choice for September 2024, and this is part of my coverage of the bundle. If you are interested in the game and it's before October 1st, 2024, consider picking up the game as part of the current monthly bundle.Why won’t you do the job? Stranded Alien Dawn is made by the same company that makes Tropico and Surviving Mars. For Stranded, you have a squad of four characters who survive a spaceship crash and the player will decide actions that your group needs to carry out. Players might have their team observe plants, and animals, and gather resources to build shelter. It’s a typical survival game, including alien monsters that will become very hostile. However, as I played Stranded Alien Dawn, I just got more frustrated. I wanted my characters to observe a plant. Only one or two characters could do that. Scavenging was limited to a couple of characters. For most of my playtime, two of my characters sat around being idle, and the game didn’t give me clear guidance on why they did nothing. Perhaps it’s about the actual skills the characters had, but they should have had enough. There’s a huge lack of information and it became far more frustrating than anything, and before I knew it I was bum rushed by 16 beetles, who killed my team because I hadn’t researched Weapons yet and couldn’t defend myself. Admittedly, some of this will probably come from tutorials and more. But it also just doesn’t feel intuitive at all to understand what characters are thinking or wanting to do. There’s a level of micromanagement here that seems unrealistic for what the game is offering. Pick this up if you’re willing to invest a long time into the game. However, the frustrations I felt with Stranded are similar to the Frustrations I had with Tropico and Surviving Mars. It’s probably just what this developer wants to make at this point in their career. There’s a solid fanbase for this type of game, but it’s like pulling teeth just to understand what’s going on. If you enjoyed this review or want to know what I think of other games in the bundle, check out the full review on or subscribe to my Youtube channel:

_childDocuments_.review: Bought on impulse and was pleasantly surprised. At the time I'm writing this (Oct 2022), the game is in Early Access, but despite this, it runs stable and plays well.Graphics are nice, they don't stand out, they don't distract, there's enough details to be worth zooming in and having a look. Perhaps most surprising is the stable performance, whether I play at 2k or 4k, I get to enjoy a stable 60fps.I was skeptical if I was going to like the premade characters, but ultimately I do like them. I find it very pleasurable to watch my survivors hustle and bustle, doing their chores and tasks. Sometimes the survivors priorities seem a bit off, and can require some micro-management. But this also helps build stories. Like when Katina almost let Hann bleed out after he rescued Rita from a swarm of bugs, because getting some sleep was more important. Or that time Rakha regularly got frustrated by having to do all the construction and kept going off to punch a pole or going off for shooting practice. And speaking of stories, when your outpost fails because your survivors died, you'll get a timeline with important moments, a really nice touch I enjoy.At the time of review, content overall is limited, but what's available is great. Clearly the team went for quality over quantity, and hopefully there will be more tech, more research, more ... well more of everything. The biggest downside to this approach, for the time being, after one solid successful playthrough you've basically seen everything there is. There are some randomized research options and expeditions events that change based on a random seed, but it's really nothing major.The gameplay is built with a focus on reaching the victory condition, and some mechanics are scaled around that, making an endless play somewhat difficult but not impossible. Though it's possible that this too will see some change, being in Early Access.The developers have also blessed the community with a great community manager, who's actively working on gathering feedback and communicating very respectfully with the community.In summary a great start and so much potential!

_childDocuments_.review: Stranded Alien Dawn is your typical early access colony manager, it has the minimum amount of features and a twist where there is an "end" where you build up and then build down to have your people escape one by one. It isn't finished, so if you are not a fan of "Early access" just wait for it to come out. It is on the right track and not feature complete.The good:The build system is pretty good. Looks like the one from the Planet Coaster, Planet Zoo etc which is pretty good. The mechanic of "building down" at the end is pretty cool. It isn't done yet, there needs to be more automation in place, but it is a new twist to your typical build up.The bad:Not very replayable. The characaters are static, and the maps are not procedural. A single playthrough should do it for you.The map is kinda too big. There is no way you'll use it all.Scale is small, you never really get more than 10 survivors. Game isn't "done" yet. but it is on the right track.The ugly:Nothing really. It is a pretty good game with a good future.If you are interested in the game, but haven't played Rimworld or Going Medieval I would recommend playing those first, they are better games (at the time of this review) but this game has future potential and is a pretty good game. I would just recommend Rimworld or Going Medieval over this one at this time.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is BRUTAL.You will die and you will lose your progress. In addition to that, you can softlock yourself and erase hours of progression by abandoning the entire delve, either by your own fault or due to something you could not predict at all.I'm listing some things you will see during your playthrough:-Trial and error-Jank-Getting over it-Curse management-Stamina management-inventory management-Resource management-Weapon / tool / utility management (everything breaks all the time)-Softlocks (when everything is broken and you cannot even eat)-Salt (ingredient)-Salt (emotion)-Planning, preparation and thinking-Bull****-Constantly spawning mobs that poison you and deal chip damage-Madokajacks (worst enemies I have ever seen seriously why are they like that I hate these things)Layer 3 is the worst (Madokajacks, some pitch black non-euclidean 3D maze), though 4 and 5 are also quite cruel. Bosses only require adequate preparation, patterns can be learned quickly.I'm sure some level of masochism is required to enjoy this game.

_childDocuments_.review: First things first, some simple questions that will quickly answer if this game is for you:If you , then this is not for you. Go watch the show, it's really good!If you  then this game might just be for you! With a few caveats...What  does well is present the Abyss itself as the true antagonist. It's going to get you killed, a number of times, and often in quite unfair ways, but since you've seen the show (unless you were lying when you answered my questions), you already know that!The game somewhat requires that you take a trip through an extended tutorial and recap of the start of the first season of the show, seeing Riko and Reg trek it all the way down to the edge of the second layer, just past Seeker Camp. This part of the game is quite slow, and it removes some of the more interesting mechanics that the proper game provides.Honestly, I was almost giving up on the game at first. The roughly 4 hours I spent going through the tutorial was somewhat painful. When I realised that there was no point to painstakingly collecting a lot of the things the game tells you that you CAN collect, I ended up running through a lot of the environments, opting to save them for when the real game got started. This was a wise choice! Because, oh wow, there's a lot to explore, find and collect in the game proper.Jumping over to , the  part of the game, things immediately become a lot more interesting. You start things off as a young cave raider with a grand goal in mind: Become a White Whistle and reach the bottom of the Netherworld! Sound familiar? Of course it does, you are essentially a stand-in for Riko, and your journey through the Abyss very closely matches the journey in the   and  of the show, ultimately ending at .On your way, the game presents an original story that the author of the manga was deeply involved with, making it by and large canon (with a bit of creative freedom in some regards). It kept me motivated to keep going, as I absolutely adore this world and its strange inhabitants, but the real meat of the package is of course the world itself.The Abyss is a huge, sprawling network of caverns and vistas, streams and waterfalls, settlements and wastelands, all spread out across a number of layers. Descending down is captivating. Ascending is always treacherous and sometimes literally lethal due to the curse. The deeper you go, the worse it gets. This draw, the mystery of the depths and the perils of returning from them, is truly captivating.Gameplay wise the loop consists of venturing out from Orth, the surface town built around the edge of the Abyss, and collecting artefacts to bring back. You complete quests along the way, and combined with the artefacts that you return (or make equipment out of), you slowly level up. At certain story points, you will be able to upgrade the level of your whistle, the badge of designation carried by every cave raider. The higher the level, the deeper you can go. It also comes with the benefit of making the strains caused by the curse of the abyss easier to bear, as well as unlocking the ability to fast travel in deeper and deeper parts of the Abyss. A daunting trek back from a deep layer suddenly becomes a piece of cake once you are experienced enough.Visually, the game sports a very stylized design, very closely matching the look of the anime. Characters are rendered very close to their 2D counterparts and all feature the original voice actors from the show, at least in Japanese. The beasts you encounter and the many different foods you consume over your travels are both also rendered with extreme attention to detail to the canon of the show. There are even some new environments spread through the layers you can explore, adding even more depth (pun intended) to the Abyss.Ultimately, this game is a true love letter to the show and its universe, and while the task can be somewhat daunting with a slow start and a pretty harsh difficulty spike when going deeper the first few times, I can only recommend it wholeheartedly to anyone who is a fan of the series. It’s not perfect, but the good parts by far outweigh the bad.

_childDocuments_.review: Let's start with the first major problem.Triple A pricing for a B budget game. You want your game to cost the same as major titles? But you'd have to crawl the entire game for this crap not to ruin your experience.The curse mechanic is not implemented well. Stumbling on badly made terrain where the depth goes up and down by 1 can hit you with the curse.Character creation is so limited, it may as well have been an after thought.Still with me? _childDocuments_.review: I'll recommend this game ONLY if you're a fan of the manga or anime. But wait for it to go on sale. If you don't know what Made In Abyss is, don't bother. There's quite a few REALLY annoying problems with this game right now and hopefully they'll get patched. One of the most confusing decisions by the dev was to lock the full game behind an approximately 3 hour tutorial story that is an abridged version of the first season of the Anime. Which would be FINE except it's executed in such a hamfisted way. Reg, your companion in the Tutorial, has some of the worst AI I've ever seen. He constantly gets stuck, aggros everything and dies, has only one dialog line which he repeats every few seconds for no apparent reason and, in one quest that involves the need to analyze specific enemies to complete, Reg seemed to be hell bent on killing the enemies before I could complete the process. During the tutorial, much of the game's meat and depth is either locked off from you or not explained very well. I was 3/4 of the way through the last mission before I figured out one of the ONLY things you can craft during this portion is food, something that would have made the previous 3/4 of the game much easier. You could spend hours wandering around in the Tutorial collecting relics and crafting components, but the game doesn't tell you this is all useless and wasted time. The goal of the tutorial is to just get through the story and with the exception of some basic food, you can't use any of it. Once you complete the tutorial / anime rehash, the game does expand a great deal. There's a few skill trees for crafting, fighting and cave raiding. You're free to explore wherever you want and do whatever you want. This is all fine but you're going to get annoyed real quick with a couple horrendous problems. The worst is some of the most frustrating enemy spawning I've ever encountered. They spawn wherever you're not looking. 3 squirrel looking things? Kill them and they immediately re spawn behind or beside you just out of view. This also happens when you're climbing, which is incredibly problematic because you use stamina to climb, and also to swing your weapon. So continuously spawning enemies are kind of a game breaker since you either have to take damage or use stamina to fend them off and probably fall because you run out of stamina.  This is also incredibly bad because attacking enemies contributes to your weapon degrading and breaking. You can burn through one very quickly fending off non stop spawning enemies and find yourself defenseless after you run out of crafting materials. EDIT: Now that I'm more than half way through the game's main campaign, I can add a bit more. The rapid spawn mechanic is apparently by choice. After you spend too long in an area, low HP enemies spawn rapidly to push you along. There's apparently an item that temporarily pauses this mechanic, but it's still an odd choice given how much the game wants you to take your time and explore.  What the Deep In Abyss mode does get right is the sense of danger and careful planning it takes to successfully dive and make it back. Your inventory is extremely limited if you stock up on survival items and doesn't leave room for valuable relics to earn money and experience when taken back to town. But you need food and weapons, not to mention your clothing which takes up a significant portion of your available inventory. Weapon degradation is a real problem if you go around attacking everything you see. So the game pushes you to avoid conflict in this manner and encourages you to pick and choose your battles.  The more weapons you take to compensate for the degradation and breaking, the less room you have for other stuff. The Deep In Abyss mode has incredible potential. The sense of depth and scale translates very well to the real danger the Abyss presents. If you go down to layers 3 or deeper, it's a huge commitment to return with the valuable relics you can find. There's no shortage of exploration and secrets to find. The crafting system is just deep enough to make it challenging without being too complex.  Unlocking new parts of the skill trees gives you access to things that make delving easier and less time consuming in the upper layers. The environments are unique in each layer, which is nice. But the graphics don't get any better the deeper you go. There's just enough to convey the terrain and that's about it. I still stand by the reccomendation ONLY if you're a fan of the series. It's worth the playthrough to explore the Abyss yourself.

_childDocuments_.review: is not the game that an amazing series like  deserves. It's janky, buggy, unpolished, and frustrating in several ways. That said, it's the only  game we have for now, and for those of us who have already watched the anime and read the manga, it's the only other official content to tide us over until the next volumes and seasons come out, which could be years from now. And despite the jank, it's not a terrible game--there are some things I really like about it. But still, I struggled with whether or not to recommend the game, and ultimately decide that I can recommend it, but per the previous disclaimer, only to huge fans of the series who can wait for a sale and tamper their expectations.The game is split into two parts, "Hello Abyss," which is basically a tutorial that recaps the first half of season 1 (), and "Deep in Abyss" in which you create your own cave raider and work your way up from being a lowly bell rank to a legendary White Whistle. Hello Abyss can be finished in about three to four hours, but it's barely worth playing unless you want the achievements. It's missing a lot of the mechanics that make the rest of the game interesting, and the retelling of Riko and Reg's story is abysmal. It doesn't do the anime or the manga justice at all. While they did at least get the same voice actors from the anime, the developers didn't license any of the animation or music from the series, except for a few intro scenes. Instead, they rely on poorly animated in-engine cutscenes that lack any of the emotional impact of the anime. I think this entire section of the game was outsourced to another studio, and it really shows in the lack of quality throughout. Deep in Abyss is much better, and it has kept me hooked on the game for 40+ hours despite all of its faults. In this mode, you do the actual work of a cave raider: preparing for your trip, delving into the abyss, collecting as many relics and other materials as you can carry, and trying to make it back to the surface alive while surviving the threat posed by primeval creatures and the curse of the abyss. I found this gameplay loop quite addictive, and though it does get repetitive--especially towards the end of the game where leveling and crafting become very grindy--it always feels like there's more to discover, and the story of your OC cave raider's progress is intriguing enough to maintain interest, though by no means excellent.The effects of the curse/strains of ascension are mostly well done. The first and second layers cause only minor inconveniences. But in the third layer, . The fifth layer effect is a bit disappointing: it should have been more like how it's depicted in  where it , but instead it just .Other reviewers have described  as being a difficult game, but I think this is not quite accurate. It's not hard, per se, but it can be very . It's possible to get stuck which can cause you to lose hours of progress. You can delve too deep and end up not having the resources to get back. You can also follow a path downward only to later realize that there's no way back up that path if you didn't put a rope out beforehand. In most cases, there is an alternate route available somewhere, but finding it can be easier said than done.Make sure you save frequently and keep multiple different saves at different points! It's good to keep rotating saves so you always have the option to go back to a "safe" spot.Also limiting the difficulty is that enemy AI is practically non-existent. Contrary to how the primeval creatures of the deep abyss are portrayed as vicious and cunning in the anime and manga, enemies in the game mostly just stand in place and rotate around, casting attacks at random. Most of them will also leash if you get more than a few meters away, which means you can always just run past them (and usually should do so to conserve resources). The most dangerous and annoying enemies are the flying and climbing ones that harass you while you're trying to scale cliffs; the  are especially aggravating. Exacerbating this is the fact that most enemies respawn constantly without end. Apparently, there's a mod to disable that; I can completely understand why many players would want such a mod.There are a handful of forced fights in the game, including boss fights with  at the bottom of each layer. These fights are generally not hard either, but they can be aggravating due to resource management: if your weapons break and you don't have the materials to craft new ones, you can't fight back at all. Your only option at that point is to reload your previous save.There are several noteworthy bugs in the game. For example, you can exploit the stamina mechanic when climbing by standing on top of (most) relic nodes that jut out from walls. You can also exploit it when descending by dropping off the wall (neutral jump instead of downwards jump) and grabbing back on, which uses no stamina. Sometimes you can fall off a wall from a height that should be deadly, but inexplicably take no damage. If you excavate while on a wall and end up with too much weight, you'll fall off, but if you're quick enough, you can pause, discard some items, and you'll be able to grab back onto the wall before you fall to your death. I doubt any of these things were intentional.Weapons break far too easily, perhaps even easier than those in . Durability systems in games are often irritating, but I don't mind them so much when they suit the gameplay and the experience the game is trying to evoke, which is certainly the case with ' theme of survival in a hostile environment. But a 2kg metal pickaxe shouldn't shatter into pieces after whacking half a dozen rodents. Strangely, excavating relics and resources doesn't reduce your pickaxe's durability, and in fact you can even excavate without a pickaxe in your inventory at all.The role that relics play in the game is disappointing. They're effectively just glorified vendor trash and crafting materials. I do like that selling relics is one of the primary means of leveling up, given that that's what cave raiders are known for. But there should have been at least some relics with real gameplay effects (sun spheres don't count.) I was excited to finally unlock , but even these don't have any unique animations or effects. This feels like a major missed opportunity. It also could have helped explain why . is not a bad game, but it's certainly not great either. And that's a shame, because  is excellent, and the game could have been too with more care and attention to detail, and perhaps a larger budget. The core game is solid enough that I enjoyed my time with it. But I still wouldn't recommend it to anyone who isn't already a big fan of . I really hope that one day the franchise gets the high quality game it deserves.This was abridged due to Steam's character limit. Full review here:

_childDocuments_.review: So here's the deal...It has potential. The game is good if you grab the spawnrate-fix mod from . If it's on sale, it's a steal. It could be so much better with more work, and there's a ton of cut content that didn't make it to release.I've heard that the devs aren't looking at any future contributions to the game -- likely aside from bugfixes. Hopefully this isn't true, or at least the devs change their mind. Aside from that, the intro questline can't be skipped but it takes maybe ~2-3 hours if you cruise through it. No resources will carry over, so just blast your way through to get to the real meat and potatoes of the game.The custom-player mode is where the good stuff is at. Some advice and tips:-Main quest progression gates available depth (and occasionally adds some larger primeval creatures to the maps), so prioritize the main quests first.-Stamina is incredibly important while going up walls, so don't be afraid to rest on the rocks sticking out. You don't want to see your character get turned into goop after a fall.-Going up via the waypoints takes HP and Hunger, going down usually just takes Hunger. Eventually you'll unlock fast travel to take you down to the newest depth, which is much more efficient time and resource-wise, and back to Orth.-Packweight is the most limiting factor of the gameplay-cycle. Free up some weight at the itembox in your room by dumping items you don't need. You'll always be gathering more of whatever you already had. Just some food, medicine, and your tools is the ideal pack.-Armor is far and away the best thing to work towards. Always make that your primary goal; the quests can wait.-Rope isn't as valuable a resource as you might think, but it doesn't hurt to have. You can always make more.I've been loving my time with this game so far, hopefully others can look past its flaws and see the beauty underneath.

_childDocuments_.review: Made in Abyss is a fantastic anime, one of my recent favorites. So I was pleasantly surprised to see this pop up on Steam, the series has the potential for a fun video game.Given the atrocity that was the Re:ZERO game developed by the same studio, I expected just another straightforward VN-adventure hybrid. Binary Star is much more than that though. There are still VN segments, but the gameplay takes priority here and there is a full slate of stuff to play around with.Crafting food and equipment, using various tools to get around, taking in the many different areas of the Abyss, unlocking abilities on the skill tree, hunting down artifacts - it is a much higher-end production than I was anticipating and the studio has done a great job building a solid foundation.Unfortunately though, that is just the foundation, because the game takes a massive dive in quality once you get to how the actual loop works. Instead of evoking that feeling of exploration and wonder that one would expect to come with diving into the Abyss, the overall feeling I had was one of monotony. This is because the vast majority of quests are simple fetch quests, “go here and kill this” quests, or “go here, talk to this person, and come back” quests.You would think, “okay, but these fetch quests give you an opportunity to explore the Abyss” and yeah, you would be partially right. The problem there though is that once you’ve seen an area a few times, it becomes a bit boring to head back there for the fifth, sixth time to do something menial like collecting five bird eggs or fishing for material to craft a certain dish.This becomes especially annoying later on when you have to trek through like four or five different areas just to get to your objective only to have to trek all the way back at the end. I quickly realized I was spending roughly 90% of my time just getting to where I needed to be and that most of that time was spent trekking through the same areas that I had already crossed through in the previous five quests. This is the bulk of the Binary Star experience and it is a massive disappointment given the great base that the game starts with.Little things add to this disappointment too. Item weight, limited backpack size, equipment durability, and the fact that if you run out of stamina your character literally stops in place until the stamina bar regens to full. Sure, there’s an excuse for realism to be made there, but this is an anime game and a lot of these mechanics are blatantly anti-fun.The combat is the most dead simple thing ever, with your one button attacks that only expand beyond that with the skill tree that just makes the combo string longer. The lock-on is a bit finicky, the hitboxes are usually way larger than they appear, and most fights boil down to simply hitting an enemy a couple times, rolling to the side, and repeating.The game is basically divided into two parts: “Hello Abyss” and “Deep In Abyss”. The former is the “proper” story mode that tells the story from the anime and allows you to play as Riko and Reg. That said, the entire thing only adapts up to the survival training with Ozen - episode eight from the first season - and it took me just three hours to clear. I found this mode to be a vastly inferior method of telling the Made in Abyss story for what it does adapt.After completing that mode though, you unlock the full experience: Deep in Abyss - or the game mode that most of my earlier complaints come from. This mode allows you to create a custom character and tells an original story with said character. Sounds cool, but the story itself is just there to link things together and isn’t really a strong point. The rest of it is as I described earlier.The graphics are what I would expect from an early PS4 or even PS3 game, with bland textures and boring world design. The music is a bit better, but honestly nothing can compare to Kevin Penkin’s work in the anime and I guess I’m just disappointed that we couldn’t get something that at least tries to be that good.I ran the game at 4k 144fps, max settings on my RTX 3080 Ti with no performance-related issues. That said, there are some bugs worth mentioning, including voice playback randomly stopping after alt+tabbing and NPCs getting stuck in the terrain when moving. That latter one happened A LOT and it comes with an equally annoying sound effect of someone rapidly hitting the ground.Made in Abyss: Binary Star Falling into Darkness is a decent game bogged down by some incredibly tedious quest design. Exploring the Abyss can be fun, but not when you have to do so dozens of times in the same areas just to complete simple fetch quests. It’s a shame, because the studio did a fairly good job building up a solid foundation. It’s just that they didn’t know what to do with said foundation and we get a filler-stuffed experience as a result. Maybe one day we’ll get something to build on this base, but for now, Binary Star is unfortunately an easy pass.Follow my  for more reviews + videos!

_childDocuments_.review: Okay hear me out..I genuinely understand the negative points people are bringing up. HOWEVER, despite all of this i think it is a game absolutely worth checking out. Especially if you love Made In Abyss. - The general gameplay is very nice. It's your typical exploration, survival, crafting esque game and it's so much fun to explore!- The custom story (story where you create your own character and become a cave raider) even has it's own storyline and you get to see the characters everyone came to love from the show.- The visuals are actually pretty neat. From the models to the surroundings it all works really well together.- So much exploration potential!! You can just run around for funsies and bonk whatever creature comes across your path. Though some might eat you instead. You have a weight limit to your inventory (which can be upgraded) which forces you to run back home and go at it in a new run (aka. this isn't just a 2 hour game, you can spend alot of time on side quests and just explore for fun).- Learning about the creatures is hella fun. You can analyze each creature you come across and learn more about it in a journal you keep with you.- Whack control layout. That is completely true for the keyboard control. I genuinely don't understand how they came up with these settings  the good thing is that you can easily just change the keybinding and set them to whatever suits you most. Playing with a controller is a bit more comfortable though a few buttons are still questionable but then again you can still change the keybindings.- Not worth the money. I have to kinda agree on this one. I paid 60 Euro and was a bit bummed after playing for a bit because i thought that i wasted my money on barely anything fun to play.  i think alot of people haven't played too far into the custom story, got bummed out that Riko and Regs gameplay was so short, or just didn't quite expect what game they got themself into and it turned out to be a  game they don't necessarily enjoy.- Janky, Buggy, Unpolished. That is true. There's a few lil things here and there that just don't function like they probably were intended to. But it happens to the best games out there.- Creature spawn is insane. That is true as well! In certain areas you will literally be swarmed by creatures trying to attack you, even if you just stand around trying to eat something or heal yourself. There have been a few times where i got frustrated because i kept falling to my death because a moth touched my arm. If you make use of your Mail Balloons though you will be fine and it will be less frustrating.- Too Slow? I guess if you like fast paced games this is not for you. The beginning is pretty slow, having just become a red whistle you will be forced to simply struggle along and run back home after getting a scratch on your knee. But that changes as soon as you start going to the 2nd and 3rd layer.- Side characters talk TOO MUCH..... that was something i struggled personally. Whenever you have a mission that requires someone to join you on your journey into the Abyss, they will talk to you. All. The. Time. Whenever you pick something up they throw 3 sentences at you in a row.. I want to pick my flowers in peace leave me alone please.If you like exploring an unknown world, learn about it's creatures, survival + crafting, and have a little bit of patience? I think this game is worth checking out. If you're unsure about it's pricing.. wait for a discount :)8/10 recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game that has all the elements in place to be great- a large world to explore, crafting, survival, talent trees, quests/side-quests, and best of all, being placed in the world of Made in Abyss.Sadly, the execution fails, and the game is marred by terrible design decisions. I don't know if there was zero play testing, if people were afraid to give feedback during development, or if leads were too arrogant to listen to that feedback. It's unfortunate, because it's not a case of needing more budget. They could have played the game for five minutes and seen how the game's systems get in the way of enjoying the game.It's a grouping of several small issues that on their own can easily be overlooked, but combined make gameplay truly tedious. Like companions repeating the same two lines every 3 seconds (no joke, you dont get more than a couple of seconds of silence at best before they repeat the same lines on a loop). The ability to place 99 custom map markers, but will disappear once you go to town (lol, seriously, why?). Enemies that respawn a second or two after killing them, combined with low weapon durability and limited inventory space. Slightly different from the last point, flying enemies that spawn infinitely around you when you've been in an area for ~5 minutes (again, combined with durability and inventory space make this quite tedious). Apparently this was actually patched a few months ago, I can't even imagine what it was like before.As can be expected, maps are quite vertical, meaning you have to deal with the curse every few seconds. Combine this with the plentiful climbing, where every 5 seconds of climbing you have to pause for ~7 seconds so the curse can fade. Now add in the infinitely spawning flying enemies swarming you while climbing, your weapon durability, and the limited stamina.Those who know the story upon which this game is based, know that this world is brutal. I expected difficult and unforgiving gameplay. Instead, the game is actually really simple, the only difficulty comes from the tedium of these mechanics and the jankiness of the game. I feel like I'm not fighting the creatures inhabiting the world, nor the Abyss - instead I'm fighting the developers and the game itself. It completely breaks immersion and it's such a shame.When I saw Spike Chunsoft made this game, I was both excited and fearful. Some of my favorite games are by these folks, but from my experience, action games are not their forte. I knew what I was getting into, I knew this wasn't going to be triple A, and quality would not be high. But it didn't need to be for this game to be a success.I will continue to play in the hopes that the game gets better, because ultimately I still love the world the game is based on, and I'll update if things change. However, at this moment, the feeling I get from this game is disappointment in such wasted potential, especially because a lot of these issues could have been fixed so easily, and should have been identified immediately within just a few minutes of playtesting.One last note: If you decide to pick up this game, I would seriously recommend skipping "Hello Abyss". It's not a difficulty setting, and despite what people say, it's not a tutorial either. It's a barebones version of the game that offers a highly watered down version of the first few episodes of the anime, and where basically none of the systems are in place. You will be punished for exploring, and for looting pretty much anything you find. You will likely spend a huge chunk of your time managing your inventory and deciding what to throw away. Reaching the Seeker Camp made me want to cry from how sad one of the fights was, and the cutscenes did not do the story justice. I was ready to uninstall after completing that, and thankfully I decided to give the main game a try (and if after this rant of a review I'm still thinking that the main game is a drastic improvement over Hello Abyss, just think what that says about Hello Abyss).

_childDocuments_.review: Play this if you love Made in Abyss but hate yourself. I personally really enjoyed it, but that's not because it's a good game. This game is actually bad. For example: an Orb Piercer should be able to 1 or 2 shot your small child body and skewer you for an epic death cutscene by the time you first meet one... or you can repeatedly hit it with the first hit of your "combo" instead of actually using the "combo" (that you spend skill points to unlock) to stun-lock it forever and ~never~ get hit at all. It's very stupid, but so is all of the combat in this game. However, somewhere in the jank... I enjoyed it. There is something compelling about getting completely lost in the maze of the 3rd layer after having "you-know-what" happens, or getting bodied by the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ madokajack hitboxes while struggling to find enough food to even climb out of the Great Fault.I increased my enjoyment of this game by installing several mods, and if you do pick up this game I would implore you to do the same through the MiA:BSFiD modding discord server. Buying it while it's highly discounted should be the only time you consider buying it, but I did buy it at full price because I am a MiA slave. Sorry, but not sorry. Oya, oya, oya, oya, oya, oya...In summary, this makes me yearn for a true Made in Abyss game to be made: a competent game, a complete experience. Unfortunately, you'll find none of that here.

_childDocuments_.review: Middling recommendation, with several CAVEats. (Ha!)If you've seen the show, and thought the world and especially the Abyss were fascinating, there's a lot to like here, albeit mixed in with a whole lot of budget problems and sometimes weird fanservice. Note: I didn't really care about rehashing RIko and Reg's journey in a slightly worse way, so I only played the other game mode. It's got a number of tonal issues whenever you're talking to anyone, is my main critique. Riko, the incompetent and frankly insane loser who technically flunked out of orphan school for committing suicide, is now some sort of weirdly legendary character. Everyone assumes you've heard of this amazing person and her incredible exploits, despite her being... pretty much a nobody in the anime. And often it feels like people don't take the dangers of the abyss seriously at all, even when they're supposed to be professional cave raiders. Even Riko knew it was dangerous in the anime, she just didn't care. But you'll see even black whistles be totally nonchalant about everything.There are also bloody stumps of cut features all over the place - for instance, a lot of characters will, after completing a specific quest for them, have some dialogue in the vein of "Give me a call if you ever want me to join you on an expedition!" It's pretty obvious a lot of planned features were designed around and then awkwardly torn out. The whole game feels buggy and unfinished, in an old-school Obsidian kinda way. My favorite bug is when you kill a boss with a weapon, the weapon breaks, regardless of its durability level, including relic weapons. Thanks QA! (I'm joking, I know they didn't have the budget for a QA department)The game requires a mod to be enjoyable - play it for a bit until you see what I mean, then go get the "disable constant enemy spawning" mod. Otherwise you can never stop and look around, which is... weird in a game that you're mostly playing for the scenery.With all of those out of the way... Yes, I really like this game. For all of its flaws, as an exploration/survival game, it's fantastic. I've never seen a game where a weight limit was as harsh or as necessary, because what you don't necessarily realize going in is that this is not an action game, or an adventure game. It's a hiking sim with mountain-climbing elements. I'd say 90% of your time will be spent either slowly trundling into some increasingly dangerous place with your comically oversized backpack OR climbing a rock face (the remaining 10% of your time is spent managing your inventory). You aren't an action hero, and while combat is often necessary, you are MUCH better off running away or otherwise avoiding fights most of the time. Your weapon won't survive more than a few swings, and weapons, especially GOOD weapons, are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ HEAVY. You can only carry a few, unless that's the ONLY thing you bring with you. In many ways it forces you to think carefully, consider the dangers of a course of action, and treat things with a lot more gravity. Especially gravity, because boy will gravity kill you a lot. And I love that slow, careful exploration. It's where the game truly shines. It's not perfect, there's a number of things I'd change and places where it's held back by various concessions (mostly to budget, occasionally to accessibility, annoyingly frequently to tone-deaf fan service). But I can't think of a single game like it, really. So, if you are...1. A fan of the show,2. A fan of slow-paced, grounded, careful survival/exploration,3. Willing to overlook bugs (as well as insects) and a blatantly incomplete game,then I would give it a somewhat muted recommendation. I like this game a lot. I don't think it's  good, but it does certain things uniquely well, and those things are pretty great if you like them. Pick it up on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: I completed this game.  It's imperative that I inform you that you should only be buying this game on sale if you value your quality/$ metrics.  That said, it should at most be worth $30 if you don't want to feel robbed.  The 60 hours I am shown to have put in was the time I spent completing the game, so there is quite a bit to do if you also factor time into your tolerance for pricing.You should also know that "Hello Abyss", the first segment of the game, makes up well less than 10% of the time you will spend to finish the game.  Don't over-invest yourself in playing "Hello Abyss", because "Deep in Abyss" is what your money has been spent for.  At this point, the game thankfully no longer demands you to unlock "Deep in Abyss" by playing "Hello Abyss" first as many initial players had to deal with.  If you want to determine whether or not to refund, "Hello Abyss" is a red herring mode that will inappropriately represent what the game will be like, and it may take long enough to time you out of the refund period; play "Deep in Abyss" from the get-go instead if you listen to this and are still unsure if you'll like the game.Deep in Abyss is a delving simulator based on the world of Made in Abyss.  Yeah, I said SIMULATOR.  Don't expect fun, streamlined action and adventure all the time.  The game is amazing at delivering an experience of the day-in-day-out delving job where you brave the wild and seek out relics to sell back in Orth.  The journey down will be a chore, and so will the journey back... at least until you start getting promoted and can fast travel amidst layers.You will manage hunger, stamina, weapon durability, cargo weight, and the curse of ascension traversing the Abyss.  You will make judgments about fighting or avoiding creatures.  You will plan out items to bring with you and seek resources and/or food ingredients to pick up and craft/cook with on-site to facilitate your excursions (if the show/manga didn't make it clear that eating is an essential aspect of survival, the game will force-feed you the wisdom one way or another).  You will revisit some areas multiple times, especially if you have charted it as an optimal route to where you need to go next.It will feel like a slog at times, and that's probably what actual delvers in the world would feel; dare I say, that could be considered immersion of its own kind.  If you value the idea of eating some humble pie and immersing yourself with that sensation, Deep in Abyss shares a bit with old-style Monster Hunter games (note: the versions BEFORE World and Rise) in how you can identify as and take pride in being a successful delver through the act of careful preparation and work applied using what you've learned through experience.I didn't care so much about the jank of the controls (arguably appropriate to approximate a delver's struggles in the Abyss, but I cannot anticipate whether or not you will be frustrated), the general graphical quality, or such.  Even the parts of the game that others despise (constant butterflies and birds for daring to climb, the third layer, etc.) I considered part of the trial of triumphing over the game, and everything is achievable.  I did like the ambient intensity of the music (I didn't expect electric guitar bits, but they worked where applied), though Kevin Penkin's work might have added a bit of beauty to the setting.  All that said, I found the value of the game was in the experience of operating as a mortal delver and the journey of improvement and progress until I obtained my white whistle.  I enjoy struggles like that.The game terminates at the end of the 5th layer.  One can hope that a future release of an MiA game will elaborate upon the qualities of the game, objectively improve graphics and interactions, and add in more dangerous trials in the 6th layer... perhaps even the 7th layer (if it takes THAT long), but I was quite satisfied with this much.  I might even start a new playthrough sometime, but, for now, I recommend the game for the MiA fan who already knows the story and wants to see how they'd fare in the Abyss.

_childDocuments_.review: This game feels like such a good idea held back by a lack of proper execution and many bugs. The visuals look nice, the voice acting is a bit hit or miss, the sound design is frustrating, and the gameplay is the most hit or miss thing ever. Having to genuinely consider whether climbing down further is the right choice or exploring a certain zone is too dangerous is so interesting. That is however made a problem by the stupid monster spawns. They will often spawn monsters right on top of you at random points for no reason. Climbing a wall? Here's a moth to annoy the ♥♥♥♥ out of you. Trying to walk around and check for relics? Have about 4 little spikey ferrets spawn on top of you to hit and frustrate you. A lot of the text UI in the game also has issues. Whether it is text going off the side of the screen or entire item descriptions that aren't completed. As for audio, you would be shocked how often the same line is repeated over and over again not just by ally characters, but by your own character as well. They all have a single line of dialogue for most actions. I can't forget the fact that Reg starts freaking out and gets stuck with any slight incline.So far this game needs so many fixes, changes, and maybe a complete overhaul before it's worth the price. My suggestion, do not buy this game for anything above $10. Spikechunsoft continues to drop the ball on every anime game they make.Quick note, a full month later and they still haven't put out a single patch/update for this game. If it doesn't get one before the year ends, then that definitely means spikechunsoft has given up on it.Another addition! Spike has put out a small patch that doesn't fix anything but makes both modes selectable from the start. They say they will release another patch. If that patch is good enough, I will rewrite my entire review. If not, I will not change a damn thing.

_childDocuments_.review: Initially, when I heard that Made in Abyss was getting a game I was extremely excited. Thinking about the world and themes of Made in Abyss, I couldnt help but feel it could be turned into an awesome game. The unique monster design, the many environments of the abyss itself, and the lingering threat of the Curse of the Abyss seemed like it would lend itself to a one of a kind gaming experience. I didnt even want much of a story, just for the devs to let me live in that awesome world for a while. But WOW, this game has dropped the ball in a big way. First off is graphics and performance. The game is not pretty, it is good PS2 to bad PS3 graphics at best and the performance is meh. Anime and JRPGs in general dont tend to be the prettiest (final fantasy excluded), but with a unique design that is crisp they can shine (Persona). Unfortunately they did not manage that here, with the models often being fuzzy and so little effort made that the dialogue wasnt even synced to the lips in some places(like not even an attempt, just a gaping unmoving maw). Its not particularly ugly, but with the pricing we should expect better.Gameplay, the core of any game. This was particularly what excited me about a Made in Abyss adaptation, there was so many unique mechanics to utilize. However, what was implemented is frankly trash. Movement is slow, bulky, and your stamina drains in about 5 seconds. I'm sorry, but you play as a kid right? Right? Why on gods green earth can they not run for more than a few feet without having to catch their breath like a 75 year old chain smoker? Oh and by the way if you let your stamina empty you have to stand still catching your breath while monsters maul you or push you off a cliff for an instant kill. Fighting in the game is slow and bulky, you are super weak, and there isnt really unique loot for killing monsters. Honestly I dont even know why they bothered to make a fighting mechanic at all? You. are. a. small. child. The entire show and manga is them scurrying around hiding. The only times they really successfully kill anything is via Regs Incinerator, a fancy tool, or using a trap. It would have been far better to make the monsters actually scary(Which honestly I dont know how they made them not scary, they are horrifying in the books and show) and improve the movement and sneaking. Instead, the monsters behave like dynasty warrior mobs that just keep spawning and slowly swinging at you. Lastly we come to the absolute WORST gameplay implementation that was done. The curse of the Abyss itself.The idea here is that if you ascend, you get sick. Its really a simple concept. The problem is how the game tallies exactly how many meters you have ascended since you last sat and had a little break. It isnt calculated by using the relative depth of the map(IE lowest point in the past 15 seconds is 500, if player crosses 485 they get sick). Noooooo, that would make to much sense. Instead they make it a sum value of any and all ascension you do. As a result if you are on a path that is roughly even in terrain, but has small bumps that cause you to rise and fall a few times as you go over it, you could easily get sick and puke your guts out while walking in a straight line. This makes traversing basic terrain infuriating as you just start getting sick out of nowhere. But thats not even the worst part. No, theres an even more egregious sin committed by the devs. In the level design they DEMAND YOU ASCEND. They literally will make you rappel down 80 meters, then walk 20 more, then climb right back up or higher on the other side. Problem is that you have to stop and take a little nap stuck to the side of the cliff like a Koala every 5 meters or you start puking! Oh and by the way to refill the hunger you just puked up you have to cook. To cook 90% of the meals you have to have salt. And its never explained where you scavenge the salt. Im sorry, but If I am starving in a death pit I dont need to season my freaking chicken!!!! Getting back to the level design, I just cant imagine any dev going "yes lets force the player to climb extremely slowly and take breaks every 5 meters for half of all the levels! What a brilliant idea!". I know this was one hell of a rant, but its honestly just such a shame to see so much potential ruined right outta the gate. I hate to say it but I didnt really enjoy any part of the game. I just tolerated it out of love for the franchise. I do have one more major point to make though, and thats the pricing.60 dollars, the price of a triple A game. That is an INSANE PRICE TO PAY. This game would barely be worth 30. I would NOT recommend buying at full price. Honestly the gameplay holds 0 lore you are missing, so just watch a video of the cutscenes on youtube if you love the world of Made in Abyss and want to consume all the lore it has. If you find it on a steep discount and want to try, sure go ahead. But be wary, the mechanics are made to infuriate. Might I suggest a stiff drink to help it go down? I certainly needed it.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll be honest. I REALLY enjoy this game,  This is a game I would never recommend this game to another person in good faith. At times it feels like there was a meeting where, as a joke, everyone pitched the worst possible mechanics, but instead they weren't actually joking and they did it.When everything is on point and you're in the flow, you really get immersed in everything, truly making you feel like you're a cave raider! When you've been down in the abyss for quite awhile and you manage to arrive back in Orth by the grace of everything, it is such a wonderful feeling. Coming to understand the Abyss like a second home and navigating it like such is satisfying because you have to have it beaten into you. I really adored getting hands-on with a world I deeply enjoy and interacting with my fan favorites from the source, all while on my own little journey to the bottom of the netherworld. that's also the same issue with this game. It tries its very best at every possible moment to remove as much fun as it can. The infinitely spawning enemies makes combat a chore and something you actively avoid, not because it's dangerous and not because of weapon durability, it's just because otherwise you'd be constantly fighting the same enemy every time you turn your camera! Combat is literally something I only engage in as a means of getting more food or because I have a quest(s) that requires me to kill X. You would think in a game about adventure and exploring you would actually be rewarded for doing so, correct? Sike, you either: death, a dead end, a waste of time and resources or, at the very best, a marginal one-way shortcut. Actually, exploring would only really serve to get you lost unless you've already unlocked  I would genuinely love to sit down to a conversation with the person(s) responsible for the mechanic where every annoying flying enemy (the butterflies and birds) hunt you if you're on a stage for 4+ minutes. Some of those stages are HUGE and time-consuming to get through unless you know in advance the EXACT route you intend on taking, otherwise enjoy not being able to climb because they WILL spawn directly on your head and you can not hit them because combat while climbing is jank or they will stunlock you because you have to wait for the curse to disappate. On the topic of the curse, it is by far the BIGGEST letdown! ANY amount of elevation and the curse starts to hit you, enjoy the uneven ground that will also start accumulating, making it so every few seconds or so you basically have to sit there for 8-10 seconds twittling your thumbs while you wait and repeat until you reach your destination. Alternatively, you can choose to sit through the animation of throwing up and sprint for a good while, since you will not get hit by the curse while you're recovering from its effect.I'm only on the 3rd layer right now, so I haven't beaten the game at the time of review but I honestly doubt my opinions would change since my issues from the core mechanics and loop of the game. I'll probably put more playtime into the game and 100% because I'm that kind of person but I very highly doubt I'll ever think about coming back after that or really even fondly thinking of the game, which is honestly a shame because there's a lot of potential if the game didn't try it's hardest to make you hate playing it.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're a fan of the Made in Abyss (Manga/Anime) series, boy are you in for a treat. This game plunges you deep into that beautiful world. It scratches that "if only the Manga/Anime could spend a little more time in expanding each layer" itch. Along the way you'll not only get to meet, but quest with many familiar faces.Ok now for the not so great, although the game was released this year, the graphics seem quite dated (you can find better graphics on a PS3 title). If you're playing on mouse and keyboard, good luck. This game was clearly made to be played with a controller. For a game that allows you to jump into each layer of the abyss to explore and hunt/scavenge/gather, it sure is frustrating that there's a persistent gameplay mechanic built-in to push you out of every area after 5 minutes. Having to deal with constantly spawning 1hp mobs that harass you after barely exploring 1/4 of a new area has to be my biggest gripe throughout my playthrough. (Glad to see there's a mod to disable this). Weapons have durability and you'll find yourself breaking (broken weapons are just instantly deleted) many all throughout the early to mid-game. Thankfully though, by late-endgame, weapon durability is no longer a significant factor to have to play around.Now, if you can get past the graphics quality and the irritating mob spawn mechanic, the gameplay loop is stellar. Diving into the abyss, exploring new layers, mining relics, gathering resources, harvesting mob parts, deciding what to keep/toss cause you're overburdened, realise you're low on food/health/poisoned, before climbing back all the way, hoping to make it back to the surface...rinse and repeat. Each tier of gear and weapon upgrades feel impactful, and can easily turn previously perilous layers into a stroll in a park. As you progress through Red to White Whistle, you are rewarded with very nice quality-of-life buffs like curse resistance and the ability to teleport back to the surface from a previous layer at the cost of hunger and life. Despite the mob spawn mechanic, I was able to complete the game progressing at a relatively comfortable and casual pace (umbrella might be the best relic in the game imo lol).All in all, I thoroughly enjoyed the game very much and to be able to travel down the same paths taken by the Manga/Anime characters, this is very much a must-play for any Made in Abyss enjoyer.

_childDocuments_.review: Good ip, poor game designBeing one of the top fans of Made in Abyss, I bought this game immediately, but quickly got disappointed by the several factors in the following:1. Ridiculous Key bindsIn most 3rd person RPG games, you click left mouse to attack, right mouse to aim. In this game, left clicking your mouse is Crouching, and right clicking does nothing. You hold Z key to aim, and press X to attack. The worst part is you can’t change the key bind to your mouse in settings. Left shift is supposed to be sprinting and Q or E to open your inventory. No. You need to press TAB to craft and open the full inventory. You sprint by holding left control. I haven’t even complain that mouse wouldn’t work in selecting anything except a few option buttons. Instead of scrolling down with your mouse wheel in menu, you are forced to spam W and S or Z and X keys to go up or down and left or right on the panel, respectively. By the way, spacebar always closes the menu, ESC is useless just like left mouse.2. Reg’s AI is profoundly defective. He is controlled by an AI that has a health bar and would respawn after losing all health. Sometimes he helps you to neutralise threats. But most of the time he attacks any hostile monster even if they are passive, he could’ve just ignore them. But he decides to attack anything and wastes health. Then by the time you need him, he’s always on his way to respawn.Sometimes he is stuck in one place. He can’t climb unlike Riko with spacebar, and decides to stomp around. If you don’t have any food supply, ignore him and move on, because trying to lead him will waste your hunger bar. 3. some map design flaws that would trap you forever if your hunger bar is empty. First, you lose hunger when you enter the next map. Second, In the reverse forest, there’s a spot on the only path that you must climb. Climbing costs you hunger and stamina. And when your hunger bar is empty, your stamina bar is also empty. That means you can’t climb or use weapons. And to recover your hunger, you need food. There are barely any food in this map and only by hunting the birds you have a chance to loot 1 egg from 1 bird. You need 2 units of eggs to craft 1 unit of food, and each unit will only sustain a couple more times to attack and steps of walking. Then you might want to rely on Reg, and he is not reliable in the game.Conclusion I really want to ask for refund but my play time is well over 2 hours. Console version is probably better speaking of the controls. Whoever makes the steam version has never played any RPG games on PC. If you have bought this already, you have paid a premium well beyond any of the triple A games. At least not worse than bf2042.

_childDocuments_.review: A lot of premature reviews here. It took me 3 hours and 12 minutes to beat Hello Abyss (story mode). This isn't the full game. The crafting is extremely limited in this mode, and the game doesn't tell you that. You are not meant to gather and explore in this mode; it is purely to tell the story of the anime (up until Riko leaves Seeker Camp).The real game is the mode after you beat story. The crafting system, armor, weapons, etc. open up to their full potential in this mode (a lot was hidden in story). I've only played 50 minutes of the second mode and have noticed a rather annoying glitch. Enemies spawn right behind me as soon as my camera looks away. Literally anytime my camera is not pointing in X direction a Mon-toyer or whatever the weasel things are called spawns right on top of me. It's really annoying when you have no pickaxe and can't get 2 hard stone. I like the game. Try it out if you want. But a lot of these reviews are unfairly premature

_childDocuments_.review: I desperately wanted to like this game. But I cannot in good faith recommend this to anyone, fans or otherwise, of Made in Abyss. To start off, the game has two modes. You play as Riko and Reg, two of the main cast of the anime, as they descent to the second layer of the Abyss. Completing their mode is considered the "Tutorial", and you make your own original character child and experience what cave raiding essentially would be in this world. That is a fantastic setup for what could have been an anime aesthetic punishing-but-fair action game with Tsukushi's messed up mind making up about 3/4 of the monsters you'll encounter in the game. Instead what we get is a crash course in bad game design and budget restraints causing a developer to pad game time with arbitrary meter management that becomes next to impossible near the end of the game.-It sure is Made in Abyss-Moments of actual awe and wonder as you reach certain areas and get to explore places from the manga-Side quests are generally of the "Gather 50 in X zone of Y Layer", for every zone of the layer, or "Kill Z monsters in X zone of Y layer"-The design of the layers feels like most of the budget was put into layers 1 and 2, and they ran out of money to finish the game.-If you navigate the world, you will eventually NEED to ascend in order to continue going down, whether a walk up a hill, climbing a tree, or scaling a cliff. The Curse of the Abyss introduces a very fun and exciting mechanic where you have to stop moving for 30 seconds in order wear off so you can continue to ascend. This never improves and there is no resistance stat like cave raiders develop in the Anime's canon.-Enemies are spawned constantly behind your camera. This can become exceptionally frustrating when you're navigating sheer cliffs.-Related, Moths and other flying enemies spawned behind the camera can navigate into your model, causing you to be stuck in place until you fall to your death.-The durability of your weapons is just slightly too low to not be frustrating.There may be more but this is what has come to mind. Finishing this game was exhausting and I wish to never touch it again.I've beaten the game, 100% achievements, and I did it in spite of the game and its poor design choice, not because of the game being enjoyable.
