_childDocuments_.review: A fair game, once you understood the mechanics you can break the difficulty really easily. Mech fights could use more flare or special characteristic to them. Only time I was surprised was when . Maybe make a sniper mech that doesn't move from the corner and alter the arena to make it hard to approach or something. Just an idea.Fights can have several days in between where nothing happens and you just free roam. This stretched the game for seemingly no reason. You can cut most of them out without much change to the game.Those are pretty much my biggest nitpicks. The one positive thing that stand out from the rest is how solid VA did their job.The game is overall still enjoyable and would give it a recommend for someone looking for a simple turn based mech game. Would definitely like seeing a second game fleshing out the mechanics a bit more.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a relatively short game if you rush through it without doing the extras, but I think it's a nice experience for it's price.I'd almost recommend playing the game until you lose in a main story match, because that way you can keep the game a somewhat challenging, as buying the best gear or getting bonus parts from extra content can quickly make you ridiculously strong.The good:+ Great soundtrack / voiceacting+ Fun characters + Good art & aestheticsThe bad:- The daily traveling takes more time than the fights- The gameplay gets incredibly repetitive- Fights are easily cheesed as long as you're not too underpowered, as the opponents don't really plan ahead- Obnoxious symbolism stuffed everywhereI'm gonna give it a 7/10. The dev loves 7's :D
_childDocuments_.name: Wolfstride

_childDocuments_.review: Being someone who played their fair share of Mecha Flash games growing up, I have to say that Wolfstride ended up being a wonderful sub-20 hour experience. a. Core Gameplay Loop: Stylish 1v1 Mecha Duels Definitely my favourite element of the game, both due to the variety of equipment, moves & stances that you can mix & match to fulfill your desired playstyle as well as how stylish all the battle animations are. b. Story & Characters: One that needs time to growWhilst some of the characters are initially rather off-putting (looking at you Mr Tiny Robot), I found that over the course of the game that many of their characters arcs turned out to be rather quite satisfying - if a bit unresolved by the end of the game. Personally, I ended enjoying Shado's & Nebraska's arcs the most.c. OST & Sound DesignExcellent on all fronts & marvelously compliments the rest of the game.Overall Rating for me would be an 8.5/10 - well worth your time & money.
_childDocuments_.name: Wolfstride

_childDocuments_.review: I was gifted this game from a friend who thought I'd enjoy it. _childDocuments_.review: First week over, early review timeI'd been looking forward to Wolfstride for a while and it's honestly pretty damn good!The voice acting is decent, the music is fitting and the aesthetics rock a solid design with pixel overworld, awesome mech fighting and stylised art for portraits and cutscenes.The world has a few references dabbed in here and there and it's overall a fun time.There's a good build up here and I'm looking forward to playing through the rest of the game!

_childDocuments_.review: Story - 9/10A pretty good-written story with some twists. The side plotlines are a bit cut in my opinion.Visuals - 9/10Nice simple style, very high quality.  Though some parts are missing - many scenes lack close-up faces, mostly in the 2nd half of the game.Gameplay - 7/10The battles are...me(c)h. I mean, if your objective is to specifically not hit the torso and the target does not hide behind a shield, it is pretty straightforward. Still fun to see how characters interact during the fight.The mini-games are sort of dull and for their quality I would expect more quantity, at least in the next part.The visual novel/travelling part was the most annoying though. Like, can we please get not the "skip all scenes" button for long animated parts and get the fast travel function instead? Or at least make the levels smaller to waste ~5 seconds instead of 10?Overall this is a nice mech game, hope some stuff will be fixed in the next partm which feels to be in plans so far.

_childDocuments_.review: The game took just about 22 hours to beat and I did pretty much everything, I'm only missing 2 achievements and one of them is grinding the battlepass in the in-game video game to max.It is very very heavily story focused, everything and everyone is voice acted. The mecha battles are mandated by story progression, not a freeform tournament or anything you go through at your own pace.The writing and the voice work is quite good for every character and that's really the main focus, though there are a few eye-rolling moments when things get a bit too emo or edgy. Even the robot who has a stupid high pitched voice and says PEEEEE as a censor, grew on me by the end. The "real" story is only told in tiny bits and pieces with foreshadowing until the very very end, you're really here for the characters and their journey through this mecha tournament, with the backstories of everyone as a side focus, I feel like. The battle system is pretty simple but engaging enough, but once you get the hang of it the story battles are never challenging. After each story battle you have a chance to go grind for money to buy the best parts for your mech if you feel like it, probably so you cant get stuck.You can target specific body parts of your opponents to disable their attacks using that part and move left/right in a line grid battlefield. Getting your opponent (or yourself) locked in the corner gives a damage buff.There's 2 sets of optional challenge fights you can do that can be tough depending on how well equipped you are at the time, but once you're geared and have a good basic strategy they aren't that hard either.The art is really nice when its there, for character portraits or mechs with the occasional full screen art piece. Otherwise most everything is done in pretty simple pixel art.I was expecting it to have some super robot anime tropes where there's some grand power up or world changing event (ala Gurren Lagann and such) but honestly it stays very grounded.
_childDocuments_.name: Wolfstride

_childDocuments_.review: It's a VN on the most part. With additional mini-games and JRPG style turn-based mecha combat. Weebs and mecha fans will find a lot of references and easter eggs.Plot is all over the place yet fits comedy/parody style with some drama inserts almost perfectly. A lot is going on simultaneously, political struggle of superpowers unleashes in background, subplots (sometime ridiculous) develop in your town while you are just trying to make ends meet and fix/upgrade your mech for the next fight. Devs left a lot of loose ends so sequel seems quite possible.Humour and jokes vary especially from character to character so I think everyone will find something to laugh at.Voice acting is quite solid though I think they overact at some TEH DRAMA points but it's quite subjective.The biggest fault: grindy as hell and a lot of running around the town map that simply wastes time and annoys. But maybe it's just my play style of searching every nook and cranny.Overall: recommended to mecha/VN/turn-based combat lovers.
_childDocuments_.name: Wolfstride

_childDocuments_.review: How to make a cool game with anime qualities - Take mechas & a bit of over-the-top artstyle from Tengen toppa Gurren Lagann, mix in a dash of strong characters with interesting backstories from something like Cowboy Bebop, pepper it with strong language, then wrap it up in basic premise from Redline to kick off the story.AND YOU HAVE A WINNER LADIES AND GENTLEMEN!I cannot stress enough how much I enjoyed this game. The main turn-based combat system is fun, it is nicely animated to convey the brutal oil-spilling action, and it feels great to slowly upgrade your mecha. The minigames are a nice distraction. The music is just brilliant and often I would just chill in the hangar, enjoying the atmosphere. But the well written, fully voiced (SO DAMN WELL VOICED) characters and great story really made this one of my instant all time favourite games.My only complaint would be too much unnecessary running around the city, looking for new events at every location, EVERY DAY. Often I would run all the way somewhere to find that nothing has changed from the day before. But still, it was all worth it for me in the end.Now... I just sit here with a void in my heart after finishing the game, wishing for more. Best mark of quality in my book.
_childDocuments_.name: Wolfstride

_childDocuments_.review: Cool mecha game with a ton of style and heart. The dialogue sometimes feels a little tryhard and I'm not sure if the subplot introduced toward the end of the game was super necessary, but overall, a very fun labor of love that commits hard to its unique look. _childDocuments_.review: Ohhhh this is really good. Really, really good.Sometimes you find a game that's just pure gold, something where they had a vision and stayed true to it. _childDocuments_.review: This game has full VA cast, you don't have to read anything in this game, the chars speak out the speech trees for you, and your choices in this game really matters, not to mention it literally has epic gameplay, interesting chars and very very cool graphics, the style will remind you of what anime/manga mech battles are about, it reminds me of metabots in a way as well.

_childDocuments_.review: As Ota Imon Studio's debut game, they absolutely knocked it out of the ball park.Wolfstride is an indie masterpiece, filled with gorgeous art, colorful characters, and a great story to wrap it all up. At its core, it's a story-rich linear narrative game with mecha fights sprinkled along the way. Characters have unique and humorous personalities, and the voice acting is superb. The story is over-the-top dramatic and the game is very self-aware about it. There will be small subplots you can piece together over the course of the game by visiting locations often, but its mostly "hidden" dialogue and have no huge impact on the main story. The game is separated into days, and new events can occur on every day minus Free Roam days, where you can do whatever you want. The fighting aspect of the game is great! you maneuver around a battlefield separated into sections with buffs and debuffs to your damage. There are a huge variety of mecha to fight against, although the COWBOY will be your only ride throughout the game, as it is central to the story. New parts make your mecha stronger, watching movies gives your pilot new stances (gives bonuses doing certain actions, like blocking, pushing, etc), and your trainer robot can sell you new moves. Of course, upgrading your mecha will cost money. While winning fights does pay prize money, most of your cash will be earned grinding out short minigames scattered throughout Rain City. if you over prepare and grind way too much cash, it might get boring, but in my experience I never really had to grind that much. Some minor nitpicks:-large amounts of backtracking, visiting old locations. Can't be helped since Rain City is a pretty small place.-minor bugs that the developers will no doubt patch in the future. -For those looking for a pure mecha brawler turn based strategy game, sometimes that aspect takes a backseat compared to the main story. However, later unlocks in the game allows you to do just that with non stop battles. -Some humor is a hit or miss depending on the audience. I enjoyed it because I didn't take it too seriously, but other people might find it way too dramatic.Game length is about 20 hours or so give or take.For the price this game is at and the amount of love the devs fit in its little 3.4ish gigabyte body, this is a steal. Definitely check it out!
_childDocuments_.name: Wolfstride

_childDocuments_.review: A fantastic turn based strategy game. Classic anime style artwork. A unique style of combat with many different strategies. The story is deep and developed, and you can tell the developers put a lot of effort into this game.If I had to rate this game I would give it 10/10.Seriously, if you like turn based combat, this is THE game to play.

_childDocuments_.review: I picked this game up on a whim. _childDocuments_.review: So I just completed what I believe is a 100% playthrough (all achievements at least) and I enjoyed the game for the most part.Pros:-Mech battle system is very fun. I enjoyed the positioning mechanics, and it felt like a great medium for storytelling.-Characters are enjoyable. There are many archetype subversions that I found enjoyable. (looking at you Oyabun and Boss Hog)-Artistically very fun. Black and white worked. Shockingly well. Pixel art + fleshed out portraits was great.Cons:-Battle system feels unfinished. There's a very clear way to build a mech, and deviating from that will meet you with disappointment. I'd love to have changed my mech for who I was fighting, but doing that only seemed to make my mech weaker compared to a generalist build.-Not enough parts for the mech. I felt like I got no real new options past day 30ish, which is roughly the halfway point. That was kinda a bummer.-Stances and a fair amount of systems are a bit unbalanced.-Pineapples? I'm still not 100% sure if they change the story or not, but they felt kinda pointless. I was hoping for more bonus dialogue, or something for getting everyone all the pineapples. They kinda just give things to make jobs easier.-Ending felt bad. Without giving any spoilers, the narrative ended up feeling circular and counter to the growth moral the rest of the story pushes.
_childDocuments_.name: Wolfstride

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely worth a playthrough if you like mechs, or you like story.The Story - It could be a little cringey/corny at times but overall I loved it. It took some time getting used to how quick the tone shifts and the story's focus changing but after a while I got used to it.Voice actors - The voices were awesome. They did an amazing job. Enough said.Gameplay - Gameplay was split into 3 sections: Overworld, minigames, and mech battles. Overworld: It reminded me of the later persona games with you wandering around and talking to npcs. So if you know how those are, you get the idea.Minigames: These were quick and easy ways to get some cash and earn some new parts (after a while you do outpeform anything you can be given from these but they are easy cash so big deal). There were 4 major minigames that I remember. When you play them you need to learn them on the fly (they give you very little warning when they start). But you can repeat them as much as you want with no downside.Mech battles: These are similar to fencing, with both mechs on a line. Depending on where you are on the line, you can get bonuses or penalties to attacks (simple plus or minus damage values). You have 4 options to you during combat: movement, attack, defense, and one thats a bit of spoilers so you'll have to play to see. Theres some more stuff I could go into but if you like any of this, give it a try. You won't regret it.TLDR: Games good, play it.
_childDocuments_.name: Wolfstride

_childDocuments_.review: The game is better than the demo. Full voice acting by folks with chops, a soundtrack with longer cues, a great script that paces things out way more than back-to-back fights - it's a big step up.This is a fantastic game being held back by some rough edges. While art, music, writing and animation are all good to great... in order to go somewhere, you have to walk through a street zone before reaching the real zone. There is nothing to do in this street zone and it doesn't seem to change. Good for mood? Maybe? It's hard not to read this as padding out the game length.You're able to go to a hospital at any time. So you head that way and you walk aalllll the way down the street. Then your protag helpfully says "there's nothing to do there". And you walk aaallll the way back. You can talk to people, but you can't tell if you're about to listen to a new conversation or hear an older one repeated. You can go anywhere, but your protag has ideas about where to go first, and won't tell you what they are until you're halfway there. There's a lot of time being wasted here. It feels like this game should have been a visual novel but really, really wanted to be No More Heroes, tried to pull it off on a more modest budget, and was ultimately hurt by the attempt.Again, I want to stress, I do recommend this game. It has a lot going for it! Get in there! I just wish they'd taken a hard look at some elements in those final editing passes.
_childDocuments_.name: Wolfstride

_childDocuments_.review: Easily one of the best experiences I had with indie games this year, an easy 9/10 and the developers of this game should be proud of what they made it.Incredible Artstyle and just style in general.10/10 voice action and really surprised me with how much of this game was voice acted, I really can't think of anything in the game that is not voiced, from random conversation or background NPC, everyone has a voice that fits and its well performance.Really fun combat, just wish the last couple fights in the story itself was a little harder. Of the final 4-5 gauntlet fights I was able to win 3 of the on the first turn and another on the second, but the fight with queen took some more time and it was really fun.Biggest problem with the game was probable the amount of time you spend walking around, I feel like you could had cut the screen you had to talk before you reach your destination and it would had being fine, hell I would even make the second screen shorter and disable the running to compensate, or maybe its just my love for the walking animation talking, really the walking animation looked really good.Aside from that there was some small thing I would change like how some transitions from scene to scene were just the game going to black and all the sound cutting, a little jarring where you just finish a sad/important scene and don't really had time to absorb it.Also, some bugs and softlock, but I'm sure the developers of this game love their project and are going to patch it.But anyway, this game could probably cost more than double and I would still give it high praise and say it's worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: Damn does this game makes an entrance. I am at work right now, but I stayed up till almost 4 am just so I could play this a little longer and I haven't been more excited to go back and play a game in a while. I will update my review when i get farther in the game, but I felt it deserved a thumbs up already.The love child of Cowboy Bebop, Gurran Leggan, and Red Line. This game oozes style and personality. Every character is rich with charm and I have really enjoyed the pacing. Some people might find it slow (in the first few hours there is only three fights, but honestly I really liked that. When a fight happens, it feels epic because its been built up through the story)The music is on par, the voice acting is really good, and I don't even have to mention the art direction but I am constantly baffled by how cool and unique each new character I meet looks. They also each have several portrait drawn for their different emotions, some of which completely changes their entire look and its awesome.It really is a time to be alive, seeing so many games that are influenced by anime, but aren't actually anime, which allows them avoid tropes and put new spins on things. I HIGHLY recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.name: Wolfstride

_childDocuments_.review: The consistency and precision with which this game hits its vibe is honestly ridiculous, every time I thought it couldn't evoke another reference or callback or hit that sweet 90s mecha style again it DID. The music, the visuals, the dialogue, all of it is so perfectly accurate to what I wanted after I played the demo. There are a few road bumps and flaws but overall a thoroughly enjoyable game.As I'm the type of person to look for the negatives in reviews more often than the positives, I'll list those here:- The "map" is a simple location selector, but in order to get to the main point of interest for each location you have to run through an extra street before actually arriving at the important part of the area. It can get a little annoying and repetitive.- I found the battles generally pretty easy, especially with how money becomes very easy to grind making it all the easier to have the best equipment available.- One particular resource is extremely grindy to get but essential to getting some of the best gear in the game.Once again, for effect, thoroughly enjoyable game.
_childDocuments_.name: Wolfstride

_childDocuments_.review: Okay, trash! So you need to give this baby some time, eh? The build-up will be slow and sometimes cheesy also tedious but maaaan, if you have the patience and will to survive the first few hours, that's where the real game begins... Once you can upgrade your Mech, your piloting skills, and have the option to fight virtual battles, the whole thing suddenly opens up. Too bad it took so long. - Traveling between locations is a slow and unnecessary process (which hurts the pace quite often), a fast travel option would have been very welcome. The mini-games are more funny and cheesy than entertaining or useful, but thankfully there aren't too many of them. - The story seems interesting, it's just as confusing and muddled as your regular anime storyline, but that's probably intentional. (And I'll probably update this section when I finished the game!). - The dialogue is mostly great, sometimes it is a little too "cool" and edgy for its own good, which hurts the otherwise quite nice character development arks. - The art design is amazing (and unique!), the music is excellent and the voice-acting is exceptionally good, although some of the recorded lines don't really match the facial expressions of the characters which can be off-putting.- The Mecha fight side of the game is solid and tactical, deep enough to really make you think, but not hardcore in difficulty, so you're unlikely to be stuck on a boss for too long and you won't need mathematical formulas to win.- For all its faults, this game has a real personality and a SOUL, which is perhaps the most important aspect, because all other "issues" are mostly a matter of taste, and most of them can be corrected with some fine-tunings, patches, updates, etc. So, again: Give this baby time and patience, because it will reward you with love, and you'll have a heck of a good time.
_childDocuments_.name: Wolfstride

_childDocuments_.review: I never bother to write reviews, but this game is so good I have to make an exceptionThe artstyle (Both pixel art and detailed character art), writing and story is all superb. The voice acting is great and fits and makes the characters so much more enjoyable to listen too. One of the few RPG's where I don't actually skip dialogue as I read and instead just let it all play out.While some might not like the running around the game has you doing, it isn't that bad, and while it can feel like padding, events happen enough to always keep you interested. The actual combat is simple yet interesting with a good amount of tactics and thinking required.I don't really know what else to say other than, buy the game, play if for two hours, and if you aren't hooked by then, ask for a refund.
_childDocuments_.name: Wolfstride

_childDocuments_.review:
Wolfstride is a role-playing game about three former partners-in-crime coming to a turning point in their lives. When they inherit a junkyard mecha called Cowboy, they reunite to enter the planet's most elite mecha competition: the Ultimate Golden God Tournament.

Each member of the team lends their unique experience as they prepare to outwit the best mecha opponents from around the world. Between dog-mechanic Duque, mecha pilot Knife Leopard, and jack-of-all-trades Dominique Shade, the core crew's got just about everything covered.

That is... until their simple mission to make money unfolds into a deep, slow-burning exploration of their complex lives, the dark choices of their past, and their inevitable fate
_childDocuments_.name: Wolfstride

name: Stray
detailed_description: Lost, alone and separated from family, a stray cat must untangle an ancient mystery to escape a long-forgotten city. Stray is a third-person cat adventure game set amidst the detailed, neon-lit alleys of a decaying cybercity and the murky environments of its seedy underbelly. Roam surroundings high and low, defend against unforeseen threats and solve the mysteries of this unwelcoming place inhabited by curious droids and dangerous creatures. See the world through the eyes of a cat and interact with the environment in playful ways. Be stealthy, nimble, silly, and sometimes as annoying as possible with the strange inhabitants of this mysterious world. Along the way, the cat befriends a small flying drone, known only as B-12. With the help of this newfound companion, the duo must find a way out. Stray is developed by BlueTwelve Studio, a small team from the south of France mostly made up of cats and a handful of humans.

Stray is a third-person cat adventure game set amidst the detailed, neon-lit alleys of a decaying cybercity and the murky environments of its seedy underbelly. Roam surroundings high and low, defend against unforeseen threats and solve the mysteries of this unwelcoming place inhabited by curious droids and dangerous creatures. The battles with the police bots, were really fun. The jailbreak was thrilling and overal it gave the game an unrealistic, but fun POV of a cat going through adventures, which I always like.The animation and detail in everything was so good! I even saw little Zurks behind these fleshy walls which I really didn't expect. Even just playing the storyline that was required, I received enough lore to understand the game and it's story. I said it to my friend and I'll say it again: 'It's as if I was watching an interactive movie'The detail was so precise, every feeling the game was supposed to give the player, I felt it. And don't forget the amazing hard work, though I didn't see all credentials, I saw only 3 animators worked on this game; and although I'm not part of the IT or Movie world, I find that impressive!Not too many cutscenes, no unneccessary ones and enough gameplay. I was however disappointed when I wasn't allowed to walk through the city after I opened it, but even then, it was still a fun game.Coming from someone who generally doesn't interact with cats well IRL: I will definitely play another time, to search for more lore and the hidden achievements!Recommended to all animal lovers, adventurous gamers, people who love lore and overal anyone who is seeking a new game to play.

_childDocuments_.review: Post cyberpunk is in!Of all the silent protagonists, a cat is definitely the best type. The world design stops being about creating spaces for humanoids but instead is able to intrinsically lean on things that make puzzle style levels so great - sanctioned and unsanctioned spaces. The feeling of being able to squeeze through bars, under some insignificant drainage or just scale a building totally sells everything about the cat's relationship to this world.The remaining helper robots - strays in their own right - are also brilliantly executed and while the lack of life is the point, the little, repeating actions as if caught in a loop really light up the areas they inhabit. Memories of who they used to serve, perhaps.Finally, the art and lighting is something out of a game with 10x the budget, the gamepad controls feel fantastic, with the use of vibration actually having nuance.

_childDocuments_.review: Ending completely ruined it.Imagine a version of Final Fantasy X that plays out exactly the same as normal -- except, once you get to Zanarkand, Yuna just performs the Final Summoning and then the game abruptly ends. You haven't even finished crying over Yuna's fate, and the game is just over with no closure at all, leaving you to sit there and ask, "What was even the point if we couldn't save her?" And it's only once you stop crying, after the credits have stopped rolling, that you pause and realize that the ending that the writers chose completely contradicts what the rest of the game was trying to do thematically.That's Stray.The first 99% of the game is wonderful and beautiful. The art direction is incredible, the music is lovely. The atmosphere is more effective cyberpunk than Cyberpunk 2077's. The world feels real and lived in. The characters are all distinct and likeable in their own ways. The cat protagonist is animated and lively and feels like he has a personality despite being unable to talk. His relationship with B-12 is one of the most touching ones I've come across in gaming in quite some time.And then the last, like, five minutes happens and it all goes to ♥♥♥♥.Do yourself a favor. Play this game, and then once the cat protagonist and B-12 get on the subway, just stop playing. Pretend that's the ending and just stop. Let yourself believe that B-12 and the cat escaped together and went on to re-discover the beauty of the world together. Because, while that's still inconclusive as hell, that's a way better ending than what we got.*** SPOILERS AHEAD ***This game feels like it was made by a bunch of people who got too high on the smell of their own "What if humans are the real virus??" farts during the pandemic. For the vast majority of its runtime, Stray seems to be a game that's about perseverance and hope and the kindness of strangers -- a game about how we're all better off when we work together instead of going it alone -- only at the very last second to turn around and go: "Now that the last trace of humanity is gone, the planet can begin to heal."What????The characters you meet and form bonds with along the way? No follow-up, no closure at all. Their stories end exactly where you left them. How does anyone actually benefit from the achieved goal at the end? Impossible to say, because the game ended before it told us. The protagonist cat goes through so much growth throughout the story only to have it all wiped clean at the end when he just... goes home. There's not a moment of hesitation from him, not even a Frodo-esque "how do you pick up the threads of an old life?" moment. He's just home. It's fine. Shut up.What was the purpose of what B-12 did? What does opening up the city actually do for anyone? Why on earth would the writers choose to have the cat protagonist just run off into the sunset instead of going back to stay with the people who took him in and became like family? What was the point of any of those connections, in that case?Why is humanity the sudden enemy? B-12 tries to make this make sense with a line about how he has hope for the future because the robots turned out so great -- and this is said after it's established that humanity basically wiped itself out -- but how is that true when the robots behave exactly the same as humans? Humans are painted as bad because of the power-hungry police states that they formed in the wake of a plague -- but the robots are also oppressing each other! That's, like, the entire point of the Midtown sequence! How is that any better from what humans did?I wept openly over what happened to B-12, but I cried even harder during the credits when I realized that what happened to him happened for no reason at all. There was no reason for the writers to do that to him, neither from a narrative or a thematic perspective. It was like he never mattered at all -- that that bond between him and the protagonist cat never mattered -- because the protagonist cat just goes back to his old life anyway.If you write a story where you purposefully get the audience attached to a character just so that you can make that audience mourn them later and that's it, that's the whole point of the character because their death has no thematic purpose...... your writing is Bad, Actually.There's no justification for what happened to B-12. The ending is sad for the sake of being sad. Don't get fooled by "the story made me feel an emotion, therefore the story is good." No. No, it isn't. Stories can make you feel feelings and still be bad. Hell, David Cage made an entire career off of stories like that.The bonds you form with people don't matter. The trials that you overcome in life don't matter. The people you've met along the way don't matter. Sometimes people will just disappear from your life with no closure as though the connection never mattered at all, because it didn't, no matter how important it may have felt at the time. Humanity is a virus and we should just hand the world back over to nature. That's the message that Stray gives the player in the end.This game broke my heart, and not in a good way. I loved this game. I really, really, really was in love with it. I was ready to give it a 9.5 out of 10. But that ending seriously knocks it down to a 5 out of 10 for me. It's really that bad. So, I can't recommend this game to anyone. Not in good faith. Because what the game ultimately delivers in the end is not what was promised during the bulk of it.Just like my example with Yuna -- What the ♥♥♥♥ was the point of it all, when you can't save the person who came to matter most? Why bother telling the stories of Momo and Clementine if they never get resolved? Why bother developing the character of the cat protagonist, only to put him right back where he started at the end? Why go through the journey if the journey doesn't matter?Why waste your time and emotions with this game?

_childDocuments_.review: i would recommend the game ONLY if it is on sale!!!!spoilers probably;game IS visually appealing and it does fulfill the playing-as-a-cat gimmick well, but that's about all the substance the game has. you only get to hang around with other cats for the first 10-20 minutes of the game---the rest of the game is basically just chase sequences, and "open world" where you venture around in a cube of cityscape and can get repeated one-liners from every single npc, all of whom have a name for some reason?basically every bit of progression tied to npcs is a fetch-quest. the story boils down to SoCieTy KiLlEd HuMaNiTy..........! and has very little substance outside of this. the parasites are said to "eat anything" the entire game, but for some reason have not chewed through walls and doors (made of metal, which they are confirmed to eat) to lay waste to the rest of robotkind. also the parasite nesting material grows bigs demonic eyes for....... fun?i think the game would be considerably improved without dialogue, or at least dialogue that isn't directed at the cat. having a big text box pop up everytime i "talked" to someone was extremely immersion-breaking. having the cat instead listening in on conversations (which could be spoken in something made-up, with english subtitles), or your droid buddy pointing their light at/hanging around text on walls to casually direct the players attention would be better. having your droid companion recount memories while you travel instead of forcing you to sit still and read a paragraph would make interactions with them feel more natural... though that wouldn't fix them having little/no emotional depth. writing issue!I also think the game would be improved if it was truly open-world. while i don't think the current approach (a few different maps that you spend time exploring vertically) is awful, the way the quests are designed makes the enclosed maps seem even smaller.

_childDocuments_.review: BlueTwelve Studio's "Stray" transcends typical gaming experiences. It's an immersive journey that occupies the mind long after completion, its neon-lit dystopia and robotic inhabitants refusing to fade from memory.The game's feline protagonist is a marvel of digital craftsmanship. Every movement, every interaction captures the essence of "catness" with uncanny precision. For cat lovers, the experience hits particularly close to home, evoking a poignant longing for our own feline companions, particularly those we've lost.What's remarkable is the universal appeal. Even non-cat enthusiasts will find themselves drawn into this meticulously crafted world. The entire universe of Stray, and all of its inhabitants are equally captivating in their level of detail and creativity. "Stray" taps into our innate sense of wonder and exploration, creating an environment that demands to be experienced.For those who seek total immersion in their media—be it film, literature, or music—"Stray" offers a rich, sensory-laden landscape. It's a testament to the power of nuanced world-building and thoughtful design.In an industry often fixated on spectacle, "Stray" stands out by prioritizing atmosphere and emotional connection. It's not just a game; it's an experience that showcases the medium's potential to move and inspire.For anyone questioning whether to embark on this unique experience, the answer is clear. Step into "Stray." Let it envelop you.Thanks devs and team for making this. This game meant a lot to me personally.

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr - poetic way by Gary to sum up my feelings for this game: But in more seriousness:- The controls are fluent (I've only played with a controller so far and it's even encouraged by the game).- Graphics are delicious.- I've grown up with cats and can confirm that a lot of true-to-cats-stuff is happening (like, when you make them wear something how they start to kind of crawl or just lay down flat on the ground).- Haven't experienced much from the story so far but seems very intriguing (coming from a person who hasn't looked up much about Stray).- And the game, to my pleasant surprise, runs really, really well! I honestly expected more of a rollercoaster and am generally rather cautious before I spent money (for new games), but this here is a smooth ride so far. It's rather relaxed and it appears like you can't miss a jump. By standard, you push "a" to jump and can only do so when the game gives you that option. The game kind of does most of the targeting in that regard for you, though not at all in a way where it would seem like it's babysitting you (not to me at least).It's a smooth experience, lot's of interactables and things to discover, I'm impressed and don't regret a cent I've spent for this game. The developers seem to have poured A LOT of love into this work of art. Truly a gem.Really, if you like cats, it's a no-brainer. There is even a button for meowing. I mean I've only played for roughly an hour so far (when I first wrote the review) and noticed the love that the game got in a lot of details already (walking on keyboards/piano strings, pushing stuff over the edge with the paw...). Should you own cats, you'll probably see their funny behaviour reflected in a lot of situations in this game (and that's somehow a really worthwhile experience). :DSo, if you're unsure, you are still able to return it after said hour (as long as you don't exceed a playtime of 2 hours or possession of the game for more than 2 weeks (exceptions can apply) if I'm not mistaken).So what are you waiting for?

_childDocuments_.review: Funny thing first and beware some really small spoilers: I started this game close to its launch but for some reason, probably something medical related, I just did not have the time to go through this beautiful gem of a story. So just yesterday I played the rest of the story, I was about an hour into the game and I finished it in around 7 hours (If that is interesting for you so you know that the game entertains in a rather casual gameplay and without collecting everything, but the most, in around 8 to 9 hours. I would say that prbly fits to every first time playthrough from what I spoke about with other people.). Now the funny thing is that halfway through, after the major Zurk encounters I noticed I forgot that the game had a sprint button. I switched to Controller for my contiuation, I remembered the story from the apartement on pretty good but I forgot about the control scheme. Be aware it can be a bit unusual but you will see that the devs very well had a great intention behind this - it is just natural for the feeling of the whole game concept and its deeper meaning that you exactly use this type of control scheme on the Controller. So many little things I will not spoiler, make this game truly beautiful and lively, wich should be an intentional overall paradoxon I guess - even the detail of MC-animated robots to reflect the possible soul of humans in them.... I don't want to spoiler any more, the game can be short if you play it through without paying too much attention, therefore do so, I found many interesting notes and newspaper infos, the context expresses itself in the detail. Therefore it reminded me a lot (also due to the lighting) of the Game "Homesick".Now to the issues: The control scheme might be an issue at first, also that, if you want to play from an old cloud save like me, you might not get an direct reminder for the control schemes like other games do - that could have been done better but to be absolutely fair, guys, who stops playing a 10 hour story game? Thats like skipping the rest of a piece of cake. But personally I found it a bit frustrating, even with sprinting later on, how difficult some missions suddenly felt. I am not sure if this was also part of the intentional metaphors, that the game really makes you sweat suddenly in some levels, but I think this can be a bit overwhelming because you would not expect this from a game that has a rather Telltale-Control Scheme and similar gameplay style vibe to it. But see for yourself, even if it can be challenging, it is absolutely not problem to to master after some three or four tries, therefore just the heartliest recommendations for this game! :)

_childDocuments_.review: What I expected: well made but gimmicky game about cat in a cyberpunk city, since cats and cyberpunk are trendy topicsWhat I got: a fascinating look into the relationship between organic and synthetic beings, a downtrodden but hopeful tale about friendship, an intimate description of humanity through the perspective of a small innocence creature. A deeply touching experience that I respectfully object to every single claim that the game is somehow "wholesome" (it is not! It criticizes the fantasy of elevating humanity's physical form to something higher, more advanced, more less-human-as-if-our-flesh-and-bone-is-the-weakling-part-that-should-be-peeled-off, and cite the innocence of the orange cat as one of a few little good things scattered left in this world). It is not a "cat game" by any means, it doesn't make you feel like a cat, it doesn't give you total escapism from the human's perspective and the fulfillment to be a creature that is not us, but rather to showcase the trajectory of how that creature, much like us, smaller but not less emotional, would go and achieve such human objectives.If anything, the perception towards Stray fascinates me. The people who dislike it look negatively at the game because of how simple the gameplay is, how non challenging, how unsatisfying, how clunky it might feel, how it doesn't provide the utmost level of real . The press and game journalists leaving a thousand words praising Stray through buzzwords that sell the game to cat lovers, as if they think our plain brain demands pure  all the time. What do you people crave for, an utterly accurate cat simulator that satisfies your cowardy inner nihilism who's too afraid to walk out of the basement and shower a cat with love? Because if you do think Stray has the duty to jerk off what fantasy you want out of a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ storydriven game starring a cat, then you are unsalvageable.But take my words: you don't need to be a cat lover to enjoy Stray. Empathy extends to any being with a single cell of organism. We don't owe anyone to be born good, to do good as if it's an invisible duty. We do it because humanity is inherently good, and we don't need a video game starring a little cat in a dismal future to fool ourselves that he  kind,  cute, and  pure, so he is the last bastion of beauty in this universe, while human is despicable and we deserved everything bad happened to us. Stray is a humane story. We might not be a fluffy cuteball, we might not understand them fully, but we are also kind and unwavering, our love is unconditional, just like how far the cat is willing to go to get back home. We are life, we are human, we are us. Never forget that.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not a cat person, so I didn't know what they hype was all about with this game. I still got it, completed it and I must honestly say I still don't know what they hype was all about. This is fine game, quite enjoyable for the 5-6 hours it provides, but doesn't really go beyond that.The game is very simple and mostly very linear. It's also at the best when it is linear. The control scheme is very simple - you just move with analog, and if something is highlighted nearby you can jump on it with A button. All the jumps are pre-programmed and you cannot fail at them. The gameplay mostly has you figuring out how to proceed trough the current corridor.There are two open areas in this game. Those are very dense, with multiple levels you can jump on, including roofs. It's possible to run around there for a long time doing random stuff to NPCs or looking for hidden items. The bad thing about those ares is the save system - or the lack of thereof. The game only saves during control points. In the open area it usually also saves when you get an item. In the second open area I was playing for 45 minutes with no save in sight. Quitting a game doesn't save it, so you lose progress if you decide to quit. While usually it never goes above 2-3 minutes, in open area you can be screwed. Also, I found the chapters taking in those open areas to drag. There are few sections in the game when the gameplay changes a bit. There are chase sequences, very light stealth sequences, and you also unlock some temporary abilities. All those provide nice change of pace from the usual find-your-way gameplay.The story is alright. There are few not-very-memorable characters you meet on your journey. During most of the game you have an ally that translates stuff for you, and most of the story is about them, not the cat.Now, the cat. The cat is strange. Sometimes it's treated as animal and it's cute. You can walk on a computer keyboard and write random stuff, or toss books around and make a mess. Like a real cat! But then the story for the most part treats you as a human, and the further you go the more you'll think "why am I even playing as a cat?". I could suspend my disbelief for the most of the game, but last 3 chapters just went too far. I'm a cat, I don't know what you mean by "turn on computers". All I can do with computers is step on the keys and write random stuff, like in chapter 3. Ultimately it bothered me a lot during final stretch.The game looks really good. I made a ton of screenshot. There are a lot of nooks and crannies to explore, and you might want to do that for the collectibles. There are only 2 types of collectible - big and small memories. I think the big ones are mandatory for the story to progress, while small ones are hidden around the world. You can see postcards of the places where the memories are hidden for the current chapters, but those are all glitchy and corrupted to make it harder to find. You also can see how many are you lacking in chapter select. Some of them are very easy to find, while others require you to work for them. Each memory will have your ally say a sentence or two about his past. You won't learn too much from the small memories, but big memories tell you a lot.The city you explore feels like Midgar from Final Fantasy 7 in many regards. It's all dark and gloomy, with neon lights and strange languages on display. I dig it. There are also places where nature is taking over, so it's not very monotonous. There's also plenty of colour inside houses(and you can enter a lot of those). You encounter intriguing robot culture, which is explored a bit, especially if you talk to everyone. You can see if you walked to someone, as the prompt changes, so it's easy to keep track of who to talk with.All in all it's worth playing at the asking price, but it's not amazing. I suggest it for a nice distraction for a slow weekend.

_childDocuments_.review: Oh i could start telling you it's lovely to play as a cat, to have a dedicated button to meow and to be able to jump and throw things off surfaces.. and well, it's what i just did :) But this game is way more than that. it's a harrowing depiction of a post-cyberpunk world where things went awry in a sad, realistic way. So no humans, few animals, and a world populated by machines. it's not all gone though. In this intricate daedalus of a city, that I wouldn't call a ruin given the strong yet artificial living populating it, life keeps pulsating in different forms, from the most archaic to the quasi-philosopical. Colors and lights are few of the little things left to express oneself in the city, and that gives us an extraordinary palette of vibrant, electric colors. The price of this game might be a bit steep for the amount of hours required to complete it, but it's absolutely fascinating and you'll love every second of it. Except the Zurks. _childDocuments_.review: I once knew someone who pirated this game when it came out. They told me that they did this for most games, to "try them out before they wasted money on something they'd regret". They beat the whole game, even using a guide get all the collectibles, (not shaming). When I asked them what they thought, they told me that they were glad that they never bought it. Claiming that the game devs were insane to charge $40 for such a short game with barely anything in it. "The whole selling point of the game is that you get to play as a cat," they said "People are stupid if they spend money on this, there's nothing else in this game."When I bought Stray much later and played it for myself, I can see THEY didn't like it. They're shallow person, with no appreciation for art and only see value in games with swathes of "content".Stray is a beautiful, hand crafted gem that I believe everyone should experience. Every single part of this game shows the clear love, talent, and dedication of the developers to create something they were truly passionate about. Every part of this world feels lived in. The attention to detail in the environments and the NPCs are truly amazing, showing so much personality in the art design, so that every character you interact with and building you enter fells unique and alive. I loved simply exploring the game world, buildings a lit with neon and filled various trinkets, walls covered with grime and art, and the NPCs going about their days, looking for secrets and talking to everyone, and not once did I feel like the game fell short. Even the infested areas felt real and threatening, making me feel uncomfortable like I had entered an alien world filled with dangers.The animations are purrfect, especially with the cat. The way they move, jump, and interact with the world feels real, and shows just how much the devs cared and hard work they put in to make it feel just right. And finally, the writing is beautiful. Every dialogue with the various characters is filled with personality and charm that adds to the world building and story. I never had a bad experience talking to anyone, and they all felt believable, whether they were casually going about the routines or voicing their complaints. The story is surprisingly tragic, and tells a beautiful tale of desperation, adversity, friendship, and hope that I have very seldom experienced before, and I'm unafraid to say I teared up multiple times throughout.I don't regret purchasing this game in the slightest, anyone who says that it has nothing in it, clearly needs to reevaluate their Idea of "content". I loved every part of Stray and I can absolutely see myself playing this again in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fantastic game. It had a good story (albeit cliche), beautiful visuals, and a great soundtrack. _childDocuments_.review: Stray is a third-person cat adventure game set amidst the detailed, neon-lit alleys of a decaying cybercity and the murky environments of its seedy underbelly. Roam surroundings high and low, defend against unforeseen threats and solve the mysteries of this unwelcoming place inhabited by curious droids and dangerous creatures.See the world through the eyes of a cat and interact with the environment in playful ways. Be stealthy, nimble, silly, and sometimes as annoying as possible with the strange inhabitants of this mysterious world.I can't speak about the story without getting into spoilers. I recommend you play the game without knowing too much about it!This is obviously a major thing in games, You are playing as a cat (obviously). The developers seems to have made the controls as realistic as possible without making it not fun etc. You press left alt to "meow", You cannot jump on command, You are forced to go near a ledge or somewhere you can climb up to be able to jump. I personally like this, I dislike the idea of being able to jump whenever you want as it would make the game look very goofy.I am really enjoying the game so far, It's very calming when you are exploring, The music adds to the exploration and it can be pretty enjoyable doing puzzles and trying to find items in the game!The game is very good looking, I was blown away at how good the game looked. The smallest details can be seen in this game. Looks like the developers had fun making the game and put lots of love into the game.So far. This game to me is honestly the best i've seen so far this year. I'm mentioning again that the developers have put in a LOT of effort to this game. I appreciate the effort they put in. I'm going to rate it a solid 10/10. Amazing work, The feelings at the end after progressing through everything just wowed me.I'm not going to "cry" about bugs here, I'm only mentioning them so others can be aware of them. Includes spoilers, So be warned!

_childDocuments_.review: Prior to playing the game I had only seen the trailer, hell yeah cat game! Stray is a unique game set in a cyberpunk world where you play in the pov of a cat who plunges into the mysterious walled city. Clear of humans and only inhabited by various robots that you meet along the way, Stray is a unique take on the cyberpunk genre. The world of stray is separated by semi open world spaces that provide you with enough guidance to find your way along to progress, with plenty of little tidbits to interact with.Controls: The controls are simple to use. I'm not sure how it fairs on keyboard but experience with a controller was very smooth, you'll have to control the camera pov yourself. _childDocuments_.review: The story of Stray as a project is a fairly interesting one. The project was presented as “Project HK” back in 2015 with a few pictures and tweets, the most interesting part was that they also had a few pipe UE4 blueprint videos for the game, which at the time already had the current elements of what would become STRAY. 5 years later, Annapurna Interactive took the project to publish it - It’s now 2022, 7 years after the initial picture of Project HK we got the game, STRAY is finally here. Is it worth your time? Did it deliver a good experience? Let’s find out.Rusty pipes, cracked concrete and wild vegetation. This is the first thing we see through the eyes of our feline protagonist, perhaps an abandoned structure? We don’t care because we are a wild cat with our pack until one day, exploring the decaying structure we fall into a dark pit.Defendless, scared but still curious we wake up inside the structure, a dead city. No one to be found but we follow the signals that ask for our help, is somebody there? It won’t take long before we encounter strange life forms on those empty streets and a few disconnected robots but soon we discover who is asking for help, B12, a sentient AI that will need your help and will go with you in this adventure. This is an unknown world with tons of secrets to discover like what happened, what’s going on and most importantly, how do we return with our pack.Make no mistake, there’s a story behind this game. While it might seem that the narrative aspect of the game is merely formulaic, it presents a very interesting premise in which AI and their robotic bodies started evolving by creating a language, imitating human life and even started to have feelings and emotions. I won’t spoil the story because I consider it an important part of the game but sooner rather than later we will find out we are in the distant future in which, apparently, there are no longer human beings in this city but instead there are quite a few charismatic robots that will open new branches of this enigmatic place. If there’s a topic from the game I want to share with you is that our planet is precious and we should take care of it, it’s our home.Remember when I said “our feline protagonist” well, I made that distinction because I consider B12 as “our robotic protagonist”. Both characters do have an important role together in this story, kitty serves as a transport and as a way of keep going through the story while B12 is the narrative element of our duo, the one that will open fractions of the past and present and the one that will help kitty to get to the surface. In this case I think it’s fair to say that this ain’t a story about a cat, it is a story about a cat and an AI. The more you traverse these streets and the further you go, the more you will learn about your companion.There are quite a few more characters during this adventure like Momo and the rest of The Outsiders, the Slums and midtown people and while it’s interesting to talk with them (sometimes they share some cool tidbits about the world) they lack depth, which isn’t bad per say, it’s just that they merely have a narrative purpose and that’s it, they are not meant to be extremely detailed.When it comes to details I think about the world and its visuals.STRAY is absolutely gorgeous. The game’s city is based on the walled city of Kowloon, a piece of land in Hong Kong where jurisdiction was under a different administration and as so, buildings were able to be built in ways that were impossible to do under regulated areas, the result? A big city in which buildings were built one above the other and it has served as inspiration for countless fictional products like STRAY.You will notice that there’s a decaying cyberpunk feeling on the streets. Dark corners, water drops everywhere and neon lights, tons of neon light. Buildings are extremely detailed, you can see how nature is reclaiming the space it lost and how the parasitic creatures are spreading, there’s beauty in all scenarios waiting to be explored. At a graphical level STRAY sometimes looks like an animation movie.Kitty is extremely well done, robots have a lot of personality and a really cool design. In general there has been a lot of effort into making this a really meaningful visual experience.Something I wanted to mention before I jump into the gameplay loop. The more you look at the game, the smaller it seems to be and that’s right, STRAY is quite contained but at the same time it feels enormous thanks to the small size of our feline character. The size illusion makes it look like the city is huge while in reality it is us who are small. This is actually really clever and the fact that the city is so detailed (as said previously) makes it even more impressive because it lets you explore quite a lot of it.And here comes the gameplay part which is extremely simple but surprisingly engaging. There are a few basic actions, jump, run and talk (exactly, meow!) but the fun part begins here. The way you traverse the multiple levels of the city is by acting like a real cat jumping from roof to roof, throwing some things or interacting with objects to see the reaction. Do not expect combats nor deep interactions, it’s simple but effective. Thanks to this combatless or, let’s say, liviane situations you can do funny things with kitty.Movement feels natural most of the time and interactions are well done, while sometimes it might do some weird things, the overall experience is delightful. It is lovely how they portrayed this cat’s behaviour to feel so natural, like for example, putting a paper bag in your head or scratching a surface, the results are hilarious.They also did a great job with music and sound effects. In general, there isn’t a lot of music, however, it has this semi-chip effect that makes it sound futuristic while at the same time it feels intriguing. It helps a lot building an atmosphere in which you feel immersed.There’s also this guitar folk at the slums, you might want to give him the music sheets, some pieces are really cool.Finally I think it is time to talk about performance. Much like in my latest review, I played this game entirely on my Steam Deck and performance was good, extremely good I would say. It’s already verified so there’s no point talking about which Proton version I did use, however, I must say that I have been playing with medium settings at 60% resolution scale at 800p and the visual quality was impressive at the 7inch screen.There were performance dips at each new level but once it loaded the section, it didn’t stutter nor drop in performance, overall I would say that pre-cached shaders did a really great job, so there’s that.And that’s it, STRAY delivered exactly what I expected, a great cat experience exploring an unknown city and surprised me with a story I wasn’t expecting at all with sci-fi touches that weren’t shown previously. If you are looking for a visually appealing experience, a relaxing walking game or a cat and robot adventure, I think you will likely enjoy the game. It took me around 7 hours to finish by doing most of the side stuff (I’m going to 100% it) so keep that in mind but I think it was well worth the money they ask for.In general Annapurna published titles doesn’t disappoint me and this wasn’t the exception, STRAY was a really great game and easy to recommend, I thought it was an engaging little adventure and sometimes that’s exactly what you need, an adventure.I hope you all enjoy STRAY as much as I did. Have fun and congrats for the developers for the successful release.

_childDocuments_.review: Stray is the game which has the most conflicting reviews. Some tells that it’s good, relaxing and Cat is very cute, other tells it’s to simple in gameplay and plot. While I played the game I experienced all the above sensations. And Stray has something, that keep the game interesting, because of which you want to play this game.At the very beginning, we are introduced to the mechanics of the game and the normal daily life of a cat. And one day, during an unsuccessful walk, the cat falls into the abyss. The protagonist woke up in some kind of sewerage and with a damaged paw. This is the first 10 minutes of the game.Later we find a friend - B12. It's not just a drone, B12 becomes: a bag, a flashlight, a hacker and a translator.During the attempt to get outside, we can help B12 recover his lost memory by finding certain inscriptions and pictures. Also along the way, we can help local robots.While the little fluffy's attempt to return home, he is confronted by unidentified creatures who wish the cat dead. As well as deadly police drones. In general, the plot is good, but at the same time very simple and easy to understand.The main game mechanics of fluffy are revealed in the first 10 minutes. B12 game mechanics are added a little later with the ability to communicate with surrounding robots thanks to our drone translator.The game is very linear and it is strongly felt. We cannot jump wherever we want, but only to certain places, we cannot sharpen our claws anywhere and sleep wherever we please. But on the first pass, you mostly will ignore this.The game can be completed in 2 hours (there is a special achievement for this), but the first passage will most likely take 4 hours. The player, like the cat - for the first time in a new place and the game helps with immersion, you don't know where to go and just hitting all the corners to learn at least something.But basically the game looks like this - a certain robot will help you with the main quest task, he, in turn, needs a thing. You can get this thing from another robot, and he wants another thing or a task from you. And between all these actions, you have to communicate a lot with other robots.The game is really relaxing with a very simple plot. There are puzzles, but they are not difficult. The picture is good. The cat is cute and there are moments when you worry about him. Mechanics of the game are unique in their kind, the behavior of the cat is conveyed in sufficient detail.In the middle of the game, I felt a slight boredom, innovations end, and the gameplay is delayed by the same type of tasks - go to him, look for that thing, then look for another robot, and do that. I personally looked for an opportunity to play Stray, I mean the difficulty was that I wanted to enjoy the game, and for this I needed a certain mood. This game is unique in its kind - not for avid gamers, those who get high for example from Resident Evil etc will not be able to fully enjoy Stray. On the question of recommendations, I would generally like to put - "maybe".  The game is good and the Cat is cute. But it can be easily disliked, simply because it doesn't have the amount of action that is now common in other games and game may feel bored.

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:+ It's fun playing as a cute cat (A meow button, climbing on things, knocking things over)+ It's cozy playing around in a shanty town and talking to robots in the first quarter of the game+ It's fun to solve puzzles and find hidden secretsCons:-The game's only about 6 hours long, with little replay value (unless you're a perfectionist and want all the achievements), and it's just not quite enough to justify the $30 price tag. (I don't regret buying it, but I kinda wished that I waited for a sale!)-The game can't seem to pick a theme, there's about three chase sequences and two stealth sections - it's very out of place with the rest of the game and I feel kind of lied to about what experience I was actually getting.I really would have preferred if the game stayed consistent with the first section but have the locations vary over time, but then I guess it would have felt like a walking simulator. Also, what's up with the Zurg creatures? There isn't really an explanation for why they exist or how long they've been around. I thought this was a game about a cat exploring the remnants of a city that's inhabited by robots, didn't expect nor need monsters thrown in the mix. It was really jarring for me, personally, and I actually put off playing the rest of the game for two weeks because I wasn't sure if I could immerse myself in it anymore. But, I pushed on - with unsatisfactory results.-The ending felt rushed and left some questions unanswered, it felt unsatisfying.Spoiler:  +++++++++I wish I could give this a neutral review, it's a fun game with good graphics but it feels rushed and a bit shallow.I'll rate this as a 'Positive' since it wasn't a bad quality experience, and it didn't crash or have any bugs that I saw, but I will leave these suggestions below regardless:-If you really, really want to play it for yourself, wait for it to go on sale first! -If you're unsure, I suggest watching someone else play it on Youtube.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely delightful gem of a game. Fluid controls, natural parkour playground, the story was actually quite interesting and it led into a possible sequel with an entire world left to explore. I got this game on sale, obviously, but I would have paid the retail price and not regret it. You can complete the game in less than 2 hours (there is an achievement for it) but the game is worth taking your time and witnessing the beautiful world they (the developers) had crafted for us.
_childDocuments_.name: Stray

_childDocuments_.review: So, I finished Stray...I had pretty good time playing this game. BUT. Cat. In theory and by watching trailers for this game you may assume - you playing as a cat. In practice, I had quite a lot of confusion and find it hard to believe this is how normal cat would act. You can replace cat with human in this game - nothing really going to change. It's doesn't really works well in my opinion.Story.  Story is basic and not really catching. I pretty much enjoyed beginning of the game, I was really excited about exploring this world, but there is nothing to explore. Middle and the end is pretty boring. It's poor and really bad written story, with interesting background/world building. But it's just not there, you know?Gameplay.  It's bad? There is not much of gameplay either. When I saw the most first trailer of this game, I was expecting a lot of interesting puzzles and riddles, if it makes sense. The reality is: Please, take this thing from A place to the B place to make progression in the story. Frustrating and sad. A lot of potentional, but seems like devs decided to go with the most simple way and thought cat is all you need to enjoy it.In the end, really interesting idea, lovely graphics, art-direction and very poor realization of all of those ideas. In my opinion, the main point of this game - you play as a cutie cat. But it's just isn't enough to create a good game.
_childDocuments_.name: Stray

_childDocuments_.review: Stray is honestly one of the best games I have played,The visuals, even on a low spec gaming laptop like mine are absolutely beautiful, and the game went in a direction I completely didn't expect. The story and side missions are all pretty fun to play, and the way you interact with the environments is very unique.The enemies in the game are fun to play against and it can get very intense in some sections trying to weave between hoards of them running at you. In later sections, the drone enemies also pose a new challenge, although they are much easier to avoid.My only complaint really is that there is no punishment for error, jumping over obstacles can only be done when it is possible, and there is no way for the cat to fall off unless it is a scripted event.This does however help the game stay very linear, and overall the positives completely outweigh the negatives.I don't want to give away too much about the story itself, since the game isn't super long10/10 game

_childDocuments_.review: Mostly a walking cat sim with simple puzzles and the limited interactions kind of guide the puzzle solving. The ending is a little weak.  Despite all of this negativity, I'm going to recommend trying it.  You play this game not for the action or the reward - it's more for mood.  And after finishing the game, go hug your cat and contemplate life.
_childDocuments_.name: Stray

_childDocuments_.review: You play as a cat. You see from the cat's point of view (fun experience, you are so small comparing to the environment). You can ride in a basket (aww!) and navigate the city by climbing places. The game is set in a post apocalyptic world which reminded me of "The Fall" games. Absolutely worth the price for players who like cats and enjoy creative atmospheric games. I don't care if it is "short" (arguably) because i am not speed running this. So much work went into creating well-designed levels, i actually want to take time to explore them and to collect all achievements. Meow.Edit: I am nominating this amazing game for The Game of The Year Award because it deserves it. My cat said so.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is about a cat who falls into a city of sentient robots and wants to find their way back home to its family. The city is built under a dome and is locked down ever since a pandemic seems to have destroyed all human life, even the sky is artificial in this city. Most of the robots do not want to step outside the city but the few that do help the cat( i.e you the protagonist). On this journey you will make friends, explore, collect stuff, run errands, solve puzzles, fight zurks, avoid being sighted by enemies, help the robots and receive help from them. You will also witness sacrifice, face betrayal and emerge triumphant.

_childDocuments_.review: "Stray," developed by BlueTwelve Studio and published by Annapurna Interactive, takes players on an extraordinary adventure through a cybernetic metropolis, offering a unique and captivating experience that seamlessly blends exploration, puzzle-solving, and heartwarming storytelling.Visually, "Stray" is a masterpiece. The game's futuristic cityscape is a breathtaking amalgamation of neon lights, intricate details, and a lived-in atmosphere that truly immerses players in its cyberpunk world. The attention to detail in the environments is remarkable, with every alley, rooftop, and hidden corner telling a story of the city's past and present. The dynamic lighting and weather effects add a layer of realism that enhances the overall immersion.The protagonist, a stray cat equipped with a small backpack, serves as an unlikely but endearing guide through this sprawling urban jungle. The animations and movements of the feline protagonist are remarkably lifelike, creating a bond between the player and their virtual companion. Navigating the city from a cat's perspective adds a unique dimension to the gameplay, allowing for creative and unexpected solutions to puzzles.The narrative in "Stray" is delivered without conventional dialogue, relying on environmental storytelling and subtle cues. The mystery of the city's past unfolds gradually, keeping players engaged and encouraging exploration. The game strikes a perfect balance between a sense of wonder and a slightly eerie atmosphere, creating an emotional connection that resonates long after the credits roll.Gameplay mechanics in "Stray" are intuitive and accessible, making it easy for players to navigate the vast city and solve puzzles without feeling overwhelmed. The game cleverly integrates the cat's abilities, such as climbing and interacting with the environment, into the challenges, making for a seamless and enjoyable experience.One of the standout features of "Stray" is its exceptional sound design. The ambient sounds of the city, combined with a hauntingly beautiful musical score, contribute significantly to the overall atmosphere. The attention to detail extends to the lively and diverse soundtrack that adapts to the player's actions, enhancing the emotional impact of key moments.While "Stray" is not without its minor flaws, such as occasional camera angles that may require adjustment, these are overshadowed by the game's overall brilliance. The developers have created a unique and memorable experience that sets "Stray" apart in the world of indie games. It's a testament to the potential of video games as an art form and a reminder that a well-crafted world and story can elevate a game to a truly extraordinary level.In conclusion, "Stray" is a must-play for anyone seeking a fresh and emotionally resonant gaming experience. With its stunning visuals, compelling narrative, and innovative gameplay, "Stray" stands as a shining example of the creativity and potential within the indie gaming scene.

_childDocuments_.review: I am going with a thumbs down for this one, and I'll explain why.I loved most of this game, and the cat was made perfectly, from the sounds it makes, to the movements too. But at one point, near the end of the game, it turns into a stealth game.Now, I usually steer clear of stealth games, but this had no indication anywhere it might become a stealth game. It means that a feel-good, heart-warming game became a 'tear my hair out' game, which I cannot finish, even after many, many tries, and also looking at walkthrough videos.You will probably love the game up until that point, and if you do buy it, be aware that the later stages of it may reverse all the 'good vibes' that came before.

_childDocuments_.review: My expectation for this game was high, I mean it is a cat game after all. You get to play a cat, scratch things, sleep, jump into boxes, and meow. 10/10 for the cat.Unfortunately, both the narrative and gameplay turned out to be disappointingly shallow.. The simplicity in mechanics and linear progression robbed this game of genuine challenge and engagement, resulting in a disjointed and detached player experience. The incomplete story offered in-game, coupled with a lack of meaningful resolution, significantly diminishes its overall value as an RPG experience.The so-called escape sequences involving bugs ended up being more infuriating than fun. While there were fleeting moments of delight they were overshadowed by the game's shortcomings. It's hard to recommend Stray to those seeking an engaging gaming journey. While the portrayal of the cat's behaviour was cute, and the grim yet beautiful game world must be appreciated for its portrayal of a dystopian future), the overall experience falls flat.

_childDocuments_.review: I wish Steam had a recommended on sale option for reviews.I enjoyed Stray, but I feel like it didn't live up to the hype it received. It's a pretty short game, and the majority of it is spent on what I feel are the weaker aspects of the game. The best part of Stray in my opinion is finished in the first hour or so.After the first couple of tutorial-esque chapters you get to the slums, and this is where Stray really shines. It's open and full of places to explore, rooftops to traverse and has a couple of small side quests which are really fun and really promote the exploration aspect of the game. This made me really hopeful that more of that was to come, but after you leave the slums, you just go back to linear platforming. There are only 2 other open areas in the game, and both are pretty small with barely anything to actually do in them.The platforming itself isn't necessarily bad, but in a game where you play as a cat I'd have thought free jumping would've been a thing. In truth, you're never at risk while platforming, every action is predetermined and on rails. I just feel like Stray could have been so much more than it was. It's wasted potential, and honestly, I don't think it's worth the full price.
