_childDocuments_.review: I know this review will be lengthy, but I hope you stick around to read the reason why I adore this game, as it is very personal to me.Firstly, a game like this is the last kind of game someone like me would buy. I'm not big on puzzle games, chill games and the like, certainly not games where I play as a cat. I like the action, shooter, strategy kind of stuff. So why would someone like me buy a game like this?Well, let me start by saying something even weirder: I'm not a cat person. Or at least, there was a time I wasn't. Then one day at work, in the auto detailing shop I work in, a stray cat wandered into our shop, pregnant with a litter. My mom managed to catch her, bring her into one of the rooms of our shop, and turn it into a place to take care of her kittens until they were able to be given away. We designated the mama cat "Mama Kitty", and eventually called her "Mama" for short. After we got them homes, we got her fixed so she couldn't have kittens anymore. During this time, I was going through a lot of depression problems, and once again, the last thing I expected was a cat would be a companion in this time, but Mama Kitty became just that.After her kittens were all gone, she fell into a deep depression, and was alone in that room. I watched her, and my heart sank. For her, her kittens all moved on, were given new homes, and she was left here, alone. I related to exactly how she felt, feeling like everyone around you was moving on with life but you couldn't. We tried to get her a home, but it didn't work out. She just wasn't an indoor cat. So what happened? She ended up staying in our shop, literally making the whole shop her home. She followed me almost everywhere I went, and for two years, I would come into work and there was Mama Kitty waiting for me to feed her, and fill her day with love, affection and joy. She found a home, and she found peace at our shop, and for me, helping her move on with her life, no longer needing to worry about kittens, and getting to just be a free-spirited cat, was all I needed to help me with my own depression. She fit in so well. She would literally just find a spot in the shop, lay there and watch you work, and occasionally want so much attention, she'd interrupt your work, demanding you pet her, or feed her.Why do I speak in past tense? About five or six months ago, Mama Kitty disappeared. One Friday she was there, on Saturday gone. She had gone off many times before, but was always back by the end of the day, and she had this little makeshift bed in a bush that she slept in every night, and napped in every day. She was just gone, and I have never seen her since. The Monday after she disappeared was the hardest day of them all. It was the first day coming back to work and she was not there waiting for me. I didn't want to be there, falling apart, trying not to let people see me an emotional, pitiful mess. My little Mama Kitty was gone. I miss her meow (which the cat you play as in this game reminds me so much of), her playfulness, and just how spoiled she was.I don't know where Mama Kitty is, or if she is even still alive. By now, I'll never know what happened to her unless she miraculously turns back up at the shop. Cats have been known to do that, particularly strays. The other day I caught myself wondering if she wandered off for the last time, got herself into serious trouble, and then died all alone, without me to be there with her in her last moments, and it eats me up to think about. I loved that cat with all my heart. But I know at least I can have the peace of mind that I did everything I could to give her a wonderful life while she had it, even if it was two short years.  I don't regret it, and I pray she'll come back to that same life.That's why this game hits me on a personal level that no game does. When I heard about this game, I was immediately reminded of Mama Kitty, and just had to get it. For the first time in my life, a game has reached me on an intimately emotional level. Thank you to these developers for making this game. I bought this game for Mama Kitty, in remembrance of her and how much she helped me as I did my best to give her the best little life I could. This game is a joy to my heart, helping me with the memory of my own cat, a little stray, whom I had the privilege of loving.

_childDocuments_.review: With under six hours of gameplay, it probably cannot demand its $30 list price. But, I think this is a game that you should get to experience eventually. Let's say that you fed an A.I. with every video game ever made, and asked the resulting model, "Make me a French game, from Annapurna, featuring a cat." "Stray" might be what you'd get: a sort of cyberpunk Paris, filled with a Daft Punk-ish soundtrack, and simple puzzles al la Gobliins or Twinsen. This isn't to say it's formulaic. It's just that, despite its novel wrapping, it's maybe a bit too simple. The controls are easy, but not precise. There's limited places where the cat can actually go, and there's really no skill or luck involved in getting the cat into high places. The characters you meet are designed for localization -- which is to say that none of them speak English, and instead all speak in short text-boxes. Most of those boxes are petri-dish-shallow, with a character being defined more by their clothing and activities in the world than any text. And that's where we get to the part that's special. Stray's world is LUSH. There's so much detail EVERYWHERE, and it is all carefully polished to be alien and yet familiar. The artwork is to the level one would expect from an Annapurna game.There are a few cute points and some genuinely laugh-out-loud moments. There is a dedicated 'meow' button. The story often drags you along before you're done exploring. I think I skipped most of the midtown section because I found myself through the one-way advance-the-plot door before I'd even explored half the town. I am quite bitter about this. This goes with the bipolar pacing that starts slow and gentle at the start, but does a mad-dash downhill race to the finish that leaves you feeling disappointed in the game's length.It appears I can go back and pick up whole chapters and assuage my completionist tendencies, so maybe I can get a second chance at the midtown section. But otherwise, I don't see an ounce of replayability in the game. With rare exceptions, the game is on rails, and the only deviations from that are a tiny number of hidden collectibles, and a slight re-ordering of when you collect certain items. There's certainly nothing that changes the experience or the ending.In the end, I'm a little disappointed in the game's short and linear story, but it has a beautiful world and an endearing player character.

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished the game / all achievements, and people wanted a serious review, so:To get one thing out of the way real quick that I've seen some people ask about:: Here's what to expect, if this is something you are concerned over: There's a cutscene at the very start of the game where you suffer a great fall and have a limp afterwards, but you recover in a few seconds. Somewhere around mid-game, you get ejected from a high-speed cart, and again you hit the ground hard and limp for a little bit, but nothing major. There are also hostile headcrab creatures that can swarm and kill you (no gore or anything -- they just cling to you, the screen goes red, and then you collapse if you don't shake them off in time). Near the end-game there are drones that will outright shoot you. Those are the only occurrences of the cat getting hurt - so you can make the decision for yourself whether it's no-big-deal, or too much to stomach.Moving on to the usual categories:: I thought the game was quite beautiful. The colors are great and there is a ton of detail in the world at large. It was a lot of fun to go exploring and just admire the views. The only visual drawbacks occur when you hit a big dynamic loading zone, because some stuttering will occur. : Very ambient, atmospheric, and chill - but also playful, which I think makes sense considering that this is a game where you play as a cat, haha. : The gameplay is smooth for the most part. It's fun to cat-parkour your way up a building. However, I got lost from time to time, as sometimes it wasn't obvious where I needed to go. I was also unsure what the cat's max jump/leap distance was, which made some jumps harder to eyeball. There were some jumps that seemed impossibly far and yet I was permitted to make them, and some other jumps that seemed reasonable but the game wouldn't let me do them. Other than that, no real issues. You can meow, you can scale stuff, you can scratch the crap out of everyone's furniture and push things off ledges... it's great.: A full playthrough (going for all collectibles) took me about 6 hours, exploring and taking my time. There are 12 chapters in total - some are quite long, while others are very short. My first attempt at the speedrun achievement took me 1 hour and 40 minutes, going at a brisk pace knowing exactly where everything was. Then there's the hour-long catnap achievement. So all in all, you can expect maybe 9-10 hours for doing everything. : There is a chapter selection feature so you can go back and mop up any achievements you missed. Though as of this review, the Scratch achievement is bugged and doesn't trigger on the PC version when using mouse and keyboard -- it only works when using a controller (and even then you may have to adjust your trigger settings - which is what I had to do, using an XBox Elite controller). The Territory achievement may also be bugged, in that I had to do it all in a single run (chapter select didn't work for that one on my first file even though I scratched the same surfaces). The Can't Cat-ch Me achievement is really frustrating in its randomness - all I can say is to hard-cut across/behind enemy swarms to make life easier. The whole "zigzag" advice didn't work for me.: The game starts off simple enough, but as you progress you start to realize you're in a very strange place under strange circumstances. While the broad strokes are predictable, I didn't think it detracted at all. The characters are pretty humorous and they help add some levity to a bleak, dystopian situation.: Do keep in mind that this particular game, at least right now, at launch - has bugs that various people are encountering, ranging from softlocks to hardlocks to crashes. Different people seem to be hitting different bugs. Personally, I didn't have any of these bugs aside from the two achievements. I am sure the devs will iron out all these issues soon enough, but if you were looking for an excuse to hold off for now, this wouldn't be unreasonable.: I had fun! Especially if you are a cat lover and like adventure games, this would be a solid pick.

_childDocuments_.review: I did enjoy this game enough for me to set screenshots of it as my wallpaper, look up people's Let's Plays on Youtube, and talk about it with my friends. That said, I cannot recommend it to others, at least not at full price. Don't get me wrong - a game can be worth $29.99 even if it's only 5 hours long, as long as it's a satisfying experience. The problem with this game is not that it's short, which a lot of people may tell you, except they actually mean something else. What they actually mean is that the ending happens too abruptly and leaves people with a lukewarm feeling. Many plot points are not neatly tied up, with the only way to fix it being to release a DLC in the future. If this was half the price, it would make a little more sense, but with the current price tag, I'd expect it to feel and be complete as a standalone game without thinking it should need a DLC.And not only is the story cut short, but the plot is not centered around the cat at all. The true main character is the robot companion. The cat is merely a device to drive forward what seems to be a semi-exploration but actually completely linear experience. The sets are brilliantly designed and extremely beautiful, but all of that does little to mask the fact that there is only one path you can go most of the time, because what you can jump or walk on is tightly restricted. Some so-called environmental puzzles require little to no thinking, because there is literally only one platform you can jump on following a previous one, so the solution is obvious. Many quests also boil down to what is simply a point-and-click adventure. The game markets itself as allowing players to play as a cat, which is partially true, because they do introduce cat mechanics such as a dedicated "meow" button, knocking off objects, hiding in boxes, scratching furniture etc. But given how limited your movements are and how little the storyline has to do with you being a cat, I wouldn't really say this is truly a game about playing as a cat. At least it's not utilizing such characterization to an extent that would make it worthy of praise for being a cat game.There are a fair share of bugs in this game, though I have only encountered one game breaking bug. There is one chapter where the professor/scientist is supposed to lead you somewhere, but when I got to that point, he just stood there and didn't move. I had to Google to find out that he was supposed to move in order for me to progress. Luckily restarting the chapter fixed it for me. There was another time when a hole was covered by planks and was supposed to be inaccessible but I walked right through it, and when I came out, the NPC at the entrance was missing his body. The object physics in this game are weird too; when you knock a cup off the table, there is half a chance it will shoot up into the sky and land in midair instead. Objects also easily get lodged in between spaces and become non-retrievable. If it's an essential item, then you'll have to restart the chapter. I've even seen a bunch of monsters get stuck inside a wall. Given that this game is largely linear, players always walk the same paths, and things have a set way of being triggered every time, these bugs shouldn't really exist. Think about how much more difficult it would be to debug this if the cat could roam and jump anywhere freely.To conclude, this is a good game for the new things it brings to the scene, and it is understandable why it would receive such high ratings, but it does fall short for what it should have been. It's not a super expensive game, but then I bought it expecting it to make good use of its length, so...

_childDocuments_.review: An immersive action-adventure game set in a mysterious, dystopian world devoid of humans. Here you will have the chance to do what a cat does best: meow, explore, scratch and annoy other characters.You play as a nameless orange cat that gets separated from his family and trapped in a strange, underground city full of humanoid robots. You will explore this world, meet some allies and try to both escape the sealed settlement and help your new friends with their ultimate mission.Since this is about a main character and protagonist, I’m referring to our furry friend as a , not an .Gameplay is fun and its short length prevents it from becoming boring or tedious. Still, I would have loved to play more in this wondrous world along with this smart feline. I clocked 9.8 hours at a leisurely pace, exploring the detailed environments and enjoying the experience. I managed to collect every object on my first run, and only missed a couple of memories. The puzzles are simple but effective, completely logical in its solving requirements, and make sense within the story needs. There is an adequate mix of platforming, puzzle-solving, NPC-interacting, exploring, sneaking and fighting to keep everyone entertained.This game nails the experience of being a cat. You can meow, purr, climb, fit through tight places, scratch various surfaces, push things off tables and shelves, walk on keyboards to produce satisfying gibberish, mess around with board games, sleep on surprising spots—even on top of people—and destroy stuff; and, most importantly, steal a smile from NPCs when you nuzzle up against them.The cat’s movements and animations are not perfect, yet still superbly done. He can realistically run, dash and trot; lick its paws, stretch, orient its ears and stare at stuff just like a real cat would. The animations are quite natural and a joy to look at. Only the sleeping position is not quite precise--a cat does not curl its back legs like a dog would, but this is a minor detail.Environments are detailed, varied and gorgeous. Each chapter has its very own ambience, distinguishable from the rest. The contrast between the organic and the machine is strong and meaningful, and the textures, colors, the lighting, even the platforming and exploration styles are defined per area. Most of them are relatively small and manageable, but still require attention if you are to discover all of ’s secrets. Collectibles abound, and while they are by no means numerous, they are missable and backtracking won’t be an option in several cases, unless you are willing to replay a chapter from the beginning.The story is good, bittersweet and sad; not very predictable. It is simple but it works, and leaves a lot for the player to reflect. Echoes of the global pandemic, ecological disaster and human hubris can be seen and heard everywhere, while still maintaining a fresh look on a post-apocalyptic Earth. There are lots of details, and the story is not directly handed to the player—you will have to make your own conclusions about the past, the present and the future. To me, this is not a bad thing. Rather, it is a sign of a sophisticated storyteller knowledgeable of current trends. Dramatically, the story delivers.The graphical settings are somewhat basic, and several advanced options are entirely missing.  Some people will miss stuff like ray tracing, vignette, depth of field and such. Personally, I play in a big monitor and would have loved the option to tweak the field of view—sometimes it feels too narrow, and motion-sickness might ensue. Nevertheless, the game looks beautiful.The music and sounds are great—some of them quite alien, as would be expected from a futuristic robot culture. It succeeds in setting the mood and tone for each situation and area, from the depressing and tranquil to the scary and suspenseful.Since the protagonist is completely background-less and anonymous,  could have benefited from fur and eye color customization. That element alone would have done wonders for the player to bond and care more about their cat.I paid full price with a 10% off for pre-order, and don’t regret it. It is in no way an outrageous amount for current standards, considering many games today are released costing three or four times that. Be not mistaken: experience-wise, the storytelling is carefully tailored here. Like a movie or a good short story, its quality is not defined by the overall length. It would be unfair to compare  to storyless, open-world games.Overall, I found  to be a great experience, with interesting gameplay and characters, and a fresh alternative to other dystopian, post-apocalyptic games. Playing as a cat is satisfying and novel.Mischievously recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: Stray is a game I have mixed feelings about. It does some things really well, and there is potential for a truly great game here.However, it’s also filled with some glaring flaws that make it just an average walking simulator, for lack of a better genre to insert it in.Stray has you play as a nameless cat hanging out with its feline friends, when suddenly it falls down into an underground city inhabited by nothing but sentient robots called “Companions”. Following the signs given to it, the cat finds an amnesiac drone companion called B12 that will accompany it through the rest of its journey in search of a way back to the Outside, recovering some of its memories along the way.While it’s not bad that the plot is that simple, it’s safe to say the game isn’t so much about the cat; but rather, about the underground, its story, citizens, and status as a cyberpunk dystopia.This is both the game’s biggest strength, and its biggest weakness. NPCs will often tell you very interesting information and give away small pieces of world building with most of it falling short due to almost none of the concepts being talked about being explored in depth. Even B12’s memories feel like short instances of exposition that end up generating more questions than answers.As a result, chances are by the end of the game you will end up wondering plenty of things about Stray’s world, with most of those questions being left unanswered.Visually speaking, Stray is beautiful. Not only are the graphics great, but the cats’ animations are some of the best I’ve seen in any animal in a videogame, or even animated movies for that matter. The effort BlueTwelve Studio put into making the cats’ movements as realistic as possible is commendable, and they created some of the most breathtaking cyberpunk environments I have seen in a videogame so far. The music is good and fits the game perfectly, but it’s not memorable. The gameplay isn’t great. It’s serviceable, but those who expect to be able to move around freely are probably going to be disappointed. Most actions can only be done when prompted, including jumping and interacting with most parts of the environment. It’s completely understandable that they took this approach in order to make movement and the cat’s actions more realistic.The gameplay loop can be divided into four different aspects: Puzzle solving, city exploration, action sequences and stealth sections. Puzzles tend to be very easy, with some solutions being very obvious depending on what your camera angle is when you come upon them. Cities are small but filled with small and subtle details, and one of the highlights of the game by far; finding B12’s memories is a fun task and worth the extra tidbits of world building most of the time, and the amazing landscapes make for a wonderful treat. Action sequences are pretty short, and mostly consist of escaping mutant omnivore creatures called “Zurks” and solving puzzles. Stealth sections are overall pretty well made, although they’re not difficult at all.The game does have some bugs that might be annoying, if only because you might have to restart from your latest checkpoint. I ran into three bugs in my entire gameplay, two of which were me clipping through objects or walls and being unable to progress until I restarted the game. As for the third one, the solution to a certain puzzle just wasn’t working, but restarting from the last checkpoint solved the issue. Considering checkpoints are abundant, they were small annoyances.In conclusion, I do recommend Stray, with reservations, but think it’s overall a solid game. It is a flawed and very short experience considering the price in some regions. It took me a bit over five hours to finish the game with an 87% completion rate. Despite all this, it is pretty unique and might be worth checking out when looking for a short, casual experience; or when trying to alternate with longer titles. More hardcore gamers might want to skip or wait for a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: I figured I would give this one a shot because I'm a huge cat person, and I'm sorry to say that I'm disappointed. I'll admit that maybe I'm just jaded as a gamer. This isn't a bad game. It's pretty and it plays nicely. The only real gameplay complaint I have is that I ran into some places where you would think that you should be able to jump from point A to B, but you can't. This is a problem that has long been a part of many platformers, and really that's my main point of disappointment here: this is the classic platformer formula, but you play as a cat. The novelty of it is cute, but being able to hit B to meow can only take a game so far. Maybe you'll like the story, but I couldn't get into it. I played until the point where I got my little robot buddy who started telling me what to do, rolled my eyes, and refunded. I guess my point is that, for me, this isn't worth $30 especially considering the massive discounts that this game will be getting during not-so-distant future Steam sales.

_childDocuments_.review: I was skeptical about Stray, as I am a dog person, and am not easily impressed by fancy graphics.I assumed that this game would be little more than a tech-demo with a very lifelike cat-avatar, and that the novelty would end there.  I am very glad that I was wrong.Let me address my own skepticism first.  The gameplay is a little simple, the platforming is done at the push of a button, and the puzzles, while fun, are also simple.  This may be a turn-off for some people, however, it is done in such a way to service the experience of playing as an animal.  This cat is an exceedingly good boi, however, he isn't a genius, he's not got any special powers innately (other than being genuinely the best boi), and acknowledging that allows this game to pull off a bit of a gameplay miracle in my opinion.The games' simplicity allows the story to progress at a near perfect rate.  There are no sections where you will feel hopelessly stuck, there are few points where the story feels like it's being padded, and I was never bored.  There is a narrative here, and the game frames it through the innocent eyes of this stray cat.  He is an active participant in the narrative, sure, but he is ultimately servicing the goals of the other characters you meet along the way.  His innocence combined with his instrumentality, reminded me of another legendary video game character.  Ellie from the last of us.The Last of Us is funnily enough, the closest comparison I can draw to this game, albeit with their wholesome-to-scary ratios flipped.  Both games take you on journeys through brutalized cities infested with monsters to aid the suffering populace.  Stray is less threatening, but it makes navigating dangerous activities feel that much tenser.  There are points in this game where the visuals are so striking and disturbing, that when contrasted with my cute cat protagonist, I felt helpless, and above all else, intrigued and invested in the world.  The environmental storytelling on display here is top notch.  You slink and hop through the world with the natural ease of a cat, and the story matches your pace.Your companion character's overall plotline is a little predictable, but again, it never bogs the story down in melodrama or forced sentimentality. The emotional highs this story reaches make an impact because the game has successfully illustrated the scope and importance of the journey the two of you are on together, and never takes you away from it, or each other.  You become connected to all the characters in this game, even if they are only traveling with you for a brief period of time.Ultimately the hype around this game is well deserved, and you do owe it to yourself to play it, ideally in one or two sittings, if you've got about 5 hours on hand and want to be whisk(er)ed away on an awesome post-apocalyptic, visually striking, spooky, wholesome and emotional adventure.

_childDocuments_.review: I was excited to play Stray, people were loving it. it seemed oddball enough that it might be enjoyable, and Annapurna as a publisher is a solid company.  They've published Outer Wilds which is one of my favorite game. And yet Stray just didn't connect to me.  In the game you certainly feel like a cat, and you're exploring a cybercity, but the controls felt stiffed.  Rather than a part of a large expansive city, Stray has one of the most restricted control scheme I've seen in a while.  There's places your can can "Jump to" and ways your can can walk in most areas, and if you want to try a different direction, too bad.  Every jump has to be towards a different platform, and every platform is limited. This might not have been as big a problem if the levels felt interesting.  The idea of a dead cybercity could work, and the trailers got me ready for exploration but as I played the game I realized how similar so much of the game felt, there was always something telling me where to go, whether it was other cats, or bright neon signs. The world seemed dead, which was intentional but also like a city that wasn't lived in, there's a vague enemy which the cat ran away from which clearly was designed based on the face huggers from Half Life 2, but other than that, the entire game revolved around exploration. But don't get me wrong, I'm a fan of games focused on exploration, when it's good.  The concept here had my interest, but after an hour, I started to ask myself if this was a title I wanted to keep.  At 30 bucks, it's not a full priced title, but that first hour made me question if it was worth the price and at the end of the day I decided I should refund the game.I truly love the elevator pitch, I love the idea of playing as a cat.  It might have been interesting, but Stray really didn't hook me in the first hour and at the end of my time an uber cutsy robot came to life but I just kind of sighed and gave up.I know a lot of people love this game and swear by it, but for me I just don't think it was worth the 30 dollars, and at the end of the day, I might wait for it to be on sale before I give this another go, or more likely just play something else from my backlog, because Stray was merely ok in my book.   Or perhaps I stopped just as the game was "Getting good" but the fact is the opening hour wasn't compelling and I felt like I was watching the clock to ensure I wouldn't lose my ability to refund it... that's not a strong opening for a game that will run people under 8 hours. If you enjoy this game, I'm glad you found something special here, and maybe I'm the odd man out, but the more I think about it, the more I'm shocked so many people took the risk here.   Perhaps this one just isn't for me.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is absolutely stunning. The visuals are on point, it isn't a very demanding game, and everything about it is so immersive and beautifully done. For being such a straightforward game, you're faced with challenges and action packed sequences that are occasionally very difficult to figure out.This game had me fixated for hours without end, enjoying every moment and struggle. Along with the visuals, the soundtrack and sound design for this game is phenomenal. Every; step, crash, fall, clang, bang, voice, and shuffle can all be heard as if it is really there or truly far away from the player.The perspective of being a cat is amazing, it offers new challenges since you can't just open a door to what you need, you have to work around things to get what you need. Every turn is filled with new ways to solve a problem in the eyes of a cat- it provides a well needed and fresh outlook on gaming.I personally believe this game is beginner friendly, you don't have very basic controls, but you don't have very extensive ones that you have to keep thinking about. Once the muscle memory kicks in, you're set. That being said, this is a very enjoyable game. I saw the trailer back when it was first released, and while I couldn't wait to play it, I didn't have high hopes for it. Needless to say I was blown out of the water with it. Never have I been so immersed into a game before.While it may be a short story based game, I don't want that to turn anyone away. For me personally this has been my favorite game to play since it is filled with such a large variation of approach and style. I think this is absolutely one of the top games this year, and while it would be great for it to be longer, I think the entire plot line finishes itself in a very nice way. Think sort of 'The Last Guardian' if you will. A beautiful but heartbreaking story that ends in an amazing way, this game I believe is the 2022 version of that.Definitely a go-to game for myself.

_childDocuments_.review: Stray isn’t just a game. It’s art.It transports. It evokes deep, complex emotions.It’s said that familiarity breeds contempt. In a time where most people are sick of other people and the things they do to one another; the world of Stray takes us as far as possible from it all.We are just a cat. Our friends are sentimental robots just trying to get by. And the memory of humanity is so distant that, in the bittersweet melancholy of Stray’s rotting, growing world, we miss people.Transported so far away, we see humanity posthumously, through the lens of fear and wonder.

_childDocuments_.review: In this captivating game, players are transported to a beautifully detailed futuristic city through the eyes of a stray cat. From the moment you start exploring, the vibrant world, rich with neon lights and towering skyscrapers, draws you in. The city is teeming with life, offering a unique blend of exploration and puzzle-solving that is both engaging and immersive.The storyline, while simple, is deeply emotional and poignant. It follows the stray cat's quest to return to its family, and the narrative is woven seamlessly into the gameplay, making each discovery and interaction feel meaningful. The game excels in environmental storytelling, using its surroundings to convey the history and atmosphere of the city without the need for lengthy exposition.Gameplay is intuitive yet innovative, leveraging the cat's natural agility to navigate obstacles and solve puzzles. The developers have done a remarkable job capturing the essence of feline behavior, from the way the cat moves to its interactions with the environment. This attention to detail makes the experience feel authentic and adds a layer of charm that is hard to find elsewhere.Graphically, the game is stunning. The art style is a beautiful mix of realism and stylization, creating a visually striking world that is both immersive and enchanting. The lighting and textures contribute to a vibrant and atmospheric cityscape, while the character animations bring the stray cat to life in a way that is both endearing and realistic.The soundtrack and sound design further enhance the experience, with a hauntingly beautiful score that complements the game's tone perfectly. The ambient sounds of the city, from distant chatter to the hum of machinery, add to the immersion and make the world feel alive.In terms of pacing, the game strikes a good balance between exploration, puzzle-solving, and narrative progression. The puzzles are clever and challenging without being overly frustrating, and the story unfolds at a steady pace that keeps players engaged without overwhelming them.Overall, this game is a memorable and heartwarming journey that stands out in the gaming landscape. It offers a unique perspective and a fresh take on the adventure genre, delivering an experience that is both emotionally resonant and visually captivating. Whether you're a fan of exploration games, puzzles, or simply enjoy a good story, this title is well worth your time.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm going back over my review again.At the time when I first wrote this, I was only 5 hours in. People are claiming that the HLTB says 5 hours is the main story. However, I took my time. Soaking in the ambience, talking to everyone, and making my best effort to grab all the collectibles and quests along the way. I felt like the game was about 80% positive 20% negative.After finishing the story at around 9 hours (maybe 8, I did get the 'sleep for an hour' achievement), I put this at 110% positive. This game is an absolute fn' masterpiece. There WILL be spoilers later on.The short of it is this: there's a lot you can fairly criticize the game for. The platforming is very much 'on rails', the puzzles aren't puzzles, I wouldn't even say there's any real challenge to the game.You might think those are major problems to have with a *game*, but Stray is absolutely a winner in the 'games are art' category. The adventure we go on with Stray (who I will thusforth refer to simply as "Cat") is incredible. I'm not even kidding when I say I finished the game an hour ago and yet I'm still sniffly about how it ended.If you're looking for 'LOL CAT GAME ROFL', this isn't it. It has cute cat moments, but that's ancillary to everything else. If you're looking for Catsassin's Creed', this isn't it. I would even venture to say that the platforming is a deconstruction of platforming games. Platforming is impossible to fail at; in essence, the platforming element has been distilled to its purist form. There's no worry about failing, it simply is a way to navigate.What this game is is a deeply emotional story that you are experiencing not through the eyes of a cat... but more as a cat's friend.The last thing I'll say before getting into spoilers, is that I honestly hope this game doesn't have DLC or a sequel. My spoilers will explain my feelings more, but essentially I think the ending was flawless (which is something many disagree with). I think the ending is something that with time, people will learn to appreciate as ending exactly how it should have ended. To introduce further adventures with Cat will cheapen the adventure we just had with him.This particular spoiler is not a major spoiler but does involve the very end of the game. It doesn't involve plot points and I don't think it will affect you, but I want to point out why I think this game is beautiful and will be a game people remember for years to come.The very first minute of the game begins with ///More major spoilers begin here involving plot points.///And that is why this game is a 10/10, flawless masterpiece. No game has EVER genuinely made me feel what I feel even now, hours after finishing the game, and no sequel or DLC will ever recapture that.Thank you BlueTwelve. This was a Triumph.

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty good game. I am a cat person, but playing as a cat is kind of frustrating, so that's not why I think the game is good. It's a very cinematic game, and I don't mean that pejoratively. It's also beautifully realized and stylized, but unfortunately that does lose its appeal after about an hour or so of playing, which is why I think the game's relatively short runtime is actually a bit of a blessing.The story is alright, there are a lot of repeated beats, including 4 or 5 separate instances of the classic "go on without me, I can't come with you" kind of trope. The gameplay is very intuitive and the game goes out of its way (most of the time) to direct your attention towards the way forward, which was nice, but there are some sections that are pretty unintuitive and will probably require you to use a guide, which is doubly frustrating when the rest of the game is so well designed. The base mechanic obviously lends itself to this action-puzzle kind of gameplay, and this is the predominant gameplay style. There are a few sections where you're running away from enemies, which were annoying, and three decent-sized stealth sections, which I found myself having terminal skill issue problems with. The section where you get the ability to mow down enemies with a flashlight is very cool and fun though, I would've played a whole game that was just that.Overall, like I said, I enjoyed the game. I would buy it on sale if I were you though, like I did.

_childDocuments_.review: About 4-5 hours of playtime. Only had about 3 times where my frames hit 30. Never below; it kept a steady 58-60 frames per second on my little GTX 1650 Super. There is absolutely zero loading screens, too. You just play it from start to finish.I became immediately invested right in the intro sequence! Then again though, I might be a little biased because I love cats. Anyway... Here are my thoughts on certain aspects of the game as well as an overall rating.: 8/10 - Smooth like butter at times, but my 1650 super did have like 3 moments where it struggled to load the world for a few seconds. Nothing major though. Very doable. There was only one very obvious issue where an entity was caught behind a wall, but it didn't stop me from moving forward at all. As a matter of fact it was actually pretty hilarious lmao.: 8/10 - Pretty smooth. Controls are simple and straight forward, and you get the hang of em pretty quickly. So much so that you could likely speed run this game a bit below the average 4 hour mark if you know where you're going and don't use any exploits. (not that I know of any lol). There are surfaces you can jump on in the game, but very rarely there are spots where you have to do some slightly awkward positioning to get the jump prompt (jumping isn't a function you can do on your own at all times). Sometimes the camera will also position itself oddly if you have auto-cam on. You can disable this with one click no problem though.: 9/10 - It's short and sweet, but incredibly interesting. The environmental storytelling is just as good as the direct storytelling from interacting with characters and cutscenes. You can very easily (but slowly) put together what happened within the world of Stray, and it is damn interesting. Just wish there was more of it!: 8/10 (subjective) - They looked fantastic for my little 1650 Super, so I'm positive they'll look great on higher end GPUs.: Meow/10 - Dedicated MEOW button instantly gave this game a positive view from me lol. The game does a wonderful job at making you feel like this small and fragile creature in a dark scary world. : 7/10 - Did I mention scary? There is a whole part of this game that is legitimately off-putting in an amazing way. Lots of gore, too. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ awesome. Again, just wish there was more of it.: 7/10 - The characters you meet in this game are pretty neat. The main ones are sweet and pretty funny at times, and likable. Unfortunately there isn't a whole lot of dialogue to go through, and the dialogue will get exhausted after like 2 or 3 times when talking to someone. Not only that, but since the game is so short, I couldn't really get attached to many of them besides one that is with you the whole game. Other than all that, the characters are pretty damn solid and won't take you outta the immersion/experience.: 8/10 - LOTS of stuff to explore and find. There are optional things to collect as well with all the exploration you can do. The world is pretty, ugly, scary, lonely, and cozy at times. Amazing. I loved it :): Great game. 8/10. I think it's worth the money. You don't need a super computer to run it, and if you like cats, you'll absolutely love it. (I personally give it a 9/10 because I love cats).

_childDocuments_.review: I finished this game on 100% now, both ingame as well as steam achievements - because I love it so much and wanted to play it to the very last drop. That's a rare thing, at least for me. But anyhow - the gameplay is smooth, both the controls as well as the difficulty of the riddles. You have to think about it a bit, but not for too long that it would frustrate you.The worldbuilding, however, is what really sucked me in. I love the way we learn bits and pieces over the memories and have to puzzle the full picture together in our mind; imagining of what was and will be eventually. The more time you give yourself to explore, the more hints to the world you'll find - and god. I wish I could read a book about this world or something, because it really intrigued my interest and I want to know *more* than is possible.Big recommendation from my side. This game truly deserves all the love it gets at the moment.EDIT: While I still recommend the game, I had to realise that the localisation to German was most likely just rushed through Google Translate. It's bad - *really* bad. Which is a shame, because the game feels so refreshingly polished otherwise for todays standards in the industry. Please invest in an actual localisation team next time.

_childDocuments_.review: Writing this review is just about the most enjoyment I got from this game. It just did not do it for me and honestly, how it got the rating it has is beyond me. It plays a lot more like a kids game where you pretty much just follow along as the game guides you from one needed item to the next. Sure sometimes the "what's next" takes a little more to figure out and getting to the items can be a little challenging at times, but beyond that there is just not much there...not even for only $20. Jumping from one place to another is a big part of the game yet there is no free jump which really takes away from the game in my opinion. It's a matter of turning this way and that until you see the jump indicator....which can be a little finicky at times too making it difficult to execute a jump. It's not because it's a more challenging jump either....it's much more of a buggy type feel. Regardless it gets old pretty quick. The best part of the game is the world you (the cat) get to roam around in. The color scheme and overall design are beautifully rendered. Playing as a cat is a cool concept too and for the most part that works as well. I am a cat person so I did appreciate how the cat looked and moved...it was indeed cat like. It's just all wasted on a very weak story line, poor character interaction, clunky game mechanics and linear and very predictable game play.In the end I enjoyed the game...for a little while anyway. Then it just sort of got a little tedious. I played mostly while binge watching Top Chef and my cat character fell asleep or sat idle a lot more often than I paused Top Chef. I just cannot recommend this game....at least not for a serious gamer. It would be a good game for a child or someone who enjoys simple cute easy to play games. It just did not work for me.

_childDocuments_.review: This is an outstanding game. The storytelling is great, it has an interesting story to tell without ever being annoying or boring. It even takes the common trope of a post apocalyptic world in a completely new direction, making it so much more interesting than usual. The gameplay is smooth and satisfying, beautifully capturing the nimble and agile movement capabilities of a cat, letting you swiftly traverse across any environment. The characters are awesome, all being really charming and unique despite being robots; and the world design is stunning. Every area is beautiful, flawlessly built, and such a joy to explore.I've seen some reviews say this game doesn't hold up, and just plays on peoples love for cats without actually being a good game in it's own right, but I don't think that's true at all. The gameplay is great, the plot takes a boring trope and makes it interesting, and the world this is set in is absolutely wonderful. I do think the game is much too short, and that one eldritch horror part that gets left with no explanation or elaboration is absurd, but overall I think this game definitely holds up as more than just a gimmick, it's really something special.

_childDocuments_.review: What some modern game devs don't understand is that sometimes, you just want to play as a little critter roaming around and exploring. With an orange tabby, a little robot companion, beautiful graphics, anthropomorphic robot society, and a designated meow button, it's definitely GOTY worthy.
_childDocuments_.name: Stray

_childDocuments_.review: First of all, this is the kind of game I love. Putting a cat in a dystopian cyberpunk world is one of the greatest idea I've ever seen. Our feline protagonst and B12 develop a very special relationship which everyone would like to see. Exploring and fighting with a little sentient AI by your side make the game more enjoyable. Especially when the gang of Zurks crosses your path.Although the game was a bit too short, I find the plot perfectly balanced. I got everything I needed. My eyes were almost watering at the end but that's all. I don't wanna spill any spoilers. I added myself some extra hours by exploring the world and seeking easter eggs so It took me about 10 hours to complete the game with its all collectives.When it comes to details and the visual side of the game, I think Stray is absolutely gorgeous in every possible way. I totally fell in love with the locations, especially with those dark corners and big neon lights scattered everywhere.As a person who enjoys taking screenshots in games I find not having a photo mode in Stray a missed opportunity. That would be a great feature and I think the game would be better with it.To sum everything up, maybe Stray is not a massive open world game as The Witcher 3 or RDR2 but you will be impressed how easily It can draw you into its own, specific universe and its perfectly built story. I mean, how can you resist the cuteness of the cat and the AI?If you consider whether to buy this kitty game called Stray or not... You SHOULD. It's definitely worth buying! I hope you enjoy the game as much as I did ^^

_childDocuments_.review: First off Stray is a fantastic game. Let's get that out of the way.  It plays well, reacts well, has a depth of story I didn't expect.  It boasts an enjoyable interactive world and delivers more than it promises. But what's more is that it is totally worth the full price tag to break out of the monotony of modern triple A games. Repetitive mechanics plague the gaming landscape to the point where a new game is ANYTHING but new.  Just the endless recycling of the same ♥♥♥♥ pushed into new environments voiced by new characters. But it's no one's fault, new and inventive ideas are hard enough in any medium.  But the joy of Stray is discovering that it's not just a walking simulator, but it's not some full on RPG either.  You'll be scratching doors for pleasure. Finding spots to nap.  But then right after you can be solving puzzles by knocking paint cans off roofs, or perhaps scaring robots, and with that you'll feel pressed to test your luck on more random cat activities for no apparent reason,other than wanting to see the effect. If you want to play a 40 hour game of grind right now -  then this isn't for you.  But if you wish to play a videogame for the reason of pure enjoyment and discovery.  Then this is for you.Crushable in 4-6 hours with a high multiple playthrough potential, I fully recommend Stray and look forward to future projects from BlueTwelve Studio

_childDocuments_.review: I never want to see this game again. Deleting isn't enough, I want to dunk it in bleach. This game started so beautifully. _childDocuments_.review: I opened the game expecting it to be a gimmicky experience, one that plays on the fact that you're a cat. However, Stray quickly proved me wrong and exceeded my expectations. The game's atmosphere is just lovely, seamlessly combining a cool cyberpunk feel that ties in with overgrown nature, creating a visually stunning environment, from the neon-drenched streets filled with life to the very top of the city.One of the things that stood out to me was the game's ability to convey so much emotion without relying heavily on dialogue. It's a rare treat to feel so connected to a game's story with such minimal words. The game's filled with heartfelt moments such as reuniting Doc with his son.The soundtrack is great and significantly enhances the overall experience. The tunes align perfectly with the mood, adding depth to the game and making each moment more memorable. I also enjoyed Morusque, the robot who serenades you whenever you bring her music notes, a charming addition. Listening to 'Cool Down' (music note 6) unexpectedly brought a smile to my face. Since we're still talking sound, the game earns extra points for letting players embrace their inner DJ, scratching vinyls in the club, a commendable feature!Regardless of your fondness for felines or your desire for a captivating platformer, Stray offers an excellent experience. I'd confidently give it a 9 out of 10.

_childDocuments_.review: Stray is a wonderful little game. It’s not a title that pushes the genre forward, nor is it a game that’s all about the microtransactions and making a quick buck. This is classic video-game territory; a title that just wants to tell an emotional story and allow players to explore a beautiful world.Split across 12 chapters, the story follows a stray cat that’s lost and separated from its family. As a result of its travels, the cat is thrust into an ancient mystery involving a long-forgotten walled city and its robot inhabitants. With a self-contained story and some memorable characters along the way, this is certainly not a game to be missed. And given the playing time is around 6-8 hours, it’s accessible even for those with a lot on their plates. With help from a small flying drone, you’re going to explore the city, solve puzzles and help residents along the way, all the while trying to return to your family above-ground.Each chapter has a pretty linear direction, combining platforming with puzzling to great effect. There’s a combination of safe code combinations, light physic-based puzzles and simple but effective fetch quests peppered throughout, breaking up any niggling feelings of monotony that may settle in. There’s nothing too strenuous here either, but there’s equally enough that requires you to think outside the box on more than one occasion.Graphically, Stray looks fantastic too. Whether it be neon lights reflected off puddles on the ground or something simple like your feline traversing on the rooftops, every part of this game looks fantastic. There’s a mixture of vibrant and dingy colours, whenever the script calls for it, and you’ll find yourself itching to explore the next area to see what else this game has in store for you.We’ve been graced with some wonderful Indie games over the years but Stray is certainly one of the most unique experiences out there. There’s a lot of love that’s gone into crafting this game and Stray deserves its plaudits. This is a fantastic game and easily one of the best I've played this year. 10/10 Recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: A real treasure of an adventure game. Reminds me of the old point and click era, especially in later sections- disable camera to get a casette tape to put in a boombox to distract a guard so you can steal a hat.Graphics and music are well done. Best part for me is, there is no platforming, no timed jumps. Good for a casual romp in a strange city.The story falls flat by its own making though.When you meet a significant robot character, you bond, then *gasp* he can't go with you to the next level. Go find the next important robot!Ok... find the next important robot. You bond then *gasp* they can't go with you to the next level!The game literally conditions you to find a character then leave them. To the point where late in the game, you are trying to find a key to help out a robot, I thought it was some random robot until I realized far later than I should that it was one of the named robots that are important to your adventure. But yet again, that one can't go with you. It's supposed to be an emotional moment, but for me it was just like all the others the game had trained me to just leave behind and was met with an unenthusiastic "meh, ok."

_childDocuments_.review: Stray is an excellent, polished indie title that doesn't overstay its welcome. It lasts about 6-7 hours (I just spent a lot of time ogling the visuals). I'll get the negative stuff out of the way:The story isn't very good, it's kind of bland and uninteresting in its themes, and the characters leave zero impression on you. It's not bad or anything, but there's really nothing to keep you invested in the world. Writing is wholly forgettable and even though it tries for emotional moments, it just doesn't land.The game has occasional shader compilation stutters, and some extremely minor bugs, but really nothing that will spoil the experience in any way.Now to the good bits: the game is gorgeous and the art design is doing some REAL heavy lifting here. The devs weren't afraid to use bold, saturated colours for the lighting and neon-drenched cityscapes, and as a fan of cyberpunk and synthwave, I loved every moment. The neighbourhood looks tightly packed together like the Kowloon Walled City, and ledges and AC units and pipes are aplenty, letting your cat protagonist climb and jump wherever it pleases.I spent way too much time just exploring these compact spaces, doing little side quests, and marvelling at the bright neon lights. The level design is great, and buildings and rooms are interconnected, so you'll keep finding new ways to go from point A to B. The side quests weren't deep or absorbing, but they were fun little distractions that gave me incentive to explore more.The game doesn't try to get too fancy with new mechanics, and it sticks to its main strengths for 80% of the game: exploring and climbing. Which suited me just fine, this was a chill and relax type of game for me.FYI, this isn't an open world game by any means, each 'city' space is more like a small tightly-packed neighbourhood full of tiny activities and characters. But the advantage is that you become intimately familiar with each space, and everything you see looks unique and handcrafted.More than anything, I appreciated the sense of place this game offered. Each location felt real and lived in, and though there wasn't that much of 'environmental storytelling' you see in Fallout or Witcher, wherever I went, I couldn't help but wonder what this city would have looked like when humans lived there. And the fact that you play as a cat means you approach the world from a very different perspective, where everyday objects are much bigger than usual, and turn into a maze of boxes and pipes and windows and roofs.All in all, I really enjoyed my time with Stray, and if you're into games that know what they're good at and stick to their strengths, you'll like this a lot, too.
_childDocuments_.name: Stray

_childDocuments_.review: Stray is a distinctive adventure game that offers a refreshing perspective by casting players as a lost cat navigating a mysterious, dystopian city. The game beautifully merges exploration, light puzzle elements, and stealth mechanics, all seen through the eyes of our feline protagonist. The city itself is a character, rich in neon-lit ambiance and inhabited by robots with human-like dilemmas, which adds a poignant layer to the game's narrative.Graphically, Stray is a visual treat. The attention to detail in the environments is meticulous, from the flickering lights of a robot's shop to the somber, rain-soaked alleyways. The sound design deserves equal praise, with a soundtrack that perfectly complements the eerie, sometimes melancholic tone of the game. Where "Stray" slightly stumbles is in its gameplay mechanics, which, while initially engaging, can feel repetitive as the game progresses. The puzzle solutions are often straightforward, lacking the complexity that might keep more seasoned gamers on their toes.Despite these minor gripes, Stray is a heartfelt and innovative title that successfully delivers an experience unlike most in the genre. It's a compelling blend of storytelling and exploration that resonates emotionally, particularly for cat lovers. This game is about the journey of a stray cat, a commentary on loneliness, resilience, and the quest for belonging, making it a memorable addition to the gaming landscape.I would rate Stray an 85 out of 100.
_childDocuments_.name: Stray

_childDocuments_.review: I have beaten Stray about three times, and honestly the atmosphere of this game is beautiful. I definitely recommend this game if you want something relaxing, but can still be engaging. I will make a note though, there are a couple times that this game isn't as relaxing, but I mean that in a good way. Should you buy it?? Yeah.Edit: I beat this game when it came out last year, probably three times, and it has stuck with me. Still today I want to go back and explore the world of stray. Awesome!Gameplay: I haven't got too far into the game but it seems fun, how you'd imagine a playing as a cat to feel like. There are elements of puzzle solving and collectibles too. Interacting with robots and engaging in side quests adds a fun element to the experience.Overall, Stray offers a unique world but falls short in gameplay. _childDocuments_.review: tldr; good game, 9/10Let me get the obvious fact out of the way. Playing as a cat? Best decision any devs have ever made. There's a dedicated meow button, and you frequently do cat things like knocking things off tables and sharpening your claws on couches, as cats do. The cat is very well made and acts realistically. Super cute.Now, onto the main story. It's a 4-5 hour story, and honestly is pretty damn well written. They use the fact there's a cat to draw you in, and then the story keeps you engaged. The world building is pretty good, as you truly understand what goes on, even if you're just a cat. No spoilers but you feel connected to the environment and the NPC's. Speaking of the environment, it's super well made. Since the game is so small, it's full of detail, and every single room is hand crafted to portray what it's really for.There's a few very minor bugs and glitches like minor clipping, but it's mostly aesthetic and doesn't impact the gameplay. Can be excused because it's such an early release. I did have one instance where I clipped out of an elevator, which meant I had to restart that particular section, but it wasn't a big deal.Overall this is a very cool game. And I love cats :)

_childDocuments_.review: I recommend this game to you with a very special caveat: You must be a cat-lover. Not because the game is bad if you’re not, but because I don’t think it’s made for non-cat-lovers, and so it’d be wrong to judge this game from the perspective of its unintended audience.By this I only mean to highlight the fact that this game is - fundamentally - a walking simulator. Most of the fun I had was just from simple things you can do like abusing the meow button and feeling this warm fuzzy feeling inside while controlling our tiny little feline hero. If that’s not your thing then you’d probably be playing a very different game than what I’m about to describe and in all honesty I feel I lack both the perspective and the objectivity to judge whether this alternative experience is worth recommending.That said, Stray offers (to cat lovers) a unique and immersive experience in a BEAUTIFULLY animated world full of personalities and intrigue. I love how the story remains as cute as its protagonist throughout except a couple moments of ingenious Lovecraftian horror. It ties up really well and feels surprisingly (in a good way) emotional. Also I’m surprised to find out the cat was entirely animated and there wasn’t any mo-cap involved - that it captures the quintessence of our perception of feline movement in the end is a testament to the tremendous talent the team must have for this game to be this good. Also the score is one of the best I’ve heard yet, really makes the world come to life and adds to the wholesome tone of the game.All in all just a fantastically made game and I hope it gets enough fanfare to spawn another sequel, or at least a spiritual successor? A dog game, a spider game…you name it.
_childDocuments_.name: Stray

_childDocuments_.review: While this game ended up being something different from what I expected, I still enjoyed my time with Stray. I was thinking this was going to be a bit more stealth or action orientated but it ended up being more like an adventure game, filled with the classic item trading. While that isn't bad, the game sort of ends up not being about the cat and more about the companion, and then just sort of becomes like any other game rather than something unique. I do think there could have been far less dialogue and more atmospheric story telling, or even just flesh the game out with skills or further game-play elements, but what is here is just sort of fine. The game is very short too, being easily beaten in 5 or so hours, with not a lot demanding a revisit. I'd say maybe wait for a sale since the price might be too steep for what's here.

_childDocuments_.review: After finishing and beating this game I still have no idea what engine it was made in - I reckon Unreal 5. Regardless, this is one of the most gorgeous adventure games I've ever played. The cyberpunk aesthetic of every environment, even the natural lighting of the outdoors, looks absolutely wonderful. When you go to an area like Midtown, it looks better than Night City - no apologies that's just a fact.The soundtrack to the game is stellar, too,. Whether it's the absolute bangers the robot guitarist plays when you collect the sheet music or just the normal music, this game has excellent music from beginning to end and I can see why the soundtrack is sold separately for $9.50 right now. I had no idea what to expect going into this game besides cat + robot = fun, but the story is surprisingly developed and interesting. It may not be the most original thing in the history of stories - no story is, but the themes it borrows from the past century of media whether it's post-apocalypse stuff, eldritch horros from Lovecraft, or the exploration of a post-human future, the story has quite a bit to offer.The weakest aspect of this game is the complexity and length of the gameplay. Stray doesn't offer much more than most action adventure games -  some stealth, some platforming, collectibles and basic puzzle solving - but the gameplay is only meant to get you from one point of the story to the next. A great, short game that's absolutely worth giving a chance.
_childDocuments_.name: Stray

_childDocuments_.review: It's a game about a cat. It's not a proper Cat Game - you can do Cat Things, but they are mostly absolutely irrelephant to the core gameplay and few and far between.It's a game about a city. A city forgotten by time, a city without hope, a city without the sun. A city without a kitty.It's a game about humans. It's a game .It's a game you can complete in an hour and a half if you run really really fast. It's also a game you must sink at least six hours into if you want to 100% it, probably way more if you aren't using a guide (badge achievements aside, everything else is very easily findable and obtainable if you have at least one working eye - and I say that as a person with 0.9 working eyes).Yes, it looks like it cribs design decisions from Half Life, Last of Us, any Walled City-related piece of media ever made (DREDD 3D? Shadowrun? Chappi?), but it still manages to tell a compelling and, at times, moving story while using a viewpoint character whose contribution to most of the dialogues is meowing.Trust me: it's not that expensive, it's not that long, and it tells an infinitely better post-cyberpunk post-apocalypse story than Remember Me had ever tried with what is probably a quarter of its budget and triple the visual quality. Unless you're ideologically allergic to media containing cats, headcrabs or Advancing Wall of Doom gameplay elements, you're probably going to enjoy this ditty about a kitty in a doomed domed city wallowing in self-pity.
_childDocuments_.name: Stray

_childDocuments_.review: Stray is a true gem in the indie game world. What makes it stand out is its extraordinary perspective: you play as a cat, exploring a rich and detailed world through the eyes of a furry little adventurer. The movements, behaviors, and interactions feel so realistic that you really feel like you’re roaming the streets of a futuristic city yourself.The graphics and sound design create a dense, atmospheric environment. Neon lights, narrow alleys, and intriguing inhabitants bring this world to life, making it both welcoming and mysterious. Every corner is filled with detail, inviting you to explore and uncover its secrets in a playful, charming way.The gameplay is another standout feature, blending exploration, puzzle-solving, and a touch of suspense. The controls are intuitive and smooth, which is essential in a game that emphasizes movement and agility. Stray strikes a balance between a relaxed pace and moments of excitement, making it perfect for players who love to take their time while exploring and discovering new things.For anyone looking for a fresh gaming experience and a unique story, Stray is a must-try. It manages to deliver a deep, atmospheric experience with minimal dialogue, creating a journey that will stay with you long after you’ve finished.Rating: 9/10 – A beautifully atmospheric adventure from a new perspective that captivates players from start to finish.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR - Every single point about this game is less than average, by far Things look nice most of the time. Except the meowing. That's the only selling point. The meows are cute.Alright, I've gotta change my review to negative. I'm sorry but it just in my opinion is not even worth the current selling price. First things first, I tried not to spoil anything, but not too hard. There isn't much to spoil.  But there still might be some, so be careful.The story leaves more questions than answers. It seems to introduce an absolutely great story line or plot twist and then just... forgets about it. Never talks about it again. It's crazy how many times I've thought to myself "THIS has to be what I was waiting for!" Just to be absolutely disappointed, over and over, every single chapter. Even the ending, I thought to myself, "ok, NOW is where the story gets detailed." Nope, just credits. Explains absolutely nothing. They could make 100 different games off every cliffhanger or loose end they left while telling this story. It's absurd. It's also extremely short, but that could have been excused if it wasn't so poorly written.It's absolutely the MOST linear game I have played in ages. Not a single thing you do to the robots, whether that's meowing near them, or rubbing on their legs does a single thing. They just show little hearts on the otherwise AFK robots, it has absolutely zero effect on the story, how they think of you, nothing. You can't do anything in any way other than the way they lay out for you. Even the 'extra routes' are usually leading to dead ends without even a nice view. There are probably three spots that actually lead to anything worth traveling to in the first place, no matter how small the reward was whether its a Memory or a view of an area.Speaking of which, the gameplay and the atmosphere. Yes, the game looks nice, most of the time. There are for sure nice looking lights and scenes, but you hardly get to experience those because of A)How linear the game is, most routes are blocked preventing you from getting anywhere higher than one story. You also don't revisit most areas but briefly for a few chats, then they are closed off and cannot revisit any of them. And B)How limited the gameplay is in general. For the entire aspect of the game being focused on being a cat, you can only go up to maybe two stories high in most areas, and only in the areas they want you to. Most 'air conditioners' or 'ventilation systems' that are NOT already covered in what seems to be 'anti cat spikes' only reach up one or two floors, and the ones that don't have these anti cat spikes you just can't seem to get to. You can see across the street plenty of things that may or may not lead to a secret area, only to find out you just simply cannot reach these areas. You're forced to "explore" or "climb" such an absolute minute amount of city its laughable. Yes you get a good screenshot or two, but you're forced to leave that area to continue and you can't go back, and you HAVE to go the way THEY are directing you towards. Even the little "side quests" I was doing before moving on to the main story, weren't even side quests. There was ONE time you had to just get three different colored flowers for a robot, and it did nothing anyway. You could have just as easily not have gotten these, it wouldn't have mattered in the slightest. The other times I was doing what I thought was an extra quest, it turns out you need to do this for this item, that for that item, and these things for those in order to progress anyway. It's like an excuse to explore the area you're in, which is small to begin with.The characters and the story are the most absolute basic bare bones I've experienced in even a small indie game in a long time. The characters talk to and about you like you are some mystical, whimsical cat from some crazy land far away, that could NEVER make it down to where "they" are. Without spoiling what is basically the ENTIRE game, let's just say they introduce problems that have been a problem for entire generations, and all you had to do was trade them a poncho to do it. Or replace a battery. And then it's never talked about again, or brought up in any way ever again. The robots you save turn into NPCs that stand around. The one robot you work with to get to the end game just gets left behind in the most anticlimactic way possible. There is also some "PG Berserk" type stuff introduced about halfway through, and all you do is run away from it, and it's never talked about in any fashion ever again. It's absolutely mind boggling just how basic and bland the story and characters are, every single one, yourself as a cat included.As for the core gameplay, you jump a lot right? From ledge to ledge, rooftop to rooftop, etc. Why does it seem so choppy? And so... bland? Again? Every animation you jump with stops what you're doing for a split second, plays the animation, and lands in some awkward manner that orients itself as you move. The cats in the beginning cut scenes, your cat in cut scenes or 'gameplay scenes' all just seem so choppy. The robots. I get it, it's hard to perfect something like that, but it's what the ENTIRE game consists of. It's the absolute main mechanic. Besides meowing. And yes, meowing is cute and it sounds great. You can meow during cutscenes and while you do different things like sleep and drink, so props for that. It's super cute, I can't lie.As for BEING a cat in this game in general however, even that is yes, you guessed it, bland. There are a handful of paint cans you can knock off in typical cat fashion, or rip up a carpet or a door, and yea I can see the cuteness and appeal to that. The first time. But it does again absolutely zero. The paint cans have no consequences (besides one you MUST knock over to get into an area), ripping up carpets or doors does absolutely nothing. There are bottles and stuff you can knock over by walking into, but again, why? I get the appeal for the first thirty minutes, but that's it? You're a cat and can knock things over? There is absolutely nothing, not even a fake 'emotion meter' or something to make you want to do these things. Absolutely zero.Overall, this game is cute. That's literally it, and only for the first maybe thirty minutes or an hour. The worst part is how many plot holes and things left unexplained there are. It's just absolutely extravagant. Introduce some cool concept or gadget or plot twist just to never talk about it again. Yes I said this at the top but it's just so unbelievably empty and basic. It's unreal. I'd give it a genuine rating of probably 3.5/10. It seems like some stretched out tech demo for what could have been an amazing game with an amazing story. I genuinely thought when the game was ending that maybe it was only the first chapter ending, but nope just credits rolling.

_childDocuments_.review: So... This game is one of those games that on the first playthrough, it WOWS you with all the visuals and the idea of being a cat, but even then leaves you with a feeling like it was very unfinished by the end of the game. Then you playthrough it again and take off the rose colored cat glasses and honestly, this game is subpar at best. The first area of the game is definitely the best. Collectibles, memories, and trading quests to do, makes you really dig around and stick your nose into every hole you can find looking for more. Definitely when the game is at its peak for exploration and enjoyment. Then comes the part after this area.....Remember that part where you had to run from some weird things. There is going to be A LOT of that, or you can just use a mechanic it gives you to completely trivialize any of the suspense of these sections. Then you find the next area and looking at it from a distance you think to yourself 'MORE STUFF TO EXPLORE' but you are going to be sadly disappointed by the nothing in it.Then sadly, your reach the last area of the game, where your disappointment will be at an all time high. This area is HUGE with lots of amazing things to look at, but almost nothing to actually do in it. You run around digging into every nook like the first area only to realize that there is nothing to find so you continue the main story. You enter a 'stealth' section, but there is no actual stealth because it turns out you are faster than the people trying to catch you and you can just jauntily run past them on your way to the next objective.I wish there was a neutral option on Steam, because I would still recommend people play this game, as it is very fun to just jump and climb and claw things as a cat, but at a $30 price tag, this game just seems way to unfinished and lazy to justify that kind of money. TL;DR Good game. Lazy Design and Unfinished Feeling. Play it, but wait for a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: 8/10Giving Stray a score has been really hard. One one hand I think the game accomplishes what it aspires to do almost perfectly. On the other hand I think that the asking price is a little steep and that what the game ultimately is is not amazing to the point where I can comfortably give it a higher score. With that said, I completely understand people who loves this game wholeheartedly, it does things that few other games do.In Stray you play as a cat in a futuristic world. You live on the outskirts of a city shielded off from the outside world. One day you accidentally fall into the city, now inhabited by humanoid robots and metal-eating bug-monsters, and lose you cat-family. Now trapped in the city you traverse different areas and try to both find your way home to your friends as well as try to piece together what has happened to this once flourishing place.The controls and the perspective of the cat is what sets this game apart from others. It is truly designed with a cat in mind and you truly feel immersed in the body of a brave (and impossibly clever) cat. You meow, scratch, tip over, jump and run through the city and with the help of a small robotic companion solve puzzles and explore to your hearts content. It clicks right away and no area ever feels poorly designed for the controls or the tools you are given. The game is never hard but still manages to challenge your ability to perceive and intuitively figure out where to go and how to solve puzzles.There are not too many nitpicks to mention about Stray. I did not care much for the story or any characters, they fit the theme but failed to make any real impact on me. The robots have very little personality and the game is so short that there is no real growth or development. It is fine, really, but I would have liked a little more focus on characters, as the game is absolutely FILLED with unique NCPs that COULD have been interesting. Finally, I think that the game is slightly too expensive. I have played through it twice and speedran it and after completing it 100%, achievements and all I only managed to rack up 12 hours. A normal playthrough with no focus on extras should last between 4-5 hours, which is on the shorter end for the asking price. However, the game clicks so hard that I can understand that others may feel as though the experience is well worth the money. Me, I would recommend getting this on a sale.
