_childDocuments_.review: After broiling in Early Access for what felt like eternity, seasoned with a mix of Lovecraftian and 80s Horror spices, Dread Templar is finally up for grabs. To start with, I found its emphasis on secrets sensible. Aside from being a distinctly oldschool attribute, hidden caches are a great source of dopamine, so to bet on them was a good idea. Albeit, I can't say the same about the game's story, which is dull and anti-climactic. But I'll bite. This plot plays up the camp by taking itself seriously and The Templar isn't the type to dispense quips, is all. Instead, the humour is relegated to droves of loving nods to legends like Quake, DUSK, Blood, etc. These references don't mumble "I know this thing" like inbred fools but regally state "I learned from it".And it shows, starting with a hard thing to nail - the difficulty balance. The second hardest, Hell, felt just like your classic Ultra-Violence, providing enough resistance in the form of devastating incoming damage and resource scarcity. Both of these perils can be mitigated, besides, hitscan doesn't run rampant here, so the uphill battle of exorcising satanic spawn felt fair to me. It could've been trivial if this game relied on the usual savescum, but the save point system in place kept me in check. I appreciate it when a shooter forcibly makes me focus and strategize instead of apathetically scattering my gibs around the place in a trial-and-error marathon.The game consolidates several styles at once, but I think I can safely call its looks industrially gothic with a comicbook edge, given its dark overtones of satanic influence, pits full of skulls, and contrast techno-hellscapes feeding into surreal otherworldly macabre. The guns and monsters look badass and their minimalist look impressed me with how much panache was conveyed through so few facets. A clean low-poly image with pixelated textures is enhanced with modern tech like complex geometry and artistically applied lighting. It's evident that developers understood the amount of scrutiny their environments would be subjected to, making them a focal point of Templar's design.Fire with detail, the scenery pops with complex architecture and striking colour palettes of 2018's Mandy, accompanied by similarly sick music that facilitates dramatic chanting and choruses, changing alongside the landscapes. Some of it reminded me of Painkiller, but later the soundscape goes its own strange way. Speaking of which, I'd say the guns bang alright, but enemies' sound cues are barely audible. I'd like to hear them scream in pain, not just whimper out of existence. Incoming damage feedback is muffled, too, and projectile blares aren't pronounced enough, sometimes being silent altogether. I couldn't always tell what killed me.With this game, I couldn't always tell where I was, for its levels often go in and out of the realms of R'lyehian abstraction. After bathing in the blood light enveloping gloomy graveyards, shooting your way through the deceitful corridors of a soul-melting factory leading to forbidden libraries of a dark castle towering over a fishing village, halt and gawk at the vivid sights of many haunted realms, their ice-laden temples and canyons sprawling across cyclopean landscapes of crimson splendour I don't even dare to describe. Much like DUSK, this game drives itself increasingly mad with each passing level, yeeting you along with it into the infernal depths of shrieking chaos and colours out of space.Mechanically, these places aren't exactly your intricate puzzle boxes as seen in Doom or Quake. There are barely any monster closets, no key card calamities or sprawling mazes, however, each level is more than a set of arenas to beeline through. The maps on offer aren't less complex, they only seem unambiguous thanks to their strong internal logic, well-designed loops, shortcuts, and prominent landmarks, which make the geometry of temperately labyrinthian order easy to follow. Yeah, I miss diabolic monster closets and think that it was a mistake to brush them off like that but, at the same time, T19 reimbursed by giving the whole genre a push in terms of secret design.Progression is based on secret-hunting, otherwise, you'd be lacking resources. Searching for secrets demands a high level of engagement with your surroundings, procuring immersion. The levels can be vast, although fluid movement and neat loops made hunting feel snappy. Aside from numerous twists I won't spoil, look out for your common strangeness with the torches, hidden buttons, and opportunities for acrobatic feats. The latter doesn't look scary here. You don't slip off the edges or get caught on them and the jump's length is just right, so platforming efforts normally end up exactly as you anticipate.What I didn't anticipate was how the action made me contort in my chair like I was partaking in NASCAR. You run like wind, yet enemies are also quick. Evading their blows and projectiles is part reaction, part precognition, part slo-mo ability, which restores on kills and can be useful in a pinch. Gunplay feels kinetic. Foes flinch and fall over with subdued ragdoll or explode in splashes of gratuitous blood and gore. Ammo scarcity ties in, raising the importance of secret stashes, and makes weapon-juggling your lifeline. Your arsenal includes a katana and a bow, dual pistols coupled with SMGs, great pump-action and double-barrel, two rocket launchers producing surprisingly feeble explosions, an infernal magnum revolver, and a demonic gauntlet that claps hordes and bosses like flies. Instead of alternative fire, almost every weapon has an alternative weapon! I kid you not.But what you can do to these lookers is even better. This is where all these runes and gems you find lead to - the Upgrade Altar. Okay, these aren't something too new and exciting. You can encounter a few of those in any level and use them to rebuild at any time, free of charge. Upgrades are a substantial. Not just adding ammo capacity, damage, fire rate (a double-edged sword) but providing an option to, say, make pistols more potent while going Max Payne, to turn your pump-action into a sniper workhorse, or conjure even more drastic transformations to play with. I see it as a kind of difficulty customisation through your arsenal. If the going seems tough - go back to the table, perhaps you missed a killer combination.Onto said killing then. Typically, most bosses are bimbos who exist to look good and die fast, but enemy design compensates. They're all really dumb even by the boomer-shooter standards, but they stand out in other ways. Not just due to bigger health pools or damage output, too. Some rush you, some spawn trouble, some are immune to explosions, some cast fog around them. The game steadily drops uneven heaps of foes on your head, it's an unpredictable romp of ever-escalating intensity. Small-scale corridor brawls flow into massive battles, then dial back to tight set pieces, chock-full of demon knights, grenade-launching "not ogres", flying eye apparitions, pesky warlock summoners, eldritch Fiends, acid-spitting sisters of Vores, swift ice Alien scum, Wanamingos...I'm running out of space after barely scratching the surface. And look, I didn't use these pop culture comparisons because the designs are derivative. Some are, sure, yet mostly I couldn't find the words to describe all the imaginative things I saw, resorting to shortcuts. Unlike me, the game doesn't cut corners. Given the insane variety and fertility, Dread Templar perfectly maintains its consistency of gameplay and art style, staying good and true from cover to cover. It inherited Quake's pacing and precision, sweeping me off my feet with how relentlessly it ramped up. This is it, chief, knock yourself out.My curator

_childDocuments_.review: Dread Templar is yet another fish in the sea of recent boomer shooters. It's a competent game, but misses the mark when it comes to personality and finding it's own identity. If you're looking to scratch that retro-shooter itch, you could do a lot worse than Dread Templar - just don't expect it to be on the same level as Dusk and Amid Evil.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: Dread Templar is an old school First Person Shooter where the player character must fight through hordes of demons in a hell dimension on a quest for revenge.•	Movement speed is fast, allowing you to circle strafe enemies and sidestep incoming projectiles. You also have a dash move which can be performed on the ground and in mid air, which is useful for quickly escaping nearby enemies and jumping over bottomless pits.•	Killing enemies fills a special meter which lets you activate bullet time, helping you to deal with large groups of enemies in slow motion.•	There are many different enemy types, honestly I don’t even know how to describe most of them, just really strange looking demons. There’s the usual mixture of melee, ranged, flyers, summoners and a few large bosses.•	You can carry all the weapons simultaneously, including katana, pistol, SMG, single and double barrel shotguns, bow, magnum, rocket launcher, and gauntlet. •	Hidden around each map you’ll find tokens which let you upgrade weapons to increase damage, ammo capacity and fire rate, or improve your character’s health, bullet time, and dash cooldown.•	Each weapon can also be upgraded to its infernal variant, which changes how the weapon functions. For example, the SMG has all bullets in one big clip so you don’t need to reload, the double barrel shotgun fires wave of energy, and the rocket launcher fires three homing missiles.•	Maps are quite maze-like, full of side paths and secret areas, where you’ll need to collect coloured key cards and activate switches to unlock the path forward.•	Hard difficulty was a fun challenge for an experienced FPS player. I had to survive several tough fights on low health, and I died a few times, but was never stuck for long.•	It took me just over 9 hours to complete the game.•	Controls are fully rebindable and work great with mouse and keyboard.•	I didn’t have any problems with bugs, crashes or framerate.•	Excellent heavy metal soundtrack which is fast, loud, and perfectly complements the speed of combat.Dread Templar is an excellent game which FPS fans should consider a must play, especially if you enjoyed similar games like Dusk and Amid Evil.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: You can turn two swords into a throwable sword and slam the f**cker into a distant enemy, only to watch them explode into red mist. It looks like Quake, kind of feels like Quake as well. It's totally level-based, just like the classics, and you'll be finding keys and activating switches and the like. But there's also bullet time, plus upgrades for your weapons. Honestly, it's a lot of fun, even if it doesn't do anything all that different from anything else. If you want another FPS that's like Quake or Dusk, this scratches that same itch.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: Painfully average.After finishing the second chapter in around 6 or so hours I went back to my initial thoughts of playing the game and realised they hadn't changed whatsoever.I love the boomer shooter genre and the more of these the better right?well... sort ofDread Templar has all the makings of another classic in the vein of Quake and Blood but seems to just be missing something and my whole time playing I'm still unsure as to what. The combat is very fluid and fast paced, Weapons are all exactly what you'd expect, following the genres classics like a (woefully underpowered feeling) super shotgun. The more unique weapons are still relatively plain, The recharging bow is fine not much to say about it, the throwable katana is just another recharging slightly higher damage weapon that when you use it you have to wait for another cooldown before being able to melee or toss it again (I really don't understand the love for this weapon) and the inf. Gauntlet which is a charge high ammo costing blast that acts like a railgun for a few examples. I think the problem comes in any kind of unique selling point. Everybody talks about the movement in this game like its the second coming and its not quite fast enough for that satisfying quake style of gameplay with bouncing and rocketjumping around. But its certainly not slow, The level design is great and its corridor shooter style is generally pretty spot on for its movement style (although i think the dash cooldown is a little too long for its platforming sections) the level design and secrets are fun and very satisfying to roam around.Oh and can we sort the spammy bosses please. Good god are they insufferable. some good ideas for how they interact with you (such as the giant hearts lasers staying in one spot but you can kill them to free it up) but everything devolves to "circle strafe around the arena shooting it watching its huge health bar chip away until it calls in fodder to waste your ammo" and they can spam the same aggravating move en masse and its just not very fun. The final boss of episode 2 spent 90% of its time in an invincible state shooting down purple lightning at me while I stood in one of two spots waiting,  It wasn't challenging or difficult, it was absolutely miserable.The game looks great but never really grabs and holds my interest which i think is down to an underdeveloped art style to the world. The soundtrack is decent if a little droning at points I never felt the need to listen to it out of gameplay which considering its industrial vibe is very strange for me it just doesn't have that kick to really capture me. and the presentation is clearly above average but just lacking that memorable factor.Dread Templar despite what seems like a wall of my complaining, is fine. It plays well and it looks good but I think in a world of Dusk, Amid Evil, Ultrakill, Project Warlock and other contemporaries this game doesn't do enough and doesn't have the real raw passion to make itself stand among them as tall. If you have played a lot of its ilk and are just looking for more of that its perfectly playable and you will have a good time, but all these reviews about how its more satisfying and better designed than Doom Eternal or the true spiritual successor to Quake are utter bollocks
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: Not a bad game by any means, but average at best. If you've ever played a boomer shooter, you've played Dread Templar. Serviceable visuals, basic enemies, very mediocre weapon arsenal, cliched maps mostly based around castles/dungeons/caves, cool upgrade system hidden behind hundreds upon hundreds of secret areas in every map, nice soundtrack ruined by terrible looping. I've had fun, but I see no real point in finishing it. The problem is, boomer shooters evolved so much in the last couple of years and this one, ironically, feels dated. Every encounter plays pretty much the same - you go into a room, quickly dash back into the corridor and shoot enemies rushing you through the chokepoint. Rinse, repeat. It's pretty fun in doses, but that's about it.Don't know what else to say really. It's an okay game. If you haven't played a boomer shooter in a long time, this might do the trick... or just replay Dusk.

_childDocuments_.review: Worth your time if you like retro fps. Kind of feels like a mix of Quake and Doom Eternal. Dread Templar has the chunky Quake aesthetics and the weapon swapping and enemy prioritization of Doom Eternal (although not as emphasized as Doom Eternal). Dread Templar rewards precision and headshotting is very fun.It takes an episode or two to get into. My first impressions of this was that it was generic and uninspired, but the game really becomes enjoyable when you have more weapons and the level design gradually improves. Main gripes with the game is that the save system can be occasionally buggy. The music, while really good, becomes repetitive quickly. Some songs play again across different levels. Imagine playing a level for 20-30 minutes having the same 3 minute song loop, then you start the next map, and the exact same song loops again. Do yourself a favor and turn the music off and play something else you like in the background. It's a shame there aren't more ambient tracks and tracks in general because John S. Weekley (composer for this game) makes awesome music.Overall fun game and a standout for me in the retro fps resurgence.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: Dread Templar is great, the gameplay, the design, the music. It's all really good. The game is still in early access which does result in a small amount of playtime/content but that small time was great. The levels are all very well designed and never found too hard to combat my enemies. I sometimes got a little lost on where I was required to go but after some wandering I was able to continue. The shooting and general combat is solid. All the guns feel powerful and purposeful, I was really impressed with the amount of weapons. The game has a very large line up of guns for all purposes. The guns feel modern and also feel very quake/doom like. The art in the game is as expected, it's a modernised version of the classic fps visuals. There's some extra lighting tech that really helps push the game a little further and the enemy designs really stood out as intriguing. It's certainly not anything to be excited about but I did enjoy seeing what the locations had on offer. The music is probably some of the best you can get from the genre, the early levels have the best tracks, they are heavy, fast and have tons of power behind them. The performance is quite good, some fps dips in places which is odd with the low poly count. They were not awful but it happens at times. A big issue I had was my frame rate being extremely high which was causing me to work harder than it needed to because the game has no frame cap. A frame cap would have been a great setting to have and would have helped the game perform better. There were little to no bugs within the game, some very small inconveniences but nothing ever bothered me. In conclusion, the game is great. There is not much here currently which might make some avoid it, i was able to beat it in 4 hours on normal difficulty but If you're looking for more old school shooters I'd certainly add this one to your library. Note : purchased via Humble Bundles - Boomer shooter bundle.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: I want to enjoy this game, I really do, but it's not that engaging. Dread Templar is just so by-the-numbers that it doesn't have anything unique to it. I mean, sure, there's the bullet time mechanic and the ability to throw your melee weapon as an emergency ranged attack, plus the soundtrack is freaking awesome, but this game is so freaking boring.Let me put this into perspective. You play as a gunslinger working for an unnamed "Lord," who sends you out on a quest to rid the world of demonic forces. Sounds bog-standard, but we're not really in it for the story, we're in it for the gameplay. We want to go out and slaughter demons and other foes that stand in our way. And Dread Templar does that. So what else does the game have to offer besides an excuse plot and a Hellish setting? Not a whole lot. You have some interesting weapons, such as dual pistols, dual SMGs, an infernal rocket launcher and revolver, a bow that recharges ammo, and perhaps most interesting out of all, a pair of blades that you can combine together to make a spear. That's about it, really. There's an upgrade system for the weapons, where you collect red tokens to unlock upgrade slots and then collect the upgrades themselves, and then slot them in for different buffs. The level design is semi-linear in scope, in that you mostly travel in a straight line across the map, pick up keys, then double back to their respective doors and continue forth. Oh yeah, I forgot to mention, the save system is checkpoint-based. You walk up to blue crystalline devices and save your progress there. That's where the decent stuff ends, unfortunately.The bad stuff... hoo boy, where do I begin? Well, let's start with the combat. It's dull. The enemies are decently designed and their AI is serviceable enough, the weapons feel good but lack significant oomph and thus feel weaker than they're supposed to. I mean, sure, the bow is powerful and capable of taking down some of the stronger enemies, but the rocket launcher and revolver feel like NERF toys. Even with the upgrades. Oh, btw, the weapon upgrades are boring. You get the bog standard ones, such as increased ammo reserves, boosted damage, etc., but the real disappointing ones are the gold upgrades. For instance, the dual pistols' gold upgrade turns them from a pair of M1911s to a pair of demonic slugthrowers. Sounds nice, yeah? However, the pistols' bullets now have travel time. That's right, the bullets change from hitscan to projectiles that have travel time. I dunno about you, but that sounds like a step back for me. And that's not getting to the glitches. At one point, when I was about to face off against a boss, I fired my rocket launcher at it, but for some weird reason, the rockets fired *away* from the target, even *backwards*. I was only able to circumvent this glitch by activating Nvidia ShadowPlay; yeah, that's right, turning on ShadowPlay not only made the rockets travel straight to the target, but it also smoothed out the framerate. How do you mess that up?Actually getting upgrades is a slog, too. The tokens needed to unlock the slots are sparse and are mostly found in secrets, so unless you're adept at finding those secrets, you're gonna have a hard time unlocking the upgrade slots. Even then, the tokens don't net you enough to unlock all the slots. I still haven't been able to upgrade my rocket launcher or revolver fully because I was constantly short of tokens, even at the point where I left the game. And the upgrades themselves are numerous, but many of them are redundant. End result: you end up with more upgrades than you do tokens to unlock the upgrade slots.The level design sucks. I said earlier that the levels are semi-linear in scope, right? You travel in a straight line for most of them, but that's not the annoying part. Are you a fan of first-person platforming? And no, we're not talking about Mirror's Edge here, we're talking about Half-Life 1-esque platforming. Jumping from platform to platform over instadeath pits while getting shot at by enemies is guaranteed to make you rip your hair out, because a lot of times, you'll end up either missing a platform or you get knocked off of it because you got hit by an enemy attack, and therefore, you fall to your death. And the levels' secrets are a pain to find because there's a lot of points in the levels where you *think* you can reach them, such as ledges or cave entrances, only to discover that they're blocked with invisible walls. Ergo, you fall to your death. Again. Exploration is slim here, as a result, because of the invisible walls and instadeath pits.Not worth the $10. Skip this one and go find a different boomshoot that's on Steam.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: A very lengthy shooter.  Memorable?  Not really though I would consider one boss encounter memorable.  I thought the level design good,  the weapons great but the majority of the boss encounters lacking.  I played on normal so perhaps it was matter of being too good for the difficulty. :)   Dread Templar's campaign is substantial and challenging.  I was engaged the whole way through.  Enough enemy designs to meet expectations.  A twist are the runes which change weapon or player abilities.  Some of them are over done but I appreciate their inclusion.  Recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: Combine Quake 2 with Doom and perhaps a bit of Painkiller and you might end up with something like Dread Templar. Even though that does sound like a 'killer-combo', I'm not sure what to think of this game.The game starts off pretty slow and it takes quite a long time to step up the pace which gives me hope that in the future this could be a really fun game when finished. Like in most 90s/Retro FPS games you will be running around killing creatures and finding keys or levers to unlock doors. Obviously there are tons of secrets to find which contain ammo, health or perks which you can use to give your character extra health or extra pistol dmg and so on.The problems I have with this game is that killing creatures is not really that fun compared to some other games I've played + the maps are not that interesting. Especially the earlier levels are a borefest, nothing you have never seen before. The weapons are fine I guess. Obviously it's getting harder for developers to come up with unique weapons.Like I said before; At one point Dread Templar starts to become more interesting and comes pretty close to Doom (2016) using the Quake 2 engine but not long after that you will have finished the game since it's still in Early Access. I do have to say that the heavy metal soundtrack is pretty good and keeps you in the mood. Dread Templar certainly is not the worst game of the bunch but at the moment I can't really recommend it compared to the asking price.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: I can't really recommend this game until the developers take the time to put the finishing touch on the product before moving on to their next project. 4/10 if I'm being 100% honest. It plays like a mediocre GZDoom mod with some interesting, yet flat footed execution. Slightly more detail down below, I have not finished the game but likely will at some point. (playing on the "hard" difficulty as of now)This game is severely lacking movement tech/options to more reliably dodge incoming attacks. A myriad of levels in this game are just absolutely jam packed with enemies, and this would be a positive note if not for the fact that the dash is SINGLE USE and set to an almost 30 SECOND COOL-DOWN. You CAN upgrade the cool-down using one of your already limited upgrade slots, but as of playing I just beat the boss of Episode 2 and still have only found one upgrade for the dash. It did ALMOST NOTHING. I still find myself trying to bunny hop and strafe out of the way of enemies I legitimately just cannot outmaneuver, because strafe jumping and bunny hopping do literally nothing for your movement speed. It's just downright disappointing.The game desperately needs a balance and QoL passover, because as it stands the game is just unpolished with some MAJOR potential. Such as dying immediately upon falling into pits instead of taking damage and being thrown back up onto a nearby ledge. Why is such an archaic mechanic still implemented into something that is supposed to be a retro shooter with MODERN elements? There is nothing modern about absolutely trash ass platforming sections being coupled with insta-kill death drops EVERYWHERE. The AI also definitely needs some work, it's extremely in the realm of "everything that doesn't shoot at you literally just runs headlong into your bullets until one of you is dead." Finally, just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ add ledge climbing. Do it, just shut the ♥♥♥♥ up and do it. There is no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ reason to not have it. I'm tired of pretending that it isn't a borderline required mechanic for a tightly designed, smooth, and responsive boomer shooter. This has been my TED talk. Maybe buy the game if you like inconsistent and quite frankly frustrating experiences with mechanics that make little to no sense.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: Not a bad game by any means, but it blends into the sea of retro shooters that released recently. It's a competent shooter, but it doesn't really excel at anything in particular compared to other games.Thoughts after finishing:- EP1 was notably boring, episodes after it were definitely better.- There were some neat levels, but a lot of them blend together since all the levels in each episode generally share the same set of textures.- I don't really know how to quantify *why*, but even though the levels had lots of secrets, I didn't really have much fun exploring them compared to CULTIC and the new Quake episode.- Game starts to pick up when you get enough runes to get your ideal loadout (around EP4ish for me), but runes/upgrades are often locked behind obscure secrets so playing with a guide is pretty much mandatory. The mandatory secret hunting for character upgrades soured my experience quite a bit.- Feels like most things slightly underperform at the baseline and require you to use runes to make them feel good (ex. 1shotting bugs with the pump shotgun requires you to stack multiple damage upgrades or else they get left with a sliver of HP). Rune system would be more fun if there were less pure stat boost upgrades and it was mainly just playstyle changes (gold runes do a good job of this).- Needs better sound feedback in general. Most notably, enemy attack sound cues are barely-audible/completely lacking on a lot of enemies. Risk of Rain 2 does a superb job in this regard, as every enemy has a distinct attack noise that can be easily recognized mid-combat, and projectiles make noise mid-flight so you can hear when they're whizzing past you.- Music ended up being really repetitive due to being on a short loop. Super unfitting when you're spending 30 minutes checking every nook and cranny of an already-cleared map trying to find whichever runes you missed.- NEEDS AN OPTION TO DISABLE INTERACTION CUTSCENES. Straight up died a few times due to getting locked in place when pulling a switch, getting killed immediately when the cutscene ends.Minor notes:- No matter what combination of upgrades to the dual katanas I used, I couldn't get them to be very useful at all in either fire mode. Best I could do was stun things with the Lightning Spear upgrade, while their actual damage output was lacking.- All of the Gold Runes for the Trap Launcher that I got seemed to be a direct downgrade (multi explosion removes the shock, bug turret is funny but comes at the cost of being able to shock, defense bubble was awkward to use)- Would be nice if the Reset Slot button refunded the Blood Gem as well, since the only way to re-spec those is to Reset All.- Noticed certain enemies (ex. the ice spike enemies that charge you) have a tendency to clip directly into you which ends up being kind of awkward.- Wish the flying enemies would die in 1 bow/revolver shot. It's really awkward that they get left with a sliver of HP that requires you to pistol them to death. I'm assuming the intended solution is to stack multiple damage upgrades.- Quite a few levels have awkward invisible wall placement. I noticed 1 level in EP4 where a small healthpack was completely inaccessible because of it.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: Terrific, fast-paced boomer shooter with a simple story and explosive action. This game doesn't waste your time with unnecessary filler and clearly understands why old school FPS design is having a renaissance these days. It easily won me over with some modern elements and classic mechanics. Highly recommended for any demon-slaying fanatic.Pros:- Interesting upgrade system;- Good arsenal;- Responsive controls;- Great level design;- Awesome soundtrack;- Lots of secrets;- Great optimisation;- Bullet time;- Good enemy roster;- Customisable retro visuals;- Satisfying combat;Cons:- Mediocre bosses;
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: The reliance on upgrades and level design are what kill this game.  You have to upgrade to stand a chance in later levels, but finding the items to upgrade your arsenal requires hunting for extremely obscure secrets.  Now, I'm a nerd, but not nerdy enough to want to double my play time by running around swinging my melee weapons at walls.  The levels themselves are extremely lazy and sloppy, especially after the first 1/3 of the game.  You can tell that they wanted to get this thing done.Gun play and arsenal are good, but the level design kills the encounters.  I'd recommend this if it weren't for the fact that there are plenty of other (better) "Boomer Shooters" out there.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: + Often great level design+ Varied secrets, mostly reasonably hidden super secrets+ Wide arsenal of weapons (8 weapon slots, 16 weapons total with upgrades that swap some of them out for different versions) with good incentive to use all of them+ Instant weapon switching makes for great potential for effective and satisfying combos.+ The most common upgrades are incremental, but the most impactful ones are designed to have drawbacks, so you're not simply choosing the thing with the highest number.+ Upgrades can be swapped out for others to fill out 3 slots per weapon and 3 character upgrade slots. You don't need to commit to a specific build beyond unlocking the slots themselves.+ Fairly long campaign, bonus wave defense mode, secrets incentivising replaying levels.+ Well placed checkpoints instead of a quicksave system.- The gamepad controls are entirely unusable and even if you'd want to suffer through the game with them there's no aim assist to use as a crutch.- As good as the music is, you're going to want to turn it off. The music is made with combat in mind, but there's no dynamic music system, so you're just listening to the same 3 minute loop of intense bgm on repeat while just walking around areas. At least one of the tracks is reused for 3 consecutive (long) levels, to give you an idea.- The game's progression system is tied to exploration. If you're not interested in hunting for secrets, at least some of your weapons will be less effective in combat and you'll effectively miss out on some weapons due to how much mods can alter the guns' characteristics.- Annoying enemy designs - they're faster than you, their projectiles are fast enough to always hit you in close to mid range but slow enough that reversing the direction you're circle strafing in will almost always get you hit by an attack fired 10 seconds ago. A lot of attacks are also explosive so even when you avoid the projectiles themselves you will get hit because there's just not enough space to manoeuvre around the splash radii.- Most enemy attacks have no sound effects and the rare SFX that are there don't always play- Enemies see, attack, and hit you through walls often- A couple of the levels are unfun to navigate due to reuse of assets and lack of variety their geometry.- The game really wants you to get into every little suspicious spot, but a lot of them are clipped off, which results in disappointment, getting you killed or stuck (forcing a reload). This gets worse in the latter parts of the campaign.- Bosses aren't all that great and get totally melted by high dps weapons to the point where they might take just seconds to take down with an optimised build instead of minutes.- There is no pocket reloading, so you need to go through the routine of reloading a few of the weapons after every encounter. It's also annoying to switch to a weapon just to see that you've forgotten to reload it in the last few minutes.- Enemy animations are fairly lacking, which makes it hard to see when they're attacking.- The damage indicator always claims you're taking damage from the back (unless it just looks that way for some reason).- The movement doesn't give you much to do when just exploring the large levels. It's missing some small, timing based movement tech that would allow you to travel slightly faster, just to give your hands something to do.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: Dread Templar is a fairly competent game that may or may not scratch an itch. It's Quake, more or less, with a few extra bells and whistles. Mainly, Slow-mo, melee, a dash, a bow, and upgrades. It's really hard to say this, but even though the gunplay is good, the levels and enemies are so incredibly uninteresting that I just can't recommend it. I like spaghetti but I don't want it three meals a day.Pros:-runs great-controls and game feel is very good-upgrade system adds a little incentive to explore-Some cool weaponsCons:-extreme amount of music repetition, I like metal but the tracks are re-used well beyond what's tolerable.-enemies lack depth and are introduced rather slowly. Enemies either run at you, shoot at you, or both. It becomes monotonous after a couple hours.-upgrade menu UX is kinda bad-environment aesthetics are very uninspired and all the levels I played were basically interchangeable. Bright primary colors for markers/lighting just add to confusion and make the game uglier and harder to navigate.-LEVEL DESIGN IS VERY BAD. levels are fairly aimless and are utterly crippled by assets and bright colors being reused everywhere; every room looks basically the same, lots of backtracking, lots of hitting switches and then a door arbitrarily opens on the opposite side of the map or perhaps a place you've never even been.Summary: This is a one-note experience with very little nuance or creativity. At a quick glance, you'd be forgiven for thinking this is a good game, but a game like this just doesn't work without good level design, and the level design here is abysmal. Some will love it because of its Quake similarities, but I need a little more substance. The FPS genre has evolved a lot over the years, but despite having the new bells & whistles mentioned at the start, Dread Templar doesn't feel like a new take on a classic to me.

_childDocuments_.review: Oh boy where to begin with this gem of a game. Out of all the retro FPS games that I am waiting for to leave early access (and that's no small number) this one right here might be my most anticipated of them.First off this game doesn't do a whole lot different than other retro fps games out there (not to say it doesn't have some amazing ideas and set pieces and enemies, weapons etc) but what this game does is take what makes a retro fps great, and polishes it to a perfect shine.The Music: I have to praise the soundtrack, honestly this is one of the best game soundtracks i've ever heard and in my opinion beats Doom Eternal's stellar soundtrack. Its metal mayhem with amazing synths and dark chanting and other amazing instruments. Every single level has an amazing soundtrack to accompany it and I even find myself listening to it outside of the game.The gunplay: These guns are great, you got your standard fair of shotgun, double barrel, pistols (duel wield), smg (also duel wield) Rocket Launcher that can be swapped for a 3 shot launcher, but then you got weapons like a revolver straight out of hell that sounds like a cannon going off, a launcher that shoots stun mines, a katana that can be turned into a throwing weapon and launch it like a javelin, the games own BFG (which looks amazing visually and just melts anything you need to kill) and a bow that can be used as a sniper rifle. All the weapons are very useful and fun to use and have very punchy sound effects.Abilities: You have a bullet time ability that fills up as you kill enemies which slows down time letting you go full Neo on everything, you also have a dash too which is great for platforming and dodging enemies.Enemies: The enemy design is great and each one both looks unique, stands out from the rest, and all have interesting attacks. Later in the game you start to run into enemies that have really interesting attacks and abilities and things can get chaotic very quickly. You got your grunts, fast moving humanoids, snipers, flying enemies, tank enemies, grenade throwing enemies that remind me of the ogres from quake, and much more. A personal favorite of mine is the necromancer mage that summons a purple enemy that is stronger than normal to help it fight. All the enemies are visually distinct enough to stand out to help the player prioritize targets and have tell tale sounds and delightfully gib when killed.Levels and secrets: The Levels are all wonderfully done with some light platforming here and there, interesting set pieces and puzzles, honestly can't think of a single level that I hated. The secrets are all well hidden and each level has a bonus area indicated by a red x in the terrain that if broken, leads to a side area that is a major step up in difficulty but rewards the player with upgrades and ammo and even sometimes hidden weapons.Upgrades: The game has an upgrade system where you can find these red crystals to unlock perk slots and the perks themselves are hidden all throughout the levels. Some of these perks are standard fair such as more ammo or damage or fire rate. But some are really interesting such as one where it makes your pistols do crazy damage and have infinite ammo when you use bullet time.Visuals: The visuals are retro fps goodness, nice detailed models that still have the retro look. Honestly not much to say about the visuals every part of the game is distinct and looks great and the game has a lot of color so you won't be seeing constant brown like some retro fps games.The only thing that I think this game could benefit from is either faster movement speed or the ability to move around the terrain faster by bunny hopping. While you do move fast you can't use your dash a lot and being able to bunny hop around would really add to the chaotic combat.Overall this is an amazing retro fps and I cannot wait for the full release, if you haven't gotten this game yet I highly suggest purchasing this gem. You won't regret it.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: (playthrough difficulty set to hard, not sure how things change in hell/nightmare atm)I don't really get the people calling this game mid, this is honestly a solid af boomer shooter that sets itself apart via the rune system, from basic stat upgrades to playstyle-enabling gold runes this game basically lets you play however you want while also encouraging secret hunting (cuz most of the good stuff is hidden behind secrets and super secrets)there's a good amount of level variety (with a lot of nods & references mostly found in secrets/super secrets), the enemies are well designed (for the most part, the flying bugs that explode can go bite me), the weapons are cool and fun to ♥♥♥♥ around with, again for the most part. The main outlier here for me is the rocket launcher (& by extension the tri-rocket launcher), they both feel awfully weak even with max weapon damage runes and you can't rocket jump at all for some reason, which is weird because one of the gold runes for the rocket launcher significantly reduces self damage, so you'd think that would let you rocket jump but that didn't work :(Regardless, I had tons of fun blasting demons in 6 gorillion pieces while listening to some baller heavy music (shoutout to E3M5 best track if you know you know)Also this is a solo dev project lol they had me fooled i thought this was a small team at least considering how polished it it but no it's one person, mad props

_childDocuments_.review: Very serviceable boomer shooter. It's an appropriate length (8ish hours) with a wide variety of sets and enemies. Guns feel a little weak in my opinion, especially the shotguns and SMGs. Secrets can be incredibly obtuse but hold some of the best weapon/character upgrades, so a lot of time spent mashing on walls or running in circles to find secrets. However, it's still fun to play. I would say a 6.5-7/10 in regards to boomer shooters. Don't play this if you're not actively looking for another game in the genre to scratch an itch, but if you are it works.

_childDocuments_.review: This past week has been big for the oldschool-styled shooters, and I've reviewed a few of them now.  White Hell, Dread Templar, and KUR are all worthy additions to my library for different reasons.. and they're all cheap enough that you'd be crazy not to pick up at least one or two of these great games if you're into the genre.Dread Templar probably looks a lot like a Quake game, though its selection of weapons, and its upgrade system set it apart from that.  It also includes a bullet time mode that can be recharged by killing enemies the regular way, and things that cool down or charge up after use, such as throwing your swords, using arrows after you find the bow, and using your dodge-dash/air-dash.I'd say it also focuses more on exploring more complex environments than you find in your classic Quake experience, always treading the line between giving you a bunch of enemies to deal with, then leaving you to find your way through, or locate secrets and extra supplies scattered around.  Some of those secrets contain the medallions that are used to upgrade your own abilities, and the capabilities of your arsenal, and each medallion has a specific upgrade, giving you some reason to seek out specific ones.  How many of these upgrades you can actually apply at a time is governed partially by another collectible, but don't worry, your overall profile in this game is a consistent thing that you carry whether you're working through the story linearly, or using the Level Select mode to return to previous stages to hunt for things you may have missed.. at least until you choose to reset it, if you wish for a new, clean playthrough.Anyway, with the variety of enemies, environments, the mix of puzzle solving, exploration, light platforming, and combat.. the systems that all mostly work in harmony with each other, and the levels of challenge on offer (I'm playing on normal and it's just right for me, but there are higher ones, including a hidden difficulty), I would say that in a market that is starting to feel flooded with these types of shooters, this is one of the ones worth owning.  Buy it now, or wait for Early Access to be over, the decision is yours, but at least keep it on your wishlist.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: While I understand the release timing of this game for Realms Deep, I cannot currently recommend this game. It feels unfinished and unpolished in it's current state, something that should be expected for a beta, but 15 bucks for a version 0.9 EA release in this condition is too much at the moment. I do understand the timing of the release, as this should work as a means to secure funding to further develop the game (given this isn't another EA scam.) The game isn't awful, but there are likely better retro style shooters to play that you may have not had the chance to get to yet.A lot about this game takes elements from Doom Eternal, and does nothing to add to it or feels like a lesser version of it. All guns feel familiar, but are unbalanced. The bow in particular is absolutely worthless. It's your standard fps gameplay at it's core, which is fine. If you like boomer shooters you will feel right at home. I really like the textures and gun models, but not much else about the game stands out. Environments look bare and lack detail. The second set of enemies are unique, but the first are your run of the mill zombie type enemies. The lighting is not dynamic and colored lighting looks a bit too funky in my opinion. The music is okay, but there aren't enough tracks for each stage yet so you will be hearing some of the same tracks over and over. The djent/death metal hybrid is starting to get a bit too cliche for me. The second chapter stands out in comparison to the first. The first chapter is very drab and contains no interesting level design elements. There are 3 levels in the 2nd chapter that are great and the rest are just okay. While I expect some issues, there are some things that need to be addressed immediately and I'm surprised to see it in a 0.9 build. Some doors and switches would not visually activate. This led to confusion as to where to go. It took me a good 15 minutes once to figure out that a door was open but looked closed and I had to walk through it. This happened around 5 times and each time tripped up the flow of the game. Enemy hurtboxes are also wonky while they are stunned from traps. The biggest purple enemy particularly lost his hurtbox while stunned and I was shooting rockets through them. I was walking through some enemies as well. Speaking of the menu options, they are currently lacking. Not to a horrible extent, but definitely needs work. Some nitpicking here, the katana throw is great in concept but very annoying to use. After throwing it you need to immediately switch to another weapon as there is a cooldown for the throw. There should be an auto-switch to your previous weapon. There is also no auto-switch toggle for when you run out of ammo. There should be an option for this in the menu. And why do arrows recharge and have such limited ammo? What is the point of this? And the bow does so little damage there's no point to using it, unless there are emblems that drastically rework it that I didn't collect. Dash is annoying. I don't see a need for the long cooldown and it's a little frustrating to have to use an emblem spot to shorten it and it doesn't shorten it that much. Bullet time is worthless. While you do get an increased rate of fire while in it, you are still perfectly vulnerable. I made it through the entire game without needing it. It should be reworked so that it becomes more of a required mechanic. The first two bosses are a wash, but the final boss is simply unfun. It's not terribly difficult, but has aggravating slowdown mechanics. Most of the attacks do little damage, except one that killed me at 80 health on Normal difficulty.  The entire strategy for the boss was just positioning to not get hit by slowdown combo into that strong hit while everything else was trivial. However, I did like that I had to have a game plan for my weapons used during the fight. The font is annoying and looks like Harry Potter. Audio/visual feed back is lacking when you take damage. The playthrough of the game in its current state took me roughly 2 hours to complete, which is not worth 15 bucks to me. I'm sure there's other stuff I could harp on, but I think you get the point of what I'm getting at. It's an EA game so I'm not surprised by any of these issues. I will try this game again on it's full release, but for now it just feels too run of the mill for me to play again anytime soon.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: This is a weird one.This is mostly a solid Doom Eternal-ish indie shooter with varied and mostly great-to-look-at levels, mostly satisfying gunplay, and all that jazz.But it's just bogged down with design decisions that are just bizarre, man. And not the good kind of bizarre.What is this save system? Why are there survival horror save points in my fast-paced boomer-shooter? Why does the game autosave after an absolute non-issue like me pulling a lever, but not before the gоddamn boss fights and not at the start of the level? I HATE E2M5 with passion precisely because of this.Why is the main progression system almost entirely locked behind secrets? Why are some of those secrets platforming challenges?Why does a 6/6 on ammo counter means that I have 6 shells left? Why does the rocket launcher splash damage zone look way smaller than it actually is? Why do half the enemy attacks lack any visual feedback for damage taken? Why does the Gluon gun variant lack literally any impact whatsoever? Why can I just casually walk right past the pre-final boss gauntlet?All of this isn’t a big deal by itself, but man, this stuff adds up quick and makes this game feel mediocre as a result. If you're new to indie shooters, there are dozens of better ones out there. If you’ve already played them, you can still get some enjoyment out of this, I guess.6/10
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: It doesn't bring anything new to the table, but it's tightly made - and that's not a bad thing; a solidly made game doesn't need a gimmick to make itself stand out. All of the weapons (except the shotgun) feel good to use, the maps are mostly passable, and the game can look beautiful when it wants to. Particular props to the art direction of the enemies in the game, which are all distinct and give easy visual cues as to their purpose almost immediately.The only problem is that with the slight beefiness of some of the enemies, and the speed at which they move, the game starts to fall into Serious Sam Syndrome on occasion - falling into the "hold S and shoot type of gameplay, thanks to a lot of concentrated mobs that are hard to kill and which are chasing you at high speeds. This is only really a problem occasionally, in episode three specifically.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: The action is fast, the game is hard and the feeling is right, in fact it seems to be back for a few minutes to Duke Nukem 3D or Quake or similar games. I've tried other titles in the same genre (Hellbound, Project Warlock) and I didn't like them, at all. This one is actually fun, this one has actually a gameplay. It's more on the side of Ion Fury or Dusk. For this reason the vote is positive, despite some problems. Highly recommended if you like these old shooters.What are the problems? (as requested by the developers, the criticism is to improve the product)- Checkpoint saves. It's quite manageable, but it's there, and I don't think it can be fixed- Some opponents take too many hits to fall. Things like this should be limited to large spaces like arenas (Serious Sam style), but certainly not in narrow corridors or small rooms- In several moments I ran out of ammunition- Sometimes (like in E3M4 but not only) you are forced to throw yourself into a dangerous area where a lot of demons of different types (which would need different weapons) shoot and come at you, all together, with no possibility of shelterThere are of course some very positive things. For example the dual mode of some weapons (quickly changeable with a right click). It's a great thing, because it adds strategy: the powerful mode consumes more ammunition.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: This is the best of the boomer shooters to me. I own most of the ones that are out, like Dusk, Prodeus, Amid Evil, Project Warlock, HROT, and I forgot what else. I saw this and thought it had potential, but it is really the most enjoyable of the retro fps games I've played.I love that you have a katana that you can make into a spear and throw. It does a ton of damage and I regularly use it to 1 hit enemies. The bow is also fantastic, as well as the supershot gun. There is a dash ability, and it charges, and you can find items to make the recharge faster, or your shotgun stronger, hold more ammo, etc for all weapons.The music is pretty amazing too.Really surprised, I haven't heard of this and saw a couple of reviews, and just thought I would give it a try and I am glad I did.

_childDocuments_.review: Glad I got this game for only 1 USD on Fanatical because after 3 hours of playing it I was bored to death. This is probably the most cookie-cutter boomer shooter I've played. The best analogy I can come up with - Dread Templar is like "The Best of" compilation album of a mediocre tribute band. Nothing it does is particularly bad or wrong, but there is no original bone in it.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: Felt like leaving a review since this game's flying under a lot of people's radar and unjustifiably so. The recent full release was a great opportunity to revisit it after having played through the first 3 chapters about a year ago.There isn't much story and these kinds of games really don't need one. The ending's Tchernobog-esque where the big bad wants to siphon off your accumulated "dread force" only to, predictably, get annihilated instead.Speaking of Tchernobog, this game knows its ancestors and is ripe with homages to them. In fact, you'll be hard-pressed to find a single classic FPS that isn't referenced in one easter egg or another. Pretty cool.As for the gameplay, it feels great. Really responsive with a good selection of weapons (and upgrades) and good flow of combat. There's really nothing in particular I was missing. If I had to name one shortcoming, it'd be the OST. While the individual tracks are good, there's like only 1 track per chapter and it gets repetitive after a while. I'll chalk it down to this being a one-man project.All in all, this game does not have any major flaws but, on the flipside, doesn't have anything outstanding or memorable going for it either. Just solid all-around.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely nails that nostalgic 1999 vibe.The movement and shooting is pleasing, which is good because that's the majority of the gameplay.A lot of weapons to choose from, to the point that you can forget what you have.The weapon / character upgrade mechanic is simple enough without disrupting the pacing.Levels design is a hit or miss, but the soundtrack slaps so hard it's easy to overlook some of the less fun areas.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: I decided to give this game a shot despite the middling reviews. Sadly, they're right.A boomer shooter lives and dies by its gunplay, because that's all it has to offer. A boomer shooter without visceral and tight gunplay is like a pizza place that can't make a good pizza. You can be a hamburger place and make a mediocre pizza, and that'd be fine. But you are a pizza place, Dread Templar. The hit feel is simply not there in this game. So much so that the developers clearly felt the need to add hit markers. I can see why, because if not for the hit markers, I wouldn't be able to tell when I'm hitting an enemy and not. It's *that* bad.This may be mostly because of the gunplay but; killing most of the enemies is a chore rather than being satisfying (especially that one tanky *and* fast melee enemy). I'd describe them as "annoying" instead of being "challenging". The visuals aren't very impressive. The music is well composed, but still quite generic. Level design is "passable", though way too linear. (Come on boomer shooter devs... DOOM laid out the blueprint only.... literally 31 YEARS ago) Everything about the game is "just enough" or "mediocre" or "not enough", it's not impressive whatsoever, doesn't break any new ground. So I don't see why you would play this over any other boomer shooter on the market right now, of which there are many. Nothing about it stands out.Hopefully the developers learned a lot making this game and will use all of it in their next game. Best of luck for the next one, but sadly this isn't it, chief.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: While Dread Templar is a pretty good retro-inspired shooter and gets a lot right; from the guns to the story to the action, I feel the overall experience for me was weakened by the mis-use of the power that is John S. Weekley’s work. Can it be fixed in future updates? I don’t think so. Should the developers seriously consider a more adaptive music approach to the sequel; please, yes, please; the game was good, but not worth the literal headache after 16 hours of game play.The final outcome here; for me at least, is a game that has so much engaging action and interesting game play mechanics, but over the long run time falls short on longevity and consistency, with the noise turning a normal exploration for tokens into a frustrating speed run without breath or air. I shouldn’t crave the sense of relief I get at the end of the map, just to have a moment to collect myself in a brief instance of pace change, as the tracks change, sometimes, between maps.Give Dread Templar a try, but take some breaks, unless headaches are your thing. But also, if you miss this one, you’ll only regret that awesome weapon customization mechanic.

_childDocuments_.review: I was having a lot of fun with this game for the first 3/4, but stuff happened irl and I wasn't able to finish it. Finally I reinstalled the game and decided I'd just start a new playthrough, only to find that the gems you get for perks in game were completely absent from where they were supposed to be. What you're supposed to do before starting a new playthrough is click the setting the resets all blood gem locations, the only issue with doing that is that IT DOESN'T ACTUALLY RESET ANYTHING AT ALL. Furthermore, I've learned this has been a problem for multiple people dating back months ago and the dev still hasn't fixed it. It's a crying shame, because the game itself is fun and the music is amazing, but I can't recommend something that breaks new games.

_childDocuments_.review: A solid old-school shooter, with retro graphics, a fascinating background, creepy enemies, classic weapons, and a dynamic and fun gameplay, pumped by a powerful soundtrack. There are some interesting mechanics, like , but overall the game is rather similar to the classics of this genre, especially to the first Quake. As in all old shooters, you can carry all the weapons you want, your walking speed and agility are very high, and you can pick up health and armor. After a while it becomes a bit repetitive, but after all, this is the bane of all shooters. I recommend it if you like bathing into the blood and guts of your enemies while running around at superhuman speed in a desolate and nightmarish landscape. Can you ask any better?Cheers guys!

_childDocuments_.review: is a "fast-paced" retro style FPS, with a story that is quite simple. You are a Dread templar seeking revenge in Hell. The game really has problems keeping up with consistency.- Graphically the game is what you expect, it has that Quake-ish style to it.- Performance is smooth- Enjoyable soundtrack that matches the fast paced gameplay- Variety in enemies are pretty good- Boss fights are challenging and fun- Secrets to explore, and Side areas, which are actually not a bad idea in games like this.- Steam achievements- Maps look great and they are designed pretty well.- The combat is a mixed bag, sometimes it's awesome and then it just feels straight up garbage. It's weird.- Some audio sounds low quality- Hitbox issues, and there are a ton.- Some weird design choices, like dodging some enemies' attack is straight up impossible as they will hit you no matter what you do. I guess this forces you to use the bullet time mechanic every time these kinds of monsters get close to you.- Episode 3 so far is the worst designed episode in any boomer shooter I've played in a long time. The game is not yet finished completely, It's only halfway done and when the full version will be released. I'll give the game a rating. Right now, there are many many things the developers need to fix and overhaul. Especially the combat that cannot keep up consistently in my opinion or I've approached it very differently as they expected players would.Nonetheless, if the developers makes some changes to the combat, and enemies while keeping the maps challenging and fun, not frustrating, then the game could be a success.

_childDocuments_.review: Very promising game. Love the graphics and gameplay so far. I'm currently stuck on what I think is the last boss.Since this is an early access game, I guess you'd like some feedback, so here it goes:Please mute the music when the game is paused or minimized, and please make the music slow down a bit when the action stops. I like the heavy metal soundtrack, but it's a bit too strong when you're looking for secrets or just trying to find the way to go. The game works well on my ultra-wide monitor (32:9), but the ammo and HP in the corners is too far away to see on my monitor. Please keep HUD elements closer to the center.The secret platforming section with the circular saws and poison gas was a pain due to a lack of visibility - it's not clear which part of the pipes the gas comes from and how big their hitbox is, and the saws are completely flat so it's hard to judge how distant they are from you. Crouching feels a bit awkward. Maybe crouching should be just automatic when you approach a small hole? It doesn't seem to be useful for anything else - maybe it should have a second purpose?I think there should be a separate button for punching boxes/vases. Having to switch back to the katana is a pain, especially if I just threw it, and have to wait a few seconds to get it back.I'm guessing that the upgrades interface isn't finished. It's not very satisfying to upgrade your character. The menu needs more sound effects and shiny visual effects - it would be cool if you could see your character while you choose upgrades, and he holds the weapon your are currently modifying, for example.I also assume voice acting and story is still a work in progress - I would really love a little bit of cheesy spoken dialogue, like the game DUSK or something similar.Overall it's a very cool game and I'm looking forward to seeing it finished!

_childDocuments_.review: What I really want to rate this game is a Neutral. It's a solid 5 or 6 out of 10 for me, reason being that whilst it ticks all the " Modern FPS with a Retro Nod" boxes, it doesn't excel in anything and feels lacking in some core aspects. Combat wise, Gun design is ok, but the differentials in its utilities are not very prominent. I've reached E2M2 on the "hard difficulty equivalent" only really using pistols and shotguns. The only time I used any other weapon was when I was fighting a boss and ran out of ammo for those guns. The katanas are cool, but again, I have no reason to use them aside from when I've run out of bullets.Enemies are quite varied, and yet not varied enough. I approach most of them the same way, using the same weapon,  Strafe, double shot gun, strafe double shot gun. Occasionally switching to pistols to conserve ammo or to deal with enemies that are further away.  Last of all there's bullet time, which I also did not use at all aside from the tutorial. There was simply no challenge that seemed to require it and I tend to forget about it being there until i see the resources scattered around the map and go "ahhhh.. i really should use that more often".The upgrade system is cool, but it is locked between 2 levels of locks. Firstly you need to find resources to enable the upgrade slot, then you need to also look for the upgrades. I think given that finding the upgrades themselves are already a challenge, I see no reason for having slot unlocks linked to such a progression system. It punishes players who dont look for secrets, limiting their "fun". My last critique on the upgrade system is that the guns don't feel cool to use until further skills are unlocked, so the difficulty associated with actually getting to use them locks out the fun of the game from other players.Level design is servicable, with secrets scattered throughout. Nothing that really differenciates each encounter from the next. They aren't Duke Nukem or ION Fury levels of "cool secrets", but some are quite enjoyable to find.All in all, I think if you are an FPS fan, you might find something to enjoy here. I would definitely continue to play the game despite my criticisms of it. But if you are looking for a game to showcase what modern boomer shooters are amazingly capable of, unfortunately, I don't think this is the game to do that.** Review after additional 7 hours: The game definitely gets better midway through episode 2 in terms of enemy design and lay out. Im enjoying it much more now. I still feel the same in terms of how the guns feel, and how the progression system is set up. And for the game to pick up so long after E1M1, ultimately it is still difficult to recommend this game. If you enjoy boomer shooters, and enjoy looking for secrets, this is a good game, or else I'd probably suggest picking this game up discounted.

_childDocuments_.review: Dread Templar is a high quality old school ‘Boomershooter’ FPS that will likely split folks. It looks nice, it sounds nice, it plays nice and has a varied play style of play due to its upgrade system. It even has some imaginative environments and fun boss fights in the later half of the game! Unfortunately to get there you have to trawl through a couple of highly uninspired chapters that scream “generic” more than any other old school FPS that I’ve played in the past 5 years.I want to make one thing clear. Dread Templar is really good. If you are a hard-line boomshoot connoisseur, then you will absolutely devour ol’ Dreddy here to the same degree that e-girls create drama. If you were to break it down to its mechanical parts then it not only does everything right, but takes other concepts other modern boomshoots have used and refines them nicely. The act of pulling the trigger on a gun, with both the audio and visual feedback of firing is satisfying. Enemies die in spectacular ways and the gibs from their exploding bodies are some of the best I’ve seen. Exploration in the sprawling levels is rewarding. The movement is absolutely spot without snags that plague some other unity titles, and it straddles the balance between Quake’s simplicity and Doom Eternal’s chaotic meta. It is a title that not only nails mechanical reliability, but also expands on the basics that so many games have used until recently.Two elements about Dread Templar help it stand out (mechanically at least) come in it’s recharging meta and its upgrade system. While neither are strikingly original, they seem to be sublimely balanced.First is the way it treats its recharging resources. Aside from a slow charging dash (which I will add is quite well balanced: fast enough to charge as to not be forgotten as useless and slow enough to charge as to not be over spammed) there are the constantly recharging throwing spear, the arrows for the black bow and the charge-on-kill bullet time features. While I have noted some folks forget about these features, when used frequently they vary up the gameplay a lot. The dash and bullet time are useful for huge, difficult fights, while the throwing spear is a single shot, alt fire for your melee weapon that does high damage to multiple enemies. The bow finally is a 4 shot, long ranged sniping weapon with a tiny charge time. These two weapons help enormously not only with ammo efficiency but also act as great long distance tools. All these elements mean that even when the player may end up in situations where resources are limited there is always an option to use bar the basic melee weapon. Granted it is not 100% clear about this, and I can imagine a few folks not cottoning on to this and finding the game frustrating, once the player understands the meta it becomes a whole bunch of fun.Even with these rechargeable extras, as the game goes on the fights become increasingly difficult in the enemy attacks where the base weapons just won’t cut the mustard. Thankfully the upgrade system helps overcome this problem. Here player expression is fully realised, giving players the ability to enhance their abilities and weaponry to suit their playstyle. Do you like the black bow and you want to lean on it more? Enhance the number of arrows it has, enhance the damage and then make it so each successive arrow does more damage than the last. Like crowd control and weapon switching? Get the ice shotgun and then enhance the revolver so it does more damage to frozen enemies. Make dashing cool down faster, incoming damage less, increase bullet time, turn some guns into overpowered versions of themselves. It really does have a huge variation of styles that allows for any player to lean into whatever playstyle they prefer, and even if they don’t like their choices, they can be reset later. Unlike Forgive Me Father’s style of upgrades, which is peppered with useless junk that cannot be changed, here you can play around with enhanced shotgun damage or overpowered bullet time pistols and then, come the next upgrade station, you can switch things out to hellfire pistols or longer range shotgun blasts.After all that praise one would presume that Dread Templar would be amongst the pinnacles of the throwback shooter genre, rubbing shoulders with Ion Fury and Dusk, though here is the part of the review where the predictable “BUT” comes in.For all its mechanical fanciness Dread Templar falls short for the first two chapters. Here it is a matter of taste, but it is clear that there have been absolutely tons of boomshoots in the past few years and to stand out from the crowd you need to have some unique elements. As much as people can speak about “gameplay is the most important thing”, aesthetic is a major element in which people emotionally attach themselves with in media. 2022’s Fashion Police Squad for example was somewhat flimsy in places gameplay and level design wise, but won out with the over-the-top settings and charming settings.Dread Templar does not stand out. It is another game where you crawl through hell as a bad-ass dude out to kill all the zombie enemies hunting down Satan for vengeance, shooting double barrel shotguns while relatively cool heavy metal plays. For the average person who has not got the greatest attention span, you have played this before. You have played it many, many times before.This is worst in the first two chapters. Initially you will have not accumulated enough upgrades to make the weaponry interesting and, as such, everything seems to be so generic that it becomes predictable after a level or two. It is not bad, just bland. This is made considerably worse due to these chapters effectively remaining in the same setting and using the same music over and over. Differentiating E1M2 from E1M4? It is you fighting through crypts of zombies, just as E1M1 was, and E1M3 was, and most of E1M5 is all the while the same sounding Rob Zombiesque OST plays endlessly. I can see this easily putting folks off very quickly, playing for about 30 minutes and then just thinking “What is so special about this?” before casting it aside and then proclaiming the whole old school FPS genre has become stale.The most frustrating element is once you pass the second episode the settings really unfurl with their more wild concepts, such as deserts made from the sands of time collapsing in on themselves due to your actions, or fighting through a huge celestial library / castle place where it becomes clear that the worlds are stored in paintings. If the crypts were held back a world or two then the first impressions would have been much better, setting the player up with some cool upgrades to be able to carve through the predictable crypt levels to reduce the monotony, but as it is you need to play for at least an hour and a half before you start to get to the good stuff, and I cannot see too many folks to have that kind of patience.In summery, Dread Templar is a good game. A game I would advise to both the old school adherent and to people with the patience to cut through the opening levels. However if you are starting to have got your fill of these types of game and need a shakeup of the formula, Dread Templar is just too slow to get to the fun stuff and will no doubt bore you with its predictable opening chapters. A good buy then, but only for those who absolutely need more boomshoots in their life.

_childDocuments_.review: Embrace the Dread Force and Unleash HellDread Templar is a masterful blend of classic 90s shooter nostalgia and modern FPS elements, creating a heart-pounding and exhilarating experience that leaves players on the edge of their seats. From the moment you pick up the controller (mouse and keyboard), the game captivates you with its impeccable pacing, making it difficult to tear yourself away from the relentless action.One of the standout features of Dread Templar is its exceptional pacing. The game manages to strike a perfect balance between intense combat sequences and moments of respite, creating a dynamic flow that keeps players thoroughly engaged throughout the entire journey. You'll find yourself constantly on the move, strategising and adapting to the ever-changing challenges presented by the fiendish enemies. The difficulty level is expertly crafted, ensuring that as you progress, the challenges escalate proportionally. The game doesn't hold your hand, but it also doesn't feel unfair. Each encounter provides a learning opportunity, forcing you to refine your skills and tactics to survive the relentless onslaught. This finely-tuned difficulty curve keeps you motivated, as overcoming obstacles feels genuinely rewarding.Weapons play a pivotal role in any first-person shooter, and Dread Templar delivers in this aspect. The arsenal of weapons at your disposal feels incredibly responsive and satisfying to use. As you unlock and combine dozens of upgrades and skills, you'll find yourself mastering the art of destruction, turning your enemies into artistic displays of red-mist. Speaking of enemies, the monsters in Dread Templar are not to be taken lightly. They are cunning, ferocious, and relentless (especially those gun wielding zombie dudes), always ready to exploit any moment of weakness, where a momentary lapse in focus can lead to being swiftly overwhelmed, these typically manifest from situation where you are not paying attention to monsters further off in the distance(I am referring to those purple brain monsters who can mortar fire for days) or just bumb-rush you until die. The feeling of danger lurking around every corner keeps you constantly on your toes, adding an extra layer of excitement and challenge to the gameplay.Dread Templar doesn't just offer a high-octane experience; it takes it to a whole new level. The gameplay can escalate from 0 to 100 in a matter of seconds, immersing you in adrenaline-pumping battles and heart-stopping moments. It's an experience that will keep your heart racing, your hands sweaty, and your mind utterly absorbed in the chaos.Considering that Dread Templar was developed by a small indie company, it is nothing short of remarkable. The dedication and passion poured into this game are evident in every detail. From the polished mechanics to the captivating level design, it showcases the studio's talent and potential in the gaming industry.If you're a hardcore FPS enthusiast seeking an adrenaline-fuelled challenge, Dread Templar should undoubtedly be on your must-play list. Embrace the Dread Force, unleash your inner hellish fury, and embark on a journey of revenge that will leave you begging for more.PS: That side mission with the mining cart, that sucked.

_childDocuments_.review: Dread Templar is an old-school shooter elevated by an incredible soundtrack. The guns are largely staples of the genre, though the trap launcher and bow add some welcome wrinkles. From what I've played of the games 25 levels thus far, environments are interesting and varied and there are a plethora of enemy types. If you're a person who likes deep and involved stories, there isn't much of that here. There is narration between episodes, but I found this to be boring. The environmental storytelling is pretty solid though, and there are lots of secrets to find so it pays to search each level thoroughly. Overall, this is another boomer shooter with all of the trappings you'd expect. It's not going to revolutionize the genre, but it's a lot of fun and a welcome addition to any enthusiast's collection.
