_childDocuments_.review: Don't write Dread Templar off, like I did at first.It may look like "just another Quake-like", but it really nails the kind of action and level design I expect from a Quake-type game. Not to mention, this game manages to make good use of an upgrade system, which I find some games don't quite do well enough. Mix and match passive buffs and perks, as well as weapon upgrades, to your heart's content, as you acquire more throughout your time playing. Don't like your chosen batch of upgrades? No problem, just switch out what "runes" you find, mid-mission. Not even weapon alts are permanent, if you don't want to keep one equipped. This ties really, really well into the secret hunting. The more secrets you find, the more powerful you end up becoming, and the secret hunting, as well as the puzzling Super Secrets, are really satisfying and cleverly placed. I don't mean to draw too many comparisons to Quake, but it really does remind me of the best of Quake community maps, particularly Arcane Dimensions. And, unlike certain other recently released Quake-likes, the level design is FAR from bloated. Levels are really tight and well-paced, with a lot of verticality, nooks and crannies, and impressive views.My only gripes may be that the art direction causes a lot of environments to look... overly samey, like a lot of similar, very detailed texture work and colors. It gets a little mushy. Also, I don't care for the neon fuchsia atmosphere of the "hell" levels. It looks like a Tiktok influencer puked all over it. IDK, maybe they were going for a "color out of space" type look, but it doesn't work for me. The only other thing is, so far, the "story" is unironically edgy. Like, maybe it's just such good satire that I cannot tell whether the writing is being genuine or not, but the narration and origin of the titular Templar is a bit... corny. Its nothing terrible tho.Overall, I'd say this is an easy recommend if you want a fairly well designed Quake-adjacent experience. I keep finding myself being pushed (just on the normal skill as of now) to actually switch up my weapon use and, for once, use the bullet time at vital moments. And those upgrades to your arsenal/buffs are vital to improving, or even changing the experience. Talk about a rewarding time. I often find some games either have arsenals that don't really feel purposeful in their implementation, or the "oh so popular" bullet time ability is needlessly tacked on for some cool factor. But that is not the case here. I am far from dreading spending more time with this game, its just the kind of thing I love. Color me impressed.

_childDocuments_.review: Silver upgrades are flat enhancements like Damage, Rate of Fire, and Spare Ammo capacity.Gold upgrades are interesting enhancements that change how the weapon works.Pistols and SMGs have reload mechanics, but no other weapons have this except for the double-barrel shotgun with a gold upgrade.There are 3 ability icons: Melee Throw, Regen Bow Ammo, and Dash. To make better use of these, there should be an instant attack button for "Melee Throw" and for the Bow. Additionally, the number of arrows should be shown on the Bow's icon. The Bow regenerates its own ammo and has its own icon.The maps seem a bit too big and there is no map. The fear of missing any upgrades kills the flow of the game.Pistol/SMG ammo and shotgun ammo are clear, but the other ammo types are hard to understand. _childDocuments_.review: Dread Templar is what you get when you mix Quake 1 and Painkiller. But sadly it wasn't as enjoyable to me.Good looking and fun for the first 2 episodes, then the game becomes a gamble : if you haven't unlocked enough perks this far, you die. That simple.I played on Normal difficulty, it was pretty nice the first episode with the discovery of the arsenal and overall level design, the door unlocking routine etc.The second episode is leaning toward Doom Eternal mechanisms : you need specific weapons for specific situations. Thus making it more of a challenge. A bit harder, but still manageable and satisfying.After those, the game is throwing a ton of sh!t at you for the sake of it regardless of your stuff.I love games like Duke Nukem 3D and Brutal Doom. And whenever an indie gem shows up I feel the urge to take a bite.But maybe I am just too old for these "hardcore" fps. I am definetly too lazy to go any further at that point. The game is too demanding. Perhaps if I chose the easiest difficulty I'd say otherwise, but it's meant to be played the default way right ?Difficulty aside, Dread Templar may be better if :- it wasn't so perks-dependant because the enemies grow stronger the more you progress, and you must upgrade your character and items. Perks shouldn't be mandatory in games imo, especially when they are hidden.- it had a weapon wheel system to ease gun selection during critical action.- the "you are hit" feedback was more obvious. You don't always realize how low HP you are, cuz there is no hint except the little scream covered but music and sounds.- better ragdolls. The weapons have a nice vibe to them, but it flattens right away when enemies just drop down or explode. They don't fly and bounce, it's a shame. Ragdoll is the easiest reward in gunfights.On the positive side of things, I really like the aesthetic of the game. And the soundtracks is gorgeous !Didn't come across any bug neither, pretty clean job.Despite my bitter experience on the game and the fact I gave up on it, I want to give devs a chance and recommend it to others, should they be aware of what they step in : not a walk in the park.

For me it opened up somewhere around the end of the first and the start of the second playthrough; invest some time into exploring secrets and as the game progresses the runes start coming together, synergy cranks you damage output to eleven, new ways to deal with enemies come up, and finally you start to feel like an unstoppable dread force plowing through packs of monsters. greatly vary in visuals and presentation; first is kinda meh I guess, full of dilapidated ruins and withered vegetation, somewhat brownish; second is tombs and castles painted in blue and violet tones. Then come the icy expanses and frozen villages of the third episode, strangely reminiscent of Alice Madness Returns' underwater world. Fourth is abandoned desert settlements, and while I generally detest desert levels in games, in this case they were pretty good, and music easily makes it my favorite episode. Fifth, by way of music and you traversing backwards through rehashed pieces of earlier maps, is very Dusk-ish, not in a bad way; good episode, except for a couple fleshy levels which I really don't care for. are rather short, and that works to game's advantage; you are never really lost or looking for a way out, combat encounters are spaced out well with an occasional squad of mobs here and there to keep you on your toes. Ammunition is abundant if you are willing to look for efficient weapon combos to take monsters out; more is hidden away in secrets, if you're really hurting for ammo. are fun, sound meaty enough and look amazing (okay, shotgun is kinda bland and its banshee variant looks weird).  Golden runes, if you're willing to look for them, can turn some of them into completely different versions of themselves, making you adjust your strategies or synergize with other weapons: dual SMGs become monster-melting hail of death burning through your whole ammo supply in a couple second (frankly, they are a panic button of sorts), shotgun chills enemies and makes them open for double damage from Lethal-slotted revolver, rockets burst into forward cones of ice needles and so on. The most underwhelming weapon is the rocket launcher actually, with way less damage output than you would expect - on higher difficulties only the first-tier enemies can be killed with a single rocket (with 3 level damage rune at that), and while ammo supply is plenty, it just takes too long to kill anything as opposed to, say, split second combo of banshee+revolver, which takes down most enemies in one go. is good. It can get a bit repetitive in the first episode, especially if you're hunting for secrets for the first time, but later episodes have some beautiful pieces. This is the kind of soundtrack worth listening to even outside the game. Fits episode themes  nicely and helps further set distinctive mood for each level. are okay. Placement is usually logical, so you can usually tell that something's there if you look around a bit, although there are some brutally miniscule wall indentations and hard to discern texture misalignments (aggravated by the game being somewhat sloppy with texture alignment generally), but they are pretty few, most of them I got by sheer luck and from erc's guides. Secrets have runes, ammo and much needed health and armor - especially in Nightmare difficulty, which only has health packs in secrets, so it's worth it looking for them.Most of the levels have super secrets, which have an element of puzzle to them, and it's always fun discovering a piece and wondering where it should go. are few and mostly related to level geometry, a missing piece here and there; in a couple levels state of objects is not saved properly, so after loading a side area count resets to zero, or keys spawn again even if you opened the doors already. Nothing gamebreaking. There was only one time when I had to load after getting stuck in some dark hole in a broken down ship.All in all, after working my way from Hard to Nightmare+ in four consecutive playthroughs, I consider Dread Templar one of the high-tier fast-paced shooters, worth playing and replaying.

_childDocuments_.review: Wait until it's fully released. Right now there's 2 episodes, 10 levels total. Roughly 2 hours of playtime right now. If you care about finding secrets, you'll probably get more time out of it. Overall, the levels are a lot of fun. This game isn't as polished as something like Dusk, and the level design and loadout aren't quite as good, either. The trap shooter weapon in particular feels a bit out of place and not super useful. I like the rest of the guns, though.There's a foundation for a good game here. The level design is good and the enemy design is really cool. Unfortunately, right now there just isn't enough to it to justify a $15 price tag. Even the $12.74 sale price I paid for it seems kind of steep, considering you can beat it in a day or two.Also, the boss of episode 2 (what is currently the final boss) is brutal. Like, so annoyingly difficult that it's not fun. I'm not a fan of bosses that can kill you in one hit, especially when they also have moves that slow you down, thus making it a lot easier for that one hit kill to land. To top it off, he's just a giant bullet sponge. The "shoot at it until it dies" philosophy of retro FPS games works best when bosses don't take ages to kill. Granted, the final boss of Doom can be beat in 5 seconds. That's no good either, but it's better than what this game is doing. I spent about 30 minutes on that final boss before finally giving up.Anyways, the reason I'm not recommending this game is primarily because there just isn't enough content for it to be worth the asking price right now. And I'm salty about that boss. I would imagine that when the game is fully released and all 5 episodes are there, I'll give this game a positive review.

_childDocuments_.review: It's good. Nay, ace. No doubt about it. If it wasn't up against the stiff competition that is the years upon years of high quality 'boomer' shooters, this would be a completely unqualified early access recommendation. Ultrakill, Ion Fury, Post Void, Project Warlock 1 + II, Amid Evil, DUSK, HROT, Maximum Action, GTTOD, Prodeus, Cultic, etc - be they full games, early access, or just demos, the retro, 'boomer' shooter genre really is booming. I also cannot wait for the likes of Into the Pit, Fortune's Run, and Forgive Me Father.  I started up a playthrough on the hardest difficulty and finally got a handle on  getting through levels whilst taking minimal to no damage. It was a blast. The one thing Dread truly nails is superb action committed to dodgeable projectiles and no-hit runs. Presentation is gorgeous and refreshingly colourful. Golden upgrades transform a weapon such that you can carve out a unique playstyle. It takes a significant investment in the weapons to unlock the privilege after all, yet it also doesn't force you to commit to anything you've invested. Great stuff. I like the quick switch between similar weapons. For an amateur like me who can't do the fast weapon switch method used by speedrunners in Doom Eternal, RE: Village, etc, this really delivers the illusion that I can. The bullet time is a great ability given how finger-click fast the action is. Level navigation is ace and well paced with save points, even if it's not the most inspired level design in the world. It's all very readable and I enjoyed seeking out secrets (including references!). Action is silky smooth and gives great gory feedback. Certainly no complaints there. Dashing makes platforming much more interesting. There's some flirtation with more 'out there' enemies, weapons, and level design, but as it is I need a lot more like the electric trap launcher and the power fist. The soundtrack fits it like a glove. Bosses are a highlight, particularly the (current) final one wherein you have to be cognizant of aerial damage. Panic inducing, that one. Despite its excellent name and action, it lacks something definite to call its own other compared to its genre compatriots. Bullet time, a dash, and its upgrade system, sure, but elements like its power glove tease something more. This is a derivative and nostalgic genre by nature, but perhaps there's some way it can become more distinctive going forward., I feel the dash and the katana throw both need to disrupt the player flow less with their cooldowns. Dashing like a maniac is liable to get you killed anyway (I'd assume) and I can't see any reason why I can't switch back to my normal katanas right after a javelin throw. Creating these clamps on player power and killing momentum feels antithetical to the fun of the genre for me. It's hard to have bullet time and not be immediately compelled to slide and dive. Med kits on the hardest difficulty being reserved for secret areas is perhaps too brutal.  That seems unnecessary. Everything else feels pretty reasonable. Even committing to med kits as secrets feels okay given the game's focus on avoiding all or most damage. It's doable.

_childDocuments_.review: There's a lot of thoughts I have on this game, and if you had to ask me what my thoughts are for episode 1 and 2 I'd say the game is excellent. Dread Templar knows what it is, and what it sets out to do, but whilst progressing throughout the game past episode 2 there are cracks which start to form. Some levels do a bit of work stitching these cracks back together, and almost make you feel as though you're back in the first two episodes, but their appearance is few and far between. Whilst I know this sounds bleak to start with, I actually do recommend this game, but not by that much, as the game is just *fine*, and as I got further into the game I felt as though I had more of an obligation to complete it rather than wanting to complete it, and upon completing it I felt as though a curse had been lifted from upon me. There are DEFINITELY worse games you could spend your money on, especially if you want something which has a LOT of playtime for such a small price which even goes on sale for around $5.: 6.5/10Moving onwards from episodes 1 and 2 however, the game starts to take a turn that most other games in the "boomshoot/retro FPS" space don't, in that it actually starts to slowly become.. Worse? It's weird. Every single FPS I've played within the same genre space have only gotten BETTER as they've progressed, with Dusk almost blossoming into a work of art in some specific levels, Incision only ramping up from the beginning, and Cultic improving throughout. Dread Templar doesn't do this, and if I had to present a graph signifying my enjoyment of the game it'd look erratic. Overall, Dread Templar could've cut out about 70% of the levels from Episode 3 and 4 and ONLY kept the good levels and then the endings and it'd be a more compelling and interesting game than it currently is, as many of the levels feel just like an after thought. Episode 3 itself is a point of contention for me, as whilst the first two episodes featured enemies which rushed at you, Episode 3 feels almost like they tried to take the games combat flow into an entirely new direction, as if someone new was designing this episode. Episode 3 adds an enemy which is faster than you, and spawns in large groups to the point they feel almost as if they're the primary enemy in this episode, taking it from something where you're meant to rush into a group and take them out one by one, to a backpedaling simulator. Episode 3 is also where some levels almost begin to feel.. Incomplete? There's weird level geometry in many places, almost as if the design of the levels feels as though it was rushed, and this only more apparent as you progress further into episode 4, with there being weird pits you can fall into which don't equate to instant death, which could effectively soft-lock the player into a reset.Weapons in Dread Templar are both powerful and superfluous, with many of the counterparts of certain weapons just feeling lackluster as you get further into the game. Dread Templar's Bazooka ends up succumbing to this within episode 4, with it requiring an exorbitant amount of ammunition to be able to down certain enemies. On top of this, there is an upgrade tree which can alter your weapons, but many of the weapons don't get meaningful upgrades which make them worth using outside of very specific cases, and even if you do acquire these upgrades they require increased ammunition to use them which cuts into the reserves of the alternate weapon for that key which makes it feel as though it's almost not worth picking them up.Bosses are... Wtf are the bosses in this game? Easily some of the absolute worst bosses I've ever seen in an FPS, in terms of both mechanics and difficulty. NONE of them are hard whatsoever, as I beat all of them except the first boss in a single try on Hell Difficulty. Realistically these add nothing in terms of difficulty or complexity to the game, and whilst I understand they were likely added because they were meant to be the capstone for each episode, they could've been removed and killed in cutscenes and I wouldn't have felt as if the game was any better or worse.

_childDocuments_.review: I covered Dread Templar in an article, as well as many other games from Realms Deep 2021, which you can read and see screenshots from my website -  -_____________________________Dread Templar just released into Early Access, and have seen some more recent gameplay of it, I broke down and decided that I would go against my will of Early Access games, and bought it. I'm sure I'll regret it later when I'm unable to finish the full game till launch, but that's a problem I'm willing to deal with to give Dread Templar a try, as there isn't an up-to-date demo on Steam.The demo levels I played are here, but altered to flow better, and not have just one BIG map that I could get lost in. The path of the levels were simple, but offered some exploration and alternative paths to go. Secrets are plenty and range from easy to find to multi step puzzles to get the best secrets. What really helps Dread Templar is the inclusion of a metal soundtrack, which I say even rivals Doom 2016s soundtrack! Combined with the gothic ruins, monstrous creatures to kill, and powerful weapons with fast movement speed is the perfect combo for addictive gameplay! Oh and mix in some slow-mo as well! One nit pick I do want to say, not so much about the game, but about some people commenting about the game, is saying the movement system is better than Quake. Those people clearly never played Quake. Dread Templar lacks any form of bunny hopping or a way to increase your movement speed like you can in Quake. I tend to jump around or bunny hop out of habit in every FPS game, so I would have noticed if there was a way to move around faster, but there isn't other than the short dodge mechanic, which doesn't really make you "faster" in any sense.The weapon selection is pretty good and covers all the basics. Starting with your duel katanas that can then be combined to be a spear which kills most basic enemies in one shot. You also start with Duel pistols, and eventually you pick up Duel Uzi which share the same weapon slot, but can switch between on the fly by pressing the same weapon slot key. The same works with the shotgun and double barrel shotgun. You also have access to a magical bow that regenerates shots after a short time, a trap launcher which acts like your stun gun or trap layer, and your rocket launcher type weapon, with more to come later. On top of that, there is also an upgrade system! Each weapon type can have two basic emblems which do simple things like give more ammo or faster fire rate or recharge time or damage. You can also equip one legendary emblem which can drastically change your weapons, such as giving your pistols and Uzi no reloads, electrifying your katanas, pistols having infinite ammo during slow-mo, turning your shotgun into a sniper rifle, and that was just the few I found in the first episode! However, you can't just go and equip these right off the bat, you have to unlock the emblem slots with Blood shards, which you will find as you progress through the game and in it's many secret or the harder "side areas". This really makes you want to look through the maps and try to find everything you can.Now I only completed the first Episode and stopped. Not that I was bored, but because I needed to finish up some other games. Plus this would give me some time for the game to get some updates with more content and closer to the full release, then I can binge the whole game at once. I know that kind of goes against my logic of playing something through to completion before I review, but again, this game is in Early Access and not the full game. Things can and will change.Either way Dread Templar is great fun and I can't wait for the full release in the future!

_childDocuments_.review: If you're a fan of old-school first-person shooters with a modern twist, Dread Templar is a blast from the past that you shouldn't miss. The game masterfully captures the fast-paced, adrenaline-fueled action of classics like Doom and Quake, but adds enough unique elements to feel fresh and engaging.The gunplay is incredibly satisfying, with a wide array of weapons to experiment with—dual katanas and shotguns are personal favorites! The combat system is smooth and brutal, and the level design encourages exploration with secret areas, upgrades, and clever puzzles.The art style blends retro pixel aesthetics with modern lighting and effects, giving the game a gritty, old-school charm. Plus, the soundtrack absolutely slaps, though i'd definitely add a bit more variety of it.What really stands out, though, is the game's progression system. The Templar skill tree lets you customize your playstyle, unlocking abilities and perks that make combat even more fun. You get to approach battles the way you want, whether that's close-quarters carnage or long-range destruction.If you are a masochist, go ahead and play on the maximum difficulty since it's just painfully hard. If you’re a sucker for fast-paced, blood-soaked shooter action with a hint of nostalgia, Dread Templar hits all the right notes. It's a love letter to the '90s FPS era, with modern sensibilities that make it more than just a tribute.

_childDocuments_.review: Among modern FPS titles that are deliberately classic "boomer shooters", Dread Templar is the most mediocre and bland game I've ever played, and honestly I don't know how I feel about this one, on paper, I should have enjoyed it since I enjoy "boomer shooters", but in practice I was left dissatisfied and frustrated, and by hour 5 or so I just wanted it to end already.For me, the main downside is the AI behavior, AI spawn system, upgrade/rune system which falls flat and to a lesser extend, the lack of sound feedback and cues from enemies & the environment.Cons:- Enemy design is just mediocre and cheap, as soon as enemies spot you, they just charge at you or spam projectiles mindlessly, and that is it, that is the only behavior of enemies, even 20+ years old games have better enemy design and AI behavior.- Enemies are extremely fast and spammy, imagine 10s of them spawning right in front of you, spamming projectiles while the rest rush on you.- Most weapons feel underpowered and require you to use runes to make them perform okay, and even then most of the runes felt underperforming or not worth using at all. - Many runes are locked behind secret areas.- Rune descriptions are vague and don't mention all the details completely (have to look for guides to completely understand the details).- Player projectiles getting stuck in level geometry, walls, ground, etc.- Enemy projectiles sometimes going through walls.- Lack of sound feedback from enemies and some of the environment.,- Lack of ambient & environment sounds, they're extremely on short loop.- Music is extremely repetitive and plays in short loop, (had to mute it after 30 mins).Pros:+ Optimization and smoothness across the levels is the only positive thing I have to say about this game, it plays very smoothly.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: I was excited to give this one a go. As someone who grew up with Doom on my old 486, this had my interest peaked. I grabbed it on sale for $5 US and man am I glad I got it for that price.I figured just do a normal run to get familiar with things before diving into max difficulty, but omfg I am so burnt out on this. The big problem are the horde sizes. I'm not looking for my hand to be held on a boomer shooter, but sometimes there's so many enemies at once that missions in episode two and beyond just feel far more burdening than they ever need to be. Twenty-three hours in doing campaign, side quests, and hunting for secrets and I'm genuinely exhausted to the point that if I finish E5M2, let alone the campaign, it's because I forced myself to.And I'm fine with that. It's a decent game that is just incredibly unbalanced, and I definitely got my ten bucks worth. Had I paid full price I'd be a little more pissed, honestly. If you grab it on sale for a couple dollars, give it a shot. I can't suggest it off my experience (with the game and boomer shooters overall in my existence), but if you enjoy a struggle (and not in a Dark Souls way) maybe you'll find more to enjoy here than I did.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: Every enemy aggros and attacks within a millisecond of seeing you. Ranged enemies will pre-fire wallhack you when you try to peak out to take shots. Imagine having to dodge an attack from every ranged enemy before you can kill them. Way too many enemies spawn from monster closets or just pop out of the ground right by you and instantly attack.After dealing with that you spend the next 20+ minutes running around an empty level looking for obscure secrets that you need to power your character up.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: I want to like this game, but everything about it is kind of boring. It checks all the boxes of a boomer shooter in the most rote, by the numbers way. You have a Mick Gordon-esque soundtrack, that frankly isn't very good. All the boomer shooter weapons are there, but none of them feel particularly good to use or have any interesting gimmicks--from the hour or so I played I didn't see any gimmicks. The levels go for that classic boomer shooter design emulating the best stuff from Doom, Quake, and Levelord, but the exploration is unrewarding.The game has a good look, but other than that I don't have anything positive to say about it. It isn't necessarily bad, it's just kind of boring and generic, which is kind of the name of the way for boomer shooters. It's hard to recommend this when there are other games of the genre that have come out and done it better in recent years. If you're desperate for another boomer shooter and have played most/all of the others out there, maybe give this a look, but don't expect it to be your favorite.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: Dread Templar does everything right and rarely falters in any of its facets. Gameplay is as tight as you should expect from a game of its kin. Move fast, dash, slow down time and combine your katanas into an unstoppable spear of death on your way to victory.Weapons pack a wallop just as a good arsenal would. You got your standard accoutrement of armament ranging from your dual pistols and SMGs, shotguns in both single and double barrel flavours to your long range Bow and Arrow (with an infinitely refilling quiver on a cooldown), angry Hell Rocket Launcher and Revolver and - Dread Templar's BFG - the Infernal Fist that erases everything in its path; disappointment is not a word in this game's dictionary.Graphics are instantly reminiscent of Quake with its crunchy 3D models and textures and brown colour palette in the first Episode, cosmic green skyboxes with a world drenched in purple haze and neon pink ooze in the second Episode - and its incredible closer - and a massive library occupied by phantom clerics wherein - upon interacting with a painting Mario 64-style - it leads to frozen scapes and shipwrecks with ghostly crew still on board in Episode 3.Clever level design with passages and pathways that lead you right where you need to go after you flick a switch or grab a key and side areas that are riddled with enemies and hazards but reward you with much-needed upgrades, though I got lost but those occurences were few and far between.Oh yeah, upgrades. The game has an upgrade system that thankfully does not adhere to the derivative tree scheme and instead opts to ask you to gather Emblems and Blood Gems in order to unlock upgrade slots for your weapons or your person (using Blood Gems) and equipping said Emblems. Be sure to find every secret you can because your benefit will go beyond the simple armour or ammo cache.Music is majestically metal and legitimately the best soundtrack I've heard in a good while courtesy of the much underappreciated PRIMEVAL - who should receive as much recognition as Hulshult does. If you don't know who he is, he has composed the soundtracks to many Doom mods including the immensely enjoyable Ashes 2063 and Ashes Afterglow. I was very impressed with how good performance was, considering how often my laptop gets brought to its knees by even the least graphically potent games. However, bullet time did consistently tank my performance so that remains to be addressed.At the time of writing, there are two complete Episodes with three boss fights, with a third currently in the works. The game is planned to ship with five Episodes. The first level of the third Episode has been released and it's stunning. I was able to finish my first playthrough on Normal difficulty in a little over three and a half hours with some light secret searching. I spent another hour replaying levels to unlock achievements I had left and obtain some upgrades. I saw nearly everything in about five hours.Overall, Dread Templar scratched ever itch I have in a boomer shooter and it's one that you should not skip if you fancy yourself a good Retro FPS. It's a very polished and competent shooter that has barely any bugs even in Early Access and will seldom leave you bemused. The future is looking bright for 1C and T19 and I'm very excited to play every subsequent content update.

_childDocuments_.review: Having watched the trailers on the steam page, I can say that Dread Templar plays significantly better than I expected it to. It lacks in a lot of places and is not a very polished game, but the OST is a head-banger and the movement is fast and fluid, it has that reload/recoil cancelling weapon switching from doom eternal as well as an upgrade/perk system. Solid 7, maybe 7.5 overall. Definitely get this game if you like secret hunting in old FPS'es, as there is a super secret puzzle in every map and a campaign-wide ultra secret as well.

_childDocuments_.review: Another great Quake and DOOM Eternal inspired FPS with solid shooting/weapon swap mechanics.Great amount of content for the price.Wish the progression was faster, the game could use an active ammo management system, audio/music could be better, the secrets should've been handled in a better way; almost all of them are just invisible doors.But issues aside, the game is great just because of the great combat. Much better than the more generic boomer shooters that over saturate the genre.8.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: A mid game, not bad, but still mid.A very old design philosophy, simple enemy behavior (mostly charging at the player) and a focus on secret hunting (wall licking)The repetitive music doesn't help either.Buy on heavy discount only AFTER playing other, better boomer shooters like Turbo Overkill or Dusk and want to turn off your brain.

_childDocuments_.review: Boring, don't bother.Nothing about this game is interesting or original. Almost all of the levels are visually uninteresting, expect for a couple exceptions.Most engagements start by going into a room or around a bend and getting jumped, then kiting them back around to kill them, just playing round corners; because the AI is super basic. Every enemy aggros instantly, and either runs directly at you, or shoots you as soon as you show your face. If you try to play more aggressive, you just get swarmed with enemies and projectiles, then die, because the dash is on a three second cooldown and there are no other movement options.All of the weapons seemed designed around what this type of game SHOULD have, without any thought for why that's the case. Most weapons have one or two others that do what they do but just better. And when you upgrade them, you can turn most weapons into generalists, so you only have to switch when you run out of ammo.Speaking of upgrades, they currency to get them is only in special secret rooms, but are required to have any fun in the latter third of the game, as every enemy becomes a bullet sponge, or just straight up immune to certain weapons. (Why is the horde enemy immune to rockets? This is not fun.) So you better hope you were getting those early onAlso the bullet-time mechanic. Your meter lasts for about 5 seconds, and refills are sparse. What is the point of this mechanic if you don't want the player to use it?What is the actual core of this game? This is a patchwork of borrowed ideas and sloppy execution that seems to have to underlying spark of creativity or drive.A few more things real quick:- The story segments are just cringe, and the voice acting is bad.- The movement and jumping feel loose and unrefined.- Bad sound design across the board (I've never heard a more flaccid shotgun in my life)- Every retro filter looks like it's bad on purpose. Why even include them?- I've played this for 11 hoursSome good things about the game, the first area is pretty good and the save system is a good idea.Bleh
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: Dread Templar is a beautiful looking game, I love how the weapons look, how the enemies are designed, the levels look great and there are cool visual effects used everywhere such as waterfalls of sand and strong winds and burning buildings and dense fog and so on. Weapons feel meaty and powerful to use. Soundtrack is solid. Some optional side arenas bring a nice change of pace to the combat based levels. I loved the one where you had to run uphill and dodge giant boulders rolling down. But...   Art alone is not enough to carry a game. The movement feels terrible. There is no acceleration/deceleration curve, you just stop instantly midair when letting go of the arrow keys. Crouching just snaps your camera up/down with zero smoothing. Then there is a slow motion mode that I forgot even exists after the tutorial. Your dash move is always on cooldown when you need it. There is a reason all the platformer games reset your dash cooldown once you land on solid ground instead of putting it on a timer. You can upgrade it but it barely helps.   Speaking of the upgrade system, it's terrible. First you have to find a type of currency on the levels to purchase upgrade slots and then you have to find the upgrade items. The upgrade items are everywhere but the currency is insanely hidden and limited that I only had half the slots unlocked by the end of the game. You end up with tons of upgrades but nowhere to use them. This should be the other way around, everyone should get the slots but only the serious explorers get to choose between the items to put in the slots.   Combat is pretty awful too, you spend half of it reloading because that's fun in a boomer shooter. Enemies have infinite range so they attack you from the other end of the map. The particle effects from enemy attacks stick around for far too long making you wait before you can pass through and engage in combat. A bunch of enemies just jump/charge inside you from behind corners making you get stuck inside their collision, hard to tell if it's by design or a bug? Either way it feels horrible. After combat arenas you'd expect to find healing items and ammo to restock but half the time they just aren't there so you have to be super conservative with your approaches to everything. Good way to kill the pace. Not much fun though. This would be fine if you could quick save/load but that is not the case here, all you have are rare checkpoints and manual save points scattered on the map.    Level design? Invisible walls everywhere. Instakill death pits everywhere. See that ledge over there that looks like leads to a secret area? You jump to it, only to be stopped by an invisible wall and fall to your death. Oh look, a cave entrance? Looks promising. Nah, it's just a fake blocked by an invisible wall. Reward exploration? Nope.   Then we have these annoying cutscenes that you get after pressing buttons that open doors. Very janky and take you out of the game for no reason. I'm not even going to talk about the mediocre story/voice acted cutscenes between the levels...   One final thing, the music goes on full blast 24/7 no matter what is happening on the screen. Are you exploring or fighting? Safe zone or combat zone? Boss fight or trash mobs? Does not matter. Music just does not care or react to anything.

_childDocuments_.review: I am in genuine awe as to what lays before me.Who in their right mind thought it would be a good idea to hide the game’s most interesting and useful upgrades (the one half decent innovation this game has) behind the monotony of scouring its insipid levels for obtuse “super secrets”? Imagine, in a genre all about fast, frenetic action, putting such emphasis on one its most riveting aspects, secret hunting! Yes! The mechanic that is often there to reward observant players with EXTRA (i.e ADDITIONAL) pick ups or easter eggs, is now mandatory! That is of course, unless you’re fine with just playing a mediocre boomer shooter without engaging with its central upgrade mechanic.In addition, these “super secrets” range from obtuse, to stupidly simple. This begs the question, what the hell is even the point? It wouldn’t be such a problem if the game didn’t constantly make it feel as though you’re missing out by not slogging through its levels mashing the use key on every pixel or deciphering poorly worded text box hints.This is only exacerbated by the fact that by embarking on your search for these “super secrets” you are also unwittingly signing up to participate in what I can only assume is part of a new wave MK Ultra experiment. While you slog through these levels searching for these precious upgrades, you will be tortured by what is one of the most appalling soundtracks I’ve had the misfortune of listening to. Generic, flaccid approximations of “metal” infused with, for some ungodly reason, sea shanties and what I swear are samples of “Flight of The Sugar Plum Fairy.” This infernal mix will lay siege to your eardrums with a ceaseless one minute loop on replay from the moment you enter a level until the moment you leave.The kicker here is that the few moments of mercy this game allows you when it finally shuts up after a boss fight and allows it’s ambient sounds to kick in, are actually somewhat atmospheric and pleasant.The upgrade system the game totes and some of its reviewers laud, is one of the only things that it does decently. Even then, it is given far too much credit. I’ve seen mentions of “builds” and i cannot think of a more hilarious way to describe what is an incredibly  bare bones system. You are quite literally slotting in ammo and fire rate upgrades of varying levels. These upgrades seem to stack, which does sort of allow you to equip two fire rate upgrades, for example, which allows you some variety. Thing is, I’m not even entirely certain this works. I’m only hoping it does, because it’s the only semblance of a “build” I can manage. It’s not like the game provides any observable numbers or stats to help fine tune a “build.” As a matter of fact, the game sometimes doesn’t even explain what the hell some upgrades do. What on earth do you mean I’m “luckier” ? Are critical hits a thing? Are critical misses a thing? Is that why some of my shots seem to disappear into the void? Is there a chance the game will uninstall itself and load a good game? This luck upgrade is a GOLD rune by the way, implying it’s one of the big, game changing, must have upgrades.Some of the gold runes do alter your weapons enough to where it’s a bit cool. Pistols turn into infernal pistols with slower ROF and higher damage (wahoo) and your katana become electrified and can stun surrounding enemies for the nano second it takes you to swap to a weapon that doesn’t blow.The only compliment I have for Dread Templar is that the gameplay itself isn’t terrible. It’s decent. It’s a stock standard boomer shooter with an alright bullet time mechanic. It has mediocre enemies, the grand majority of which bum rush you and perform Old School Runescape-esque animations. Other enemies include the average summoner enemy and the “pepper you  from afar” variety. There are some palette swaps introduced as you progress.I can sum up Dread Templar with my very own #dreadtemplarmoment which was solving one of its super secrets and arriving at an amazingly accurate recreation of the Quake difficulty selection room. I was then immediately reminded that I could be playing a much better game.Dreadful indeed.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: It's pretty rough around the edges, but there's a lot of fun to be had for retro-shooter fans! The most important thing I can tell you is that Dread Templar starts off rather weak, and then builds up substantially as you get further. Except for that last episode, that one is a bit of a rush to the end, but it's alright. That penultimate episode is an absolute gauntlet though and I think that's where Dread Templar peaked for me.Once you get enough runes to upgrade your arsenal in various ways, the game becomes a lot of fun. There's a lot of cool upgrades and you can really hone your weapons to how you want to use them. There are some overpowered ones that carried me through the entire game once I've got them though.The game is a tad janky, the animations are very stiff, voice acting isn't good, story.. what story? (no idea what's going on lol), sound effects are fine in general I guess. Music is good, there's definitely some great tracks, it's a bit of a shame that some are repeated for multiple levels, it's one of the quirks I always enjoyed about retro fps's - each level having its own destinct music and theme, but I suppose there simply wasn't the time or budget.Where it lacks in music variety it definitely makes up for in the environment. The level design is all around great and varied, you'll travel through dungeons, cathedrals, hellscapes, mountains or even an egyptian desert. Arsenal is also all-around great, I especially enjoy the Black Bow and some of the hellish variants you can upgrade your basic weapons into. The only weapons I didn't really use is the Katanas and the Trap Launcher. The RPG also kinda fell off for me towards the end, but I can assure you the game is perfectly beatable even when you don't use everything. I didn't even touch the bullet-time mechanic the entire game, as I personally don't find those very fun, but from what I could tell, it seemed to be executed fine in this game.This game will also definitely click for secret and easter eggs hunters - there's a *lot* of those in Dread Templar.------Overall, game's fun, it has its jank, but the core aspects that are fundamental for a retro fps are there, and they're done well. If the animations will ever get improved, then this game would really be elevated to an 8-9/10. For now I'd say it's just about above average. It's not anything we haven't seen before, but it's mostly well made and fun as you get further and further.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: Dread Templar's not , but it isn't good either. There's just too much thrown together in regards to the player's arsenal and skills that combat becomes messy, and it falls apart when combined with the poor enemy and encounter design.There are twelve total weapons, with ten of them available by the start of Chapter 3 (of 5). Add the rune system on top of that, which allows you to modify each weapon or pair of weapons, and you've got a lot of customization. Except it doesn't do much for you. With such a large weapon pool, weapons are bound to overlap in their effectiveness; the Black Bow, Inferno Rocket, and Inferno Revolver all serve the same purpose— hit things from afar. The SMGs, Shotgun, and Super Shotgun are equally useful in close combat, which makes the rune system partially obsolete, as you really have more than enough at your disposal for most encounters. Having too many options isn't an entirely bad thing even if it may make some of the runes obsolete, as long as the encounters are fun. However, on the higher difficulties, you're stuck to either corner peaking far distance enemies or back-peddling close-ranged enemies. This isn't an issue in the first two acts of the game, but it becomes very prevalent in the last three. The health and hitboxes of enemies feel a little off as well, with every flying enemy requiring two shots from the Black Bow, Inferno Rocket, or Inferno Revolver, no matter which runes I use. Head shots, which you can perform with the Black Bow and the Inferno Revolver, don't exist for most enemies, and for large enemies, are either very easy to hit, or very difficult to hit which makes enemies feel like bullet sponges. Secrets are a huge part of Dread Templar and the normal secrets are obtuse at times, too often hidden behind walls with misaligned textures, but the super secrets, hidden in most levels, are way too hidden for the average player. I think I found two or three in my first playthrough while actively searching for them, and with the super secrets rewarding golden runes, it feels like a shame to miss out on the gameplay altering runes. Blood gems, which are used to unlock the slots for runes, are tied to these secrets, so if you aren't an avid secret hunter, you'll end up having a worse experience.The rune system, which is initially interesting, is too dull the majority of the time. There are two types of runes: silver runes, which might increase ammo or damage, and golden runes, which alter how the gun actually feels. Silver runes are useless progression. Wasting blood gems to get to the golden rune slots feels bad because getting 60 more SMG ammo doesn't change the way the game is played. This is only exacerbated with the Inferno Weapons that require more blood gems than normal weapons, and it practically requires you to find the secrets to use the golden runes.Bosses are more of a footnote than anything else, as they're all very easy to beat with circle-strafing. Bullet time feels tacked on as you're not really encouraged to stay in the heat of combat. Music never ends and can feel grating after a while, especially if you're just looking for secrets after clearing a level of enemies.Dread Templar has a lot of minor issues that drag it down, which is a shame, because it's first two chapters, while reminiscent of older shooters, feel really good to play and have solid weapon progression.

_childDocuments_.review: I initially did not recommend this game.  I've left my original review down below.  I opted to give this game another chance and the gameplay was good enough to change my mind, but consider this a thumbs up with a massive asterisks.   However, my initial sentiments were spot on.  This game locks power progression behind secrets, which are often obtuse.  I do not enjoy secret hunting, and ultimately used a guide to find the ones in episode 1-3, giving up around episode 4.  I do believe the time spent was worth it as I had additional upgrade points I would not have had otherwise.  The problem was this was work, not fun.  Really big miss from the developer.  If you are willing to put up with some BS, as well as an incredibly generic episode 1, this game is fun enough.  I played it through on hard.  I did have fun.  Fun that was unnecessarily hampered though.  If the developers make a sequel I would simply suggest remove the secretgating and make more of the same, and you'll have innovated enough.  Original Review:Upgrade system is gatekept by secrets.  I do not enjoy secret hunting, thus I am locked from the best part of the game.  I am moving on.

_childDocuments_.review: Generally when you start up a game, it's like planting a seed. You start with something simple(or at least simpler) and then branch out into something more complex. From the start, the mechanics hint at what's going to come, what interesting tools you'll have and what interesting enemies you'll face, what cool potential areas you can run into, the first steps of the plot suggest that some very cool stuff is going to happen later.After half an hour of Dread Templar, what I mostly feel is that I've already seen all the game has to offer, nothing about it seems to suggest that it's ever going to get more complex in any real sense. I run down corridors, enemies go "blargh!" I back off, shoot them while they go blargh and fail to kill me, run forwards again. The art design makes the original Quake's brown tech corridors look exciting. The weapons are generic FPS fare bland enough to make me miss Doom's loadout. As far as I can tell there isn't even locational damage or anything of the sort to spice up combat even slightly.Other Retro shooters, like DUSK and Cultic, have engaged in some of the same heavy metal horror aesthetics, but they brought a lot more of their own to the playing table, their weapons were more satisfying, enemies more interesting and levels more fun. The few times I felt some excitement when playing Dread Templar was when there were actual open areas where the Doomguy levels of fast movement were actually part of the gameplay. Every interior area is just completely wasted.There's some sort of vestigial RPG/upgrade system, but as far as I experienced it, it just gave me extremely vague damage bonuses. The level design also suffers a lot from relapsing into unreality. I understand that this is probably an intentional retro move, but it robs the game of a lot of interest. Most other shooters have areas that feel like real places in some sense, they have a believable size, shape, structure, rooms have purposes other than being brown and filled with gross water. It helps the gameplay because you can predict something about the shapes and sizes, you can perhaps intuit that between room 1 and 2 there ought to be another, secret room or that you can drop down from room 4 to reach room 3 that you had to bypass earlier.That sort of stuff makes secret-hunting fun. It makes you use your brain to find secrets, Dread Templar's secrets are just "here's a brown hole on a brown wall reached by jumping on a brown ledge." There is no satisfaction to finding them, especially since they seem to generally just contain supremely generic pickups.The soundtrack is pretty good, though. I enjoyed listening to it even if nothing else about the experience was particularly motivating.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: So much fun. Weapons & upgrade system work well together. Level design and sound is awesome. A lot of secrets and super secrets. Especially the super secrets and the 1 mega secret are so fun to discover/hunt. So many references to classic games and  movies. That last boss after using the book, I just couldn't believe it. The medieval and desert episodes reminded me a lot of Serious Sam, which is of course a good thing. Guardian mode is also very playable. No crashes so far. Imo a steal for that price. _childDocuments_.review: ★★★✰✰ - Alright 8 Hours Normal	- Boomer Shooter. Similar to Doom Eternal.  Low max ammo causes you to switch between weapons often.	- Minimal. Eyerollingly Edgy. Not to be paid attention to.	- 1990's Retro PC\PS1 Graphics.	- Varied. Great use of Colour. _childDocuments_.review: Great shooter with satisfying gameplay. The level design starts a little basic but gets progressively better as the game goes on (EP 4 being the highlight for me). Levels are full of secrets and references to other games and movies. Some secrets are fairly basic (open the wall to reveal hidden supplies) and some are super secrets that require you to pay attention to clues around the level and often have multiple steps to complete. Finding secrets is highly recommended since they hide runes witch  you need to upgrade your weapons. This game is clearly a labor of love and hopefully a start of more good things to come from the developer.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: A shockingly good boomer shooter considering, i bought this in early access on a whim and didn't expect much more than basic arena action. Dread Templar is fantastic in exploration and level design, finding runes that drastically change the look and feel of your weapons, solving puzzles to super secrets that are both satisfying and rewarding, and the levels themselves are just fun to roam around in. Combat is basic, shoot enemies until they explode into gibs or ragdoll to the ground, nothing extraordinary but the guns feel good, sound ok, and enemies are the right amount of annoying to not push you over board. A criminally underrated gem in the genre, and 100% worth the $20.

_childDocuments_.review: I'M ONLY RECOMMENDING THIS GAME BECAUSE I BELIEVE IT IS A PRODUCT WORTH INVESTING IN.Otherwise i don't think i could recommend this game in its current state. It's fun, fast paced and stylish but has many many flaws. From what I've seen of the game going from open beta to early access the team behind it are working hard and trying to make the best product they can, that's why i think its worth buying the game to support the devs.The things i enjoyed:-Gunplay is nice and responsive-Wide array of weapons to choose from and have fun with-Really good art-style-Interesting and varied levelsI think the thing this game has going for it the most is the really fun gunplay, its super satisfying to pop an enemy with a shotgun blast or lay into a big enemy with loads of uzi shots.The downsides of this game:-2 hours of gameplay for $20aud. (going to be fixed when out of EA)-No option for newgame+, i found this really odd considering that half the stuff i was unlocking for my weapons wouldn't be able to be equipped unless i replayed the campaign twice.-Really annoying final boss. (i understand that a final boss should be difficult but some of the ♥♥♥♥ it throws at you is just cheesy)-Personally i found it hard to manage all the weapons i had, they're all fun and varied but swapping to the right one in the middle of combat i found tough.-The bullet time may as well not be in the game, for how long it takes to charge to full and how little you get to use it when you pop it... there's no point even having it in the game. Needs a big buff.-Easy to get lost if you don't remember the map very well, a map screen would be a nice addition.-It's so hard to tell when you've been hit by an enemy, especially in the final boss fight. Without glancing at my health-bar i wouldn't be able to tell how low or high on HP i am.There's probably more but my short term memory is so bad i can't think of any.The cons far outweigh the pros, but from what i can tell it's definitely a game thats going to get much better with time and love from both the devs and the community playing it. Honestly in it's state rn i'd play it over and over if they added newgame+... thats all i really want, everything else is meh but still a downside.TL;DRno newgame+, game short rn, worth buying to support devs otherwise not worth $20.

_childDocuments_.review: Dread Templar perhaps most resembles the Quake games.It's a solid FPS, with a dash & bullet time.There will be plenty of moments where you will enter a room and die (or lose most of your health) almost instantly because you had the wrong gun out for the situation, or encountered one of those flying hitscan enemies that you couldn't have known was there, or got bum rushed by something nasty.  In other words; unless you have the reactions of Neo from the Matrix, you are going to have a fair few unforseeable deaths, and can do better the next time knowing what is around that corner.  Fortunately checkpoints are pretty frequent, and you aren't heavily punished, which makes this entirely bearable to me.The game lets you augment your weapons, though i found myself just adding basic + damage +ammunition type stuff, and it wasn't until about 3/4 through the game that I got to really play with the cool upgrades that would change how the guns function.  Levels have plenty of secrets in them, some of which are cumulative, as in: you find might find 3 secret items on a level which can be used somewhere to uncover a bigger secret, or lead you to a secret level.  Some secrets will reward you with parts you can use to upgrade your weapons, so there is quite an incentive to try and find them unlike most other FPS's.In terms of polish;  I encountered a crash a couple of times in the same place.  The game has its fair share of invisible walls/boundaries.  It seems like they didn't polish up the later episodes much at all when it came to these, which really put a dent in the exploration, it in fact discouraged me from looking for sneaky ledge jumps i might be able to do to track down secrets, because i expected to smack my face into an invisible wall and plummet to my death.Music is a mixed bag.  On the one hand, the tracks are great, mostly a mix of slow thrashy/industrial metal and dance techno.  On the other, well hearing the same track for 90 minutes, no matter how good it is can get a bit too much.  The game needs more tracks!If you don't go in expecting anything groundbreaking, and were happy with the level design in games like the Quake series, you should have a good time.  The greater rewards for finding secrets is something I want to see in more FPS games.  Dread Templar is one of the better retro FPS's to come out and for me a solid 8/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: It's ok in general, but each episode after the second feels a bit less polished than the previous. "Dread Templar" incorporates a lot of things that could have been done better: enemies that are a tad too spongy, invisible walls, instantly killing falls, some of which are not properly indicated, and so on..
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: In the - still rolling - wave of throwback-shooters, this one has its spot not far from the crown. Fast, gory, fun. Yes, the look is OG Quake-y, if that rubs you the wrong way, better stay away. If you don't mind that or even - like me - appreciate it, you're in for quite the treat. From what is on display so far - this is still early access mind you - there's little to complain and a lot to love.Weapons are mostly variations of your standard FPS-arsenal, but they all look and sound just the way you want it (the shotty feels good, and if you nail that, you're a winner in my book), the enemies are diverse and creative, the level design is intricate enough to not be boring but not so much as to confuse the player too much.Apart from your regular rootie-tootie point-and-shooties you're equipped with three timed abilities, a dash - which is solid, a katana-throw - which is fun when I remember that I have it, and bullet-time - which I somehow never use. It's not bad, it's just that I never feel the need for it and eventually forget about it.Saving your game is done at fixed savepoints in the level which aren't too far between; the system feels fair.There's also an upgrade system for your weapons and abilities in place which could feel a bit more impactful, especially on the damage side of things.If you're a fan of the genre and feel like playing a mash-up of Prodeus and Wrath - buy this. If you feel uncomfortable with shelling out coin for unfinished products, you can make an informed decision by checking the roadmap on this here steam page to see what's already there and what's to come. (There's also the option of getting this game in the "This is my Boomstick Bundle" by publisher 1C, which also includes the brilliant Viscerafest and Forgive Me Father. Just saying.)

_childDocuments_.review: Dread Templar (AKA Hell Hunt) has been a game I've been following for quite some time ever since the beginning of the decade when this got announced. I was very excited for it, but after many disappointments in the Boomer Shooter market, many of which I've talked about my problems with in previous reviews of this sub genre, I was a bit weary if I was truly going to like this especially with many people complaining that it's a very generic game altogether. Yes, it might be a bit on the unoriginal side of things, but that doesn't mean the game is not fun, because it actually is! And Dread Templar improves upon many aspects that many other games have implemented in it's design.First off, I want to get my only real negatives out of the way first. Like most Boomer Shooter games, the story here is hot garbage. It's edgy nonsense that thinks it's so cool when it really isn't. It's grating and annoying. The main character of the Templar sounds like if Postal Dude was trying too hard to be edgy and cool. Thankfully, all the cutscenes can be skipped which is always nice so you can just get into the action immediately. Aside from some immersion breaking things like how the Templar has two different pitched sounds when getting hit and jumping (which is mostly a nitpick but I really do care about being immersed in games nowadays) and Episode 4 being a bit on the easy side, everything here is solid.This is a hardcore styled shooter in the same vein of Doom Eternal. I thought I was going to have another Turbo Overkill situation where the game was just overly hard for no reason and copied the hardcore shooter style without getting why, but thankfully, Dread Templar's difficulty takes notes from Doom Eternal and makes some massive improvements to what that game did as well. One of the best things about the game is the weapon management. It's by far the best I've played in a Boomer Shooter recently. Every gun has it's use for one reason or another and nothing went to waste. Weapon combos to defeat enemies from a double shotgun to a regular shotgun blast is very satisfying and with the right mouse button being to switch to different weapon variants. The developer here has done a great job at this and should be commended for understanding Boomer Shooter/Old School game mechanics and putting a modern feel to them.As for the gameplay, it's a super fast twitched base style that works extremely well here. Dread Templar takes notes from Doom Eternal yet again and by being a challenging but never cheap game. Even if you don't get something at first or die for reasons unknown, you'll know immediately how to deal with the situation next time. The gunplay is nothing extraordinary but can still be solid when facing multiple enemies at once. Another thing this game does well is it's upgrade system. Again, this is the best I've seen in the Boomer Shooter market, tons of diverse upgrades, easy to find and unlock them, whether it be in the open or going through side areas and all having different effects that you can stack up on top of each other. When Doom eventually returns, I hope they take notes from this game here. Because this is the best of the best I've seen in a long time when it comes to upgrades.Some other quick notes to make are the graphics. While the game does have a similar style to Quake and early 3D Shooters, it's never an eyesore and is never uncompelling. The graphics here are excellent and the replication of the old school shooter is tasteful and effective. The boss fights are also very challenging as well. The final boss does take some time to understand how to defeat him, but I found a nice plan on how I used my weapons to be effective in battle. The side areas are also quite fun as well. Some are combat oriented while some are challenge oriented. The Mine Cart Area and Boulder Slope area were some of the most interesting of the game and the side areas do get better as you go along despite most of them being combat oriented.Finally, Dread Templar has a pretty kick ass soundtrack. The songs here take on different styles each fitting the respective area and episodes of the game. There is never a bad song and it fits with the action nicely, even if nothing will truly stick out in the coming weeks. Another thing as well is the campaign can be beaten in about 6.5/7 Hours total, making it unusually lengthy for an FPS Game. This might be nice to some who want more playtime, but I felt a more tighter, 4-5 Hour length would have made the game sturdier. It overstayed it's welcome by the end and I just wanted it to be over despite me enjoying the game.So I did enjoy Dread Templar. Boomer Shooter fans will find lots to like and admire here as it improves upon many gameplay and design aspects of recent Boomer Shooters and Old School Shooters good and bad. I never found myself frustrated with it totally and it does a good job at replicating the hardcore style difficulty of Doom Eternal well enough. It's not the most original game of the bunch, but that's just a thing that's lacking currently in the Boomer Shooter market at the moment. Overall, a worthy FPS that you should definitely check out.

_childDocuments_.review: There is a lot of content here for an Early Access title. Dread Templar is very challenging with good level design and a plethora of enemy types. _childDocuments_.review: The best thing that happened to so called boomer shooter revival was DUSK. that game set the standards high and that was just the perfect thing because this game and some others I played are not even close to that standard. I played most of the 90's shooters so I like to think I know a thing or 2 about these kind of games.I don't like doing this, writing a bad review for an indie title is really not my thing.So most of negative reviews say that this game is ok, average, mid etc and yet only 2.8 % reached the middle of the game and 2.8 % finished the game. I finished it on hard and here are some of my thoughts.I will start with the positives first. The guns are ok, the upgrade system is ok, 10 % levels are well designed, some secrets smartly hidden.Now, the first thing that I want to say is that this game is not finished, you can run through enemies, get stuck in enemies, there are glitches, bugs.... Look, I would get over bugs and glitches but running through enemies like they are ghosts and getting stuck in enemies is unacceptable. Most of the levels are just copied and each chapter feels like one level, large open levels and they are badly designed. The other thing I can't stand are invisible walls and there are a ton of them in this game so how about an idea - build a visible wall - ! Overall poor level design.The music is heavy metal of course but only one track is playing on repeat on every level so just turn it off. One thing that I almost never complain about are graphics, you can go through my 400 + reviews and you can find only a few. This game looks mostly crappy and I am being polite. Quick save , no reloading are not included so you will have to save manually on save stations OMG and reload of course,Look, I thumbed down Ion Fury ( and that game doesn't look bad at all after playing Dread Templar ) so I have no problems when I say that this game is not good. It lacks identity, has poor level design and it could use 10-15 patches. I wasted my time so you don't have to.

_childDocuments_.review: I played this during its final playtest just over a month ago and left a scathing review. Let me just say, this is the largest improvement I have ever seen in a game in such a short span of time. The massive jump in quality, and the implementing of player feedback bodes well for this game being in early access. I absolutely loved this game. Heres a quick breakdown of pro's and cons.Pros- Satisfying Gunplay- Great weapon sounds- Substantive upgrade system- Solid (but unremarkable) level design- Polished visual style- A lot of content, especially for a brand new early access title- Fun, fast movement (minus some cooldowns being too long)Cons- Melee is mostly useless- Movement cooldowns need tweaking- Ammo is a little too plentiful even on hard difficulties- Story is more of a hindrance than a help at this point- Unable to use the full upgrade system at this stage of the game (not enough upgrade tokens)- No way to go back and replay levels with upgrades and new weaponsOverall, this is a phenomenal title, and I am someone who went in highly skeptical after the demo and playtests for the game. The developers seem to place great importance on player feedback, and have implemented tons of it since the demo and playtests for the game. If you like boomer shooters, buy it. ♥♥♥♥♥. Kidding. Dont kick my ass.

_childDocuments_.review: Hi there!Yeah, yeah, we're here again. Steam nominations and all that stuff. The time of the year where hundreds of forced reviews show up haha. Ok I'll keep this rather brief I think and will put a TL;DR right at the start here:Great action FPS game with a lot of nods to classic/retro/Boomer-Shooters with a pumping "industrial death metal"-soundtrack (no vocals) and fast gameplay (although you can play it slower too if you like). It features unlockable skills, diverse environments, different enemies and some huge bosses. Also lots of secrets in every level. No quicksaving - but save spots!So yeah, if you grew up playing all those boomer shooters, you might feel right at home. Although not all of our ancient shooters featured a high tempo like this game offers. And not all offered a story too. Yes, this game has a story but it doesn't bother you too much if you just wanna jump right in it. To keep things short: you are a/the Dread Templar and you are on a quest for revenge. Your "quest" if you want to label it as such takes you through different times and places and lots of killing will take place. All along the way you'll improve your powers and weaponry with artifacts called "blood gems" and runestones.That's cool and all but what about your arsenal? Your first weapon is the (dual) katana which you can use to melee or combine to a spear you can hurl at your foes. You don't have to run to your "improv spear" to pick it up as it is tied to a skill with a cooldown. After a while, it will reappear in your hand ready to switch to melee mode or take your shot at another throw again.Then there's different kinds of pistols, a single and double barreled shotgun, some kind of "electrical mine thrower", rocket launcher and more. You'll even be able to use the "inferno gauntlet" which kind of is like this games BFG9000. Some weapons also feature alternate variants for specific playstyles or targeted towards different situations.And what about those skills? No way that I'll spoil it for you and list all there is, but... here's a little "teaser": some skills decrease cooldown timers for various weapons, like the cooldown of the "spear katana" to return to your hand. Pretty self explanatory. Then there's of course possible damage boosts or increasing the maximum amount of ammo you can carry. And then there's kinda "ultimate upgrades"; for example, your shotgun can become the "frost-banshee" - hitting normal foes will freeze them or your pistols will be their "inferno" variants with higher rate of fire to bathe your enemies in a whirlwind of bullets. Mind the ammo consumption though.Movement isn't limited to walking and running, you can also dive (I think there's no air timer you have to watch for in this game) and dash while in the air and on ground. No double jump though except I just haven't unlocked that yet (I still have to finish the last episode)."Ok, what about the levels?" you may ask. Ok, I have to be honest here, caves, tunnels, dungeons, ancient sites and hellish mines are somewhat prevalent. But there's still variety, like a wintry landscape containing an small archaic town with wooden houses and the almost expected well. There's giant libraries. There are some huge contraptions and buildings to explore. Excavation sites, frozen caves, some supernatural stuff (one level is called "Soul Melting Factory" FYI lol). Everything is garnished with pillars, chests, demonic statues, switches, elevators, platforms and on top of that each level features a good deal of secrets and one super secret. What's a super secret? Well, you might have a clue if you played Blood. Usually there's something exceptionally hidden or different objects you have to find and return to a specific location and your reward most of the time is worth the trouble. On top of that: of course there's easter eggs included which I won't spoil here.EDIT:Each level usually also has a side-area with additional loot and monsters if you want to go for the 100% run.Since you can't quicksave wherever you please, how's the save system set up? You can only save your game at specific "save spots" (glowing blue symbols scattered around the maps). In my opinion they're close enough to each other as to not make this game too hard or frustrating.Your enemies? Puh, some are rather weird. I don't actually know how to describe some of those... Cenobyte-Zombies? The usual host of demonic and occult looking beasts, ice ... insects? Acid pus flinging lovecraftian blobs? Bomb throwing ogres? Body horror crawlies with big eyeballs? These are just some words that come to mind and might give you a general idea of the enemy roster.The music I described as "industrial death metal" was done by John S. Weekley from PRIMEVAL Music. It features lots of electronic sounds layered with distorted, down-tuned electric guitars and a pumping drumset with these powerful "80s snare sound". I guess one could also drop the word "djent" here or there, although it doesn't go overboard too much with it. And sometimes there's a bit of "ethno" sound to the songs too (listen to E4M1/E4M2 for example). You won't have any real vocals, no growling here - but there's the occasional supporting "choir" sample. If you liked the modern Doom games soundtracks by Mick Gordon or music made by Andrew Hulshult, chances are you'll be a-ok with this too.Sound FX wise there's not too much to complain in my book. I think the shotgun could've used a beefier sound, something close to the inferno revolver but it doesn't sound as weak as the single barrel shotgun in Quake. You remember that one? You got one jumping sound, lots of booms and bangs with your whole arsenal but honestly, I'd like to keep the music in the foreground. As you'd expect, enemies react to you and the world with their own samples. All in all I'd say the soundwork is well done (and will definitely benefit if you have a subwoofer lol), although nothing exceptional comes to mind.Performance-wise I never had a problem with my 1080 Ti and 12700k CPU, it was always running super smooth. And it rarely crashed. In about 30 hours of playtime I had when I was writing this review, I only had few and I might've provoked those because I was doing stuff in the background.All in all, I'm having a blast with this game. Well done T19 Games & Fulqrum Publishing.If you should have any unanswered questions regarding this game, feel free to ask. And remember: this game has no toilets.

_childDocuments_.review: yes, but dont expect a masterpiece, theres some jank here and there and some strange enemy behaviour, but the gunplay is fun if you use the following weapons, pistols, mac's, shotgun, inferno rocket launcher, inferno revolver, and the 2nd gauntlet that drains all around you (kind of like a BFG 10000 from Quake II but without the projectile, it just channels on everything you see as long as you hold the button)The secrets are fun to run around and find, i think the upgrade system is interesting, but could perhaps be better, the level design compared to other indie games is definitely more vertical (ive seen too many games going for the wolfenstein 3D route, i.e; flat) so that gets a big plus.Again i think the guns i listed are a ton of fun to use and i especially like the alignment they have, they dont cover 40% of the screen like waaaaaay too many games do these days, probably the best gun alignment ive seen in a long ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ time, so that gets the biggest plus. my favorite is probably the shotgun, i used that up until the point where things needed 5 shots to take an enemy down, but thats when the upgrades swoop in to save it, the frost upgrade for it was the saviour. probably used the shotgun 75% of the entire games playtime which is a bout 9 hours, (less if you rush ofc). the super shotgun... it was not good, felt like a wet fart in comparison to its single shot counterpart.The bosses were interesting, but some of the movements they did requires you to slow down reality in real life to react to, cause even with the bullet time mode in game, their swings are still lightning fast.Some of them had fun mechanics, where my favorite might have been the fire boss.overall i'd give it a 73%, i found some enjoyment, but some things annoyed me.
