_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this game but I think my biggest gripe is lack of cohesiveness if that's the word. - I mean the UI definitely leaves something to be desired, functionally as well. The UI almost does not exist for me whenever I'm playing the game. It's hectic action and the appearance of it all definitely does not catch your attention on important information. The flash and sound of a skill being up is nice but is not pronounced enough imo and could be portrayed better with the distance between it and the other two skill icons so you can just tell from position, or possibly even design of the flash and sound cue. I don't think the health goes red when you're low and the armor value is always there in the same color with no quick way to see what it's around on the corner of your eye.- There's also stupid superfluous information which is the maximum number a value could be. This is denoted with health and ammo and possibly other elements. The hierarchy of information is just not presented well enough for a game that is meant to be as fast as this game.- I think we can all agree the upgrades menu is really bad but that's not hugeBut other than the UI- The separation of different icons connected to a switch is nonexistent. All that needed to happen is the change up the color but there are separate doors with the same icon in the same area that don't respond to the same switch for no reason. - The AI seems really basic with the only command of "run directly towards the man shooting you"- The information that is presented to the player of the monsters intention is lacking in my opinion- BUT WHY IS THERE NO ANIMATION CANCEL FOR RELOADS? Every single good FPS puts animation cancelling in its game. A game that is fast paced should definitely include it in the game since you'll be running around switching weapons. If there is no animation cancelling on reloads, it could be way simpler to just make the end of the reload have more flair. The double barrel shotgun I say is the worst offender. Partly due to animation cancelling the reload is second nature and also the end of the animation is a slow pull of the barrel upwards instead of a huge snap, like slamming the shells in. Minor things- Quite annoying that you are unable to melee with the katana in throwing mode when you have it, but you can when you threw the katana. This makes breaking boxes and other destructible items an absolute chore to hit if you have katanas in javelin mode. - Why is the second version of the pistols silenced mac-10s. That's the weirdest choice ever. I had fun with the game. The katana javelin feels great, having weapon secondary action being swapping to the weapon that consumes the same ammo is great. The music fits the game. The environments feel an appropriate amount of dreadful. It's just such a shame for me that not being able to reload animation cancel the super shotty and UI shortcomings  is going to lead me to not play this game any further.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't really play FPS a lot, but I am interested in this genre. Dread Templar picked my interest, so I decided to give it a go. Movement feels good and responsive, guns shoot, music rocks, enemies slay and are being slayed too, retro-style graphics are stylish but detailed enough to contain more... details; power-ups are plenty but the currency you pay for installing those upgrades is not, which is a good thing - it makes you choose between preferred guns and therefore between playstyle. But that's pretty much it. Dread Templar has seeds of a good game scattered here and there, but they did not grow in some memorable and engaging mechanics.The music is just there... it's not a bad music, it's just metal. Metal everywhere. Even when you're just walking with no one in sight. Feels goofy. Save system is weird. I mean, where is autosave? I'm not against having an option to save in different slots but after two hours of playing I started question myself why would I need different slots anyway? It's not like if I find more secrets the ending would change, is it? And why do I need to press several buttons to save in the only slot I use? Too much work for something trivial. Also, sometimes (at least in the first chapters) these checkpoints at which you can save are close to each other which doesn't really makes sense. You can save here or 50 metres away, it won't really matter.The enemies lack some sort of interactivity. Yes, they are different in their attacks, but all you can really do is shoot them. The only reall difference in that sense is target's size and (sometimes) speed. But it honestly looks uninspiring and feels boring to just walk and shoot. Would be cool if some enemies reacted to your arsenal differently depending on what guns you are choosing to use. Because for now it seems like you just need to use weapons that deal more damage. That is until you run out of bullets.Also, explosions. I want to see their impact. But really you don't see the explosion itself, there is no immediate visual responce. Yes, enemies die around some radius, but it's not as satisfying when you actually see fire and smokes. Just a side note.Normally I don't ask for a refund of games I find nice, but for now I'm not in a position when I can buy whatever I want. Right now it cames down to a question whether I should keep Dread Templar or not, and I decide against it simply because I didn't find my limited playtime promising. The only thing I hold against Dread Templar is lack of more nuanced directional and artistic approach. It's just a game. Not bad, not good.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is G.R.E.A.T GREAT.Ive heard some people compare it to shooters such as quake, which it shares only a similar aesthetic in the first chapter, chasm and even duskThe game however, shares only aesthetic similarities and a similar weapon loadout to those gamesThe game is more similar to modern shooters such as doom eternal, as unlike dusk or quake, the movement is alot more deliberate. there is no bhopping or momentum in the movement, However, the game makes up for this with its bullet time mechanic and dash move, both of which force the player to time their movements in response to the current situation or the environment. this means that you dont bhop around insanely fast like a cracked up ♥♥♥♥ but your forced to make deliberate movements in order to succeed.The weapons too are similarly great, weapon switching is heavily encouraged through reload mechanics and a fast swap time, while this may seem ♥♥♥♥♥♥, it encourages the player to make the most out of their loadout and utilize every weapon appropriately. The level design is great, however the first act is quite boring and borrows heavily from quake. The best levels are the latter half of episode 2, and the one episode 3 level playable now is the best, with an awesome aesthetic and great verticality, the level reminded me alot of that one underwater stage from mario 64 with the ships its great.Ultimately, the game is still in early access, however, the mechanics which make it good already exist and the dev is still actively creating the game and its definitely something worth playing for any shooter fan, if you can get past the initial slog of the first 2 levels

Hiding so many upgrades and powerups behind secrets is the mark of an amateur, not to mention a telltale sign of a micro penis or some other mental illness charade. The game's cutscenes, which seem to be under the false impression that they're telling some kind of story, are a clear indication as to why it is a bad idea to hire voice actors from fiverr. Main character sounds like the protagonist from Party Hard. Weapons don't tell you what they do when you first pick some up so get ready to fire one as an experiment and load the most recent save. Also no quicksaves, because then you might be in danger of going at your own pace and not starting a six minute segment over and over again until you run out of life and your flesh withers into dust. _childDocuments_.review: Dread Templar is a retro, low poly first person action shooter/brawler and spiritually a ripoff of 1990's games like DooM and Daikatana.  However, it's not the 1990's anymore.  Oops.  While the game is well optimised, it's incomplete and unfinished.  There's a slew of issues here that gamers should be warned about. The game has been in Early Access since 2021 and while it's still getting updates, it's deep in Development Hell.  There's no reasonable expectation that this will ever be completed, as the game is now nearing the developers promised deadline to complete the game, but is far from finished.  Whether the developer lacks the time, funds, or skill/talent required to complete a video game isn't really something gamers should be expected to accept as an excuse.From a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.The game features lazy low-polygon "retro" assets and low resolution textures, making this look like a barely functional 3D game from the 1990s.  It's unclear why the developers weren't able to arrange high quality, high polygon count contemporary assets for the game, and also irrelevant... what matters is that this looks bad as a result of their decisions, a compromise PC gamers shouldn't have to put up with.These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.Unethically, the developer sold keys to this abandoned Early Access game into cheap, nasty game bundles, where they knew it would be advertised and sold as a complete game.  This seems to have been done in an attempt to mislead gamers into buying a knowingly faulty, defective and incomplete product.  When a developer does this for a game they have zero practical intention of completing, this is essentially a scam, an intention to get paid for a broken/unfinished product.  Often this is done as an exit strategy, as the developer takes the money and runs.  No refunds have been given, the developer kept all the money they took from gamers.The developer has used a number of Unity assets for the game, which in itself is certainly no crime, but they fail to acknowledge the use of the work of others in this game.  Claiming the work of others as your own, failing to properly advise gamers and credit those who did the actual work for this game is highly unethical.Dread Templar has a laughable, eye watering price of $15 USD (for an incomplete game!), for which you could easily get any number of older AAA games, let alone the sheer number of free games available on Steam.  Given the defects and shortcomings, it's impossible to recommend this.  If you want a good, frenetic action shooter, try the Doom reboots (available cheaper than this unfinished game).

_childDocuments_.review: Dread Templar is a game of mixed quality. The levels in episodes 1 and 2 are great, while in 3, 4 and 5 they vary from good to borderland terrible.  The devs could easily have cut 70 - 80% of the maps in episodes 3-5 and combined the remaining maps into a longer great final episode.The weapons are similarly mixed, there's lots of them and they're quite varied but in order to make most of these guns even remotely viable in the later episodes you need to upgrade them.  This is a fine system on paper, the problem is that most of the really good upgrades are hidden behind incredibly obscure secrets, as in borderline impossible to locate without a guide obscure.  I did my 1st playthrough on hell difficulty with a guide open to find all these secrets and with the loot and upgrades from these the game generally felt very well balanced.  If I didn't have the guide open I guarantee my guns would have hitting like wet noodles and I'd constantly be on the verge of dying from the lack of heals and ammo.  It's a strange choice balancing your highest difficulties around locating secrets.Another choice I don't understand is the lack of quick saves, quick save/quick load spam is a key part of any good boomer-shooter, Cultic, Doom, Dusk, Ion Fury all great games and each allows you to save anywhere to your hearts content.It's not all bad, some of the levels are very good, the ability to freely change your weapon and character upgrades at any upgrade alter is great, the boss fights are surprisingly good for an fps.  Though I did end up using only 3 main weapons for most of the later episodes every weapon except maybe the trap launcher along with the alternative RPG and Infernal Gauntlets all fill a niche use.  I was having to swap weapons frequently to deal with different enemies which helped keep the game engaging.7/10, Dread Templar is absolutely not a bad game but it does suffer from the overall quality declining the further through the campaign you go and a couple of questionable design choices hindering player enjoyment.

_childDocuments_.review: Quick Summary: Dread Templar is a game that starts out strong but gets relatively stale around the halfway point. I'd give it a 6/10, it's far from a terrible game but leaves a lot to be desired. I would only recommend this game if you've already played the amazing "boomer shooters" on this platform and are looking for something new and want to pick it up on sale. Full Summary: Dread Templar's first two episodes are pretty well-done, the levels are enjoyable and the enemy placement is good. There are also enough supplies to comfortably get through them on the higher difficulties. Unfortunately, the level design for episodes 3-5 is varied, but I mostly didn't like them. A mixture of boring areas, increasingly confusing secrets, and seemingly unfinished levels really hindered my enjoyment of the levels in the latter half of the game. This is a game that basically requires secret hunting, so I'd spend 30-50 minutes in each level to find skill points and upgrades for your character and arsenal. I would recommend using one of the guides on here if you plan on playing at all, you'll need them. In the third episode onward, there were tons of invisible walls in levels that hindered exploration for secrets and even some unfinished environments. It feels like they forgot to do certain things, like notify the player when they're about to leave the level or switches no longer playing cutscenes showing when a door or area is opened (the first two episodes featured this prominently). Also, the levels seem to have either too much or too little ammo and health, no in-between.The upgrade system seems kinda forced. You find silver and gold medals to upgrade your character and weapons, allowing two silver medals and one gold medal. For whatever reason, the descriptions for the upgrades aren't clear; if I get a medal that increases damage, it doesn't say how much damage is increased by.The weapons are interesting and pretty varied which makes it all the more disappointing realizing how spongy the enemies are from episode 3 onward. By the end of the game, I found myself using the revolver that can sometimes one-shot with a gold medal upgrade just to clear the hordes of bulky enemies as fast as I could. It's disappointing since there are some pretty cool weapons that are made obsolete by how annoying it is to kill enemies.The enemy design is mostly interesting, but most of the combat in this game consists of walking backwards while melee enemies try to hit you and ranged enemies walk around until they can shoot you. There are a lot of enemies in this game and the levels usually put them to good use, but the enemies introduced in episode 3 and 4 are very bulky and annoying to deal with, especially the flaming dog things that shoot you on sight.There's also a tower defense mode, but I didn't play it all that much. More of the same, but your upgrades and weapons from the campaign are basically required. The music is alright with some good tracks, but it'll loop a lot if you're looking for all the secrets, with most tracks being about 2-4 minutes. Tracks are also used in multiple levels, usually back-to-back.Overall, the game took me 17 hours to get 100% achievements on, but cheats can be used to speed things up a bit. I hope my review is helpful!

_childDocuments_.review: Old school vibes with some new flavor.  You will recognize some of what I will assume are the games that gave the devs their inspiration.  You can tell they took the love of the old school games and added cool weapon ideas and a sort of balancing act in the skill tree.  Want to focus heavy on shotguns?  Go for it and when that doesn't suit the level re-balance your character traits and try again.  Weapons you think might be kind of pointless at first have a strength that you have to experiment to find.  Combos of tech, abilities and weapons may take the creature down faster.  It is fun to get faster at switching weapons in the heat of the moment.  I think my favorite part is the secret areas.  It takes me back to the old Spear of Destiny days and the game even takes time to make fun of its self for having so many secrets.  Even if you missed the games back in the day or maybe you weren't even alive when they came out I think there is enough here to keep most shooter fans happy.  Just when you think you are figuring out the enemies they know when to stick a grenade in your shorts.  Happy hunting oh and by the way the cool pistols on the game banner are in the game a little later.

_childDocuments_.review: Recommended, but with caveats. I'm being generous here after having seen the ending credits and seeing that pretty much everything was done by one guy; with that in mind, it deserves a bit more appreciation. Still, there are issues:-Chapters 1 and 2 are pretty decent. Chapter 3 falls off towards the second half. Chapter 4 was really really rough. Chapter 5 was fine. Overall, the levels would come to like a 7/10 overall-Secrets are neat, and the upgrade system allows a bit of building, but the game is balanced around secret hunting which was rough, especially when levels can be 10 minutes long sometimes, but secret hunting drags them out to 30-40 minutes of backtracking and looking around.-The game doesn't really innovate on the genre; it's kind of just more of the usual retro shooter fare. In 2018/2019 I would've been fine with this, but having played games like Cultic and Turbo Overkill, I'm now looking for a bit more from games in this genre.Overall, a 7-ish seems fair, and on that mark I did enjoy a good chunk of the gameplay. Pick this one up on sale if you don't mind the caveats above, since it's a net positive time overall.

_childDocuments_.review: This was bought for me as a Christmas present and recently finished it, so I can thank my friend for gifting this to me; I genuinely did enjoy my time playing it until the final episode.Dread Templar is a good game and satisfies that itch for a quick bloodbath, but it does suffer a few issues. The music is good, composed by a guy called John S. Weekley, and fits the game rather well; if you plan to just blaze through the campaign. The music can get a bit much when you stop to secret hunt like I did, though. The sound is good enough, but one or two weapons sound a little lacklustre, like the rocket launcher.The gameplay and gunplay are quite fun and has some variety to it as well as a bullet time mechanic. You get upgrades you can make to each weapon which you can swap around to find what suits you. These upgrades are fairly heavily locked behind secrets, however, which does give you some incentive you explore but are very well hidden and are many. There are a lot of different enemies allowing for some varied encounters and quick target prioritisation. The game also has things it calls "side-areas" which are a nice little addition and meant to be a little harder, early ones introduce tougher enemies sooner, while later ones are more gimmicks and/or platforming.Now for my complaints. While the enemy has variety it lacks in intelligence, most will just beeline for you and if the ranged enemies start attacking when behind cover, their shots may go through that cover. The bosses are too easy in all honesty; my deaths to them being my own stupidity. The last complaint I have is with episode five of the campaign, E5M1 is fine, but the last two maps before the final boss just weren't up to the standard of the rest of the game.I wish the best of luck to the developer for future endeavours and hope they do make more.

_childDocuments_.review: A cool game with a ♥♥♥♥-ton of issues.I found myself enjoying the game during my second attempt at finishing it (the first one lasted about 30 minutes due to the first levels being rather uninspiring). Generally its shooting is nice, the weapons feel appropriately punchy and the feedback (animations and gibs) are satisfying. The movement is a bit boring, but since the levels are typically small it does not hinder the experience all that much. The idea behind the throwing sword and the bow is cool as well as they can be easily incorporated in-between combos.The upgrade system is an interesting idea that is, in my opinion, botched by the way said upgrades are acquired, that being my finding secrets. Although some upgrades can be found on a few levels, many of the golden tokens which change weapons in a more substantive way seem to be exclusive and can be easily missed without a guide. This destroys the idea of player expression as a fun gun type can be accidentally omitted and many can be found in the later levels making them obsolete by the time they are acquired. A more fitting system, I think, would be to use the tokens to buy a given upgrade which would actually allow players to choose the options they see as the most fitting.That being said there are some baffling design choices that do, actually, hinder said experience. The save system is just unpleasant to use (why can't I simply interact with the crystal to create a quick save?) and feels like a more convoluted and less balanced checkpoint system. The aforementioned save crystals can be very close to each other and because of their placement they encourage save scumming which leads to another issue - the music. The music is fine. Great, even. Too bad almost every track is used twice in a row, making them overstay their welcome. Because there is no dynamic music in the game, the player's ears are being bombarded with blast beats during 15 minutes-long secret huntings which gets irritating fast. Not only that, but when the game loads the song starts from the beginning which furthermore adds to the auditory tedium. Also, weapons reset as well which results in the need to readjust each weapons after every respawn (especially the sword as it is not ready to be thrown without a semi-lengthy (in combat, at least) animation, cool).The levels? Usually fine, sometimes bland, other times fun and creative. Their creativity shines the most when they diverge from the generic FPS levels (frozen caves with ghost pirate ships are my favourites from the bunch). The secrets, however, are rather cheap. Many of them rely on wall-humping (yes, the wall textures differ slightly, but it is often hard if not impossible to notice) and the way the player interacts with them can be rage-inducing - especially when there is no feedback after using a wall or a button or if the interaction area is very small and a wall I used just did not open and lead me to believe that there was no secret there (thank god for the guides). I also got stuck twice and had to reload the save. Many enemies are also annoying. I especially hate the flaming rabbit-looking ass which is unnecessarily tanky and its projectile is barely visible while hitting like a truck (it is a common issue with projectiles in this game - they tend to blend with the environment). I often felt like I was playing Doom 3 again - after being hit by a corner-peeking ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ for the 10th time (ranged enemies tend to attack too early after going around corners which also sucks and creates unfun combat scenarios) I had to adapt and abuse the AI in order to scrape by (the health pickups on the Hell difficulty are way too scarce IMO).And you know what? Despite all of these issues I completed the game, had fun, and I am willing to finish it again on the Nightmare difficulty (because the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ achievements for finishing the game on Hell and Nightmare cannot be unlocked by doing the latter, thanks). Do I recommend the game? Yes, but only if one is ready to endure some amateurish design and, dare I say, jank.Oh, and the Defender Mode is fine, too. It's way too cramped and easy, but it's a fun treat nonetheless.

_childDocuments_.review: Summary:A fun, fast paced FPS that combines elements of Quake, Blood and FEAR to good results. Dread Templar has a well-judged difficulty curve despite being a challenging game, meaning you're unlikely to give up even in the hardest areas. There's a decent plot and some interesting puzzles, all handled in a way that doesn't slow the pace of the combat or disconnect you from the game.Cons:- Some weapons are too weak to use effectively even after extensive upgrading- Upgrading and time-slowing systems feel a bit superfluous- Doom 3 style enemy spawns can make the game very trial and error at timesNeutral:- Most secrets are embedded in complex puzzles that are easy to miss and sometimes very hard to figure out- Game doesn't seem to pause when saving, which can lead to cheap deaths if you're rushing to save e.g at one point I thought I'd cleared an area, saved, and on exiting save I got blown up by a straggling kamikaze that had flown right up to me while I was saving.- Frequent use of invisible walls and imaginary boundaries can make exploration confusing at times. Again can also result in sudden death via you falling through spaces you thought you could walk over because they look the same as others.Pros:- Brilliant synth metal soundtrack and gothic/eldritch horror atmosphere.- Combat is smooth, fun and incredibly satisfying when you start to nail it.- Encourages you to approach battles strategically and pick the right weapon for each job, leading to extra satisfaction when you figure a strategy out, and an overall feel that the game is never a slugfest- Very well judged difficulty curve with no real spikes or walls to come up against, that gradually ups the challenge firmly but fairly throughout the game.- Literally tons of contentConclusion:Dread Templar is a rapid fire eldritch horror FPS that provides a stiff but fair challenge across a very large game. It makes you approach combat thoughtfully and gives you lots of different strategic options. Although the time-slow and RPG aspects feel tagged-on at times, the game gives you control of how you play and which parts of your arsenal you focus on, and as such each player can mould their own playstyle. With 5 very large episodes and multiple side areas and secrets, there is absolutely tons to do, and plenty of reason to return to the game after completing it. Add to this the fact that the game performs smoothly like butter, and Dread Templar is worth everyone giving a try, you're sure to find something you like regardless of your gaming preferences.

_childDocuments_.review: I always find myself comparing this to another retro style shooter- Wrath: Aeon of Ruin. Both are very good leaving out the fact that Wrath is still only in early release. _childDocuments_.review: For the most part, I had fun. The upgrade system was interesting, and most of the levels looked cool and the overall aesthetic was good. That said, some of the gameplay leaned towards being a bit frustrating (lots of bullet sponges that move faster than you do, lots of enemies that fire the instant they see you, some giant lads popping out of boulders in the 3rd episode). I felt that the earlier levels were stronger than the later ones, as interesting layouts gave way to wide open spaces full of large groups of enemies. But, weapons were fun to use (I liked the bow) and some of the upgrades made the spongier enemies late-game easier to deal with.Some of the secrets were interesting and fun to track down, though they seemed to become more sparse late-game (or perhaps, way better hidden). And there were a few interesting levels I really enjoyed, though again, most of my favourites were early-game. Another comment I have is, the player movement felt a bit too slow. Though, it's possible it felt slow because many of the late-game enemies move faster than you do.All that said, it was made by a _very_ small team (end credits all fit on one screen!). For what it is, and as someone who likes the genre even when it's a bit janky, I enjoyed it. It's no DUSK, but it doesn't have to be. If you like the genre and can forgive a few rough edges, I'd say it's worth picking up.

_childDocuments_.review: Can't be arsed to complete. Beautiful environments and weapons. Well designed overall. There are two big problems with the gameplay. You are severely limited in your movement. The dash cooldown is too much and you should be able to dash more than once. The enemies are ridiculously spongy especially in later levels where you fight waves of them. There is nowhere near enough ammo pickups considering how many bullets it takes to kill one enemy.

_childDocuments_.review: I knew this was going to be a faster paced boomer shooter, as movement abilities looked to be emphasized here, but I had no idea how different from the norm this would end up being. If I had to find a comparison point to put it against, it really reminded me of Quake, but faster. Enemies don't die quickly and they feel like they are placed in such a hateful way. It's a struggle of a game, but at the same time, a true joy. The underlying gameplay is fantastic, it just so happens that it is a really difficult game. I really enjoyed that aspect of it actually once I got used to what was to await. The game does a lot different so it's worth breaking down each aspect that really shined for me. While initially I didn't find the upgrade system to be very interesting, it really grew on me as time went on. The gold tier unlocks actually can drastically change how you are playing the game and layering on silver upgrades to help boost that ends up being a fun discovery process. The secrets are actually pretty challenging to find, so you are not always able to find every upgrade the first time you go through a level, so there is a replay value there to try to figure that out. The other aspect I want to call out is the levels. Each episode has a dramatically different theme and a different feel to how they are traversed. There are layers to some of the levels that help boost the overall immersion of playing the game. Some feel like the typical slog (that isn't necessarily a bad thing) while others feel more like a build engine influence. It's a fun balance to keep things fresh for what ended up being a longer game than I was expecting.

_childDocuments_.review: Dread Templer is what they're calling a boomer shooter these days!And for what its trying to do, it seems to nail it.  The gameplay is appropriately fast, the weapons are tuned well, the music is pumpin'.  There's also a few things that make me wish were a little different such as more variety in the music, a more streamlined upgrade system, and different schema used for secret areas (or a map).  But its when your complaints are small and clearly identifiable, that you know they've nailed the important stuff.TLDR: It scratches that doom itch, if you've recently contracted it!

_childDocuments_.review: It's a really good game with some of the bet aspects of classic shooters combined with some of the awesome stuff that a lot of newer shooters have. For instance, there's to weapons that do massive damage and have infinite ammo but they require a recharge. There's also a huge array of things that you can do to change your characters stats. The only complaint is that you can go kaput from fall damage and get sent all the way back to the last save point. Honestly, that's one of the aspects of classic shooters that make the game significantly less fun. It's a boring difficulty curve that can be super frustrating.That's literally my only complaint. This game is a 8.5/10 and I recommend it to anyone who likes finding secrets, using super cool guns, and supporting some really creative developers!

_childDocuments_.review: The best parts of Dread Templar are the beginning stages, it really drags a bit later on. All the guns except the trap launcher feels nice to play with. The music is for the most part awesome but occasionally it gets repetitive and non-fitting for what is going on at the moment in the game. Enemies and level design can be very annoying and frustrating sometimes, especially in the later stages. The "story" is kinda non-existent, just some minor dialogue after each chapter. It's basically run and gun all the way through, the story telling through the gameplay is very very vague and confusing at times. I found myself closing the game and picking it up later way more often than any other shooter I've played earlier. I wanted to like this game more than I did since the theme of the game is cool, guns are nice and the beginning was so great. It is still a pretty good game and I'm recommending it for anyone that loves old-school style shooters. Looking forward to seeing that this developer cooks up next.

_childDocuments_.review: Awesome combat, smooth movement, good level flow, and a progression system that made me legitimately excited every time I found a new gold rune.The final chapter feels rushed and unfinished, but the game is so long and otherwise well fleshed out that it hardly matters in the grand scheme. I also wish Dread Templar had a bit more of its own personality and a more developed world/story/lore in the manner that games like DUSK do.Other than that, I loved it and it was a remarkably polished experience for a practically one-person developed game. Dread Templar is clearly crafted with love and care.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: Dread Templar: the perfect case of ''I wish there was a 'mixed' button in steam's reviews.Basically, the game is.... fine. Yup that 's it. It's enjoyable in a discreet way, but... I don't know. This is my first time reviewing a game that, in paper, ''should' be good, astonishing even, but in reality... is mediocre (but still, perfectly enjoyable.I gave it a little thought and I believe is this : the game tries to 'put' a lot of mechanics (not just fighting ones) together and, for that, doesn't achieve greatness in any of them.Case in point? gun play: weapon feel... weak, but you can upgrade them... only that doesn't seem to improve that much (maybe the third upgrade, but even that feels like a reskin in some cases). Or what about level design: maps are big but convoluted, with a lot of secret hunting (my favorite thing to do in a boomer shooter). Problems? welp, maps are big but empty, convoluted but they look all the same: add that to the almost boring gunplay, junky enemies, 'woobly' performance, a story that has no bite (and a little bit too edgy without being fun), Doom 2016 wannabe soundtracks that are repeated for most levels and not that great (srly, people. Boomer shooter doesn't mean rock blasted into you ear, it must follow the pace... speaking of...), an unsteady pace, graphics that could be good but wasted in uninspired scenarios...welp, I'm not that eager to search for any secrets (and some of them are really well designed).... or to finished the game....Ok, after all my ranting, why the thumbs up?Because the game has been done with some ''love'' for the genre, it's almost undeniable, but it tries to hard to unite things without really knowing how. Anyhow, I believe in supporting such developers and hoping their next game will be.... better. (And, again, the game is enjoyable, and if discounted, it is recommended).
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: Dread Templar is a solid boomer shooter. It's unabashedly edgy, but in a fun way that doesn't detract from the game. The soundtrack is solid, the visuals are fine, and the guns feel good to fire. It's not that long of a game if you're just going for the main story (which is what I did), but if you go for full completion without leaning on guides I think you could eke 20+ hours out of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Dread Templar is an OK old-school FPS. Not all weapons are equally useful, some need upgrades to be useful, which is a bad thing. I would rather have guns that are fun to use from the beginning and upgrade them from there.Level design is okay, nothing mind blowing. The later episodes become a bit of a drag.6/10

_childDocuments_.review: Now that Dread Templar is fully out of early access I can wholeheartedly recommend this title. It's a boomer shooter so expect the usual, fast movement speed, dash move, fixed health and armour, a full roster of weapons to choose between and a slow-mo bullet time mode. There are plenty of secrets hidden in each level, the finding of which is immensely fun and rewarding. There are more often than not, side rooms containing extra challenges in either combat or platforming, but mostly combat. There is a robust upgrade system that doesn't unlock static skills or abilities, but allows you to unlock slots under specific weapons and you find runes that have enhancements to those weapons. You can swap these runes around at certain points in levels and allows you to mix and match for your playstyle. The level design is great in most levels, a few are a little lacking or sometimes lack a little direction but these are rare cases, most levels flow nicely together and are often expertly laid out so you revisit areas previously locked off helping you gain a stronger understanding of the level. The weapons are good, have decent feedback and all pretty fun to use. As the difficulty climbed I found even the weakest of the guns useful in certain situations I was often stuck in. Specifically referring to the trap launcher that helps you stun enemies for a few scant seconds to help give you some breathing room. While most enemies are programmed to bum rush the player, having added effects like some enemies slow you on hit or others that are immune to rocket damage help to make the lineup of creatures varied and fun. I often found myself reaching a new room full of enemies and taking a quick second to analyse the best one to focus on first instead of just mindlessly circle strafing until everything died. Boss fights are a little underwhelming but this is a boomer shooter so that is to be expected. The story feels like it was ripped straight out of an edgy 14 year old boy's notebook, this is a good thing. It's light on details, doesn't bog things down and is just plain stupid fun. If you're a fan of boomer shooters or curious to see what they're like, this is hardly a bad place to start. Fans of these shooters can expect to find a ton of fun and cheeky references to past titles like Blood and Quake.

_childDocuments_.review: Dread Templar, a game that seems to receive a rather mixed feeling from those who have played it.It's a little difficult to describe, on the one hand, those stating the game is mediocre aren't exactly wrong, but to consider it bad because of mediocrity would be unfairly judging it.Everything Dread Templar does, it does right, from the pulsepounding metal soundtrack, the sound effects, the guns, the enemy variety, the visuals, level designs, it's all exactly what you could want from a retro-fps.  There's nothing particular that stands out about it, but that's ok, because if the worst thing that could be said about it is that it feels like every other retro-fps, then that means it's a very fun and enjoyable experience that you'll slip in to like a comfy pair of pants and have a blast with.Since buying it in early access, and playing it in to full release, I've been having a lot of fun with it, dashing around blasting bad guys, finding secrets and playing around with the upgrade system.  It feels a lot like Dusk, but with a hellscape level design instead of a boondock village, with blade wielding demons in place of chainsaw hillbillys.  If you like Dusk, this is more of the same in a different skin, and given how immensely successful Dusk is, that's pretty high praise.  Bonus praise has to be given to the soundtrack, which really amps up the frantic shooting and dodging with it's heavy guitar riffs and thumping drumbeats.  It's a great example of a retro-fps being what a retro-fps should be, and well worth the low price it's being sold at.

_childDocuments_.review: A retro-inspired FPS that struggles to set itself apart from other games in the genre, but still manages to deliver good quality gameplay through a solid upgrade system, weapon switching combat akin to Doom Eternal and a great metal soundtrack. _childDocuments_.review: Many enemies in Dread Templar are as fast or faster than the player, which seems designed around a slow-mo meter mechanic that simply builds up too slowly and drains too quickly. Each episode swaps out its enemies for a new set of equally bad ones -- some choice enemies include ones that are both faster than you  slow you down if they get too close, enemies that immediately create a fart cloud as soon as they see you and snipe you from inside it to make themselves impossible to hit, and enemies that are straight up immune to explosive damage and come at you in swarms when you would most want to use explosives on them.Since the vast majority of combat encounters in Dread Templar are fast swarming enemies coming at you from the other end of a long corridor (along with some snipers in the back), the first guns to come out are generally the single shot accurate high-damage weapons like the bow, inferno revolver, and explosives (which is funny when the game introduces the enemies that are immune to explosive damage, meaning you have one less tool to deal with them). Once enemies get close enough, the next weapon to come out is the trap launcher, to avoid getting swarmed, and maybe some slow-mo (if you even have any). When every combat encounter plays out the same way, every combat encounter feels like the same combat encounter.Dread Templar has maybe 1-2 music tracks per episode and loops them throughout entire levels, back-to-back, without breaks. These tracks are 100% energy all the time. This means you're listening to the same high-energy metal for up to 2 hours at a time. Worse still, some level ambiance is tonal and not in the same key as the background music. At one point, I simply turned the music off and played in silence.Later in the game, I got an upgrade that turned my SMGs into hand-held miniguns that chew through ammo but absolutely obliterate enemies. This is cool, but I realized I was running into the Doom 2016 problem: a self-perpetuating upgrade system in lieu of good encounter design built around a well rounded roster of weapons. Every combat encounter in Dread Templar is a chaotic mess designed to be dealt with by an upgrade system that didn't need to exist. At the very least, the upgrade system in Dread Templar makes secret hunting feel very rewarding.

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:-Tight, fast, exciting gunplay!-Environments are varied and really weird, very fun to explore-Great variety of guns to find and upgrade-This game's version of "BFG" feels awesome to use-Wide variety of enemies to fightCons:-Secrets are both a pro and con. They are fun to find, but you won't ever find them all by yourself. You will need to alt+tab every few minutes to see where the next one is. It's honestly kind of annoying, but also a central part of the game.-Normal difficulty is too easy-Soundtrack is appropriate and fits the theme well, but can get a bit repetitive after about 20 minutes into a level. I also don't particularly enjoy metal type of music-Story is pretty surface level. Not much to it.I haven't had this much fun since Amid Evil! _childDocuments_.review: It’s a surprisingly good throwback shooter! I acquired it back when the game was still in EA and decided that I won’t touch it until its full release. And boy, the wait was worth it, because playing it from start to finish in a matter of few days was a great experience. In terms of the oldschool gameplay, the basic but satisfying shooting is there along with the mid-90s era graphics and all provide a very good reminiscence of the good old days, plus it being coupled with a plethora of weapons to choose from and additional unlockable skills only adds to the already rewarding experience.However, the biggest downfall for me is the lack of better weapon switching mechanics for mouse + keyboard, as in the brink of the moment with lots of enemies on screen you want to utilise the weaponry as best as possible, but doing that while there’s a lot of stuff going on screen and with constant movement it’s hard to swiftly select the best weapon for the current situation – a perfect solution would be adapting the weapon wheel for all control devices or providing a better graphical indication of what’s currently chosen. Maybe in future patches?Nevertheless, what matters the most is already there and it’s a must for anyone wanting some old-fashioned shooting with an additional skills progression.

_childDocuments_.review: Pro:+ The movement is fantastic, commands are responsive and tight+ Very good weapon roster that gets even better with upgrades+ Very well designed roster of enemies, each of them stays relevant for the entire game and along with your weapons it allows for different approach for each fight+ Very good level design, the game does nto shy away from variety in its levels, from confined prisons to large eldricht vistas+ Fantastic soundtrack, each one its a bangerCons:- While the art direction is fine, even great in some point, of all the recent boomer shooter this is the first one that feels 'ugly' too look at, might be personal preference but it feel more rough than something like Dusk with which it shares the minimalistic visual style- Some jank like very prominent invisible walls in some of the later chapters maps and enemies clipping into the walls while strafing or jumping- Overdose of secrets, while secrets are an amazing addition to any fps, Dread Templar sort of overindulges in it and when most of your level have 10+ secrets you simply stop caring searching for them, especially some are quite obtuseDread Templar is a very competently made boomer shooter with fantastic moment to moment gameplay that will keep you entertained for 10 to 15 hours depending on your difficulty of choice (i played at Hard) and if you want to find every single upgrade in the game. That being said if you are player new to the boomer shooter genre there are more polished and suitable title to try before this (Prodeus\Amid Evil\Dusk\Ion Fury) but if you are a lover of the genre it is surely a game worthy to stay in your collection.Recommended with 7/10

_childDocuments_.review: All in all the game is pretty good. The gunplay is rewarding and incentivises you to switch around and try out different strategies. _childDocuments_.review: Dread Templar is a very enjoyable boomer shooter that doesn't quite reach the heights of the modern genre greats from past few years due to some design decisions and other minor flaws that hold it back, but it is definitely worth playing especially if you are a fan of the genre.Weapons feel satisfying, there is a good amount of weapon variety and every weapon (or weapon type in some cases) comes with some amount of customization that lets you tailor your arsenal to suit your playstyle. While I loved the idea of the customization its progression was perhaps too closely tied to finding secrets in the levels as instead of making you feel like you are rewarded for the optional exploration or discovery, it instead turns exploration in to a sort of mandatory part of the game which hurts the overall flow and pacing.This is in part due to the level design which is probably the weakest aspect of the game, not due to the structure of the levels themselves but because of the lack of visual clarity which is in part due to the visual fidelity of the textures and in part because the game doesn't really do a good job of utilizing typical level design tricks that subconsciously point the players attention where it needs to be. There were quite a few occasions where some of this result in breaking the flow of the game and especially when combined with seeking out secrets it sometimes really brought the pace to a halt.Soundtrack is excellent and generally goes pretty hard, which is something I enjoyed a lot and felt like it works really well as long as you maintain that steady flow of advancing ahead mixed together with a steady intake of fights. However the moment that the gameplay flow gets interrupted be it due to looking for secrets, not figuring out how to advance in the map or even using the manual save points (more auto-saves or a quick-save function would do so much for maintaining the pace) - it can become repetitive, as your attention gets more directed to the music while the gameplay is not keeping you fully engaged.That being said, despite its flaws I had a blast with Dread Templar and found this one to be an easy recommendation especially for the fans of the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: Awesome boomer shooter, with some nitpicks.The great:* Awesome weapon variety. Most weapons have 2 variants (think pump shotgun/double barrelled, or dual pistols/dual uzis). * Great upgrade tree/tier system. Incremental upgrades for each weapon category(pair) for things like damage/ammo, then gold(ultimate) upgrades that can change the weapon playstyle completely (pump shotgun to freezing shotgun for setting up combos)* Solid headbanging music* Level design and overall aesthetic is great. You start slow with swamps and catacombs, then you are steppign through paintings into a frozen cave helping a ghost pirate captain, then in a hellish floating cathedral/castle* A ton of secrets, and super secrets that reward puzzle solving and sometimes knowledge of retro shooters.The good:* Enemy variety is very solid, and their patterns a fairly predictable, so very little that's unfair. Only complaint is sometimes they spawn behind you (rare), and that the relies on recolors, which do admittedly do different things... but a sprinkling of 4-5 more across E2-E4 would solve it* Difficulty seems well balanced too. You have your standard easy-normal-hard-hell(very hard), then a secret Nightmare difficulty if you really want it. The lower levels scale damage down, but the higher levels make health packs spawn less, finally limiting them to only secret areas. This is fine... but I'm playing on Hell, and while I play a ton of these, I am generally flooded with ammo. Scaling ammo drop rates down a touch on Hell E3-E5 would be good, and would force me to swap to new weapons more, and change up my strategy, rather than relying on the same combos.The neutral:* Secrets, progression and upgrades. Seemingly 90% of your upgrades are found inside secret areas. Harder to find secrets can have gold upgrades(special weapon variants/abilities) and Super secrets that have puzzles attached which always have gold upgrades and sometimes new weapons, earlier than you would otherwise get them. This is fine for me because I like to secret hunt, but if you don't enjoy that, it will hurt your playthrough a lot.The not so good:* The music tracks (which is great) reset to the beginning when you load or die. If you are struggling on a section, you will hear that opening section over and over again. This is just straight up annoying, and can make you dislike the otherwise great music, by pure repetition.* The sounds effects that exist are great, but there need to be far more. General atmospheric sound like fire etc is limited, and the in between parts of levels can feel a bit static without them. More importantly, enemy attack sounds and spawning need to be much more audible and distinct (or exist).* General level creation jank. I get that this is probably a single developer, but level jank like walls floating slightly above the floor, misaligned textures or being able to exist level boundaries is simply painful when you **hide secrets behind these kind of things**. I have left levels more times than I can count, wandered around and never been 100% sure if I was meant to be there, or there was as secret I was missing. Is that patch of wierd wall a secret, or a mistake? Better spam E to make sure... which is fine for me, but I can see if driving many players up the wall.Overall, a great game with some serious love and dedication put into it. Just needs a tiny bit more polish to be truly excellent, but I would still recommend it regardless, if you know what you to expect.

_childDocuments_.review: Playing the first chapter during early access had me concerned, but things pick up considerably starting in the second. Dread Templar gets a lot of things right - for example, no hitscan enemies - and the weapons start to feel pretty great after you've discovered a few gold runes throughout the game's numerous secrets. I wouldn't say anything about Dread Templar necessarily *excels* compared to the elite of the new wave of retro shooters (DUSK being the most obvious comparison), but it marks a quality "B" entry in the genre for anyone looking for more. Normal mode can be a bit easy, the 5th chapter tails off somewhat in quality as the game stops introducing new enemy variants or map designs, and I never really came around on the trap launcher. But overall I had a pretty good time with Dread Templar and I'll definitely be keeping my eye on T19 going forward.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: The level design of the first episode did not wow me but the gameplay was so fun it left me deeply intrigued.By episode 2 I realized I was playing a game with potential to be great.By episode 3 I was convinced - this is the best boomer shooter I've played in... possibly ever?DREAD TEMPLAR takes the best elements of all my favorite shooters - Doom, Quake, Serious Sam, Blood, Duke Nuke Em, and somehow ups the ante. It succeeds in the areas where these other games fell short. The level design is sufficiently complex without ever feeling tedious. The secrets are rewarding and encourage the player to explore the levels in-depth without a penalty for time spent exploring.The handling is smooth and the action is intense, keeping you on the edge of your seat as you slaughter your way through hoards of enemies. There is a wide enough variety of enemies that the combat does not feel repetitive or forced.Sure, the story is lack-luster, but if I wanted story I wouldn't be playing a boomer shooter. This game is phenomenal, fans of the genre will be thoroughly pleased.

_childDocuments_.review: Another of these old school FPS games that gets a lot right, movement is slick, enemies are challenging and pretty much all the weapons have a use even in later levels thanks to how customisable they are.Some of the levels about halfway through the campaign start to get a bit too cramped (with movement as good as this you really want to actually have some room to jump about)the music is extremely good and you'll be headbanging during combat downtime, just wish it didn't restart the track every time you die.Also I didn't make these rules but it is an unwritten rule of FPS games that if you have an enemy that summons clones of itself, the clones have to die when you kill the original, that's just how it is..The game could also benefit from a bit of a redraft as a lot of the tool tips and I suppose dialogue are clearly written by someone for whom English is not their first language, it's by no means illegible there's just some bits that could do with tightening up

_childDocuments_.review: If you love indie darlings and boomer-inspired shooters, then Dread Templar is for you. If you love hard-rock inspired themes to rock out to as you send every blasted demon to hell, then Dread Templar is for you (the composer, John S. Weekley, has done a phenomenally good job here). If you love having the ability to use slo-mo, then Dread Templar is for you. If you love games that throw their narrative to the wayside, and instead let you turn off your brain and just have fun, then Dread Templar is for you.Now, the weapons themselves may not sound as punchy as they ought to, but they certainly kick ass. The variety of firearms is equally grand, and the ability to upgrade them, and even change how they appear and act (similar to Forgive me Father) is equally stunning. Note: Upgrading the Gauntlets with the 'Boss Killer' tag, is basically a cheat.Now, weapons are only ever as good as the enemies they go up against, and Dread Templar has a good selection of monsters, none of whom are hit-scanners, thank Christ. The enemies in the first two episodes probably evoke a closer feeling to Quake, as do the environments, though as you continue into episode 3, you will see some truly unique creations, along with some Dusk inspired levels in the final episode. That said, I feel the levels in episodes 3 and 4 are not as strong as they were in the opening two. I especially am not a fan of the invisible walls that are implemented to stop you going places you shouldn't.Moreover, as you progress, you will see upgraded reskins of  prior monsters, which basically become bullet sponges - probably the games way of keeping up with the player as you upgrade your health and weapons.On a further note, finding the secrets is incredibly rewarding and fun. The occasional puzzle solving needed uncover the 'super secrets', adds another layer of immersion and creativity.On a technical note, the game ran buttery smooth. I encountered one glitch (I needed to pick up a map, but I initially could not), though loading a previous save fixed this. I also noticed, enemies could occasionally shoot through walls - that was a tad annoying. That said, no known problems.Dread Templar is an easy sell. Think Quake married with Dusk, and you have the right idea. What's not to love?

_childDocuments_.review: Boy, oh boy, Where to start?Welp, I loved the game for the first two chapters or so, the levels, the enemies, the design, and the gunplay, were all pristine; it was fun to get new weapons, the gunplay was great and meaty, the enemies kept melting whilst I would use all of the repertoire of my arsenal; it was a darn good time... And then, the damn game turns into a slog fest with a complete unbalanced level of difficulty...This happens for two reasons: First, the game has health pickups, no regen; which is fine, it's a "boomer shooter" after all, but here's the thing; the pickups aren't well scattered nor well given to the player... Some areas have more pickups than others, sometimes they're arbitrarily scattered through some of the later levels, it's very messy...Then there's the second reason, perhaps the worst of them all...The game isn't properly balanced... At first is excellently balanced, the first two chapters are great, but as soon as I hit the third the problems started, sometimes you get into areas where the game keeps throwing enemies at you, other times the game chooses to lock you into very small areas filled with huge enemies giving you a very small room to maneuver; Worst of all? The damn game has a mechanic in which you're slowed down when getting hit by an enemy for some strange reason; you can change it and by getting an upgrade but...You have to find this upgrade, they're runes that you can find throughout the level which can give you higher damage, fire rates, or even cool things like removing this obnoxious mechanic; but you have to find these items first they're not just given to you for the most part... Not only that, but to actually equip them, you have to spend blood crystals, which is a type of currency -also-, scattered throughout the levels.In the end you're left with two choices to push through these issues; you either persist despite how frustrating the game can get, or you drop down the difficulty and deal with how boring the game becomes...So in the end, because of this, sadly this isn't a recommended game for me.It's such a shame too, because I really, really liked the game at the start.

_childDocuments_.review: 6/10 - It's a good game, it could be improved a lot though. I like the level design of this game a lot, music is also very good. The boss fights are cool, they have actual mechanics which isn't that common in FPS games.Unfortunately I feel like the game falls off a lot in the second half, the first half of it is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ amazing, up to an 8/10 level game, but then its just starts to go downhill. The biggest problem is the weapons. They literally feel the same, within their effective range most weapons do very similar damage. This would make some sense if this was a multiplayer game, but it is not, so...Enemies are very bulletspongy, and the weapons makes this feel ever worse. Like it takes 3 close range shots with the sawed off shotgun to kill a regular enemy, rocket launcher is the exact same but to mid-long range. This is the most limp ♥♥♥♥ rocker launcher I have used in recent memory, it is more of a threat to yourself due to splash damage than it is to the enemies. Like 3 direct rocket launcher hits to kill a regular ass enemy? Thats just not good. There is the glove weapon that really stands out being the most powerfull but you barely get to use it because there is no ammo for it.There is some upgrades but whenever I got a new one, it didn't feel like anything has changed at all. Like give me a slight boost to one of the weapon classes but in the same time the enemies get stronger too so it's like absolutely nothing has changed.If they would change the weapons to feel different it would immediately improve this game a lot. There is a bunch of things they could do to make them better. I would either remove reloading, or make it much, much faster. This would also make weapon comboing much more effective. Adjust the damage numbers to separate weapons a lot more, adjust available ammo accordingly or raise enemy numbers or make them more aggressive.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: This game perfectly encapsulate that nice feel of Quake. Movement is nice and fluid, the guns feel great and unique, and the level design is magnificent. There's a little bit of "Where the hell am I?" now and then, but most levels have a nice linear fashion to them that will stop you from getting too lost. Highly recommend to anyone who enjoyed Amid Evil. And thanks to the devs for not using flat sprites for enemies, which can look cool, but suck in reality.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: Well, also a "boomer-shooter", part of the humblebundle  "best of boomer shooters". If you like PlayStation (1) graphics, and the strange feeling that you are the only entity in the game that gets punished by any hits at all, and no monster reacts to being shot in any, and I mean ANY way, then this game is for you. Not for me, tho. Play GZDoom instead, get the WADs from GOG. Have 99% more fun than with this shooter. Promise!
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: Having now played through all five episodes (normal difficulty), I can say that Dread Templar is a good game. It has very smooth controls, the gunplay feels great and the perk mechanic goes well with the otherwise oldschool gameplay. What´s missing here in my opinion is a good story / more background information about the character (he stays very bland) and the game world. I really don´t expect cutscenes like in Turbo Overkill, but at least a story which holds the episodes together would have been nice. It still feels you are thrown in different settings just for the sake of some variety, but it´s not very believable. I think the devs recognized that at the end of episode 5 and therefore threw some "Dusk"-horror in, but this just feels out of place at the end.Same goes for the levels - while some of them show a lot of creativity (e. g. the pirate ship in episode 2), others are kind of generic and repetitive (especially episode 4). Check out Cultic, Turbo Overkill, Dusk or Hrot and you will see what I mean. Anyway, in terms of pure gameplay, Dread Templar gets a clear recommandation from me for all fans of oldschool FPS - even if it´s not a game to come back to after the first playthrough.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't finished it yet so this might get updated when I do.Cons: - It's a bit darker than I would like and I'm not sure if it's intentional or not - Lack of map (the level design is very well thought out, but I would say in this case is more like nice thing to have since I do have some occasions that I get a bit confused, but nothing major)Pros: - Gameplay is smooth, responsive and fast - Music is great and goes well with the flow - Some of the weapons are interesting and the others are basically in every boomer shooter, but if it works don't change it and I like we have headshot system (makes the bow quite useful) - I love secrets and this game has a ton of them and some are really well hidden (super secrets) - Maps have this horror diablo like theme to them and I like it. The layout of the maps is also well done and there were some small occasions I got...well not lost, but a bit confused, but I would say nothing major.Overall I really love me some good boomer shooters and this one satisfies that itch quite nicely and I totally recommend it!
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: Better than Dusk.Nearly everything about this game is sheer perfection in my experience. It is to the point where I struggle to find anything negative to say about the game. Weapons feel satisfying to use. Soundtrack is amazing. Every single weapon litteraly feels useful, and the whole rune upgrading system works brilliantly, giving you options to try out different playstyles. Want to rely on bullet time more? Use the upgrade that grants you more bullet time per kill and combine it with the "Neo" rune, allowing you to mow down tons of enemies with the basic pistols. Want to rely on oneshotting monsters with the infernal revolver? Pick the fatality rune for it and along with the Lucky rune to grant it a 55 percent chance of oneshotting everything except bosses. Or build the Infernal revolver around dealing double damage to stunned enemies, which other runes give synergy to... Just an amazing and very well thought out system. Dusk has nothing at all like this. Another interresting and unique thing this game does with the "normal" shotgun and supershotgun is that you have to reload the SSG inbetween shots, so you cant just quickswitch like crazy inbetween the 2. You haft to reload it, switch to normal shotgun fire, then shoot the SSG and quickly fire off the regular shotgun, allowing you to fire 3 shots almost instantly. There is even a rune that buffs the damage of firing the shotgun like this with quickswitching.Your basic katana serves as a recharging throwing weapon, that you will often be switching to in order to save ammo, instantly killing a demon while instantly switching to another weapon. The quick weapon switching on this game suits this gameplay loop with the katana well. Katana also gets its own rune slot.The super secrets in this game are brilliant. All of them are fun and satisfying to find, and grants you much needed runes and blood gems. Game rewards you for exploring everything, rather than punishing you for "wasting time". The side areas are also fun. Absolutely worth doing. There was even one of them that had the layout of de_dust1 from CS which was great. The game is also filled with references to other games.Sounds in this game are particularily satisfying. Everything from the monsters, weapons and other enviromental sounds are exellent. I think the main reason I like this game so much has to do with the sound design. Level design is great, not that many problems getting lost.I have some very minor complaints, mainly about a specific enemy that sometimes outranges you so much that none of your weapons can even reach it except the bow. This happens very rarely, but it was a minor annoyance. The bosses on this game are... good, but I would not say they are amazing. I think they are better than the boss fights in Dusk tho, as both games kinda lack a good boss fight, but Dread Templar comes out with the better fights here imo.I think this is the best boomer shooter I played so far.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: While the first stages were not very interesting to me, the game got progressively better and I have really enjoyed episodes 2 and 3. As you advance, you have more options regarding weapons and upgrades, enemies get harder to deal with (though ambushes/hordes can be a bit too much), and in my opinion the setting of the levels gets better (in the sense that the graphic elements follow a theme closer, and scenery is more spectacular and it seems like it has more work behind it). The slowing time mechanic was very nice too. Just don't expect an interesting and deep story, that's not a point of the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: Cool little boomer shooter. The difficulty spikes pretty hard in the final episode with some of the most annoying enemies I've ever seen. The weapons are all mostly useful due to the "rune" system. Pretty promising early access title.Update: Game just hit 1.0 and the last episodes are alright but nothing too special. The voice-acting is just as retarded as ever. I wouldn't recommend buying this for full price, the combat gets gimmicky later-on with the focus on precise head-shots. I'd probably give this a 6/10 at best.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: It's too bad this game makes such a "meh" first impression, because it absolutely BANGS. Episode One is mind-numbingly easy, kinda ugly, and weirdly balanced (breaking destructible objects leaves you absolutely SWIMMING in ammo). Also the bare-bones story is presented in the most boring way possible: literally just text on a black screen.That said, once you get to Episode 2 the enemy roster gets MUCH better and the challenge starts to ramp up. The visuals get nicer as you move out of samey crypts and into wide-open outdoor areas. It keeps escalating to a boss battle that legit had me sweating.And then episode 3 hits and GOT DAMN. It's beautiful, it's challenging, the music is better than ever...it's almost like a completely different game! The finished version is going to have 5 episodes and it's already worth the price.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: Really fun and generally great Boomer Shooter, It's upgrade system adds an insane amount of replayability and it's one of the few Retro Shooters where you can make your own full unique builds. I'd give this like a solid 9/10 just some super high quality shooting with no glaring flaws in my eyes, though I feel balance on some upgrades could be changed a bit.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: Even at this stage you get a great experience for a fair price. Movement and shooting itself feel great and the upgrade system provides an incentive for further playthroughs. Level design and the themes present really sell the mood well and music fits with everything and cranks up the rush of gameplay. Cannot wait for the full release.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: Bought it from that Humble Bundle sale a ways back and finally got to it.Episodes 1 and 2 easily put me in a trance state where my jaw goes slack because the gameplay loop was just that tight. Episode 3 broke me out of it cause they went with much bigger/intricate level design that didn't really work for me. What really really matters for classic shooters is the movement and weapons which were still great even in weaker levels. It was still good but the hooks were slipping out of my brain during EP3. Love the perk system and how hard they go with some of the level 3 ones. As-is DT's pretty great overall and I look forward to the full release.And good aesthetics and music and vibes yadda yadda it's good game.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: Petty cool little boomer shooter, if you skip all the secrets the game is only like 4 hours long but even so its super fun with cool weapons to choose from and a bit of character customisation to do with perks.The game isn't too hard to 100% either so if you're looking for a pretty ez but fun game to 100% this is it.Its def worth the asking price already but if its on sale you shouldn't have a reason not to pick it up.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent game! Looking forward to what more is to come. My only real criticism is the score could really use some work. Parts of it are good but I turned it off during the first level and never turned it back on. I really like the genre of music but it just sounds like a couple cords on loop constantly,  it could use some variety, maybe ramping up when you're fighting and when you're exploring maybe have some calmer music. Also is it just me or does the bow, the jump / jump dash and revolver REALLY feel familiar.. that's all I'll say about that.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: So, I originally played this hidden gem of a game after it was brought onto Steam in 2021 for a Beta test. I initially went into the game thinking it would pretty much be a poor knock off of Doom, but it has surprised me.While it definitely takes more than a few of it's inspirations from the early Doom games, it's still really enjoyable. The movement is really simple and easy to get the hang of, the weapons are also relatively easy to use and great fun, and the sword is a great little addition and option for when you absolutely have to YEET something at the one spider that's gunning for you. I mean, you'll be running and gunning. That's all this game in really. Think Devil Daggers with less ominous void.The levels are very well designed with enough hidden or secret areas to keep you guessing and questioning all the walls, doors and buttons you can find, and the enemies are pretty good at keeping you moving and shooting. The music is great, and definitely makes you feel more like a demon slaying monster, although even as a lifelong metalhead I have to admit it can be a little repetitive at times.Regardless of anything else, this is a delightful little game that really makes you feel like a kid again, and I would highly recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: Don't sleep on this title in particular if you like Quake or modern FPS games.There's something about the fine mix of the classic quake FPS experience and style mixed with modern mechanics like upgrades and special weapon abilities like head-shots and reloading that I absolutely adore. I understand that reloading in a boomer shooter isn't the most welcome design decision but I personally don't mind it because reloading seems cool, dunno how to explain it really and plus the reloading isn't necessary for all weapons and even when it is necessary it's not that disturbing. There are 11 weapons and only 4 need reloading by default: Pistols, SMGs, SSG and the revolver.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: First game I consider to be a decent successor to Quake 1. Of course it's still quite different and there a few flaws that need to be ironed out (much smaller team!) but this has soul! Most weapons especially the basic guns, shotgun and bow feel amazing but the rocket launcher lacks oomph. Good enemy variety and great mix of level design with ambushes, secrets and traps though the first episode has a pretty slow start with a lack of surprises and challenges. Bunch of bosses, even hidden optional bosses and lots of abilities to unlock for your weapons. One of my favorite aspect is that there's quite good worldbuilding with several levels having a theme and fun bits of visual storytelling as well as "super secrets" in each level that often take the form of mini side quests with items to use to reveal paths. Lots of love's been put into this.Last but not least: The OST by Primeval absolutely slaps!!! New track every couple level and even several boss themes. It goes all in!
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: +great setting+fun powerful punchy weapons+good upgrade system+you can throw your katana. need i say more.+full secret optional areas. not just secrets. basically mini levels hidden inside of the main levels+fun gameplay loop+great level design and sense of direction+awesome ost+varied enemy types+good checkpoint system that doesn't hold your hand but is still somewhat generous. good balance.-upgrade tokens are too infrequent -no ammo pickups on some boss fight arenas-movement options are lacking-no cheats without mods
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: This game is addicting. One more level. One more level. The soundtrack is killer; crunchy and motivating. Often found myself just chillin' and listening to the riffs.Love how each chapter has a different theme and different enemies.The guns all serve a purpose, no redundancies. All fun to make a mess out of monsters with.Recommend if you like to feel like a badass.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: Are you looking for a retro shooter with an amazing metal soundtrack?If your answer is yes, then I can only recommend this game, it isn't your run and gun shooter, some encounters do require a little thought process unless you want to die ofc.Which is one of the things I love about this game, plus it just feels and looks like the good old shooters from an era where shooters, weren't full of regenerating health and what not, and ammo wasn't just thrown at you like money at a stripper who knows what she is doing. So if you are a true retro fan, this is a game you should not miss out on.

_childDocuments_.review: overall the game is fun, graphics are great, the weapons feel good and you can get satisfying gibs. people say its more like doom or quake but i disagree, its way more like serious sam. not much unique movement aside from the one dash and in one of the episodes, you'll find yourself backpedaling and dashing away from enemies who run straight towards you. level design is okay, its really easy to get lost in some parts because you didn't realize you had to press E on something when you weren't told to interact with anything6.5/10 for people who like id games, 7.5 if you like serious samgood buy if its on sale

_childDocuments_.review: This game is pretty awesome, it takes the starting-to-get-stale boomer shooter formula and takes some risks with it, adding a ton of customization options, snappy and responsive movement, a large arsenal that can be modified to your taste and lots more.
